I've currently put around six hours into this game at the moment and some would say that maybe isnt a sufficient amount to merit writting a review, but I don't really care.
From the little I have played of the game I have to say I am quite impressed with what I have seen, with the attention to detail being one of the things I have to say is a strength of this game as well as being a really good looking game, especially in the winter months with everything covered in a blanket of snow is when the game looks at it's best, but even the summer time is pretty on the eye. But things like villager animations looking smooth. On the visual front there really isn't anything to complain about and gets an easy 10/10 from me.
Gameplay is equally as good it has to be said, there is something strangely satisfying about surviving that first cruicial winter with the little resources you are given, but even after then it is a blast to play with multiple factors you are constantly having to take into account, and you find more and more crop up as you progressively make your town bigger. It is a clever game because it requires you to be sustainable with certain resouces but at the same time provide your citizens and businesses with what they need to survive and produce things like tools and coats, so the micro-management side of it really pleasing and rewarding when you find that correct balance, I'll give it a 9/10 for that, and the reason it isn't a 10 is stated below.
Mainly I have not encountered any bugs with this game which is really good, however there are one or two minor things I would love to see in the game to give it that more of an edge, the main one being that you can't place things like crop fields, pastures and things of that nature into any shape to fit the terrain like the edge of a meandering river, or a the edge of a large hill, and instead you have to stick to squares and rectangles, which doesn't allow the player to make full use of all the space especially if they are playing on smaller maps.
The other minor thing is I would love to see some sort of ground leveling tool for ting hills/bumps, I found it on a couple of occasions where  wanted to build something on what seemed like a large area of flat land but there is actually a small hill/bump preventing me from doing something and therefore had to alter my plan, but if this went unchanged I wouldn't mind because it's a small thing but the inclusion of it would again help players make use of all the space they are gven.
In a nutshell i've run out of superlatives for this game despite a few tiny things i would change, but as the game brings out updates it's all subject to change of course and i can't wait to see what this game does next and i'll no doubt look forward to it and i suggest it strongly to anyone.

Heres what you should know about The Crew:
Tuning
The Tuning Garage is more of a bolt on parts shop. You dont actually tune anything. You select a part and put it on. These parts are unlocked through races and events. I was a bit let down on the whole 'tune your car' thing, since you arent really tuning your car.
Customization:
There are lots of colors and vinyls to choose from, but it feels lacking in the customization department. Again, a letdown. Yeah, its got body mods and stuff, but it fails to meet expectations set by NFSU2. For instance, you can pick a wide array of stripes, but not choose their color.
Multiplayer:
This is NOT an MMO. Yes, there are thousands of people online. However, you will only see a few at a time. At no point will you ever see 100 other drivers at the same time. Ive seen a few people, and we have largely ignored each other. 7 other drivers is the maximum it will ever show you at once. They wont always be the samer drivers, but that it the limit. Thus far Ive done everything alone, though Im still pretty new to the whole thing.
Now, the game is fun. Especially with a wheel, pedals and H shifter. They will require about 1/2 hour of tweaking to get just right - but its very enjoyable when done. People said not to use manual and hardcore driving assist (which is zero assists such as traction control and stability) but quite honestly, I find this the best way to drive. Granted, I have just under 20 years driving experience and have had my fair share of street and drag races IRL. Manual transmissions are natural to me. The vehicles simply act slightly more natural with everything off. I think the visceral experience of shifting and turning a wheel really add to the experience...Im not even sure Id enjoy the game half as much without it based on the lack of customization available.
The game's storyline plays out like a cheap ripoff of a FF movie. Given the arcadey nature of the game, thats ok with me. Cheese is good sometimes. There are tons of short mini games involved such as hitting as many targets as you can, jumps, 'go fast and stay  on the road' races and such. There are plenty of odds and ends to keep you busy for quite some time if you are a completionist. The races and storyline events can be tough, requiring a few shots at it to learn the track before a victory can be eked out most of the time.
My most major complaint is the lack of actual tuning and customization. Everything else seems to work as it should at this point. After some hours of trial and error, I have the steering wheel decent enough to handle the game and feel pretty ok with it. Its not perfect by any means, but serviceable.
If you want a game with a storyline like a bad Fast & Furious movie, driving style along the veins of NFSU 2, and just a [fair] bit of customization, this might be what you are looking for.
If you're looking for realistic handling, deep customization, in depth tuning, and a more serious/sim style experience, this game is not for you. It has none of those things.
Im going with Recommended because its not super broken out of the box. Everything works, its fun, but its still a bit of a letdown. I was hoping for real tuning and deeper options for customizing your ride.

Horror movies very rarely seem to scare me. Horror games on the other hand when done right scare the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of me! Neverending Nightmares is a fantastic example of a horror game done right that had me on edge throughout the entirety of my time spent playing.
At it's core NN is just an exploration game. But at it's heart it is much more. NN presents a physhological horror experience of the kind I have never experienced in a game before.
Let's start with the sound design. This is what builds up the experience. Ambient noices are present throughout the entire game. They help to build up the fear amazingly. Each sound is designed to absolute perfection. Everything sounds like what it should do and when put together they create a perfect tension throughout the exploration. Their is also a brilliant soundtrack featuring creepy songs such as out of tune record players that build the experience. The only issue I have with sound design is the voice acting. Some of it isn't great. Luckily there are only two characters that speak and they don't speak very often so this is a minor flaw. But it could do with some improvement.
Then there's the graphics. It is the most unique choose of graphics I have seen in a game and it is a fantastic choice. The whole game is presented in a handdrawn sketch style art view. NN is a work of art in this mean. The detail the artistic has put into it is an unprecedanted masterpiece. The small details are paid close attention to. Everything from the cracks in the wall to the creepy paintings on the wall help to build up the horror experience.
What about the actual horror element? Well it's definitely not for the faint hearted. There is a "lot" of gore. I mean a huge amount. You see things like the character chopping their own arm to pieces in excruciating detail! It is extremely disturbing. Now I am not a person that usually get's cringeworthy at gore, but this game had me cringing a few times.
But the real horror comes from some of the jump scares. There are few of them compared to other horror games but they are done extremely well. They are not cheap overdone jump scares either. Each of them is well thought out and unique in it's own way. They definitely all come at a suprise. All of them really, really scared me. And as I said before I don't find myself getting scared at jump scares in films but in games it seems completely different. Maybe it's just the fact that you feel like you are actually experiencing it yourself by playing as the main character.
The enemies are something of a pleasure as well. Each are very unique. You will often find yourself running from enemies during the game. And that's not because the game is making you but because you are running from your own fear. This paragraph may contain spoilers if you don't want to know about any of the enemies you will be experiencing.
The story is mildly intriguing. It is one of the least standout parts of the games though. I don't know quite how to explain it without spoiling it though so I will just leave it at that. But it seems to get resolved rather quickly at the end of the game and then it just ends. It was a rather disappointing but suprising ending.
I have seen in other reviews peoples main complete being about the length of the game. I don't see this as a bad thing. I experienced everything that the game had to offer, including getting every achievement, in just under 3 hours. I think this is a reasonable length. Anymore and I would have found myself getting bored of it. But you may think differently so you should put this into consideration.
So I would definitely recommend this game. It is one of the best horror experiences I have played to date. Most things are done to perfection and it is very unique. The only thing that may put people off is the price point of £10.99. I personally think it is well worth this initial price though. I really hope people consider this game and don't put it off to play one of the bigger 3D horror experiences that have nothing on the pyschologial experience neverending nightmares presents.

I picked up the HD remastered versions of Final Fantasy X/X-2 on PS3 when they came out last month, and I replayed FFX for the first time in probably at least 10 years. I remember really enjoying when I first played it and I was worried my memory of the game would be greater than what the game actually was. But I enjoyed it quite a bit a second time around and it held up pretty well aside from the horrendous cutscenes. It's crazy to think about how Square just churned out hit after hit of amazing classic RPGs from this franchise in the 90s and early 00s and then to think about what garbage the FF series has given us since this game.
A quick sidenote for those who never played a game in this series or are otherwise unaware: The stories and battle mechanics of each game in the Final Fantasy series are completely unrelated. Each game in the series has a completely new cast of characters and settings, and there's nearly always a different battle system with different battle mechanics and rules. The series has some common elements and reoccurring motifs; for instance there's usually magic or summon monsters and for some reason there's almost always a character named Cid that appears somewhere in the game. But you don't have to have played FF9 before FF10 or anything like that.
FF10 (or FFX for you Romans) follows the story of a young man named Tidus who is a star blitzball player from the futuristic city of Zanarkand. Blitzball is some kind of crazy combination of football and soccer, but played underwater. It also serves as FFX's primary minigame. It's kind of broken and clunky, but the football fan in me enjoys it despite its faults. Anyway, in the game's prologue, the Zanarkand blitzball arena is suddenly attacked by a massive whale-looking monster known as "Sin". Sin magically transports Tidus 1000 years into the future to another world called "Spira". While searching for a way to get back home to Zanarkand, Tidus learns about the world of Spira and befriends some of its residents. He learns that Spira has always been under constant torment by the same Sin monster he encountered in Zanarkand. Tidus soon befriends a young girl, Yuna, who is training to become a summoner in hopes to obtain a summon monster powerful enough to destroy Sin. FFX's main storyline deals with Tidus, Yuna and her guardian's journey across Spira and their quest to defeat Sin.
I found the story and pacing for FFX to be both very good. Now the thing that's an absolute trainwreck and nearly ruins the game are the voice acting and cutscenes. Final Fantasy X was the first game in the series to be voice acted, and it definitely shows. Each cutscene is more awkward and cringe-worthy than the last. You may have seen the infamous laughing scene on YouTube before. Yeah, that's pretty much how all of the cutscenes in this game are. Now the actual story that is behind these cutscenes is pretty good. But oh man, those cutscenes. It might actually be better to watch them on mute. You have to try to focus on what the game is trying to show you, not how the game is showing it. If you can't do that, you'll probably find this game's story pretty laughable. No pun intended.
Final Fantasy X's battle system is pretty tight and well balanced. Information like damage, status effects, and weaknesses are clearly communicated to the player during battle instead of having to guess which enemies are weak vs. which elements or try to figure out whether the status effect spell you just cast was successful based on what color a sprite is. If you equip your party with the proper "sensor weapons", you will even see strategies on how to defeat specific enemies, their HP, and what their weaknesses are. It's the kind of useful information the FF series always used to hide in the background instead of telling you straight up for some reason. There's a good variety of enemies that all have strengths and weaknesses to different members of your party. For instance flying-type monsters need to be taken down by a ranged fighter, while Tidus' sword is effective on smaller more nimble monsters. Still others may be weak to magic spells and require a Mage to defeat. It's a fun, strategic turn-based battle system that will have you rotating your party members in and out in order to try to exploit enemies' weaknesses.
FFX is notable for not having a world map to explore, which is normally a series staple for Final Fantasy. I was afraid this would be too much like FFXIII, a game which I hated for having linear corridor after linear corridor strung together as level design. But you never really get that feeling in FFX. The level design does a good job with divergent paths and interesting things to do and people to talk to in all of the areas to make you forget there's no world map linking everything together. The level design and pacing is pretty good in this game... except for the puzzle solving sections in stupid cloister of trails areas. People who have played this game before know what I'm talking about. Tedious, time wasting puzzles with random arbitrary logic that you have to solve by trial and error. Terrible game design. Whoever put these in the game needs to be smacked upside the head.
Final Fantasy X also is notable for being the first game in the series that was not exclusively composed by the legendary Nobuo Uematsu. It was a collaboration between him and some other dudes. It's still a excellent soundtrack, but it sounds different than a lot of the other games in the series, and some of it sounds very un-Final Fantasy to me. Most of the soundtrack has a very electronic and synthesized sound. Still good, just different. Standout tracks include The Main Battle Theme (Nobuo Uematsu),  Rikku's Theme (Nobuo Uematsu), Battle With Seymour (Nobuo Uematsu), Besaid Island (Masashi Hamauzu), and Illusion (Junya Nakano). It's easy to hear each composer's different style and which tracks they contributed to the soundtrack.
The soundtrack to the HD version was remixed, which I was a little disappointed in. Even though it had been 10 years since I played this game, I have the soundtrack on my phone and listen to it all the time, so some of the remixes were a little jarring to me. The HD remix soundtrack grew on me eventually, some tracks are more subtle and little less "in your face" than the originals and probably more appropriate in certain areas. But at least include the option for me to switch back to the old ones if I want!
Summary:
Overall FFX is a pretty solid game. Solid battle system, excellent soundtrack and good story. Terrible voice acting. I would actually recommend it as a good entry point for newcomers to the series if it weren't for those cutscenes. As it stands though, I'd probably tell Final Fantasy newbies to start with the masterpiece that is FFVII. It's may not be as polished, refined or pretty looking as FFX, but at least it doesn't have the infamous laughing scene in it.

It has clean, crisp sprites, fantastic gameplay, well written dialogue, an interesting story, and somber fitting music, but all of it is tossed out the window for the single most overused, boring and cliched ending to any zombie-centric story you can think of. Yes, its THAT ending. I dont even need to tell you which one it is and you'll already know. It's a huge spit in the face.
While the ending is a massive stain on this otherwise clean game, it has a few smaller stains as well. The entire train maintenance system seemed tacked on in the end, as all it really did was prevent you from hearing whole conversations, or having to burn resources just to hear your passengers speak since it would take longer to hear it all and they would get hungry/bleed to death in the mean time. The way the machine gun replaced the pistol also bugged me, as by that point I had a fantastic pistol and the machine gun just didnt feel as good. Although earlier I mentioned an interesting story, that too can be an issue at times. The story is vague and leaves room for thought, but it also leaves TOO MUCH room for thought. Not enough is explained, and while that isnt personally a turn off for someone like me (why would anyone tell the ♥♥♥♥in Conductor what's going on in the world, right?), it could be a massive turn off for someone invested in it.
I've been harping on the game a ton, but I do genuinely like this game. The way they reveal just who the Conductor was calling the whole game was great, the way your fellow conductors would contact you on your train, how the people would gossip, it's all so well written. The atmosphere and the lighting made me feel so tense, and the sound in those areas was stellar. The scene where you ride passed all the pods was a great example of all that.
The game is like a damaged, solid sheet of gold: It's a wonderful thing, and if you can get past the hole on it then you have something you'll really want to have in your possession.

I had some pretty high hopes for this game, I mean. It sounds amazing in concept. Keep your train running, Scavenge for supplies to keep said train running. However the game has a couple of issues.
First of all it barely has anything to do with trains. The meat of the game is spent in a 2D sidescrolling not-zombie shooter. Which, In my opinion isn't really well thought out. At first i thought it was brillant. Throw objects at zombies to conserve ammo, Use heavy punches to knock off armor plated not-zombies
However shortly after the game just kinda gives you guns and ammo basically screaming "Hey player! How about a group of not-zombies?" I don't feel like a scavenger if literally everything i find is because in the next room over i need to use it to survive. (The breaking point for me was when the game gives you a shotgun and you find a note saying "Don't go into the subway!" And you are, Unless i ♥♥♥♥ed up. Forced to go into the subway)
Back to that train, It's basically a whack-a-mole game as another reviewer described. red "!" appears over a console or person and you have to either play a minigame or give them something. I was really hoping for more meaningful train mechanics. Other then busy work until you get to the next station.
Now, This game does do a lot right. For instance the story is told in a very creative way and the atmosphere is expertly done. For example you have a text message console that allowes you to communicate with other train workers. And your passengers will talk about the lore of the world allowing you to fill in the gaps of the story (if you rescue, and keep them alive anyways) I'll probably keep playing for the story alone to be honest. It's got me hooked. I really wish steam had a neutral button instead of thumbs up/down as this game deserves a neutral in my book.
TL:DR Buy it on sale - Story so far is great - Gameplay is meh

Getting a crew, and doing CoOp is very much possible, however, I think it is reigon locked, as I seem to be unable to connect to European players and vice versa, for example. There are quite a few people playing, but depends on when you play, like any game, work, school, social events will flux the population. The game is NOT locked at 30 FPS. This USED to be true in the beta, but if you actually enter your settings for the game, you will see the option to "frame limit" to 60. Now in my personal oppinion, 60 is bare minimum for an acceptable PC frame rate, I run a 120HZ monitor and that nothing new to the PC, so I do expect PC relases to hit 60+ without fail. Also, remember, when assessing a game, if you have bare minimum specs, your experince will be drastically different from a high spec machine, so do remember that when publically reviewing.
Now some Server stability, there have been issues here, mostly in the midday/late morning, they are not terrible, but for sure more frequant then deiserable, I suspect this will clear up soon. Uplay is almost useless for this game, now I am not a fan of it to start with, but it litterally tells you it is going to use steam to launch the application, if you launch from uplay. Good grief Ubi, just retire Uplay already.
Thats it for this review, anything else I have to say about it is purely my personal oppinion and has nothing of relivence for the game.

TL;DR
It's very good. For sure Codemasters best F1 game to date. But has notably problems like fairly passive ai. It's also buggy and Codemasters tend to spend little time fixing bugs. Could be truly great if they put effort into improving it.
Having done my first two career races I can happily say it's good. Not perfect, not by a long shot. I'd stop short of the glowing review above, but it's good.
Notable down sides, bugs, there's quite a few, including a hilarious one where I'd got distracted by real life so had to restart my first race (I hate restarting). Apparently when I restarted, Haryanto was going through a foam sign at the time, so when we restarted I noticed that the game had decided to remember that. His car had foam constantly bouncing out the back of it. It was amusing if not somewhat distracting.
My biggest criticism however is the AI doesn't seem as punchy as it was last year (one of last years highlights). They have gone back to the, oh, I'm on the outside, I will back off now mentality. Also, and this annoys me, they refuse to cut across if another car is on the outside around a corner. So in Bahrain where I had a ridiculously good position on the grid compared to Australia, (either luck, learning how to drive or a balance issue) I saw Hamilton and Rosberg spend about 6-8 corners side by side..... That, kinda, wouldn't happen. So it seems the ai isn't aggressive enough. I haven't seen any ai tangle with each other yet.
Also, another thing, the ai is weird on the first lap, they all bunch into a close nit line. Now, I don't know if they use different ai on the first lap, or, there's a weird catch up thing going on, (god I hope not), but it feels very weird. They all seem to go the same speed (or close too) After the first lap it's fine though. Once you hit the first round of pit stops there's cars doing all sorts of things, which makes it feel really alive, if not slightly hard to follow.
The strategy, both race and long term development is fantastically done. There tyres really feel like a choice. The pit crews often (too often), gives you alternative strategies to switch to during the race. I say too often, because as I was desperately trying to cling to 11th with 2 laps to go in Bahrain (it didn't work, I feel to 14th), it was just, really distracting. No, I don't want to pit with 2 laps to go. Stop asking. Also, stop telling me you'll let me know if there's a storm front on it's way. In Britain, sure, but I'm racing in Bahrain. It just sounds silly. So, the radio is still a bit annoying, even if it is much better. (The options you have to interact and the information you can get are much better).
Obviously the game is build to be used with (if you like) voice commands for the pit wall, however I haven't seen any way to actually make it respond to my headset. It would be disappointing if it wasn't in built in this years version, (last years required an external program).
Oh, another thing and this really ♥♥♥♥♥ me, I use a G27. If I hit a button on the keyboard, the little tooltips for what each button does relates to the keyboard, it'll tell me F5 swaps pages in the set up screen or something. But if I hit a button on my wheel, all the tool tips turn to Xbox controls. What button on my wheel is X, I ask you. Unless the game is being played with a controller, it should never come up. Why can't the tool tips just reflect what's in the settings menu? Why not let the player customize the out of race bindings as well?
Oh, another thing, the VSC is awesome, but, it needs to show your delta in the middle of the screen and have it larger. (I'm sure mods will make this happen). Because the pint sized text box on the right is damn hard to see when you're trying to keep to is through a series of corners as well as trying not to run into anything or miss a braking point. Also, entering the pits, you have to manually slow the car. I like that. But, it's damn hard to make sure you're going 56 and not 61. (Melbourne was not a good race for me).
I really like this years game so far. But good god, a lot isn't bugs. It's just, obvious stuff they they either haven't got around to or are oblivious too. It's painfully obvious that it's a port.
Worth noting, it runs very well and it's looks good as you would expect. The sound is good, but the volume of the competitors is too high, so you think there's a car coming up behind you and he's actually five or ten seconds behind. There seems little difference in sound between a car on your gearbox and two corners back.
So, that's my thoughts so far. Defiantly their best game. Far from perfect. Driving as K-Mag's team mate in the Renault. 0 points for the team so far. Solid start I think. But I am beating K-Mag.
A quick few things that are great, the rivalry system is just, amazing. The race starts are fantastic the physics are really a highlight I think. Sound is solid, the career mode is back and is well done. Although, really it should be standard fair. The last bad thing I'll say is this, unlike most games I buy, I have little hope that Codemaster's will significantly address issues with the game (apart from game breaking bugs). The tight schedule means they don't spend any time really improving the game post release. I hope that mods can fix some issues, but from last year they basically killed off the modding scene as they made it impossible to mod most things.

EDIT: I *tentatively* recommend this game to *some* people. No updates makes me bummed out.

In Dark Souls II, I have been killed because enemies have used weapons through walls, shot arrows around corners, died because I attacked in a completely different direction of my targeted enemy so the person I was fighting could backstab me easily. (to name a few annoyances)
It feels like you move forward slowly, pick off enemies one at a time (because if two attack you at once, you are out of luck) and hope that a bonfire is just around the corner.
Don't get me wrong, it's still a lot of fun and VERY challenging, but it just feels like the game can be unfair on occasions, and I'm pretty sure that never happened in the original.

this is a Great game, although with some blatently lazy things in it. ( I'm Looking at you Covetous Demon,  Magic Elevator, and Blue Smelter), and most of the bosses are just a large, humanoid being with a weapon.  But regardless, this game holds some incredibly great things.  The DLC in particular are incredible.  some of the bossfights, such as Sir Alonne's and Sihn's, are flat out unforgettable.  The Covenants are each unique and very fun, and the multiplayer is incredible...  Save for one little thing...  Soul Memory.   Now, I can see where they were going with this,  By matching players based on how many souls (for those of you who don't know,  thats the ingame currency) they've acquired, you should be matching players of similar skill, equipment, and level, therefore avoiding twinks and making each online match enjoyable.  However, Soul Memory has proved to be far less effective then matching players based on Level, as the first and third games do.  This unfortunately has botched many of the covenants,  especially the Way of the Blue/blue sentinals and the Rat king's Servants.  But all in all,  this is a very, very enjoyable game, and while it doesn't quite live up to the First Game, it remains and incredibly enjoyable item that I highly recommend to any one coming from Demon's Souls, Dark souls I/III, Bloodborne, or any other game in the genre.

First off I would like to say, I have more experince with this game then alot of reviews I have seen, I was a beta tester after all.
Here is what you get, a large, open, racing game that takes place in the USA. While not a perfect replica, most major reconizable areas are present, graphics are very good. The content can be realistically beaten in a couple of days if you just run and gun the story. However there is unlimited potential for VS, CoOp and Leaderboard *friend and worldwide*.
I will now address some of the falsehoods posted in a few reviews. Getting a crew, and doing CoOp is very much possible, however, I think it is reigon locked, as I seem to be unable to connect to European players and vice versa, for example. There are quite a few people playing, but depends on when you play, like any game, work, school, social events will flux the population. The game is NOT locked at 30 FPS. This USED to be true in the beta, but if you actually enter your settings for the game, you will see the option to "frame limit" to 60. Now in my personal oppinion, 60 is bare minimum for an acceptable PC frame rate, I run a 120HZ monitor and that nothing new to the PC, so I do expect PC relases to hit 60+ without fail. Also, remember, when assessing a game, if you have bare minimum specs, your experince will be drastically different from a high spec machine, so do remember that when publically reviewing.
Now some Server stability, there have been issues here, mostly in the midday/late morning, they are not terrible, but for sure more frequant then deiserable, I suspect this will clear up soon. Uplay is almost useless for this game, now I am not a fan of it to start with, but it litterally tells you it is going to use steam to launch the application, if you launch from uplay. Good grief Ubi, just retire Uplay already.
Thats it for this review, anything else I have to say about it is purely my personal oppinion and has nothing of relivence for the game.

The Final Station is a game where you ride a train and fight not-zombies while uncovering a hidden threat. No, it's not Kabaneri of the Iron Fortress. However, it's very similar to it in that they both have garbage endings that make the work you put into the media to that point feel worthless.
See, Final Station is a great game. It has clean, crisp sprites, fantastic gameplay, well written dialogue, an interesting story, and somber fitting music, but all of it is tossed out the window for the single most overused, boring and cliched ending to any zombie-centric story you can think of. Yes, its THAT ending. I dont even need to tell you which one it is and you'll already know. It's a huge spit in the face.
While the ending is a massive stain on this otherwise clean game, it has a few smaller stains as well. The entire train maintenance system seemed tacked on in the end, as all it really did was prevent you from hearing whole conversations, or having to burn resources just to hear your passengers speak since it would take longer to hear it all and they would get hungry/bleed to death in the mean time. The way the machine gun replaced the pistol also bugged me, as by that point I had a fantastic pistol and the machine gun just didnt feel as good. Although earlier I mentioned an interesting story, that too can be an issue at times. The story is vague and leaves room for thought, but it also leaves TOO MUCH room for thought. Not enough is explained, and while that isnt personally a turn off for someone like me (why would anyone tell the ♥♥♥♥in Conductor what's going on in the world, right?), it could be a massive turn off for someone invested in it.
I've been harping on the game a ton, but I do genuinely like this game. The way they reveal just who the Conductor was calling the whole game was great, the way your fellow conductors would contact you on your train, how the people would gossip, it's all so well written. The atmosphere and the lighting made me feel so tense, and the sound in those areas was stellar. The scene where you ride passed all the pods was a great example of all that.
The game is like a damaged, solid sheet of gold: It's a wonderful thing, and if you can get past the hole on it then you have something you'll really want to have in your possession.

First of all it barely has anything to do with trains. The meat of the game is spent in a 2D sidescrolling not-zombie shooter. Which, In my opinion isn't really well thought out. At first i thought it was brillant. Throw objects at zombies to conserve ammo, Use heavy punches to knock off armor plated not-zombies
However shortly after the game just kinda gives you guns and ammo basically screaming "Hey player! How about a group of not-zombies?" I don't feel like a scavenger if literally everything i find is because in the next room over i need to use it to survive. (The breaking point for me was when the game gives you a shotgun and you find a note saying "Don't go into the subway!" And you are, Unless i ♥♥♥♥ed up. Forced to go into the subway)
Back to that train, It's basically a whack-a-mole game as another reviewer described. red "!" appears over a console or person and you have to either play a minigame or give them something. I was really hoping for more meaningful train mechanics. Other then busy work until you get to the next station.
Now, This game does do a lot right. For instance the story is told in a very creative way and the atmosphere is expertly done. For example you have a text message console that allowes you to communicate with other train workers. And your passengers will talk about the lore of the world allowing you to fill in the gaps of the story (if you rescue, and keep them alive anyways) I'll probably keep playing for the story alone to be honest. It's got me hooked. I really wish steam had a neutral button instead of thumbs up/down as this game deserves a neutral in my book.
TL:DR Buy it on sale - Story so far is great - Gameplay is meh

| VERDUN |
|*BREIF*|
Verdun is an engaging and at times visually stunning game - given certain circumstances it beautifully portrays war (in perticular, the first world war). It can be frustrating, infuriating and mesmorising all at the same time. It really is one of the 'I'm a big boy' military shooter's. It does come with it's flaws however which I will be going through below, first off however the positives.
|*POSITIVES*|
- Visually stunning at times given you have the computer to handle it (more on that later)
- The weaponry used in the game is specific (to an extent) to the time era, you aren't going to be able to use WW1 'Smg's', use fancy optics or be able to paint your gun in lovely patterns. Your gun will feel basic but overwelmingly powerful if used properly.
- Depending on how you like to play fps games, the maps are very well sized and can really immersify you into the battle, if you have the right amount of players in the game.
- The realism aspect drives the game forward and adds to the immersion and atmosphere.
- There's a straight forward weapon progression setup in place where you're rewarded with different weaponry based on your performance on the battlefield rather than the rank you hold.
|*NEAUTRAL*|
- The game seems to have technical issues from low end to high end, which can be a pain at times as you really do have to tailor your settings around on some rigs regardless of their power, you do get the occasional frame drop however it isn't enough to damage gameplay, at least on my end.
- The wave defense mode is a little too easy, it's an easy way to gain XP provided you have a good squad with you, I have been in games where we have picked off the whole wave 50-60 yards off.
- Some weapons (In perticular the RSC) weren't used all that much in the war, it's quite OP and be an♥♥♥♥♥to come up against. Sticking on the grounds of realism, the rifle wasn't readily available to all soldiers thus it was quite the sh*t storm on the field, which ironically reflects on the game.
|*NEGATIVES*|
- The squad element of the game includes 4 options for you to choose from, if all 3 slots are taken you're left with the final slot (usually this is the officer slot, for the prime reason you start with a pistol and bino's). Prefer long range shooting? Tough, you've got the pistol stop complaining.
- The game has recently seen a decrease in the amount of players in the server, this reflects in games. Verdun doesn't have the large scale element added to it, battlefields can be quite scarce and plain unless the game has 30+ players in it and even then it can seem rather bland.
- The spawn system (despite being realsitic) can be frustrating, especially in high player matches. Your time in each play if someone wants to be a sh*t on the opposition can be as little as 30 seconds. Esepcially if said sh*it is sitting in a trench picking you off one by one with his MG.
- There's not many game modes to choose from, additonal game modes would be a nice touch.
- As said above, there's technical issues. I'm placing this in the negative tab too as it can affect other players despite me not getting much issues with it.
|* OVERALL SCORE*|
Graphics: 8/10
Sound: 7/10
Gameplay: 8/10
Replay factor: 9/10
Multiplayer overall: 7/10

Originally posted as part of The State of Busy Gaming - 2014: Evolving tastes for portable, PC, and console treats in bite-sized portions:
I bought this game on impulse during a Humble Indie Bundle flash sale, and it's one of the best PC games I've enjoyed in years. It's basically one of those cooking/restaurant management "sims" similar to Cooking Mama, which I enjoyed briefly on the Nintendo DS. But this one grabbed me and won't let go. I liken it to BioShock: If you read my review, I would try to savor that game by playing for brief spurts and then I'd shut down my console - only to reboot it just minutes later. This became a cycle that continued until I gave up and powered through the story. I'm doing the same thing here, only it only takes a second to reboot and about five minutes to play through another day in my restaurant's life.
You also can use a keyboard or DualShock 4, but I have the iconic Xbox buttons memorized better than the PlayStation buttons - which makes reading and reacting to the on-screen button cues easier. One small error can ruin a "perfect day" and the resulting $250 bonus. The game includes enough distractions to throw you off your game, from online dates who demand difficult dishes executed perfectly (and then text you as you're completing the evening's orders) to robbers who must be identified from a witness description to prevent a costly loss in hard-earned revenue. Building the right menu to succeed requires strategy and sometimes extra practice with complicated dishes to maximize profits and build buzz. You also must complete clean-up chores to avoid a devastating health inspection.
I only wish there were a console version (the iOS version's free demo convinced me that tapping isn't nearly as fun as using a controller). I might just have to try the HDMI output on my laptop so I can play this on a bigger screen.

This is my personal favorite restaurant sim!
Sure, if you really think about it it's just a stupid typing game, but no. It's actually something more than typing. Owning a restaurant isn't as easy as you thought and so proves this game. You start off from a crappy restaurant in a tower, putting ketchup and mustard on corn dogs and serving burgers. But as you move on, you'll be serving soups, pastas and other top notch foods, becoming the finest restaurant to date.
But it's not just that. You must arrange your menu, depending on the weather, the people and what the VIP like (when they come), earning additional daily buzz, which means more money in a day.
With the restaurant there are also problems. You must do things like wash dishes, trap mouses (on the first steps) or flush toilets. But there are things such as the Protection Due, the -previously mentioned- VIPs and robbers.
What makes this game addicting is the fact that it has a lot of ways to play the game. You can start by saving money for buying a new food, or for upgrading another one. There are bets, Steam Leaderboards and extra stuff that really make this greater than most cooking sims.
You like fast paced gameplay and cooking? Then Cook, Serve, Delicious! is the thing for you.

This game is definitely not for everyone (and yes, it IS a game, ♥♥♥♥ you), it's firmly in the "love it or hate it" catagory, but for what it's worth, I personally loved it!
I think a big part of that is because the story really resonated with me on a very personal level, in more ways then one, and I really liked the way it used environmental story telling to present something of a character study; by the end of it I really felt like I knew all these characters regardless of the fact that you never physcially meet any of them in the game. Also, even though the whole game takes place in one house I think the level design is really good. This is gonna sound weird, but it reminds me of Demon's Souls, as you explore around you find shortcuts, areas that loop back around on themselves to minimize backtracking, and it doesn't feel artificaly at all, it feels like you're exploring a house that people have been living in, and it serves to drive home the atmosphere very well.
Hell, when you consider that to run this game on my toaster I had to crank all the settings down as low as they'll go, and I still got a framerate of about 5 FPS, but I liked the rest of the game so much that I soldiered through it, that should serve as a pretty good mark in it's favor right there.
You'll notice that I havn't talked at all about what this game is about, and that's intentional. I didn't know a whole lot about this game going in, and I think that's the absolute best way to experience it, go into it as cold as possible, play through the whole thing in one go (it's about the length of your average film so that shouldn't be too hard), and just give it a chance. If you can enjoy a first person, narrative driven, experimental type of game with an emphasis on characters, pacing, and environmental story telling, then I think you'll find the story this game tells and the way it tells it to be something very special.
I do think the full price seems a tad expensive for this sort of experience, but I'd absolutely reccomend it for a Steam Sale pickup.

Verdun, set during the First World War portrays a variety of different aspects of World War I combat. There are several game modes that one can play in Verdun, including "Frontlines" and "Team Deathmatch". Frontlines simulates the actual World War I trench warfare in a realistic, and interesting way. Though some of the mechanics of firing, jumping, reloading, etc. still need some improvement, over all the combat experience is fantastic! Within the squad that you join in Frontlines, you can advanced through several classes, with several different weapons that are able to be used by each class. Some feature weapons most have never heard of (but are still historically accurate), while featuring more popular weapons such as the Springfield 1907, the Trench Gun, the British Webly, and the infamous Lewis Gun. Other squad roles include Squad Leader (Corporal, Sergeant, etc. depending on nationality), Rifleman, Machinegunner, and Grenadier, among others. Each nation has it's own unique weapons set for both the Allied and Central powers. The combat even features mustard gas and artillery strikes, as would be a daily event for any soldier fighting in the Trenches. The historical accuracy of the game is quite good, having family that fought in World War I on the Western front, the gameplay seems to match accounts of real first world war combat. I would recommend this game to anyone who is a fan of First Person Shooters, Historical Games, World War I, or just interested in trying something new. The development team has truly found the spirit of the First World War, and put it into a playable game mode!

Fascinating concept for a game. You actually have to manually operate your weapon.
The game is procedurally generated with regards to the placement of enemies, ammunition, and the objective collectibles.
Your success can depend on what weapons, equipment and however much ammo you start with, all of which are random. You can start with anything from a .44 with a dozen rounds, or a 9mm with three measley bullets.
The gunplay is satisfying and tactile, and the game is arranged such that you won't need to do the dozen things involved with operating a gun in a hurry. The pace is slow, and you have as much time as you like to get ready.
It's possible to get up a list of keyboard commands on screen to help you know what to press and what does what.
In all, a great concept, very well designed. Hopefully we see more like this in the future, with more scenarios perhaps, or some sort of multiplayer deathmatch.

For $10, this game is a blast. Although it may not be as polished or bug free as other open world game, the gameplay and exploration is this games strong suit. After many patches since the games release, I feel this is the version they wanted to put out.
Pros
+ Large, highly detailed open world
+ AI is (usually) pretty smart, they will flank behind you and kill you if you don't pay attention
+ No regenerating health, health packs are scarce, and you can die in about 3-4 shots which makes the game really  challenging on the hardest difficulty
+ A good amount of gun customization, allows you to change attachments on the fly
+ The guns feel heavy, killing enemies is satisfying
+ Amazing graphics on Ultra settings, also has a texture resoultion upscaler if you have a powerful PC
+ Very smooth, barely droped below 45FPS (my pc isn't that powerful to run ultra at a constant 60FPS)
Neutral
* The co-op mode is fun, if you can find players for it.
* Sound design is a little weird at times, sometimes certain sound effects are either too loud or too quiet
* The motorbike allows you to travel around faster, but there isn't much open room to go really fast, and there are enemies every where so you can get shot off if you're going too slow
* When the AI isn't being smart, they are doing some weird stuff, like sprinting around for no reason at all, or getting stuck in somewhere they shouldn't be
* Story is at times interesting, other times cliched and uninspired, but it's easy to not pay attention and still enjoy the gameplay
* No way to completely turn off the HUD or to make it smaller/more opaque. I can ignore the minimap when I don't need it, but I wish you could move it out of the way some more, it's pretty big
Negative
- Some minor bugs that are seemingly easy to fix, but still persist in the game
- The DLC doesn't add a whole lot to the game (get them on sale if you want them, also the last DLC they are making looks to be one of the best they've made)
- Wish there were more "base" guns (guns that aren't converted)
- Stealth is mediocre
- The ♥♥♥♥ing radio is so goddamn annoying. Your radio is always blowing up with messages from 4 different people at once. Too bad you can't change just the volume of the radio, instead you have to turn down the volume for all dialog
Overall, while this game does have it's flaws, I believe this is one of the best games to come out of 2016. I'm a sucker for open-world FPS games, and this game gave me what I was wanting.
7/10, buy it on sale.

Despite the flaws included in being a 7 day FPS entry, I still seem to be drawn back to Reciever.
It's frustrating, because at some point you'll forget to add bullets to your magazine or you'll stumble while trying to run from one of the many hellish floating zappy robots that inhabits Reciever's levels, but the simple element of having to treat your gun like a real firearm makes Reciever something else. It gains more imersiveness than could be added by having Tomb Raider (2013)'s visuals or Half Life 2's character animations. It makes the game more of a realization that you are not the killing machine Call of Duty has trained you to be. It shouts in your face, "you can't even run from a fan with a taser strapped to it!"
It might also be the quick loading time that makes Reciever an easy game to get into, usually I only end up playing 15 minutes before getting frustrated that I got the revolver again (I don't really like the revolver, it loses the complexity that the 1911 and the Glock have), only to come back half an hour later for more.
Reciever may not really be a game, but it certainly shows that if you add complexity to any game mechanic, the game might be more interesting.

Adds a lot of improvements to Dark Souls I, but tried to change the original, and so, was shunned by the playerbase.
The game was apparently made without Myazaki, and usually, people consider this alone to make it a bad game.
-Universe-
In Dark Souls III, you basically play Dark Souls I all over again, same NPC, same areas, even same areas sometimes.
Dark Souls II adds it's own universe, who still feels like it's in the Souls continuity. In Dark Souls I, you are in a messed up world, in Lordran, it's a ruined kingdom with monsters and undead everywhere.
In Drangleic, it's a peaceful atmosphere wich lure you into a sense of security, then bite you in the♥♥♥♥♥ The world is really interesting and fledged out. You have 4 path wich each leads you to one lord and one king. (The iron king being both). This game also create at least 70% of Dark Souls III logic, by creating the idea of cycle and immortals souls.
You will meet more NPCs than in Dark Souls I, and they have a more logical impact on the game, the rock collector sells you rocks, the merchant gains wealth when you buy from him, allowing him to have a bigger stock, and the laddersmith... Makes ladders.
If you follow the 4 path logic, the game actually feel way deeper, most people dismiss it as being "many areas mashed into the same world", but in a franchise where you can find a giant lake under ruins and lava, it doesn't stand out that much. I mean, there is a fortress made entirely of iron in a volcano, guarded by an army of knights with electrics katanas, how isn't that amazing ?
-Gameplay-
The game add actual dual wielding, each weapons has it's own off-hand moveset, no longer you will block with a dagger, my friend ! This is actually a gigantic change, for it makes a weapon in the offhand viable. Also, powerstancing is a thing, remember the requirement for weapons in DS I ? If you exceed it by 1.5, you can "powerstance" the weapon, it means you can assume a stronger stance, wich replace offhand attack by attacks with both weapons. At 99 strenght, you can powerstance two gigantics clubs, allowing you to just look amazing.
The interconnectivity is gone, and this is an aspect that has created most of the controversy. You can teleport from the beginning of the game, and the hub allows you to choose 4 different paths, but those paths are all separated, unlike in Dark Souls I, when you could go from one area to another by walking, allowing you to go through the entire world without a single loadscreen.
However, Dark Souls III does the exact same thing (even worse, because unlike in the II, you HAVE to teleport from the first level), but it was made by Myazaki, it was actually a good idea all along !
The game is also waaaaaay more forgiving on infusion, separating them from the upgrade, in DS I, you had a lot of different titanite type, wich were really niche (like, allowing you to upgrade from +5 to +10 for flame weapons), in Dark Souls II, there is only one type of titanite, and a type of rock for each infusion, allowing you to power up a weapon from 0 to 10, and then decide how you want to infuse it, you can even reverse the infusion to put another one instead.
The PVP is, IMO, one of the most balanced of the soulsborne. Convenants are really interesting, having differents goals, (there even are co-op and PVE covenants), there even is a convenant that makes people invade you, and a fight club covenant.
Some moveset have changed, and there is a new type of magic, the Hexes, wich uses both faith and intelligence, and can be cast with chime (talismans) or staff. But the biggest difference is definitely the offhand moveset. The game is a LITTLE faster than the first, but still way slower than Bloodborne dans DSIII.
-TL DR-
As long as you are not a Myazaki fanatic, the game is really good, it has taken away some things from DSI, and a lot of people never forgave that, but most of the Soul experience is still here. There are way more bosses, and the places are way more varied than in DSI and DSIII, and the lore is as solid as the first, and way deeper than the third.
If you can get past the hater, the game is solid.

Dark Souls 2 is the second installation of the DS series, and the third of the Souls games. Scholar of the First Sin is its enhanced version, which has all the DLCs bundled. In the following paragraphs I will draw comparisons between the first and second game and the enhanced edition.
One of the strongest points of the sequel is the improvement of the visuals. Everything feels way smoother. Lightning effects are great, texture and model quality is better. This is especially true in the case of the enhanced edition. Also, the game do not need any third-party mod to function properly. Visual menu contains a handful of options which let you configure the look of the game.
In terms of world design DS2 is definitely weaker than the first. Places while look good, they are not as memorable. With the introduction of a teleport option for every bonfire the world is not traversed enough to even become known enough. In addition the areas are more linear and "where to go" options are also limited most of the time due to a missing key/item or high level mobs. While the characters in the world have plenty to say, somehow they are not as memorable as their predecessors. I am currently playing the two games side-by-side, so I would not say that nostalgia would come to play in this case. However, one thing is definitely worse in the second installation, the bosses. About 50% of these creatures are badly designed, sometimes dissapointingly easy, even recycled at times. Without going into details there are a few bosses which are hard because they have lots of health or extreme amount of poison, curse or similar damage. Their intelligence and pattern variety rarely reaches the level which was seen in the first Dark Souls.
Gameplay is maybe another area where the game improves upon the previous one while introducing problems. It feels more fluid. Camera and auto-target however is still pretty bad, and with the faster combat they are more and more in the way. The system itself is also more leanient in the end. You can equip heavier armors without the serious movement penalty. An extra stat is added to improve max equip load, so endurance is not going to give any more. Way into my second playthrough, now with SotFS I mostly go for strength and dexterity because I need them for my greatswords. Because of this I do not have enough points to improve my stamina, health and load. Starting stats are also much lower. As a deprived I started with everything on 6. Getting everything to 10 took a lot of time, but they are decent on that level. I would say that there is a 5 point difference between the two games. Leveling is much faster. After 40 hours I was level 76 in the first, while level 133 in the second game. Above 20 most of the stats barely hold any advantage, so progression becomes quite hollow after a while. One more thing that was annoying is that sometimes the direction of an attack is misaligned with targeting on. The character attacks in the wrong direction. Something which is horrible, and I do not think that it was this bad in the first game, is the hit detection. This becomes obvious mostly when playing against others. However, there is one boss with multiple encounters throughout the game, namely the Pursuer, whose "curse-attack" has a huge hitbox contrary to the animation which is a thrust at a point. I got cursed every time during these fights, most of the time standing next to the sword at appropriate distance after a dodge, still my character teleported onto the end of the weapon and got cursed losing its humanity in the process. I already mentioned pvp which is the worst I have ever seen in any game. Invade items have higher chance against lower tier players, so you are screwed twice. Also, got invaded by people living in Mexico and Australia for example, which is hilarious, unplayable and frustrating as hell. Tiers used to determine the pool available for co-op and pvp, but instead of character level, soul memory is used. Soul memory is the total amount of soul gathered with the character. This is once again an extremely bad design decision as for someone like me who buys a lot of stuff - like armors, spells, etc. - this means that I got invaded by much stronger people who spent most of their souls on either leveling or equipment upgrades. Overall, I think the quality of the core systems of Dark Souls 2 is a step back from the first game.
Sound is mostly the same as it was in the first game. The game has a decent soundtrack, similar to Dragon's Dogma and other rpgs which were developed in Japan. They have a unique style regarding music. Voice acting as always is less important as there is not much to listen to. The characters in DS2 have more lines, while voice-overs being better quality by the same amount. Atmosphere-wise the game delivers with frightening noises and immersive ambient sounds.
The base game itself is quite lengthy, while it mostly depends on the style of the player. I usually grind in early-game, so it becomes easier, thus I tend to finish the game later. One of the strongest parts of DS that I would mention is the amount of unique armor, weapons and spells. I can always find new stuff to play with and improve with rare minerals that I find along my journey. SotFS contains all released DLCs, so the game has content for many hours. NG+ also gives a few extra challenges with added encounters and strengthened foes. One of the new features is the ability to level up areas. So, you can level up a bonefire and the corresponding part of the world to NG+ and above. This means that there is more options for the player, but also a few items have more use encouraging the use of these strengthening items. I do not necessarily think that this serves the game.
While I would say that the original Dark Souls 2 was a good game, the enhanced edition changed things mostly for the worse. For example, one thing which was also there in the first DS in some form is the heide knight. A tough, non-respawning, optional enemy who would drop rare loot. In SotFS they are regular knights, except they become hostile only after killing a specific boss. This also makes Tower of Flame a crowded place after the first boss. SotFS also placed a few extra stronger mob and previous bosses around the world with the same effect as I mentioned before, over-crowding various areas. This is the kind of unfair added difficulty which makes no sense. Intelligent placement of enemies were a strong point in From Software games. This is just plain bad at times. Dark Souls' Demon Ruins featured three of the earlier bosses as respawning enemies, but they were not as pointless and frustrating as the Flexile Sentry in Sinner's Rise. Right now, I feel this is a worse version than the original Dark Souls 2. The only thing which makes this more recommendable is the bundled DLCs and bigger active playerbase.
While being a Dark Souls game DS2 is still a rushed package made for a wider audience. It is a mixed bag which can be just as great as terrible sometimes. After spending a decent amount of time with it I consider it a huge disappointment. While many people tend to defend DS2 it is still the worst Souls game out there and not a valid representation of the series. It is a shame that the third is the last DS and it might have been better to wait a few years instead of getting out a half-baked game like the second.

This is game that sadly commits the worst sin of story telling imaginable; it TELLS you, rather than SHOWING you.
“Gone Home is what would happen if you took a click-and-point adventure game in the same vain as  Deponia, and tried transferring it into a first person perspective. A game where you could [in theory] click on and interact with your game world in a dynamic way that makes that world feel alive. Gone home however has seemed to miss the biggest part those click-and-point adventure games had; a compelling story and actual interaction.  Rather than focusing on characters that were interacting with each other, the player instead plays the cameraman. You as kaitlyn have no point in the story because you didn't have any interaction when the game starts. The game instead should have focused on the father coming home, only to realize his daughters gone and discover an entire world he really didn't know about. That would have been interesting because the father could have commented on his opinions and views of what happened, and we would have actually seen character development as the father realizes he'd done something wrong.
Instead, what they did is focus on a character who didn't have any major interaction and instead acts like the cameraman. It would have made more sense story wise if you weren't even in the game. The parents would have been interesting cameramen because they would have had revelations about their daughters world they largely ignored or pretended didn't exist, you as kaitlyn don't have that option because you weren't their to have those original interactions. Instead, the story entirely focuses on the wrong characters and the WRONG interactions. It committed a sin, and a game to focus solely on the story and have the story be a failure leaves little to grab onto.

This is a fantastic game, and I cannot recommend enough that you purchase it.
You open a restaurant in an office tower, and your ultimate goal is to raise it up to a 5 start restaurant that everyone will want to eat at. You manage your menu to make sure you have food that fits the weather (sunny or rainy), fits the clients (maybe that hot chick from a dating site is coming, or even a VIP guest) and keep your menu items fresh (you've had fish on the menu for two whole days, switch it out!). You can also upgrade the food to make it better (and allow you to charge more for it).
The game is fast paced and very hectic. You prepare and serve the food as the orders come in. Some things are simple, and some are not. Pretzel? Serve it plain, with salt, with butter, or with both. Fried chicken? Deep fry until cooked and put a basket and serve. Nachos? If they want meat, you have to cook it, if not don't worry. Then you need to make sure you get everything on the nachos they want. Soup? Make sure the noodles are correct, make sure you add the right ingredients, and don't forget to individually chop the vegetables. See what I'm getting at?
The beauty is that this allows you to essentially make the game as easy or as hard as you want. You could make the game hard by serving easy to prepare food, or hard to prepare food. You could serve soda, making sure you choose the right cup size, pour the right flavor, figure out if they want ice, etc. Or you could just serve beer and fill a mug and give it to them. It's brilliant.
You also do chores; throwing out garbage, flushing toilets, and cleaning dishes, all of which must be done while you take orders and prepare food. What, you think you hire help at this place? Nope you're a one man show. There's a lot of micromanagement involved; take the order for the pasta, cook the noodles, make someone a salad, pour someone a beer, come back to the pasta order and add the toppings, flush the toilet, etcetera.
The keys for each task can also be binded individually as well, so if you don't like it, change it. The art style is pleasant, and the music fits the game really well. The little additions like taking on catering jobs and additional cooking challenges, and being able to earn money by making in-game bets for in-game money just add to it.

Neverending Nightmare is a horror adventure style game. This game was released in September 2014 on Steam.
You play the role of Thomas, the idea behind the game is that you keep experiencing nightmares, but you keep waking up and going straight into another one.  Each nightmare gets worse and worse every time - and the gameplay elements in them become harder too. The game also has a pretty cool save system in that if you die, you end up waking up just a few moments before in the same nightmare.
The actual gameplay is fairly simple - it almost works like a point and click adventure game, but you walk around either using WASD or a controller. As you navigate around the levels, you encounter certain objects which can be interacted with or picked up to use in someway, such as a candle. You will also face a couple of enemies which you have no way of killing, you just have to either avoid or sneak past.
Graphically, Never-ending Nightmares is a 2D hand-drawn line art style. This looks really cool and really puts across the point that this is a never ending dream; all of the colours are the same every room looks identical to the last but with subtle changes.
This game comes with three different endings, I haven't figured out really how to get different endings to the one I already have got, but there are guides online if you are into that sort of thing.
My first run through NM took me about two hours to complete. This would of been considerably shorter if not for a few irritating moments involving sneaking past a difficult monster, but I felt this time was OK for this type of game. Like I said, there are two other endings which will make this a pretty decent length title, but others may be looking for a bit more longivity for the price this is on sale for.
I didn't have any technical problems whilst playing, I did however see something which I think should be mentioned - no loading screens. I don't think games get enough credit when they implement something like that, having no loading screens at all really keeps you immersed in your surroundings and the game.
My final thoughts would be to pick this game up if you are into the atmospheric horror genre of games; but don't go into it expecting fast paced action because you will be thoroughly disappointed as there is virtually no action here. But for what it is, which is a well presented horror game with an awesome looking art style, then you'll get some enjoyment out of it. Personally I think that the £10,99 is a bit steep, maybe wait for it to go for -25% off before picking it up just because of a single ending only takes 2 hours to see.

A simplistic yet endearing game. The plot is barebones, relayed to you only through collectible tapes hidden throughout the world. The game takes place in a seemingly abandoned building inhabited by robots and machines out to kill you. This is where the gameplay shines. It's an FPS, yes, but you only carry a single pistol with VERY limited ammunition. In addition to this, you have to go through EVERY single step of using a gun. You'd have to manually insert the rounds into the magazine, insert the magazine, release the safety, chamber the round, and take aim all manually. Reloading has no automation whatsoever. Even then, you have to keep track of any ammo you have by checking the magazine as well as checking the chamber manually. On top of that, you die in one hit, while enemies take two to three hits on average.
That's the main premise of the game, the interaction with the firearm. It's a bit shaky at first, but when you reload a gun just through muscle memory alone, it's the greatest feeling.
Oh yeah. One more thing. You're gonna need that flashlight. If you don't spawn with it, you best find it.

The final station is a side-scrolling survival game that tells the story of a train conducter delivering special cargo to various stations around the world. During your travels you'll find survivors that can travel with you on your train, but you will have to take care of them by providing them with aid and food.
Don't go into this game expecting a FTL light or a 2D open world survival game. The game is a nice mix of various genres but only really shines in it's storytelling. It is also a very linear experience that will try to do it's best to get you until the end by using save points. Ammo and first-aid kits are definitely limited though, so don't go wasting them!
Even with the limits of it's 2D pixelated art, it manages to show a world that's aware of it's impending doom but tries to keep going anyway. Through the conversations the survivors have during your train rides and newspapers you can buy in towns that are still operating, you get a small idea of what's causing the coming apocalypse and what mankind is doing to try to stop it. Even though you have a role to play in that plan, this is mostly a story about you, the conducter.
Unfortunately, the ending leaves you with many unanswered questions and the game could really use an epilogue to explain a bit more, but overall I quite enjoyed it.

I'll review each game separately (Maybe some spoilers? Not really but you never know what people will consider to be spoilers).  I may be blinded by the nostalgia goggles a little bit, especially for X-2, but still a sincere review.
Oh lord, where do I begin.  First played this game when I was 10 years old.  I'm turning 20 in two days and I'm still in love with this game.  In my original PS2 file, I have well over 300 hours in it, and since then with different save files and with the PS3 version and now the Steam version, I probably have nearly 1000 hours total (in FFX alone, not counting X-2).  Its captivating story is a good way to experience every emotion a good story will produce: anger, happiness, sadness, heartbreak, you name it.  It's a game from 2001 and made for controllers, so its graphics and keyboard layout are a little lackluster and frustrating, but graphics don't always make the game.  After you're finished with the story, there's always loads of extra stuff to do like stat maxing, celestial weapons, and Blitzball (however I seem to be the only person that thoroughly enjoys Blitzball).  With the Steam version, the addition of the Function key hacks make grinding far more bearable, even though there are some things that still need to be ironed out that probably won't (would be nice if in battles when you have the speed hack active it would disable dialogue so there wouldn't be long pauses between moves when someone talks, and sometimes it takes a while for whatever reason before a fiend casts magic.  Would also be nice if Blitzball would be affected by the increase in speed because those games can drag a bit if you have an enormous lead with an OP team).
tl;dr: Great game with an amazing story with lots to do. 10/10
There's a lot of hate surrounding the game which I can understand I suppose, but it's pretty annoying to see all the time.  The game is focused around Yuna's story in a changed world from FFX.  Of course it'll be different.  FFX is an amazing game but the atmosphere after its ending would obviously be different.  There are several times in the game that makes me incredibly sad for her.  The percentage in relation to optional story missions makes exploring the game without a guide a LOT of fun (especially when I was a child and was still in awe by every video game I could find), and then playing with a guide is a lot of fun because there are several hidden things that would be near impossible to discover by yourself, not to mention the satisfaction of watching the percentage go up every few missions (be warned though: there are several guides that are wrong in their order/vague about what to do.  I haven't checked the guide on Steam so I can't say anything about that).  The Creature Creator is sort of tedious and obnoxious but is a great way to level grind/get more items that are exclusive to a single playthrough and whatnot.  The New Game+ option is great because then you can keep all of your stuff and ignore certain missions and choose a different side to experience another aspect of the game.  When I think of the FFX story, I pile the FFX-2 story with it because, in my opinion at least, the two complement each other nicely and make each other whole.
tl;dr: Ignore the hate for X-2, it's a good game if you don't try to play it in the same way as FFX. 9/10

FFX is one of my favorite RPGs of all time. It has a great intro to get you hooked in, and then sprinkles new elements throughout the game as you go on to keep your interest. All of the characters develop pretty well as the story goes on, and the story is pretty enjoyable overall. There are a ton of side quests and games you can do, but the vast majority of them open up to you after completing about 80-90% of the main storyline.
Every area in the world tells a different part of the story. Some areas are war torn. Some are troubled, but hopeful. Some are thriving. Some are corrupt. There's a lot of real-life similarities in storytelling, like touching on things like discrimination (Al Bhed), religion (Yevon) , politics, and death. And the characters all act appropriately to how they were developed and the progression of the story. Some characters will feel strongly against or for something, only to develop into a different mindset.  Even minor side characters will show differences in their feelings from start to finish.
The method of leveling up is practically perfect (Sphere Grid). Every character has their own path, but if you have the right tools you can break off and into another character. If you want, you can make your character as the game intended, and if not, you can have them jump to another character's leveling path to get their similar stats. But with enough time and patience, it is possible for every character to have everything the paths allow them to.
The soundtrack is a solid 10/10. I've listened to the original version on the PS2 copy so many times, but the remastered is actually pretty good too, except for a few tracks.
Honorable Mention of other things I like: Customizing Equipment, Customizing your summons, The ability to talk to the enemy during battle, Tons of variety in weapons/armor/items, Blitzball (Though it's pretttty hard), etc.
After completing about 80-90% of the main storyline, the entire world opens back up for you to explore and quick travel. And you also get a ton of sidequests (Dark Aeons, Omega Ruins, Monster Arena). It's great that there's so much for you to do, but the difficulty spike is insane. There's no middle ground here, you just go from pretty standard fights to practically impossible instantly. For example,
. I really wish they would have added a better form of a middle ground rather than grinding like crazy to get your characters to get to higher levels AND grind for certain items that make leveling up easier.
The story is absolutely disrespectful for everything that happened in the original. But...the gameplay is probably my favorite out of any FF game. Where as FFX is turn-based, FFX-2 is Active Turn-Based, where it still goes by turns but if you don't do anything the enemies will keep attacking. And there's more user involvement to the gameplay (Trigger Happy, Yuna's skil, requires repeatedly mashing buttons for more damage)
It kinda upsets me because what they did the story is almost unforgivable, but then the gameplay is just A+ 10/10 great.
Buy it for FFX. If you fell in love with it and understand the story is about to get a lot worse, go into FFX-2.

Homefront: The Revolution should be judged on what it has become.  It started of as an ambitious project to create an open world guerilla warfare FPS.  However, on release it fell short of that mark...severely so.

Nonetheless, the shooting mechanics are solid.  Each weapon has it own feel and you'll grow to love one over the other depending on your play style. The equipment you are given and can upgrade will make your play style individual - whether you go in guns blazing, stealth play or build a RC car with a bomb attached to really spice things up.  The story line isn't the greatest, but decent to keep you engaged to the next set piece.
For what the game is now, it is worth every cent.  Don't expect a game changer, but a truly solid game to wile away the hours.  Persist with it and have fun.
