TLDR: Prefered the first installment but this is fine too, and technically superior.
I just recently got into the Dark Souls franchise, played the first quite a bit and after finishing it a few times I aquired this one, of which I just finished my first playthrough. So do keep in mind that this is not a "Veteran" review.
And while I did enjoy my time with it, I couldnt help but feel somewhat dissapointed.
Now the first game was a gem, a diamond in the rough, and so comparisons are somewhat skewed from the beginning, but I still feel like the game is falling short in some major areas. Before I go a bit deeper, do understand that I recommend this game for anyone who liked Dark Souls and could go for seconds, but for anyone that hasn't played Dark Souls (1) yet, I would recommend that one.
DS2 is technically superior, which shows in three major areas.
1. No frameratedrops - the game runs smooth 60 FPS throughout, while DS1 was locked at 30, could only be "modded" into 60 and kept dropping in some areas like Blighttown.
2. Sliiiiiightly prettier graphics (but mostly reused assets from he first game! This is very dissapointing but more than half the armor, weapons and monsterdesign was seen before!)
3. No Multiplayer-Extra-Tool required
However it falls flat on some other areas.
1. The Characters - After my first DS1 run, I had a decent understanding of who all these people were, desperatly tried to find ways of keeping some of the NPCs like Sigmeyer or Solare alive and found myself reading up on some of the more interesting characters like Artorias or Sunbro. In DS2, I didnt care about a single one of the NPCs and where all the Bosses in DS1 were inspired and seemed to make some sense as to why they are there, with some being outstanding like Sif, The Bosses in DS2 felt like a checklist. Not sure how many knights I murdered but they all felt the same, I couldnt even name all of them now and a lot of bosses seem to have as their only reason for being there "because a level ends in a boss".
2. The World - DS1 has quite the small world if you think about it. And thats a strength, not a weakness. In DS1 every corner has something interesting, there are no useless rooms, every place remains a memory once gone, because everything happens just once, all the places are interconnected and follow a theme of one Big Castle with its garden and crypt a.s.o. (with Anor Londo the exception) . In DS2 I honestly am not sure right now how many knights-filled castles I went to. Also, barely nothing is interconnected, the only time I found that two areas connected was the Bastille which can be reached by at least two routes, everything else is a one-way-street.
3. Difficulty - DS1 was hard - no doubt - but it made sense. I was challanged all throughout the game, but always felt like it was "doable" (with exception to Capra Demon, which, while now quite trivial, I feel is too hard for new players and wayyyy harder than gargoyles)  - In DS2 the difficulty is all over the place. I found the start to be the by-far hardest part, the player is given 4 possible routes in the beginning, this means theese four routes are very close in difficulty. But since the player gets stronger with each, the difficulty for these 4 is actually inverted with them getting easier instead of harder. I am pretty sure that I aquired more than half of my all-together-deaths in the first and possibly second Area. After these the Levels get very linear, but interestingly not actually harder, meaning that most bosses can be murdered on the first or maybe second try.
4. Upgrades
In DS1 you always felt like you were getting stronger, at least for NG, because you would finish a normal run somewhere between LVL 60-80, so you would know what to level, and the best weapon would be aquired later in the game or at least could be reinforced later.
In DS2 you can reinforce you weapon to the highest point way before the midgame, but cant buy additional (big) titanite until very late in the game. So I upgraded my Katana to lvl 10 (the new max) after a few hours and couldnt find a better weapon throughout 90% of the game - and it wasnt necessary since, as stated before, the game doesnt get harder but easier. I finished at Soullvl 130, even though I dont think I actually got stronger since lvl 60ish, because I already had 40dexterity (the maximum amount that makes sense) and just started upgrading everything else for giggles.
5. Gamelength
I am not entirely sure why, maybe I just got better from playing the first game, but I finished my first very thorough runthrough after 24 in-game-hours. The first game took me almost twice as long, even though it had WAY less bosses and areas.
6. Multiplayer
While in DS1 (with the Multiplayerprogram) one can find multiple summon signs per bonfire, In DS2 in the 24 hour run, I was invaded by another player ONCE and found TWO summon sings from other players. Either the Multiplayer is broken or noone is playing it anymore. (Granted I am not using a multiplayerprogram for DS2, but I do not believe such exists.)
So in the end, the game is pretty good, but it just couldnt captivate me like the first game and I will definatly return to that one - after being done with the third game.

I'm sick of all that "B-team this, B-team that" bull.
At least Dark Souls II is its own game! It's not a lazy homage fest like Dark Souls 3 which has a statue in criticland. Sure, both have their references, but "A-team" Dark Souls 3 didn't even bother to
From Soft. was so "scared" of making another "atrocity" like DSII that they basically made a Dark Souls 1 reskin of Bloodborne. That is what mob psychology does to games.
Dark Souls 2 improves on a load of things, like variety of weapons, armor and character builds, actually competitive caster classes, built-in challenges for end-game, playable PvP etc. The only objective complaints that can be made, we have heard a thousand times. It's about the level design not quite bringing the magic back from the original. Also, some people may find that a few areas offer only "cheap" difficulty, especially in the (now included) DLC.
The changes made in the Scholar of the First Sin edition are minor. There was a one-year gap between my playthrough of the stock version and I can say the differences are rarely noticeable. It's mainly about blocking off some of the areas in the game to avoid confusion for new players and make the game more challenging for the old players. Some enemy and item placements have been changed, usually for the best. Finally, the graphics were supposedly improved.
Personally, I have put way more hours in this game than in the rest of the series and for good reason, though I won't deny that the true magic of Souls shines in the original Dark Souls. But after you're done with that, drop anchor in this one. You needn't go any further.
If all "bad games" were like this, I feel the games industry would be MILES ahead right now.

I'm not going to say this game is absolutely fabulous, because it does have problems. That said, for me this game is wonderful because it evokes wonderful nostalgia of the 90s. I came into gaming via Herinteractive's Nancy Drew PC game series, which are point-and-click adventures, and this game is a lot like those. You don't interact with people, but rather with the protagonist's (Katie's) little sister Sam through her notes and momentos she's left around the house. The point of this game is to explore the house and take in the story.
A lot of people will derisively refer to this type of game as a "walking simulator," which is fine. There is nothing innovative about point-and-click adventures, especially ones without much adventure. The dialogue is one-sided, with Sam speaking to Katie and Katie unable to speak back. There are no NPCs, one of the things I really like about the Herinteractive games, so you are quite alone in this endeavor. Going solo actually adds a lot to the isolation that Sam felt in the house because it enables you to see and experience things as she did: alone.
The ending is nice and complete, albeit sad. There is no possible way to fail this game, apart from giving up. I would have liked some more variance in terms of failures. Even Herinteractive has come up with clever ways for Nancy to fail. Still, given that this is an Indie title created on a small budget, the game is excellently crafted. Sadly, there's not a lot to do beyond reading, listening, and unlocking containers with combinations you've found. I recommend this game for its story, which touched me as an elder sister to someone really similar to young Sam. Play this game for the narrative and you will enjoy it, but if you're looking for something innovative and full of action... skip it.

Neverending Nightmare has a subtle, dark atmosphere. What it doesn't have is context. 
And this is the main problem I am seeing in this game. When it starts, you see impressive visuals and amazing soundtrack by Skyler McGlothin. And it works great - in Neverending Nightmare darkness is scary, not because of what you see or hear, but what you think you see or hear. The game's description tells us that 'a dynamic lighting system gives the ever present darkness a character of its own'. This is spot on. Developers were able to replicate that feeling, when you walk in darkness and start to see silhouettes in your furniture and you feel disturbed.
But later on it all goes away - when the plot only starts, it is wrapped in mystery, yet as it unravels... wait, it actually doesn't. The plot is weak. And when you have a horror game it is not music or art style , which fuel the plot to make it stronger. It is the other way - the plot gives context to all 'scary' things to make them matter.  Otherwise,  it is just an equivalent  to a person who makes silly faces while jumping out of a corner.
Neverending Nightmares is stated to be 'a psychological horror game inspired by the developer's (Matt Gilgenbach, creative director of Infinitap Games) actual battle with mental illness'. Yet it doesn't feel like it. It indeed has a
distinguished feeling of crushing darkness, of somebody watching you from behind, but you can’t base your whole horror game on 'that feeling, when I go to toilet at night and it is kinda creepy'. Mr. Gilgenbach also wrote a novel 'Deconstruction' which dealt with the same personal problems of his. I didn't read it, so I can't say what is the reason behind poor writing in N.N. - technical restrictions or just lack of ability.
Continuing discussing problems within the plot, I want to address the issue of endings.  The game's page on Steam states that 'branching narrative features 3 completely different endings'. And this is true - endings are completely different, I would even say that they have no connection to each other or what we have seen previously in the game. There are symbolic elements which, combined, must give us a complete picture of what was going on, yet when these elements must apply to different meanings, we get a mess. Each ending can point at something which was previously in the game and say 'these things led you to this me'. Yet none of the endings can say that about every plot-element. And when you finish one branch, you start to re-play to get other endings , and you get bored, because they doesn't differ that much in their scenery and gameplay.
By the way, about gameplay - it is primitive. The only thing you do is just basically go forward and avoid monsters, which becomes boring fast, because these monsters are very easy and one particular type shows too often and basically overstays its welcome.
In conclusion I want to say that the game doesn't hold up to its great visuals and music. It doesn't have thought put in it and it will leave you disappointed.
Currently Infinitap Games started a Kickstarter for their new game 'Devastated Dreams'. It already has a demo, so I checked it out and I saw 'Neverending Nightmare 2.0'. It is a polishing of what they did - it seems to be better in terms of setting and gameplay, its visual style has improved even more. Yet I don't have a feeling that they dealt with issues N.N. had, it doesn't feel like a next step. Right now I doubt that I will play D.D, but I hope I will be proven wrong, because there is a lot of talent in the dev-team.

The final station was a breath of fresh air to me, as I am a huge fan of indie games with a retro look, and boy did this game look gorgeous! You can tell a lot of care and attention went in to its many sprites and level designs; this is always a big plus for me in indie games as many seem rushed and unimaginative.
The gameplay itself is very simple in nature, which was perfect as I found the shooting and taking care of survivors and the train itself to be just minor things, there to keep me occupied whilst I was trying to piece together the story, and watching the beautiful scenery go by – I really struggled to put this game down after it hooked it’s claws in, and was a visual and auditory heaven for every second.
The main character is a train conductor, just going about his work when a strange attack happens which causes people to turn in to blood firstly killers. With all the city’s being shut down, your objective is to transport an important cargo, and the survivors you pick up on your way, to your destination whilst trying to survive.
The main goals are pretty standard; each city you arrive in requires you to find a code for the train blocker, which will allow you to move onto your next destination – As you explore the various areas, you will find resources, survivors and the infected; one word of advice, try not to waste bullets as they are few and far between. You will also need to maintain your train as you travel between cities.
Overall, The Final Station is one of the few games that has actually left me satisfied at the end of it – As a single player, story driven game, it does not follow the fads of other indie game titles; the core concept of the game itself was well thought out and executed well. As short as the game is it does evoke some emotions, and if you are just wanting a fast passed shooter, leave now as the first 30 minutes are a slow burn that sets up a great story.
I would most certainly recommend this game to anyone, but I would have to say it’s best to wait till it hits a sale on steam, even though I loved this game I think the price point is a little high; for that reason I’m giving this game 8/10
This game is also available on PS4 and Xbox One.

Neverending Nightmares offers a breath of fresh air in a genre dominated by experiences like Slender: The Arrival and Amnesia: The Dark Descent.  This side-scrolling game combines hand-drawn aesthetics, unsettling atmosphere, and sparse but terrifying jump scares.
One of my few issues with Neverending Nightmares arises in what I consider to be lazy storytelling. Although I enjoy abstract and cryptic plot-lines, I couldn't remember the name of the hero's sister after finishing my first playthrough.  Considering that Thomas and Gabby are the only two characters in the game, you would hope I'd be able to tell you a bit more about them than I actually can.  (I know they're siblings, and I know Thomas is older than her, but that's pretty much it.)  Secondly, the story occasionally sacrifices depth for shallow creepiness.  Sure, I thought the lecture in the asylum was creepy—but did it reveal anything about the protagonist?  Not really.  That said, the story does have one thing in its favor: multiple endings establish this game as one with high replayability.
Secondly, even though Infinitap Games claims Neverending Nightmares seeks "to promote a greater understanding of mental illness," I rarely felt as though the game actually discussed this.  While one of the endings delves into this theme, it is easy to miss if you play without first reading up on the backstory behind Neverending Nightmares. The goal was commendable; it's too bad the implementation wasn't there.
My complaints, though valid, pale in comparison to the many positive qualities of Neverending Nightmares.  Some people might be concerned about the simplistic gameplay—over a period of two to four hours (depending whether or not you choose to find all the endings), you will do nothing but walk, run, and interact with maybe a dozen objects.  I admit this sounds tedious, but in reality the game's simplicity results in a sort of streamlined horror:my limited options heightened the tension because I knew I would be unable to hide or fight back.
Not that the tension needs heightening.  This game possesses an incredible atmosphere, dark and dense and forbidding. The atmospheric tension starts with a unique art style: the black and white dichotomy creates a sparseness that elevates the few colors in Neverending Nightmares.  My pulse spiked whenever I saw the vivid redness of blood, and I grew paranoid when I discovered a yellow candle.  An under-appreciated aspect of the art lies in its incorporation of shadow.  Dynamic shadows based on light sources swerve and flicker around Thomas, and thin lines of blackness darken rooms.
Of course no creepy atmosphere would be complete without audio, and I'm happy to say that both the music and the sound design are well done.  One of the Kickstarter rewards for Neverending Nightmares allowed backers to create a sound that would appear in game, and the variety of these sounds helps make this experience even more nerve-wracking.  Additionally, all of the audio is specially crafted for headphones.  The way certain sounds only register in one ear or the other kept convincing me that there was someone behind me.
While the jump scares don't quite match up to the superb atmosphere, they still frightened me.  Some of these scares are traditional: expect to be chased by several humanoid monsters.  That said, there are plenty of unexpected surprises as well.  I won't mention them here, but rest assured that you will be jumping at many different moments.  (Now that I think about it, I guess you shouldn't rest assured.)
Ultimately, Neverending Nightmares is horror with a message.  If you are willing to spend fifteen dollars on a two to four hour game, you'll discover a beautiful, terrifying experience.  Like me, you may be left wanting to know more about Thomas and Gabby...but nonetheless, I recommend fans of the horror genre pick up this indie title.
FINAL SCORE: 8.7/10

Summary at the Bottom.
The Crew is a game I was quite excited for since I played the Beta, though it is suffering from some massive issues and probably more as I play more. My review style is usually pointing out the negatives, as negatives are easier to see then positives, which positives clog the list up if you try to find them and it becomes a mess.
Note: I didn't pay fully for the game with my own money(I sold TF2♥♥♥♥♥♥on the market), so I am not biased by how much money I invested.
Lets get started..
•AI
-The AI is the type to mimic what the player does if it's not in 1st place, you'll notice this if you're already playing.
-And they just do things that are outright impossible. In the video Jim Sterling made at the 8 minute mark, there's a AI controlled car that just does what he is doing except at a ridiculous level and still is faster. This is a massive problem when you're racing AI and they pull this.
-Source of the ridiculously bad AI;
He's not even racing him cause it's the prologue and he's doing this cause that's how they're coded, and in races they do the exact crap.
-There are also times where they go through civilian traffic vehicles to keep up with you, it's extremely unfair and frustrating.
-Faction missions where you have to race these very AI for an hour or 2 is just the most infuriating thing imaginable, imagine that AI, doing insane stuff and keeping up with you while you're trying your best to not slam into traffic in crowded cities at 150-200mph and the AI is going through it like it doesn't even exist with no consequences in handling. Not fun at all and I'd say avoid ones that have you racing the AI in those long missions.
•Customization
-Kits are another issue, many kits aren't done yet which should of been if the game had to be delayed.
-Kits like the raid or circuit, you can't customize the body for the few cars that currently have it.
-You can't color your rims(Which would be so easy to put in), so you're stuck with Grey/Default, black, white, and sometimes gold)
-There isn't too many selections, for instance in Dirt, if I wanted a certain headlight setup, with fog lights, I couldn't do it, I had to have fog lights with a different setup of headlights. A tad restrictive and could possibly be easily fixed seeing as the fog lights are ontop of the model.
-Vinyl's are somewhat dull as well as restrictive seeing as what you see is what you get, no color changing what so ever, so you'd have to tailor your core vehicle color to the vinyl or just either have no vinyl or pick a different one.
•Cars
-Pretty much a 14 year olds wet dream, there's a bunch of Exotics and Muscle Cars with barely any Japanese Cars.
-When you start, you have the choice between 3 identical looking American boats, or the one Japanese Car, barely much variety to start with.
-There's some Civilian cars that look pretty damn good and would add greatly to the selection, but they chose to make them just cars to pass by or get in your way.
-Tuning is pretty much non-existant, the only thing you're doing is upgrading parts, not tuning. Static upgrades. No body tuning, or engine tuning. The spec kits are the only thing that 'tune' your car.
•Misc
-G27 and other wheel controller support is still awkward and the Force Feedback is not good to play with, it jerks the wheel randomly and you're constantly fighting it, no matter if your on Sports or Hardcore, you have to turn Force feedback down to play with a wheel enjoyably
-Personally I don't really like nitrous boosts in games, but that's just my peeve, the mechanic is there so note that.
-Crew system has problems with disconnecting at the end of missions, instancing, etc.
-The Police are ridiculous during missions or higher level stars, like they're psychopaths who got a Police car and want to kill you at the cost of killing themselves, and suffer from the typical AI problems.
-Physics are ridiculous, as the community calls them Cat-Physics, your car will try it's best to stay on all 4 wheels, which causes ridiculous things to happen if your wheels get off center.
-Text Chat censors such stupid letter combinations making it impossible to have normal conversations.
On the topic of drifting; If you want to know what kit is best for drifting, it's Street. It use to be Dirt, but the handling changes made the the dirt kit less optimal for that.
•Summary.
-The AI is Terrible and Unfair
-Customization is more limited then it should be(It doesn't need to be NFS Underground, but it can easily be better then what it is)
-Car selection is very uninspired and bland.
-Currently doing missions in a crew has issues and kicks people out of the game and having their rewards lost.
-Nitrous is a mechanic and is pretty much needed to be used in missions.
-G27/Wheel support needs work
-Assets in the game that should be used but aren't.
-Game is still unfinished even after a Release delay, unobtainable kits cause they're not "finished".
-No user radio for immersion sake, and the music selection is very boring. You'll have to resort to listening to your own music outside of the game.
-Missions due to the AI aren't fun
-Popo are not fun and you might as well let them catch out outside of missions if your star level is too high.
-Text Chat censors are terrible, and was rushed.
-Physics are counter-intuitive and can mess you up especially during jumps.
-There is no Tuning, changing Specs is the only 'tuning' you'll get.

Some guns have you press V to change firing modes or to turn on or off the saftey. It might sound an annoying ammount of things to deal with but when you are doing it successfully its pretty rad. TLDR: Prefered the first installment but this is fine too, and technically superior.
I just recently got into the Dark Souls franchise, played the first quite a bit and after finishing it a few times I aquired this one, of which I just finished my first playthrough. So do keep in mind that this is not a "Veteran" review.
And while I did enjoy my time with it, I couldnt help but feel somewhat dissapointed.
Now the first game was a gem, a diamond in the rough, and so comparisons are somewhat skewed from the beginning, but I still feel like the game is falling short in some major areas. Before I go a bit deeper, do understand that I recommend this game for anyone who liked Dark Souls and could go for seconds, but for anyone that hasn't played Dark Souls (1) yet, I would recommend that one.
DS2 is technically superior, which shows in three major areas.
1. No frameratedrops - the game runs smooth 60 FPS throughout, while DS1 was locked at 30, could only be "modded" into 60 and kept dropping in some areas like Blighttown.
2. Sliiiiiightly prettier graphics (but mostly reused assets from he first game! This is very dissapointing but more than half the armor, weapons and monsterdesign was seen before!)
3. No Multiplayer-Extra-Tool required
However it falls flat on some other areas.
1. The Characters - After my first DS1 run, I had a decent understanding of who all these people were, desperatly tried to find ways of keeping some of the NPCs like Sigmeyer or Solare alive and found myself reading up on some of the more interesting characters like Artorias or Sunbro. In DS2, I didnt care about a single one of the NPCs and where all the Bosses in DS1 were inspired and seemed to make some sense as to why they are there, with some being outstanding like Sif, The Bosses in DS2 felt like a checklist. Not sure how many knights I murdered but they all felt the same, I couldnt even name all of them now and a lot of bosses seem to have as their only reason for being there "because a level ends in a boss".
2. The World - DS1 has quite the small world if you think about it. And thats a strength, not a weakness. In DS1 every corner has something interesting, there are no useless rooms, every place remains a memory once gone, because everything happens just once, all the places are interconnected and follow a theme of one Big Castle with its garden and crypt a.s.o. (with Anor Londo the exception) . In DS2 I honestly am not sure right now how many knights-filled castles I went to. Also, barely nothing is interconnected, the only time I found that two areas connected was the Bastille which can be reached by at least two routes, everything else is a one-way-street.
3. Difficulty - DS1 was hard - no doubt - but it made sense. I was challanged all throughout the game, but always felt like it was "doable" (with exception to Capra Demon, which, while now quite trivial, I feel is too hard for new players and wayyyy harder than gargoyles)  - In DS2 the difficulty is all over the place. I found the start to be the by-far hardest part, the player is given 4 possible routes in the beginning, this means theese four routes are very close in difficulty. But since the player gets stronger with each, the difficulty for these 4 is actually inverted with them getting easier instead of harder. I am pretty sure that I aquired more than half of my all-together-deaths in the first and possibly second Area. After these the Levels get very linear, but interestingly not actually harder, meaning that most bosses can be murdered on the first or maybe second try.
4. Upgrades
In DS1 you always felt like you were getting stronger, at least for NG, because you would finish a normal run somewhere between LVL 60-80, so you would know what to level, and the best weapon would be aquired later in the game or at least could be reinforced later.
In DS2 you can reinforce you weapon to the highest point way before the midgame, but cant buy additional (big) titanite until very late in the game. So I upgraded my Katana to lvl 10 (the new max) after a few hours and couldnt find a better weapon throughout 90% of the game - and it wasnt necessary since, as stated before, the game doesnt get harder but easier. I finished at Soullvl 130, even though I dont think I actually got stronger since lvl 60ish, because I already had 40dexterity (the maximum amount that makes sense) and just started upgrading everything else for giggles.
5. Gamelength
I am not entirely sure why, maybe I just got better from playing the first game, but I finished my first very thorough runthrough after 24 in-game-hours. The first game took me almost twice as long, even though it had WAY less bosses and areas.
6. Multiplayer
While in DS1 (with the Multiplayerprogram) one can find multiple summon signs per bonfire, In DS2 in the 24 hour run, I was invaded by another player ONCE and found TWO summon sings from other players. Either the Multiplayer is broken or noone is playing it anymore. (Granted I am not using a multiplayerprogram for DS2, but I do not believe such exists.)
So in the end, the game is pretty good, but it just couldnt captivate me like the first game and I will definatly return to that one - after being done with the third game.

For a game made in a week, it's pretty great. It's inherently satisfying to manually reload your weapon as quickly as you can, once you have a grasp on the mechanics. It's tense and fun when you hear a drone around a corner, look out for its camera light, and time it just right to shoot and disable it unscathed. There's some nice use of adaptive music, a scarcity of ammunition forcing you to make every shot count, and some terrifying flying drones to escape from.
However, being made in a short amount of time, in Unity, and using randomly generated environments, I've run into framerate issues, repetitive environments, graphical whoopsies, and situations with no chance of success. As well, the objective of collecting tapes involves listening to a monotone voice drone exposition that is often heard over and over again after respawning. You can fully mute the voice volume in the settings, at least.
It's worth the $5 pricetag, but I was happy to pick it up on sale if you catch my drift.

I'm sick of all that "B-team this, B-team that" bull.
At least Dark Souls II is its own game! It's not a lazy homage fest like Dark Souls 3 which has a statue in criticland. Sure, both have their references, but "A-team" Dark Souls 3 didn't even bother to
From Soft. was so "scared" of making another "atrocity" like DSII that they basically made a Dark Souls 1 reskin of Bloodborne. That is what mob psychology does to games.
Dark Souls 2 improves on a load of things, like variety of weapons, armor and character builds, actually competitive caster classes, built-in challenges for end-game, playable PvP etc. The only objective complaints that can be made, we have heard a thousand times. It's about the level design not quite bringing the magic back from the original. Also, some people may find that a few areas offer only "cheap" difficulty, especially in the (now included) DLC.
The changes made in the Scholar of the First Sin edition are minor. There was a one-year gap between my playthrough of the stock version and I can say the differences are rarely noticeable. It's mainly about blocking off some of the areas in the game to avoid confusion for new players and make the game more challenging for the old players. Some enemy and item placements have been changed, usually for the best. Finally, the graphics were supposedly improved.
Personally, I have put way more hours in this game than in the rest of the series and for good reason, though I won't deny that the true magic of Souls shines in the original Dark Souls. But after you're done with that, drop anchor in this one. You needn't go any further.
If all "bad games" were like this, I feel the games industry would be MILES ahead right now.

(**This is a pretty neutral review, but Steam reviews don't leave that much room for nuance**)
**Here's a quick TL,DR: A unique and interesting horror/adventure hybrid, that lets itself down and falls a bit flat, but does still do just enough to stand on its own.**
Oh Neverending Nightmares, you stood on the precipice of greatness, but then you made a few mistakes, and those misteps drove you down a considerable ammount. As it stands, rather than setting the world on fire and becoming a revolutionary classic, you're an above average, competently executed horror/adventure hybrid.
Before we get to why this game falls short, let's take a moment to acknowledge all the things it does right. First off, it is creepy and unnerving throughout. The atmosphere is incredible. This is accomplished by a beautiful, unique, and simple (yet also nicely detailed) art style. The detailed closeups of items scattered throughout the world are a very nice touch, and do a lot to help flesh out the world. Backing that up is some of the best sound design I've ever encountered in a horror game. No exageration, it sounds every bit as creepy as you could want. Not wanting to spoil anything, the third section of the game made me so genuinely uncomfortable because of the sound design, that I actually had to walk away from the game for a little bit.
Beyond atmosphere, I want to commend the game's designer for being so openly influenced by mental illness. I don't have much to say about that right now, but that took guts, so, well done. Knowing this information going in helps significantly appreciate a lot of design choices.
Finally, in addition to the atmosphere, the level design is great itself. While only existing of pretty straight forward hallways and paths, the world itself gets a lot of distance out of this simplicity, even as the vast majority of movement occurs on a 2D plane. The paths you can take branch out, twist around themselves, and generally seem to shift around you. It's honestly creepy, and unnerving as you try to make sense out of the impossible geometries the game builds and lets you explore.
It's worth noting that this game is not particurally long. As many people have pointed out, it only takes about an hour or two to finish a playthrough. However, I won't hold this against the game too much, as its length feels appropriate. It does what it wants to do, and then ends without overstaying its welcome. And yes, $15 dollars for 1 hour of play is a bit steep in comparison to a lot of games, but the budget conscious among us could always wait for a sale to save a few dollars. It's worth noting that despite the cost and relatively short length, I didn't feel ripped off or cheated out of my money.
So now, we come inevitably to the part where I need to break out the criticisms. First off, and this is the most minor of my criticisms, as big as the game world appears to be, it seems to consist of a lot of empty space. There are plenty of uninteresting dead ends, as well as some repeating elements that start to lose luster very quickly.
Next up, and more damaging to the game overall, is the enemy design. The game starts out with positive points in this category because you've got absolutely no offensive capabilties, and no defensive capabilities beyond running away, and even that can only be done for short distances. These facts make enemies legitimate threats, and keeps this from approaching anything actiony, and keeps you feeling disempowered and helpless, the key elements of horror. However, from this strong start, the game quickly surrenders the advantage.  There are a very small number of enemy types throughout the game. While this isn't the end of the world, the enemies are largely uninspired. They are mostly humanoid, not truly anything too horrifying or mostrous. But again, this could be overlooked, or may even be something some people like. But what ultimately is the final nail in the coffin on this issue, is that dealing with the enemies is just dull. They are mostly just tests of patience, more than anything intrinsically interesting to encounter or deal with. They are easy to figure out how to deal with, and once you accomplish that, they do little more than add arbitrary wait times to each encounter. There are a few puzzles which use the enemy mechanics to interesting effect, but to be honest, other than serving as the essential threat to life itself, the enemies serve little purpose. In a game with as great an atmosphere and understanding of pacing and discomfort, it's practically criminal that the enemies are so weakly designed.
And finally, my biggest criticism of the game comes up. This has to do with the structure of the story. I'm going to try to avoid all spoilers about specific events and occurances of the story, but I will be talking about narative structure here. The important thing to know is that the game has multiple endings based on which paths you take throughout the game. These are mostly subtle choices, that honestly you won't notice until you get told by the game where the choices were at the end. Having multiple endings is the greatest flaw of this game, despite how well they are integrated into the gameplay. To explain why, you need to understand that the game is drenched in symbolism, from small details of the environment, to enemy design and even gameplay mechanics. But by having three separate endings, the developer essentially rendered two-thirds of the symbols encountered in a given playthrough completely moot and meaningless. While having the multiple paths does pad out the length of the game, as you backtrack to find all the divergent paths, I'd rather have one very solid ending than three weak-ish endings. The only real defense that I can think of for this is that having multiple endings contributes to the themes of ambiguity throughout the game, but this is a pretty weak justification. These endings are also mostly cliched, and not particularly exciting, especially when contrasted with the incredible atmosphere on display.
So, if the game is short, has weak enemy design, has an ultimately dissappointing story, and generally has weak gameplay, why is there a big thumbs up next to this review? Well, for all of the criticisms I can fairly levy against this game, as I said, I never felt ripped off by this game. I was engaged for as long as I played it, and even the ending, while abrupt and weak, wasn't a deal breaker by any means. It also is one of the few games I've found that describes itself as psychological horror, and does enough to earn that title. While there are a few jump scares, they are used sparingly enough as to not weaken the game, and the rest of the game puts you in a disempowered place and truly messes with you, leaving a lingering sense of fear and unease. If you're a fan of real horror, and not the empty meaningless YouTube-bait horror with exclusively meaningless jumpscares, definately give this game a shot.

When I first heard of this game, I was very excited. Kotaku advertised it as a game built around environmental storytelling, the likes of which made games like Bioshock and Fallout very enjoyable. Instead of true environmental storytelling, however, the player is "treated" to literally nothing but audiologs. It reaches a point where I might as well have just purchased a movie because all you do is walk around the house, pick up objects, and listen to a teenage monologue. The environments themselves don't even make sense. One location in the house is a TV that is still on with VCR tapes of the X-files lying around. It creates a sense that something happened suddenly to the characters, but you later learn thats impossible so the TV was either on for days and no one shut it off, or it was just placed to set a rather inappropriate mood that fits nowhere in the plot. The whole point of environmental storytelling appears to have been lost on the developers, who seem to beleive notes and audio messages are somehow the same thing as meticulously creating a scene that contains an implied story. Thats the thing about environmental storytelling, you're not supposed to use words.
Other than that, the game doesn't have anything that makes it feel special. It has zero replay value, the story is experienced so passivly by the player it might as well have been a movie, and the game itself is barely 2 hours long. I've purchased games for less than a dollar that delivered more content than this.

Neverending Nightmares is a game that delves deep into the darkest corners of the human mind and exposes your most terrible fears. It is a piece of psychological horror at its finest. Loss of identity, decay, suffering, death, insanity, can all be found here in a unique and original display.
Do not be deceived by the apparently undetailed graphics, the art of the game in fact contributes to much of the feeling it creates. From desorientation, disgust, fear to sheer horror, this game has it all.
The multiple endings derive from confounding identities, and, as you will see, each nightmare introduces new threats and explores a different theme of fear.
Though I would not recommend this game for its gameplay (which is extremely simplistic) or its story (which is rather ambiguous), it is a must-play for any fans of the art of horror.
Pros:
+original setting, graphics and ideas
+very opressive atmosphere
+very scary at times
+possibly the creepiest game I've ever played
Cons:
-very simplistic gameplay
-design is repeatitive, at times you will simply lose track of where you are and that may easily break the immersion
-overall a bit hollow, just wandering around does get boring after a while. Introducing some puzzles or some other decent way of of interaction with the environment might have helped
-story is ambiguous and difficult to follow, but it is creepy and disturbing
-short, overpriced and doesn't have much replayability value
Overall, I'd say it deserves at least a 7/10 for the brilliant way in which it illustrates almost everything that psychological horror is about. I suggest you don't buy it on full price though, because you might get disappointed by how short it is, especially since, except for unlocking all nightmares and branching pathways, it has no replayability value at all. But I definitely recommend it on a sale.

The Final Station is a Methodical Side Scrolling Zombie Shooter with Train Rides in between.
You travel from zombie-infested town to town with your train. At every station you have to find a "blocker code" in order to unlock your train an continue your travel.
The zombie shooting/city exploration part is actually quite interesting. It's mainly about acting methodical, not rushing, not pannicking and conserving your ammonition. The level is very good if a little linear. However after a few hours of play the zombi shooting parts becoma a bit repetitive because at least for the first 3 hours of play you will only have two weapons (pistol and shotgun) and only encounter 4 different zombie types.
The train ride sections are imho the weak part of the game. It is a silly minigames where you have to keep your train running by adjusting various levers on a timer. While doing so, you can try to listen to the chat of your passengers (survivors you have picked up along the way) but since there is no voice acting I had a hard time keeping up with the text while trying to fix my train and feeding the passengers.
The story is mainly told through a lot of small notes, E-Mails and chat snippets you find throughout the game and is very intriguing. Together with the amazing art style and environmental details this creates a pretty cool atmosphere and was encouraging me to explore more about what really happened and how it will all play out in the end.
However as fascinating the story and the world was, I'm a mechaincs focused gamer at heart. And while the zombie shooting/exploring parts were fun for two hours or so, they got very stale afterwards and the tidious train rides didn't help either. Therefore overall I cannot reommend the game to anyone who has similar priorities as me.

The good: Great atmosphere, genuinely creepy in some places. Exploration is rewarding. On foot in the towns and stations, gameplay is fun. Combat is solid and fun, with a surprising amount of variety for just a few basic enemy types. Levels are really well designed.
The less good: The translation isn't the best, so the dialogue is sometimes weird and incomprehensible. It's kind of amusing and charming, but it makes it hard to follow the story at times. The game is really short. I managed to beat it in under 4 hours. I don't think it's a problem. It's short, to the point, and never wears out its welcome. Some people may hesitate to pay full price for such a short game, though.
The bad: On the train, gameplay is very tedious. You constantly have to keep tabs on survivors who seem determined to starve or bleed to death. It's less This War of Mine and more Tamagotchi. One part of your train will always be on the fritz, and fixing it is a boring and repetitive chore. A handful of moments in the on-foot sections can be cheap and frustrating, especially when you have to deal with enemies waiting for you in a small room at the bottom of a ladder.
The overall: Good! ... for the most part. It's certainly worth playing.

The Final Station is a 2D survival adventure where you are the conductor of a train that you must maintain, and keep moving onward to the next station.
While on the train, you need to keep up on repairs on only one train component at a time, as well as tend to your passengers with food and med kits. You can also craft ammo and med kits with the spare parts you’ve scavenged. The journey from one station to the next gets tedious quickly and every trip is essentially the same.
You will need to explore each station you arrive at, and find the key code to unblock the train, in order to depart for the next station. Since supplies are fairly limited, it is strongly recommended to search the area thoroughly. Watch out for for the infected hordes though, as there will be plenty of them to kill or avoid. There is a fair amount of combat at most stations, but I’m a little disappointed that there was never any on the train.
The game took me just over 4 hours to complete, and aside from achievements, I can’t see any reason to want to replay it.
The Final Station isn’t a bad game, but it starts feeling repetitive quite early on. I didn’t hate the game by any means, but I feel like they could have done a lot more with it. It needs something more to keep the train rides and exploration fresh and exciting because doing the same tasks over and over gets stale quickly. Then you top it all off with the actual ending, it’s disappointing, and I find it hard to recommend the game, especially at full price.

Final Fantasy X broke the PS1 era mould a little bit by bringing FF back to its traditional turn based roots. I personally think the game is better for it, but objectively it may be a little bit slow for people who are used to the faster ATB system. It also allows you to switch characters freely during battle (with only three active characters at once). The switch system adds an exciting element to the battles, because it feels like you can freely exploilt enemy weaknesses on the fly, and you can use every character instead of only focusing on a few.
Another way it broke the mould was by removing the traditional level up system and using a level up grid called the
. This has both pros and cons but is essentially a more visually stimulating standard level up system. Choice doesn't really play a big role here unless you use the expert grid, but generally you won't be using the expert grid due to issues you have later in the game. The benefits of the sphere grid system lie in the fact that you can see future abilities you will acquire and notice significant power increases after moving for a while on the grid.
The character balance is fine throughout the main storyline, but there's one character that tends to be weaker than the rest due to the fact that he has no specialisation and feels a few steps behind whoever he decides to tail on the grid. Post game balance is pretty bad with the fact that you'll only use 4/8 of the characters. This is less important as obviously post game content tends to be done with efficiency in mind so players probably won't mind.
In terms of the writing, the characters are pretty consistently good with a few common anime tropes thrown in. They're all charming though, even if some of the scenes can be a little bit cringey. The writing is good, and the overall plot is actually very interesting. It avoids falling into some of the shonen cliches and the game is definitely better for it. The world is grim and it definitely lets you feel the main themes of the game, which are death and hope.
The music is top notch with a great leitmotif that they use at the correct times to make you feel the beats of the story more accurately. The theme of the game was a song called "Suteki Da Ne" which I personally don't care for as much as 'Eyes on Me' or 'Melodies of Life'. Not to say that it's bad, I just don't enjoy the singer too much so I find it hard to listen to it as much as the other main FF themes.
Ok, here's a quick pros/cons list to finish this review off.
+ Interesting plot, good writing, great music and quality world building. Standard FF fare.
+ Tactical combat means that you feel good for beating tough enemies
+ Standard story is harder than normal FF's, if you're after a challenge this might be for you. (without grinding)
+ Tons of post game content, that is actually very tough and time consuming.
- Sphere Grid gives the illusion of choice.
- Some voice acting is a little bit cringey
- Animations are a bit... off.
All in all this is a solid game (and port) that lives up to the FF name superbly, and I would recommend to anyone looking for a great experience.

stand up in free game world and if you enjoy shooting the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of things, you would not waste your time on this game.
It is not in any way flawless. In fact, every single aspect of the game has flaws, just because its a free title, and the good news is all of them are not deal breakers and will not kill the fun.
The gameplay has two main diversions: PVP (or Player Versus Player) and PVE (or Player Versus Environment).
The PVP section have a Counter Strike theme to it, in a good way. You have the main popular modes and you have the ranking matches.
It also have a daily quest like objectives in form of contracts which are fun to do. All and all, even if Warface might not have the best PVP experience among the competitors but it will bring the fun and enjoyment.
The PVE section, well personally, I did not see anything like it anywhere else. You might not expect much from it, but in that case, Warface will surprise you.
Like PVP there are two ways to play PVE:
One by doing shorter daily missions which thanks to a smart system in level design, are in fact the same 15 or so levels over and over again but the trick to it is the levels are followed by different levels and the route might get reversed. So even if the environment feels repetitive, the gameplay will not go down that way easily.
Or two by doing one of the three accessible longer missions (there are more longer specific missions but only 3 of them are accessible every season) at different difficulties to test your teamwork and individual skills.
Speaking of teams, you can either team up with up to 4 other people in a PUG (Pick Up Group) system or create your own private dedicated servers to play aside your friends.
There are a lot of other things to talk about like how the reward system is appealing, how the game announcement of in-game events feels right, how teamwork in higher difficulties become a crucial factor and etc. but just read this:
The net code is not the best but admittedly they did a very good job considering the title is free. If you are playing in the closest server to you (they have EU, US and Turkey) and a fine internet connection, you will most probably experience a smooth gameplay.
It’s over 400 hours and I still feel like there are a lot more to discover. There are more than 100 individual ♥♥♥♥ing guns in this game! Yes, you can obviously see repetition like in real world but again a single smart trick made it feel right. The repetition is spread among different classes. You can find FY SMG, FY Sniper Rifle, FY Machine Gun and FY LMG which in my experience did not feel repetitive at all because I found the SMG version superior on its class in my arsenal for a long time while not much of its Sniper Rifle version.
And of course there is the famous Crysis customization system. Enough parts to make it your own.
Simply put: its good because it is simple. And sometimes here and there you will find your needed option in the exact right place.
The main plot is about two military factions called “Warface” and “Blackwood” and you already know who are the bad guys and who are the good guys. Through shorter missions you will hear high ranks of Warface officers chatter about Blackwood “Bad activities” and “Bad intentions” and you will learn about one or two high ranks of Blackwood on longer missions, that BTW are poorly scripted, and that’s it. There is no higher purpose in this fight or higher goal than fight or any simple twist in the plot. I’m not expecting Bioshock, just give me a better reason to kill those blackwood ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s than "they are trying to win the war against us"! And why are we fighting again?
Did I mention the scripts are horrible? Also I’ve seen better voice acting in mobile games!
Although having a simple interface have its own benefits but I need to be able to communicate with my teammate in middle of the fight to tell him “Dude, I got this section, I know a trick, you try and push forward” or even plan a strategy ahead. There is this in-game chat, but no indication of new messages and no history. That was just an example but more you play the game more you will find yourself in those situation.
Another example is this market to sell or buy some of fancy gear or weapon which you would normally earn from opening random boxes, but guess where is it! ON THE ♥♥♥♥ING WARFACE WEBSITE!

Definitely one of my favourite city builder games of all time, and I've been playing them for 20 years!  Incredible that this masterpiece is the work of one man.  Not to mention that, apart from an AI bug I actually prefer to keep (animals walk under water when they travel!), the game appears to be completely bug free.
I do, however, have to warn you that this is also one of the hardest in the genre.  Expand too slowly and you'll be stifled by old age; expand too soon and your town will starve to death.  The resource management is key, and is incredibly sensitive to fluctuation.  Find yourself on a downward spiral, running out of resources?  You're probably already doomed.  Managed to harvest in excess?  Store it up so you have a buffer zone.  Not enough workers?  Accept some nomads, or help your population to breed.
The game might appear to be a little shallow - once you've built all that appears in the menu, that's it - but I promise you, there's so much to this game if you're interested in making a successful, expansionist town, especially if you're after the achievements.
It's not a quickfire game either - you need lots and lots of patience to survive, and even more to master it.  Before you know it, you'll have spent hours on this game without achieving much, but having grand goals for your town in mind.

I just found one of the 3 endings of Neverending Nightmares (in 1.4 hours). This intrigues me for the replayablity factor that is presented,  however the thought of trudging (and I use that word literally to describe the speed at which the asthmatic main character moves) through labyrinthine corridors deters me from pursuing them for the time being. Even if I were to find all 3 endings, I'm not sure I'd ever revisit this title though. There are some games I do revisit from time to time, this is unfortunately not going to be one of those titles. I'd say the current 68/100 metacritic score is accurate.
What the game does well:
The atmosphere is done well, and I particularly enjoyed the Edward Gorey aesthetic used in the design, as well as the use of color to draw attention to specifc details. The few frights and encounters kept things interesting, as well did the atmospheric music (definitely play with headphones).
The running is short-lived and easily expired, which presents the user with choices to make especially when present in more dangerous situations.
Non-reliant on Jump scares:  Neverending Nightmare might have a few tricks of its own in the jump department, but its focus on the environment and sound are its strong points.
What could be improved:
The Pacing - The character speed could probably be sped up about 1.5 to 2 times their current speed with as much walking around is required. I'd liken the current speed to that of wading through knee deep water,,, for the entire game.
If you want to make a character move that slow, then the atmosphere needs to be more engaging (whether that be more benign haunts, more background detail to focus on, or slow changes to environment as the character moves though it). Neverending Nightmares does provide all of these, however it feels as though it's not quite enough as you slowly  navigate its corridors.
Considering I found one ending in 1.4 hours, you could argue the speed is artificially extending the play time.
The Ending(s) - I've only seen one ending so far. It was more like a quick scene rather than a fleshed out closure, so the payout felt a bit weak considering the narrative through scenery the game otherwise provides.
Who I would recommend this to:
One of my friends got bored, maybe getting past the first nightmare only and then moving on. However, they tend to be more action oriented rather than savoring that slow build-up.
If you enjoy games that focus heavily on exploration ("wander quests" as I call them) and enjoy a slower pace in a dark room, then you'd probably enjoy this title. For anyone who enjoys horror games, this is a nice title to have especially if you can look past its faults.
For the brevity of the game though, and what little it does perform, I'm not sure I can recommend this game at it's 14.99 price. I have a hard time spending slightly less on that for a movie theater ticket as is.

As the developer and publisher describe it The Final Station is part ‘train simulator and exploration game’ and part ‘hardcore sidescrolling shooter.’
My expectations for The Final Station were relatively high. This is in part because I enjoyed the Reddit AMA that Alex Nicihiporchik from tinyBuild and developer Oleg Sergeev created to hype their game. As a former marketing student I am of the opinion that Reddit can be a great – and cheap – marketing activity to promote your game (or any product for that matter). I believe that you have to take every opportunity that you can to communicate with potential customers. It’s not something that nearly enough developers are doing.
The game is approximately four or so hours in length. However, the first half an hour or so of the game builds up to the main gameplay. I personally found this period to be very slow and tedious. It doesn’t do enough to generate interest and keep you emotionally connected to the game. It’s not until the game is well and truly into its meaty portion where I felt in sync with the gameplay.
In the AMA Igor makes the claims that the game is one that many people will want to play numerous times in order to completely understand the game. This is generally true for most media. The more you play something the more its secrets are revealed. You will discover something that you didn’t previously know. However, I don’t believe that most players would want to play the game through multiple times. This is because the game is extremely linear.
There may be things that you wish you knew earlier in a game to get a different outcome. For example, I’ve read reports of numerous people not realizing that you could craft items on the train until late in the game.
I would suggest that those who are likely to play the game multiple times are the achievement hunters. This is because a number of the game’s achievements require you to meet certain numerical requirements in order for the achievement to unlock. This isn’t always going to happen on the first or even the second playthrough.
Bravo to the devs on outstanding level design. The greatest asset that the game has is its level design. Although replayability is minimal because of its linear approach the actual level design makes an initial playthrough an exciting adventure (after the initial starting period). The decision to make everything behind a closed door dark was brilliant. This provides an air of mystery for everything that you do. Finding out what is lurking in the darkness is a rewarding experience.
Arguably the most significant criticism that I have with the game is in a disappointing way combat becomes trivialized. Once you learn how to manage your available ammunition the risk almost feels non-existent. This is because of the overly generous checkpoint system. Whenever, if ever, you do die you don’t ever get put back very far. This means that aside from ammo management players can be as reckless and as carefree with the enemies as you would like. I’m not asking for a game that is as punishing as a Dark Souls game where every misstep carries a significant cost but I would like to know that I will be penalized proportionately for poor play.
I appreciate the design that went into the actual train simulation The creation of a number of mini-games is intelligent and keeps players engaged throughout the rail journey. Having to maintain and repair parts of the train through mini games was fantastic. They are all easily accessible to most gamers and are engaging. I also liked the little onboard messaging system with other characters within the game. I felt that this added to the game’s narrative in a clever way.
The fact that you have to do this at the same time as tending to the needs of your passengers also gets a thumbs up from me. It mixes the realities of the customer service aspects of train travel with the hard work maintenance. Of course, the reality is that real life train services have multiple people doing these jobs but it is still interesting and well-designed nonetheless.
The pixel graphics have been designed by Oleg and he has done a masterful job in their creation. I have a tendency to believe that pixel graphics have been overdone lately and that they don’t suit every game style. However, I believe that they really help build the atmosphere that they were hoping to achieve. It is one of the standout features of the game. I love the contrasts that they achieve in relation to shape and size.
The Final Station has Steam achievements and Steam trading cards. This makes the game Steamified.
I am honestly on the fence in regards to The Final Station. It’s a game where I truly wish I hadn’t had my expectations and hopes raised for it. There is a high likelihood that I would have enjoyed my time with the game that much more had I not. The Final Station isn't a bad game but it's certainly not as good as it could have been. I can recommend the game to those of you seeking a relatively short survival adventure game especially to those of you not seeking significant replayability. If you're looking for anything more then you may be barking up the wrong tree.

A very enigmatic (borderline broken) storyline gives some semblance of a driving force for the game, but the overall experience is lacking.
Pros:
Neat mental exercise
Combat is well done
Music
Artwork- particularly the backgrounds.
Cons:
-Maintenence of the train is less balancing resources and maintaining, as it is pressing a single button every few seconds as your frantically run back and forth to feed/mend whatever survivors you have.
-A large amount of dialogue is between passengers on the train. You can't read it though, because if you do, your train will A) Shut down, B) Stop giving passengers oxygen, or C) one of them will die within seconds. You basically have to choose between keeping people alive, or listening to a portion of the plot.
-The Plot is convoluted and highly open to interpretation in the same way that an art piece involving a bundle of steel wool could be. The story is there, somewhere, but finding it involves making huge logical jumps and digging through tidbits of information. The problem is that there's no baseline. The whole thing handles like a mushroom trip.
-Writing suffers from poor translation and makes it that much harder to glean any kind of understanding.

Game is really fun. If you like arcade racing games it is a must have.
Pros:
-The way the car drives is pretty customizable and even though you can't make huge changes like making it a sim, you can definitely make it drive to your taste (as long as you enjoy arcade driving).
-Game creates the perfect challange. You can win most races with relative ease, but getting that gold medal definitely requires some skill.
-People have been bashing the graphics, but for an online-focused open world racing game the graphics are really impressive.
-Online experience seems pretty stable. One problem I always have with online racing games is how crazy things go when playing online, cars popping out of nowhere, suddenly stoping or accelarating, etc. So far I have experienced no major problems while playing coop events.
-Variety of car classes and events for those classes. There are car classes build for different terrains and conditions and events for those different classes.
-Don't like playing with other people? You can go completely solo. Even though the game is online-focused you can ignore everyone around you and play it like if it was a singleplayer game.
-Even though it's an arcade game you can feel the differences in handling of each vehicle with ease, making car choices come to preference.
-That huge map! Travelling from one city to another is already a lot of fun and there are kind of mini-games in every road that include jumping, slaloms, driving fast and on the road, etc. All to keep you busy on your travels while also rewarding you.
-The performance is flawless. Some people may be worried about performance since it's a Ubisoft game, but I have a pretty old computer and can still run the game flawlessly with mixed high/ultra settings.
Neutral:
-There are not many visual customization options as I though there would be, but customizing your car is still pretty fun, even though I feel it could be better.
-Soundtrack doesn't fit the game well. The songs don't give you that adrenaline that make you want to drive fast and recklessly. But I believe no one cares for game soundtracks anymore, since most people just mute the game music and use an external music player.
-The story feels kinda dull. The story is amazing the first minutes of gameplay, but once you hit the road it doesn't feel like a big deal anymore, but all online-focused games are like this. I haven't completed the game yet, so take this one with a grain of salt.
-Cops are lazy. You have to do some real♥♥♥♥♥♥for them to go after you, just driving a clearly illegaly modified car 100Km/h above speed limit won't do it. Some people will love it, some others will hate it. Sometimes they also appear during races and don't do anything. In events where they're the main deal it's a different story, of course.
Cons:
-The car sounds are pretty bad, they just don't sound reallistic. Sometimes I feel like hearing an engine that came from a 2005 game.
-You win performance parts in every event, which completely makes the performance shop useless allowing you to make a lot of money very easily since you have to spend very little of it to progress through the game. Remember that I haven't completed the game yet, it may change at some point.
-You can't play the game offline, as far as I know. People who don't have access to a decent connection all the time must be very careful when buying this game.
Some people have been saying this game is horrible, it is not. I haven't experienced bugs, lags, freezes, ctds or anything like that. The game is just great, even though it's not amazing. It's a great game that will give you a lot of fun specially if you play with your friends, but there's nothing really groundbraking about it.
Also, don't pay attention to those people saying that the game's handling and physics are horrible. It's an arcade game and it was designed to be so, so don't expect reallistic collisions, steering, car damage or anything like that. It has very good mechanics for an arcade game. It's not just an "accelerate and steer game" and you can still make mistakes in it, considering that you're playing on hardcore mode.
I give this game a solid 7.8/10
If you have any doubts if you should or should not buy the game, feel free to ask me any questions ; )

In conclusion, F1 2016 seems like the culmination of years of development of this series. A near-perfect F1 / Racing game. Well done Codemasters.

This was one of the times I pre-ordered a game solely based on its trailer (and it will probably be the last time).
The Final Station's trailer really impressed me with its music and atmosphere, the retro-style graphics and the gameplay it presented. Looked quite simplistic and a bit melancholic. that is exactly what I was looking for.
I hoped to be tought how to play the game, advance through better weapons and better zombies as time moves on and experience the story of this game in the manner it was presented in the trailer. I expected the gameplay to be a bit hectic and varied, how it commonly is with retro shooters. The train segment looked fun as well, a bit of micromanaging in between - sounded good to me.
The big problem is: I was left sorely disappointed. Let me tell you why.
This game is not at all what I hoped it was going to be. First of all, you do not get tought any controls from the get go. There is a little tutorial, but if you don't look up the controls yourself at some point in the game, you won't get to know em. This is a very minor thing to be honest, but it confused me a bit. Why drop me in a tutorial where you could go through every single control option perfectly... and just not do that? Doesn't make sense to me. This theme carries on to your first actual train ride, where you are gives a bunch of things to keep track of without being told how to. Yeah, you can figure it out yourself quite easily, but again it's extremely weird that the opportunity to at least *label* the options was not taken. Also the status of the passengers isn't labeled either, so you have to figure out yourself that this white drop means "bleeding" and that the guy will take continuous damage over time until he dies.
But anyways, these are smaller things that I just found odd. My main two points of critique are a bit heavier. First point: the way of storytelling. You are just dropped in there with no context, no idea who you are, where you are, what you are doing and so on. The story just kinda unfolds and you have to roll with it because you have no details at all to cling to. Everything is just "given". Like you are playing a video game adaption to a comic book, where it is expected that you already know about half the story. The way it is conveyed didn't appeal to me either. Just a bunch of rambling from the train guests that you *miss anyways* if you have to micromanage something in the front part of the train. the speech bubbles just disappear. Really odd design choice again. Also there are a lot of missed opportunities along the way. Why can I only talk to *this* person and not the others? I wanna know more! Why does my character never reply at all? I mean - he does reply, but for some reason it is not shown on screen so I have no clue what he said. Well, sometimes he makes a little "..." speech bubble, other times he doesn't for some reason, the result stays the same. What put me off even more were the two situations I came across, where you were actually able to make a response choice. That only happens during little in-between text chat segments when you are actually able to see your own answers. The first one was a choice between "..." and "Thank you!" which I am sure had no effect on the story prograssion at all and the second one was a choice between exactly one option. I have no clue why they even made that a "choice" you had literally no alternatives and usually the character talks by himself anyways. All of this felt weird and extremely inconsistent.
Second point: The actual gameplay. It's just a bit... boring. Fighting zombies gets repetetive *really* quickly and is just weird sometimes. Melee hits don't connect, bullets seem to not deal damage - maybe I just suck, but there were situations where I really felt like something was off. Anyways, the fights get repetetive really soon and even adding new zombies or a new gun later doesn't get that stale taste out of my mouth. The whole "limited ammo" aspect is also not pushed proberly either as you do run out of ammo - yes - but melee combat is just so chunky and a bad alternative usually. It doesn't really depend on skill, it just depends on which zombies are left after you ran out. For example you are rarely given any means of defense against sprinting zombies. Combat doesn't feel good at all.
Apart from that I really dislike that you cannot get any information on cities further down the road or get info on your next objective / place to drop people off (so you could calculate if its worth keeping that bleeding dude alive or not). Again a really odd choice.
So, to conclude, that is my opinion. I'm certain a bit of the sour aftertaste came from my high expectations and the good trailer, but surely not all of it. I am just really disappointed. I *wanted* to like this game so much, but I just can't. The fights feel stale, the ambience doesn't really get me at all, Communication an interaction is really unappealing and inconsistent.
Overall this game had a ton of good ideas, even in a genre that is as oversaturated as zombie shooters, but it kinda failed to deliver. As I said, I really wanted to like it, and I don't want to trash-talk it in any way, but I really can't see much to praise except for the absolutely stellar soundtrack.
You have to decide for yourself if you want to buy it. I'm sure some people could really enjoy it. But i can't and maybe I can make you reconsider your choice.

A neat game, but definitely not what I was expecting. I heard about The Final Station on Giant Bomb, and expected to play a roguelike-y post-apoc Oregon Trail with trains. What I got was a neat adventure title with so-so combat.
The game's loop is made up of two parts: Exploration and travel. Exploration involves pressing E on every interactable object and killing gross guys. You can also find survivor-types during the exploration phase, who disappear after you press E on them they'll reappear in your train during the travel phase.
I picked the game up after taking one look at the game's travel phase for two reasons: Trains are cool and I like getting stressed out about resource management. Sadly, what I got was a lot more fiddly than stressful. Most of the "repairs" you end up handling on the train amount to no-effort minigames, and saving survivors doesn't feel all that great either. You have to feed and medicate them until you hit a safe (metropolitan) station. They reward you with cash, weapon upgrades, or a nice conversation after disembarking.
The Final Station's english translation is really bad. The game's narrative is a bit enigmatic, and it's a lot tougher to parse when the sparse dialogue doesn't make all that much sense.
Despite all these complaints, though, I had fun playing The Final Station. It's a neat concept, if a bit more half-baked than I'd like. If you like narrative games, trains, and searching with the E key, then you'll probably enjoy.

This review is based on 34 minutes of tutoral viewing and interacting with, and my impression of the game is based on this time and the fact my son has been playing the game for about a week now and loves it, though he finds it difficult and a challenge, which are reasons for him to like it! Graphics 9.5 - based on the fact they are WAY better than I could do and if I were programming the game, creating the graphics and designing it as I went, those graphics would be at the level of Zork-none! Gameplay 9 - Appears to be a better mix for children whose parents worry about violent content, although this title kills peple off in droves at times - it's Maw Nature doing the killin' and that makes it all right in anyone's book! Keeping up with the demands of hungry, homeless, freezing citizens of your village will prove to be a constant war, and there will be deaths aplenty, as in any war for survival. Realism 8 - Not higher because, let's face it, without the bloodshed of other city builders and civilization startup games, those little people dashing about will get bored and eat even more of the scarce food supply, making their lives and your life, a bit more frenetic. However, I love the fact there is no fighting in the game. I play other games for the satisfaction of tracking, hunting, shooting, and generally being a NRA, flag-waving, machine-gun toting destroyer of all who give the finger to my beloved country. But, once in a while, I would like to see a peaceful creation of a nation, and Banished provides that opportunity to me. Stats? Yeah, there are a few, (thank God!), but not too many in my opinion. Gameplay is balanced, there are births but Maw Nature is a hard task master and she is above all else - unforgiving. Put a hunting lodge in town and you'll be watching a townful of "starvin' Marvins". Same for shelter. Just like in real life if we don't eat - we die. No war means I can concentrate on how best to serve my minions rather than worrying about being attacked. Instead of building armies that consume resources, (listening to this DOD?), I can put the people to work building houses, schools, hospitals, and all the other things necessary to a strong infrastructure and more resilient society. Overall "feel" of the game 10 - Look, one person plays civilization games and finds them frustrating for many reasons. In their mind is the image of a game that pits a few human beings, outcast by society and left to die on a small island with enough resources to allow growth, if the outcasts are especially careful of every single facet of their existence and are cooperative in all things, that is. I like this game, I plan on playing a lot over the next couple of weeks and I'll write a better, more detailed review of it after that.
