[UPDATED REVIEW]
6.2/10
So its been roughly 7 months since the game has released, and to be honest, the game is dying. Ubisoft has been changing things within the game and making balance tweaks, but there are some overlying problems that prevent this game from reaching its full potential, outside of what I mentioned in my first review below.
One of the main problems is the lacking of the "team" or "crew" based racing. Each time you explore the map and get 7-8 other players in your session, there is no incentive to actually race or interact with them. The fact that you can only get 7-8 players in your session is another downside, although technology is probably to blame for that
The car roster is still fairly weak, even after the four DLC packs as part of the season pass and the newest cars added. There are still only a few Japanese cars in the game, and now the count is at 4 different Corvetes (Which I don't mind, but not many people are huge Corvette fans).
Once you've upgraded your cars to the maximum level, there is basically no end-game other than PvP, which is also boring as almost everyone competitive uses the same cars.
This game had so much potential, but it fell flat. As much as i hate to say it, I can't reccomend this game anymore.
--------------------------OLD REVIEW------------------------
8/10.
No Lotus cars and too many Mustangs
But seriously, this game is getting a lot of flak for little reason in my opinion. Yes it is not a groundbreaking achievement of gamer kind, and Yes, Ubisoft has a crap reputation for its 2014 games, but The Crew is pretty awesome (at least in my eyes, Racing games and MMOs are my thing).
Pros:
HUGE map. Seriously, it takes ~40 minutes to drive coast to coast in the highest performance cars (assuming you don't crash at all which is near impossible)
Each car feels different. They mentioned this in one of the trailers, but driving the different cars (even the starter cars) feels fairly different from others on the roster. From the zippy and nimble Abarth 500 and Mini cooper to the powerhouse Corvette and Viper to the juggernaut-like strength of the Hunner H1 Alpha and the Jeep Grand Cherokee.
No mandatroy drift events. Not everyone likes drifting (i don't), and aside from the challenges, it doesn't force you to drift at any point during the story or in the challenges.
Cons:
The Story is bland. Gang member kills your brother who was the leader of the gang, you get framed for it. You then team up with cops and slowly work your way up until you beat that gang member and take over the gang. Sure there is more along the way, but the story is more of an afterthought.
Microtransactions. While the most expensive cars aren't the best (The Laferrari, The Hummer and the  Agera), the cars are priced it a way that makes it difficult to earn more cars just by playing the story. You either have to play PVP, do faction missions (both are unlocked at level 10), or grind skills endlessly to earn money, or buy cars/unlocked upgrades with real world money.
PvP. Speaking of the PvP, it is difficult for new players to get into it and stand a chance. When the game was first released, it was possible to enter events with low ranked cars and still stand a chance, but now that its a month and a half after release, a lot of PvP players have max performance cars that will completely stomp any new PvP racers.
Overall I still reccomend this to racing game fans. If you were looking for a true MMO though, you may find yourself fairly dissapointed.

I'll start this off with a brief summary of everything I'm about to say. This game is fun, but not worth the full price. The controls and gameplay is alright. The visuals good as far as pixel art goes. The music is quite nice at times. The level design isn't great. The plot is vague and confusing. The ending is borderline terrible. Maybe wait for a sale of <50%.
Now for more detail.
Gameplay: The Final Station can be very good fun at times. Those times would be the chase segments, in which the game suddenly becomes a fast-paced storm of "zombies" and bullets. Most of the time though, you're carefully preparing for the worst as you open up each room in your current location. At the best times, this is suspenseful and actually quite enjoyable. At the worst times, it's boring.
"Open door. Nothing. Open door. Nothing. Climb ladder. Nothing. Open door. Kill monster. Loot locker. Repeat."
And that is to say nothing of those irritating segments where you repeatedly climb a ladder, land a few hits, and retreat until you've killed all the monsters.
I guess I should mention the train segments. Coming into this game, I assumed the train would play a large part, and I suppose it does. The train gets you to each new level and ultimately your goal in each level is to find the code that will allow your train to pass to the next one. Regardless of all that, the time the game has you spend on the train feels largely pointless. In the train rides between each level, you'll usually have to maintain parts of the train that are failing, as well as bring food and medicine to your constantly ailing passengers. After a few levels you'll reach a safe station where the passengers will get off, paying you money and items for your help. Money can be spent at a few stations to gain food, medkits, ammo, and gun upgrades. This seemed pretty simple to me, until I realized that most of what you get from them is largely useless. Medkits and ammo can be crafted using the plentiful materials found in each level and food is only for feeding passengers. Some of the gun upgrades are somewhat useful, but you can probably get those just with the money found in the levels. What I'm saying is that you'd probably be better off just letting everyone on the train die, looting their bodies, and doing more important things with your time and resources.
With all that said, some of the game's best visuals can only be seen during train-rides, so there's something to them. Speaking of which...
Visuals: It's pixel art, which means I'm already liking it. Actually though, the visual quality of this game varies quite a bit. Sometimes it's lovely (much of the train-ride scenery, a city built around a giant [REDACTED]) , but there are a few areas that are well done but seem poorly designed. (an oddly shaded mountain, an office in a tower, that damned tunnel segment). Still, pixel art is pixel art. You can't go too far wrong.
Music: I'll be honest, I had the sound off for most of this one. When I was playing with sound though, it was actually very good. I guess I really can't say too much here.
Story: This is likely the worst part. It's difficult to write about this because of spoilers. But it's really no spoiler to say that the whole thing is SO. DAMNED. VAGUE. If you're partway through the game and thinking "Oh, that'll be explained by the end!" you're wrong. Unless it's the Guardian. You actually do get a bit of info on that. If you enjoy being in the dark about basically everything in the game's world, this might be for you. Also, the ending is awful. When I was most of the way through the game, I was talking to a friend who had already finished it. I told him where I was and he said I had about an hour left to go. My first thought was "Wow, they're really going to start moving quickly to finish this thing up!" but that's not what happened. I just kept going through standard levels, getting increasingly concerned about how the game was going to end. When the ending finally came, I didn't even realize it was the end until about halfway through. By that time, I was already irritated. I begrudgingly played through what was essentially a long walking simulator while the game tried its best to end dramatically. It failed. Maybe if I had known anything about what was going on, I would've felt something other than disappointment.
I'm tempted to write a paragraph about that tunnel segment, but I think I'll pass.

An excellent, immersive, emotionally satisfying game.
Take note, though: Homefront The Revolultion is not 'like' a Far Cry game - it IS a Far Cry game.
Really, the mechanics are exactly the same, from stealth to combat to weapon procurement.
And even though this is so, there's nothing wrong with that, particularly if you're a Far Cry fan.
Voice acting by the man characters is excellent, and the game storyline -though taken from all the classic dystopian movies- is paced very well.
Characters that pehaps when you first meet them are irritating -Dana, for me- become like family while you're in this game world.
The music, though limited, is fantastic, evocotive of the original Terminator, and really puts you in the setting.
Gameplay is excellent, though achieving all the side goals can be a bit of a grind.  When you liberate an area and have freedom fighters running about things can get chaotic as they battle in the streets against your occupiers.
Enemy blimps trawl the skies above, seeking out rebles, and if you get caught in their view all hell breaks loose as they call KPA troops down on you.
Very glad I got the game and pass during the Christmas sale, was well worth it, particularly if your a fan of dystopian or post apocalyptic worlds.
The only issue I had was that frame rates dropped if battles were too huge and a lot of bodies began piling up.  The only work around for this is taking a break from the game and coming back to it - wich is actually a good thing since it's engaging enough to play hours at a stretch.

is an open world FPS, similar to the likes of Far Cry but it sure feels like a far cry away from a successful game and franchise.
I've played this in 2017, long after its shaky release and optimization wise the game runs quite smooth actually. Not hickups, no stuttering, it's runs pretty well compared to the mess it was at launch. But let's set aside the technical aspects of the game and lets focus on the things that really matter; the game itself.
Let's start on a positive note and say that this game is a vast improvement over its predecessor. In every single way. The gunplay is entertaining and is actually one of the few saving graces of the game. You can customize your weapons on the spot, each weapon having 3 different types of transformation and that sure allows for variety in you want to take out the enemy. It's sort of reminiscent of Crysis and I guess it's not really a coincidence because this game is based on CRYENGINE, which while it might still look pretty you cannot help the fact that the models seem a little bit dated at times. Visually the game is pretty nice looking. The ruined city of Philadelphia looks fitting for the revolution theme that the game tries to create. The gameplay alternates between the
and the
The red zones are all out combat, you liberating various points on the map for the Resistance, either by killing everyone or hacking something... and that's about it. There are a couple of variations and mini-puzzles (?) [not really as in you have to find a different way to access part of the objective) but basically it all boils down to doing the same thing over and over again. It gets repetitive really fast and mostly it feels like a chore or a means to get influence over the area rather than actually going and liberating a part of your city. After freeing an outpost/stronghold, that place becomes part of the resistance, allowing you to quickly change your loadout, sell/buy stuff and upgrade your equipment. You can also recruit resistance AI teammates but doing so will probably annoy you more than anything but we will get to the AI later.
Yellow zones are the still standing parts of the city in which the KPA are patrolling the streets. The game switches to a more stealth oriented playstyle i.e avoiding patrols, quietly killing guards, helping people in need. Essential you have the
meter which you need to fill to 100% by sabotaging KPA posts, capturing stronghold, freeing civilians, assassinating KPA officials. The game actually show hints of brilliance in the yellow zones and the transition from red to yellow is certainly one of the better aspects of the game.
Which bring me to the failing point of the game. The AI is dumb. Like ridiculously dumb. I can understand that trying to balance between stealth'em up and FPS might be hard, but the AI really drains away the immersion the game is so desperately trying to push. You kill a guard from a distance in silence and the rest will just act all jittery for a little and then proceed like nothing has happened. It's feels stupid, it looks stupid and it plays stupid. The moment you make some noise or miss a silenced shot, you're
discovered and unless you find a safe spot, endless waves of enemies will come after you. They will even enter your 'liberated' outposts and start shooting resistance members like a 18th century soldier. Standing directly facing the enemy and shooting till something dies. I've seen better AI in games from the 90s and the comical situations I've encountered in Homefront: The Revolution are plentiful and that's not always funny. Your AI teammates will block you, they will follow you like puppies having no sense of self preservation or intelligence and they behave more like toddlers rather than revolutionaries.
The story is cheesy but not the 'over-the-top-so-bad-is-good' cheesy. It tries to take itself seriously and the whole premise is ridiculous from the get go anyway. North Korea has control over the US and they're essentially tormenting the entire population. Nonetheless, there's some good dialogue in the game and some interesting themes that play out and I should give credit to that. Mostly the whole revolution/violence is not the magic bullet that will bring the country back together. There are collaborators, there are parts of the population who abhor violence even after the banner of freedom, there are people who think of all the innocents who get caught in the crossfire. It's actually kind refreshing to see that theme being explored a little more rather that just having a supersoldier killing everyone for America.
Finally, the longevity of the game is less than I expected and the ending is very abrupt and rushed beyond all belief. The DLCs are about 90 minutes each while playing casually and the main character actually suffers from Gordon Freeman disease, that is to say he's mute. It's really baffling why they did this in a game which features plenty of dialogue between members of your own faction. He actually does get voiced in the
DLC but it's too little, too late.

Receiver is an experimental, FPS roguelike, with the goal of collecting all the tapes in the level while managing weapons that handle some-what realistically. Instead of Pressing R to reload, you have a myriad of buttons to eject magazines, empty the chamber, refill bullets, turn on/off safety. It's all reminscent of games like QWOP and Ampu-Tea where it is difficult to play, though the game is not necessarily trying to torture you, even though the game is awfully difficult. I do hate these controls though - I don't have a big problem with the revolver, but I never found out how to insert bullets into a clip of a pistol despite pressing nearly every key on my keyboard, so I would always run out of ammo unless I found a clip, even if I had bullets on my person. Whenever you die or reset the game, the level is regenerated, placing the rooms in a different order and connection, so the rooms are still familiar, but will be encountered differently.
I can definitely see a rewarding factor here, as death comes from one hit and it feels good to aim down the sights and put down a bot that could easily kill you - It's reminescent of the first time using ADS in the early Call of Duty games that became the standard for most shooters. As much as I respect this game, I absolutely do not like playing it. I like my games to be "gamey" and I want to enjoy the gameplay of managing the gun like a real gun, but I'm sick of fumbling around with the controls trying unsuccesfully to reload a Glock or 1911, failing to flee with the "repeatedly tap W to run" mechanic, and wasting ammo because a turret wouldn't die after shooting five bullets into it. I do respect that shooting a bot in its different parts will have different effects (hitting the camera remove it's vision, shooting it's ammo box removes its ammo, Shooting the battery disables it). But I know I won't be entertained by fumbling with the controls, dealing with the extreme difficulty to just listen to some tapes that will probably end up all sounding overly pretentious.
That said, there community that loves this game, kind of like those who love the Dark Souls series. I don't mind the difficulty and like the fact that death is one hit, requring you to be extra careful. I can do without the paltry fall damage. I don't have any interest in wrestling controls and trying to remember 8 different buttons just to manage a gun. I'm interested in seeing some shooters try having to handle your gun much like Reciever, but without awkwardness of needing to use so many buttons and gun parts and invetory floating around your face. Watch videos of other players and see if you think you can handle what is offered - be ready to accidentally lose bullets and magazines because you're chambering and pressing the wrong button to insert a magazine or bullet. The game seems worth it's price and if you can get all the tapes, then you will have seen nearly all this game has to offer.

Receiver is a very interesting little experiment that bases its gameplay around the mechanic that you have to manually reload your weapon like a puzzle, essentially a on the fly FPS puzzel game.

I bought Homefront: The Revolution on a steam sale even after reading a bunch of mixed reviews.  Unfortunately, mixed is probably the best way to describe it.  Homefront gameplay and design is essentially a combination of more successful games but lacks the fluidity, narrative, and variation to sell it.  It does some things well: the cover system mostly works, guns look and sound unique, and the environment is initially interesting.  Unfortunately, that's about all the good that I can list.  Within a few hours, the missions are all virtually identical, the storyline is short and uninteresting, and the characters are forgettable.  I found myself listening to podcasts while I essentially ground out each area.  It wasn't particularly difficult; just very vanilla gameplay.
If I had to name the number one sin of the game, it's the lack of any variation.  If you play an hour of the game, you'll know exactly what the rest of the game is going to be like.  At no point do you have any real sense of urgency or connectedness to the people.  It's just... boring.

Lets tackle this right out the gate... The radical feminist "Fight the patriarchy" stuff is nowhere as bad as some dummies would have you believe. Its a minuscule little magazine that is quickly forgotten about and is not part of the games overall message in anyway. Now onto the game,
This is an explorative story game about young love as a homosexual, and if that is to "SJW" for you just f*ck off and play a different game. Although honestly I'd suggest most people to play another game anyway because this is a very very short game.
Gone Home doesn't really dive into much more than the young love story, but it tries to dip its toes in other bigger topics... That is where it fails for me not properly handling the big topics, and glancing over them like there no big deal. I will say I did have a lot of fun exploring the house and the atmosphere was superb. There were times I genuinely felt like I was in a dark stormy house all alone. For me the story didn't grab me like I felt it should it just came off pretty bland, but the potential for a story is all around. It could of been a lot more if it truly dived in and tackled the big topics instead of using them as a light seasoning. Overall I didn't get why this game is the punching bag people have made it into its not really worth that level of hate. This isn't anywhere near the level of atrocious as something like Dear Esther. Its just a short explorative story driven game... with a sub-par story.

Initially, I didn't want to recomend this game. The gameplay is essentially a two hour arcade minigame from an old Sierra adventure game, and is incredibly frustrating. The motifs are relatively tries and repetitive. And it has the problem that alot of brawlers have, of a 2d character on a 3d plane. But, something rather interesting happened when I finished the game last night. This morning as I type out my review, I am incredibly tired, for all last night, my dreams were all night terrors. Everytime I blink, I see the world in cross hatch. And this kind of immersion I hacen't expererienced since I first played and saw Pyramid Head staring at me from behind red bars. And that was when I was seven. There is actually a bit towards the end of  the game that is an obvious rip off of Silent Hill 2. This game is described as an experience of a life with ocd, but feel this description could apply to any mental disease. Actually, I think the best way to describe it, is as a nightmare Eric Chahi might have after watching a box set of Vincent Price films. In the end I'd recomend this game to three types of people; anyone who'd like to understand what it is to be mentally, anyone who never got the chance to play PT before it was removed from the PSN, or anyone whose a fan of excellent atmosphere. It's a little bit Edgar Allen Poe, and a little bit of Clocktower, and a little bit of B-Movie gore, and a lot lot lot (that's three lots) of Silent Hill. Without meaning to spoil anything, the ending is frustrating, and doesn't offer any closure, but it isn't a deal breaker. Oh, and don't tell me it's open to interpretation. Blade Runner is open to interpretation because I know what I'm supposed to be interpreting.

Review for: Banished
Date: 3/8/2014
My Pros:
Graphics are nice, weather had realistic sound effects, visually appealing.
My Cons: I read that this was a simulator game, i was under the impression simulator means to show someone how to do something or hands on, ect. That is not the case here, you are given zero instruction, and you can't even control the people.
They do all the work, all you get to do is click the icons that you want to build, and you watch them build it. Thats it.
I was disappointed in reading how this was a building strategy game (one of the tags it has) yet there is no strategy involved, you can click an icon and the place you want it, thats the strategy.
Sure people die of starvation, but logic is to have food production.
That is not simulation, there is no 'hands on' type work that teach you how to survive or build. If i knew this beforehand, i wouldn't of bought it because i feel there is a false description wether it be by the tags on the game, or the description itself about the game, i don't feel it was accurate.

I'm not into driving games, infact I haven't really played a driving game since Need For Speed Most Wanted on the PS2. I decided to grab the gold edition of this game because I had some extra steam credit, and god it was worth it. The driving feels really nice, and there are a couple cool types of races. There are regular street races, off road races, and raid races where you try to destroy/damage the opponent's vehicle by ramming into them. The MMO aspects of the game are awesome, It's cool seeing 10 to 15 (you can only usually see around 10 people in one city, and driving around you'll come across different players) driving in the same area as you. The map is also massive. I drove from Michigan to Tennessee to Georgia to Florida, seeing cities like Detroit, Nashville, Atlanta, Miami, and other various small towns you can encounter in the countryside. You can literally go across the entire US. (It took me 10 minutes to go from Detroit to Nashville, so I'm assuming it'd be about an hour or so to drive from east coast to west coat and vice versa.) The Crew aspect which makes the game unique is also very fun. You can team up with random players or your friends and race or do missions. Overall, It's extremely fun, and It really suprised me since I'm not a big racing/driving game fan.
TL;DR buy this game, you won't be dissapointed.

A simple game, a simple objective, yet so much fun and intensity obtained by a 2D side-scroller. Released only yesterday on the 30th of August, it already obtained nearly 200 reviews which rate it "Very Positive" on the Steam Store page.
At first glance The Final Station appears to be a more fast pace zombie killing side-scroller. However, right from the beginning you can tell this game is truly a more survival and story driven game. So, do not jump into this game hoping to get your fill of zombie killing action. Instead expect a very well crafted story, and solid gameplay mechanics.
The objective of the game is to go from train station to train station in your trusty old locomotive gathering supplies such as health packs, food and ammunition, as well as survivors of the rapid zombie apocalypse.
The dialogues between your passengers and people you see in the city are quite interesting. If interested, you could also find notes in various houses in the city which tell a little about the people who live/work there and give you an opportunity to speculate what may have happened to them. For example: I have found a laptop with a conversation open talking about a work colleague who spends a lot of time in the bathroom, once I entered the bathroom and opened all the stalls, one zombie actually popped out and surprised me.
Overall this is a game definitely worth getting, but I advise you to wait for a sale as it is quite expensive ($14.99)

I hate to compare two different games when I'm doing reviews like this. I really, really do. But I'm going to open this review by doing just that.
Verdun is the game that Battlefield 1
it could be.
Verdun absolutely nails the feel of the first World War. There are various game modes, but the main one (and evidently the most popular, judging from the number of players I see whenever I go to join a game) is Frontlines. In Frontlines, two teams, the Entente Powers and the Central Powers (read: France, the UK/Canada, Belgium and the U.S against Germany, repsectively) battle over control of various trenchlines, with one team attacking and the other defending. For every trench a team takes, they score a point. If the attacking team's push fails, then it's their turn to defend. It's like an incredibly-lethal game of football, and in many games I've played in, the end result is a draw, with everyone ending where they started. This reflects the back-and-forth nature of the Great War incredibly well, as countless men would die for almost no gains in territory: the Battle of the Somme, the bloodiest battle in the first World War, left over a million men dead. The end result: the British and French took only six miles (or about 10 kilometers) of ground.
Which brings me to my next point in Verdun's favor: the lethality. You will die in this game. There's no getting around it. You'll be shot in the face from across No Man's Land, cut down by machinegun fire as you try to cross No Man's Land, cut down by barbed wire while trying to cross No Man's Land, blown up by artillery as you're leaving your trench to cross No Man's Land, gassed to death, shot, stabbed, blown up, and clubbed. A few shots from most handguns will drop anyone; a single shot from a rifle will kill you.
There's not much I can say about the graphics other than that they're beautiful. I can't, at present, run Verdun at anything other than the lowest settings, and it still looks gorgeous. It's a bit of a resource hog, sure, but it's worth it. The sound design is also top-notch. The firearms sound like they should, the artillery is appropriately-terrifying, and when you slip on your gas mask all you can hear is the muffled sounds of gunfire and the ragged hissing of your own breath through the filter. And with the Horrors of War update, the game got a whole lot gorier; shotguns and explosives will tear limbs off, and sometimes when you die you won't actually die for several seconds but will instead squirm on the ground gasping for one last breath, then one more, then another until you finally can't.
The weapons are period-appropirate, consisting primarily of bolt-action rifles. There's no prototype personal automatic weapons here; closest you'll get are the German MP18 and the American BAR. There are, of course, also a handful of other automatic weapons, but most of them are machineguns, and must be braced to fire (well, some anyway. The Lewis and other CAN be hip-fired, but the only machinegun that can be aimed without bracing is the BAR).
There's a good variety of squad types to use, each with their own tactics, loadouts, and specializations. The Canadians, for example, specialize in trench raiding; they have comparatively few long-range options, but they're absolute monsters within the confines of a trench, if the Canadians know what they're doing. German Alpenjäger squads are marksmen and infiltrators, creeping close to enemy lines and eliminating enemy snipers and machinegunners while calling in recon planes to mark enemy positions. German Pioniere suqads are combat engineers, sweeping enemy trenches clean with smokescreens, white phosphorous artillery, grenades, and the ever-deadly
American Doughboys are your standard line infantry, but with the BAR's ability to lay down accurate heavy fire while on the move, they can easily cut a path through No Man's Land. And this is just a small sample of what available; this doesn't even cover Landser squads, Stosstruppen, British Tommies, the Belgians, or any of the 4 other squad types I haven't named.
Not everything is great, though. As I mentioned previously, the game is a serious resource hog; if you don't have at least a decent rig with a good graphics card, you might not be able to play Verdun. I also have some issues staying connected to servers between matches, but this is likely an issue on my end. Other than these issues, though, I have no real problems with Verdun. I would like to see a bit more variety in maps and squads, though. While I'm aware that Verdun focuses on the Western Front, I'd very much like to have the opportunity to play as the Austro-Hungarians, or the Italians, the Russians, or even the Ottomans. But these are less "things that are wrong" and more "things I'd like to see."
To summarize, Verdun is
best World War I FPS on the market today. And while that's not a very large niche, Verdun outdoes every other game that has even attempted it,
Battlefield 1. Verdun's slow-paced tactical gameplay, harrowing and unforgiving combat, and the respectful, thoughtful approach that it takes in portraying the Great War shows that M2H and Blackmill Games understand World War I
better than any triple-A studio does. DICE could, and should, learn some lessons from Verdun.

Dark Souls II. Dark Souls, II. What a game, what a masterpiece. Does this entry in the Souls' serie deserves the name that it currently has? Yes, YES it does. A lot of people hate(d) the game, because of its hitboxes, because of the fact that the game was not immersive as the first one because the areas made the game feel more of a dungeon crawler because the connection between them was just that thanks to the bonfire(s).
Still, this game manages to do it. Mechanically speaking, the game improved a lot from its predecessor and for some parts it's even superior than it's sequel, boss fights are memorable, even though the bosses themselves are quite frankly humanoids apart from a few of them. The base game is amazing, but the DLCs?
The DLCs are on a new level. The DLCs are where the game TRULY shines for its beauty: boss fights like Fume Knight's one, Sinh's, these are the best bossfights a game - in my opinion - or better, the developers, managed to deliver.
Is the game the best in the serie? Probably yes, thanks to this version (EDIT: I don't mean lore-wise, I'm talking about gameplay mechanics, and other stuff like PvE and PvP, the latter it's amongst fan's favourites in Dark Souls II: SotFS). The base game had a lot of problems, technically speaking but SotFS' version manages to get them fixed.
Hitboxes? Yeah, they're kinda ♥♥♥♥ed up. NOT THAT MUCH, not, that, much. They're not worse than DS1 or DS3, in fact all of them from a technical viewpoint are ♥♥♥♥ed up. But this series is amazing, nonetheless. Even if this game, Dark Souls II, has its flaws, the game shines no matter what.

This is a brilliant game, I have to say. It only has three guns, and it only has two types of enemies, and it isn't full random generation (Like games such as Starbound), more on that later. However, the game is so much fine. If you think you can come into this and hit R to reload and see your ammo in the bottomright corner, then NO. This game is much more than that. You have to move every individual piece of the gun by either holding or tapping a button, and if you get ONE thing wrong, by the time you go around a corner and attempt to fire the gun and you realise a drone is flying towards you with its taser on the ready, you're basically dead unless you're me.
The game features permanent death. If you die, that's it, all of it is erased, but if you get hit by something ONCE, and that includes your own rebounded bullets (Or bullets you accidentally shot yourself in the foot with), you die. The game generates the world via procedural generation. It basically takes a load of giant buildings, adds some custom things to that giant building (Bullets, enemies, etc.) and then connects it to another giant building. All of the giant buildings have three floors. The game then spawns you in with a random weapon, a random amount of magazines, a random amount of loose ammunition, a random amount of ammunition in magazines, and a random state of your weapon, also it decides whether or not you will spawn with a flashlight and decides whether or not there is an enemy looking at you just as you spawn in to challenge you. You then tuck into a corner and get your weapon all ready. If you find yourself ejecting live rounds out of the side of the gun and then pulling the magazine out of the gun and dropping it off a building or similar, you should press the ? key to bring up a context-sensitive help menu. What this means is that it will show all the things you can do, however things recommended to get your weapon into recommended operation (As in, full auto off, ready to fire, safety off etc.) will be coloured white, and things not recommended will be a dull grey.
The enemies in the game consist of only two types. There are actually four types, however two of them were cut for time restriction reasons (Or I assume), as this game was made in a 7 day FPS challenge. The two enemies in the game are the immobile machinegun turrets, which will now be called turrets, which spin around slowly with a blue light on them, and when they see you, the blue light turns yellow, it makes a beeping sound, it tracks you, and very shortly after the light turns red (to indicate "THREAT DETECTED") and then it opens fire. You have to either sneak past it or kill it if you want to advance in that direction most of the time, and the way you kill it is not just "fire until it has no more HP", you actually have to aim and shoot at something and if you shoot, for example, the camera, it will not be able to track you, or shoot at the magazine and it will not be able to chamber any more rounds, but that still means it can still fire one bullet, and I've heard that it tends to trick you, as in hold fire for a few moments to indicate you probably shot out the firing control, and then fire that one bullet straight into you, though no confirmation. There is a small chance for you to be able to hit a nonvital area on an enemy and shut it down, however most of the time absolutely NOTHING will occur when you do this.
There is also these shock drones, which most of the community tends to call them taser bots, or just drones (However don't get into that habit - there is another type of drone that isn't in the game but may be in the game sometime in the future), however I will just be calling them shock drones from now on. They fly around, they find you, they then have the same lights on them as the turret, but then they engage, they rush at you, they try to taser you. These are flying death if you don't deal with them shortly after they spot you, they will even hide above or to the side of doorways and wait for you to come out so it has a tactical advantage, they are VERY intelligent but they have no fear of you, keep that in mind.
The two unreleased types of enemies are: The mobile turret, which is basically a turret on wheels, it looks like it'd go quite slowly and would obviously have the inability to go up stairs, but it'd be terrifying. The other type is a drone with (what I assume is) a gun on it, which would be one of the most deadly enemies to ever exist if I think I know how they'd work, however they probably wouldn't fire nearly as fast as an immobile turret (Nor would the mobile turret) or be as accurate, the turrets are deadly accurate and will one shot kill you if you aren't moving, and even if you are moving and not running they still have a high chance of shooting you in one shot.
I've told you alot of the game mechanics, you should get a basic idea of it, however I haven't told you about the story or the objective.
The objective of the game relates to the story, therefor I have to give you a basic understanding of the story for you to fully understand the objective. I will try not to go into detail at all, the story will probably be much more advanced than I describe. Here we go:
Alot of this is not implemented such as the cleartape things or the repeatedly listening to tapes, but it will give you an idea of the storyline. You have to collect the 11 tapes before being killed.
The game has mod support, and it has a quite popular mod which adds a firing range aswell as a few new weapons. There is something you should do with this mod to get you started, it's an exercise I created: Basically, you go to the firing range, activate the weapon selection, and then choose the first weapon in the list, and then hold L to reset your game. You then need to put the weapon into full operation order without making a single wrong action, this does not include pressing a button that does nothing, however it includes things like dropping the magazine. You have to repeatedly do this correctly and discharge the weapon a few times without making a single true mistake and as fast as possible, you have to set the amount of times you want to do a weapon, I recommend 3 to start out with, however after a while move it up to 6. If you perform one error, you need to hold L, reset your score, and then try again.
Once you get to the limit, you then select the next weapon in the list- I'm out of space.

I have a few mixed feelings about SotFS that I would like to address. First off, SotFS does not run on the same multiplayer servers as vanilla Dark Souls II. If you want to view this from a technical standpoint and assume that FromSoftware didn't have the ability to merge both servers into one, then fair enough, but this splits the Dark Souls II community into two regardless of the fact. Secondly, SotFS drastically changes a lot of the enemy placements in the game. This can be a huge improvement to some people, but for me, it's certainly a double-edged sword. Some of the more annoying areas that are present in the vanilla version of Dark Souls II were tweaked to make them less of a nuisance, that being the decreased amount of certain mobs or simply the replacement of another mob present in the game, but there are also some areas that were unecessarily altered to make them even more aggravating than they should be ( Few examples: The giant dragon before the bridge to the Old Dragon Slayer and the increase of Desert Sorceresses in Harvest Valley ). That said, you can be the judge on whether or not these new enemy placements affect you negatively, but take it into consideration if you're a vanilla Dark Souls II player. If there's one thing I really like about these changes, it's that It makes the game feel refreshing. If you have general knowledge about the enemy placements in the vanilla version, chances are you might be surprised a few times throughout your playthrough.
The visuals, most noteably the lighting, have been improved to give the game a better atmosphere. The darker areas of the game are... actually dark! This makes the torch item quite useful for once. The improvement isn't necessarily drastic, but it's certainly noticeable.
Overall, I had an enjoyable experience. Do I prefer SotFS over the vanilla version? Yes. I think SotFS is the definitive version of Dark Souls II and is a must-have if you haven't played the vanilla game before. Despite my seemingly negative perspective on some of the enemy placements, I do feel like it keeps the game fresh and significantly more challenging.

Homefront The Revolution (HFR) is a First-person military styled shooter set in the future area (2029) the US has been invaded by North Korea.  HFR is the sequel to Homefront (2011).  The game continues along the same plot but the story is new and takes place on the east coast in Philadelphia 2029, just two years after the rebellion movement on the west coast (Bay Area) in Homefront.
The game project was started and sold multiple times before finally ending up in Dambuster Studios/ Deep Silver.  As a result this is a project with many developers hands in the mix so it shouldn't be too big os a shock it wasn't exactly what many had hoped for.  For starters, the best part of Homefront (2011) was the multiplayer, which was very similar to CoD, only to be ignored and left out of the sequel.  Instead a Co-op mode was provided in its place. This did not set well with the community which caused a backlash of predicted negative reviews before anyone even had a chance to play the game.
The game is open world but you have to follow a progression to go to each new section.  In each section you will follow the main story as well as have the oportunity to complete side missions.  While these can be fun and even challenging at times, they feel repetitive.  The plot is interesting but the delivery is lack luster.
The gameplay is the standard FPS feel.  The controls and UI are adaquate but do not invent the wheel, just more of the same things sound in other FPS shooters like the Fallout and Farcry series with weapon/item selections and crafting.  The coolest thing in the game is the weapon mods that allow you to turn you weapons into just about anyhting bt switching upper receivers and other items allowing you to carry an arsenal without carrying 20 weapons.  The gameplay is smooth but there is a collision problem when taking cover up against walls where you can see thru them.
I wish the collision problem was the only bug but it is not.  The game's release was bug infested to the point I gave up trying to play it and waited months before trying again. Most of the game breaking issues like the fps drops and crashes seem to be resolved, but the collision issue is ever present. There are also issues where you can jump thru a window but not back in which makes no sense. Co-op is difficult to find matches for and inviting friends isn't as easy as it should be.
The AI can be deadly with aimbot skills killing you with only a single shot to the head. However, the AI also feels broken in that at times you can kill someone stealthly and move along with your mission. At other times, you take someone out stealthly with a silenced weapon only to be rushed by multiple enemies, overrun, and killed. The AI will also see you in a building if you stand to close to a wall and begin shooting at you or alert other AI to your presence. This is usually resolved be stepping away from the wall, but not always.
The game is built on CryEngine which is used in games like Far Cry, Crysis, Sniper Ghost Warrior 2, Kingdom Come Deliverance, and Roberts Space Industries Star Citizen. Needless to say the engine is capable of breath taking visuals.  While the game looks good and is immersive, it was poorly optimized and felt as though it did not have the graphical fidelity other other titles on the same engine.
As stated earlier, the team deathmatch/domination style multiplayer modes were removed and replaced with a multiplayer co-op version of the game.  While the co-op game mode is fun, it lacks the replay appeal of a true multiplayer game mode provides. People have complained of connectivity issues with multiplayer as well as isssues of teaming with friends.
The game has been patched and runs well enough to enjoy now although the gameplay does feels repetitive.  If you're ok with completing similar missions throughout the game, like you would in a Far Cry game, pick it up. The game isn't bad and I have had fun with it, but it does fails to deliver that I cannot stop playing feeling I have experienced in other games. I do believe it is worth playing especially if it is on sale so I am going to give it a Yes on my Recommendation.

After about 50 hours of "Banished!" I highly recommend this game to fans of the city-building genre.  At first the game seems very simple but you quickly find it has a ton of depth to it and can be quite challenging.  "Banished!" doesn't have combat but you'll find yourself constantly battling hunger, cold, and resource management to the point where you'll be glad there aren't any invaders knocking on your door.  You will have to make some tough decisions early in each village- "Do I spend my vital resources on food production?  but I don't have enough workers to man those buildings... so do I build houses in hopes of increasing my population?  but then I won't have enough food and my people will starve..." These predicaments are endless which makes it extremely satisfying when you get your population to a meager 50-75 citizens or more.  The only downside is I feel like once you get a village to a certain point it is way too easy, however, the game will be mod-able soon and that should bring tons of new options to add onto this already fun game.  At a price of $20 this is a no-brainer.  Not to mention the fact that this game was created by a SINGLE PERSON, it's nice to know that the money is helping support a very talented indie game creator.

I went into this game hearing that it's the oddball of the Soulsborne series and, hungry for more Souls, went into this one anyway after only beating Dark Souls 1 to give it a chance before playing 3. There's some things I prefer about this one and some things I prefer about the first, so I'll compare them in the following review.
What's better in Dark Souls 2:
+Improved weapon upgrade system. The seperatation of infusion from base weapon upgrades makes a lot of sense.
+Greater build variety. The changes to stats' impact on infusions and elemental bonuses really encourage trying different stats to level up.
+Enemies despawning after killing them so many times. Knows that you're obviously having trouble with something else down the road, saves your time.
+Vastly improved online. Much easier to summon, invade, and leave/rate messages.
+Better covenants. Much more purposeful, especially the covenant that gives you access to three new areas and an exclusive boss fight. Don't join the Company of Champions though. Ugh.
+Improved UI. Going through your inventory is a lot easier on the eyes than the first due to its new grid view.
+Better visual engine. Shadows and lighting look much better.
+Much more optimized than DS1 on PC. No need for any mod akin to DSfix.
What's better in Dark Souls 1:
-The level design. Too many cheap deaths in DS2, a lot of enemy placements and hazards make death feel cheap and undeserved.
-The areas themselves. DS1's areas were all unique and interconnected, DS2's areas and world feel uncreative and lazy.
-Enemy variety. While DS1's enemies were all unique, DS2's enemies are mostly armored dudes.
-The boss fights. Much more creative than DS2's boss fights.
-The roll mechanic. Rolls in DS1 clearly show what frames will be i-frames, DS2 roll i-frames are unclear and you will often be hurt mid-roll.
-Estuses. Using an estus in DS2 is slow and difficult to upgrade due to the focus on lifegems.
-The hollow system. Part of DS1's genius design was its encouragement to experiment. DS2 ruins this by cutting your max HP by up to half every time you die, only reversible by using Humanity.
-Online matchmaking. Matching you with people that have gathered around the same amount of total souls as you rather than the amount of times you levelled up is stupid.
-Bonfire warping. You shouldn't have access to warp right away, makes farming too easy and makes travel too convenient compared to DS1 which had you earn the privelege.
-The atmosphere and story. DS1's atmosphere was one of the best I've ever played in a video game thanks to its deep lore and fantastic world. DS2 doesn't come close and you never really care about the story or lore.
-Why the ♥♥♥♥ is there a boss in DS2 that you have to pay a humanity fee every time you want to even attempt it??
So yeah, DS1>DS2, but still not a terrible game. DS1 is more creative, has a more interesting world, and has better gameplay mechanics, while DS2 has better online, visuals, and improvements in some aspects.
And yes, I'm the guy that made the review with the really bad puns for DS1 :D

Gone home is an unconventional game. That's all I have to say. It's a very linear experience, with its fair share of optional secrets. I went into this game with zero sequences spoiled for me which means I constantly expected ghost sightings and because of that everything felt very eerie and weird. I felt really uncomfortable expected something would happen and then nothing did. That's the beauty of this game. You're constantly expecting something to happen, something to scare you, some event that is going to pop and then when it doesn't you don't feel sad or stupid, you feel amazing because you realize the atmosphere is what makes this game. It's all about atmosphere from the setting to the sounds you encounter during your little investigation. Also everything is a huge 90s fan service nostalgia trip.
SHOULD YOU BUY IT?
Having all that in mind, I'd say don't buy the game at full price. The 20 euro price tag is way too unrealistic. It's a 2 hour experience and I've read almost everything in the game. Wait for a 50% sale at least. I got it in humble bundle and I'd say for that price it's really decent.

The Final Station is a very short and sweet game. I'll go over the pros and cons.
Pros:
-Good art direction, backdrops that the train drives through are pretty cool most of the time, and there is a cyber-punky aesthetic to the cities and tech in the game
-Combat, simple yet has enough depth to make you think about how to engage your enemies
-Story, there are many hidden tidbits to find that reveal more of the story to you and the storyline is somewhat mysterious
Cons:
-Very short, took me about 3 and a half hours to beat and I was somewhat taking my time with it
-Price, a little too expensive for less than 4 hours of gameplay
-No replayability, I was expecting a NG+ mode or something like that but there's nothing
-Very easy, only one system malfunctions at a time in the train and it's pretty easy to stay on top of the system and 6 passengers, even if 2 are injured. I always seemed to have enough supplies if I just explored all of each level
Overall it's a pretty good game but given the price it is too short and does not have enough replayability.
I recommend you put it on your wishlist if you're interested, and buy it when it goes on sale.

Dark Souls II. Dark Souls, II. What a game, what a masterpiece. Does this entry in the Souls' serie deserves the name that it currently has? Yes, YES it does. A lot of people hate(d) the game, because of its hitboxes, because of the fact that the game was not immersive as the first one because the areas made the game feel more of a dungeon crawler because the connection between them was just that thanks to the bonfire(s).
Still, this game manages to do it. Mechanically speaking, the game improved a lot from its predecessor and for some parts it's even superior than it's sequel, boss fights are memorable, even though the bosses themselves are quite frankly humanoids apart from a few of them. The base game is amazing, but the DLCs?
The DLCs are on a new level. The DLCs are where the game TRULY shines for its beauty: boss fights like Fume Knight's one, Sinh's, these are the best bossfights a game - in my opinion - or better, the developers, managed to deliver.
Is the game the best in the serie? Probably yes, thanks to this version (EDIT: I don't mean lore-wise, I'm talking about gameplay mechanics, and other stuff like PvE and PvP, the latter it's amongst fan's favourites in Dark Souls II: SotFS). The base game had a lot of problems, technically speaking but SotFS' version manages to get them fixed.
Hitboxes? Yeah, they're kinda ♥♥♥♥ed up. NOT THAT MUCH, not, that, much. They're not worse than DS1 or DS3, in fact all of them from a technical viewpoint are ♥♥♥♥ed up. But this series is amazing, nonetheless. Even if this game, Dark Souls II, has its flaws, the game shines no matter what.

I have a few mixed feelings about SotFS that I would like to address. First off, SotFS does not run on the same multiplayer servers as vanilla Dark Souls II. If you want to view this from a technical standpoint and assume that FromSoftware didn't have the ability to merge both servers into one, then fair enough, but this splits the Dark Souls II community into two regardless of the fact. Secondly, SotFS drastically changes a lot of the enemy placements in the game. This can be a huge improvement to some people, but for me, it's certainly a double-edged sword. Some of the more annoying areas that are present in the vanilla version of Dark Souls II were tweaked to make them less of a nuisance, that being the decreased amount of certain mobs or simply the replacement of another mob present in the game, but there are also some areas that were unecessarily altered to make them even more aggravating than they should be ( Few examples: The giant dragon before the bridge to the Old Dragon Slayer and the increase of Desert Sorceresses in Harvest Valley ). That said, you can be the judge on whether or not these new enemy placements affect you negatively, but take it into consideration if you're a vanilla Dark Souls II player. If there's one thing I really like about these changes, it's that It makes the game feel refreshing. If you have general knowledge about the enemy placements in the vanilla version, chances are you might be surprised a few times throughout your playthrough.
The visuals, most noteably the lighting, have been improved to give the game a better atmosphere. The darker areas of the game are... actually dark! This makes the torch item quite useful for once. The improvement isn't necessarily drastic, but it's certainly noticeable.
Overall, I had an enjoyable experience. Do I prefer SotFS over the vanilla version? Yes. I think SotFS is the definitive version of Dark Souls II and is a must-have if you haven't played the vanilla game before. Despite my seemingly negative perspective on some of the enemy placements, I do feel like it keeps the game fresh and significantly more challenging.

The beauty of this game is in the complete freedom you're given from the square 1. GTA games give you a sandbox and then tease you by restricting sections, blocking vehicles, and holding your hand. Skyrim delievers a sandbox that's expansive but offers little in what you get to do in it. Just Cause 2 has no such reservations, dilemmas, or issues.
Want to immediately ignore the storyline, collect weapon crates, and steal helicopters to blitz offshore oil rigs? Okay.
Want to wreak continual, nigh unstoppable havoc on the military of the island nation with your grapple? Sure.
Want to scour the land, looking for generals to assassinate? Go for it.
Ever wanted to hijack an airplane on the runway by speeding a motorcycle next to it? And then fly said airplane, stand on the outside and steal the attack chopper scrambled to take you down? Just Cause 2 lets you, and with an equal measure of challenge and ease.
I enjoy this game immensely. If I want to play something, but nothing especially involved or complicated, and enjoy myself for an hour or so, I load Just Cause 2. There have been numerous games I've installed, beaten, and then uninstalled to make room for something else. This game, since I bought it 4 years ago, has never left my hard drive.

The graphics are simplistic, sure, but the soundtrack is pretty cool, if you like chiptunes (if you fondly remember the NES or Sega Genisis game scores, that's you). There is a definite sense of characterization, (crew members will worry about those still missing, and go exploring after being saved) and the plot is interesting. Simply beating the game is relatively challenging (evil moving tower!), but the trinkets...Those will induce hair pulling.
The game takes a simple mechanic, the capacity to flip your personal gravity (drop from floor to ceiling, or vice versa) while on firm ground, and pushes it to the limit. Add in some clever save point mechanisms, and you have a very smart little game. The game is mostly non-linear, and it is relatively short-first runs last less than ten hours in my experience. There are bonus stages and trinkets, if you want more challenge, though. Good price. Anything else?

Also the "survival" aspect it seems to play up on isn't there, this is a story based mission game, you go from place to place and find the code at the end of a level behind a locked door every time. There is so much pontentil in the map design, enemies could chase you back through the level, more vertical options to bypass large groups, but its content to have 3/4 guys attack you each time. Only once is there a horde I've seen, it you pretty much given a "theres only one guy on the right so keep walking thattaway!" They can't catch you if you just keep walking, so the tension isn't there.
Storys got some cool parts, but isn't super special, plus the MC doesn't talk meaning conversation is pretty basic. All the cool dialoge between the surviviors you find is rly hard to listen to because you have to keep running back and forth between the 3-5 different train parts to stop it dying on you
and all the food and medical stuff is on the other side of the ship, so if a guy is hungry and bleeding welp you better have caught that beforehand, since the warnings don't pop up until they're nearly dead (or in one case, didn't pop up at all and the guy died infront of me). The survivior conversations and everything is really interesting though, I like what the story has going for it, its just so painful to try and gather everything. If the machine near the front of the train is "the one" that needs monitoring (and its only ever been one for me so far) then it makes trying to listen to the conversations frustrating.

TL:DR: this game is an expensive flash game
The game has an interesting concept, but fails to make any relevant progress. It tries to become a survival horror, but takes shortcuts that make it feel more like a flash game than a full product. The best comparison is with P.T. which uses a similar idea: revisiting the same small area with minor changes at every iteration. Unfortunately, the game has you go into several rooms with no real progression. Each time you make a startling discovery or die, and end up in your bed. but the time to reach that climax is slow, stagnant, with an abrupt change. It lacks crescendo. There is a bare-bones stealth area where you hide in a closet while a grotesque baby-faced grunt shakes it. This mechanic is poorly developed, as you only have two directions to flee, and it is a matter of waiting until they are off-screen.
I played one session and did not return, because only 1/5 of the game is actually content, and relies heavily on jump scares and exploration of mostly static environments. Items that you do examine are paintings with no interest or plot progression, as if they were added for either showing off artistic skills or lengthening gameplay.

If you want to sell folk on VVVVVV, you'll be staring up a hill with a near-right grade that's pestering you to climb it. For one, try to initially wedge mention of it into polite conversation; it's unpronouncable. Should you manage to settle on a verbal interpretation of the title eventually ("vee vee vee vee vee vee", "the letter 'V' six times", "vvvvhhh"), then you've got to sell anyone left remaining on the threadbare graphics and a difficulty that escalates like Wonka's Glass Elevator.
It looks like VVVVVV is daring you to love it in the face of stark circumstances. You'll end up liking it, though; the music, speedy gravity-swapping play and psychedically basic visuals create an impressionable space-warping saga of authentic - and repeated - sacrifice. Captain Viridian is one of gaming's truest badasses, which goes a fair jog toward invoking the cliche of being deceived by appearances (much like the rest of this game does.)

I want to say something about this game, and I want you all to listen please.
When I play my single player story games, I like to Role Play like i'm really that character (I know it's weird, but hear me out).  I like to make decisions like I actually would in real life.  This War of Mine had a certain sequence that almost made me cry (a suicide from doing too many bad things).
This game, as short as it is, evokes some emotions.  I won't spoil anything.  The game is slow to start, but don't buy it expecting to shooty shooty bang bang all kinds of weird zombie-like people.  The first half an hour is a slow burn that sets up a great story line.
You are a train driver man who is driving his train, which apparently is a little bit in need of repairs, but you drive it.  Through the story you find out something is going on.  SOMETHING.  The way the first part of the game sets up the story is amazing to me, and I stand by that 100%.  I'm a guy who played through Skyrim the first time and had almost 200 hours because i loved to talk to everybody and enjoy the story line.
This game does a great job at placing little gems in the environment that will give you clues as to what is going on.  Now, don't get me wrong.  You can just run through this game and the intro may seem boring if you are looking for a shooty game.  But if you buy this, enjoy it.  talk to everyone.
As you can tell, I love this game.  I wish it was longer.  I hope there is some DLC/sequel coming out.

It's up to you.  I highly recommend this game.  Do I think it is worth the asking price?  I played this game and so far I enjoy it.  If you like the looks of the game, and the preview videos do it justice, buy it.  If you are a person who is critizing the price, wait a while and it may come up on sale.
I recommend you buy it.  Thank you.

Verdun is honestly one of the funnest games I've played. It feels different to a lot of other FPS games, not only in the theme but in the gameplay mechanics too. I particularly enjoy the NCO role in squads giving access to command auras and abilities such as mortar strikes, smoke screens, air recon, and gas attacks.

The weapons are very fun to use and I feel there is a good and interesting variety, with the vastly different fire rates of weapons, along with the different requirements of no man's land and trench fighting, I feel there is a lot of tactical thinking that can go into gameplay and deciding how and when to take your battles.
I really enjoy the team focused elements of the game and I feel that the Verdun community is one of the friendliest and more welcoming communities in online games that I've experienced.
Progressing, gaining ranks, medals, etc. All of that is nice as well and gives a real sense of achievement and I often screenshot the scoreboard and my medals when I've done particularly well, and looking at the screenshots in the community hub, I'm not alone in doing this.
All in all, it's a very wonderful, sure there is the occasional bug but I feel the developers are pretty good at fixing these and I wouldn't say they impact gameplay much at all.
I would definitely recommend Verdun!

**** Initial Review **** More Detailed Review Below ****
Just over 4 hours in and this is a much better game than previous versions.
Had a lot of fun with the R&D in Career mode.  The tasks are like mini-games you have to complete in order to progress.
Learning to drive with the new physics. Cars feel like they slide around a lot more this year (no assists).
Graphics are improved significantly with some of the biggest improvements being the lighting and reflections on the cars.
The sound of the cars is realistic, and the commentary and voice work is varied and of a good standard. The race engineer has a lot more to say than before and can now even read your lap times for you.
Great game so far, very challenging.
**** More Details ****
Off the bat, it is clear that this is the very best version of the F1 series made by Codemasters so far.
Presentation is about as good as you can expect from any modern racing game, and the way it is done here has the potential to immediately suck in any F1 fan.  A very smooth and simple interface allows you to quickly jump into any race around the 20 circuits available on the calendar as any one of the 22 drivers and 11 teams on the roster this year.  For a more in-depth experience you can play the Career mode which allows you to select your own driver avatar, name and number and pick which team and team-mate you race with for the 10 season campaign.  Career mode is beefed up this year, in addition to your laptop, you get access to an agent and an engineer who assists with contract negotiations and R&D updates respectively.  These are simple tocuhes and whilst updated on previous iterations (the motorhome and laptop 2013 - I think?).
The Career season itself is customizable allowing you to set anything from Full Race Weekends to various shorter versions and race lengths from 3 Laps to 100% Races.
The difficulty settings range from Very Easy to Ultimate, and new level more difficult than the previous highest difficulty setting - Legend and there's something for everyone.
Unlike previous games, leaving on the driving assists doesn't actually do much to slow the driver, so you are not rewarded as such for driving with no assists vs assists.
R&D tests are offered during Practice Sessions on Career Mode which add a few fun minigames which can be done during practice laps. Success in these tests are rewarded with R&D points which can be used to improve your car over time allowing a Manor to eventually have enough parts to challenge a Merc (in theory).  The results of the R&D tests can be viewed, and actually an help the player become more precise at placing the car and making the tyres last longer.
The podium is available for the winner and two runners up. The animations are better than previous games, and are just a nice little touch which you do not get with simulators such as Assetto Corsa (another fantastic racing game/sim).
Replays are available after races, with the standard range of cameras to review the race. The ability to flip between drivers has remained and makes for some good fun watching incidents and accidents between other drivers.
Time Trials have new features as well as keeping all the old ones from F1 2015.
Now you can race rivals and also get access to the setups of all the other drivers on the leaderboard allowing you to benefit from the tried and tested settings.  I personally love this as I am horrible at setting up a car myself.
There is also the ability to download various car setups posted on the Steam Workshop from other players (thanks guys! :) ) which is immensively helpful to everyone from the complete novice (like myself) to a budding engineer aiming to be the new Adrian Newey.
As of yet, I have not delved into Multiplayer which now has Lobbies and also a time delayed Multiplayer Co-op championship (I think).
Just about everything you could want for this game exists here in this version.  Short of adding a part where the player can be Lewis Hamilton during his time off, there's not much more that could be done.
Over time, I think there will be better and more immersive versions of this series, but for now, this is as good as it gets.

Warface had me addicted for a few good hours. At one point, I thought I'd play it much more than I did. In the end, it gave me ~40hrs of fun. Here's how I feel about it:
As an avid FPS player, I do like how the game rewards aiming for the head. Sadly, this can easily lead to people hackusating even the most decent of players. Some assault rifles seem to one-shot people if its a headshot, and that can be frustrating if you're new to the game or just overall very casual. I personally don't have an issue with that but I know people who do.
I also like how the game seperates the servers into two level groups. You start out in the beginner servers which are for players level 1-12, and once you become level 13, you're able to play with anyone who is level 13+. This is nice because it gives players a few hours to gain a grip of the game while playing against people who are just as new. The playing field is made more fair and more balanced, and it keeps everyone as engaged as they should be as they are learning a new game.
An issue that arises with this is, for one, smurfs. Nothing is stopping a veteran from making an alternate account and going on to the beginner servers and curbstomping everyone. I also did this, simply because I wanted to play with lower level friends. Sadly, this issue isn't a new one, and it plagues many games. Pretty much nothing can be done about it, but it deserves to be mentioned.
Moving on, lets discuss the array of weapons. Again, I have mixed feelings about this.
There are many weapons, and each class has just as many as the last to choose from and try out. Sadly, some weapons don't seem to be different enough from others and in some cases, some weapons are straight upgrades from another, rendering one useless. Some weapons are unlocked at certain levels, the majority of them become unlocked at level 13. Sadly, some actually stay locked after you reach level 13, and the game gives no real explanation as to how to unlock them. Rumor has it that a few guns have actually been removed from the game due to being unbalanced, but people who had gotten them before they were purged were able to keep them. This is an obvious oversight on the part of the dev-team and should be adressed.
We haven't even discussed the "crown" weapons...
Each of the four classes has a few weapons that can be unlocked with Crowns, an in-game currency you can earn for doing special ops missions, co-op missions, contracts, etc. You cannot buy these Crowns, but the missions that you are required to do to earn them take hours. Believe me when I say Crowns are hard-earned. The weapons that you can purchase with these Crowns are all blatantly overpowered. The way the dev-team attempts to balance this out is the fact that none of the Crown weapons can be purchased permanently. One week is the maximium amount you can have one. But, if one was to play enough, you could probably earn enough Crowns to purchase another Crown weapon in one week. Basically, the game rewards griding for an overpowered weapon that other people may not have the time or skill to grind for. More or less unfair but it could be justified.
The same general gist goes for armor as well. There are pieces of armor that seem to be straight upgrades. There is also Crown armor. There are also exclusive pieces of Armor that you earn via special missions, etc, that you only get for an hour and the timer starts as soon as you earn it, meaning if you happened to be done playing for the day, welp, too bad, your exclusive reward will expire unless you play for another hour to experience it.
The progression also seems to hit a plateau at about level 15 or so. Not going to go into detail about this too much because frankly I'm tired and plateaus are self-explanitory. If not, refer to

This is one of the best city builders out there. It's extremely focused, so there's not very many buildings to mess with. Micromanaging is limited primarily to how you divide up your workforce. This gives the game an aesthetic elegance where others can get lost in feature bloat.
The game's primary challenge comes from surviving each winter. Rather than being a capitalism simulator, this game feels more like a civilization simulator. This comes at much relief for those of us who want to engage in more meaningful activities than simply making a bunch of money. In fact, there is no money in Banished. You an barter however, and this proves to be one of the more powerful foundations for a massive town.
The game is not without some faults. Large town suffer from an AI that begins to break down as you expand over great stretches of territory. This is a shame because the AI is fantastic otherwise. Also, players with massive towns may feel as though limited by the small number of buildings in the game. No game is perfect, and this game's simplistic aesthetic which is of such benefit to small and medium sized towns just makes large towns feel homogenous after a while.
I'd recommend this game to anyone who enjoys city building games. Starting over again in new terrains at the highest difficulty for an ultimate challenge is where this game truly shines. Those looking for simulations that can handle the management of large towns may find that they grow tired of Banished, but not until they've put a good number of hours into the game. It's well worth the cost of the game even then.

Quite simply, an amazing game. You may get frustrated. You may want to curse the developer. But 99% chance when you get mad and want to curse, it's your own fault. A brilliant, simple game, that keeps you coming back for more.
If you dont know the mechanics of the game, they are simple. I will give a simple example, to not spoil anything.
Say you want to serve a Baked Potato in your restaurant. It might have two recipes. ABCX and ABCY. So customers order one of the two. You hit those keys, serve it up, get your money and everyone is happy. Perhaps you want to serve a steak? You buy it from the food menu. Maybe it has 4 different types of steaks that people order, for example HGFF, HGFY, HHFY, and DHFT. Now you have two items, with six recipes you have to recall. At first it's easy, brilliant. But then it just keeps going and going. Add other issues like flushing the toilet (perhaps Arrow Up, Arrow Up, Arrow Down, repeated 4 times) and it just gets to be crazy fun.
Its a brilliant game, well worth the money. When I mess up, I want to blame someone else for it, but I know its just a simple game, and it makes me want to continue. Just about as addictive as it gets.
If you suck using the keyboard, then this isnt the game for you. If you prefer the mouse, I doubt this is the game for you. But if you suck at the keyboard, you still have a chance as you can change ANY recipe to what you want. So if you mess up an order, its your fault.

I recommend this game, unless you just are terrible at the keyboard. Otherwise, its a surprising and challenging game that keeps me coming back .  I would be honored to work for this developer.

Finally got around to this game. Took a while, but better late than never - and in this case playing Gone Home was well worth the wait. Though it ocassionally veers into heavy sentimentality, Gone Home is for the most part a profoundly affecting experience. The atmosphere is rich, full of objects to be explored, listened to, and read. The specificity of the atmosphere allows each new room to gradually accrue the full emotional heft of a family whose own dynamics have been buried in the mundane material of living for years. As Kaitlyn, a college student returning home from your own globe-trotting adventure, your arrival is met only by absence, a family missing without explanation. In their absence, the material of the house itself becomes the trace of your family, and in coming to know their hopes, sorrows, and loves, your family is somehow more present than if fully rendered characters appeared alongside you.
It's a beautiful experience. Brief, but lovely - like the last few moments before your heart breaks.

I am an unashamed fan of these "walking simulator" titles, a term I truly despise because it implicates itself as pejoritave. However, I can understand why people who don't like them think that way. That said, this isn't so much a walking simulator as it is a "going through people's stuff" simulator, a term I also despise even though I just made it up, because rather than just holding down a button to move forward while the story plays out around you in the scenery, you have to go looking for it.
In Gone Home, you decide how much time and energy to invest in uncovering the character arcs. The main plot unfolds by being fed to you through notes that are easily discovered. It's the easiest of all the stories to uncover. But where Gone Home truly shines is the way the creators handle characterization of minor characters in a truly filmic way, they show more than they tell. The father, the mother, and the childhood friend all have narratives that are opened and (mostly) closed when the credits roll. In addition, the creators allow you to decide how much time to invest in discovering all of this backstory. Don't want to read a short story written by the protaganist as a child? That's okay, it's not entirely necessary. But if you decide to invest the time, it will only elevate the story and your appreciation for its craft that much more.

While appearing to be a food service simulator, Cook, Serve, Delicious feels more like a mini-game compilation in the vein of WarioWare. You are in charge of single-handed running the busiest restaurant in the world, and are expected to prepare and serve each meal promptly and to order. This is simple with cheaper dishes such as corn dogs and fish filet; however, as the game progresses, and you are asked to prepare more complicated meals, the pace mounts exponentially. Balancing your menu not only involved making sure you don't serve the same thing too often: it also involves balancing your menu so that you don't serve too many difficult dishes at once. For those not satisfied with the normal progression, random bets and Steam challenges are here to give you the opportunity to grab extra bragging rights.
Honestly, CSD is one of the best cooking games I've played, and it's definitely worth the full $10.
