Quite simply put, this game excells in its atmosphere and in terms of subtlety, an aspect that is lacking in most games nowadays, especially horror titles. There is very little jump scares involved in the game and the few that are involved in ways that fit the atmosphere of the game. The imagery is frightening (and gets pretty disturbing at points), the subject matter gets incredibly dark, the audio presentation is amazing, and the story manages to be abstracxt enough to get your own interpretation, yet clear enough so that you can be entertained by what you are seeing. It is a game that rewards thought, which is a rare aspect of stories in games.
There are only a few complaints I have, the first being that, while the art style is well drawn and adds to the atmosphere, I found there to be a slight bit of eye strain due to the amounts of small lines of various different monochrome shades that represent the darkness, which tends to just look incredibly awful in motion, which is even worse due to the flickering when the screen moves, so you may want to pass on this if you have especially sensitive eyes.
The other being that the game is kind of simplistic gameplay wise, and you spend most of the time just walking left or right, while occasionally trying to figure out how to slip by an enemy, which is in a rather simplistic way each time. The game is also light on content and can be beaten in about 4 hours, although it can be a bit longer if you take your time. Overall though, I highly reccomend this game. It really knows how to handle horror and atmosphere incredibly well and is one of the most underrated games of 2014.

Verdun is honestly one of the funnest games I've played. It feels different to a lot of other FPS games, not only in the theme but in the gameplay mechanics too. I particularly enjoy the NCO role in squads giving access to command auras and abilities such as mortar strikes, smoke screens, air recon, and gas attacks.

I really enjoy the team focused elements of the game and I feel that the Verdun community is one of the friendliest and more welcoming communities in online games that I've experienced.
Progressing, gaining ranks, medals, etc. All of that is nice as well and gives a real sense of achievement and I often screenshot the scoreboard and my medals when I've done particularly well, and looking at the screenshots in the community hub, I'm not alone in doing this.
All in all, it's a very wonderful, sure there is the occasional bug but I feel the developers are pretty good at fixing these and I wouldn't say they impact gameplay much at all.
I would definitely recommend Verdun!

This game is presented in an interesting way, but the mechanics, pacing and "teaching" make it frustrating rather than fun. In short, the game needs more time to realize its potential.
Conversations need to be meaningful - they should contain interesting information that actually help me discover items or improve my chances of survial. Ofc some convos can be just about story, but there needs to be some gameplay centric ones as well. Right now it feels like I'm reading a story frustratingly distrubted across a set of NPCs.
Combat needs refinement and mechanical variance: the gun need to be able to wound an enemy (leg shot), slowing them down, headshot for instant kill (or at least more damage) and then simply shoot. See Matthais Worch's GDC talk
. Melee attack needs a purpose (why can't I pistol whip?) over and above a weak version of using the pistol - see HLD, Halo, etc, etc. Environmental objects (that can be used as weapons) need to feel like something I'm smart enough to discover, rather than a necessary means of conserving ammo. Can I shoot an enviro object so that it explodes? Can I cause things to fall on enemies? Can I kick a chair at them to give me time to climb a ladder? Can I hide in a locker?
Level design needs to be less linear, see Mark of the Ninja. I feel like I'm simply walking from room to room, rather than masterfully recognizing and overcoming encounters in smart ways.
It probably sounds like I want a different game, and it's true I do, because the concept behind this one simply isn't fleshed out enough.

I was skeptical at first, I must admit. 4 hours in and I am more than happy with my purchase of F1 2016.
So, last years iteration caught a lot of flak due to the game being practically incomplete (no safety cars, career mode, ect.) Not only that, but it was riddled with bugs to the point where it was practically unplayable. Now, normally, I would be irritated by this, but I cut Codemasters some slack. It was their first shot at an entirely new game engine. Surely, F1 2016 would be an improvement...
Well? It most certainly is. With my expectations being low, Codemasters BLEW them out of the water. While the game is not PERFECT, I am finding it far more enjoyable than previous F1 titles I have invested in. There are minor graphical glitches here and there (stupid little things that won't hinder your gameplay, at least not that I've encountered). Better Yet, not once in 4 hours did the game crash to the desktop! I'm in awe!
All in all, thank you, Codemasters, for listening to your fan base. You have done us a service releasing such a well done game. Here is to the future! We can only move forward!

Be warned, this is a long one. If you are looking to buy the game then maybe this will help.
Where do I start? F1 2016
the F1 game that we have been waiting for. Immediatley starting to drive yielded noticable improvements that made me feel much more satisfied with this years installment. Now, if you were like me, you watched almost every single pre-release video from the likes of xMattyG1 and Tiametmarduk, so there weren't any huge surprises with any big new features. Despite the element of surprise not being there, I was still excited to start my Career Mode, and to see the all the detail in the paddock.
I want to go over one thing more than everything else, which will be summarised below, and that thing is Career Mode, and things that you will encounter while racing in it.

Career Mode is back and better than ever. With a more in-depth look at the life of a Formula 1 driver, you will be sucked into the game more than ever before. You are given ten seasons to compete in, either moving around to get to the top, or making your favourite team the one to beat. You are able to fully customise your avatar, choosing from a multitude of appearances and helmets (which you can customise further). You are also able to pick your own number, besides ones that are either in use or retired.
Testing gives you a whole new reason to do Practice sessions, and allows you to upgrade your car. For now, they are a fun and informative way to see how you can be getting the most out of your car. Later on, they will probably just be another thing to do to get those research points. Tests include the Track Acclimatisation Test, the Tyre Wear Test, and a Qualifying Pace Test. All fairly self explanatory. The only issue I have encountered has been with the Tyre Wear Test, as I couldn’t complete it at all. It wasn’t because the tyres were degrading, but because I couldn’t set a laptime that was quick enough for it to count. Although that was frustrating, it boils down to my skill with the game, and how I am driving a Sauber for my Career Mode seasons. Car upgrades are chosen by you, and you have multiple areas for improvement available. Other teams will upgrade around you as well, so if you aren’t moving forward as a team, you’re moving backwards. Upgrades are done with research points, which you gain from the practice testing. The better you do in the tests, and the more objectives you hit, the more points you get to create a dream team.
The formation lap, manual starts, and manual pit entry add a greater sense of realism and difficulty. The formation lap allows you to heat your tyres and brakes, while warming up for when the lights go out. If there is one thing I would highly suggest is to use the manual start feature. It isn’t hard, and allows you to get a great start, as opposed to every other version where you would be guaranteed to not get away well. I have found around 12000RPM is a good spot to be in, although that was just me testing in a few different cars. Manual pit entry lets you brake for the pit lane, which could allow you to gain on, or even overtake other drivers. Penalties will be awarded for speeding, so practice trying to find the perfect spot to start braking. Just make sure you don’t get a “speeding in the pits” penalty while serving your previous infraction for speeding in the pits.
A new damage model gives the gameplay that ever needed realism. Instead of just a “Full” damage option, there is one more called “Simulation.” Now, if you hit the wall, or touch the rear wing of another driver, you will lose parts accordingly. When your tyre does come off, it is attached to tethers, which will keep it with the car.
What goes hand-in-hand with complete carnage? Safety, because you can’t have one without the other. The safety car makes its return to the game, and brings along its younger sibling, the Virtual Safety Car, or VSC. While the removal of the safety car in previous versions might have just been a PR move to “bring it back” for more hype, I can’t complain now that it is available. You have complete control under the safety car, but I wouldn’t go passing other drivers while it is on track, or pass the safety car itself. Bad ideas. While under the VSC, you must keep to a delta time between the cars around you, or you will get penalised. Like the safety car, you still have full control under the VSC. Maybe try changing your strategy when the safety car comes out, and also be ever alert when it is returning to the pits. You can make up serious ground on those around if they aren’t paying as much attention.
The one issue that I have ran into is how the menu stays on the last selected item. If I quickly want to rewind, but I last went to the garage, the selection is still on Back to Garage. It has cost me qualifying quite a few times. Not sure if this issue is "working as intended" or if it is something that could be fixed.
Multiplayer works really really well from the races I have done. Side by side battles worked out flawlessly, and there was no hopping around. The aliens have disappeared!
If you are worried about the recommended spec level, I run with a Xeon E3 1231v3 and a GTX 970 with great performance.
I love this game so far, and Codemasters has really stepped up their game from last year. Community input, testing, and communication shows that they do care about our racing experience. I look forward to playing it whenever I can.

I bought this for €12 and it's quite OK for that price so I'll give thumbs up. But I really hesitated with this rating, trust me.
Spirit of the revolution is really great. Music is empowering. There were moments I just wanted to turn off my computer and get out to destroy cars with baseball bat and beat up some evil North Koreans soldiers. Overall atmosphere is the best thing about this game and authors really nailed it.
List of bad things is much more longer. Bugs are everywhere. Bugged locations, mission, jobs, enemies, spawns, achievements. A lot of small annoying bugs. Enemy AI is terrible. Like when you're hidden perfectly, nobody saw you hiding there, but enemies end up standing near you and keep up firing to inpenetrable wall behind which you're hidden. Spawns are terrible. You can see enemy soldiers spawning and sometimes also disappearing right in front of your eyes/crosshair. And so on.
Weapon modding is not too bad, but it feels a bit weird. You can carry only three weapons but you can carry up to 9 mods and like 10 attachable equipement pieces? Alright, whatever. You'll end up using maybe three weapon all the time. Best of all is definitely battle rifle. Guerilla tools are incredibly uncreative. The same variants for each tool. Upgrades as well. Oh dear lord. I nearly forgot. This is so frustrating I you just tried to force it out from my brain forever. Motorbikes. Fun and quick way to go around, huh? Nope. Story is generic and boring, characters as well. You have very limited money income for upgrades. But at the end of game you have ridiculous amount of absolutely useless tech points for unlocking new stuff. But you've already unlocked everything at the third location.

Surprisingly enjoyable. Patches seem to have reduced the framerate problems to the occasional hiccup. Game runs smoothly and seems to be optimized (by removing select volumetric lighting effects, etc) enough that my computer barely feels its weight.
So far as story is concernced, there isn't much of one. Homefront also drops its introduced characters fairly quickly, opting to drop you into a small sandbox environment, allowing you to complete activities and unlock the small area bit by bit. Though, the overall world map is very large later on. Taking a page from Far Cry, Homefront sees you completing small tasks while disrupting radio signals and invading strongholds. However, it is in the setting and gunplay where the game really becomes fun.
You might be surprised by the lack of customization options for weapons, but you'll quickly realize that 2-3 full weapon mods (ripping apart a pistol on the fly and making it an smg, for example) for each of the 5 weapons with full attatchment options (sight, barrel, underbarrel, etc) per mod make for some epic combinations. The story and characters aren't really there, but the gunplay feels fantastic and the game shines as you rip apart your shotgun, turn it into a fireball launcher and burn a score of enemies, allowing you to unlock a portion of the map and see all the other fun things to do nearby.

While appearing to be a food service simulator, Cook, Serve, Delicious feels more like a mini-game compilation in the vein of WarioWare. You are in charge of single-handed running the busiest restaurant in the world, and are expected to prepare and serve each meal promptly and to order. This is simple with cheaper dishes such as corn dogs and fish filet; however, as the game progresses, and you are asked to prepare more complicated meals, the pace mounts exponentially. Balancing your menu not only involved making sure you don't serve the same thing too often: it also involves balancing your menu so that you don't serve too many difficult dishes at once. For those not satisfied with the normal progression, random bets and Steam challenges are here to give you the opportunity to grab extra bragging rights.
Honestly, CSD is one of the best cooking games I've played, and it's definitely worth the full $10.

The steam achievements, steam cooking challenges and leaderboards give the game a competitive aspect.
In my opninion the game is very simple but it works. It's fun and addictive. You can easily play Cook, Serve, Delicious! for 30-40 hours until you have fully completed it.

Gone Home seemed to have potential. In general it was pretty creepy and you expect something to eventually happen, but (sorry if this spoils it) nothing ever does. The game is probably better if you start off with an expectation like that because you'll either A) decide then to never play Gone Home, or B) play it while keeping your hopes low. The story is okay, you find clues and then the game usually confirms your suspicions with sporadic pieces of monologue. Sound and music-- there isn't much. There is mostly silence and the occassional thunder and I liked that. When the game's music does come up it's because you triggered it and it has these warm tones that make you feel kinda good. Then there's the punk cassettes. The songs fit the game, although I found them to be annoying, barely tolerable at best. There isn't much to the gameplay. Not a whole lot of purpose to your inventory. You can interact with almost any object but there usually isn't any significance to it. Overall my expectations were too high going into this game. I kept thinking something scary was going to happen or something hugely serious, like finding your sister hanging from a noose in the next room, walking in on your parent's beating one another, your Uncle's ghost chasing you, or stumbling upon your old neighbor who came back for his Street Fighter game and is now going insane chopping up your whole family while you were away relaxing across the world for a whole f*cking year. Seriously, how well off are you that you can go on vacation for an entire year? Anyway, at one point the game basically tells you straightforward that you're going to walk in on your sister banging. And you're like wow! This game is nuts! This could be hilarious and interesting! Then the story turns and it doesn't happen. Like I said, nothing ever happens. Gone Home is really just a waste of a few hours. It's like reading a fairly dull short book that you can move around in.
I originally bought this game because a friend and I thought it looked hilarious, yet people were saying that it was good. Ya know how sometimes you just want to watch a movie or play a game that seems like it might be so corny that it becomes entertaining? At worst, I figured even if it's not funny apparently it should still be a good game based on people's reviews. I got it on sale. Thought we'd have a few light beers and a lighthearted time, but the game's funny-but-not-supposed-to-be parts are too few and far between and the serious parts are too frequent that you can't even enjoy the game in that cheap way either.
So if you can't enjoy Gone Home in a serious way, and you can't enjoy it in a ridiculous way, then I have no idea why you'd still want to try to play this game.

This game is essentially the entire history of East European Science Fiction compressed into a five hour experience. Never have I simultaneously felt so accomplished while realizing almost everything I did was pointless. Final Fantasy X/X2 HD comes finally makes it to PC. The good news is the wait has been worth it. It is a port of the HD remaster for PS3/PS4. Traditionally Square Enix Final Fantasy ports have been hit or miss for one reason or another. Some titles are ports of their mobile counterparts which doesn't translate well to PC.
I am glad to say that from the time I have spent with the game thus far the game has run at a steady frame rate on my i5 with a GTX 750 ti 2gb Vram OC'ed and 8 gb of total ram. I have not yet experienced a crash of any sort. Perhaps the game was easier to port from PS4 given the similar architecture. I am unsure if this is a port of the PS3 or PS4 version. What I will say is that the game looks great and comes with a variety of resolution options as well as windowed, full screen and borderless window.
In addition to those options the PC port also supports a variety of other video options including antialiasing, color correction, shadows, anisoptropic filtering, tex quality, post filter aa, unsharp mask, and Ambient occlusion.
These options are certainly welcome and a good step up from other ports from Square. Though it is disappointing the game still appears to be capped at 30fps. Its not a deal breaker as this isn't a fast paced shooter or anything where frame rate really matters.
The game also features a number of 'cheats' ranging from encounter rates to max items, gil and skill unlocks. These are nice options for people that may just want to experience the story. As you might expect acheivements are also available.
With the technical stuff out of the way, this is the same game you remember and love from the PS2 with a new coat of paint. If you never played the original or the remake. You play as Tidus a star Blitzball player and embark on an adventure to defeat Sin. On the way you will meet likeable characters and upgrade them using a sphere grid to unlock new abilities. There are plenty of side activities to partake in including Blitzball, finding all the aeons, acquiring Legendary weapons and more. X-2 is also included which is a matter of take it or leave it for some folks.
All in all FFX/X-2 HD for PC is a solid port and is something Square should carry forward from here on out and seek to raise the bar even higher.
*UPDATE*
I forgot to mention that the game features international content as well as rearranged music. Purists can still opt for the original soundtrack though. One of the only criticisms I really have is the same I had with the remaster on PS3/PS4. The updated main character models are quite nice. But the other NPC's don't really match the same attention to detail paid to the main characters. I realize though that overhauling the characters for all of the NPCs would have taken considerable time. But its a disappointment still.

Probably the coolest game I've seen in very long time.
This is an experimental "simulation" FPS, stealth, survival w/ permadeath game with an out-of-order storytelling style, the story of which is revealed through 11 audio tapes which are also your primary objective.
Receiver simulates most or all of the aspects of real life gun handling, but NOT in the horrific, "Surgeon Simulator" way that sounds.  This is by far its most fascinating--and fun!--feature.  It also sports a simple and unobtrusive soundtrack that, for me, draws me straight into this dark, simply rendered, rough-around-the-edges, strange, and wonderful place.
The controls take some getting used to, mostly because of the complex actions they are used to perform.  FPS veterans: forget everything you think you know about first person shooters for this one.  The panic that sets in at the disheartening *click click* of an empty chamber, unloaded magazine, or an uncocked hammer, as an enemy bears down on you, is wonderful and frightening.
Still, not terribly long into my first session, I found myself, mostly through muscle memory, ejecting a magazine to peek at how many rounds I have left, loading it back into the gun, peeking in the chamber to make sure I have a round loaded, taking a deep breath, and rounding a corner to fire directly into the camera of a robotic sentry gun just as it "beeps" in hostile recognition, seconds from destroying me.  Only after the encounter was over did I realize I was completely on autopilot.
Receiver is definitely the most unexpected, fascinating, and mechanically interesting game I have played in a long time.  It is breathtaking in its visceral simplicity.  It requires a certain sense of open minded wonder to fully appreciate, and it is certainly filled with flaws, both in terms of polish (it was made in 7 days for a competition) and in terms of its unusual game mechanics.  However, at $5 full price, it's a deep breath of fresh air, and I find myself wondering whether--and hoping--other shooters  will look to Receiver for inspiration.  I won't hold my breath.

It's a typing game about food. No, wait, it's a food game about typing.
It's Typing of the Dead without the zombies, but with more hamburgers, steaks, lobsters, and cilantro. OK, there's no cilantro. But there's anchovies. And when someone wants them on a pizza, you have to oblige no matter how much it hurts.
It's frantic. You're juggling multiple orders while new ones keep coming in in a roughshod attempt to get them all in perfect order. A maintained combo means better pay at the end of the day. Rewards await those who pull off the perfect day. Juggle a menu between highly complicated dishes with expensive prices and easier ones that don't quite make as much. Customize your menu to match the requirements for, and then beat the pants off of, the daily bet. Compete in Iron Che—I mean Cook. Iron Cook, yes—challenges. Grow from a meager hole-in-the-wall diner to a five star establishment, complete with whiny, needy celebrities to indulge!
Try to keep up. You won't. You'll try, but you won't. And then, one day, you will. It will be glorious. And all the while you'll have one hell of a time.

Cook, Serve, Delicious! is a high octane restaurant sim, complete with typing elements and a whole lot of stress. The game is simple and enjoyable (as long as you can handle making a few mistakes here and there) and is also surprisingly replayable and long for a petty price tag of $9.99.
Players are tasked with building up a menu of food items and successfully getting through a day with serving as many customers as possible with a minimal number of complaints. In order to cook the food on the menu, players must either use their mouse or keyboard to assemble all the required components of the item - more complex food (like sushi or salad) require more components, whereas simpler items (like coffee and pretzels) require less components. The player then has to find the perfect balance between high-income food items and low-complexity food items in order to turn a hefty profit and insure that customers don't walk out of the restaurant with an empty stomach. Over time, catering missions, contests and better food becomes available - these make sure that you don't get tired of playing the game after a few hours, and trust me, you won't.
The graphics are a simple art style that is neither good nor bad. The music found in the game changes depending on the time of day - Spanish fiesta music plays during the afternoon whereas calm and weary music plays before closing time. There isn't much of a story, except for the goal to constantly improve the restaurant's star rating, but you will find that the game doesn't need one since it is more or less an arcade title.
For $9.99, you're going to find that this game is a great deal. I picked it up during the WInter Sale for $4.99 - maybe keep a look out for it in the upcoming Summer Sale if you want to save money. This game could easily serve as a time-killer OR a full-fledged personal favourite, depending on whatever mood you are in. The bottom line however: it's great, buy it and you won't regret it.

This is not a game I expected to like.  The sample images turned me off, and I only got this game because of buying a charity bundle at some point.
But I finally tried it, and I have to say, for the most part, it definitely works.  The atmosphere works tremendously well--and that's saying something for a short indie game.  The look and feel of it all, along with the utterly fantastic ambient music, create a constant feeling of dread as you move through the game.
Now there are pros and cons.  The line art for the backgrounds is amazing and incredibly detailed--but close-ups and anything in motion look terrible.  The endings are abrupt and unfulfilling--but you won't regret the journey getting there.   When the game is subtle, it's fantastic--when it's direct, it falls short; not every jump scare needs a crescendo!
Should you buy it?  Maybe when it's on sale.  But it's worth playing, definitely.

A nice short narrative with a solid linear gameplay design. The Final Station isn't exactly a deeply complex game, and it's also in no way a rougelike despite its resource management and survival gameplay. However, what's here is a game that's worth a playthrough for its plot, great world building, lore, fantastic atmosphere, and awesome visuals.
The combat feels very tactile and tight, giving you a feeling of total control of your weapons, with enemies being sufficiently tough without feeling too weak nor being on the verge on being bullet sponges. A lot of times, you're encouraged to run away or use certain environmental objects such as boxes, chairs and barrels to dispose of enemies, along with a basic melee attack so you can conserve your ammo for larger mobs.
The level design in terms of gameplay does get a bit repetitive, but the game's length is just about right so it never really verges on the feeling of overstaying its welcome. Going back to the visuals, one of the best things about The Final Station is behind its artwork, especially evident during train rides with beautiful vistas and barren wastelands evoking a very atmospheric environment.
Detailing further on the survival elements and resource management, The Final Station takes a similar approach to the Metro games rather than modern roguelikes. Shops are far between levels, and the game just provides a little bit more than enough resources to equip yourself while making sure every person on your train can come out alive, as long as you're playing it smart.
One of the most glaring issues behind The Final Station is perhaps on the fact that the game isn't also really all that difficult despite the survival elements. You can easily get the hang out of the resource management and train maintenance an hour into the game. Another thing, the game is also really generous when it comes to checkpoints, so deaths in the game rarely feels frustrating, making deaths feel like a light slap on the wrist. Despite being relatively light on the challenge though, it's still feels a lot of fun to go through and outsmart a large group of enemies using just barely enough weapons and resources. There's also an undeniable sense of accomplishment too when you are able to get all of your passengers to their destination alive and well, on top of the rewards you're handed out with.
Overall The Final Station isn't something you play for its length or replay value, but if you want a good solid linear experience after getting burnt out on open world games, or just want to trek through a nice entertaining train ride while looking at pretty scenery, The Final Station provides enough polished content to make it worth a playthrough.

The Final Station is one of those few single-player story-driven games that have left me satisfied overall and doesn't follow most of the fads of most indie-titles from recent times. The concept itself was interesting already, and the execution didn't leave much to be desired in the end. This is one of those games that has a simple concept and gameplay as a strength, which is further enhanced by the narrative and satisfyingly fleshed-out world the game takes place in.
What is good:
-The art is very atmospheric and detailed enough without being too distracting or non-specific for its style.
-The controls and gameplay are simple, yet satisfying. You can shoot, you can scavenge, you don't feel like you're limited in a contrived manner.
-The narrative and how it is told. All the events were made in a way that they felt they mattered, especially the supernatural and key story events.
-The concept, surviving on a train to get to the next stop, rescuing people, finding supplies. Survival is important without taking all the priority and overshadowing everything else in the game like some recent titles without any narrative.
-The heavy inspiration from Russian/Soviet science fiction and how the world is fleshed out without revealing everything.
What could have been done better:
-When on the train, it's hard to follow the story because keeping people alive and fixing malfunctions in the train systems requires split-second decision making and takes your full attention. You want to read what the other characters have to say, but you can't because either one will starve to death if you don't exit the train immediately or you're too busy running for a medkit so someone doesn't bleed to death.
-While the way the story is structured and told is interesting, the more abstract parts of the story (unnamed reoccuring characters with their own plan outside of the main narrative, the ending, for example) are far too abstract and confusing. To be honest, they feel a little bit out of place because they make at best 2 appearances total. This is one of the few times traditional story structure would have helped.
-(POTENTIAL SPOILER) The ending. I get it, happy endings are too mainstream and whatnot, but it would be best to get a more traditional ending that gives at least some answers and more closure. The traditional indie-game endings are far too cliche now, while this one isn't the worst. Would be nice to have something better next time. The worst thing a game can do is make you feel like all you did was for nothing.
-The game hooks you in with the levels, story, and setting, but doesn't feel like it lasts long enough (this point is clearly subjective).
Conclusion:
The story, setting, gameplay, and art are this game's strong points. While it has some small flaws that do not detract too much from the main experience, the game is satisfying overall and is very close to what I wanted and expected from it. I hope that the world of this game is expanded further and we get a sequel that expands the story, answers more questions, and fixes the previous game's flaws.
Thanks to the developers for their hard work, I hope to see more.

Like the creator, I also suffer from both depression and O.C.D, so before the game came out I wondered how it could possibly depict what it's like to suffer from these illnesses, especially O.C.D. as it isn't an illness that I could imagine working well within a game. However, having now played the game, I actually think it does a really good job of showing the kind of mindset people who suffer from these kinds of illnesses experience.
Not only do I think the game does a good job of showing what it's like inside the mind of people who suffer from these illnesses, but I also think it does a good job as a horror game in its own right. Whilst some of the more frigtening moments are just jump scares, it does very well to create a very creepy environment that really made me feel like I had to escape.
I also liked the cool, hand-drawn art style. Being creepy, yet simplistic, it manages to fit in well with the eerie World in the game, whilst at the same time fitting in with the underlying tone of the game, that is trying to get across what it's like to suffer from depression and O.C.D. as suffering from O.C.D. often makes simple tasks a source of great distress and anxiety, which the art style seems to be a metaphor for.
To summarise, whether you just like horror games, or whether you're interested in getting an insight into what it's like to suffer from one or more mental illnesses, Neverending Nightmares is a game I'd recommend.

The Final Station is a story/adventure game which keeps the story filled with lot's of blanks leaving you to imagine and make your own theories until the end when everything is revealed.
That's what I'd like to say.
In reality, the story does have lot's of blanks leaving you guessing and making up your own theories as to what's going on until the end, where it stays like that and nothing is answered.
If you like the idea of having to live with your own theories about what happened and leave it like that tthen great. However if you are like most people who do eventually wan't answers to the story then you may as well click off now.
I made the mistake of pre-ordering The Final Station as when I saw the youtuber previews which consisted of about 20 minutes of gameplay I was super excited and took advantage of the pre-order sale.
First off, it's not in anyway shape or form a survival game. While it may look like one it really isn't. You have passengers which you must feed and heal if they are injured. However these passengers mean nothing, you don't get anything other than some money or rewards and an achievement for brining them all in. If they all die it has no impact on anything.
The looting is completely scripted. If you loot the whole level you will always have "just enough". If you die you just respawn at one of the many checkpoints which seem to be every five metres away, leaving no penalty for dying or healing yourself. This game is not hardcore in anyway.
The combat is brilliant, the gun play feels simplistic, but in a good way. The little heart attack when you open a door and an enemy pops out is great, it keeps you alert every time you open a door for fear you will get rushed. I really did like the combat and the main part of the game I enjoyed.
The main issue for me apart from the story is the length. In the game there is a map of all the stations in the game which any person would think means all of the stations you will go to as the game never says otherwise. The gameplay is four hours (I have played this game 3 times, mainly for achievements) and for the price is not worth it. Especially when you are in one of the last stations and the game makes you think you are barely half way on the map. Considering the un answered story I feel it is not worth what you pay.
TL;DR
The Final Station's ending leaves you with lots of questions which you will never have answered. The combat is great but for the price and the length (four hours) I do not find it worth your time. A DLC was released which should have been free or a euro which is the main reason I havn't bought it as it's just the same old.
If you really like the look of the game and don't mind spending the cash then go for it, but don't expect any updates by the developers, at least not free ones.

Obligatory header to the review: I focus on four primary areas whenever I review a game: gameplay, story, graphics, and sound/audio/general things that go into your earholes. Gameplay and Story get a rating scale from 1 to 10, and the AV stuff gets a rating from 1 to 5. My philosophy on this is that there are some instances in which a game may not necessarily have that much in the way of gameplay (take Amnesia for example), but the story/atmosphere/whatever it may be is reason enough to pick it up. Also, take the cumulative score with a grain of salt; it's just a numerical feeling about the game as a whole. That's part of why I do these subscores. Also, keep in mind that I'm not going off of school grade based rankings. A 5/10 denotes what I feel to be an average game. Likewise, 7/10 is a game that I think is pretty cool, and something that gets a 2/10 is near-abomination level. Pinning scores to an even further obfuscated rating scale is kinda senseless, but for the sake of my backloggery, I'll repeat again that 1.0-2.7 is a one-star game, 3.0-4.7 is a two-star game, 5.0-6.7, 7.0-8.7, and 9.0-10 are three, four, and five stars, respectively.
Gameplay: Definitely one of the more interesting FPSes I've played. It's easily described as Slender but with guns, and while that's not bad, it does miss what this game is truly about, which is to emulate gun mechanics as accurately as possible. No longer in this game are you able to press the easy reload button. Instead, you have to go through the motions for each and every gun. While that may sound tedious, it's actually pretty fun in execution. Much like Slender, this game does have a very randomized nature to it, which can be both a benefit and a downfall. It's always disappointing being met with three turrets in a row whenever you've only got three bullets in your magazine. This game can be completed relatively quickly (hence the short playtime, but there's another reason for that), but it's still a pretty fun game nonetheless. 7/10.
Story: Hey guys, do you like The Matrix? If so, you'll be able to tell ALL of the "inspirations"! But hey, they did it in a non-linear manner, so that's pretty neat. 6/10.
Graphics: The sore spot of this game. The game looks alright for a game that was submitted to a game jam, but HOLY BUTTS IS IT UNDEROPTIMIZED. Apparently the reason for this is because they used an older version of Unity, but even after using the mods (the reason why my playtime is apparently only 50 minutes), the game still ran my GTX 760 through the ringer. This is also apparently because of how the lighting is handled. Plus, there's some pretty obvious and ugly gaps in the level geometry. There's also loading zones here and there that bring the game to a screeching halt so that things can load or something. Either way, the graphics side of this game, even though it was for a game jam, is potentially a deal breaker for some (since they may not be able to run it). 1/5.
Music: Well, there is none. The voiceacting is pretty uninterested (presumably one of the devs), but the gun sounds are alright...? I dunno; nothing too remarkable here. 2/5.
Overall score is 7/6/1/2; 5.0/10. Again, keep in mind that this game was made in seven days. However, this still doesn't excuse how bad it runs, as it just feels like I paid money for a throwaway project. A decent throwaway project, but a throwaway project nonetheless. It's still fairly fun, though; pick it up when it's like $1 or something.

Everything Test Drive Unlimited should have been, and almost like Horizon on steroids... It's not very often we get a racing game like this on PC, if ever.
The Good:
-Handling far improved from the Beta, especially if using a controller
-Tuning/Customization is one of the most fun aspects of the game, it's not perfect and I'd love to see some more options like airride and ornamental lighting, but a very well implemented system none the less
-Huge Open World, drive wherever you want with no boundaries, tones of US landmarks and official Race Tracks, one of my favorite aspects
-In-Game Purchases: Now you may ask "why is this listed under the good?", let me explain.. I in no way condone in-game purchases or P2W modeled games, but in here it's different. While you can pay real money for cars/customization objects, EVERYTHING in the game can be bought with ingame credits, and even if you make an in-game purchase like I did for a vehicle, you may have a slight edge to beginwith in your story missions, but by the time you hit end game content everyone is really even, so not necessarily "good", but it's for those of us who want instant gratification rather than grinding.
The Bad:
-Car Selection.... As much as I love Muscle cars and the usual cookie cutter Exotics, where are the Japanese imports? Especially for a game with that Fast & Furious feel. Nissan is the only JDM Manufacturer in the Game and only includes the R34 Skyline GT-R and the 370z, I'm a Subaru fan myself and in a game with offroad aspects it was very sad to see them not make the cut.
-The Story, while I did enjoy some aspects of the story, this is definitely an MMO style game first and single player game after. It's not terrible, but it does feel like it was thrown in as a simple way to introduce all the mechanics of the game.

Final Score: 8/10

This game grabbed everything good from the Need For Speed games, Burnout games and even Test Drive Unlimited 2.
After the gap left in my heart by the NFS series and its... turn to the worse... I was in need of another racing game...
For a few moments, Test Drive Unlimited 1 and 2 along with Midnight Club 3 and L.A. kept me entertained... and then there was nothing...
But look no further! This game will scratch your street racing itch in a way only Need For Speed Most Wanted (the good one) did!
EDIT (Wild Run expansion): The Wild Run expansion added a whole bunch of new features, giving the game even more content! Although I still feel like there are a bunch of flaws (looking at you, Monster Trucks...) I think it's definitly worth getting with the Wild Run expansion!
EDIT (Calling All Units expansion: Ergh... they dun' goofed...  this expansion, unlike the previous, adds close to nothing aside from a few re-skinned cars to look like cops... aaaaaand this brings us to the horrible chases...
Chases -could- be fun and done right (like in NFS: Hot Pursuit)... but instead we have chases where about five cops spawn in front of you out of nowhere AND that are somehow able to keep up with you (because Crown Victorias are -surely- capable of going alongside a tuned Pagani Hyura...)... but, to be honest... this is understandable.
BUT... the PvP chases ARE NOT... you can get busted going 300 KM/h just because the other player is keeping up with you... and then you have the class differences...
If you start a chase it doesn't matter at all what you are driving... if you want to level up your Street Spec, good luck... most cop players will catch up easily with their Perf/Circuit specs... again, not a problem... you can start the chase right after being Busted.
Buuuuuuuuuuuut the same cop will be called and you WILL be harrassed by said cop... every. Time. You. Restart.
Now, on the cop side, you'll be lucky if your "fellow" interceptors don't knock you 10 miles in the opposite direction because reasons... same with other player cops...
As for single player content...
The new character is awful. Seriously. Absolutely horrible.
The missions are boring and easy... and there aren't many of them.
So...
TL;DR
The Crew - It's a good racing game with a whole bunch of content! Not perfect but not bad! 7/10
Wild Run - Amazing. Does exactly what you want from an expansion; more content and more hours of fun! 8.5/10!
Calling All Units - Utter garbage. I do NOT recomend this expansion. At all.
But yeah. The game is great fun! Calling All Units crippled it slighly, but it's still great!

If your looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an outstanding pie recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie
Directions:
1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.

Although this game has its issues, it's fun at its core. It was a steal for about 15 dollars, and highly worth the money.
The multiplayer has lots of customization options. From what you were before the KPA invaded (which number is in the 20s) to the amount of different helments, gas masks, shinguards, etc. in the game (which is at least 200+), it isn't too hard to find a look that meets your needs. The missions are fun and challenging on the "hard" difficulty.
The main game is good as well. Although the story is somewhat cliche, the different places you go to look amazing and provide you with lots of eye-candy. The gradual change in the environment from KPA to Resistance also is refreshing.
The gun custimization is somewhat limited but good as well. You can attatch silencers to muzzle-breaks on a multitude firearms, and all of them do their job quite well. The addition of allowing you to change your firearm's attachment and "mode" is also refreshing and very useful. For example, if you have the modification, you can transform the long ranged, silent crossbow into a flamethrower to decimate and roast infantry (literally).
Although the capturing of the different zones has been labeled "repetitive," I actually found it quite varied. The tasks for each point you captured were different and forced me to think about how to liberate each one. One notable one I remember was when I came across a capture point where you had to somehow get a motorcycle onto a roof to charge a generator and capture the area.
The voice acting, I must admit, was only alright, and there still exists multiple AI bugs and glitches that need attention.
Another thing I would like to touch on is the the cap of 20 skills per character in the multiplayer "Resistance Mode." Although well intentioned, this cap only limits your character's potential and forces you to use more than one character.
Overall, this game is well worth the cost if it is on sale; however, if it is not so I suggest that you wait until another one comes along.
Thanks for reading!

Brilliant game, the atmosphere is chilling and the art is wonderful. The first time I played this game, I was truly blown away by how gorgeous the enviroments were accompanied by an abundance of detail. The storyline is amazing, and the end left me speechless; a beautiful tale of love (as well as showing that love can be felt and received by anyone). The lighting in this game can create some gorgeous sights, and the lack thereof can send chills down your spine, granted the game isn't a horror, and I don't know whether it was intended or simply my own paranoia, but there are some cases where you may get a little scared, I'm not going to post any spoilers; but let's just say the house has plenty of backstory.
Gameplay 9/10 (Controls are smooth, game works as you want it too; occasionaly getting stuck in doors)
Level Design 9/10 (Beautiful area, the house gains more complexity as the game continues, but stays gorgeous)
Soundtrack 8/10 (Throwback songs, not to mention the chillingly haunting tunes whenever a note from Sam is played)

I can't really recommend this game.  It really IS a walking simulator.  There's really only one puzzle in this game, and all it is is finding two halves of a combination (also, there are several "dead end" locks and combinations that literally don't lead anywhere aside from a sidestory or two that feel shoved into the game enough as it is).  In fact, most all of this game is in fact optional (the path to the ending can be opened up within the first two minutes of "gameplay" if you either know where to look or just check EVERYWHERE).  If you're expecting something like Myst or other point-and-click adventures, you will be SADLY disappointed.
The story is, admittedly, not BAD, but it's also (a) not all that great, either, and (b) not exactly told in the most engaging way,  I'd say "Spoiler Warning" here, but honestly the progression is so obvious that I'm not going to bother:  Your sister's gay, your parents go "it's just a phase", and she runs away with her lover just before you get home.  Obviously there's a BIT more to it than that, but not much, and it becomes VERY obvious VERY early on that that's what happened.  And honestly, this probably would have worked better as a short film or book, but for whatever reason they decided to make it a game (a term which I use rather loosely here).  Also, why do I hear my sister's voice coming from A ♥♥♥♥ING KEY and not a journal?
I WANT to recommend the music, but I can only do that for three or four tracks in this game:  The ambient music isn't bad, but it only makes up one or two of those tracks, and the stuff by the in-game band "Girlscout".  Honestly, check out the soundtrack on youtube or something, and then buy it elsewhere, but don't get this game, and DEFINITELY don't get it at full price.
All in all, pas this one up unless you're part of the hipster crowd and want to feel superior to the CoD masses - which granted I don't necessarily blame you for, but you could feel the same way by playing Fez, or Doom, or Amnesia, or...well just about any other title on Steam really.
Graphics aren't bad, tho.  Not really all that MUCH to look at, but it's got some pretty paintings in some rooms.

The first game is clunky in terms of gameplay, and the controls are slow to respond. It makes you feel mortal, feeble, and insignificant, as you should--you're being put against those with souls strong enough so as to call themselves gods. It's supposed to be hard. Quite hard. And so it was. Dark Souls II is faster, and smoother. You are cursed, yes, and you feel its diminishing effects each time you die. The curse is the focus. The land is therefore, thematically speaking, rightfully baren, plagued, abandoned, and forgotten. The first Dark Souls is certainly more vivid in color and it feels more grand because you are fighting creatures of immense mythical weight, trying to desert or prolong a long-lasting kingdom that belongs to gods. That doesn't mean that Dark Souls II is any less of an amazing game. It has its own riddles and its own respites of beauty among the disease that surrounds you. And, of course, the third game, focuses on the fire itself. Much faster than both of its predecessors and more detailed than both, it's a return to the roots of where Dark Souls came: a poetic conclusion. The gods are dead, and only their ashes and curse upon humanity remain. In the last game, you are at last allowed to choose for yourself how you wish to use the First Flame. It's a shame that Dark Souls II was cast aside. In its own way it's just as glorious as the other games--in darker tones. In it, you're essentially as much of a scholar of the old gods as Drangleic's king and his brother. It takes a step back from what is seen as the "main plot," the one that Dark Souls began, in order to analyze it and view it from an outside perspective. For that, I raise my glass and say cheers to this game with just as much vigor and enthusiasm as I would for the other games. It's no less valuable or symbolic than the others--it just has a focus on the bleak.

This game is not for everyone, but for those it IS for - horror fans with a penchant for the disturbed and a slow burn to keep you on edge, rather than the gore  and jump scares that permeate modern horror - it will resonate within your psyche for a while. If you like fast-paced action, obvious story, open-world exploration, or your sanity, please move on, because you will find none of that here. However, for what this game is - an atmospheric horror game with an ambiguous story open to interpretation - it's fantastic.
The game is short. There are 4 possible endings, and as of this review, I've completed 2 of them with only 2.4 hours on record, and even then there were a few times when I left the keyboard for a few minutes or would intentionally do something stupid just to see what would happen. Your first playthrough will only take about two hours (maybe less), then you can use a waypoint-like system to revisit earlier chapters to get to the other endings. I'm estimating 4-5 hours for completion of all 4 endings (assuming you use a spoiler-free guide to know where the branching points are, like I did).
The game is very linear. But that's not always a bad thing. Not every game needs to be an open-world Bethesda behemoth. Linear works great for this game. It's high tension, and it manages to encourage exploration while still discouraging you from getting too far off the intended path. I won't explain how - because spoilers - but that's a tough act to balance, and this game does it without breaking the atmosphere.
The art is, put simply, evocative. It holds multiple layers of detail. There were countless times when I took a closer look at a scene or a room I'd walked through before and realized the nuances I hadn't consciously observed prior, but at some level I know I witnessed them unconsciously and they added to the overall atmosphere.
Don't even get me started on the soundtrack. Oh my god the soundtrack. I want the soundtrack as a standalone purchase for my horror-themed events. It's amazing background ambience, and it's superbly mixed with haunting sound effects to deliver an experience like none other, especially through headphones (the game highly recommends headphones and utilizes a special audio mixer for that immersive experience).

I bought this on a whim after seeing a few pictures, watching a trailer and reading the synopsis: "Travel by train through a dying world. Look after your passengers, keep your train operational, and make sure you can always reach the next station. Make your way through swarms of infected at each station. Explore mysterious and abandoned stations looking for supplies and survivors." A rogue-like game where you drive around the country in a train, picking up passengers, delivering them to their destinations, maintaining the train, exploring derelict stations... hell yeah, sign me up for some of that.
And at first the game really didn't disappoint even a little bit. The first hour had me completely engrossed in the game and I couldn't tear myself away (which is not good at work!). I eagerly swooped into every station, scouring every container for food, medkits and ammo and feared opening every door. But then it started to become problematic. What I thought was a rogue-like was actually a linear narrative from beginning to end and once you figure out the secret behind the mighty fist, combat becomes far simpler, reducing what started out as pulse gripping horror to repetitive clicking. Rare were the times when the game didn't eagerly offer up some clever solution to the combat, a trick as it were, to avoid spending bullets and the later in the game, the more explosives you find littering the corridor. And if no explosive barrels are nearby the enemies themselves are explosive and with their inability to climb ladders, mere elevation is their biggest foe.
And the train simulation is more of the same. Well, no shooting or punching or exploding but a repetitive motion that you go through because... well, you have to. Or do you? The jury is out on that one as all you get for your troubles is money and upgrades and I honestly needed neither. You'll come across plenty of passengers but you're never given a choice whether they get to go on your train or remain once they're on. They all sit there, talking amongst themselves and bleeding on the upholstry. Your job then is to feed them, dress their wounds and make sure they have air to breathe, a troublesome task at first but ever so slowly it too becomes repititive and easy. The game gives you just enough of all resources plus a little more to get by if you explore the stations in detail and with the simple combat, there's no reason not to.
So all you've really got are pretty graphics, a story and heaps and heaps of atmosphere. The first times you explore stations, that first journey through a tunnel, first time exploring a city, it sucks you in and doesn't let you go. Listening in on the passengers's conversations and reading all the notes you come across paints a mental picture of the world you temporarily inhabit and the lives people lead. But little by little the story kind of gets away from you and your interest in the world vanes equally. There's a huge chunk of the game where nothing really happens and you're bogged down by repition and samey, featureless environments, the narrative sort of... taking a break before it picks back up in the third act. But at that point the gameplay is already stretched too thin to be interesting and there are a few strange design decisios that really didn't gel with me. And consequences seem to be non-existant. Keep passengers alive or let them die, fire missiles, talk with all the people, go straight to the object, explore the stations. Nothing truly seem to matter as long as you get to the end.
As such the game feels... unfinished. The narrative itself is interesting but fails to maintain interest and the gameplay isn't free enough to truly make it interesting. If I had a choice of where to go and the journey got harder, more engaging as we went then perhaps the gameplay would've been more interesting. If the resource management was more detailed and there were more options then perhaps the gameplay would've been more interesting. If my character could grow and his arsenal and train was customizable then maybe the gameplay would've been more interesting.
But it isn't. And it's a shame too because there are some breathtaking moments in this game that whispered of so much more. But the second act isn't as solid as it needs to be to carry the narrative for four hours and neither is the gameplay. Cut an hour of the game, add some more meaningful exploration and a few tough choices to make along the way and the game would've received a glowing recommendation. As it is, it only receives a thumbs up because of the graphics, what little the story manages to salvage and that first, glorious, brilliant first hour. Just don't expect a rogue like, at least not yet...

The mechanics are very cool, just the ability to manipulate every aspect of your firearm is cool enough in and of itself. Once you get the hang of it and can start filling mags, loading them and get shooting-ready without thinking about it you start feeling like a serious badass, and a lot of that is just figuring out how to get your weapon to work.
That said this game is very, very, very difficult. If you really don't understand all the little aspects of your 'mission' you're in trouble from the start, you'll probably end up dying a lot even after you figure out how to go about things.
The 'story' for this game feels more like a few base concepts. It is totally non-linear or 'structureless,' but how much actual impact it has on the game itself is questionable at best. Yes it's the 'goal' but beyond being an item to collect it seems fairly secondary. It has to be vague enough not to have a start or an end or to be collected in any order, so there isn't much really happening there. It's experimental, certainly, and a little eerie in certain ways, but that's about it, it's as open ended as the level composition and I'm not sure that it really succeeds at much of anything other than reinforcing a general atmosphere of uncertainty. That said it's not 'bad,' it just seems a little tacked on.
Either way, if it's cheap I reccomend giving this a shot, rather literally. While I don't think this game by itself is a one hundred percent ten out of ten game of the year I do appreciate what it's trying to do and think that more games like this, innovating in even simple ways with mechanics that are generally pretty staid (lookin' at you FPS' in general), are more than welcome.

The mission layout and open world nature are akin to farcry. So if you aren't into that repetitive nature, it may be best to steer clear. The story is forgettable, but it does have redeemable qualities. Being made with assets from crytek allows for this game to be above average graphically. It is no crysis 3 or even ryse son of rome, but it is solid graphically. Let it be known, this is not an amazing game, or even a great game, but for it to be considered the worst game of the year is laughable to me.

Five Nights at Freddy's 2 is definitely a major improvement on the first game with a bunch of different mechanics being introduced with my favorite being the fact that you must keep an eye on a music box which can't be forgotten or else it will be an isntant loss.
Much like the first game I made it through the entire game without suffering defeat, I was able to find the strategy to be used quite quickly.  It is a simple strategy to understand but it does have its flaws but those flaws did not hit me and I kept my flawless record even in the all 20 mode.  I was lucky to get through the all 20 mode however with the puppet not far off getting me but the clock turned 6 and I won.  Quite a close call but it left me flawless which I was happy to keep.
There are a bunch of new mechanics which I've enjoyed.
Keeping control of the music box is definitely the most difficult seeing how if it dies out you're done, from what I've been told if the wheel empties, then the classic jack in the box music sounds and the puppet takes you out.
There is a completely new enemy to watch out for which is the balloon boy, if he is able to make it into your security office then he causes your flashlight to malfunction and then you're not able to prevent foxy from getting to you.  You are able to keep everything in check, but the foxy will come and unless you're close to 6, you will lose.
Of course there is foxy, as there are no doors in this game there is no way to just stop foxy from getting into the room, the only way to keep foxy out is to flash your flashlight down the main corridor.  Foxy will show in the corridor and the game explains to flash your light down the hallway multiple times which will cause foxy to backoff.
As there are no doors to close out your enemies throughout the night the game has given you a Freddy mask, if you're in imminent danger then you can put on the mask and then when the animatronics enter the room they will simply leave again not realizing who you are, however the Freddy mask does not work on all the animatronics.
Overall Five Nights at Freddy's 2 is a decent game, by far better than the first.  All the different mechanics of the game working together made it quite enjoyable, although it was an easy game for me it may not be as easy for anyone else but it will definitely still be enjoyable.

It is a fun game that really keeps you playing for hours, but that doesn't mean it isn't without its fair share of flaws.
This game gives you all of the tools from the get-go to create a town meant for survival, but it suffers from a lack of depth in the gameplay.  There is no sense of progression aside from getting all of the buildings in your menu on the map.  After the first few hours of setting everything up, I found myself toggling between pause and 10x speed, just because of how slow the game was.  At times, I wished there was a 20x speed feature, just so I could have something to do between balancing resources and waiting for my population to increase.
Something like travel speed research, harvesting technique improvements, improved animal husbandry, etc. would greatly add a lot of customization to the gameplay.  To help balance this easier survival, disasters could be more frequent based on the number of improvements (ala under the hood point assignmnet for technology researched and increasing disaster frequency based on that).
While it provides charts and data for you to understand what's going on, the data is limited to a single window, which makes it difficult to understand the rate/net rate of resource acquisition.  This could be fixed with mods, but it would be great to have that for a finished product.  Additionally, on larger maps, it is almost required to create mini towns as opposed to districts, making for fairly redundant gameplay.
Some features that would be great for a game like this would be terraforming and possibly barges/boats to help transport resources across the map, since the AI has a tendency to have civilians starve/freeze due to long travel distances.  The marketplaces help to alleviate this issue, but since some buildings take up a lot of land, civilians still have to travel a considerable distance, resulting in death or otherwise linear gameplay (in the sense that you have to do things in a specific build order/style).  Lastly, it would be fantastic if the player could get a sort of emotional attachment to the life, from brith to death, of a civilian as opposed to looking at them as merely a tally for how many people need to fill a job.
Overall, it was fun for the first 19-20 hours, but once the game is figured out and the novelty wears off, the game loses a lot of replayability due to everything feeling linear.  Worth the price for what you get though.

Was very keen to try this one... (Watch out people, another long one. This one’s slightly personal).
…for a few key reasons!
In its description it reads “Neverending Nightmares is a psychological horror game inspired by the developer's actual battle with mental illness.”, “Nightmare worlds inspired by real life struggles with OCD and depression”. Which are all points of interest for me. I really enjoy psychology and I have had more than my fair share of mental illness myself in much of the same respects. Being someone who has also had experiences with depression and night terrors, it was almost personal to me. I had to try this game.
I’ve read very mixed reviews on this.
Some love it, others think that it’s not a horror, not scary or compelling enough to play because of its “Walking Simulator” qualities. Which I’d have to say is true to certain extents, there is quite a bit of walking, but the nature of this game is not the norm. This isn’t a typical horror game. I’d say this is more of an experience then a horror game. At least that is the way that it comes across to me.
I was very interested to see what kind of stuff would come up in this from what it’s based on. The difficult thing with dreams and nightmares is you can show and tell someone what happened, but you can’t always bring across the emotions, how you felt and the general tone and atmosphere of the dream for that very reason. An example being that I have a phobia (or Phonophobia to be more precise), an irrational fear, which I could try to explain to someone, but ultimately they’ll never understand the real feeling of having this overwhelming fear for something even you know is absolutely ridiculous.
(This is where it gets personal, skip this section if you frankly couldn’t give a rat’s♥♥♥♥♥♥)
The one thing this game brought back from the back junk filed caverns of my brain was an experience I had. I would wake up (still dreaming) in my room, and the tiniest little detail would be out of place. Whatever was out of place would “clue” as to what phobia I had developed in that particular dream. If I didn’t figure it out in time, I’d be killed. By something relating to the phobia I had just developed. For example, an out of place poster on my wall that advertised Claustrophobia. I didn’t recognise it in time, a TV turned on in my room and it showed rows upon rows of beds, pairs of which that were opposite each other would slowly move toward another, then slam together face to face. Crushing the people inside. Starting from the furthest away and working its way to me I had to force myself to “wake up”. Only to wake up in my room again, a new slightly different oddity in my room, a new clue and a new phobia.
This happened what felt like hundreds of times. Safe to say when I finally woke up for real I was sat on my bed examining my room for something out of place like a true maniac. That experience being what this game reminded me of. It’s not the exact same, but it definitely rang a few bells.
I am beyond a pansy when it comes to scary games and I was able to play this without stopping, hiding behind something and absolutely dreading moving forward like I have with traditional horror games. It’s gory, but it’s not particularly scary. Don’t get me wrong, this game builds tension and suspense and really had me and my heart rate going at times, but I don’t play many horrors games because of how big of a baby I am. If it couldn’t get my of all people’s jimmies truly rustling, I doubt it will for you.
Gameplay wise, you walk, you avoid and you run. There isn’t much to it, but where it lacks in gameplay it makes up in other aspects. The art style and use of colour is wonderful. Things that are coloured can be interacted with. A lot of things you can interest I was honestly curious as to what the significance of. Maybe they are just there for curiosities sake? Some are items you can use but most are just little things in the scene to get a closer look.
The settings are interesting and at times almost labyrinth like. I was torn between feeling like it was linear and I was on the right path and feeling like I was going in circles and was completely lost. It definitely added to the game. Wasn’t at all frustrating for me.
Finally, story. I’m not sure I would go as far as saying there is a story given the nature of nightmares. But you can tell there is definitely a recurring theme. Which is interesting! Made me wonder. This is definitely one of those games I would actually be interested in hearing the developer talk about.
All in all (thank god it’s over, right?) this is a great little indie game. I enjoyed it!
It’s an interesting experience and it’s a pretty easy 100% which is always a nice bonus!
TL;DR : (Don’t blame you) You walk a lot and gameplay wise you don’t do much. But it makes up with that with a wonderful art style and an interesting theme/story. It’s an easy 100% and I think it’s definitely worth a try. Especially if you like this psychology hoop-la, like I do!

"The Crew" is supposed to be advertised as this revolutionary "Always-Online" MMO car racing game that many people have been sitting around for years to be made. It delivers an exciting experience when read on paper, however when actually excuted makes for a sloppily made game which show obvious signs of outdated programming, and included with it an even archaic attempt to jump into the racing genre a few years too late.
The ideas presented for this game are fantastic, an always online MMO where people can join crews and race against each other representing their gang, crew or team. (Basically whatever you want to call it.)
The main problem lies in the focus that the game progression system, driving mechanics, progression system and general programming are flawed in so many ways it makes me wonder what year they drafted this game in before they took it to the crafting table.
Design wise, the game's success is at the core of it's pitch. The "Always online racing MMO car game that thrives while you are offline" with a "Progression system of great detail and complete customization". The game focuses hard on trying to give users a feeling that the world moves on without them, and you can visibly see this in (what should be) other players actively driving around the map going objective to mission points while in active traffic along side you.
Theme wise, it catches the feel of Detroit decent well, but sadly seems more or less like a rip-off towards other racing games themes that tend to stick with the south-central LA area and Detroit (Generic East Coast Theme.) There's no variation in location until the later portion of the game, and for the most part you will only see major shift changes in the locale when you move away from Detroit when you move across central USA, the dirty south, the pacific northwest, and the southwest.
The map's design is heavily (and for the most part completely) based on the idea of the whole USA as a driveable entity. It's lacking point however is that there's little to no detail outside the area of Detroit, and similarly detailed areas tend to stay grouped up within each other leaving huge spans of empty road between the different regions. (Example : Central US, Between Detroit and Florida).
Progression wise, the game tries to give users a sense of calm as progression unlocks aren't solely limited to "street races". Other goals lead to stunt jumps, checkpoint races and time attack objectives. These types of objectives spark the inner racer within all of us who prefer to beat personal times, which is great for some users. However, because progression is done with small objectives in mind to "Level" up your car to qualify for specific races, you'll spend more time driving frustratingly difficult time attack, check point, and stunt jump objectives due to the lack of responsive and "actually useable" car handling.
Car handling is heavily tied to progression as the cars at early levels drive akin to that of an ice cube sliding on the ground. The cars when driven at their base level tend to be very unresponsive at the least, and you're more then likely to spin out regardless of whether or not you slow down at a corner properly or use the emergency breaks. Early game progression unlocks help ease this problem, however like I said before, you will spend a huge amount of time on small unlocks to truly level up your car to it's max potential. The pitch for this is that higher level cars are more responsive, and thus drive better.
Mechanically speaking, the game runs well for what we've seen of it's previously noted issues. (Previously in beta, the animations were directly tied to the frames of the game data). Now that full 60fps support is "Unlocked" in the options, the lack of speed that users claimed to have in the beta is completely gone. You now have a complete sense of speed when you throttle your car above 100mph. *(160kh/m for you other homies out there.)* However, optimization in this game and it's calculation of physics and other players tend to take the game's performance below the 60fps region when in heavy traffic, but never drops below 30fps. *Hint hint* None the less, setting the graphics down in this game will tend to ease the wrath of traffic, of the obvious drawback of image quality. In addition, there are still flaws with the animation which obviously give away the fact the game was from the start developed with 30fps in mind. (Which isn't entirely a big problem, however when you play games like this which rely on user input, the resonsiveness and feeling the user gets while playing is the biggest selling point in how the game performs on a face level.)
**Plot**
I'm not going to say much, so far from what I've experienced the story seems akin to most standard street race movies.
You are the brother to the leader of an infamous street racing gang called the 510. One day he needs you to follow him to a meet up, brother is shot and you get framed as the murderer. Fast forward five years, in an effort to clear your name and find your brothers killer, and the crooked cop who framed you for the murder, you proceed to work for the FBI to rise the ranks and bring justice back to the streets.
Simply put, not exactly the best writing, character development for the lead character is non-existent and the progression of the prologue goes by so fast I honestly thought there was another beginning section I had skipped beforehand.
Multiplayer wise, you're more likely to have more fun playing with the CPU then you do with actual players. Missions introduced throughout the game have two options for execution. You have the ability for solo gameplay which allows you to compete against computer opponents and progress through the game. (The only real MMO online element begins here.)
For actual multiplayer, lobbies are formed via missions when you select the option to "race online" for that specific mission. Users are then paged, and/or formed based on who are currently doing the mission and are gathered from that method. Users past that area, or users who have not progressed to that specific portion of the game typically do not respond or bother to play online due to the lack of users because of inconsistency with progression. Half the time you will spend it again, with the CPU racing offline. With a majority of your online experiences happening at the higher levels where non-mandatory race missions are more freqent and people will be fully utilizing the "Crew" feature more.
Overall, the game is a fun chuckle. It has it's flaws, and could be a great game with fixes. Due to it's limited playability however, and it's very difficult progression system combined with a linearly designed multiplayer it falls short on the expectations created for it at it's announcement. Did Ubisoft deliver what they promised? Partly.
The game however is far from complete. For this, I have to give it a thumbs down. A game in general should be well fleshed out especially past it's multiple alpha, and beta stages which had the ability for vast numbers of user input. At this point in time it should be moderately well developed enough to not show this many flaws.
I've already spent my money, and I'll continue to play it to see how development progresses. At this current point and stage from it's inital release from CORE features that were already planned for the game and is executed in it's fullest, there's no telling what can happen.
tl;dr it's a rushed poor mans version of need for speed before EA became return of the sith
