I have no problem with it, I loved this game, but those who are looking for a more interactive experince may be let down. The game isn't very long, either. If you don't see yourself happy with about two hours of game time for the price then you may want to pass this up. At least until it's on sale, in which case I highly recommend you get it. Neverending Nightmares was a fantastic experience, and it has been one of the few horror games that I have finished and didn't stop thinking about it. The way the game is presented is fantastic and I would love to something else from the creator of this game.

"The Final Station" is a survival horror game where the main objective is to guide a train and it's passengers from station to station.
The game is divided up into two stages: train stages, where you have to manage the mechanical works of the train, and take care of the passengers by bringing them food and treating their various medical ailments, and station stages, where you have to explore a town to search for a passcode that will grant access to the next station as well as gather new passengers, ammunition, and supplies needed to make the trip. Towns are populated by humans infected with an illness that turns them into pitch black creatures who will attack you on sight. The weapons and ammunition needed to fend them off are in short supply, which adds to the overall "survive" feel of the game.
The overall plot of the game is gathered from the stories of passengers on your train, emails from your coworkers on the train's computers, and notes left behind in the abandoned cities you explore. This gives the game a very haunting and mysterious overall feeling. Part of the fun is simply piecing together what exactly is happening from the clues you find.
Overall, this is a solidly made game, but the story really engages you to play this to the very end.

Before you get into the review, let me get this out first, if you don't like the gameplay of Far Cry 4, then STOP, I assure you you’ll find the gameplay of Homefront : The Revolution tedious and repetitive, as the game takes great inspiration from Far Cry 3 & 4, although it doesn’t do it better. However, if you like the gameplay of Far Cry 4, then you might like this game.
Let me just say first hand that I love the core gameplay itself. People may deem it very repetitive, but I don’t mind. The game itself is very fun and is interesting enough to get me to finish the campaign, but MAN is this game riddled with a lot of issues. I think a lot of people reviewed this game a little too harshly, but I wouldn’t blame them for getting frustrated while playing through this game, cause I did a couple of times.
Let’s start with the positives of this game;
+ The world is absolutely detailed and believable, you really feel like you’re being dragged into a dystopian Philadelphia. Red zones looks like they were ravaged by war and Yellow zones really feel like it is occupied by the North Koreans ( Norks )
+ The gameplay pays homage to Crysis and Far Cry, which is fine and offers enough variety to keep you going through the campaign. You also have a lot jobs to take, outposts to liberate, and Norks to kill to keep you busy.
+ The weapon conversion system is an interesting concept and interjects smoothly into the gameplay, however I feel like it could’ve been done better.
+ Yellow zones are a blast to play in, where you have to employ this hit and run tactic and lurk in the alleys where you plan your next move.
Apart from that, there’s not much else that sets this game apart from the others. It does, however, have a lot of negatives which pretty much sums up why a lot of people disliked the game;
-  As I’ve stated before, gameplay does get repetitive and may force people away as they get further into the campaign
- The story is pretty generic and the ending isn’t very satisfying
- Gunplay feels clunky and is below average compared to recent shooters
- Some mission designs are abysmal
- The game is very stingy when it comes to autosaving, so prepare to be frustrated when the game crashes
- The characters, oh my god the characters, are some of the most forgettable and deplorable characters I have ever seen from any game I’ve played. They can be either generic to downright annoying, let me give you some examples;
a. The silent protagonist, Brady, I don’t get why this guy doesn’t talk, so much awkward situations could be avoided if the guy had just said a word, but he didn’t. The guy just doesn’t talk throughout the entire campaign and it’s pretty annoying
b. Perrish, this guy isn’t a bad character, but he’s not a good one either. He’s like your dad who always tries to fit in by trying to be funny, but always ends up doing it in the wrong situations.
c. Moore, the psychotic ♥♥♥♥♥ who’s backstory is so vague that you just don’t ♥♥♥♥ing care and want to stay away from her as far as possible. Her actions are always straightforward and end up being dumb and bad for everyone.
d. Dr. Burnett, the guy who complains and whines about everything. He is always against everything the resistance does making me wonder why he joined the resistance in the first place.
- Red zones, ♥♥♥♥ red zones. There are so many things that could’ve been done better when it comes to red zones. For instance;
a. Airships, they’re a unique concept, but they end up being infuriating in this game. They seem to be designed for only one thing, and that’s to track YOU. They ignore every resistance fighters they shine their light on and ONLY go red when they see you.
b. Enemies, sometimes they’re dumb and  just stand still, sometimes they’re smart and try to flank you. They also spawn out of thin air and track you like blood hounds if you’re in a red zone.
c. Bikes, again a unique concept, but falls short. Driving isn’t very fun and ends up being slower than running due to the many debris that blocks the roads in the red zone
In the end, Homefront: The Revolution feels rushed and is a missed opportunity. There are so many unique concepts, like the story and the game mechanics, however they aren’t really done properly and ends up being an annoyance that drives players away. It’s definitely not worth full price, but if you don’t mind the repetitive gameplay, I’d recommend getting it during a sale. < 6 / 10 >

Alright, so I got this game a few days ago, and from some of the reviews and many YouTube videos I was under the impression that I wasted my money. FOrtunately enough, I gave the game a go. Hereès what I found out for myself:
Pros:
- Immersive Campaign
- Variety of weapons and customizations
- Lengthy story (This is mainly if you're like me and hate driving in this game)
Cons:
- Not the best console ported game in the world
- (In my Opinion) Certain customizations don't go with weapons you wish they would :c
- Seems to be that there's no PVP mode..
Overall I would give this game an 8/10, it's great, looks amazing if your computer can handle it on highest settings and you won't regret your campaign playthrough. I can't speak for the COOP mode as I haven't even made an effort to try that yet, but maybe try to get this game on sale.

The good
-Realistic gun mechanics that show how simplified guns really are in most video games
-Pseudo-random world generation makes for a different game every time
-Extremely intense gameplay, due to permadeath
-Enemy drones malfunction based on where you shoot them. (example, shoot the battery and the drone stops rotating, or shoot the tazer and a drone will follow you around but can't hurt you) This can make for some interesting situations.
-Overall an extremely challengeing game, still haven't gotten more then 5 tapes.
The bad
-Very poorly optimized. My computer gets pretty hot.
-Quite a few bugs, my flashlight never works anymore, some stairs you cant climb without jumping.
-Visually unappealing, simple shapes and no texturing.
-Despite random level generation, the game doesn't have much replayability. You'll probably see all the rooms within half an hour.
-Only two different types of enemies.
-Sometimes you will respawn with little to no ammo, and have to die and restart.
Some general opinions
If you are looking for any of these types of games you shouldn't buy receiver.
-You are looking for a game with replayability
-You are looking for a game with decent graphics.
-You are looking for a cakewalk of a game (easy).
If you can get over these things then I say go for it. Me personally though, I kinda wish I had my $5 back (but now that I have it I'll try to beat it).

Receiver's fun. You run around shooting these sneaky little robots. The twist is that the gun that you weild is painfully realistic. Quite a few firearm mechanics come into play in this game. For someone like me who has shot guns quite a bit(FAR from an expert with guns though), I picked up on it pretty quick. The game looks nice. It's going for a minimalistic style which it achieves nicely(at least to my eyes).
However, it's HORRIBLY optimized. You've probably heard this from the bad reviews, and what they say is true. For how it looks and how much is going on, this game should not run my graphics card hotter than Battlefeild at a lower frame rate. If you have $5, go for it. It's a few hours entertainment for less than the cost of a movie ticket.

This game was really atypical and I am struggling to give it a rating. Here are some things that i liked and didn't like
Things I liked:
+ The atmosphere is perfect - At some points this is all that drove me through the game. The atmosphere really sets the mood for going through an unfamiliar house.
+The game is really simple and is pretty relaxing - For some this may be a turn off, I found myself stuck on where to go because the game has little to no direction. You have a very minor motivation that is provided to you at the beginning and that is it.
+The house! - This is probably the coolest house ever. I got a lot of fun just exploring this house that seemed pretty real and overall it was enjoyable just to be there.
What I didn't like:
-Not a lot of substance - It's hard to recommend the game at full price because the game is only an hour or two long at best and doesn't necessarily encourage replay.
-No hints - Sometimes the game just lets you wander which can be good or bad. It would have been nice if there was an optional hint system to nudge you along during a bit of a dry period.
Overall if you have the chance to play this game at a discount, absolutely give it a try. While it may be too bland for some, if you appreciate the story-telling style through bits of information left in an explorable environment, this may be a game you can enjoy.

It is a fun game that really keeps you playing for hours, but that doesn't mean it isn't without its fair share of flaws.
This game gives you all of the tools from the get-go to create a town meant for survival, but it suffers from a lack of depth in the gameplay.  There is no sense of progression aside from getting all of the buildings in your menu on the map.  After the first few hours of setting everything up, I found myself toggling between pause and 10x speed, just because of how slow the game was.  At times, I wished there was a 20x speed feature, just so I could have something to do between balancing resources and waiting for my population to increase.
Something like travel speed research, harvesting technique improvements, improved animal husbandry, etc. would greatly add a lot of customization to the gameplay.  To help balance this easier survival, disasters could be more frequent based on the number of improvements (ala under the hood point assignmnet for technology researched and increasing disaster frequency based on that).
While it provides charts and data for you to understand what's going on, the data is limited to a single window, which makes it difficult to understand the rate/net rate of resource acquisition.  This could be fixed with mods, but it would be great to have that for a finished product.  Additionally, on larger maps, it is almost required to create mini towns as opposed to districts, making for fairly redundant gameplay.
Some features that would be great for a game like this would be terraforming and possibly barges/boats to help transport resources across the map, since the AI has a tendency to have civilians starve/freeze due to long travel distances.  The marketplaces help to alleviate this issue, but since some buildings take up a lot of land, civilians still have to travel a considerable distance, resulting in death or otherwise linear gameplay (in the sense that you have to do things in a specific build order/style).  Lastly, it would be fantastic if the player could get a sort of emotional attachment to the life, from brith to death, of a civilian as opposed to looking at them as merely a tally for how many people need to fill a job.
Overall, it was fun for the first 19-20 hours, but once the game is figured out and the novelty wears off, the game loses a lot of replayability due to everything feeling linear.  Worth the price for what you get though.

I don't understand the disdain for Dark Souls II. I've played the trilogy (Demon's Souls is irrelevant here), and this one measures up just as much as the others. The first game is clunky in terms of gameplay, and the controls are slow to respond. It makes you feel mortal, feeble, and insignificant, as you should--you're being put against those with souls strong enough so as to call themselves gods. It's supposed to be hard. Quite hard. And so it was. Dark Souls II is faster, and smoother. You are cursed, yes, and you feel its diminishing effects each time you die. The curse is the focus. The land is therefore, thematically speaking, rightfully baren, plagued, abandoned, and forgotten. The first Dark Souls is certainly more vivid in color and it feels more grand because you are fighting creatures of immense mythical weight, trying to desert or prolong a long-lasting kingdom that belongs to gods. That doesn't mean that Dark Souls II is any less of an amazing game. It has its own riddles and its own respites of beauty among the disease that surrounds you. And, of course, the third game, focuses on the fire itself. Much faster than both of its predecessors and more detailed than both, it's a return to the roots of where Dark Souls came: a poetic conclusion. The gods are dead, and only their ashes and curse upon humanity remain. In the last game, you are at last allowed to choose for yourself how you wish to use the First Flame. It's a shame that Dark Souls II was cast aside. In its own way it's just as glorious as the other games--in darker tones. In it, you're essentially as much of a scholar of the old gods as Drangleic's king and his brother. It takes a step back from what is seen as the "main plot," the one that Dark Souls began, in order to analyze it and view it from an outside perspective. For that, I raise my glass and say cheers to this game with just as much vigor and enthusiasm as I would for the other games. It's no less valuable or symbolic than the others--it just has a focus on the bleak.

Neverending Nightmares, in my opinion, isn't all that great.
It's got an interesting art style, the audio is good, there's a few interesting ideas... But there's not too much more for me to say. Gameplay is... Okay, if not super simple. Mainly just walking left or right, looking for an item, some enemy avoidance or running from enemies in places, going back and forth to and fro. And that'd even be okay... But the story completely lets itself down. Playing it, I knew it was going to be a game that would be made or broken by its story, and it just does not deliver. It has all this mystery, surrealism, themes, and absolutely no pay-off. I don't want to say too much, but the game has three-endings, and not the good multiple ending kind. Basically, there's no real meaning to anything as the endings suggest different potential 'answers', and with that, are the most cliche-horror answers you could think of.
It's not terrible, worth it if interested, and there are some good scares (many front-loaded) and moments, but there's just not enough there, and what is there isn't backed up by a complete vision to be a worthwhile experience. Pieces of it are good and interesting, but let down by simplified, repetitive gameplay, and an uninteresting, cliched open-ended narrative.

I would recommend Neverending Nightmares at a discount if you are disappointed by short play-throughs. I, personally, don't care for game+ type of scenarios or running through alternate endings and such which might be something to consider also. With that said I beat the game in 92 minutes and I can say that my overall experience was pretty good.
On the plus side, the sound is notably magnificent. I really like how the directional queues in the audio contributed to the overall awareness of your impending doom. It goes without saying that sound plays a major role in any scary game or game that wants to immerse you. Equally noteworthy is the art style. You may or may not like the hand-drawn aesthetic, but I like it, though it is worth noting the entire game is rendered this way. There are also a lot of explorable areas along the way to take in the detail if you're in the mood to appreciate the labor that has been put into the artwork.
What I didn't like was the repetition. You will get winded after the first 30 minutes when, despite the inclusion of a few evil creatures, you realize the mechanics are a bit shallow. You look at things that have color, you push the shift key to run from creatures, and you try not to walk into the possessed inmates. That is the challenge in a nut shell, though it shouldn't take away from the real goal of delivering an enjoyable story which you can read all about in the game's description (it is pretty accurate).
Neverending Nightmares is a trip, no doubt about it. The game would be a great way to kill an hour or two if not indulged upon in short bites. Check it out some time.

Okay, now to the review:
Final Station is a great way to burn a weekend the same way you might with your favorite book. The developers took a very show-don't tell approach to a visual novel, and then tacked on simple, but intuitive survival elements and encounter-by-encounter combat.
Whether you enjoy spending a half second to assess a situation before having to decide how to live, or pursuing a mystery a la bread crumbs, you won't be disappointed in this one.
Pros:
-Easy to pickup, yet the mechanics don't get old quick.
-Beautifully developed and well thought out settings.
-Wish the music was more common, but the cues are delightful and well placed.
-Suspense that doesn't rely on jump-scares.
Neu:
-Combat might start to feel repetative, but encounters are well designed rarely repeated.
-Survival mechanics are probably only kept from being boring by how narrow the margins for errors are.
-Game is about 4-5 hours long with little replayability. Not calling this a con, as it felt just right for the story and what the game has to offer in general. $3/hour is nothing to complain about imo.
Cons:
-English is clearly the second language of the devs :P It is very readable, but occasional syntax errors and typos broke immersion for me.
-The ending is nothing spectacular compared to the meaty middle of the story.
-Game would be even more suspenseful if there was a penalty for dying that's harsher than losing 5 seconds of progress.

First of all, a bit of background. I've played every single Battlefield game since 1942 up to 3. Every single Call of Duty since the start up to MW2. I quit FPS games a while back because they grew stale and boring and only centered around one area for fun and that became an area in which I needed change.
I do play FPS every now and then, primarily when it's not a bread-and-butter FPS game. CoD and Battlefield remakes stretch on to the horizon and very few have any flair or charm or anything that really pulls you into the game short of just basic, solid shooter mechanics.
. . . This game doesn't even have that.
This game attempts to recrete historical battles in WWI by enacting trench warfare. This is what got my attention. It was an area that had not been really explored much by the FPS genre (excluding the new Battlefield 1 coming up soon) and the premise really intrigued me. That is ... till I played this abomination of a game.
I could continue waxing poetic-like and spinning a story about how bad this game is but I'll get down to the basics. Pros and cons. Good staple.
+ True trench warfare. You stand up, you die. Hugging the ground and hiding behind obstacles are your best chance at survival.
+ Mostly one shot bullet mechanics. These were slugs. Bullets in WWI were not aerodynamic and thus were more forceful. The game holds true to this.
+ Squad based mechanics. You are rewarded for listening to your NCO. Are rewarded for doing tasks that benefit your role, such as covering fire for the machine gunner.
Now, onto the ...
+ Terrible audio. Impossible to tell what directions things are coming from or flying half the time.
+ Bullets rarely go where you aim them. I understand this might be to 'replicate' the feeling of this historic time but it only serves to frustrate the player.
+ Exceedingly slow transition time from standing-to-crouch-to-prone and vice versa. Going from one to the other is horrendously slow.
+ Slow time to get into looking down the sights and back again. Takes almost a full second to look down the sights and another to get back.
+ Cannot reload unless completely standing still. Not even moving is allowed otherwise it stops reloading.
+ Registry feels off. Unsure on this, I gave up before I could test this more (primarily due to my bullets not landing where I was aiming)
+ Repetitive maps (yes, already I am saying that)
+ No killcam. (Some may dislike this but it assists players in learning what they did wrong and what the other player did right.)
+ Sluggish/Archaic controls. Crouch/Prone is  a toggle. Cannot change this. All movement feels as if you're slugging through a bog.
In summation, this game is something I had hoped to really enjoy. I tried giving it a fair shake to learn the ins and outs of it. However, it's extremely two dimensional. It doesn't parade to be anything else but a basic, bread-and-butter shooter with a theme: Trench Warfare. It manages this, but only barely. Even with all my vehemence for EA and their ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ child: DICE, I truly hope that Battlefield 1 does a better job at trench warfare than this abortion of a game.
I learned how to reload and fire a gun properly. In a video game! How the f*** does that even work? Try it for yourself.

UPDATED!
After fiddling with FFB and The Crew's own settings, I've actually managed to get the steering up to a level that is much more realistic, give a closer feel to actually driving. This will also make you a worse driver, competitively speaking, but that's just the nature of the beast. I'll take it, and switch controllers if I need to compete for something. Sometimes FFB turns off randomly. This seems to be a handshake problem between The Crew and the Logitech Profiler software. But it works sometimes and that's not nothing.
Still, the story, is a roadblock to your progress in the game. The rubber banding the cops have on you, the♥♥♥♥♥♥physics (they can stop you by tapping your car), makes your success at a mission totally random. You have to luck out, and I didn't sign up for a game of russian roulette with ai. There's no tactics to the game and you feel cheated because the cops and other cars always spec up to whatever your car is. Dumb story, poor mechanics. Not recommended.
INITIAL REVIEW
So here's my problem with The Crew -- I've been spoiled by Assetto Corsa. The sound, the force feedback, the realistic physics, and responsive handling of AC are phenomenal. The Crew? Falls flat in all of the above categories. The FFB is poorly integrated (no preset profiles for even the most popular wheels, such as the G27). I've fiddled around with the logitech profiler for my wheel and have successfully sobered up from Animal House wasted to Weekend at Bernies buzzed.
Visually, it's underwhelming with terrible aliasing even with TXAA at 4X. I know, it's an MMO, the servers can't handle XYZ. But damn, the cars look clunky. Where on a real car you'd see rounding in a hard edge, you just get one hard line. In short, the gist of the car is captured, but it still feels like it's a model that was made in 2008.
The cars sound like lawnmowers. There is no frequency range in the sounds -- no low frequency humming or higher frequency whining as the engine red-lines. Just a lawnmower, or perhaps a Vitamix powering up. Makes me sad.
The story, (why oh why?!) is something that should be skippable entirely. The most protracted tutorial I've been through, with most of the game kept under lock and key until you complete the story. /Spoiler/ Your brother is killed, you're framed, you're recruited by FBI. Revenge /End Spoiler/ Flat characters, not even an attempt at an original storyline. Which I'd be okay with but for the fact that my handler keeps calling me up all the time, telling me to go to the next mission. Can we just skip the story. Please?!
The HUD is somewhat cartoonish, but I understand where they're coming from. It's NFS meets...well it's NFS. But if I so much as drive half a mile, I get a pop up congratulating me at every checkpoint and asking if I'd like to re-do the past 30 seconds of gameplay. No I do not want time travel as a feature--so please stop breaking my immersion and taking up 1/2 the screen with popups. I'm drivin here!
And of course, when you buy anything from Ubisoft through steam, you have to use their absolute piece of♥♥♥♥♥♥bloatware Uplay. Almost makes buying any ubisoft game altogether unappealing. This is part of why Ubisoft is becoming more hated than EA. Origin is annoying, but at least it has become bearable to use. Uplay is like a horrible amalgamation of the Wii avatar system (why can't I upload my own profile picture?) and some bizzarro world version of steam, where everything is bright, white, and useless.
In short. If you're looking for a driving sim *SIM* placed in a huge open world environment, don't even consider this game. It's not what it was marketed as, and it's not what it is. It's an arcade game. Open world. Expansive. Lack-luster graphics and a bloated, disruptive interface. If you liked the Need For Speed series, by all means, go right ahead. It's NFS with total MMO integration, and it does that very well. What it comes down to is that this game isn't right for me -- a graphics stickler who likes racing that's more sim than arcade. If you don't identify similarly, disregard much of this review. The Crew might be a fun rehashing of Need For Speed. But it's also a souless exercise in making a game as middle of the road as possible.

Your goal is to collect the tapes scattered throughout the game and reach a state of awakening, piecing your story together as you avoid the games treacherous falls and gun-totting, tazer-wielding "Kill-Bots".
No two games you play will be the same, with randomised drops of tapes and ammo, unrelenting and uncomprimising sentry bots, and vivid and vague worlds randomly generated, which will leave you fearing, focused, frustrated, or flying-high, as you attempt to scrounge whatever little ammunition and disordered 8-tracks strewn among the highrise fortresses of a cyberpunk dystopia.

I enjoyed SotfS A TON! As you can see I wrapped up a lot of hours into it, and only few games can achieve that for me. This one did it. So let's have a quick look.
GRAPHICS - It's not too bad but it's not great either. But Dark Souls was never about graphics, was it?
GAMEPLAY - Very solid, hitboxes could use some work, sometimes you just end up stabbed even though you've clearly rolled away.
CONTROLS - As a keyboard/mouse user I've definitely used them even though the store page strongly recommends controller. The default setup is horrendous, however it's not too hard to tweak it to suit you. As it is completely tweakable. I HEAVILY recommend disabling double-clicking as the game responses to your click are then much slower. Also, the option is bugged and you have to switch it on and off every game restart. So get used to it if you're willing to stay for long.
STORY - I didn't follow it too much, but it looks like you're some kind of an undead, hollow, who needs to seek souls in order to lift the curse. And so you're told to meet the king of Drangleic, the kingdom we are in pretty much the entire game.
ANIMATIONS - Solid and fun to look at.
ITEMS - There's a great variety of items, I've been told there's a lot more than in Dark Souls 1.
SOUND/MUSIC - Great soundtrack. Some sounds do sound a bit old. Breaking for example, sounds very low quality to me. But it's good enough.
OVERALL - As someone who played really only through SotfS, I say it's an epic game, I've been really enjoying my time on it and I can totally recommend it!!

This game is a definitely a departure from most of the titles out there. As has been said before, there are no guns, no monsters, no jump scares or twisted secrets, no puzzles or deadly rooms that fill with gas unless things are done just so. It's a game where a girl goes home and explores the empty house that should have been full of welcoming family.
It's a mystery, set on a dark rainy night in the mid-nineties with lots of atmosphere and loads of character. You learn about the people involved and, in the end, probably something about yourself. It's worth the play to anyone who likes a story and has an open mind.
That all being said, it's short. Taking my sweet time it ran me about 3 hours, I played it start to finish in a sitting and may ruin through it one more time. It's more like a short book than a game really in terms or replay. If you like the story you read it again to see if you missed anything the first go 'round. There's a couple journals that are tricky to find and an easter egg buried in there but it's a game without set achievements and the only goal is simply to listen.
The controls are basic but solid, I did find it frustrating at first when I found there were things I could interact with and things that couldn't, things I could read and things I can't For example you can pick up bibles but not most other books and you can't open the books. Feels like a little more time could have been spend allowing you to open things, even if it doesn’t really add anything to the gameplay per-se it would add to the feeling and the mood of the game (which is all the game actually is). You'll also encounter a lot of drawers that are filled with papers and junk but you can't actually pick all of it up or read all of it and even more oddly you can't take most things with you in your backpack.
All of that is really beside the point. It's not about collecting loot, or picking up items that might be useful later it's about exploring and learning and not just the house and the characters but yourself as well.
Lastly, as much as I enjoyed it it's not worth full price, catch it on half or more off sale and you won't be disappointed but for $20 it's not worth the price of admission.

Neverending Nightmares is a short little game, but I would definitely recommend that any horror fan take the time to play through it. The one thing that I would strongly caution people of, is that there are parts of the game that are deeply unsettling particularly to anyone dealing with depression or self-harm issues, as some of the cutscenes and visuals strike pretty close to home in those areas. That being said, it's worth taking the time for.
The storyline is good, a simple premise that is told in an interesting way, while being relatively easy to follow. The cutscenes are informative, but not overly long and they don't distract the player from the game too much.
The gameplay itself is simple, and therefore easy enough to pick up, meaning you can jump right into the game itself without any lengthy tuturials, which is great. There aren't very many controls as the actions of your character are limited, but this simply fuels your desire not to run into any enemies, which is good since you really have no way to combat them. I tend to find that in horror titles, enemies that you can't fight have a higher psychological toll on the player and are therefore more effective generally speaking.
The thing that I love most about this game is the artwork. The visual style of the game is incredibly unique and despite not being a terrifying style in and of itself, it's used in a way that adds to the atmosphere very well. The predominantly black and white color scheme is accented perfectly with just the items of importance being colored, which is a nice way to guide the player through the game without specifically telling them what to do. It also makes for some of the most visually appealing blood I've ever seen in a video game, just because the red on the black and white makes such a shark contrast.
The one issue that I really had with the game was how slow the gameplay was in certain areas. As someone that doesn't have the best sense of direction, I had a tough time through some of the levels in regards to knowing where to go. I couldn't remember where I had been which made knowing which way to go difficult, and it became a bit tedious trying to figure it out when the character moves so slowly (though the slow movement speed does add suspense in a few places.) I also became annoyed only being able to use the run function for short distances, but it was a minor inconvenience.
All in all, I would rate this game very highly and would feel good suggesting it to just about anyone.

Banished has a sort of an old-skool feeling from the early city-building strategy games. The atmosphere in the game is nicely calm and relaxed, at least until you speed up time and half of your population dies of starvation. Beware: you are required to think, act and react.
The game is simple, yet nuanced, and at times deliciously unforgiving. At times it may seem easy, your village flourishes, and one failed crop harvest later your graveyard is full of formerly happy villagers. There is no money involved, as you juggle with various natural and manufactured resources and constantly fluctuating population. This makes the game satisfyingly tricky as you try to not neglect anything in particular to survive and expand amidst of diminishing piles of everything.
I heartily recommend this game for anyone who likes strategy games and building villages. Many, many hours can be sunk into this game, which is quite a feat from a game made by such a small studio.

Ultimately unsatisfying. That's the takeaway from this whole experience.
I jumped on the hype train for this game a long time ago, and in spite of having played no prerelease builds, preordered it so I could enter the experience early, with a fresh set of eyes, before it was spoiled for me. Turns out it wasn't worth the hype or the money.
The gameplay is simple. It's a sidescroller, broken up by chunks on the train where you play a supposed minigame by walking back and forth to deliver resources to passengers. It's not hard. The whole train element was little more than a straight line from chapter to chapter, and the 'crafting' is laughable. Click everything you walk past at stations, click all the things in your conductor's menu.
The game is incredibly short, just over four hours, including a restart I did in order to get an early achievement I missed. I don't see how this game is a gig and a half of memory, especially considering the simple graphics. I don't fault it for the graphics, because graphics are simply a medium to get a point across, and the graphical format does that well enough.
The graphics and design succeed in creating a decent enough atmosphere, if not of horror, of post-apocalyptic civilization, of a world that has been through hell and tried to return to normal. Unfortunately, there's simply not enough story to uphold that atmosphere. You scavenge snippets of story throughout the game, although I ended up missing a fair amount on the train due to the tedious mini-games getting in the way and forcing me to walk off screen while my passengers delivered atmosphere.
I feel like I might have understood the ending (and the entire ending sequence) better if the game had kept conversation logs at the very least, to let me see what I'd missed. Worse, the silent protagonist concept makes us assume what our character has said, when in some cases it really wasn't obvious. Perhaps the game is trying to leave things up to interpretation; but if so, then it's an awful choice to drop hints throughout that lead to actual answers, then not give them to us, or at least enough information that we can guess for ourselves. I'm not going to spoil the limited story, except to say that there is no satisfaction, for the player or the character.

I didn't have the patience to play the game through twice to see if there even is the possibility to do things otherwise, so I am going to be blunt with my review and possibly make few assumptions that might be untrue.
I don't know what I expected from the game, but I didn't exactly get what it looked like at first glance.
If you look at the game and expect some sort of nice survival experience where you gather survivors to your train, scrounge cities for supplies and possibly upgrade your train to hold more people and resources and fight off hordes of definitely-not-zombies, you won't find that here.
It's basically a "horror" sci-fi story. A very linear and a very short one, where your choices won't make any difference, other than getting steam achievements.
It is easily completed in one sitting, which I did. Now, I would've been satisfied with the length
if the story had delivered, but it never did. I had more questions after the game than I had to begin with, nothing was explained.
Enough with the babbling, lets get the review on.
[/h1]Here's the longer story:[/h1] (if you wish to hear things in a nutshell, scroll down)
First of all, the game was decent, it wasn't bad experience, but it wasnt exactly a rosy one either.
The game is cryptic as hell ever since the beginning and even if you go through every single paper piece of information you find, you still won't gather enough puzzle pieces to figure out what's the big picture.
About the graphics, they're good looking pixel graphics for the most part, but especially towards the end, you feel like that they just got lazy when a lot of the backgrounds look like they're high definition sprites that are just slightly pixelated in effort to blend in with the rest of the sprites, such as the train and the characters, that are more rough on the edges and more simplified. It's feels like they're from another game and that they do not belong in this one.
Maybe it's a deliberate design choice, but they still don't fit together.
The combat was lackluster, you could cheese majority of the enemies with your melee and you ever really need bullets on instances where you'd be cornered by a bigger group or when you'd face specific enemy types that either grapple you or explode.
And the way the combat was handled was very scarce. There's basically only 2 weapons. A pistol and a shotgun. Yes, I know there is a "Rifle" later in the game, but, cmon, it's just an upgrade for the pistol, making it automatic, it even uses the same ammo.
Melee was just a slap with your gun or a fist. I would've preferred actual melee weapons, for more variety.
The train sections are mostly a chore. Boring repetitive and bad minigames to keep you occupied for majority of the ride until you arrive at the next station.
If you have passengers or "survivors" on your trains, you hardly ever have the time to listen to them speak about things going on when you're forced to do your chores around the train, making sure things run as they should and that the people are well fed and not bleeding to death through the use of food and medpacks.
Now, about the story... The first 1/4 of the story wasnt good. You're dropped into the pants of this middle-aged balding man you know nothing about, in fact, you know more about the people around you, than you know about the character you're playing. You just mind your business and get to work and you're quickly on rails, and there's no turning back. You go from station to station, there's always few "corrupted" stations where you need to fight your way out to get a code that allows you to move on. Then there are these non-combat stations where you get to explore what little there is and possibly buy some upgrades for your weapons, some food, medkits and ammo. Oh yeah, and there's only like 2 upgrades for both weapons in the whole game. Pistol gets a laser sight and extended clip. Shotgun gets faster reload and extended clip, that's it, nothing fancy.
The 2/4 in the middle of the game is what I enjoyed the most. That's where all the "meat" of the game was.
The story opened a little bit but still not enough to explain what was going on.
Then came the ending that was just begging the question "That's it?"
The problem with the gameplay as a whole was that there wasnt much choice there, no matter what route you took, you'd always end up in where it was intended. There wasnt much to explore in the levels other than few dead-end rooms with possible supplies in them. Other than that, it was just running a straight line from point A to B. They introduce you these interesting cracked walls that you can break with melee or exploding barrels, but they never use them to hide secrets in the levels or possibly offer reroutes, you see them rarely and when used, they're just in the way as a nuisance, rather than a rare discovery.
While in the train, you'd occasionally get these messages from random people, supposedly from employees of the same firm you're working for. They talk with you about whatever and the game sometimes offers you to pick between 2 different dialogue choices, and sometimes only 1 for no apparent reason. These MIGHT have effect on what happens next, but as I stated before, I didnt replay the game to see if this was the case, but I assume, your choices here don't matter.
Biggest issue was that when things in the story got interesting, the game kinda forgot it's past events and completely starts a new chapter in the middle of things. It basically gets your hopes up but never finishes what it started, and before you know it, it's over.
-Buildup
-Ambiance
-Impact of surroundings
-Tension
-Artstyle
-More length
-Better Writing
-Combat variety
-Enemy variety
-More meaningful things to do
-Actual choices that made a difference
-Less minigames, more interactions with the survivors/passengers, make the train sections actually matter
-Grammar check (There were errors in spelling in some dialogues)
-Better price due to it's lack of content
That's about it.
All in all, it's a mediocre story that's constantly teasing you without ever really coming into a conclusion, and after realizing this endless loop, it literally
.
If the writing was better, the lackluster gameplay would've been forgiven, but right about now, it's only a half cooked egg with legs.
On a scale of zero to ten, I give it a 5/10.
I really wished it had this actual survival aspect to it, but it was basically just a short story that was being slowed by the occasional station runs and train minigames.
And I am still none the wiser, what the hell just happened.
Buy the game when it's on discount, the "story" is not worth 15 dollars as it stands.

So to start off the game will take you around 4-5 hours (depending on skill level) to beat the entire game. So if you judge if you should buy something off of time there you go. As for story, this game has a very interesting one that has you pick up small tid bits throughout the game to piece together what's going on. This works for those who like a mystery and want to solve it, but at the same time the story feels like it is trying to do more than it can present, and makes me feel like the value isn't worth it myself.
My biggest issue with the game is how a main chunk of gathering information is through people on a train, that you're too destracted to talk to. The game is going from station to station to reach a goal, at each station you explore and destroy creatures that occupy them, and between them is a segment where you manage the health and hunger of your passengers while making sure the train wont break down. Where one may think that the game wants you to read the information of the station you're heading too, or listening to the passengers, if you do either you're liable to have one drop dead from bleeding wounds, or hunger, or missing a bit of information trying to keep the train from stopping and everyone from dying.
The characters you meet are interesting figures with their own personalities, but with the issue presented above, you'll also notice that they won't cause too much trouble. One of the first men you rescue will make comments of taking over the train or getting his weapon back. However he will never do anything, even if you starve him out. That made me remember, oh he's just pixels not a person.
Other interactions i hated was how you 'talk' to others. The silent character is common in games to allow a person to put themselves in the mindset of the character and say whatever that character said, but in the game there are segments where you text other drivers with a choice between two or one statement, and in the stations you dont get to see what the character says, just how others react to what your person says. Also if you, say, find a man underground that looks infected in a populated area right under a military official and want to say hey there's trouble down there, or even. Infected below, you won't get a shot.
The story itself, as i said is a mysterous, interesting, but short piece. It has two main parts, one having the character go south, and one going back North. Though the second part for why isn't explained that much until you get to the end, but is hinted at throughout the game, the first part's goal is explained as it happens, and is done so pretty well through the rest stops signifying the end of an act. Some parts to me seemed to be less effective than they could have been, where i should have felt a complete loss of hope, I was more like, oh that sucks, and moved on. Though I will say the game truly tries to be the best it can be, there are just marks that didnt hit hard enough.
The gameplay itself isn't special either and doesn't give the right feelings to the game in my opinion. It's not horrible, but I'd want a way to make it more intense, where you can feel the fear the character should have in a better way. Maybe with a way to make the positions randomized, or have it so if you're next to a door a small soundclip of the creatures is heard through them, or something. I don't know, once again you can tell the effort that went into this and how they really tried to convey the dread but it once again didn't connect all to well.
A long review short is that The game is pretty good. Just not good enough for me to recommend.
I can see the effort put into the game and I'll be watching the devolopers because the potential is here and these stories are good, but need a slightly better composition somehow.

This game is a truly unique FPS-experience, and I recommend it to everyone who plays FPS, casual or professional.
Your ingame-goal is simple, but considering the challenges featured it's actually hard to achieve.
Your foes might lack sentience and versatility, but they are a strong opposition. You have an immobile and a highly manouverable type of enemy. Especially latter ones are powerful in numbers, but even immobile foes can kill you. Your reaction-time is short and you need to make the most of a second in many cases. Sure, immobile targets are easy to hit, but if you cannot see them and need to guess where they are by the noise of their machinery, you might end up getting shot.
Unlike almost every fps, you have no health-bar and one hit or even a jump from too high obstacles are certain doom.
Your arsenal is restricted to the one weapon you start with and a random amount of ammo and magazines (unless of course you start with the revolver).
Your aiming and timing are the most important things. Here comes why:
You truly need to manage your weapon. In order to load, you need to take out the magazine and reload it manually. In case you have multiple magazines (which is not guaranteed), you can prepare spare-magazines. Still, in a heaty situation like being chased by a flying drone it's still a challenge to just switch magazines.
The realistic mechanic of handling a hand-gun is Receiver's crowning-achievement and the stuff that makes this game totally unique and more challenging than the hardest PVP-multiplayer-shooters.
For 5 bucks, you get an always new layout of the map, different spawn-spots for drones and ammo, the tapes and flashlights.

First of all let me start with this: This game, feels like a dream. And I mean your usual dream where you are stranded in a place that you dont know at all. Who are you? Dont know. What are you doing here? Dont know. The only thing you know is this: You have to move forward and do this thing no matter what happens.
And that is what this game does. It tells you about the "Second Visitation". A event that seems to be rather... Bad? Good? It depends on where you stand and how you see it. But going further into this would already spoil too much.

- I have not tried to use my controller (Xbox 360) and wont try it. The K+M controls are doing very good for a game of this nature.

- A game stands and falls with its music. If the music does not fit the setting, the setting is ruined. Intense scene - Intense music.
3. The game does not directly show or tell you what happened a moment ago
- While playing the game you will come across things or will see things happening that will leave you confused or even a bit creeped out. And sometimes these events are not accompanied by music or sound to notify that it happened. And that is a good thing.

The Cons are:
1. The Cons are non

But since I love dreamlike games or stories, I am kind of willing to accept everything without caring too much about something little that may affect the gameplay of other people in a bad way. You know, like a dream basically. Sometimes in your dreams there are things that you dont like but you cant make them go away just because of that. Its a dream and it does what it wants.
End Result:

So, let's get this out of the way first: Homefront: The Revolution is not as bad as the Steam user score and many of the critic reviews said it was. Yes, it has its fair share of problems. Yes, the game was horrendously buggy on release. And yes, it's extremely derivative, and often feels like any one of open-world shooters that are so popular right now in the gaming space. Having said all that, the game isn't awful, and it's certainly playable, especially now 8 months after release, with most of the gamebreaking bugs patched out.
So, let's start with the premise. Homefront: The Revolution is not a sequel to the 2011 game (though it started out as one,) but is instead a reboot of the series, with the same premise of an America occupied by North Korea, and you take on the role, again, of an American citizen, Ethan Brady, waging guerrilla war on the KPA. Surprisingly, the premise here somehow manages to be somehow worse than the first game. While the ideas that it explores are interesting (technology with backdoors, leading to powerlessness of the military when their equipment is turned off,) the idea that Silicon Valley could have started in North Korea in the 1970's is just laughably ridiculous, even by the premises most games expect you to suspend your disbelief for. If it had been another country than North Korea (China, for example, or even Russia, stale as that would have been,) then it would have actually been a very interesting idea. Needless to say, it just feels goofy.
Once you get over the nonsensical set-up, the actual game's plot is pretty decent. It's certainly not going to win any awards, especially when compared to several AAA game plots that have been written recently, but it's definitely interesting/entertaining enough to keep you enthralled throughout its 20 or so hour runtime (depending on how many of the side activities you undertake.) It's a pretty simple story of resistance and guerrilla warfare, and it tries to put in a somewhat interesting debate about the morals of violent insurgency vs peaceful protesting, but this debate is really hampered by the fact that Brady is a silent protagonist. While the NPC characters are fun and likeable characters to be around, and are extremely charismatic and well-acted, Brady's silence means that the player has no ability to weigh in on the debate whatsoever, one of the main complaints I have with silent protagonists in games anyway, but it's accentuated here by their attempt to have some sort of moral argument. Overall, the story is decent, with a pretty satisfying ending that still allows for the possibility of a sequel.
In terms of the gameplay, I'm happy to report that Homefront is the second game that I know of to successfully capture the feel of guerrilla warfare (the first being Red Faction: Guerrilla.) This game is hard, and you absolutely have to play it like a hit-and-run resistance fighter. The KPA soldiers have better weapons and armor than you, and will always have greater numbers. In addition, the armoured cars and drones patrolling the streets will kill you in a  matter of seconds if you don't have cover. The game uses a health kit system instead of regenerating health, which is a wonderful decision for forcing you to play it smart and not a run and gun like the first game, but it can be a bit frustrating at times if you're caught out in the open without any kind of health kits. Of course, you have options for fighting back as well, and while the two weapon limit can seem restrictive at first, the game includes a weapon customization system like the Crysis games, and it really shines here. For example, your basic pistol can transform into a silent pneumatic powered dart gun, or a rapid-fire SMG, while the assault rifle can also turn into a LMG or a grenade launcher. This means that even though you can't carry a full complement of weaponry, you always have multiple for how to engage the KPA soldiers in the streets. You also have the ability to craft items such as IEDs, Molotov Cocktails, and hacking items.
The open world is split into a series of gameplay zones, each falling under the classification of Red or Yellow zones. Red zones are essentially bombed out war zones, with the KPA attacking on sight and being patrolled by the terrifying airships overhead. Here, it plays most like a typical shooter, with you capturing strike points to expand Resistance influence and stall the KPA temporarily. Yellow zones, on the other hand, are the more interesting of the two. This is where the majority of civilians live, and they're heavily guarded police zones that feel like something out of 1984. Here, you have to stay stealthy, and pulling a weapon in public view will bring hell down on you as you are attacked by tons of heavily armed KPA forces. To trigger revolution here, you have to commit acts such as sabotaging loudspeakers, killing KPA soldiers to free civilians, and capturing Strike Points here as well. even though the zones are fun, Homefront is still an incredibly derivative shooter, and whether or not you think this is a bad thing will depend on how sick you are of the model. Personally, I don't play too many open world games, so I enjoyed it, but by the end even I was feeling fatigued at the prospect of capturing more of the same kind of Strike Points and taking on jobs to earn money that are actually pretty annoying because they force you to either photograph enemies/items in the world, or kill a certain amount of enemies one set way. However, most of the activities are entirely optional, and you can skip most of them if you just want to rush through the story as fast as possible.
As for the visuals, it's really a stunning looking game. While the first Homefront (which ran on Unreal Engine 3,) looked pretty awful, this one runs on Cryengine and is a gorgeous looking game. The zones all have their own distinct look and feel, which is nice. The sound is good as well, with the guns all sounding and feeling punchy, and the voice acting is top-notch. Unfortunately, the soundtrack is rather lackluster, with no particularly good tracks that you'll want to listen to after.
Now, for the bugs. If you've held off on The Revolution for all the gamebreaking bugs that were present at launch, well, I'm happy to report that those are gone, with only mostly visual bugs remaining. I did encounter a couple bugs that prevented me from capturing Strike Points, but nothing that would stop me from completing the game.
So, should you buy Homefront? It really depends on how sick you are with open-world games in general. If you've played the Far Cry games to death and want more, you'll definitely like it. If you hated those, there's nothing here that will change your mind. But I will say it's gotten far worse press than it deserves, because what you have here is a fun open-world shooter that gives you the feel of being a Resistance fighter, with a pretty good and inspirational story of standing up and fighting back.

Is this a great game? No. Is it worth 40$? Nope. But is it as bad as a lot of people are saying it is? I really don't think so.
Homefront: The Revolution has A LOT of problems, some of which I'll list down below, but all in all, I'd honestly say this is a decent game that's worth picking up on the cheap.
Positives:
- It's gorgeous. Definitely one of the most impressive looking FPS games I've played in a long time.
- Great soundtrack.
- Decent voice acting and dialogue.
- It's a solid PC port. It has a ton of options, and it looks and runs great for me (GTX 970, i7 6700k, 16gb DDR4 RAM).
- The gunplay is solid, similar to games like Far Cry and the Metro series.
- The attention to detail is seriously spot on. It really feels like you're a part of this dystopian world.
Negatives:
- The story is pretty generic and is not even worth paying attention to.
- The sidequests are pretty terrible, similar to games like Far Cry 4 and No Man's Sky (generic fetch quests).
- The core gameplay loop is definitely the worst part about this game, and it can get awfully repetitive going around liberating outposts and stealthing around the city.
- There's a significant lack of meaningful content in this game, which is the same problem I have with a lot of modern games like (NMS, Far Cry, Mad Max, Just Cause 3, ROTTR and so on), and it really could've been something great if they focused on the story and the characters, and overall gave the world a little bit more personality.
So, overall, I think Homefront is a decent game and I really don't get why people think it's so much worse than your modern Ubisoft fare, like Far Cry 4. If it drops to the 10~15$ mark, I'd say it's definitely worth picking up.

Receiver is probably the most satisfying, and purest (in the sense of gameplay) pick-up-and-play title.  Not only is it directly based on your own readyness/carefulness, but also based on how you know either of the three weapons that you randomly tote, in various states, reserve ammo and placement.  No two playthroughs are the same; each are generated in different ways.
The enemies are one of two, a spinning sentry turrent or the more dangerous air drone.  Each having there own weakpoints to learn and behaviour to adapt to.
You can only take one bullet, which also brings up another thing about Reviever.  You die from one shot, stun or a two story drop.
The weapons, the Glock 18, M1911A1 and Colt Revolver behave realistically aswell.  On top of that, reloading becomes a very important routine, that they all differ.  You need to not only extract the magazine of the 1911, but also swap magazines, load in the cartridges, either hit the slide lock or rack it.  With such a minimalist HUD, you need to count your shots, to drop a mag for inspection.
Also nice touches such as the revolver casings expanding within the cylinder after use, requiring several attempts at the extractor and so on.
All this makes such a satisfying 'in-betweener' game.  Thoroughly recommended.

I want to preface, Dark Souls II isn’t a terrible game. It’s not even a bad game, I had personally had a lot of fun with it, and I will no doubt return to enjoy it sometime in the future. Although Dark Souls II looks, feels and acts like a Souls game, it didn’t share many of the same values its predecessors had.
Dark Souls was originally praised for the kind of difficulty it had. It was tough and brutal if you were impatient or tried to rush, but was more than fair when you were mindful and patient with the environment and enemies. Its story and gameplay complemented one another, and the world felt intertwined and real. Dark Souls II doesn’t really compare in most of these aspects.
In Dark Souls enemy placement was clever and intelligent, you would find a group of enemies and if you were slow and patient, you could challenge them one at a time and pick them off. If you tried to rush, you would run into them and have to fight them all at once, and generally die if you weren’t prepared. This was the beauty of Dark Souls, there was incentive to be patient which complemented the gameplay. Dark Souls II’s enemy placement isn’t as “fair” or intelligent as its predecessor, making you challenge larger groups of enemies instead of being able to pick them off. It tries to rush you into action, which doesn’t complement the style of combat.
The story and lore is also, in my opinion, significantly lackluster compared to Dark Souls or even Dark Souls III. Dark Souls II sits in a weird place, the lore mentions Dark Souls related things, but so vaguely that it doesn’t really matter. It feels like fanservice, and doesn’t seem to have any real significance. The setting ties into this, constantly trying to paint a picture of a desolate, depressing story of losing hope, while the world and setting doesn’t necessarily reflect that with its colors and bright world. Majula serves as Dark Souls II’s Firelink Shrine, being the place where all the NPCs and merchants eventually flock to throughout the game - but unlike Firelink Shrine, it’s bright, happy and relatively care-free. It felt out of place compared to the previous game, setting a different tone which clashed with the story and theme of the game.
Overall Dark Souls II felt flat, and made from necessity and not desire. You’ll hear it often, Dark Souls II didn’t have the same charm the original did. NPCs are rather bland and uninteresting(maybe aside from two particular ruffians), the environment feels rushed, with many blocked doors or bland undetailed/blank walls and ceilings, and similar enemies with a lack of variety, which bleeds into the overall boss design as well. However, as much as I’m bashing Dark Souls II, it’s not all bad.
Hidetaka Miyazaki (lead dev of Dark Souls/Dark Souls III) was leading development for Bloodborne whilst Dark Souls II was being made, which most likely lead to a lot of the problems fans had with this second installment. Miyazaki left some big shoes to fill, and even though there was much left to be desired, Dark Souls II was still a solid game, and actually not a terrible addition to the series. Not to mention the Scholar of the First Sin edition actually addressed many of the issues I personally held for Dark Souls II, enemy placement for example was changed to simulate the original Dark Souls a little more, although not perfectly.
The common consensus I’ve noticed is that Dark Souls II is easier than Dark Souls, and I would have to largely agree. I do think if you’re new to the Souls series, Dark Souls II is the best place to start. The story isn’t coherent compared to Dark Souls and Dark Souls III so you won’t get spoiled, you can’t really go “the wrong way” and be punished for it, and co-oping is much easier than the original Dark Souls. If you like the look of Dark Souls, or find this
an enticing explanation of the game, then you’ll be into Dark Souls II: Scholar of the First Sin

Banished has a sort of an old-skool feeling from the early city-building strategy games. The atmosphere in the game is nicely calm and relaxed, at least until you speed up time and half of your population dies of starvation. Beware: you are required to think, act and react.
The game is simple, yet nuanced, and at times deliciously unforgiving. At times it may seem easy, your village flourishes, and one failed crop harvest later your graveyard is full of formerly happy villagers. There is no money involved, as you juggle with various natural and manufactured resources and constantly fluctuating population. This makes the game satisfyingly tricky as you try to not neglect anything in particular to survive and expand amidst of diminishing piles of everything.
I heartily recommend this game for anyone who likes strategy games and building villages. Many, many hours can be sunk into this game, which is quite a feat from a game made by such a small studio.

Overall I was quite pleased with this game. It's very atmospheric and kind of disturbing. I didn't find it scary, but I don't think a lot of games are. It captures the feeling of wandering through a nightmare where you are unable to exert any control, you just have to stay on the move. However, it does have some flaws. I found that the game didn't successfully keep me in a state of immersion, so a lot of my complaints would be nitpicky for any other genre, but I think that with horror it's really important to keep the player from thinking about how they're playing a game.
The Gorey-esque line drawings are great and I liked the effects when you move into lighter and darker areas. However, you can see the seams of the 3D-looking-2D effect often enough to be jarring (the straightjacket guys turning their heads, for example.)
There's not really a lot of game here (that's not bad necessarily, there's nothing wrong with being an interactive experience) and I was sort of expecting more puzzles, especially with all the flavor stuff to look at. At first I was trying to examine every piece of furniture and object in the house and I was actually a little disappointed to realize that only things in color were interactive. Having such an obvious tell made it seem less immersive. Also, it seems like they front-loaded all the non-plot related weird stuff to look at, because there were quite a few hotspots with nightmare stuff in the first area and then nothing for the rest of the game.
I found myself getting frustrated with the slow pace, especially on replays trying to open different paths. I tend to play for long sessions and unable to not do that, and I think this game would be better parceled out gradually. There's not a lot of game here, I got it on sale but at full price it seems like a lot. I have one more achievment to get, by the time I 100% the game I'll probably have spent less than 3 hours on it. I could see myself having the desire to periodically revisit the game, though.

- I didn't feel the over-all threat of the game. Once I mastered the melee attack, bullet use became a 'I screwed up the initial melee' or '1 shot killed 5 enemies'.
OVER-ALL: 3/5

For $15, it's not a bad 4 hours of time. I've certainly spent money in less intelligent ways. (See: No Man's Sky).

"Neverending Nightmares" is a game that has a lot to offer for some but will fall entirely flat for others.
It is at its core a game about mental illness.  Not the hackneyed, insufficient portrayal seen in most media of "insanity" as a flat stereotype.  This is about mental illnesses as they really are.  This means that those who will most appreciate it are those with a mental illness of their own, or who are well-acquainted with someone with it.
The unusual art style, reminiscent of the work of artist Edward Gorey but with a more sinister bent, lends a uniqueness to the game.  Alternatingly subtle and very unsubtle creepy images saturate it, creating a tense feeling.  Do yourself a favor--play it when everything else around you is quiet, with the lights off.  It won't make you screech in horror and have nightmares, but it will make you nervous and tense the whole time.
The gameplay is really virtually nonexistant.  You wander through various unsettling areas (gore is abundant and you may find its impact diminishes over time, though this was mostly not the case for me) and the only challenges in most cases are "where do I go next?"  But even more mazelike areas are fairly linear, so when it doubt, just wander everywhere and you will eventually find your way.  There are one or two areas where you must navigate around an enemy which might sometimes be tricky, but overall, the point of this game is not to be challenging.
The multiple endings add some replay value and it is not a matter of meeting a lot of fiddly criteria to end up on the correct path--most are contingent on a spare few different actions.  I won't spoil any details but I will say that they might keep you wondering what REALLY happened.
In conclusion, "Neverending Nightmares" is definitely worth playing for anyone who appreciates a different sort of horror game, but will have vastly more to offer to those with a thorough understanding of mental illness in its many forms.

I would describe Just Cause 2 as a game just like Grand Theft Auto in that:
-You can steal every car, plane, or vehicle imagineable (firetrucks, commercial planes, etc).
-You perform missions for several gangs around the nation, which expand their influence.
-Committing crimes will send the police after you. The more havoc you cause, the greater the heat, the greater the force sent to take you down.
-The world is huge, and very open ended. The missions, it seems, are endless. There is so much to do, outside of the main story
It differs from Grand Theft Auto in several key aspects that, in my opinion, make it far superior:
-You're a CIA agent sent from America to take down and cause havoc in a communist island nation. So while you're still causing explosions, shooting cops, working for gangs, you're actually the "good guy". Much better than just being some lowlife thug. You're still a hard core fighter, but with the lack of F-bombs, and the main character displaying a level of intelligence, instead of feeling like ghetto street trash, you feel cool, classy, and in control.
-You have a grappling hook. Seriously, this is what pulls (pun intended) Just Cause 2 far ahead of any game from the Grand Theft Auto franchise. You can use it to quickly scale buildings, hijack airplanes and helicopters while in air, pull enemies off the edge of buildings, etc. It makes things more fun than any open world RPG shooter I've played.
-While I'll admit I get a good laugh from yanking pedestrians off of scooters, and crashing planes into this got a sense of humor I don't find anywhere else. Mostly, it's making fun of communism. I used to live in China, and all of the humorous aspects of it came out. The news flashes were the best. "Reports of the White Tiga taking ova the nulea facility were confirmed false. Gun shot noises tund out to be hardware malfunctions. White Tiga has been confirmed to not exist. He is a work of fiction. And when he is found, he will be executed for treason! Good day." It had me laughing out loud CONSTANTLY.
I highly recommend this game. At full price, it is worth every penny. However, I've often seen it drop down to 80% off. At $2.99, it's a steal (that's the price I bought it at). HOWEVER, I did see it drop down to FREE on 1/12/2014.

Yet another let-down. A game I wanted to love(TM). I updated the review after finishing the game.
The atmosphere is really thick and well done. Reminded me of Limbo and INSIDE in some way, and that's a compliment to a highest degree. The gameplay seems a bit bulky at first, but you'll get over it. I was sold the very first seconds. Sounds are well done, and so is the music.
The train is a weird thing. It's kind of Diner Dash mini game where you have to make sure everyone is healthy and satisfied, and your train does not overload. The customers are talking something, but most of the time I'm missing it out as I'm dashing around. I'd love to read the discussion they're having from somewhere.
But then you start to get to more combat intensive places. Rooms full of enemies, low on clips and getting mauled time after time. Death has no meaning in this game, so you keep on trying and trying. I gave up. There was a ladder, and room full of baddies. Could not get to the room without dying. Could not shoot enemies from the floor below. I HATE THOSE LADDERS.
Also, cardboard boxes and other items seem to be much more effective than the pistol. Fair enough. Ended up carrying a toilet seat half the map just in case :P
I'm not happy with the game. It just doesn't seem to have enough interesting gameplay to warrant the price or my time. All the places seem alike, and there is very little interesting things in there. Story is told via static scenery and post-it notes.. rather easy solution for game with designed levels.
Makes me wish it was some roguelike/procedurally generated game (honestly I though it would be like that based on the trailer though they did not make any claims about it. It just felt like that). Feels like a missed opportunity.
Unfortunately I cannot recommend the game in its current form (the usual I'd give it a "meh" but due to lack of it it's thumbs down).
EDIT:
Finally finished the game. Unfortunately it turned out to be quite bad. While progressing, the feeling of detachment became stronger and stronger. The story, which is actually quite hard to understand and badly written to be honest, does not have any build-up towards the ending. The ending was a huge disappointment. There was no focus on the protagonist, his motives, or background, leaving the ending quite cold and uninteresting.
The game is full of beautiful vistas and thick atmosphere, but instead of cohesive whole it started to feel like I'm jumping from scenario to another without any actual drama, and more like just for the sake of showing different environments.
Anyway. There's a real effort here, but unfortunately it doesn't not work.
Not recommended unless you get it really cheap and have few hours to waste.

This review is mostly for X, but X-2 is a solid game and isn't a bad addition to the series.
I'm sure anyone wanting to buy this game can look up tons of off steam reviews on the original game, and don't need me to delve into why it's easily my favorite Final Fantasy game.  It's a solid game, and the gameplay is great.  The game drops the map system that most Final Fantasies has, in favor of a more linear and story focused experience (for most of the game, later on you get a way to go to the previous locations for side quests).  The story is amazing, but some parts of it might make it seem weaker early on.  The infamous Tidus laughing scene is a good example of this, tho I personally don't mind the scene.   The remastered version makes the game look a lot better, and has a remastered soundtrack  ( that is completely optional via the options, incase you prefer the original).
X-2 has a weak story, but really neat gameplay imo.  Yet to play much of the port of x-2, but I beat the second boss and it worked well.
Anyway, the port is the main reason most of you are worried.
For me, personally, the port is great and has run well.  At the moment, I have a fairly weak computer and struggle to get some games to run due to the bottleneck by my cpu. The game runs at 30 fps constant(which yes, the game is locked at 30 fps but making it run at 60 fps would require an entire overhaul of the game).  Some parts of the game my fps dipped, mostly around the thunder plains, where it'd go down slightly).  The game has never crashed, and I have never had an audio or visual issue that took me away from the game.
Almost at the end of the game, and with 30 hours in it I'd gladly recommend it.  The game was my childhood and runs perfectly on the PC, with little to no problems.  X is easily one of my favorite rpgs of all time, and x-2 is a pretty fun game with a lot of side content.
