When I first started SotFS, my god was it hard to adjust to. The difficulty seemed to spike up and it felt generally unfair how often I would get plowed by enemies. But, like any dark souls game, you gotta persevere and learn from your mistakes, and now, about a year later, it still stands as my favorite entry in the soulsborne franchise.
Pros
- Easily, Dark souls 2 has the best PvP in the entire franchise. Guardbreaking, parrying all feel a lot more natural and more responsive. The online matchmaking is godly, and makes the other games feel inadequate on how easy you can invade people. No weapon is inherently useless, and going through NG to even NG+ with your basic longsword is a viable option. From a lore perspective too, DS2 took a different turn than what DS1 and 3 brought, but in hindsight, it was a welcome change from bleak darkness and the eventual giving up. DS2, having all these people in majula who care for your safety, a general lack of the jerks all over the place, really gave you hope that things will turn out well, a huge selling point for me in the end.
Cons
-Of course, the PvE aspect of DS2 lacks in comparison to the other games. This, of course, was slightly made up for in the Crown DLCs. Some of the soundtrack felt entirely the same, but still manages to get the point across. You'll mostly be telling stories of your time fighting Alonne or the Burnt Ivory King, not that time you summoned Glencour to help you fight Dragonrider. Soul Memory is and always will be the biggest downside to the online portion of the game, but if you're uninterested in taking part of it the point is entirely moot, and can in fact be beneficial for the second entryway into castle drangleic.
In total, none of the soulsborne games are perfect, but that's what makes them unique. A good game I can recommend to anyone from dark souls veterans to someone looking into starting it. 4/5

I don't know if I'd be willing to pay the full $14.99 for this game, but it falls to a mere $2.49-ish during every sale - a price which makes it unreasonable not to have this game in your library. It's your average open world game with rather nice detail. There's tons to see, tons to do, and tons of space. Personally, I have fun playing this game because of the raw destruction. A large part of the game revolves around blowing up structures while running and gunning past waves of enemies, which is a great way to blow off some steam or waste your time.
However, all of this destruction quickly becomes dry and very repetitive. After uprgading your weapons, the enemies stand no chance, even on the highest difficulty, and their AI is borderline ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ at times. My biggest complaint with this game is the story, however. It is utter crap. It was very poorly designed and the cutscenes nauseated me. I just started skipping them, which I almost never do, as the voice acting is garbage and the lips are not synced at all. To be honest, the only reason I finished the main storyline was for achievements.
Overall, I'd give this game a letter grade of B-. Perhaps that is a generous grade, but I think it's fair. I do enjoy playing the game very much, even if it is repetitive and the story is worthless. I recommend buying it with your leftover savings during a steam sale for maximum satisfaction.

An intensely atmospheric psychological horror adventure. Made by the same dude who made Retro/Grade, Neverending Nightmares takes a step into another direction towards anxiety, gore, and terror.
You'll play Thomas (hey, that's my name!), who goes through several episodes of recurring, monster filled nightmares. Driven with the need to wake up and obsession of his sister, Thomas' trails will bring you from a dark and maze-like mansion, through a blood-soaked asylum of savage lunatics, to a creepy forest littered with carcasses. How well this setting is narrated to me is what makes this game remarkable: it's incredibly atmospheric, paints everything black and white with spots of gory red, all while dissecting into a mind suffering from depression, anxiety, and obsession.
I fell in love with this game. Although a lot of parts do feel slow, short, and one particular one being frustrating, it gives me time to soak in the wonderfully hand-drawn artwork and creepy music that follows. This game gives me great hope that along with many indie games in the genre, horror is not dead. If the scares and copious amounts of blood and body parts isn't enough for you horror fans out there, then the well-delivered atmosphere will never leave you hungry.
+ A frightening and mind-provocative narrative delving into the struggles of depression
+ An equally gripping atmosphere that stuns you in its beauty before soaking you in blood
+ Filled with obstacles and terrifying monsters that require different methods to defeat
+ Branching story-lines that reach different endings
+ Several galaxies better than Depression Quest, which tried to tackle the same real-life issue of... um, depression.
- An apparent walking simulator, but with a run button
- Thomas apparently has asthma, so that run button works VERY briefly
- Sweet but short; you might wish for more conclusions to the story
- If you have a deathly fear of babies and dolls, well I have some bad news for you...

This isn't a game. This is an interactive presentation. And as any interactive presentation, it is more about the atmosphere than whether there are puzzles or really a failure state.
I didn't go into this one blind. I had chunks of the story spoiled. And still, it gripped me.
The amount of details is just enough. The pacing is near perfect, the house is believable, seems lived in. It even made me switch the lights off and close all the drawers before leaving a room again, just like it would be my place.
Bit by bit, you learn to know these people, including your own player character. You understand them, respect them as beings. Yes, you might not agree with this or that, or find a decision foolish, and yet, that is what makes them them. At a certain age, you may have acted just the same. Maybe you see yourself in them, too.
You could rush, sure, but the entire place is inviting you to explore, to look at everything. Brush off any gamey thought you might have and just literally rummage through a house of other people. Enjoy the situation, try to be in that world.
Maybe you feel something on the way. Concern, for at least one of them. Or a certain urgency to prevent what you might fear to happen?
If that happens, then this interactive presentation served its purpose.
In the end:
It is a kind of movie where you decide your own pace. It is short (~2 hours taking your time). The replay value is possibly little, and 20 bucks for it seems to be stretching it a lot, but if you have the chance to nab it cheap somewhere (like currently, it is part of the Humble Bundle), go for it.

Disclamer: My recommendation is based on the assumtion that you do use a 'dollar per hour' to decide whether a game is good value for money. I also want to disclose I picked up this game in a Humble Bundle.
Is Gone Home a good game? Is it a game at all? Well, yes and no.
Mechanically, Gone Home is a lesson in interactive environments. Pretty much everything can be picked up, examined and thrown around. There's lots to read and see and a large, well-designed house to wander around. The audio is atmospheric and the distribution of objects gievs impressive realism to an empty home recently bought.
The game runs into some problems in the narrative department though. Multiple small narratives litter the environment, absorbable at your leisure. Your character, Katie Greenbriar, has recent;y returned from Europe to an empty house. By reading the myriad of notes and letters around the house, you establish who the Greenbriar family are, what they all do, their passions and interests. You also figure out why none of them are around. Katie herself is more of a player vessel than anything, having no voice and only expressing her feelings through the occasional item description.
The issue is that only one of the narratives actually turns out to be important and it's not necessarily the one you're most interested in. There are hints towards difficulties with Katie's parents and a dark past involving her great uncle but neither of these narrative paths seem to lead anywhere. The one that does hinges on Katie's sister, Sam, and is told through various objects found around the house that trigger voice-overs.
To be fair, this story is compelling, endearing and well-written. It charts Sam's transition through high school and her relationship with a girl named Lonnie. Letters, tapes, buttons and notes scattered around give more insight into this relationship and as it develops, the boldness and confidence of the writing becomes clearer. I won't spoil it but safe to say it's original, at least in terms of common videogame narrative.
I can't help but feel Gone Home would have benefitted from a tighter focus on this one important narrative. The other trails, red herrings and false starts just made me feel like I wasted a bunch of time. I would even go so far as to say they felt like filler, put in to keep me playing for longer.
For it's current price, £14.99, I would say Gone Home is overpriced. Even rejecting the currently-popular 'dollar per hour' measure, I still feel it's too much for the experience. There's also little replayability, as once you've completed the game it's abundantly clear the other narratives have no importance and the core narrative is so short and simple it's hardly worth playing through a second time.
I would recommend you find some way of playing Gone Home, be it at a friends house, through game-sharing or by picking it up in a sale. It's well worth 3-4 hours of your time; just probably not worth 15 of your hard earned pounds.

Banished, city building and survival: an amazing experience.
You will need to develop a strategy of your own to achieve the most (fun) in this game and build your own unique town.
Decide your own speed too extreme slow to extreme fast with their own challenges to beat. There is no real best speed to play this game at, all speeds have their pros and cons and they’re yours to find out. Choose between resources to produce and buy others from traders or choose to be an isolationist and make everything for yourself. If you choose to be an isolationist, you will be rewarded with an achievement if you manage to survive and build to 300 people. Believe me, the achievements in this game are hard to get. If you somehow manage to get them all you are a true banished master and you have to show something to show off to your friends and to me.
Two major strong points of Banished:
Lots of replay ability, new challenges with every random map.
The achievements, and the general feeling of satisfaction of a proper running town.
The weakness:
The limits you can develop a single town, at a certain point you just have to scale your town up (2 tailors, 2 blacksmiths etc.). The overhead it introduces makes the game harder but you can’t do much about it. Personally I haven’t reached this point yet, but that’s where the relative low review scores come from.
I’ll go off and build another town for another achievement, good luck with your own town!

Just Cause 2 is a fun, anarchy-driven sandbox game that I thoroughly enjoyed. You play a guy with a bunch of guns going around blowing things up on a tiny island. There is a story in Just Cause 2, but it is mostly forgettable and filled with your typical video game tropes like hidden characters that aren’t really hidden and plot twists that are paper-thin. Besides, who needs story when you got stuff to go blow up and territory to go take over?
After a while, finding all the collectables and unlocking all the locations gets extremely tedious, but at that point you’ve become some sort of slaughter filled man-god. The locations also get very same-y, as you grapple-hook over them.
These two mentioned flaws do diminish from the game, but the game is still very fun. The hook itself is a fun mechanic that will amuse you for hours. And the island itself is huge and it’s littered with buildings to blow up, secrets to find, and planes to fly horridly. Overall, I think Just Cause 2 is a wonderful distraction of a game that will fill your down hours with mayhem induced moments.

Remember the fight with the cave troll in Moria in the first "Lord of the Rings" movie? The way Legolas looks at the troll, deciding whether he can risk getting a hit in without being creamed by that massive club? That'll be you in this game—all the time. And it better be, because even the lowliest tutorial enemy is fully capable of taking you down in shockingly few hits if you get careless, inattentive, or cocky for one moment. Needless to say, tougher enemies may frustrate you. But unless the mere thought of losing any fight more than once prompts you to uninstall a game, there is definitely lots of fun to be had here!
Don't put too much effort into designing your first character, as you'll likely be screwing things up a bit and reroll after you get the hang of things. I highly recommend reading a few how-to's and maybe watching a couple of tutorials before fully diving in, as there are ways of snagging a few goodies as well as hobbling yourself early on that can easily be missed.
Also, definitely, absolutely, as soon as humanly or inhumanly possible, get the "Ring of Binding." There's YouTube videos explaining how to grab it without necessarily fighting the enemies standing in your way. Without this ring, it is quite possible to get your character into a state where their HP may be so reduced that they can no longer fight a rat without getting one-shotted, forcing you to delete and start over.
Seriously, get that ring. It's literally a game changer.

I've played through games that were bloody and horrifying, yet Gone Home, a game where you play as a girl returning home from a trip to find that her family isn't there, was one of the most stressful (in a good way) experiences in my gaming history.  Honestly, explaining why is difficult.  Gone Home builds tension in a way that Hitchcock would praise.  I found myself paralyzed in some places, afraid to venture into dark rooms.  Other times, I found myself scrambling to find safe places as quickly as possible.  Furthermore, Gone Home isn't full of gimmicks and pop-up scares.  It's just legitimately bothersome.  Also, I think the thing that makes Gone Home so frightening is the not knowing.  So, if you haven't played it yet, don't read spoilers.
Having said that, SPOILERS BELOW
Okay, if I have one major criticism of the game it's that there's a part near the end that I found to be wholly ridiculous.  In one room, you find what appears to be a Wiccan-esque circle with a pentagram.  When I saw it, I just kind of rolled my eyes.  Are non-Judeo-Christian religions meant to be terrifying?  I don't mean to sound SJW-y, but it was just a silly moment.  It's as if you walked into a room with Buddhist prayer beads and a statue of Gautama Buddha and you were meant to feel like, ooh, spooky!  Anyway, that's my one, tiny criticism of the game.
If I could give it stars, I'd probably give 4/5.  Gone Home is really well-rounded and most of the puzzles are logically solvable.  I would suggest it to anyone who enjoys tension, scary houses, and independent titles in general.

Gone Home is a fairly straightforward game. Through a standard first person control scheme, you are Kaitlin Greenbriar, eldest sister in the Greenbriar family, back from an extended European holiday only to find the Greenbriar family home utterly empty. The crux of the game is uncovering the mystery behind the disappearance of Kaitlin's family.
SPOILERS BELOW. YOU HAVE BEEN ADVISED. IT'S NOT REALLY ANYTHING GROUNDBREAKING OR WORTH KEEPING A SECRET, THOUGH.
Gone Home's story is innately personal, which is why it ultimately feels hollow to witness it through the weird, voyeuristic second-hand experience of sorting through notes, filtering for meaningful information. Occasionally uncovering a milestone piece of information results in a narrated excerpt from Sam's diary, which frankly feels a little bit like cheating since the vast majority of Sam's story arc unfolds through these excerpts, rather than the notes.
Sam and Lonnie's relationship is the primary story arc of the game. It evolves from a subtext-laden friendship to a romance around the half-way point. I am nothing but sympathetic for this kind of thing; and it did hit me hardest when Sam described her mother, Janice Greenbriar, insisting that Sam was going through a "phase", "did not know what she wanted", and "just needed to meet the right guy", but this isn't a story about runaway lesbian teenagers, it's a story about an observer finding out about runaway lesbian teenagers after the fact.
This also isn't to mention the story arcs for the other characters--Terry's writing career, his obsession with the JFK assassination, his dead-end job as a hi-fi hardware reviewer, his alcoholism, and his wife's unfaithfulness--are more interesting than the relationship between Sam and Lonnie.
Gone Home's limited interactivity and 90s culture nostalgia aesthetic don't quite fill the gaps in a story loaded with cliches. In another medium, Gone Home wouldn't be considered anything remarkable. It also suffers from outdated visuals and poor engine optimization (pretty much the entire house is loaded into memory, physics objects and all).
It's important that as the video game industry reaches a larger audience and matures, we must also understand where mature criticism is necessary, where not to lump blind praise, and where to hold a game to the same standards that everyone else receives. I do not think Gone Home's praise is deserved, but I do not think its hate is either.
Gone Home is an interesting experiment in taking the kind of environmental storytelling dating all the way back to System Shock to its furthest conclusion, but not much more than that (and I feel a little insulted that the first number code in the game is 0451).

I've played the game since it was in beta testing and had a lot of fun over time. The theme is unusual in FPS games, the squad setup promotes team-work and some of the maps are genuinely challenging to advance on. There seems to be fairly regular updates, servers are often full and people seem fairly friendly.
But I wouldn't recommend it.
Not if you're after a somewhat realistic-in-feel FPS, that is.
Verdun should be considered an acrade game, and a clunky one at that. Killing enemies is a little too easy (I just went into a server after having not played for a few months - eight kills in a row to no deaths), the key controls are a little awkward, the voice chat so poorly integrated that it's seldom used. Visual effects aren't great and become repetitive quickly, the upgrades are nearly meaningless and voice controls play no real part in the game. You use them for the novelty (as in, "Oh, I haven't got my guy to say something of absolutely no consequence in a while. Let's tell the people standing around me to advance.. even though most of them won't hear it because the game doesn't pick them up very well and doesn't alert those around you that you've given an order").
The graphics, I must be honest, are pretty average. I don't have a high-end computer but on fairly decent settings the sharp edges of each object are apparent; the reflections are just variations of chrome; the further you look the worse it gets; some of the maps are designed to be night time.. which is all well and good except that it severely limits the playability of a map. It might be fun to look around a semi-dark trench for enemies but after a short while it just gets a little tedious. The game just doesn't integrate darkness well.
Crouching and laying down movements aren't smooth and you'll be caught out pressing the wrong button regularly (seriously, why is the default lay key "left ctrl"?); you can't climb over obstacles, either your person can run up an exceptionally steep banking without a fuss or you can't get over something at all. There are several lookout spots (perfect for picking off enemies running toward your trench, right?) that can't be used because if you're standing you're too tall to see through the hole in the wall and if you're crouched you're too low to see through it. Some sort of interaction with the wall, so that you can crouch behind and pop up when you wish, would be good.
There's no friendly fire. What kind of a game of carnage would hold out on friendly fire? I get that it would make it a lot more challenging, but what kind of a game tries to suggests it's even remotely close to real warfare without even having the option of friendly fire? Think there's enemies in your trench but you're not sure if the next thing you shoot at might be a friendly team member? Don't worry, there's no consequence for shooting Hans through the head because you thought he was a Frenchie.
Ambience is lacking. I know, in real life there wouldn't be any background music but there isn't enough action in Verdun to warrant silence but for the sound of your feet, the same chinking noise of what I presume is supposed to be your gear, and the occasional rifle fire. I'm sure you've recognised the hypocricy in my complaining that the lack of friendly fire makes it unrealistic but now I'm campaigning for some background noise - but my point is about enjoyment. Friendly fire would make the game more enjoyable, background audio (distant gunshots, music etc) would make it more immersive.
Verdun could be a good game if it was styled like Red Orchestra - the handling of RO is exceptional compared to Verdun. In all honesty I can't think of a game which has such poor controls as Verdun. It's not that they're necessarily bad, it's just they're clunky and awkward.
Oh, and there's no private servers. All the servers in the game (one per region, with as many games possible at one time as there are maps) are operated by the game developers. So if your connection to the only server in your continent isn't that great, you're pretty much stuck. There's no single player, so you've not got a whole lot of options.
Speaking of servers and maps, there are no custom maps. Community members can't make their own and host them (because, surprise surprise, all the servers are run by the developers). Sure, six maps may sustain a few hours of play initially but after a while people will be interested in new environments. Unfortunately if you want that you'll have to wait for the developers to release another one. Don't get your hopes up with the maps, though, as the best maps were the ones released with the game when it was launched. Every update since then, and every map that's come with it, has gradually made the game less enjoyable.
I was shocked to see this game has been released on Playstation 4. I can't imagine how they managed that. If you're thinking of getting it for PS4 I would recommend holding onto your money and buy something better.

I just did an initial playthrough for Neverending Nightmares last night. I was one of the original Backers for this on Kickstarter, and played the initial demo they had for the fundraiser to get a feel for it. Beyond that I have skipped a lot of the videos and discussions and Alpha/Beta tests so as not to spoil the experience of the game.
Now as you'll see they went with a classic pseudo Edward Gorey style of art, and this I actually like. The pen like line work is kool and the animations and overall look feel very similar to Gorey. It uses a minimalist color scheme, where interaction objects are color so you can easily spot them and know when to use them (though there is few spots to do this aside from a myriad of portraits to view, cell doors to look in and a bunch of dolls to glance at). The game only has a handful of objects to find, a candle, an axe, umm.. that's about it I think.
Most of the game is walking around this large creepy house (or an asylum) just trying to find an end to the "Nightmare". Along the way is a bevy of imagery, creepy/dangerous creatures to avoid and a few mild jump scares.
What works:
Overall sound design is atmospheric and interesting/creepy
Art design is solid
Control of the character (uses Gamepad or keyboard)
Runs at a number of resolutions, all the way to 1080p
Has enhanced audio for headphones (it has a warning that it's better to play on them than speakers)
Disturbing imagery without going overboard.
What misses:
First nightmare seems to have more creepy instances and mild jump scares than any other level
shading//lighting is too "still" (more on this later)
Music becomes quickly monotonous and repetitive
Some areas have noticeable skips where you can tell it's jumping from the end of a hallway to a new hallway when it is supposed to be one continuous hallway
The character has asthma, so you do get a "Sprint" button but you can only use it for short (1/2 a room or so ) bursts and the character makes the same whiny out of breath noises whenever you've sprinted a couple steps.
No interaction with the little dialogue that is there.
Obscure branching paths
aside from a few tense moments when you first encounter an enemy (and learn how to avoid it) the game is mostly walking and navigating.
Where this game just misses is that it feels like everything that is there, at some point was deemed "good enough" instead of "perfect" or "great". This is a trend I suspect I'll see a lot with Indie games and Kickstarter projects by small studio's. With NeN the audio design is good, it has a good somber spooky vibe to the music and the kaleidoscopic of noises that come and go are suitably "horror game" sounding. But that's all it is.. background filler. It rarely ramps up or builds to a crescendo, doesn't try to manipulate the player aside from a simple orchestra hit when something jump-scares you. And most of the atmospheric noises are heard no matter where you are, with a few audio cues added for when you are outside or in the asylum or in a bathroom.
The visual design is serviceable, but what would have made the game a lot more tense and nerve-wracking would be to make the lines creating shadows a lot less static and a lot more "noise". There is a slow crawl series of layers to the lines that create the obscured effect in the game, but they move slowly and from right to left and that's it. Horizontal and vertical lines, when thinking of it like a designer for a home or a useable space, are usually beneficial. vertical lines imply strength and stability. horizontal lines imply peace, calm, and relax a person. ANGLES cause tension. And squiggles or erratic lines also cause tension and unrest. If they had worked on the line work and shading a bit more, and created something that felt unsettled and "restless" when you are simply standing there, it would have worked wonders. I harken to playing the original Fatal Frame and how the simple detail that the view of the game was through a grainy film layer, which made every moment of every scene lack a placid stillness that felt calming, and so you were kept on edge even in moment where you were "safe".
The use of blood around the house was good in the first nightmare, but over time there is more and more blood splatters and strips and puddles. Since there is likely about a dozen or so decals for blood, you see a lot of similar splatters, and over time they end up just feeling cartoonish and copy-paste. Any atmospheric effect it could have is lost, except when you ramp it up and see a room with a LOT of blood on the walls or floor, and by that point it has lost it's shock value.
There are a lot of re-used assets. I imagine they created a lot of the objects for the game individually, then placed them around the house to create a variety of halls, rooms and areas to explore. I am not against this, except after seeing the same doll/chair/painting the 50th time. As well the fact that most of the areas you navigate are (again) static and unmoving makes it feel like " ok here is another room like this.. just need to find the door". In a lot of ways, stacking this idea with the fact some of the levels are maze-like and frustrating to navigate to the object you need or the end of the area, makes it feel like such a slog. I will admit during the second nightmare I was on the edge of shutting the game off out of sheer banal boredom.
I guess for a nightmare, I would have expected the house/asylum/areas outside to feel more "alive". organic. I want a steady stream of dolls turning to watch me, of paintings slightly fading from one normal image to a creepy one. Of stuff poking into the scene just at the edges of the screen where you almost see them, but not quite. When I played the second Phantasmagoria game and you go to work and there is a simulated "computer screen" you can check email with and do some work activities, I loved that every little while (seemingly random), words would change to other words, hard to see but if you manage to spot it you realize it's sinister and evil. It made the simple act of reading email as the character feel disturbing and you would question your sanity. When the environment feels extremely copy paste and static, so you have a good feeling of what will happen and what to expect, it ruins the tension and takes away that feeling of being helpless that makes horror games successful.
The underlying point of the game, to examine and empathize with mental health conditions, and try to evoke a sense of what it is like to have a mental illness, is really what the game was supposed to be about. I think a lot of gamers won't know to look for this or see it at all when playing the game, mostly because it is hinted at and thinly threaded into the game but not so much that it's obvious or too much (and so heavy handed). I think having the entire game be nightmares (which aren't real, and disturbing nightmares are fairly common, so not indicative of a mental disorder) actually spoils any true sense of dread. But really I am sure a lot of folk that play this will think " well i have more disturbing dreams than this, and I am not mentally ill". The idea is in there, within the bones of the game, but being buried enough you have to actively seek them out, and also play the game about 5-6 times to unlock and "see" all of the endings makes it too much work and effort to "get" the point of the game. When you consider the other issues and the fact the game is neither completely scary, totally creepy, or terrifyingly exciting, going through the first few nightmares again and again doesn't sound inviting. Considering every time you die or enter a new nightmare you burst awake in bed, the initial play through has a bit of "repetition" fatigue already. Doing it again.. not inviting.
Reccomended: Horror fanatics, Ed Gorey Fans, anyone skilled with reading into subtext/iconography in a game.This is not a "jump scare" game. Buy it cheap.

The first word that comes to mind while playing

. For you fellow STALKERS, I can't quite say it hits the spot completely, but it scratches that itch better than many other games. I recommend playing on the highest difficulty setting for best results.
Truth be told, this game scratches a lot of itches. I understand why it was critically panned: there are obvious technical and performance issues, the story is a bit obnoxious, and the characters are almost completely unlikable. But, it's far from being the "worst game ever made" that some reviewers labeled it as. The gameplay here is prime. Depending on which "zone" you're in, it sits somewhere between
,
, and
, with elements of
,
and
thrown in for good measure. It has all the gameplay notes of a cult classic.
In the "Red Zones" feel most comparable to the
series' machine war scenes. The oppressive KPA army (the enemy in
) patrols these zones with airships and drones that force you to crawl beneath rubble and ruined buildings to stay undetected and safe. The sound design, music and lighting in these areas are excellent, and create a constant sense of unease. I found myself cautiously peeking out from under cover to look for the telltale green search beams of the airships. The sound they make is... unsettling. One Red Zone even features a
-like gas mask mechanic, and although it honestly doesn’t impact the gameplay much (other than changing the visuals and sound a bit), it does go a long way towards making the game feel more hostile.
In the "Yellow Zones" things feel closer to
and
. Trash and torched cars litter the streets, and people live in extreme poverty. KPA soldiers and vehicles patrol the streets in formation, and individual officers harass civilians (much like the civil protection in
). In these areas, you need to cause civil unrest by secretly sabotaging KPA propaganda equipment while remaining undetected. It’s thrilling to observe guard patterns from out of sight, and move your way through these areas stealthily.
While it may not be a perfect masterpiece,
has extremely strong cult appeal. For the average gamer, this probably doesn’t mean much, but for people looking for something out of the ordinary, I highly recommend giving this a try. If you’re not sure, pick it up on sale like I did.

*FULL DISCLOSURE* I backed this game on Kickstarter and generally have a sympathetic view for Matt Gilgenbach, the creater of this game.
I won't sugarcoat it. You can play this game with one hand. It is a graphic adventure game with no puzzles, just a few enemies to avoid as best you can. It's not incredibly fun in the traditional sense.
That being said, there is a lot to appreciate here. On the surface it's a story about a man troubled over his many losses. The  three endings present conflicting narratives that makes one question what is and isn't a dream. Thomas is obviously a tortured soul trying to make sense of the problems that vex him.
Now to expand on that, it obviously reflects a great deal of the fears and paranoias Matt feels himself. I don't know what compels a man to want to tear their radial bone out of their arm, but♥♥♥♥♥♥do I find it fascinating.
Some of the small things in this will make you think. Like the implication of killing yourself next to your dead sister, then waking up to her. How guilty must that make someone feel, even if it was a dream?
I think that's it really, Neverending Nightmares is a lot of small, odd and/or disturbing scenes that add up to a picture of someone's suffering.
There are things the game could have done much better. It could have attempted to tie its narrative together a little more tightly, and it could have given the player a little more to interact with, and in this sense it suffers some in my book, but I'm glad I played it, and I think many would feel the same.

Banished, city building and survival: an amazing experience.
You will need to develop a strategy of your own to achieve the most (fun) in this game and build your own unique town.
Decide your own speed too extreme slow to extreme fast with their own challenges to beat. If you choose to be an isolationist, you will be rewarded with an achievement if you manage to survive and build to 300 people. Believe me, the achievements in this game are hard to get. If you somehow manage to get them all you are a true banished master and you have to show something to show off to your friends and to me.
Two major strong points of Banished:
Lots of replay ability, new challenges with every random map.
The achievements, and the general feeling of satisfaction of a proper running town.
The weakness:
The limits you can develop a single town, at a certain point you just have to scale your town up (2 tailors, 2 blacksmiths etc.). The overhead it introduces makes the game harder but you can’t do much about it. Personally I haven’t reached this point yet, but that’s where the relative low review scores come from.
I’ll go off and build another town for another achievement, good luck with your own town!

This is an interesting game that provides some chilling moments during play.  The story of Thomas Smith, while simple, pretty much makes you think a little, maybe even make your own conspiracy theories.  Both the atmosphere and the sounds give you a chill, and I'm impressed that the game manages to spook you without the use of the over-used jump scare.  There are a few problems, though.  You can finish one of the story modes in no time, I say about 45 minutes to a hour tops, so you might complete the whole game, if not collect all four achievements, with 4-5 hours.  Also, whatever enemies there are in the game aren't the scariest things ever.  You can easily get past them with the most obvious way possible.  Only thing that could make getting past the enemies more obvious was to put in neon signs, and the ones that chase you will give you at least a little bit of a problem.  That being said though, the reason why people play horror games is to get scared, and in that regard, I think it does a good job.  If you're looking for cheap jump scares, like most indie horror games do unfortunately, then this is not the game for you.  Otherwise, this is a game worth experiencing, though the length might effect how much it's worth.

I really loved Final Fantasy X when it came out for Playstation 2, so I was looking forward to the chance to play this version. As of now (22 hours of game time), I've been enjoying every second of it. As I haven't played Final Fantasy X-2 before, either the original or any other version, this review will be limited to Final Fantasy X. If and when my impressions change in the future, as I progress in Final Fantasy X and move on to Final Fantasy X-2, I'll make sure to update this review to reflect that.
So far, the game feels exactly like I remembered it, for better and worse, and by "worse", I specifically mean one issue in particular - the camera movement and control. This issue annoyed me whenever I was playing the original Playstation 2 version, and it keeps annoying me now, with this version as well. It might annoy me now even more, as I've become more spoiled, as I got used to being in near-complete control of the camera. In this game, however, unless I'm missing something, the camera movement is automatic, limited and uncomfortable. If there's a way to change that, I'm yet to figure out how.
Other than that, the game is very close to my personal, subjective idea of perfection. The story is great, combining both fantasy and science-fiction elements, alongside old-fashioned yet dark drama in a long ongoing adventure. The battle system offers a great balance - it's deep and interesting on one hand, and easy enough to learn on the other. The sphere-grid seems, even today, like a refreshing and unique twist on the standard character progression system. While at first the game feels linear and limiting, I can tell you that at a certain point, you get all the freedom you want when it comes to exploration, side quests. weapon customization and so on.
Add to that the updated graphics (Full HD at 1080p on widescreen) and soundtrack (including arranged versions) on a stable version of the game, and as far as I'm concerned, this is as good as it gets. The game looks, sounds and feels great, much better than I expected.
Whether you played Final Fantasy X before and liked it or like role playing games and never got to play it - this is your chance to play a modern version of one of the true RPG gems ever made.

Overall if you have played Final Fantasy X and/or Final Fantasy X-2 before, then you know what to expect from the story and the gameplay. The remaster has added a completely re-done soundtrack to the game, and higher resolution textures and visuals. The original CGI cutscenes introduced in the PS2 version are completely unscathed, however.
The PC version of Final Fantasy X has some added features such as Turbo Speed, Auto HP regen/Overdrive Mode, the ability to toggle on/off encounters, and auto AI battle mode. I wouldn't recommend these options for someone playing through the first time through the game as it might ruin the experience. Final Fantasy X-2 has a different set of cheat options.
My only complaint is that there is no option to skip cutscenes. This is my fifth(?) time playing through Final Fantasy X and I have to watch the cutscenes over and over again.  I understand they want you playing this game for the experience. I get it. But still not having this option in the year 2016 is beyond my level of understanding. Especially considering most of the people who are going to buy this game have probably played it before. You can still choose to skip cutscenes in FFX-2, but why would you want to miss out on that 100%?
Overall this is a good game, but not a great one. Keep Netflix or Crunchyroll on hand while playing this game to make sure you don't bore yourself to tears.

While it’s a very short game it’s still an adventure experience worth checking out if nothing else than to try something unique. The controls are pretty simple in that you move with the arrow keys, sprint with the shift key (a very limited run as Thomas has asthma), and interact with the world using the enter key. If there are two things that I didn’t like about Neverending Nightmares, it’s that the game was way too short and the endings left too many questions. The latter I can forgive as everything is built around dreaming. And anyone who remembers any dreams that they’ve had know that they can be jumbled messes that make little (if any) sense. And the former is due to the fact that I enjoyed the game so much that I wanted more. Yes, by the end of the day I left feeling a bit depressed and unnerved but that’s exactly how psychological horror works.

Neverending Nightmares is a game that puts the writing on the wall (in blood) and counts on your subconscious to fill in the details. This effect builds a lot of tension in the beginning of the game but as you move through the levels the lack of clarity makes it hard to tell if you are progressing in the true sense of the word. Is the ambiguity part of the horror of being lost within your own mind? Of not knowing what the right move is? Perhaps, but the more readily apparent consequence is that by never reaching a moment of hope or a moment of achievement that becomes more than not failing... your control of Thomas starts to feel impersonal and monsters begin to look more like mechanics than terrors of the mind.
But does any of this mean the game is a failure? The cynic in me might say yes, but he'd be proven wrong pretty easily. I spent a lot of time
to understand the world I was in, a lot of time jumping up a couple of feet and a lot of time engrossed in the atmosphere crafted through a unique and eerie art style and a haunting soundtrack. Considering one branch of three endings can be completed in under two hours, I think that speaks volumes of the quality of production.
As a kickstarter backer I'm satisfied with my purchase and I have a lot of respect for the developer, but this is a flavour of horror unique enough that a universal recommendation as a must-play would be poor advice for those who hunger after simpler dishes. For a certain group of gamers Neverending Nightmares will hit the spot - for those curious ones.
This game was so obviously crafted with love and an insane attention to detail that for the sake of everyone else I hope Matt Gilgenbach can bring his talents to bear on a future project with more readable progression.
Neverending Nightmares is an ode to uncertainty and I suspect my own perception of its meaning may shift with more playthroughs. If you're in an adventurous mood for confusion and like your atmosphere served rare, jump in - the blood's nice and warm.

Banished is very unique in its play-style. I'm a huge fan of city-builder and strategy games, and so to find a game that really breaks the mold was very refreshing. No tech trees or restrictions is a nice touch, and the idea of being a challenging survival game blended with the usual city builder element is really great. I want to love this game. I want to say its the best city builder game to come out since Sim City 4, but there's a few crucial issues I have with the game.
For the record, I've only ever tried Hard difficulty setting.
The most significant issue in Banished is that I find myself staring at numbers and messages more than anything else. It's a constant game of moving around my profession numbers. What's worse is that for being such an interface-heavy game design, the UI itself is actually not very well-designed or thought out. The micromanagement in the game suffers from a serious lack of depth. Once you've planned out your city, which is a matter of ensuring your people don't have to walk too far to drop off supplies or get to their homes, you begin your journey of tediously shuffling around professions endlessly while staring at the event log, professions and resource tabs. You're watching a number (Like food or fuel) slowly go down while you frantically try keep that number up by doing anything you can -- but a lot of the time I feel like there's nothing I can do. If my people start dying from starvation, it's nearly impossible to fix it without losing a huge chunk of my population, because when people die -- the replacements take a long time to get settled into their new home and begin work.
The game is very punishing when you do something wrong. There's no wiggle room, no room for error. If I make one too many mistakes then I'm going to suffer a major consequence - hundreds will die. This doesn't make the game challenging, it just means that due to a simple mistake I now have to wait even longer to see my city become large and prosperous. The game feels like a tedious chore more often than a strategic city-planner. The only way to prevent a few mistakes from causing all your people to die is to wait a very long time while your city stockpiles resources (especially food). It's kind of like grinding in an RPG game; it guarantees that you'll be able to progress without issues, but its boring and totally kills the fun of risky advancements.
And even when you are doing really well the game does not reward you. At the height of your success all you've managed to do was keep that illogical, arbitrary number afloat. There are no milestones in Banished. There's nothing to aspire to, nothing to accomplish except see your numbers slowly rise and build more of the same. Every building I make is just another bland-looking brown or grey construct and all it does is help the numbers move along in some way or another. Brewery improves happiness numbers. Chapel increases happiness numbers. It's a game of seemingly-meaningless numbers going up and down forever. There also seems to be a surprising lack of information pertaining to what these numbers actually represent. What exactly does 100 firewood equate to? I never feel like I'm actually planning things out, telling myself I need X amount of Y, but instead just trying to make sure I have a surplus of every resource for when that 1 extra civilian is the straw that breaks the camel's back and my economy is thrown out of balance.
If updated, Banished has potential to be amazing. Despite all of the drawbacks, I really enjoy the game, especially for its unusual survival/city-builder hybrid play-style. It was definitely worth my $20 bucks.
Rating: B+

Despite my low hours, I've played and beaten this before on PS2 (actually, I think a lot of us have already, probably you too if you're reading this). Even so, if you're a newbie to this game, here's a bit of information for you.. You've got a great cast of characters, all voiced, along with an enthralling story and amazing summons. At the time this game came out, the CGIs were amazing. There was nothing like it. And  voiced games weren't that common at the time. Also, the way the character's facial expressions changed to show their emotions was  revolutionary. Actually, now when I think about it, FFX did a lot of things first, which changed the way how a lot of people looked at games. I dont think you'd have such great and believeable characters in later games such as The Last of Us and Heavy Rain if FFX never came out. It truly was the game which forced the gaming industry to evolve beyond the ps1 era.
Looking at port quality, I really have to say that unlike a lot of their previous ports, they did a very good job with this one. You get the upgraded graphics of the PS4 version, all the international version content, original and arranged soundtracks, eternal calm, last mission, and probably even more that I'm forgetting. Oh, did I mention boosters? You can turn off enemy encounters, turn on turbo, have all basic items, get max gil, etc. Great option for people who dont have much time playing games, or those who have already beaten this game multiple times. Or well...those who just want to cheese..
Now, to be fair, it does have a 30 FPS lock, but so did the original. I've seen people be very vocal about this lock but in all honestly, if you're used to how the original plays, this shouldn't bother you. If it's still an issue for you, there's a mod coming out in a few months I heard which changes the game's framerate to 60, so you'd have to be patient for that.
All in all, if you, like me, havent played this title in ages and itching for a new FF game to replay or just want to experience  it for the first time, this is a very good version of the game to get into.

Final Fantasy X is the best Final Fantasy game they made, at least in my opinion.
Everything is fantastic, from the setting (which is a nice take on a post apocalypse instead of the normal "everyone's a cannibal now" style), to the music (all of it is well made and fits its use in the game, most of it is catchy too, even after all this time it still brings back the emotions it did when I first heard it), to the gameplay (which is not quite the normal FF gameplay, instead of ATB they went with initiative based turns instead, which I personally prefer but a lot of FF veterans disliked).
And the story is both well acted and well written.  For example a part of it where the characters supposed to be awkward is something people who havent even played the game know through internet references.  Every character has an arc, even the secondary antagonist who is the normal "I will destroy the entire world" type and so one of the weaker characters has an actual sensical reason behind his actions.
The interactions between the characters are fantastic too, though it is difficult to go into without spoilers.  As an example which doesnt spoil too much, one of the main characters has problems which are very important to him, one of the foundations of his personality.  These problems are nothing compared to what one of his friends, who too is a main character, has seen.  The second guy belittles the first guys problems when appropriate while also understanding how they effect him and and treating them with respect in general and also trying to help him work through them.  IE the way a normal couple of people would.  Which doesnt sound like much, but can you think to yourself that kind of interaction in any other game?
Even the graphics stand up well, particularily in terms of aesthetic design.  X looks fantastic even today, the HD remaster for the most part makes it look even better.  The game is a decade and a half old at this point.  A lot of good looking games came out in 2001, not many have aged as well as FFX.
I wish I could go more into how many great things this game has, but I cant without spoilers...  Which is a shame.  The purchase is worth it for X alone, and you get X-2 as well (another reason FF purists dislike X, it being the first one deemed "worthwhile" to get a direct sequel and not VI or VII!!!  Blasphemy!) which makes it even better.
The only negatives I can think of are that the soundtrack was made worse than in the original for the HD remake.  They misstepped a lot with it, but one of the worst things they did was remove some or all of the bass from most of the tracks.  And another negative is that the optional challenge content requires you to basically re-level your characters again (unless you want to exploit some cheap systems), which is kind of a pain.  That being said it isnt a huge issue because the content is optional to begin with and then there are a couple of easy ways to beat it.

This is an interesting game in that it's not as much about the story, or even the abject horror, as it is about conveying certain emotions.  Matt Gilgenbach, the creator of Neverending Nightmares, suffers from depression and OCD, and this game exists to help convey what that is like.  The player will experience anxiety, dread, and general discomfort.  Of course that is because there are jump scares and monsters that are trying to kill him, but the point is the feelings that are transmitted.  The visuals are inspired by Edward Gorey, and of course incredibly disturbing, and the sound will keep the player on edge at all times, especially with headphones.
Neverending Nightmares does have a story, but it's disjointed and intentionally vague.  There are three endings, but none of them are canon.  You can try to put the pieces together to create a cohesive whole, but it's like having 450 pieces of a 500-piece jigsaw puzzle. Connections can be made, but you won't necessarily get the whole picture, and that's the point.  Clinical depression is not a rational thing.  There is not always a reason for people to feel depressed, except that their brains tell them so.  Be aware of this when you are trying to interpret the story.
The game is also heavy on symbolism, from the enemies to dream tropes that are lying around, like blood, teeth, and even the player's own slow running speed.  While the entire game, if you go for all of the endings and branching paths, will probably end up taking less than 2.5 hours, I would still argue that it is worth the purchase for the unique experience it provides, as well as for its part in helping spread awareness of OCD and clinical depression.  This game is great, and I highly recommend it.

I was concerned about this game due to all the negative publicity, but when I played it, I found it was an incredibly well written piece of interactive fiction (IF).
With IF, you can place each game somewhere on the spectrum from 'mainly story' (games like
) to to 'mainly puzzles' (games like
).
is all story, and the good news is: the story is fantastic.
The atmosphere is brilliant; you arrive at night to a spooky home you've never seen before, there's a storm outside, your entire family is missing and your sister has told you not to look for her. Some say the mansion is haunted. I was so worried there would be a bloogy-woogy-woo jumpscare, I didn't realise what was really happening until the story fed me enough to clue me in. I reevaluated everything I'd learned up until then, and it made so much more sense. It reminded me of Adam Cadre's
which also lets you walk around with an obvious but wrong interpretation, but unlike that game,
's plot isn't a last minute twist, it's a subtle combination of several threads, each of which unravels as you progress.
I felt clever as I figured out Mom and Dad's respective situations just from the evidence they left. Lots of stories fall down because they "tell" rather than "show", but Gone Home takes the epistolic approach of having characters write to each other (sticky notes, school detention forms, formal letters, postcards, etc.) and leaving you to work out
these characters wrote to each other.
I wasn't ready for it, but the game took me on a rollercoaster ride of Sam's emotions. She felt real, and her story gripped me, I wanted to race to the end to find out if there was a happy ending or not. The soundtrack really helped here, it boosted the emotional power of Sam's diaries, without sounding melodramatic. The voice acting was also great. I really felt a teenage girl was pouring her heart out to me.
The only real negative I have about the game is that the graphics are... perfunctory. They work, and having to reach into dark rooms and turn the lights on does add tension... but once the lights are on, the graphics are flat and don't really convince me I'm in a house. I'm in a computer game simulation of a house. There are too many generic, repeated objects around the house, and the objects are all very flat.
has the same calibre of graphics, but the difference is
, so it can get away with bland repetitive graphics and concentrate all its resources on story. Compare instead with
, which is also interactive fiction, but with what appears to be an enormous budget for graphics.
One other thing: the player character is pretty much a blank slate, like Bella from
levels of blank slate. She gets medals for doing well at school and she's the parents' favorite, whoop-de-doo. She writes entirely generic postcards from European capitals. What makes her happy? Don't know. Why did she go on a grand tour? Don't know. There is little said about her, and what is said is dull. But then, the story's not really about her, so I don't really mind. Perhaps she's written that way deliberately, to be a Featureless Protagonist, but I don't really identify with being a big sister so I can't relate. She does occasionally make interjections (e.g. "Gosh, dad") and that amused me. Maybe there's more to her than I think.
Overall,
is an amazing story, and it's really worth experiencing.

- $20 is a LUDICROUS price. It takes about 2 hours to complete at most and has basically no replay value. I got it in a Humble Bundle for about $2.50, which is far more reasonable. It'll have to go on like a 90%-off sale to be worthwhile.
- It is way, way overhyped on its page. It is definitely not 'epic', and absolutely not 'the greatest story ever told'. The 'mystery' is low-end as mysteries go; you get time to speculate on what happened but the revelations aren't earth-shattering. It's definitely no expansive exploration game; it's a small (and potentially enjoyable) trip through another family's experiences that will be familiar on some level to anyone who has been a teenager and lived with their parents.
- The story is inherently one-sided. It basically forgets that you're a character too - you're not some impartial observer, but a member of the family in the story; inherently, and deeply, involved. But we never see a reaction from you (well, not to the events themselves, anyway) or hear the parents' side of the story. It didn't have to be in a positive light, but it should have been there.
- The whole "horror mystery that really isn't" problem: when you play totally unspoiled (as I did) it feels like a horror game at first. (I'm glad it wasn't, as I don't like horror games.) You've got the tagline ("You arrive home after a year abroad. You expect your family to greet you, but the house is empty. Something's not right. Where is everyone? And what's happened here?"), the note on the door, the answering machine messages from the mother begging the daughter to pick up the phone, the 'psycho house' inherited from an uncle, secret passages and hidden compartments, all the lights are off, bits of occult, persistent rainstorm in the background, etc... depending on your viewpoint, it's either a brilliant bit of narrative misdirection, or a total shill selling itself on false premises. I lean more towards the former, personally, but can imagine the latter if you have certain expectations.
In short, while I enjoyed playing it, it's a very specialized experience that really, REALLY oversells itself. The RPS review says it best: "Approach neither from the position of hype or hatred." Just take it for what it is.
And don't pay $20 for it. Seriously. That's insane.

Final Fantasy X is the best Final Fantasy game they made, at least in my opinion.
Everything is fantastic, from the setting (which is a nice take on a post apocalypse instead of the normal "everyone's a cannibal now" style), to the music (all of it is well made and fits its use in the game, most of it is catchy too, even after all this time it still brings back the emotions it did when I first heard it), to the gameplay (which is not quite the normal FF gameplay, instead of ATB they went with initiative based turns instead, which I personally prefer but a lot of FF veterans disliked).
And the story is both well acted and well written.  For example a part of it where the characters supposed to be awkward is something people who havent even played the game know through internet references.  Every character has an arc, even the secondary antagonist who is the normal "I will destroy the entire world" type and so one of the weaker characters has an actual sensical reason behind his actions.
The interactions between the characters are fantastic too, though it is difficult to go into without spoilers.  As an example which doesnt spoil too much, one of the main characters has problems which are very important to him, one of the foundations of his personality.  These problems are nothing compared to what one of his friends, who too is a main character, has seen.  The second guy belittles the first guys problems when appropriate while also understanding how they effect him and and treating them with respect in general and also trying to help him work through them.  IE the way a normal couple of people would.  Which doesnt sound like much, but can you think to yourself that kind of interaction in any other game?
Even the graphics stand up well, particularily in terms of aesthetic design.  X looks fantastic even today, the HD remaster for the most part makes it look even better.  The game is a decade and a half old at this point.  A lot of good looking games came out in 2001, not many have aged as well as FFX.
I wish I could go more into how many great things this game has, but I cant without spoilers...  Which is a shame.  The purchase is worth it for X alone, and you get X-2 as well (another reason FF purists dislike X, it being the first one deemed "worthwhile" to get a direct sequel and not VI or VII!!!  Blasphemy!) which makes it even better.
The only negatives I can think of are that the soundtrack was made worse than in the original for the HD remake.  They misstepped a lot with it, but one of the worst things they did was remove some or all of the bass from most of the tracks.  And another negative is that the optional challenge content requires you to basically re-level your characters again (unless you want to exploit some cheap systems), which is kind of a pain.  That being said it isnt a huge issue because the content is optional to begin with and then there are a couple of easy ways to beat it.

A little about my experience with the Souls series: I've platinumed Dark Souls 1, and would have platinumed Dark Souls 3 were it not for the ludicrous drop rates of Vertebra Shackles (the country I live in has♥♥♥♥♥internet and I can't PvP, so I have to grind mobs for this♥♥♥♥♥♥. I loved those two games in the series, so I went into Dark Souls 2 with high, high hopes.
It takes a while to get into. The game isn't perfect - some of the mechanics are counter-intuitive, especially if you're coming from other Dark Souls games (I'm looking at you, Adaptability). But ultimately, it IS a Dark Souls game, and unlike the first game in the series, it only gets better after the halfway point.
Things I like:
+ There is so much content. Tons of bosses, locations, armor, and weapons.
+ As is Soulsborne tradition, the DLC is amazing, and the best part of the game. Fume Knight FTW.
+ The areas may be linear, but there are a lot of different directions you can head in right at the start. There's lots of replayability here.
Things I don't:
- The game is not directed by Miyazaki, but by two C-listers who have no business being in charge of a Souls game. Miyazaki has an eye for detail that results in near-perfect gameplay in DSI and DSIII. These guys do not.
- Sometimes controls are unresponsive. Sometimes your character literally does not dodge when you press the dodge button, even when you have stamina. Sometimes your character does not heal when you press the heal button. I've died many times as a result of healing timing being ♥♥♥♥ed up by a dud button press. For reference, I'm using a Steam controller, which I also used with DSI and DSIII, which did not have this problem.
- Hitboxes. Good lord. Sometimes your sword model hits the enemy and does no damage. On many occasions, an enemy (especially bosses) will look like they miss you entirely, but nope! You got hit. It's such BS sometimes, and neither of the other DS games have this problem.

The gunplay is fun and accurate. The levels are soulless and boring random generated stuff. After about 15 minutes you have seen everything the game has to offer and are just scouring every single pixel of the random levels for the randomly dropped macguffins you need to win. It's a tech demo and not a real game.

This game is currently underrated.  That may not have been the case 6 months ago when steam/professionals reviews nominated it the biggest AAA poopstain of 2016.  Six months later, a lot of the technical/gamebreaking bugs are gone.  What's left is something of an urban Far Cry clone with a pretty outlandish story that delivers a few different gameplay elements in a pretty above-average way.  I spent about 50 hours playing it and I enjoyed myself.
Setting:   North Korea won the Korean War, uniting the entire peninsula and creating the world's foremost technological superpower.  Years later, the US is depleted and heavily dependent on Korea.  The Koreans take advantage of this and essentially take over the US under the pretense of peacekeeping.  You are a newly recruited revolutionary in the Philadelphia branch of the resistance against the takeover.
What you may like:
-Above average artistic presentation.  Good textures with limited popping.  Dynamic day/night cycle.  Quality motion-captured animations.  The resistance fighters look cool.
-Level design is top notch.  Lots of nooks and crannies for you to scavange and take potshots at the enemy form.  Very vertical with lots of parkour, with lots of open-ended methods of approach.  The different areas of the game vary enough to keep it fresh despite you doing basically the same thing.
What you may not like:
-Still quite buggy, although not game-breaking.  I was not able to complete some side jobs.  I fell through the world once. Some texture flickering.
-The story is pretty ridiculous and the enemies are kinda goofy/comicbookish.  They look like some brokeass power rangers mixed with the guy from Speed Racer.  I'm pretty sure the designers went for this look on purpose, to create a B-Movie kind of atmosphere.
-No matter how you pamper it with quality level design, capturing a tower is still capturing a tower.  This is basically like an urban far cry, so if you are tired of that, look elsewhere.
Everything else:
-Although the weapon modification system is interesting, the upgrades to the weapons are boring stat boosts
-Even though the actors did a great job delivering it, the overall writing of the story is pretty cheesy.
-The enemy AI itself is not bad.  Enemies flank, take cover, and attack in groups.However, sometimes enemies will appear/disappear right in front of your face.
Conclusion:
If you're itching for a quality urban far cry experience, this is for you.  The game doesn't stray too far from that formula. The level design is easily the best part of this game, and it kept it pretty fresh throughout.  It's still pretty buggy but the massive game-breaking bugs seem to be gone.  I quite enjoyed the different areas of its open world, and thought they were pretty varied, even moreso than many of its competitors.

If I have to pick yes or no in terms of recommending this game, I'd pick no for the average player and give some details on the actual game to anyone who I think might enjoy it.
Like most of the negative reviews, I think the art and sound design are amazing, though I did sometimes get put-off by the awkward faked animation on everything.  I'd definitely suggest headphones to anyone who does end up playing, because even the sparse soundtrack is great.  It's just great horror, aesthetically.
The problems begin when you start to learn the games tricks: nothing matters, there aren't puzzles, just walk, if you die you come back very close by.  At that point, I lost interest in the gameplay itself.  A lot of the areas drag on too, and when you start to see the same things over and over and different items rearranged in different rooms, you begin to feel like your time is being wasted and disrespected.  When you walk down the same hall five times before you see anything new, you become frustrated.  It sucks.
I beat the game and tried to go back to try for another ending, and at that point I knew more than just what the game could do, but what it actually WOULD do to me, and all semblance of tension or fun was lost from there, even as I experienced the new content.
If you're looking for a new type of horror experience and you've got fifteen bucks burning a hole in your pocket, get this, for sure.  Everyone else, be wary.

This game is short, but it has greater impact than many other horror and scare games that last much longer.  Neverending Nightmares grabs you right from the beginning: there is no tutorial that overstays its welcome; a control guide; or even an hour-long opening sequence before you dive in.  Instead, the game begins immediately, and without any GUI to distance you from the action, you being your neverending nightmare...
The graphics and atmosphere are very unique, and the hand-drawn nature of the game really helps establish a surreal setting that only increases in horror and intrigue as you progress.  The audio is integral to the experience, and pulls you in even further to this cacophony of mind-bending, psychological distortion of an adventure.
Having said that, the length is bad not because it's too short, but that it feels like there's so much more story and setting to explore.  The game doesn't overstay its welcome, but it doesn't really stay for dinner either.

*Disclaimer: I am the developer of the game, so take my review worth a grain of salt*
That being said, I thought it'd be helpful to use the review system to speak candidly about the game. Hopefully people find it helpful.
This isn't a typical horror game. It's not about startling you with jump scares. It's about creating a tense and oppressive atmosphere that mirrors my experience with mental illness.
It's not very game-y. Some may describe it as a "walking simulator". While it is true the main mechanics are walking, this was a deliberate design choice. The game is about disempowerment and vulnerability, which is important to creating a horror experience. To further the vulnerability, the main character has asthma. That means he can't run very far without stopping to get his breath, and we use the stamina to create tense situations.
We wanted to create a focus on immersion. That's why there is no UI, hud, or traditional game mechanics. We want you to forget you are playing a game and get lost in our nightmare-scapes.
It's not very long. A playthrough to one ending is between 1.5 and 2 hours. However, we have 3 different endings with unique content leading up to them, so I would recommend playing all nightmares. That will add another hour or two to your playtime.
Will you like this game? That really depends on what you are looking for. If you are looking for a unique take a horror with thick atmosphere, then I think you'll love what we are offering. If you are turned off by short games or ones without a lot of challenge, then this may not be the game for you. It's tough to make a game that appeals to everyone, but I think we've created a special game that a lot of people will really love.
Thanks for reading, and I hope you enjoy the game! :)

Did you think the first Five Nights at Freddy's game was hard? Ha. Ha, ha, ha...
Then if you like hard games you are in for a treat! FNaF2 takes the amazing story and lore of the first game to a new, bigger location, adds more than double the animatronics and completely removes the safety mechanisms you used to have [doors]. Oh, did I mention there are also three entrances into your office now? FNaF2 is a hard game, however unlike some difficult games out there it manages to keep your attention very well, especially so with the addition of pre-set custom nights (something that wasn't entirely possible in the first game due to the smaller number of animatronics there are} that upon completion award you with an adorable plushie. Also, because of this the game has a much better feel of progression to it than the first one ever did. Instead of doors this time around you are given an empty Freddy Fazbear head to put on so the animatronics dont think you're an endoskeleton and.... yeah. We've heard that before. The window of time you have to pull down the mask if an animatronic is in/or looking into your office is roughly about a second, and less than that on harder nights, making this game very, very difficult and testing your reaction times to the limit. It is however much easier than the first game at allowing you to take on and adapt to a very specific rhythm/strategy to get you through the night, however this will need to be adapted for every custom night or increase of difficulty, so because of this it is still a slightly harder game. There is also the additional mechanic of having to flash the flashlight at Foxy, the flashlight is the replacement of the power mechanic and yes, it has a battery. Yes, it does run out, however with the right strategy it can be very easy to never run out of battery. You will need to flash Foxy with the flashlight to stop him progressing up the hallway towards you as the Freddy head does not work on him. This little mechanic helps up the difficulty and can commonly break you from a perfect rhythm. However, due to all of the effort put in to making this a hard, frustrating and frantic game it just doesnt feel scary. Atall. The ambience is much less creepy than it was in the first game and can actually be more annoying than creepy, the only scary thing about this game is the jumpscares, however they can normally be predicted so the only one which should ever surprise you should be foxy's.
+ Insane Difficulty
+ Expands on Story well
+ Great Animatronic Design
+ New Mechanics
+ Custom Nights
- Not Scary
- Commonly Unfair (game will seem to cheat you out of a victory quite a lot, mainly because of how much randomisation actually affects the animatronic AI)
FNaF2 is a very worthy sequel to a good game and whilst it doesn't deliver the spooks of the first game, it keeps the insane difficulty and adds in new, fresh mechanics and a great set of pre-set custom nights that allow you to unlock little collectibles, combine that with the awesome lore and you have a really good game.

At the end of the day, if you loved FFX/FFX-2, then you'll love this remaster.  It's worthy of a "remastered" title, and demonstrates just how beloved this game is.  Every additional feature is just icing on the cake to what is an excellent game.

Receiver is a game about shooting.

Oh, were you looking for something else? That pretty much sums up what this game is, from it's concept, of course.
Now, let's start the real review:
Graphics: Made in Unity 3D, the game has simple graphics and places that seems to be missing textures. But it's all part of the game's visual art style and concept. Enemies desing are also pretty simple and you can spot then on sight (Witch is essential in this game IMO). I guess the gun model is okay, since it gives player a good vision of what he's doing with it and where he's REALLY poiting at. Skybox is dead, but you really don't need it in this game.
Gameplay: This is the jackpot in this game. The realism put into shooting, reloading, carrying and using your gun is something so nice to see in a FPS and that even most AAA studios keep forgetting that it exists. Playing this game using the device that simulates a pistol is even better. All the controls, from the keyboard/mouse/device responds pretty well and always keeps the game fluid and dinamic.
Even tough gunplay is the biggest part of this game, it also haves an objective: Collecting all your self recordings so you can finish the game. But finding then is a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥ Not only you don't have a radar, but you will die a ♥♥♥♥ING lot in this game. It IS hard. And i mean it. The enemies were created with the intetion of making the game hard in this way, and the AI woks pretty well to make sure that this is happening. Don't mess with the enemies. It's not because the game is realistic that the enemies will also be. 2-3 shoots and you are dead. Make sure of always keeping your ammo at count, or else, you are ♥♥♥♥ed.
Soundtrack: Missing. Even tough the self recording are pretty neat to hear, i just can't like this monotunus atmosphere. They could've put some songs like The Stanley Parable did (Or SuperHot) to don't let the player attention go away of the game. Mostly because that if you are not paying attention, you are dead.
Story: Most of it is explained through recordings. It's not a gigantic plot, but it does it job of keeping the player guessing. Going through uncovering the secrets of the protagonist organization and himself is quite awesome and it has a nice progression...When you find then in order, that's because the only bad thing is: If you die, your found recording count will reset, so, if you want to find a new one that you haven't heard yet/don't want to hear the same thing again from a past one, good luck with that.

Gone Home is a story driven, first person exploration based game in which you explore and eerily dark and desolate household searching for clues about your little sister. There isn't really much more to say without spoiling the story, the game is relatively short and is very effective in its use of pacing.

The atmosphere of the game is a little dismal and feels somewhat akin to the original Resident Evil minus the zombies and monsters. There is a pleasant 90's soundtrack to uncover and experience while you poke around the rooms of the house that serve to cut the tention a bit.
Gameplaywise Gone Home is devoid of any really distinguishing features, it's entirely exploration based with no real action outside of solving a puzzle or two. There are secrets aplenty and the 90s asthetic is very charming.
If you're one for a good story and enjoy empathising with characters then I cannot recommend this game enough. However if you are not one for said stories then look elsewhere. Gone Home was a short lived experience for me, but left a good enough impression to warrant me giving it a positive review.
Prepare for some of dem feels if you choose to buy this and I personally recommend taking your time in order to soak in the unique world the developer has lovingly crafted.
