Let me preface this by saying I do not think this game is bad. Homefront: The Revolution has a good foundation, and with great potential in my opinion, but almost nothing is built on it in the end.
This game is an open-world FPS title that has you play as Ethan Brady, a fresh recruit for the Resistance, fight against the KPA who hold control of Philadelphia. This game however never takes full advantage of its alternate history setting and the fact that it is an open world game. Retaking the city is pretty lackluster and repetitive. You can expect to be doing the same thing for one Zone for most of the others. You do Main missions, raise the "Hearts & Minds" percentage to 100%, do another mission to win the zone, then repeat.
I can forgive that if the rest of the game had something else to makes it stand out, but besides the weapon conversions (which are interesting, but ultimately clunky), this game has no such thing. The story is very weak, shallow, and fails to make me empathize with the Resistance. Characters lack depth and act predictably throughout the story. And while gunplay is decent, your arsenal is small and what you play with from the first zone is likely what you'll use for the rest of the game.
The final nail in the coffin for me though was how unrewarding all of it was. Most everything outside of main missions and set activities does almost nothing at all. If you killed a platoon of KPA troops nothing is gained. If you decide to capture all strongholds in a zone you only have Tech Points for changing existing weapons. All you can do is earn money, do the same activities, and finish missions. That's all the game really wants you to do.
The game can have it's moments due to the fact how you tackle each task is left for you to decide, but it's really not enough for the asking priceof $40. The game overall feels incredibly average and sometimes even below average later on in the story. Even if it's on sale I would consider looking elsewhere.
Tl;Dr - Overwhelmingly average Open-world FPS with missed potential. Not worth the price unless on (a very good) sale.

Edward Gorey.
One of my favorite artists.  His dark, gothic style of cartooning has delighted the Victorian in people for years.
Now Neverending Nightmares takes his style and makes a game out of it, and just like Goreys style, in this game there are no good endings.
The controls are basic and functional and don't get in the way of the game... The art, which is THE reason to play this game doesn't quite ring true to Gorey but is very effective in getting the hopless sense of fear and desperation out of the game and into the player.  Only black and white is allowed in the pallette, with occasional visits from other colors... particulary red.  A simple mask of blakc lines over the front of the screen gives the omnipresent drearyness  a real sense of depression.  When a color does pop up the players eyes are immediatly drawn to it.
The music fits very well, sound samples are played repeatedly with changes in frequency giving the body of the song rather than pitches or notes.  Whether is a twisted lullaby, or the screams of a lunatic in an asylum every part of this game screams at the player "Doom!  Death!  Hoplessness! Despair!" while using a the voice of a soft whisper.
If you love dark things, Victorian novels, or are a fan of E. Gorey, you will be delightfully entertained ( and possibly pushed toward suicide ) by this game.

This game took a lot of heat after it launched, with almost everyone saying it was terrible.
I cant comment on this as i dint play it back then, But i can say that in its current state, i like the game quite a bit.
The few bugs that remain are minor, and dont affect the gameplay significantly.
A few ppl still complain that its too hard, and that you can get swarmed by enemies, But in my opinion what those people dont understand is that this is one of those few FPSs where you are NOT invincible. You actually have to know when to fight AND when to run (like when reinforcements arrive), or you WILL die.
I find this game mechanic very realistic, you are fighting in occupied cities, crawling with enemy soldiers. It makes sense that once you start trouble you HAVE to do your thing fast and go away before you get swarmed.
The weapons are great imo, they actually have recoil, you CANNOT carry 10 rifles, 1 rpg, 50 grenades and a flame thrower. You actually have a carrying capacity, and you also have a reasonable capacity on how much ammo you can carry. There is also a system where you customize and even transform your guns at any time, e.g. buy the proper "kits" and turn your pistol into an SMG, add a silencer, or a laser sight, etc. Any time you want! no need to go to a "weapons bench" or anything.
Some also say that the game is "too generic", that it doesnt do anything diferent. I couldnt disagree more.
In my eyes, ->Realism<- sets this game apart. You are NOT invincible, you CANNOT defeat 150 enemy soldiers at the same time, you CANNOT carry an entire warehouse of guns & ammo, and you CANNOT endure 5 RPG hits to the head.
Here you cant just go running arround shooting everything. You have to plan your attacks, or die.
Overall i find the game realistic, and very fun to play.
Graphics are very nice, and currently the game runs fine on my less than stellar PC (i5, nvidia GTX 750ti). No performance issues for me.
Controls are responsive and easy to learn & use.
Bottom line:
If your idea of an FPS is "i am God, no one can touch me, and i will just run and kill everything i see", then you will probably NOT like this one.
If you prefeer the gameplay to be more tense, where you need to plan stuff and act fast to avoid being chopped to pieces, conserve ammo, plan on what weapons are right for the current job, and know when you need to retreat instead of fight, then you will like this one!

This is a game that I have been waiting quite a while for, and had extremely high expectations for while following the developer up to release. I feel that it hit every goal that I hoped for and expected it to.
It's not a game that focuses on cheesy jump-scares and 10-15 mins of constant fear. It's a game that offers a glimpse into the underside of our humanity and makes you feel like you're being torn from the inside out.
The themes are powerful, and leave you thinking through the game and long after it's over.
The art style is unique and well done.
The soundtrack is ominous and goes quite well with the atmosphere that the user is placed in.
A couple things that I did not like a about it though, that the hallways were a bit repetitive at times, and that the replay value is a bit lacking.
It's not the type of game that gives you a shallow terror that ultimately leaves you feeling unsatisfied. It brings you to the edge of your seat, but also gives you time to process information and build up a feeling of dread and angst. A quality that quite a few games are lacking now.
In my opinion, this game is well worth $15.00.

I played Final Fantasy X for PS2 and fell in love with the game, even though as a young, stupid kid, I didn't understand the Final Fantasy world and all of it's mechanics and gameplay. As a child, it took forever for me to get past points in the early-game that now I look at my younger self and facepalm. The gameplay is solid with it's turn-based combat.
The HD Remaster is very subtle in the graphic department, which is perfect, due to the fact that Final Fantasy X was beautiful from the start and needed very little updates to it's design anyway. Not to mention SOME games that did get a remaster (I'm looking at you, Fable) ended up going overboard and looked... weird (Seriously, Fable 1's main protagonist looks liks♥♥♥♥♥♥in the remaster compared to the original).
The soundtrack is also altered only slightly, and still resembles it's original predecessor strongly.
I never got the chance to play FFX-2, and am looking forward to it.
Disclosure:
Others throughout forums argue the game has bad-ish acting, irritating characters, the gameplay sucks, the graphics suck, etc.
Some of the complaints do have some validity to them. Yes, the acting in comparison to other FF games, and other games in general, has it's issues, but I honestly don't see it as a deal-breaker, or a game-breaker for that matter. Banished is a wonderful simulation with great graphics. Over a million different maps. Great sound additions. However, if you are someone that needs a loud-and-proud ceremony every time you do something mildly eventful, this game is not for you. Nor is it for you if you need to shoot everything that blinks an eyelid.
In Banished, you decide where you want your buildings. How many you want working there. How early in the season you should harvest. But you need firewood or coal. Did you produce that? Did you build homes? Do your people have a varied diet, do they have a faith outlet, will they be medically safe, and is there anywhere they can blow off steam? Is there a chance of being educated? What keeps them warm at night?
And even if you have all this, can you run with water to a fire, or run away from a tornado?
I do recommend this, even in its early stages. Perhaps it will have optional challenges with competition or even go the route of the Serf City style, that being, defending territory and having varied output of what's under the ground.

A little about my experience with the Souls series: I've platinumed Dark Souls 1, and would have platinumed Dark Souls 3 were it not for the ludicrous drop rates of Vertebra Shackles (the country I live in has♥♥♥♥♥internet and I can't PvP, so I have to grind mobs for this♥♥♥♥♥♥. I loved those two games in the series, so I went into Dark Souls 2 with high, high hopes.
It takes a while to get into. The game isn't perfect - some of the mechanics are counter-intuitive, especially if you're coming from other Dark Souls games (I'm looking at you, Adaptability). But ultimately, it IS a Dark Souls game, and unlike the first game in the series, it only gets better after the halfway point.
Things I like:
+ There is so much content. Tons of bosses, locations, armor, and weapons.
+ As is Soulsborne tradition, the DLC is amazing, and the best part of the game. Fume Knight FTW.
+ The areas may be linear, but there are a lot of different directions you can head in right at the start. There's lots of replayability here.
Things I don't:
- The game is not directed by Miyazaki, but by two C-listers who have no business being in charge of a Souls game. Miyazaki has an eye for detail that results in near-perfect gameplay in DSI and DSIII. These guys do not.
- Sometimes controls are unresponsive. Sometimes your character literally does not dodge when you press the dodge button, even when you have stamina. Sometimes your character does not heal when you press the heal button. I've died many times as a result of healing timing being ♥♥♥♥ed up by a dud button press. For reference, I'm using a Steam controller, which I also used with DSI and DSIII, which did not have this problem.
- Hitboxes. Good lord. Sometimes your sword model hits the enemy and does no damage. On many occasions, an enemy (especially bosses) will look like they miss you entirely, but nope! You got hit. It's such BS sometimes, and neither of the other DS games have this problem.

I've been playing this game since November 2014, and never before have I seen an FPS like this. It requires strategy, cooperation, and challenge. The main gamemode is trench warfare, which requires players to run across no man's land and capture the enemy trench. Unlike most FPS multiplayer games, if you get shot once with a rifle, you're dead. You're not some sort of super soldier that can take 100's of bullets to the face and still come back up for more.
Yes, Verdun has gone through a lot of changes and issues, in fact I was one of many who left the game in mid-2015 to try and get the developers to wake up and fix the game's issues. That and the issues the horrors of war update had at launch is why there's quite a few negative reviews.
However Verdun seems to be pulling itself together again. The optimization has gotten a lot better (well for me at least), there's less bugs, and the amount of content that's been added from the horrors of war update is amazing! It seems Verdun is going back in the right direction, let's just hope that it stays that way.
So should you buy Verdun? If you're interested in a change from your usual FPS then yes. However, just keep in mind that the devs might mess up again. They're a small development team so I can't blame them too much.

It's like someone took the core concept out of a mass-market casual phone game and made something serious, challenging, and hardcore with it.
I'm familiar with this game's strange roots, a sequel to a knockoff of a Japanese Playstation game called Ore No Ryouri that I remember getting on one of those Playstation Underground Jampack demo discs over a decade ago. Having played that, and "Ore no Ryomi 2", vertigo's previous cooking sim game, this is the tightest evolution of that concept yet.
Each "day" you play in the restaurant is like a performance. This isn't a top-level sim, you're hitting the letter keys on your keyboard or waving the mouse like a madman getting down into the nitty-gritty in preparing these foods and serving them up. In a weird way, it feels similar to playing a song in Rock Band or Guitar Hero: if you pull off a perfect day in Cook, Serve, Delicious!, you feel like a rock star. It scratches the same kind of itch that those games do, with a completely different concept.
It's not exactly the most difficult game, you can get by just fine without getting too serious, but the money you earn is tied to how fast you are with your keyboard, and in that way it can be as brutal and rewarding as you want it to be. It's a ton of fun for a small price.
Also of note, I cracked a big grin on my face when the Ryan Davis burger popped up in the game, and the achievement that popped up was a sweet little tribute to the dude.

There's a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ of indie 2D platformers with silly quirks and irreverent references to 2D games of yore, but VVVVVV stands tall above most of these games. It's quirk is that you can't jump, but you can flip the gravity, so the celing becomes the floor, and vice versa. The quirk actually significantly changes the gameplay of the standard platformer, which is more than can be said for a lot of other games. The developer's found a lot of inventive ways to use the mechanic, both in the "wow that was so much cooler than just jumping" and the "how the ♥♥♥♥ am I going to do this without jumping" categories.
As for the actual game's style, think Metroid without the upgrades (The game's map, general openness and feeling of isolation, especially) and with some classic Megaman mixed together. (It's difficult, but it controls well, and the simple graphics help the smoothness of the gameplay rather than warp it.)
It's cheap, fun, and you'll feel a huge amount of satisfaction on completing it.

Final Fantasy X review: THIS. Just THIS. This game embodies one of those times when Final Fantasy as a game series shines at its brightest. Final Fantasy X was my first Final Fantasy, and I will never, ever forget the way it blew open my world as a young teenager. They say that your first Final Fantasy is the one that will always be the best - I am so, so deeply thankful that this was my first. (FF VII lovers, sorry, but you'll have to come second.) This fact alone is even more incredible if you think about it as a testament to the quality of the Final Fantasy series, when usually your first anything sucks horse poop. Yeah. Think about it.
Anyways, this remaster basically brushes up the original game just enough so that you get sucked into the world of Spira all over again (in HD!!). Yes, the character models are a little inconsistent, in that the main characters have all gotten South-Korean perfect facelifts more in line with the CG cutscenes, while NPCs at times look like they've been injected with too much Botox with blurry textures for makeup. The infamous HahahaHAHAHAHA scene is still there, in all its cringeworthy glory. Auron's just as cool as ever, Tidus is still whiny, Yuna's prettier than before... Everything is there as you would like to remember it... Yes, even the now kinda outdated stiff character animations.
The sphere grid upgrade system still holds up after more than a decade - it's incredible how much it makes sense in terms of accessibility and enjoyability, unlike some certain other games (*cough* FF XII *cough*). The game runs smoothly without a hitch on a Geforce card, and is perfectly compatible with an Xbox controller. Oh! And finally, even though the game is locked at 30 fps, I either didn't notice it because everything was so consistent, or I simply didn't have time to care because I was too busy enjoying the game and storyline - again.
For those of you who've played it before, you know what I'm talking about. For those of you who haven't played it before - You will cringe, you will get the feels, you will laugh, you will cheer on this unlikely group of characters as they take on the world around them. So...What are you waiting for? Everyone's waiting for you. Spira awaits, with all its dreams and splendor and broken glory.  BUY THE GAME. NOW.

I've been playing this game since November 2014, and never before have I seen an FPS like this. It requires strategy, cooperation, and challenge. The main gamemode is trench warfare, which requires players to run across no man's land and capture the enemy trench. Unlike most FPS multiplayer games, if you get shot once with a rifle, you're dead. You're not some sort of super soldier that can take 100's of bullets to the face and still come back up for more.
Yes, Verdun has gone through a lot of changes and issues, in fact I was one of many who left the game in mid-2015 to try and get the developers to wake up and fix the game's issues. That and the issues the horrors of war update had at launch is why there's quite a few negative reviews.
However Verdun seems to be pulling itself together again. The optimization has gotten a lot better (well for me at least), there's less bugs, and the amount of content that's been added from the horrors of war update is amazing! It seems Verdun is going back in the right direction, let's just hope that it stays that way.
So should you buy Verdun? If you're interested in a change from your usual FPS then yes. However, just keep in mind that the devs might mess up again. They're a small development team so I can't blame them too much.

Let's make a scenario: say you're playing GTA or Saints Row, you get thrown into a vast open world, and all you can think is, "wow. I can't wait to explore every inch of this and wreck it like the kid on xbox live did to my mom" This is the driving point of JC2.
Just Cause 2 has a fairly simple story: go into the country and wreck the corrupt government so a new one can take it's place. To Progress in the story and unlock missions, you will need to cause chaos on the vast Island of Panoi. Everything is unlocked from the start (for the most part) so you just get out there and blow stuff up, and when I say blow stuff up I REALLY blow stuff up. The explosions in the game are freaking beautiful, heck everything in it is freaking beautiful, even on low settings. In the words of Nerd3, it's action movie: the game... everything has the potential to be obliterated!
Panoi consists of three main islands: an Urban/city area, a desert area, and a Jungle and Mountainous area. Just half of the desert area is roughly the size of the GTA: San Andreas map. Only half. Take a moment to think about how much space the whole world has. Yeah, a lot.
The overall gameplay is smooth and fun, whether you're doing a campaign mission, one of the thousands of side missions, or just screwing around. The HUD is limited, so there's lots of screen room to sight see. Just Cause two has insane variety in between missions as well. Side mission might require you to defend or escort someone, story missions have you taking on the government, and hundereds of bases for you to conquor inbetween. And what makes things better? Going from mission to mission is half the fun. Cops will chase you, you can steal any vehicle from ATV to Cargo Plane, all while pulling off insane stunts. The idea of having a grappling hook to pull yourself with a parachute as the main transportation is a genious idea that makes surprised, since we haven't seen it in any other game. Plus, the dedicated modders of the game just make it a millions time better plus 2.
TL;DR: Get out there, let the societal defiling commence! Whether your skydiving, driving, flying, boating, or shooting everything, you are bound to have a good time on Just Cause 2. If that's not enough, now there's a MULTIPLAYER mod so you can do all the stuff with your friends and other people! Buy. This. Game. It. Will. Be. Worth. It.

OLD REVIEW
Was a good game when I started playing (mid '15). Was full of bugs & glitches, but that was to be expected from a Beta. Game was updated fairly regularily, but ever since PS4 and XBOX 1 ports were announced there haven't been many. The game is full of Hackers, as you can be killed by players on the other side of the map, even when behind "cover" or in a "trench". High-level guns are extremely OP, whilst the Low-Level guns can't hit for Sierra Hotel India Tango beyond about six feet for a pistol, ten for an MG and twenty for a Rifle. Gas is pointless, as you can't see beyond the visor, even with your mask on, because there is a bloody vignette in the way. Bayonets are also super OP, often getting a oneshot. AI is still glitchy as hell, and they often just glitch around the map, just like the tanks and horses in this year's april fools joke. AI seems to have pinpoint accuracy and doesn't suffer from the gas like players, as they don't take damage or get an aim penalty. I think that artillery and mortars are useless, as you don't get much of a warning, and very rarely get artillery unless you are the Squad NCO. Quite often the high-level (80-100) players sit on certain, hard to find maps with lots of cover and a vantage point to kill anything in their LOS with their sniper rifles. I remember finding a mod for Battlefield 1942 (Battlefield 1917, I think) that was far better than this, as it had functional AI and guns. Bullet physics are another bad thing, as they can go off on the worlds largest tangent. They should make the gun upgrades better or stackable. I don't want the option of having a bayonet OR a scope, I would want the both at the same times. And spawn points are terrible. Sometimes on defense missions you spawn in some random point far back in no-mans land, and have to advance to the trench you need to defend and- bang - your'e dead, as super accurate High-level players and the AI rip your head off and you have to watch your team go through the same fate as you, so you can go back to the next trench and repeat. Pistols are awful. They have no range and no accuracy, their about as much as a side arm as throwing small pebbles at the enemy. Teams are a grind, as it takes several thousand xp to level up, and you have little of a chance to level up after three to four hours of gameplay (Trust me, an hour of play on one team and eventually everyone quit due to us all being level 1-10 whilst the enemy is on a high level team at levels 50-100. We got bugger-all xp. None of us, or the actual team, leveled up.). Another point is the Rifles are useless unless you have some form of super-gaming mouse with thirty-seven different buttons, as they have good accuracy, but good luck seeing through the ironsights, because you're going to have to play for a long time to get the sight, son. MGs are so innacurate that they are only useless unless you use them like an SMG, except you can't run with them. This game is very quickly becoming another Heroes and Generals, full of hackers and HLPs killing LLPs trying to actually have fun, making it not fun at all. I honestly think that "ranked battles" should be added in so that high level players play other high level players, and low level players play other low level players. German units have virtually no good level equipment, whereas the allies (especially British and French) have more accurate guns, with larger magazines. Essentially Allied bias. No eastern front - where are the Austrians and Russians, and no Gallipoli, so no Ottomans and ANZACs either. Seems to focus only on the Western front. The camoflage is too good. You can't actually see the Germans on the more grey, artillery pounded maps, or the British and Americans on the more greenish maps that haven't been bombarded. And The French and Belgians don't fit in anywhere.
However, on the plus side, the game can have its good points, and killing someone can leave them writhing on the ground in pain, screaming and rolling. It is also better than the other alternative (BF1), and is actually set in a realistic scenario, not following "Battlefield History".
Essentially, all's not quiet on the western front, as it is still a Beta and is so far from a finished game. They should have finished it before releasing it on PS4 and XBOX, and only released it now to run off of the hype created by Battlefield 1. Was a great concept, but one of the worst wastes of money (£19!) until I bought a game from CEX (for 75p) that deleted my System 32. Only buy this game if you are willing to have a bad time and pull your hair out or feel like a bad person because you hacked because their "cheat protection" just detects Cheat Engine, and eventually give up due to boredom. The game is a sniper's haven. Snipers are evil. They are so accurate, especially with the extra breathing in time for more accurate shots. Essentially, Sniper OP to the extreme. One last thing, WHERE IN ♥♥♥♥ DID THE PLAYERBASE GO! I STRUGGLE TO FIND A RUDDY GAME!

I enjoy the game. I really do, but it's extremely hard for me to give it a recommnedation, even if its discounted heavily. It's not because of the broken AI (not stupid, they're literally broken), laughable model placement mistakes (floating cars, floating debris, clipping scenery, disappearing objects when you go near, etc), broken mechanics (Drones will hunt you across the map instantly if you ever ride a bike even if nobody sees you, when hiding in bins or protable toilets in yellow zones, enemies can actually still see you and will even try to kill you by shooting and throwing bombs but they can never hurt you and your wanted cooldown will still go down. It's pretty funny actually)  or that the gameplay can be repetitive (thought personally, i don't find this to be a problem since I'm actually enjoying it).
The reason why I cannot in good faith give this a recommendation, again even if its heavily discounted, is because the game has the potential to literally ruin your computer physically. After beating halfway through Holloway (in terms of main missions), the game will HARD CRASH randomly during your playthrough from hencepoint onwards (sound will still continue to play as normal). It doesn't matter if you reinstalled the game, if you try to modify game files to make it more stable or have the latest updated version of the game. The game will crash on you so hard that it literally freezes your entire computer and your only option (unless you have a fast CPU and W10, which then you can try to "log out of user" thereby forcing the pc to do a "soft reset" by forcibly turning everything running off when it exits your Window user account) is to restart the computer.
Trying to turn just the .exe of the game alone either via task manager or right clicking to close via the task bar hardly helps. Sometimes it does turn homefront off after repeated tries, but overall doing either a full reset or as mentioned with signing out of your Window account is significantly faster and helps.
Literally I am losing files and getting system error messages (twice i even had to do a window restore because the game somehow destroyed/corrupted some important files) because of these sudden serious freeze to the whole PC because of the game. Seeing how this is very likely the final patch version of the game, i suggest you avoid this game unless you are willing to bear with the hard freezes, nevermind the glitchiness of the game itself.
Disappointing really. One of the most broken games I have ever played thus far. And what makes it worse is that I actually personally find the game enjoyable despite it glitches and understandably repetitive gameaplay.
My rig loadout is on my profile if you need reference on my rig capabilities. Also another note is that if you're using RGB products such as keyboards (Corsair K70. Apex M800), mousepads (Razer firefly, Apex MM880) and mice (Rival 700, Razer Mamba new, Sensei Wireless, M65 Pro RGB) the game WILL freeze your lighting (another indication that the game has some serious software issue). Headsets RGB doesn't seem to be affected by it for some reason, same goes for any RGB lighting for your case such as RGB fans and NZXT Hue+.
I'm not sure if the issue is because of Nvidia cards since I'm running 2 1070 (i tried running the game with and without SLI, problem still persists), so i can't say the same for AMD users. Nevertheless take it a cautionary note

Banished is a creative, simple but challenging, simulation game definitely worth the twenty bucks. However, despite the initial excitement  had with this game, its inginuity falls short of captivating past several hours of play. The game is addictively entertaining for a solid chunk of time thanks to its simple and unique approach, but all amusement is quickly exhausted due to the limited amount of choice the game offers you. To put it simply, it gets boring and repetitive.
What Banished does wrong is it takes its simple design and keeps it at just that, without actually applying it to different things. Imagine a world where every level in a Super Mario Bros. game is essentially the same as the first. Thrilling at first with a steep decline. Whether you have 5 people in your town, 20, 100, 500, the challenges and rules are the same, and figuring out how to get good at them only takes a few tries through some trial and error. Added on to that, there is a lacking sense of reward that doesn't help motivating the player to strive for that extra citizen.
To summarize, Banished is a thrilling simulation to play through for a few days, but after a while, lack of depth drives it to near boredom. If you are willing to hand over $20, go purchase it, but if not, I'd pass on this one. (7.4 / 10)

My first exposure to this game was a Let's Play by Lotus Prince.  At first glance, this game could easily be dismissed as not scary.  It certaintly doesn't look like a lot of the modern horror games.
Do not let quick impressions fool you, this game is a wonderfully creepy, scary and just disturbing game.
This is definetly a game to play with headphones if you can, the sound design is amazing.  Not only is there a mix of unsettling music, there is also plenty of background sounds that really start to get to you the longer you play.
This is also a game to play in big chunks, the more breaks you take, the more the atmosphere is broken.  If possible, try and play through to a finished path in one sitting.
I've currently gotten all three endings and I won't share any of the details here.
One of the strengths of this game is there is very little to interact with.  Too often horror games have you working on finding puzzle clues or weapons or health items.  This game you are limited what you can interact with.  The lack of busy work really helps draw you into the surroundings, and you'll find things in areas you thought weren't scary yet, slowly starting to disturb you greatly.
It also makes what you CAN interact with, and see more clearly, have that much more impact.
Yes, there are a few moments of jump scares, but this game is a lot more about the nature of being trapped in this nightmare, where you keep thinking you're waking up and escaping, and you're not.
Yes, I was one of the late backers after this game was fully funded and started to play when the Beta was available.  That doesn't make my review or praise for this game any less.  Hell it was seeing the Let's Play that made me want to help be a backer and be a part of this game.
This game has many moments where the sudden disturbing imagery made me turn away, though nothing in the realm of going too far.  Honestly some moments in this game reminded me of nightmares I've had myself, which only added to how emersed I was.
Also, do not seek a strategy guide, you'll figure out all the branches eventually.  Let youself find them alone, it's a much better story that way.
It took me a few times through some areas to figure out how to get the different branch, which helped the game feel very worth the price.

It takes a lot for me to bother to write a negative review on Steam.  I think I've done it twice in the last year (both for games that were huge disappointments and nowhere near the level that word of mouth made them out to be [Brothers: A Tale of Two Sons and Strider (2014)]).  This will be my third.
I really wanted to like this game; after not being a big fan of Retro/Grade, I decided to give this title a shot for a variety of reasons: the unique artstyle, it's a different genre from his last game, and most importantly, it's "based" off his experience with depression and OCD.  Having experienced both of those illnesses first-hand, I was hoping I could find something to relate to here, something that made me feel like somebody else knew what some of it felt like.
Instead I was treated to a repetitive game with very little gameplay and very little substance.  What little gameplay exists is moving the character from A to B and "investigating" the rooms along the way.  However, the "investigating" consists of looking at pictures or looking at creepy doll faces, for the most part.  Every once in awhile, something interesting will be there for you to examine, but the actual gameplay leaves much to be desired in the vein of exploration and story.  Further holding the gameplay back is the character's glacial walking speed -- and when you use the sprint button you quickly find out that the character must have the worlds worst case of asthma.  I know that this was done to prevent someone from just running through the game, but it hurts more than it helps, especially when you're feeling like you've seen the same hallway 37023 times and you just kind of find out what happens next.
From a horror perspective, there were a couple jump scares and a few kind of creepy moments that had me a little on edge, but nothing along the lines of instilling terror into my very soul.  There was a bit in one of the last branches I played through that had my heart racing a little, but again, nothing to really set it apart or make it worthwhile as far as I'm concerned.
The game does have some good points, even if they're few and far between, but they aren't enough to leave me feeling good about recommending this to anyone.  I thought the voice acting was pretty well done and the artstyle and animation is unique when the looming "darkness" isn't obscuring things.  Other than that, I can't say much else.
One of my friends recently played through this after backing the Kickstarter campaign because he was a huge fan of the developer's other game Retro/Grade.  He left disappointed as well and said to me that he thought the game would've been better as an animated short or something along those lines.  I can't help but think that this would've been the perfect medium for the story the developer wanted to tell as the most interesting parts of the game are the cutscenes that occurs between some of the chapters.
Overall, I found this game to be a waste of my time.  My OCD did kick in and I made sure I played the entire game and completed 100% of what it had to offer before writing my review... but I cannot in good conscience sit idly by and let people jump into this without so much as a warning.  This is probably the worst game I've played to completion in 2014 and I really feel like I would've been better off spending my money on something else.

The game divides itself between these open Red Zone battlefields and the (slightly) more civilised Yellow Zones. These are run down urban areas where the oppressed American population live under the angry, stompy boot of the Korean Army. They play out much like the Red Zones - open areas with multiple objectives leading up to a final goal - but add in a barely formed stealth mechanic and a far more stern response if you’re seen. Get spotted and it’s a case of running away, breaking line of sight and waiting out the alarm. It’s likely something you’ll be doing a lot. Because these areas are more built up it’s easier to get caught or cornered when things do go south.
Homefront: The Revolution manages to be entertaining without ever completely delivering on its open world warfare potential. There’s definitely an interesting game here if you fancy a different paced shooter. There’s just a few bits that don't quite click. The pace between the Red and Yellow Zones doesn’t flow as smoothly as it could, for example. The scrappy free roam fighting can deliver some great moments, but just as equally frustrate with loops of dying and respawning (the more restrictive set pieces fights can be especially guilty of this) and guns just don't feel... 'right'. Combined it all keeps Homefront at the level of ‘basically okay’.

Neverending Nightmares isn't so much a game, as it is an odd bit of art.
The stylized graphics and Victorian setting charmed me from the get-go.  For the past two years at PAX, this game has managed to catch my eye, even through the massive sensory overload brought on by the myriad of other games screaming for attention.  Suffice to say, it has been on my radar for a while.
Did it live up to my expectations?  Mostly.  The real strength of the game is its ambiance.  It absolutely must be played alone in a dark room, headphones cranked, with controller vibrations enabled.  The creepy music and sound effects blend smoothly with the visuals, first creating a sense of unease, which gradually ramps up to dread with a dash of "oh holy ♥♥♥♥ing hell that's disgusting."  The jump scares are definitely a big part of it, but far-between enough that they don't lose their effectiveness.
But back to my original point--it's really not much of a game.
I'm not sure what I was expecting.  Having played the demo, I suppose I thought it was going to be a puzzler.  Explore hallway, find candle.  Explore dark hallway, find axe.  Open blocked path, continue.  And on, and on.  I was kind of hoping for a horror-themed Myst.
Instead, you will spend the vast majority of your playtime creeping slowly through a (more or less) linear path, building tension for the next gruesome cutscene.   Objects that you can interact with are sparse, which is disappointing in such richly detailed environments.  It made it all the more confusing when there were special "interactable" gold-framed portraits scattered throughout the game.  It took me a while to realize that these weren't some sort of puzzle element, but rather rewards for people who contributed a certain amount to the kickstarter.
In short, this is interactive artwork, depicting a spiraling descent into madness inspired by the developer's own struggle with mental illness.  As a game, it's not exactly what I had thought it would be, but it was an enjoyable way to spend a few hours.

Starvation Simulator 2014, or otherwise known as Banished.
At the face of it it's just another city simulator, you gather materials, you build structures and off you go.
But it's not.
Your population multiplies exponentially if and the constant race to feed all of them is a challenge of itself.
It's constant growth, all over, until you just can't take it anymore, the inefficiencies of your production cycles, however minute they were, are having a compounding effect and before you know it the healthy food production you thought you had plummets like a rock and it's late summer or later. By spring you've lost 10-15% of your population and you no longer have the manpower to work your system. Firewood production breaks down, there's nobody gathering new logs, fishermen are fiddling around but not catching anything - they're freezing to death because the hunters have stopped gathering leathers and your tailor, what tailor? plucky fishermen, the odd gatherer, the priest, they're holding on. You shut down the mines, markets are down to one vendor, throw everyone at food production but it's too late, you're out of firewood and winter is coming. You're doomed. Esc, new game hit the new seed button a few times and off you go again.
Yes, it's brutal but it's also fantastically good.

*Just going to talk about how the port of this game performs*
Basically, this is the same version as the PS4 version of Final Fantasy X/X-2 HD, but they've added a couple of things not seen in any other version.
Let's talk about the pro's of this game:
+ You can switch between the original soundtrack and the remastered soundtrack on the fly.
+ There's lots of graphics settings (resolution, anti-aliasing, V-sync, texture quality, color correction, anisotropic filtering, etc.)
+ HD cutscenes. Incredibly glorious looking!
+ International content that the west never got!
+ Some VERY helpful boosters! They've got high speed (2x, and 4x), no encounters, more encounters, unlimited overdrive gauge, and some other ones that are pretty useless. Then there's the irreversible boosters like 99 of every item (no more Dark Matter grinding!), unlock all skills on the sphere grid, and max gil (99999999999999.)
+ Another Final Fantasy game without DRM!
Now onto the negatives:
- The file size is VERY large. It's a whopping 37GB! I get that it's two games, but 37 sounds like an extremely bloated number. I'm pretty sure it doesn't have to be that big!
- The chocobo minigame is still difficult, and lightning dodging is basically impossible unless you do the lightning tower trick. These are mandatory for getting Lulu and Tidus's celestial weapons.
- No 60 FPS, but this shouldn't concern anyone. Too bad it does, and if it bothers you, well here's your heads up. Honestly, a turn based game does not need to be 60 FPS! If you don't like the remastered music, lack of 60 FPS, or the new faces Nomura designed, then emulate it!

Let's make a scenario: say you're playing GTA or Saints Row, you get thrown into a vast open world, and all you can think is, "wow. I can't wait to explore every inch of this and wreck it like the kid on xbox live did to my mom" This is the driving point of JC2.
Just Cause 2 has a fairly simple story: go into the country and wreck the corrupt government so a new one can take it's place. To Progress in the story and unlock missions, you will need to cause chaos on the vast Island of Panoi. Everything is unlocked from the start (for the most part) so you just get out there and blow stuff up, and when I say blow stuff up I REALLY blow stuff up. The explosions in the game are freaking beautiful, heck everything in it is freaking beautiful, even on low settings. In the words of Nerd3, it's action movie: the game... everything has the potential to be obliterated!
Panoi consists of three main islands: an Urban/city area, a desert area, and a Jungle and Mountainous area. Just half of the desert area is roughly the size of the GTA: San Andreas map. Only half. Take a moment to think about how much space the whole world has. Yeah, a lot.
The overall gameplay is smooth and fun, whether you're doing a campaign mission, one of the thousands of side missions, or just screwing around. The HUD is limited, so there's lots of screen room to sight see. Just Cause two has insane variety in between missions as well. Side mission might require you to defend or escort someone, story missions have you taking on the government, and hundereds of bases for you to conquor inbetween. And what makes things better? Going from mission to mission is half the fun. Cops will chase you, you can steal any vehicle from ATV to Cargo Plane, all while pulling off insane stunts. The idea of having a grappling hook to pull yourself with a parachute as the main transportation is a genious idea that makes surprised, since we haven't seen it in any other game. Plus, the dedicated modders of the game just make it a millions time better plus 2.
TL;DR: Get out there, let the societal defiling commence! Whether your skydiving, driving, flying, boating, or shooting everything, you are bound to have a good time on Just Cause 2. If that's not enough, now there's a MULTIPLAYER mod so you can do all the stuff with your friends and other people! Buy. This. Game. It. Will. Be. Worth. It.

Receiver can only be described as a gun simulator. The combat is nothing special; right-click to aim with a small deadzone and left-click to fire. But what makes it a notable experiment in video gaming is the act of reloading. It's nothing so simple as pressing R and waiting for an animation to play out; you have to press a button for almost every action involved.
When you first spawn in, you need to check your firearm. There are buttons to pull back (and then lock) the slide, toggle the safety, (de-♥♥♥♥♥♥the hammer, remove the magazine, place the magazine in a specific inventory slot, remove a magazine from a specific inventory slot, holster the firearm, and load individual rounds into magazines.
If you can master the art of firing a shot, dropping the mag, holstering the firearm, reloading the magazine, redrawing the firearm, replacing the magazine, and (just for good measure) hitting the bolt release, you'll more than likely get a tingly sensation after doing it. This is hands-on gun porn.
The rest of the game is pretty basic; textures are a luxury, geometry is flat and neutral, the atmosphere is eerie in a Deus-Ex way, and the lore behind the recordings is rather interesting. Combat is tense and calculated, much more akin to chess than boxing, but sometimes the rules aren't clear enough to ease your frustration every time you die.
In the end, I'd love to see more games like this for more firearms, if only as an instruction tool for people wanting to learn how to use firearms without access to any or proper instruction.

I'll start this out by saying that this game is NOT a horror game; there are no jump scares, no chase scenes, no quick time events, nothing. That being said, this is one of the creepiest games I've ever played. The atmosphere is intense and immersive. The game gives the player little to no guidance beyond basic controls, but the ominous circumstances are enough to get you involved in unraveling Gone Home's many mysteries. This game, like The Vanishing of Ethan Carter, is short, strange, provocative, and never-ending; you'll be thinking about it and feeling its effects long after you've finished playing.

Stylized, creepy and short and MUST be played with both headphones and a game pad with vibration.  Missing either of the latter two will cause you to lose a good 50% of the atmosphere.  Great for Edward Gorey fans.
The game's strengths lie in atmosphere, sound setup and visual style, all of which are very strong.  It also does some rather clever things with checkpoints in a way that is not clear until you've gotten more familiar with the game.
It's weaknesses lie in the limited experiences offered.  The game could have been more, and one enemy in particular adds an obnoxious game mechanic which is initially clever and then very tedious.  It also fails to provide any really satisfying endings.  Finally, it's got very little replayability as once you've gotten all the endings there's little reason to return except after a long abscence after you've forgotten the pitfalls.
Your enjoyment of Neverinding Nightmares will largely depend on what you look for in a horror game.  Thankfully Slendy -- who showed up in the demo -- is removed from the final version.
If you're the kind of person who enjoys being creeped out, this does a pretty good job.  This isn't a game played for depth, but it does an excellent job with providing a unique experience your first time through.  If the art style doesn't do much for you, chances are the rest of the game won't.  If you enjoy Creepypasta however, this might be up your alley.
Warning for those squeamish about blood and gore: some paths are pretty nasty from an imagery standpoint.
Is it worth the price tag?  Depends on how much you value atmosphere.  I don't regret purchasing it, but others might not be as satisfied.  It's definitely something to get if you enjoy Edward Gorey stuff.  I would advise AGAINST looking at a Let's Play of it until after you've experienced most of what it has to offer as it will basically spoil the entire experience.

Let me get the general ruling out of the way first: this is a great game from a new and promising voice in the indie horror game scene. It tries new things and often does things by its own rules, and it does this effectively, while also following in the footsteps of tried and true horror classics. It's not for everyone, but fans of personal, artistic, exploratory games as well as fans of atmospheric horror games (as opposed to action/survival-based horror) should buy, enjoy, and support it.
That said, the game is not without its flaws, and a number of them have to do with pacing.
Hallways sometimes seem to go on a touch too long without much happening. It's a strange feeling, getting *bored* by a horror game. Luckily, several times I thought maybe I was started to get bored, something terrifically terrifying would happen and put my♥♥♥♥♥right back on the edge of my seat where it belonged. Perhaps these moments would not have been as effective without the moments of calm, but I feel that the game would have been *more*, not less, effective if a few of the rooms or hallways would have been cut.
That's not to say that all of the "pointless" rooms should be cut. It's kind of wonderful to be walking down what seems like a cookie-cutter hallway, enter a side-room, and find some new, unexpected, grotesque scene that, while serving no clear ludic function, ramps up the chills significantly and sinisterly.
By the end of the game, though, the player will likely become a little desensitized to blood and guts intended to convey scenes of horror. At the beginning, the bright sight of red blood against the beautifully pencilled black and white is a shock and reminds us that not all is well in this mansion. By the end of the game, there seems to be more red than white at times, and it becomes just another part of the macabre scenery.
Don't get me wrong, though; throughout the game, the gore is often used to wonderful effect, throwing guts in our face when we least expect it. While I'm not usually a fan of cheap jump-scares, this game does have a few, and they don't at all feel cheap. In fact, I think each and every one was greatly executed.
The art, overall, is quite nice. The way the seemingly-hand-drawn shadows scribbled their way over the light is a very cool effect and works well in the nightmarish context. The set-pieces and enemies in particular have frightening designs, especially as the game descends deeper into madness.
One enemy, though, just wasn't particularly scary or fun to deal with. Luckily it doesn't show up very often, but a few of its behaviors seemed to be a bit out of place with the rest of the games. While another, later enemy hit the sense of adolescent terror just right, this one was more obnoxious and almost silly. Other than the one, though, the enemies overall were extremely effective from both a gameplay and horror perspective.
The sound design and music are quite lovely, if you can call it that... aside from a few background ambience that sounds like someone doing an impression of a tortured Droopy Dog. I appreciated the way the music would evolve over the course of the different nightmares and a "new" nightmare's beginning would be indicated by a shift in the music as much as the narrative.
The endings (the two of three that I've played, at least), while narratively intriguing in their own rights, seem to happen just a tad too quickly and feel like they lack the weight I think they deserve. With this kind of short game I don't feel necessarily like *closure* is what's needed, but the credits seemed to start rolling quite quickly and suddenly, as if someone came into a movie theatre after the last words had been spoken and hurried the audience out so they could make room for the next group or something. That said, I like that the endings don't necessarily agree with each other. They all come from the same background, but come to different conclusions of varying depth that indicate what's **really** going on here, and I think that was a smart and cool decision.
Overall, there's a lot to praise in this game. It's at its best when it embraces nightmarish weirdness to try to throw the player off track, changing placement of rooms and playing with expectations. The lead developer, Matt Gilgenbach, has referenced *Metal Gear Solid* and *Silent Hill* as influences, and in this way they both shine through, but without becoming overbearing. If there's an ultimate takeaway, it should be that this game is a unique experience that I highly recommend. Also, supporting this game means supporting future titles from the developer, and personally I'm *very* excited to see what Gilgenbach and Infinitap does next.

Full disclosure: I was Kickstarter backer. I'm going to remain as unbiased as possible during this review, but it's more likely that not that I'll have a LITTLE bit more buy-in than others and this might taint my opinion.
I originally backed this project because I loved the art style as well as the commitment towards building something that didn't rely completely on jumpscares (I'm looking at you, Amnesia, Outlast, etc.). I'm seeing a lot of people saying that the ambience "doesn't build to anything". That it's too short and too linear.
While I'll say that they're completely correct, it was the journey, not the destination. I thoroughly enjoyed the art style as it's used to great effect. As someone who grew up with "In a Dark, Dark Room", this nailed the look. The added frosting was the sound direction, which is nothing short of amazing. Pants turn to gasps. Gasps turn to wheezing. Wheezing gives way to helplessness. Music sets the tone of neverending dread.
Some could argue that the cost doesn't justify the experience, but I disagree. I believe my Kickstarter funds went towards the exact game that was delivered. I don't regret backing this project one bit. I could complain about using the "psych ward" cliche as a means to deliver narrative, or that there was no real skill involved with beating the game, but that's not the purpose of the game. It's not here to make you reevaluate your life; it's here to be a nice, scary haunted house. A short ride that reminds you why you like scary things to begin with.
It's good. Is it $15 good? I would say so, but I'm a lone voice. If you're looking for the next Amnesia, or you're looking for something you can play over and over again for long durations, move along. If you're looking for a nice experience of dread and can part with your $15, you could certainly do much worse.

*Just going to talk about how the port of this game performs*
Basically, this is the same version as the PS4 version of Final Fantasy X/X-2 HD, but they've added a couple of things not seen in any other version.
Let's talk about the pro's of this game:
+ You can switch between the original soundtrack and the remastered soundtrack on the fly.
+ There's lots of graphics settings (resolution, anti-aliasing, V-sync, texture quality, color correction, anisotropic filtering, etc.)
+ HD cutscenes. Incredibly glorious looking!
+ International content that the west never got!
+ Some VERY helpful boosters! They've got high speed (2x, and 4x), no encounters, more encounters, unlimited overdrive gauge, and some other ones that are pretty useless. Then there's the irreversible boosters like 99 of every item (no more Dark Matter grinding!), unlock all skills on the sphere grid, and max gil (99999999999999.)
+ Another Final Fantasy game without DRM!
Now onto the negatives:
- The file size is VERY large. It's a whopping 37GB! I get that it's two games, but 37 sounds like an extremely bloated number. I'm pretty sure it doesn't have to be that big!

This is one of my favorite games ever and I'm sooooooooooo glad it finally came to the PC, I almost never thought it would happen, and it's even better than I ever thought it could be on PC.
Originally I already bought this on PS3 and it was already great-looking with amazing nostalgic value there but this version takes everything I liked about the PS3 HD Remaster and makes it even better, like including both the original music and the fancy new arrangement music to switch between.  They originally wanted to do this on the PS3 version as well but didn't bother due to size restraints.
This game is very stable and well optimized for any modern 1st-day PC release, let alone a PC port from Square Enix.  They really put some work in with this one.  There's a real menu when you hit escape instead of just opening a jarring "Close Window?" prompt in a Windows UI box appearing over the game as with many other FF games.  The aformentioned pause menu has an ACTUAL IN-GAME GRAPHICS SETTINGS MENU!!!!!!  It's got MSAA options, SMAA options, texture options, shadow options and a few others.  I personally have the settings maxed out and it looks great.  I play it on 1440p and the textures are incredible considering it's a 15 year old game originally made for Standard Definition screens now being played on an extremely large but relatively uncommon resolution above the typical 1080p that the HD Remaster was probably optimized for already on PS3/4.  Presumably this means 4K will look great as well for those with such monitors.  So far no crashing at all and only some minor choppiness in areas that have a lot going on such as in Al Bhed Home, which is perfectly normal and expected.
The XBox One controller actually works perfectly as well.  Final Fantasy VIII didn't work with controllers at all, Final Fantasy IX had controller support but it was so dysfunctional I couldn't even play the game.  This game has perfect controller support and using it feels natural: everything just works, and there's no weirdly mapped buttons.  The game also uses actual XBox controller buttons in the UI for explanations instead of defaulting to keyboard keys.
My only issues are really small ones, mostly that some minor things about the gameplay weren't addressed in the Remastering process, like the inconvenient inability to exchange spheres in cloister puzzles instead of having to find a slot to leave one sphere so you could pick up the other.  It would've been nice of them to acknowledge how tedious these puzzles are and improve it just a little bit sort of like they did with the booster options, but it would've required new animations I think.  Also the Blitzball automatic movement AI is awful, passing to your ideal shooter on the left side doesn't mean they will try to get between defenders and get closer to the goal for an angled shot and only having to deal with a defender or two, or possibly even having an open shot.  Instead, they still instantly move backwards diagonally towards the middle and seem to try gathering up as many opposing team players as possible so you're having to shoot/pass/breakthrough in quadruple coverage from center field.  Honestly I didn't expect them to fix these things anyway though, it just would've made the game that much closer to perfection.
Any PC gamer who liked Final Fantasy X back in the day on PS2, I would strongly recommend this game to them.  It's really not the same lazy quality port as all the other Final Fantasy ports, they did a very good job on this game and I consider it to be the definitive FFX experience.

This is a fairly difficult game and perhaps not for everyone, however I can recommend this on three counts
A) Are you a gun nut?
B) are you interested in or do you partake game design, especially First person shooters?
C) are you interested in a tense game with deep and interesting mechanics, a cyber-punky story and high difficulty?
If you answer "Yes" to at least one of those questions, then I say Drop the five bucks on this one. Seriously do it, Right now. For a game that was made in seven days (albiet with some post release content), I'm rather impressed on how it came out.
Sure it doesn't look that impressive from a technical standpoint and it can be REALLY hard at times, but half the fun is the learning curve. The controls are complex, but the game's help menu really helps ease you in. After a few deaths muscle memory will take over and you won't need it.
It's quite an empowering feeling when you get the drop on two drones and nail them both in two shots. In other games that doesn't sound impressive. However, in reciever it is. Because quick, percise shot placement is REQUIRED, or else you end up dead or wasting precious ammo, this of course assumes you even had your gun loaded and ready to fire.
If that sounds awesome to you, drop the five bucks, I'm glad I did!

Wow, when was the last time i had this much fun with guns? For me, shooters like cod or even bioshock are nothing. i mean they cant really give me anything good. maybe a good story, the new bioshock is kinda decent at that. I also liked Dishonored, but just because the stealth game mechanics were pretty awesome, and the world what they built for the game is kinda interesting (and i hate steampunk, so they did a pretty good job at that).
But lets forget all those arcade shooters, lets concentrate on the real thing. And when I say real, i REALLY MEAN IT. Have you ever shoot with a gun? Did you ever reload a weapon? these questions may pop up in your head when you are playing with Receiver. And also the help menu cause you will need it A LOT. I’m not kidding, getting use to this game could be frustrating at the beginning, but the time you will spent to learn about your gun, about the enemy drones and about the whole game is a terrific experience. A bit painful though, cause you gonna die and restart the game, a lot. The difficulty is a bit hard, but Reciever’s monotonic and mesmerizing gameplay gonna lure you to the bottom of this game.

I've rarely seen a game start off so stellar, then nosedive. and then suddenly be over before it barely got underway. The first half is the most eerie gaming experience I've ever had—despite the abstract artstyle—to the point where I had to shut it off and calm myself down after just 5 minutes. The few interactive items in the game that seemed like maybe pieces to a puzzle, or a secret to unravel (mostly framed portraits) appear to be just things for you to pointlessly look at.

Gone Home is not really a game; it's an interactive narrative experience. That said, there's relatively little interactivity. It actually falls closer to a modern art installation. You can walk around the gloomy halls and half-used rooms and occasionally a bit of the narrative will be revealed via audiolog tied to some specific unique object, but you are not in command of the story. You do not choose paths or change outcomes, you do not broker relations or even view characters interacting with each other. The "game" might as well not have any input at all. It is a ride at Universal Studios, minus the excitement.
The narrative is enjoyable, if cliche, and takes no risks; telling the same Sixteen Candles/Breakfast Club story of aspects of everyday life straight out of the 70s/80s. It is serviceable, and short. By god is it short. I was able to "complete" the narrative in about 2 hours, despite being, what I considered, incredibly thorough. I hate to give it a review rather than a critique, but it is simply a narrative, and not a complex one at that, and so I don't know how else to assess it. It is roughly the average length of a standard Hollywood movie, but with less plot than most, and nearly all of it delivered through exposition.
This makes a $20 cost very hard to justify. I purchased it on sale for $17.50, and still feel quite underwhelmed. Movies cost ~$12, have the same length and level of interactivity (since choosing where to direct your attention on the screen is roughly equivalent to choosing which object in a scene to pick up), and deliver more and better stories. If it were a movie, it would be dull, overpriced, and mediocre. The fact that it's on PC hardly makes a difference, especially since I see no incentive to replay it or even have a friend play it unless it was to impress upon them how dreary of a reentrance interactive narratives have made into the market (despite it's predecessor, Dear Esther, setting the bar rather low).
The long and short of it is it's hardly worth your time, let alone your $20. Amongst a sea of worthy contenders which actually have gameplay, it looks all the worse. Consider getting Papers, Please, or Cart Life, or Hotline Miami, or any number of other, cheaper, and overall higher quality media, and which actually have mechanics.

This is a horror game that shocked

Make no mistake; this is a psychologycal horror game in the truest sense - It's a game that through it's main gameplay loop (an endless awakening into another nightmare) explores the developer's daily struggles of OCD as well as intrusive thoughts. It's all presented in an Edward Gorey-like artstyle, that also brings to mind the works of Edgar Allan Poe. Even more intriguing than it's artstyle is the absolutely fantastic sound design which consantly keeps the player tense for the horrors to come. Is this the scariest horror game I've ever played? Well, no. But like the best games in the psychological horror genre it focuses on being thoroughly unsettling throughout - a feeling that intensifies upon reflecting on the real life mental struggles that inspired it.
Common complaints target the game's short length and the lack of player interaction - but to me these miss the point. The game should be judged by the emotional journey it takes the player through, not by some commercial formula of "X hours of gameplay for Y amount of money". To me this is a great game, and the few complaints I do have - i.e. some of the character animations, lip-syncing - are likely to be addressed through updates, and don't detract from the raw human emotion and pain conveyed through the experience.
Two thumbs up.

Receiver is a game that was slighlty surprising to me, but was it a good or bad surprise?
Gameplay: 6.5/10 - Receiver is a game with a lot of good ideas, including the excellent gun simulation. Before I go on with this topic however, I must mention that I've never held a gun in my entire life, let alone fire one. With that said, let's continue. Even if the gun simulation is wrong (not saying it is), there is a lot of achievement that comes with playing Receiver. However, with all that feeling of achievment comes a lot of frustration before it. For example, it will take you a lot of time to truly understand the mechanics of the game which can be quite time consuming and frankly, boring. Luckily, once you do get a hold of what you need to do, Receiver is very rewarding.
In Receiver you will need to remember a lot of keys, but this adds to the feeling of realism that the game tries it hardest to present to you. This also means that when you remember how to do something without looking at the massive control panel, you will feel great. You will have to do everything that you would have to do in real life (as far as I know), to actually use the gun properly.
Now, aside from the gun simulation, Receiver is fairly basic. You will basically just find yourself walking through a maze like area, while mostly trying to stay hidden from turrets and other machines that will kill you quite quickly. Of course, you could fight these so called enemies, but you would be much better off just sticking to the shadows, because they are not easy to kill.
I suppose there's only one more question to ask about the gameplay; is it fun? The answer if you ask me, can never be correct. The right question would actually be - Do you want an excellent gun simulator, or an action packed first person shooter? If your answer is an excellent gun simulator, then you will find many hours of enjoyment out of Receiver, but otherwise, it might catch your interest for a bit to only fall into your large library of games that you never play on Steam.
Presentation: 5.0/10 - The style of the game is extremely simplistic in the sense that everything feels like a block or rectangle lacking texture; because everything is. The world you play in is confusing like a maze, and quite interesting, but your actual surroundings look very bland and untouched. Luckily the game has some interesting lighting effects that stand out above all the grey and colorless environments that you will be traversing through. So, Receiver isn't the best looking game, but at five bucks I didn't expect too much from that aspect.
Plot: 5.3/10 - This where things get quite odd. In Receiver, you will search for tapes. These tapes will be littered around the map and don't really move the story forward, but instead adds some more depth to the background of the game. Unfortunately, I'm lacking skills to collect all tapes, but it seems interesting how they've done the story. Finding out things in little bits and pieces has a kind of modern murder mystery feel to it, which I quite enjoy. However, even if this is an interesting idea, it adds very little to the game, which is quite dissapointing.
Overall: 5.6/10 - Mediocre.
I'd say that if you're not into guns and how they actually work, don't waste your time and money here. If you do like guns and how they work, then absolutely go for it, at only five bucks it's a steal for a person like that.

Lately I have been very crazy about this game. I think there are several things make it so special.
The first thing is absolutely the difficulty. This game is so damn HARD. My first hour playing this game is nothing but dying. The begin part is so tough that I cannot get what this game is about at all and even try to give up. However, it feels so worth once I get to understand the fun of this game. Difficulty is a good thing, especially for hardcore players. After years of hardcore gameplay, I become fastidious and go on from game to game just to find some challenge. This game totally fits me. What’s more, the difficulty of this game is so comprehensive. It’s not just the battle part. How to build your character, which class, what weapon, what spell, where you can go to find the next dungeon, how to solve the puzzle or even where you can find a puzzle to solve. It’s just a dangerous secret world unfold in front of you, a poor soul surrounded by dark and don’t even dare to move a step because there could be a trap everywhere. I totally love this immersive experience of the game.
The second thing is the build of a character. You are totally free in this game. You have a class but it limits you nothing as well as bears you nothing. What you can do all depends on how you spend your attribute points, choose your weapon, armor and spells. You can be a tanky warrior, a agile rogue, a cleric, a mage, a dark mage, or you can be all of them at the same time. There are just so many things to chose from and you can mix them freely as you want. In one word, there are no boundaries.
Besides, as I mentioned above, every element in this game fits each other so well that together they make a whole comprehensive experience, a poor soul in a dark world watching for every step he moves. With every step you move, you become stronger and stronger. Finally, you will not be sacred any more, because you are the most powerful one in the world.

Honest review: This game has been around way before Battlefield came up with the WWI idea. In my humble opinion it executes the historical accuracy far better.
Realism is this games forte, nothing arcade like in the ways of BF/CoD or black dudes/women running through the trenches (because they did not, no matter how loud you shout racism or patriarchy. Go learn some history). There are no F1 accelerating tanks or no-trench maps. This is actual WWI, as it was intended to be. You play as a forgotten soldier in the muddy and rainy trenches of France. A bullet can kill you, or fatally wound you. Gas attacks or barbed wire can be very troublesome either. There are also several modes to play and the biggest thing they have is the trench warfare style move forwards and backwards maps. It is true that the game requires a good rig to run smooth but if you have it and if you like realistic shooters on WWI, then I say it is good enough. You get the most bang for your buck. Have fun and see you in the ghastly trenches of war !

For a game that was created in a single week, it runs exceptionally well and is quite addictive.  This game, unlike other FPS's, take the approuch of being as real as possible: Every single thing you do with the gun is another step for you to take.  Unloading a clip?  Reloading?  Safty?  All of those need to be done one at a time.  Although this may seem risky, this game does it to a whole new level and makes it interesting.  Mechanics are a bit awkward to get a handle of at first, but after about a half hour of play-time, you begin to get the hang of it, gaining some progress in the game.  I can almost memorize all the buttons required for reloading.
Enemies are nothing special, though: they basically boil down to stationary turrets and flying robot helicopers from SpyGear with tazers that go *zap*.  Nothing unique, but far from being easy.
This game does a good job of making it a challange without making it either laughably easy or insanly hard.  At first, the game is difficult, but then you get a hang of things and it begins to get easier.  It's well paced.
Randomly generated areas also help the game's overall success.
This game is fantastic for what it is.  The best part is that I didn't even need to pay for it: They announced that if you pre-order their other game, "Overgrowth" (which is an excellent game as well; I highly recomend it) you get a free copy of "Reciever" as a thank you gift.
Thanks, Wolfire games!  ~Ohyoupokedme

Receiver is one of those 'weird' games that you're either going to absolutely love, or hate with a passion of a thousand suns. To help you with your decision, I've offered a quick bullet point breakdown of what this game is, what it offers, and from there hopefully you can make a decision.
- Procedurally generated world design, enemy placement, starting loadouts, and loot. No two games are going to be the same.
- Permadeath. Get killed and you restart.
- Brutally efficient enemies, which come in mobile (air) and static (ground) variants.
- Realistic gun handling and bullet physics
Simple in design, yet deep and addicting in play, Receiver is one of those few games that had me hooked for HOURS. At first glance this seems like a low rent, indie developed FPS title - but then you learn (yes, LEARN) how to reload your gun and that's when the game's design starts to sink in. Exploring hallways, rooms, and open areas becomes an experience of both elation and absolute tension. What kind of enemy is in the next area? Do you have enough ammo? Is that a shiny pile of bullets? Which path do you take? What's that noise?
This is the world of Receiver, one of experimentation, frustration, and then pure satisfaction. You will take down turrets, find tons of ammo, and maybe if you're lucky you'll stumble upon some of the hidden audio tapes. Then you'll get murdered by a flying sentry and do it all over again, with a smile on your face and a newfound determination to do better.
