I should probably preface this by informing you that I took place in the pre-alpha testing of Neverending Nightmares as a reward for backing the game. I have been exposed to the game much longer than most people probably will.
So obviously, you know that it’s a horror game, but not in the same way Amnesia: The Dark Descent, Outlast, Slender, or SCP Containment Breach are. Those use a first person perspective to create more personal jump scares and to create a more realistic atmosphere; Neverending Nightmares doesn’t have nearly as many jump scares as those do and focuses on enhancing a very foreboding atmosphere and telling a story. Neverending Nightmares has a lot more in common with Gone Home then the other titles mentioned.
The story in NN can easily get confusing and requires some analysis to fully understand. Depending on which ending you get, you may be greatly disappointed in the game. I feel like only one of the endings actually has closure while the other two are much better if experienced after the first ending. The game tries to push the player to the first ending, but there is one branch that I feel could have been done much better in pushing the player in the right direction (SPOILER: it’s at the end of the asylum level. I feel like most people will probably jump off the edge just to see what happens, even if there’s a teetering animation. This is problematic because the way to the first ending is by going back into the asylum).
The horror in NN mostly comes from the atmosphere and imagery; not too much from the feeling of being chased or stalked like in SCP or, Slender. If you want something like those games then you’ll probably be somewhat disappointed with NN. Not to say that NN doesn’t have jump scares but they’re placed throughout the game very sparingly like in Amnesia, or Silent Hill. Silent Hill is somewhat similar to NN, but Silent Hill had more of a puzzle focus than NN does. The puzzles in NN are pretty easy and even become easier if you can’t seem to figure it out (note, that these “hints” are designed not to break your immersion, so there will be no word box that appears; rather, something in the environment will change to lead you in the right direction). If you expect the cryptic puzzles found in Silent Hill, then you’ll probably be disappointed.
From my interactions with Matt Gilgenbach, the creative director, and my many playthroughs of the game, I figured that immersion is probably the biggest priority in this game. Many things that are just looked over in other games have a reason for it to happen; for example, every time the player dies, he wakes up in a bed as if that death was just a nightmare. Other games would probably just throw a “game over” screen and have you try again—and there’s nothing wrong with that, but NN creates a narrative reason to player deaths, which boosts immersion. Immersion also works well with the way the game tells its story since attention to the game environments is expected to fully understand many of the details in the story. I feel like the game’s short length also encourages replays since it’s a lot easier to study the environments of a two-hour game than a twenty-hour one.
So in conclusion, for what it is, NN is a great experience that I would recommend it to anyone who likes disturbing horror with a thought-out story, and a very distinctive art style. The game isn't really going to make you scream like other horror games, the game will give you more of an uncomfortable feeling while playing. This game is very, very reminiscent of the Tropico series rather than Cities XL or SimCity.  Individual lives are more important than big-picture thinking, resource gathering is a matter of watching visual feedback---you can see your people at work---and the in-game economy is very much dependent on producing enough to export so that you can get what you need from foreign trade.
Then again, that might be this game's problem.  It's Tropico set to Battletoads difficulty for reasons that often don't make sense.  Citizen resource consumption rates are set high seemingly as a difficulty construct, random (negative) events occur at the same frequency they would in the aforementioned Tropico's "Are you loco, Presidente?" setting, and the game never reaches a point that's the most rewarding part of the genre---the ability to sit back and enjoy what you've built.  There's always _something_ horribly out of true, or if there isn't, it's only a random event away.
Which makes it a great Ph.D-level program for master city builders (I've been playing this genre since SimCity Classic and have played every major and some of the minor series to come out over the last 25 years).  What it doesn't make it is a game to just relax with and enjoy.
A hesitant recommendation.  Know what you're getting into and don't force this game to be something it's not and you'll like it just fine.  It's well-constructed.  It just too often crosses the line between fun and frustrating.

Platforming with a twist. VVVVVV is an excellent example of a good platformer that has been made better by adding an original, interesting core game mechanic. In VVVVVV, you play as Captain Viridian who must rescue his crew after a disaster nearly destroys his ship. Traveling all around a strange new universe called "VVVVVV", you must rescue each crew member in their own zone of the map. Each new zone introduces a new game mechanic such as moving maps, bouncy ropes, and NPC co-op.
VVVVVV's system of introducing new mechanics allows you to adjust to each challenge before entering the last stages of the game which require you to navigate maps containing every mechanic simultaneously. This isn't an easy game, but not too hard to beat if you're persistent. Many of the most challenging puzzles are previously-optional challenges which are required to reach a treasure. Veni Vidi Vici. After completing the main story and collecting every treasure, you receive a special reward.

Full disclosure: review copy provided by developer/publisher!
“Neverending Nightmares” is one of the more aptly named titles for a game on Steam (y'know, besides "Shannon Tweeds Attack of the Groupies"), because that is exactly what will plague you upon playing it: never-ending nightmares. This is bleak, brutal, and brief – like every good horror should be.
As Thomas you wake up from a nightmare... only to realize that you're still asleep, still dreaming. And like a Freudian Dante you'll make your descent down the increasingly bizarre and menacing circles of your inner Hell searching for your Beatrice... of sorts. The world is sketched starkly and wildly in black and white (like a schizophrenic's scribblings) with the occasional accent of blood red and sickly yellow to mark manipulable objects and pretty much every childhood fear, irrational or otherwise, you still foster in your beating heart: darkness, gore, claustrophobia, self-harm, asylums, creepy porcelain-skinned, raven-haired girls, dolls... it touches on them all. ♥♥♥♥ing dolls. ♥♥♥♥ing dolls and raven-haired girls, man. Some people are afraid of heights. Some people are afraid of clowns. I'm afraid of dolls and women with black hair and fair complexions. And if you aren't, you will be.
The atmosphere is thick in this one. As you progress slowly from room to room and area to area, the game will do its damnedest to put you on edge. China will crash to the floor with no prompting, birds slam into windows with suicidal intent, and shadowy figures dissipate as you draw close. Then the tension will ease off, and your guard will be lowered. That's when the game will hit you. And it will hit you relentlessly. As I've said, this will touch on all your creeping nightmares... and perhaps some new ones will blossom. How great for you! “Neverending Nightmares” utilizes its jumpscares effectively. While they are numerous, they're only as scary as the atmosphere allows and let me tell you, it abides.
According to the “About This Game” section, “Neverending Nightmares” is in part inspired by a developer's own struggle with mental illness. And that absolutely comes across in the game. The jarring, not-initially-clear story, the imagined monsters... and the real ones; the soft, distorted, plinky music and “mental ward sketching” look of the art... it feels very personal. And the game benefits from it. This is a man's soul laid bare, complete with an intimate, artistic peephole into his troubled mind. It gives the game character. More importantly, it makes it that much more terrifying and tangible.
“Neverending Nightmares” doesn't overstay its welcome, keeping it fresh and frightening. And with the divergent endings you'll likely get some replayability, but don't expect to revisit this one over and over as it's fairly linear. It isn't all that challenging either, though that isn't why I play horrors. I play them to have a story told to me... a story told to me by an unspeakable horror that has me bound to a chair in basement with a lone, swinging light bulb above my head. And it's on the fritz.
“Neverending Nightmares” is one of the better ways to ring in a new spooktastic October.

Neverending Nightmares is a psychological horror game based on developer Matt Gilgenbach’s personal experience with OCD and depression. You can clearly see that a lot of work and effort went into creating this game but the big question really is: is this game enjoyable for and accessible to anyone else who doesn’t suffer from these disorders ? Is this game not too personal ? Let’s review:
I’ll immediately answer that question for you. No, the game has not become too personal and it has become a game anyone can play. What you make of it is totally up to you, however. Even if most of what you’ll see is fairly obvious.
When I said that this is a psychological horror game I wasn’t being entirely honest with you. Because the game - well, it doesn’t really rely on them, but it uses them anyway – also has a few jump scares in it. But, these are rare and more creepy than scary.
The game does an amazing job at creating an unsettling atmosphere. It felt uneasy the whole time I was playing this. Not many horror games have managed to do this so that was a pleasant surprise for me.
This is a traditional survival horror game where you don’t possess any weapons (nor will you pick any up later on) and the idea behind it is to create a sense of dread or helplessness. And with success.
You’ll navigate through a mansion and other environments to find out what’s happening with you and at least one other major character. I’m not going to spoil anything here, because this is a game that should be experienced and talking about it too much would just detract from that.
The whole world is in black and white with the exception of some objects that you can interact with (like doors and paintings) and things like blood. It’s part of why the atmosphere is so good, because there’s no clear distinction between objects. You can’t possibly know what to expect.
You’ll navigate through the environments by just going through doors in the hope that it’s the right one. There’s no map and especially in the beginning this can lead to a bit of backtracking. The fact that the environments subtly change doesn’t help either. But once you realize how the game works it will actually become easier to understand.
Neverending Nightmares is a short experience, and I finished my first playthrough within just an hour. After completing it I noticed that the game actually has branching paths and thus I actually missed 3 different endings. This was entirely unexpected because the game doesn’t play like a game where you can make choices. It’s all very subtle. So, anyway, I continued closest to where it would branch off and tried a different path. And what do you know ? I came across different settings/environments and had completely different scares, along with a story that wasn’t even remotely similar to my first ending. Very impressive and because of that you can easily add a couple of hours to the playtime here. I think first time players can and will finish the first story in 60-90 minutes, though.
And I almost forgot to mention; should you die - and it doesn’t matter where - you will usually wake up in your room. Going through the door will usually let you continue close to where you died so you won’t have to backtrack much. It’s a clever system that once again adds to the creepy atmosphere it tries to create.
Graphically this game is a stunner. Usually I don’t expect indie games to have high resolution art in them, but Neverending Nightmares has some of the prettiest and sharpest graphics I’ve seen in a 2D game so far. People refer to it as pen-and-ink style and I can only agree. It’s something that has to be seen in motion to be appreciated and understood.
There are so many details found in the environments and in the animations of your character that it’s nothing short of impressive. I’ve seen the character stopping and panting after running for too long, with perfect lip syncing and I’ve seen the belly of a monster moving. Usually developers don’t put much time in animating everything there is to animate so it usually comes down to limbs and heads. This is absolutely amazing.
The music and sounds are ominous and exactly what you would expect from a horror game. Don’t expect any happy tunes here.
Now, ‘is there nothing wrong with this game’, I hear you ask ? Well, no, not really. If there’s one thing I had to mention then it’s that it’s a bit slow sometimes and that it’s a bit repetitive once you get used to the scares and atmosphere. That’s literally the only thing I can think of. Honestly.
I hope Matt’s Neverending Nightmares will be a huge success critically and financially, because it really deserves it. And if it can make people aware of OCD and depression at the same time then it deserves even more credit. I just hope that the people who are going to play it will also try to actually finish it because, let’s be honest, that is its ultimate goal.

Disclaimer: I took part in the Kickstarter campaign in order to get this game funded. As a result I’ve been playing the game for a good number of months in its Alpha/Beta stages, giving feedback and talking with the developers about the game.
-TL;DR version-
The game is a wonderfully crafted psychological horror game that builds its horror around crafting a dark and foreboding atmosphere. It also does a great job at emphasising a slower, more disturbing tone than a traditional startling tone. The game being inspired by the visions and thoughts of someone with mental illness give a very genuine and unnerving feel to everything, which as a result makes for one of the best horror games that I’ve played in recent times. Definitely worth your time if you’re a horror fan and want something that’ll truly get under your skin.
-Long version-
Neverending Nightmares is a psychological horror game based upon the intrusive thoughts that have plagued developer Matt Gilgenbach over the years as a result of his mental illness. You play as Thomas, a man who initially when the game begins wakes up from a nightmare. From then on the game is shaped around Thomas’ descent into his mind as he keeps waking up into new nightmares. One major factor is consistent throughout almost all of Thomas’ nightmares, the presence of a girl named Gabby. How she and Thomas are connected remains unclear until one of the games multiple endings. As a result the player is given multiple possible theories to play around and work with; is she your sister? Is she your wife? Is she just a friend? Is she an enemy? The narrative gives the player enough to work with so that they are constantly guessing up until the very end of the game. This constant questioning plays into the world of Neverending Nightmares as you are never certain of what is reality or what is simply a figment of the nightmare you are currently in. As explained earlier the game features multiple branching pathways that lead to multiple endings (3 in total). These branches change the story of the game in various unique ways making the entire motivation behind the nightmares different in each ending, as a result it is encouraged that you playthrough multiple times to acquire all the endings and experience new nightmares that can only be found on that pathway. This added replayability should give you around an hour or two extra playtime once your first playthrough is completed.

The gameplay of Neverending Nightmares follows a 2D adventure format. You walk around various environments, interact with objects and explore your current nightmare in order to progress forward. If there’s one shortcoming that can be levelled against the game it’s that the gameplay itself, on an objective level, is rather basic. The formula doesn’t change too drastically from nightmare to nightmare, with only some minor puzzle solving elements being introduced when dealing with enemies. However there’s enough story and horror to help strengthen the gameplay, making you intrigued to progress further. In terms of actual control Neverending Nightmares adopts a very simple control style, with the only major functions being move, interact and sprint. This simplicity however doesn’t detract from the overall product in a major way.  The controls themselves are spot on, with the player being able to move Thomas in any which way they please, as well as being fully re-bindable. The controls also play into the horror as Thomas suffers from asthma, so he can only sprint for a short distance which requires effective management so the player isn’t left in a compromising situation. There are also other sections that play with the controls in interesting ways, however you shall have to find those out for yourself.
But what’s a horror game without the horror right? Well you’ll find your needs met with Neverending Nightmares. As this is a semi-autobiographical product a lot of the horror has been drawn from real experiences and visions, which really adds to the game's atmosphere. Some of the visions and imagery you experience in Neverending Nightmares is truly disturbing, especially with the added context of it being taken from a very real place. From body mutilation to overwhelming darkness, there are multiple instances where you will be truly afraid or horrified of what may or may not be around the next turn. Often times you’ll find yourself simply walking down a hallway, however the game slowly begins to twist and bend the environment to play with you. Distant whispers, growls within the darkness, words written in blood are simply some of the tactics that start to put you on edge. From there everything only builds and continues to build, making the player wonder “When is something going to attack me?” “Where’s the next safe spot?” “What will happen if I go down these stairs?”. Often times you will have never even seen an enemy that could potentially kill you and you’re still on edge, just waiting…Waiting for the inevitable. All of this contributes into creating a horror game that understands that the best way to create fear is to let the player scare themselves. However for those who like and appreciate the more startling aspects to horror, there are still elements of that in here with some well crafted jumpscares that are never too abundant to become tiresome.
One aspect of the game that can be critiqued is the brevity and challenge of the game. Neverending Nightmares isn’t the most challenging of horror games. Often times you are able to bypass enemies with relative ease once you determine their behaviour and the game is decidely linear which leads little room to get lost. As a result the game in one playthrough can be finished in around 2-3 hours, however with the added branches there is an extra hour or two of gameplay added on top. With that said, the game is much more focused on the experience than challenge. By focusing more on the experience, the team at Infinitap Games are able to create a very lean game that packs all of horror into one sleek package. As a result the horror itself is a lot more impactful rather than being bogged down by repetition or filler. How you feel on the matter however is something that should be left up to you, just be aware that the game isn’t particularly lengthy or challenging before going in.
Finally the visual/audio design is superb throughout. The Edward Gorey inspired art design stands out as being something unique within the genre, it also creates a storybook-esque style that meshes well with the horrific atmosphere. The audio design is top notch with subtle flourishes of music and ambient noises that play on your mind all throughout the game. Voice acting, whilst being slightly underplayed in the story as a whole, conveys the suitable amount of emotion required to make you empathise with Thomas’ struggle and dubious of Gabby’s true intentions.
All in all I can say that the money I spent on Kickstarting this game was not made in vain. Neverending Nightmares succeeds at crafting a satisfying horror experience that toys with the player in a wonderfully fresh way. The semi-autobiographical angle gives the whole game a very grounded and real atmosphere, making you see some of the worst that mental illness does to people.
In my opinion, it’s one of my favourite horror games in recent memory and definitely worth a purchase for any horror fan.

So far im going to start off by giving this a mixed review, not a thumbs up, not a thumbs down. I'm going to be honest and give as much info as i can to anybody starting this after ds1

a lot of changes will have you on edge after starting off. You dont start off with an estus flask until a bit in, you start off with healing gems, your estus flask also only starts with one charge, you upgrade this with shards you find compared to using humanity to further how many charges you get at the bonfire in dark souls 1, you also no longer level at any bonfire, you level at a lady next to one of the bonfires you run into. another concept at the start which bugs me is that when you die, you hallow out, but as you die more, you hallow out more and more and you will notice the visual changes in your character. as you die more and hallow more you will start off with less of your actual health bar making things even more difficult, you reverse this by using a human effigy to restore your humanity instead of using an actual humanity based system in this game. npcs will also invade you while hallowed. Bought this game for around $23 when it was on sale. That's a fair price. I had fun playing this game, but I doubt I would play it again. The atmosphere and graphics were on point. I tell my friends this is a mashup of Assassin's Creed and Far Cry, with some Fallout-level destruction thrown in there. Running around the "Red Zone", shooting snipers, then running to a different position while avoiding air ships was fun. And seeing a guard abusing a civilian and slitting that guard's throat was satisfying.
All in all, I'd give this game a 7/10 for the $20 sale price. It'd be 6/10 if I paid full price.
Tl;dr: Wait for the game to go on sale.

I have been enamored by this game from the first time I saw it. In fact, this is the first game I've purchased at full price in a long time. Many will describe this game as cross between a city builder and a survival game, and these descriptions are spot on. When starting, you will want to play the game slowly and deliberately to ensure that every ounce of productivity is squeezed out of your population. After a few years, though, and once your citizens have the basics covered, you can start expanding your village and numbers. This expansion requires a certain level of balance, as you want to ensure that you citizens have plenty of food, clothes, tools, and firewood to continue surviving for another year.
There have been many reviews that criticize the game for losing its difficulty after a few hours. I would agree with this to a certain extent; once you have expanded to a certain point, the intense focus on survival tends to phase out. However, the new challenge at this point becomes maximizing productivity, population, and the utilization of the land. The creator has added a number of achievements that actually are
, some of which can be pretty difficult to obtain.
On top of all that, the modding community for this game is incredibly active, and guarantee a fresh change for your additional playthroughs!
There are a few minor gripes to be had from the game, mostly dealing with citizen AI, but nothing that breaks the game for me. The creator is working on patches for the game at this time to fix some of the most major issues, after which he plans to add Mac/Linux compatability and modding capabilities.
All in all, I highly recommend this game! There isn't another game quite like it, and I think there is plenty here to make worth the $20 asking price.

I actually played the game before, back when it was released. But I didn't finish it back then and it was quite laggy on my old PC. So now I decided to grab it for such a great price (-80%! I wouldn't compare this game to GTA series as some reviewers did, but it might be compared with Saints Row - a type of sandbox openworld where all you care is the fun and sometimes you can sacrafice some (lots) realism to get more fun. So don't expect much of the story, simulation, common sense... but do expect quite a load of fun!
Oh, and did I say fun? Fun? FUN? FUN!!!
The main feature of the gameplay - the grapple - allows you to put a lot of enthusiasm and creativity in killing enemies and bringing chaos. A simple example: shoot the guy with a grapple then tie him up (simply with another shot of a grapple) with a rocket then shoot the rocket and see the poor thing fly straight to the heaven... You can also go headshoting and exploding everything - it's up to you.
I was very excited by the graphics back when the game was just out. But even now it looks decent. The island is nicely detailed, distances are quite insane even by modern standards - you can fly on a jet from the ground and above the clouds and the surroundings will have a nice level of detail at all distances. Your clothes are getting wet from the water and your car might get washed by the rain... And of course the explosions: much boom, such wow!
If you're in the mood for some really good old-school platforming, spend the $5 and enjoy yourself.

I'm just going to start off by saying I prefer Dark Souls over Dark Souls II. I know I sound like some 'genwunner', but hear me out. While Dark Souls did have problems, it was thematically coherent, with the best level design you will ever find in a video game, and contained a slew of original and unique bosses that were all brilliant with a few exceptions (Bed of Chaos, Seath, and the fact that there are three 'asylum demon' type bosses, though I believe that Demon Firesage is alright, Stray Demon did not need to exist). Dark Souls II, on the other hand, is just incoherent both thematically (without DLC anyway) and level design-wise, with a LOT of bad and unoriginal bosses (The Royal Rat Vanguard, Prowling Magus, Dragonrider,  Velstadt, Belfry Gargoyles, Covetous Demon, Flexile Sentry [underutilized its full potential] and Ruin Sentinels [just a dumb boss that is nothing more than throwing three enemies at once that will mess you up unless you summon or are actually pro]). It's also just rather drab in the aesthetic department apart from a few areas (Dragon Aerie, Heide's Tower of Flame, and Shrine of Amana). However, it is still souls, and though parts of it are just honest-to-God cheap difficulty, the DLC does make it a better game. I still think this is quite a good game, with a strong PvP component for those who enjoy it. A worthy game that I still immensely enjoyed.

Arriving home after a long trip away, you find the house empty. Searching around will reveal why you're alone, and along with it a touching story, wonderfully told.
This isn't a horror game. But it does have that unsettling feeling one might experience when coming home and finding you're all alone during a thunderstorm. Newspaper clippings, letters, files, audio tapes (etc) gradually reveal what has happened since you've been away, and though the game can technically be finished in about 30 minutes or so (once you know exactly where to look and which paths to take through the home), you'd be denying yourself a wonderful narrative if you didn't explore the home and the items in it on your first play through.
With that said, the game likely has little to no replay value, aside from maybe wanting to experience the story again in the far future.
I recommend it if the above interests you, and I'd say stay away from it if you need your games to have action/danger or want challenges to overcome that can be failed.

Don't let this game's intense reputation dissuade you, this is an absolutely incredible game.
There is indeed a great amount of challenge, and sometimes your death will feel greatly undeserved, but it's worth every lost soul. It is a beautiful game that challenges you to truly work and strive for every victory, and then have an immense sense of relief and satisfaction when your work pays off (which it will if you stick with it).
The combat in this game is fantastic, and is the centerpiece of the game.  You have a wide variety of classes and weapons types at your disposal, and each weapon type truly allows for an incredibly different playstyle from the others. The melee combat is where this game shines and is truly what the franchise is based upon, but there are also “safer” methods of play with ranged magic or bow builds (which you get wrecked with if you ever play PvP).
The online combat is also terrifying and fantastic, as you could be on your last legs trying to get to the next bonfire with 20k souls when you get the notification that “dEEzeNuTZ69 has invaded your world.” You best run like the dickens son.
Overall, the game has fantastic combat with a gorgeously designed world and story. Things aren’t shoved down your throat (expect arrows and swords and fire and metal), and you have the option to discover the rich lore and story or just say “bunk that” and just go off and adventure. This was a great entry point in the Souls franchise for me, and I will be a lifelong fan of this series.

The uninhabited world (well, house) WORKS ITS♥♥♥♥♥OFF conveying realism and character to keep us engaged. Meditative. Rewards snooping. I think it's a proof-of-concept for virtual house tours. Replay value of bubblegum.

Experience: PS2, ps3, PC complete playthroughs of X, ps2 playthrough of x-2
So I got done through a playthrough of FFX on PC, including penance/nemesis.
Good:
-Support for 4k. While few if any assets benefit significantly from that resolution, its nice that its there.
-speedup option. Makes grinding the monster arena easy.
-Choice between original and re-imaged soundtrack (original is far superior IMO)
-decent stability. One problem with crashing, but was able to get through.
-autosave feature. It skips the (frequent) cutscenes, so it makes retrying fights a lot easier and quicker.
-"cheats" that speed up the game, increase or eliminate random encounters, and can make the game easier if desired, or signficanty less "grindy"
Mixed:
-The new character models are hit-or-miss.
-Not all models and textures are updated.
-large install size (~37gb). likely due to HD video and (lossless?) audio.
-the international version can make certain missed content much more difficult to re-obtain compared to the original NA version.
Bad:
-30fps in all but menus.
-unskippable cutscenes, of which there are (emphasis) many.
-Voice-acting is often poor (bad Dynamic range) or obnoxious (ex. tidus laugh)
Overall, I like it. FFX has always been a favorite PS2 title of mine, and the remaster on PC is, in my opinion, the definitive remaster. It contains features not on the PS3/PS4/Vita versions, and doesn't suffer from any significant issues that would place it below the console versions.
If you haven't played FFX before, definitely pick it up if you're remotely interested in japanese or turn-based RPGs. Like many games in the genre, it is a fairly lengthy RPG, fortunately, unlike many others, it has a decent difficulty curve (with a noticable bump near the endgame), where grinding is completely optional. Additionally, it has plenty of replayability via player-made challenges, such as NSG (no sphere grid, equivalent of a level-1 run). The endgame content can take a lot longer and is grindy, but it can be done in <30 hours total with the added features/cheats (less time than it usually takes to get through the story of the original ps2 version).

So Banished, what can I say? I've been following the development blog for this game for the last 2 years. I begged to be a tester, begged to get a pre-release demo, begged to throw my money at Luke before release date. In all that anticipation I think I may have developed an unfair expectation as to what I thought the game was going to end up being. Let me tell you some of the good first. Then I'll explain why I do not recommend the game.
Graphics - Not AAA great, but certainly a lot better than most indie games and this comes from one guy! DX11 makes this game feel so much better and it was a good idea to upgrade the graphics to support it. The river is entrancing, the trees have individual 'leaves' and sway in the wind. It's all just great.
Sounds - The environmental sounds are perfect and give a great sense of immersion. It's nice to hear sounds that are not taken from some stock foley repository.
Building - It's a building game and this game does that pretty well. Unlike most building/simulation games where you are limited to the types of building available until you build a certain other building or research it or attain a certain goal; Banished gives you all the buildings upfront. It's up to you to decide how and what to build. Build too fast and nothing will get done, build too slow and your people will suffer.
Rouge-like - I think of Banished as a rouge-like building game, because one small mistake can send your whole village to the grave in the matter of a season. It's actually quite fun to watch as people starve to death and freeze because your builders just wouldn't finish that last 10% of the hunters lodge from early spring to late winter, even though all the materials were already delivered and you frantically cancelled all other build orders. The lack of winter meats caused the firewood guy to starve, but you didn't notice who was dying while in the grasps of furiously moving the map around looking for the 4 assigned builders, wondering wtf they were doing other than building. No firewood meant that people began to freeze in their homes. Suddenly, you realize just how horribly mangled and mismanaged your efforts have been and you decide to restart.
Therein lies the reason I cannot recommend Banished. It's fun, it's polished, it's a good time killer, but it's not a fun game. Sim City 4 (let's just forget 5 ever existed) allowed you to plan for growth and set your own goals for the future city planning. Cities XL let you build theme based communities i.e. tourist town, farm town, industry zones, then link them all together to power a metropolis. Settlers gave you the need to conquer. Anno the need to evolve. Tropico the need to manage people's needs while meeting exterior goals. Banished doesn't provide any of those things. It's fun to watch how horribly wrong things can get, but it's not fun in the interims between. There is no goals, there is no end, there is no outside aggression. There is only build and manage.
I think just adding in a social aspect to the game would have made a huge impact. Feeling a personal connection with the townsfolk's would give you a reason to keep building. Currently you can follow people around, but you can't really zoom in on them. You always stay at a broad distance to the people your planning and caring for. The lack of outside aggression means you need to have an internal dialogue, but that is lacking from this game.
I do still hold out hope though. Luke has been full-time working to patch this game up and he has eluded to adding in more features, namely, mods. I think the modding community will be the saving grace for my own personal experience. However, as it stands just after release, this game is slightly boring.

I tried it, and didn't like it one bit. Got a refund. I would spawn, instantly (or near enough as makes no difference) get sniped, and sit and wait 30 seconds to respawn. I honestly just thought it was not a good game. Like, to the point where I can't think of one good thing to say about it, other than the original concept is great, but everything after that has been done wrong.
Might you be able to spend hours and weeks on end adding up to months out of your life banging your head against this wall, hoping to get good at it and overcome this stuff? Possibly. If you absolutely dominate these games maybe you'll have a different experience than me. I wasn't willing to risk spending the time. I loved the idea of a WWI shooter, which is why I bought it, but everything about it is glitchy and wonky and frustrating and just not right. I would avoid this one, utterly. I bought it on sale for $10, and got a refund, which should make my opinion clear: this game is not even worth getting on sale. Unless you just want to spend money hoping that some other developer will see that there is money in WWI and try to make, you know, a decent game that you'll actually WANT to play.

I'm just going to start off by saying I prefer Dark Souls over Dark Souls II. I know I sound like some 'genwunner', but hear me out. While Dark Souls did have problems, it was thematically coherent, with the best level design you will ever find in a video game, and contained a slew of original and unique bosses that were all brilliant with a few exceptions (Bed of Chaos, Seath, and the fact that there are three 'asylum demon' type bosses, though I believe that Demon Firesage is alright, Stray Demon did not need to exist). Dark Souls II, on the other hand, is just incoherent both thematically (without DLC anyway) and level design-wise, with a LOT of bad and unoriginal bosses (The Royal Rat Vanguard, Prowling Magus, Dragonrider,  Velstadt, Belfry Gargoyles, Covetous Demon, Flexile Sentry [underutilized its full potential] and Ruin Sentinels [just a dumb boss that is nothing more than throwing three enemies at once that will mess you up unless you summon or are actually pro]). It's also just rather drab in the aesthetic department apart from a few areas (Dragon Aerie, Heide's Tower of Flame, and Shrine of Amana). However, it is still souls, and though parts of it are just honest-to-God cheap difficulty, the DLC does make it a better game. I still think this is quite a good game, with a strong PvP component for those who enjoy it. A worthy game that I still immensely enjoyed.

I am sick of most FPS games.
I got really stoaked for Battlefield 1 for a while..... until I saw actual gameplay;
yet another automatic weapon death match just like all its predecessors (not to say Battlefield has not had some titles that I have enjoyed in the past, just I wanted the unique feel of a WWI game).
I came across Verdun and I am very pleased.
+Best Squad-based tactics I have played since Gears of War 1 (I have been playing with mostly randoms since I got the game and most are actually pretty receptive to following the NCO's orders)
+The squads/classes are all unique, requiring an adverse range of tactics to counter/use them
+Verdun's unique "desertion" dynamic keeps the battle constantly shifting between offence/dence for both sides and discourages players from being able to simply circle around the map and shoot every one in the back
+The weapons give the game a great deal of authenticity because few are versitle
-There should be a voice chat channel for NCOs to speak to each other in order to create a comprehensive battle plan entailing all squads
-It is far too easy to unlock every load out for each class (however, the coop exp portion is still very rewarding and unique)
-Possible that the player base will die out after this $10 sale
In short, it is obvious that this was a labour of love from the Devs.
It is a very unique game which puts a terrific spin on the shooter genre.

Don't let this game's intense reputation dissuade you, this is an absolutely incredible game.
There is indeed a great amount of challenge, and sometimes your death will feel greatly undeserved, but it's worth every lost soul. It is a beautiful game that challenges you to truly work and strive for every victory, and then have an immense sense of relief and satisfaction when your work pays off (which it will if you stick with it).
The combat in this game is fantastic, and is the centerpiece of the game.  You have a wide variety of classes and weapons types at your disposal, and each weapon type truly allows for an incredibly different playstyle from the others. The melee combat is where this game shines and is truly what the franchise is based upon, but there are also “safer” methods of play with ranged magic or bow builds (which you get wrecked with if you ever play PvP).
The online combat is also terrifying and fantastic, as you could be on your last legs trying to get to the next bonfire with 20k souls when you get the notification that “dEEzeNuTZ69 has invaded your world.” You best run like the dickens son.
Overall, the game has fantastic combat with a gorgeously designed world and story. Things aren’t shoved down your throat (expect arrows and swords and fire and metal), and you have the option to discover the rich lore and story or just say “bunk that” and just go off and adventure. This was a great entry point in the Souls franchise for me, and I will be a lifelong fan of this series.

It’s rare for a video game to enable the player to see life so effectively through another person’s eyes and with such sincerity. Sam reveals herself with a lot of honesty through her journal entries and the excellent writing and voice-acting serves to back this up; and it all means that by the time you’ve spent the three hours needed to complete the title, both she and her story will have left a lasting mark on you.
However, that’s not to say that I think it’s for everyone. Gamers who don’t have enough patience to investigate every cupboard and drawer within the house, who would prefer to plough through the plot to get to the end and achieve a goal rather than experience the title as a whole, won’t find much here to please them. Instead, it’s a thoughtful slow-burner whose characters get under your skin and leave you feeling for them. It tells a believable story that’s grounded in the real world and focuses on people as complex individuals.

This is the game that Dark Souls 2 should have been.  While vanilla Dark Souls 2 was quite good, it suffered from the inevitable comparisons to its legendary predecessor. So Banished, what can I say? I've been following the development blog for this game for the last 2 years. I begged to be a tester, begged to get a pre-release demo, begged to throw my money at Luke before release date. In all that anticipation I think I may have developed an unfair expectation as to what I thought the game was going to end up being. Let me tell you some of the good first. Then I'll explain why I do not recommend the game.
Graphics - Not AAA great, but certainly a lot better than most indie games and this comes from one guy! DX11 makes this game feel so much better and it was a good idea to upgrade the graphics to support it. The river is entrancing, the trees have individual 'leaves' and sway in the wind. It's all just great.
Sounds - The environmental sounds are perfect and give a great sense of immersion. It's nice to hear sounds that are not taken from some stock foley repository.
Building - It's a building game and this game does that pretty well. Unlike most building/simulation games where you are limited to the types of building available until you build a certain other building or research it or attain a certain goal; Banished gives you all the buildings upfront. It's up to you to decide how and what to build. Build too fast and nothing will get done, build too slow and your people will suffer.
Rouge-like - I think of Banished as a rouge-like building game, because one small mistake can send your whole village to the grave in the matter of a season. It's actually quite fun to watch as people starve to death and freeze because your builders just wouldn't finish that last 10% of the hunters lodge from early spring to late winter, even though all the materials were already delivered and you frantically cancelled all other build orders. The lack of winter meats caused the firewood guy to starve, but you didn't notice who was dying while in the grasps of furiously moving the map around looking for the 4 assigned builders, wondering wtf they were doing other than building. No firewood meant that people began to freeze in their homes. Suddenly, you realize just how horribly mangled and mismanaged your efforts have been and you decide to restart.
Therein lies the reason I cannot recommend Banished. It's fun, it's polished, it's a good time killer, but it's not a fun game. Sim City 4 (let's just forget 5 ever existed) allowed you to plan for growth and set your own goals for the future city planning. Cities XL let you build theme based communities i.e. tourist town, farm town, industry zones, then link them all together to power a metropolis. Settlers gave you the need to conquer. Anno the need to evolve. Tropico the need to manage people's needs while meeting exterior goals. Banished doesn't provide any of those things. It's fun to watch how horribly wrong things can get, but it's not fun in the interims between. There is no goals, there is no end, there is no outside aggression. There is only build and manage.
I think just adding in a social aspect to the game would have made a huge impact. Feeling a personal connection with the townsfolk's would give you a reason to keep building. Currently you can follow people around, but you can't really zoom in on them. You always stay at a broad distance to the people your planning and caring for. The lack of outside aggression means you need to have an internal dialogue, but that is lacking from this game.
I do still hold out hope though. Luke has been full-time working to patch this game up and he has eluded to adding in more features, namely, mods. I think the modding community will be the saving grace for my own personal experience. However, as it stands just after release, this game is slightly boring.

VVVVVV - not the most usual name for a game; but the game isn't very typical either.
In a way, it's a revival of the old 80's games; including all the low res graphics, cheesy bleep-bleep music and gameplay. And yet - it is very captivating.
The story is simple: you are the captain of a spaceship, which gets lost in a dimensional vortex. You and your crew are separated, and you need to find them.
The catchy part is the easy (and at moments very hard) gameplay. The only things you can do are: move left / right, and change the direction of gravity - but that last one is only as long as you stand on firm ground. Once you fly - you fly. This means you can not jump over obstacles as you're used to it, the whole game makes you think differently, which is nice.
The entire game can be finished within two hours, but if you want to get all trinkets - there's twenty in total - it might take you a little while (try typing "Veni Vidi Vici Trinket" on YouTube...).
I give this an 8/10 :)

I am sick of most FPS games.
I got really stoaked for Battlefield 1 for a while..... until I saw actual gameplay;
yet another automatic weapon death match just like all its predecessors (not to say Battlefield has not had some titles that I have enjoyed in the past, just I wanted the unique feel of a WWI game).
I came across Verdun and I am very pleased.
+Best Squad-based tactics I have played since Gears of War 1 (I have been playing with mostly randoms since I got the game and most are actually pretty receptive to following the NCO's orders)
+The squads/classes are all unique, requiring an adverse range of tactics to counter/use them
+Verdun's unique "desertion" dynamic keeps the battle constantly shifting between offence/dence for both sides and discourages players from being able to simply circle around the map and shoot every one in the back
+The weapons give the game a great deal of authenticity because few are versitle
-There should be a voice chat channel for NCOs to speak to each other in order to create a comprehensive battle plan entailing all squads
-It is far too easy to unlock every load out for each class (however, the coop exp portion is still very rewarding and unique)
-Possible that the player base will die out after this $10 sale
In short, it is obvious that this was a labour of love from the Devs.
It is a very unique game which puts a terrific spin on the shooter genre.

A game of truly rough n' tumble skirmishes set in the second world war. Nazis alone don't make for an edgy enough plot anymore, and zombies are a garish pink vibrating strap-on of an angle that's been utterly exhausted. Despite this, it still remains on the throne, an idea selling like hot cakes much like that decayed ol' king from warhammer 40K. So, What's next on the list? Dinosaurs? Sure, why not.
My first impressions are that the game plays rather nicely. Controlling dinosaurs and humans alike feels fairly fluid, though the 'runts' and humans are fixed in first person while the bigger dinosaurs take third. It would be nice to have the choice if there's variation to begin with. So You've got a mix of human and late cretatious characters to play as, and each team has a fairly unique roster to offer. Unfortunately, it's the Axis that are milking this historical re-jigging for it's worth, as they have around six or seven full dino variants to pick from. Allies only have the one, and the rest of your team is comprised of pink-♥♥♥♥♥ honkeys. This alone can sap the joy out of playing as an American, bar the fact the world hates you, but I wouldn't say it presents a significant disadvantage. I suppose there's just no satisfaction in beating on a dinosaur as a dinosaur, but rather playing Godzilla and crushing the fleeing people on a whim. This is presumably why teams are reversed each round.
My main gripe with this game as it stands are the maps. They seem lackluster in design and rather sparse. Vantage points are obvious and don't really appear to be very thought out, and you can't even sling a few shells through glass windows. Overall, the game seems a tad shallow and lacking potential for interesting, engaging tactics. It's a pretty standard formula (often likened to Team Fortress 2) with nothing terribly new to offer.
Nevertheless, I can't say it isn't satisfying to flatten a few yanks using a goat flung from your gargantuan jaws, or with another yank that you'd previously managed to keel over. There's fun to be had in this game for sure, but it's a quick, silly fix of entertainment and not one of any real lasting value. Would I recommend the game? Sure, for a happy drunken hootenanny or something. It's worth a chuckle or two at the least.

So, this game is awesome and here is why. This title is visceral and brutal and realistic, it is also fairly well balanced and historically accurate, making for a fun and challenging experience. There are a few occasional performance issues and net code problems, but all in all, the gameplay is smooth, precise, and exciting. The future content in the works, as well as the continuous and deligent work by the amazing development team ensure that this title will live on for quite some time, and that it can and probably will live through Battlefield One's release as it's own fruitful and enticing experience. I have enjoyed every moment of this title so far, and I look forward to the future with it! A definate buy if you like History, War games, Multiplayer, or first person multiplayer experiences.
Now to get into the nitty-gritty, there are a few things that could or should be changed, hopefully soon.
1: The insane respawn times, sometimes upwards of twenty seconds, really slow down the action and annoy the player.
2: Most of the trenches only seem to be about one person wide, which isn't entirely accurate or good for gameplay. many times I was pushed into enemy fire by friendlies because I couldn't get around them.
3: The matches need more players, 16 v 16 is alright, but to better fill out the batlefields and allow more oppurtunity for exciting gameplay, 20 v 20 would be far better.
4. The game's net code still need some work, there are moments where an enemy that has been shot four or five times by my squad mates, won't die untill he has miraculously killed half of us ( not poor aim, just net code lag.)
5: This is a great starting point for a fully fleshed out and exciting experience, but this title, which I REALLY REALLY LIKE, could defenitaly use some more content in terms of maps and factions and diversity, also some more reasons to play the different squads the way they are designed would be awesome. So a defensive squad would act more defensivly and a scouting squad would actualy have a reason to scout.
Overall I love this game, and I hope that is has a bright and fruitful future. 8.5/10

Receiver is a really interesting experiment in first-person shooter mechanics in the fact that the gun is incredibly realistic and complex. The game is all about surviving to collect 11 tapes that give background to the story, similar to collecting the Slender notes. The world is randomly generated from a series of rooms and a variety of randomly chosen preset enemy and loot locations.
The biggest part of the gameplay however is learning how to use your gun, which is a very close and very fun aspect to learn. It's no longer about running and gunning, it's about preparation. How many bullets do I have? What enemies can I see ahead? How far away are they and how can I handle them best? Surviving in this game isn't required, but it's a true testament that you constantly want to strive for that.
The only real complaints I have was that learning how best to disable the killbots is only really told through either trial and error or the tapes, which you can be lucky and spawn near three, you can be unlucky and spawn near none. I suppose it would've been nice for maybe the first spawn to give you access to the tutorial-like tapes, and have the rest of the levels be random, but given the turrets have odd shapes and sizes, you'll figure something out eventually.
For five dollars, the mechanics are complex, the enemies are powerful, the world is ever-changing and luck has to be on your side to really get far. Overall, a graphically simple but gameplay complex game. Perhaps not worth five dollars, but a bargain at -any- sale.

Like some I waited until I'd heard there had been a major patch to address the bugs this game is known for.  Waited for a discount day and decided I'd try this.  I was pleasantly surprised.  The gunplay is well done and I had a lot of fun with the weapon customization.  It didn't always make sense (like converting a sniper rifle/DMR into a rocket launcher) but there was a wide variety of weapons and equipment to choose from and play with.  The type of game where you see a group of enemies headed your way and spend 10-20 seconds deciding how you want to dispatch them each time.
Was the game bug free?  Absolutely not.  The wreckage of enemy drones or humvee's would often glitch out right as I could tell the game had timed them to explode.  Some of narrative stalls due to glitchy npc's, and there is a checkpoint scene where you follow a line of 4 or so people past a desk.  I had to reload that part about 8 times to get the npc's to walk forward when they were supposed to and not just randomly stop which prevented the scene from progressing.  Sometimes enemies would see/detect you through solid objects like police barriers when you couldn't see them.  So they definitely don't have everything worked out, but I was able to brush most of this off and still have fun.
The story was nothing impressive although there was plenty to do.  My current time played (36h) is one play through, though I'll admit I took a semi-completionist route to get about 90% of the weapons/items unlocked.  And I did find the premise of this alternate reality where North Korea has developed all the best technology in the world an entertaining one.  Basically the same route Wolfenstein: TNO took but...with far less polish and using N Koreans as a modern-day villain equivalent.
If I was as pessimistic as a lot of these other reviewers (but still objective) I'd give this a 6/10.  Optimistically an 8/10.  So a 7 is probably realistic and fair for this game overall.  Either way I'd recommend trying it.  On a sale day of course.

WARNING-GAME IS OVERHYPED AND OVERPRICED!
10/10 (This review is based on the lowered price of $2.39 USD not for the current price of $20 USD.)
Short review:
-PRO/CON-Cliche story from television, books, and movies alike, but relatively new to games from what I've played.
-PRO-Atmospheric and pretty game with great pictures and photos hanging on the walls.
-CON-High price for short game. I've played every single bit of this game and only have 3.6 hours of gameplay.
-CON-Barely any music to play, don't know why the soundtrack is so highly priced.
Long review:
Recommended if you love story games without puzzles. Not recommended if you're looking for something with tons of puzzles (ie point-and-click adventures).
I do not think the $20 asking fee is appropriate for the amount of gameplay given. Replay value, at least for me, is extremely low. I've completely completed every last bit of this game. I know everyone's stories and have searched the house top to bottom completely yet only have 3.6 hours on record. (And that's saying something as I took my sweet time enjoying the game for all it was worth.) I admit to getting this game at a low price while it was on sale-so at least for the price I paid ($2.39), I believe I got every cent's worth and then some. A fair price, in my opinion, would be about $5 or less.
I loved the story and ending, (although pretty predictable I admit) and loved the other stories integrated in the background as well. (Also the background stories are pretty cliche as well.) The art was amazing, especially the paintings on the walls (if you love watercolor paintings you'll love the detailed ones the game provides) and the photographs. The house itself was a great style with great background noise of rain and a dark backdrop. Each room was very beautiful as well, and the details were immense. I guess if I did replay the game, it'd most likely be to mess up the house and just play around instead of playing seriously.
For those looking for something scary, this is not for you. It is neither horror nor supposed to be scary. While there is a dark atmosphere, there are no scares involved whatsoever. Anything in the game that links to the maybe-ghost of the previous owner is just for storyline purposes alone and are not scary nor intended to be.
In short, this game is pretty amazing. It's atmospheric and imitates almost a visual novel/simulator mix.-A story you can walk through and feel as you progress on your journey. Handwritten notes, books, pictures, and even wall etchings detail the set of your simulated story wonderfully. Random item placement, and small jokes on magazines as well as the packages of food lighten the journey as the contrast of the storm outside darkens it.
For anyone scared easily and wanting to play this game, I recommend turning the volume down as sometimes the thunder can get pretty loud (there's a setting under options to change this volume to lower), and to watch for loudness when they play a casette or even a record. Sometimes the music is pretty loud against the almost-silence you get used to as you play.
10/10 overall for a story-based simulator-type game.

Homefront 2 didn't interest me much. I finished the first one and it wasn't a good game. On the rails shooting gallery that felt too long even with its pathetic four hours of playtime.
Second one wasn't developed by Kaos, but when I learnt that it's being cooked by Crytek UK, known as the muppets behind Haze, my enthusiasm didn't exactly grow. Plus all the trouble during development, bankruptcy of the publisher, change of dev team to Frankfurt, then back to UK, unpaid salaries of emplyoees, half the dev team leaving, then Deep Silver buying the project (followed by the return of the previously left devs, incl. game director Hasit Zala)...
No good game could have come out of this mess, could it ?
Well, according to reviews, no, it could not and it did not. For inexplicable reason (well..of course it was money) Deep Silver decided to release the game around 4 months before it was finished, at a time when console versions were almost unplayable due to low framerates, and PC version was a lottery ticket - one had it unplayable, the other could play, plagued by bugs.
To Deep Silver's credit though, they allowed Dambusters (new name of Crytek UK aka Free Radical) to finish the game post-release, via some hardcore patching. Of course, the low sales and low review scores are set.
But, patch it they did!
First the technical side then. Homefront 2 looks fantastic, almost photorealistic at times. Cryengine has amazing lightning. War zones have, particularly at night, impressive atmosphere. Framerate is pretty much perfect now - 60fps maxed out in 1080p (on 2500K@4ghz, GTX1070) without any significant drops or stutters. There are some ocassional glitches here and there, a bit of pop-in, but nothing too distracting. The patches also added ability to tune HUD (turn off almost everything) and FoV.
Now on to the game itself. Unlike the first one, Revolution is much more open affair. It takes place in Philadelphia divided into multiple zones. These zones are either Red, where most of the battles against Korea took place (Revolution takes place 4 years after the US lost the war), so they are bombed out and reminded me of the 2029 scenes of Terminator 2 (Revolution also takes place in 2029, probably not a coincindence). These zones have great atmosphere and contain the FarCry/STALKER like gameplay with taking over bases and open combat against KPA armed forces.
Yellow zones are full of civilians and instead of open combat, you need to play a guerilla rebel, taking out enemies stealthily. These most reminded me of City 17 from HL2 right after you arrive, except here you are an active saboteur, not just an observer.
Thanks to these zones the game is nicely varied, it is not constantly the same killing gameplay all the time.
Revolution has some very likeable sense for detail, you can see some here:

I like games that show their interface through ingame object - in STALKER it was PDA, in FarCry 2 you hand held the map, in Homefront you have a korean phone :)
The arsenal is great. There are not many weapons, but each can be modified in multitude of ways and each upgrade feels worthwhile. The punch and feel of the guns is flawless, the sniper rifle is one of my favourites. You can transform guns completely, for example make uzi from a pistol, or a flamethrower from a crossbow. Plus there are bombs strapped to RC cars or teddy bears at your leisure.
The game surprised me. I only gave it a chance because of the free weekend and I ended up buying it and finishing it since I enjoyed it so much. I liked it significantly more than FarCry 4 or Division, which I played right before Homefront.
That said, there are some flaws. The most significant one for me - the silent fu**ing protagonist. Oh how I hate this trope. There is even a moment in the game when another character shouted at me "Say something Ethan!" and my lovely Ethan just looked, the mute idiot that he is. Please devs, stop with this nonsense. It is not adding to immersion. It is hurting it.
Another flaw is that the AI could be better. Felt a bit too canon foddery at times. Too bad we will probably never see AI exceed or at least match what first FEAR offered in 2005.
Anyway. Great game. Give it a chance. Oh and that easter egg is effin' awesome.

Receiver is a fun "gun simulator". The gun mechanics are very in depth. You can't reload just by tapping "R". You have to eject the magazine, load each bullet into the magazine individually, then put the magazine back in. Each of these actions has its own key. While somewhat confusing at first, you can eventually memorize the keystrokes for reloading and other gun mechanics.

There is a sore lack of authenticity in video gaming. Major game companies want to focus on creating 'fun experiences' more than experiences that might last with you. Verdun is one of the latter. It sits comfortably in the vein of games like Red Orchestra or Insurgency, but shifted into a WWI trench environment. It bends slightly toward realism. On defense, you will find yourself picking off incoming dots on the horizon, sitting comfortably in your trench. The anxiety builds as a few enemies slip through your lines and begin setting up seige lanes at the flanks. Anxiety turns to full blown panic as enemy raiders begin running through murdering your teammates with semi-automatic pistol fire, sometimes accompanied by grenades or in rare cases SMGs or Flamethrowers. You engage in frantic close quarters combat against a crazed enemy, and lets say you make it through. Your lines survive and you manage to repel the invaders. Well, now YOU have to attack. You will run through machine gun fire and crawl through craters as your team tries to drop gas on the enemy. If you manage to make it through the hail of metal, you don your gas mask and sharpen your bayonet before jumping into the enemy trench. You shoot one or two men in the back, before one turns to face you. You stab him and he screams as he falls. He continues to scream. He's still screaming when you are shot in the neck running through the trench. You never saw it coming. You are bleeding out on the floor of a muddy wooden trench of France's most godforsaken hellhole. You hear your own screams as the camera pans out to look over the trench. There are limbs being blown off by mortar fire as torsos fly through the air. You respawn. Time to do it all again.

Thanks to the developers at Dambusters and Publisher Deep Silver for providing a really fun new IP for me to enjoy and escape.
As one of my most anticipated FPS games this year I never faltered even after a middling beta(I didn't play) and middling reviews(suckers buy games day one) I did my usual.I sat back relaxed and played other games while it received a few patches, updates and a price drop where I was comfortable and upon completion what different gaming universe do I live in? Homefront TR is part Dying Light, Fallout, The Division, Half-Life 2, and Far Cry and while it doesn't achieve greatness as some of those titles it does the next best thing, it provides a helluva lot of fun in both single player and surprising co op gameplay.
Lets talk about performance since everyone today seems to go ballistic if there is a minor issue. During gameplay I had all options set to high including V-sync,playing at 2560x1080 and never had any frame rate(60+), crashes or game breaking issues. In game I did notice enemies would disappear in the distance on occasion and some minor sound outages but game play for the most part is fast and solid. I Also noticed if you downsized the game to the toolbar and brought it back up you would need to restart the game as it just seems to chug. Its an open world game where minor hic cups will exsist and if you dont know that by now stop playing them.
Homefront begins with one of the most brutal opening seqences I can remember it's very disturbing and cringe worthy as are some of the melee kills and just scenes of violence. You are cast as the typical silent protagonist Ethan Brady who arrives to the front lines of the resistance for a meeting with their leader Benjamin Walker. Walker is captured during this meet and greet and this sets up the main story and thrusts you straight into the world of the revolution where North Korea(the Norks as they are called) has taken over the US due to unpaid gas bills. The story is split into 4 acts and it doesn't give a very good first impression but if you hang in there the voice work, mo cap and some moments have feeling but because you are mute with no opinion you just follow orders, whether right or wrong. HUGE problem for the story and huge mistake by the devs but overall its not bad.
While the game bills itself as open world its really divided into three zones. The green and yellow  zones are the heart of the enemy and where they are they strongest. The environments are clean and is militarized with constant enemy patrols. This is also where most of the regular population resides and these patrols, scanners, cameras and drones have a constant presence and stealth is required. The red zone is more chaotic, open and war torn. The buildings are bombed out, roads are an obstacle course of carnage and the resistance actually has a small advantage if any. This is where you can freely roam with a gun in the open, easily recruit resistance members to help with missions and you will also be given the ability to use a motorcycle to get around. Breaking these areas up into these zones keeps gameplay from being stagnant and was a great decision by the devs.
In these zones you will be given the usual main or side open world missions which involve sabotage, reconnaissance, retrieval, investigation, etc. All are familiar but depending on the objective and zone there are a lot of ways to approach each mission and end goal. This approach is highlighted by outstanding level(world) design and the tools at your disposal. One additional task you will be given in each zone is to make the people 'rise up' or as its called in game win "hearts and minds". This is mandatory as some missions and zones will stay locked until you reach 100% resistance for that particular zone. Increasing resistance can be accomplished by turning on radios know as the voice of freedom, completing flash missions, liberating strategic sites, saving civilians, assassinating targets, or just blowing stuff up. I can't tell you how awesome this feature is especially as the resistance grows NPCs begin to act different, say different things and it truly feels you are impacting the world and that's pretty cool a definite highlight for the game.
One thing absolutely clear at the start is you are underpowered and its highlighted with limited weapons, gadgets and amount of damage you absorb before falling. It makes sense the resistance is underpowered and the weapons and guerrilla tool kits(GTK) have a unique home made feel which is another cool highlight. However, being able to purchase GTKs and scarce resources at the store is sort of confusing.  Every weapon you purchase except the RPG can be converted into 3 weapons and all have different attachments. The animations for the weapon conversions are cool and the weapons themselves are solid, a lot of fun and in some cases a little too good(hello auto matic shotgun). There are also 4 GTks you can equip at all times that include hacking, molotovs, pipe bombs, and firecracker. All of these base GTKs can be converted and then used as a remote(use smart phone to detonate), proximity(land mine), or driven on on an RC car and detonated. As you explore the world you  will also be scrounging parts or finding hidden stashes to build gadgets and a reason being able to purchase them at the store is a mistake.
As for the world of Homefront its beautiful though it doesn't look like a  Cryengine game in some aspects. Graphically it doesnt compare to the likes of The Diviions but it equals it with its attention to detail. Every room, alley, street, tunnel, and bombed out building all look unique it's really impressive and it makes exploring so much fun. Character models on the other hand look impressive as do animations and mo cap.
The absolute biggest suprise in Homefront are the co op missions. A co op vetern with my friend Silver(15+ co op adventures) we absolutely loved this mode. There are 10 missions(2-4 players) that are mulit mission based and avg. about 15-25 minutes each. As it was in single player you begin bare bones and are very vulnerable at the start so a little grinding is necesary. The level cap is only 6 and money(at various prices) is then used to unlock chests which give you armor, consumbles, guns, attachments. As you gain XP and DNA you can then spend them in 4 skill trees labeled Brains, Brawn, fighter, Survivor. None of the trees differentiate themselves and once you have maxed your charcter and skills you are unable to respec those points. All that said its fanatstic co op fun and challenging.
Homefront is a pretty ambitious game that has been through the ringer of development and unfortunately due to bad release it has been killed by the casual reviewers polluting the industry. Dambusters did not waiver and have continued to provide patches, updates and support. I like the game its not perfect and maybe it was too big for this small team but its provided dozens of hours of fun and that's all I ever ask out of a game.

Receiver is a FPS created during the 7 day FPS challenge, which focuses on gun handling mechanics. You play as a person known as a "reciever" who is equiped with only a handgun, and an audio cassete with with headphone, who must uncover the secrets about a corporation called Mindkill ( or Mindtech I can't remeber ) through a complex building full of kill drones. The game focuses gun handling mechanics which instead of pressing R to reaload, you need press multiple keys to take the clip out, putting it in your inventory, getting a loaded clip from your inventory, loading the gun up, and cocking it up. The controls aren't the only challenge though, once you get hit by bullets, or a taser from the killdrones, you die and have to start all over. To add up to the challenge the tapes, ammo, flashlights, and audio cassete tapes are scattered in new locations each time you spawn. The story unravels as you collect more tapes, each with a message revealing the secrets of Mindkill ( or Mindtech ). The sound and music makes walking around the building suspensfull, and makes you think that something around the corner is going to kill you.
Overall this game is really fun, and is definetly worth getting if you want a great FPS, and a challenge.

Gameplay: You open things and collect objects and examine them. Nothing interesting happens and it's not supposed to. This is like an interactive story, with little interaction. However, that's ok with a game like this. It's not meant to be a game you "play" but something you experience. I gotta say though, it's still really boring and dull to walk, pick up random objects, find key, repeat. Mixing it up a little with some more difficult puzzles and maybe some areas outside the house would have been great.
Story: It's so generic and boring that I honestly can't believe how some people are saying "this is the greatest love story ever told". It's about an angsty teen moving to a place they don't like, meeting an even angstyer friend who trains her to be more angst because society doesn't accept them, and falling in love with her. Then they run away because their love isn't accepted. You don't even get to find out if they live happily ever after, the game just ends there. So not only does it have a lackluster story, but it doesn't even have proper closure. Congrats though, I just saved you an hour and a half of running around an empty house trying to piece together a story that you'll be disappointed in. To be honest, in the first 15-20 mins of the game you can already tell what the ending is going to be. If you want a great love story about a gay couple, go buy Brokeback Mountain. That has far more meaning, is far more interesting, and is probably longer than this entire game is. Plus, it isn't $20, an absurd price for a game of this length and quality. There's some other stories and whatnot thrown into the mix such as family history, history of the house itself, ghoooooosts~~~, and other things. However, those small stories are weak and almost as cliched as the main story itself. Most of them are like the main story in that they don't even have a proper ending. It's really really bizarre how a game based around telling a story failed so hard at its one job.
Now I wouldn't say don't buy this game. It's by no means terrible, but it's definitely not worth the price. If you see it for $5 or less, maybe pick it up. Just be warned that there is no replayability, and that all you'll be buying is a time waster. If you look past that and really think the story sounds interesting, go ahead and get it. I just hope you're not as disappointed as I was.

Game was $9.99 on sale, and $24.99 retail.  It's a mature, aim-down-sights-based first person shooter.  What do I mean by mature?  You rely on positioning and patience, spotting enemies with your binoculars, and spending part of the match crawling around in the mud to get the jump on your opponent.  Sound plays a big role as you can hear footsteps, enemy reloads, and enemy combatants audibly issue radio orders to their teammates. Bullets are strong and it will take anywhere from 1-3 bullets anywhere (1 if you get a headshot) to kill.  Reload times are long, and you will be forced to reload the entire clip before being able to shoot again.  So keep this in mind when you're in a precarious spot near the enemy.
There's several "classes" you can play, and may swap between them at any time pending a respawn / death to make the change.  The classes really have two types: those that use rifles, and those that use pistols.  Pistols are good for close to medium range fights, have a faster reload and faster rate of fire.  With the pistol classes, you will either have binoculars or a grenade.  And will have access to a set of abilities "Q" including mortar strikes and recon planes that reveal enemy locations in an area.  The rifle classes are effective at all ranges.  Their only real downside is their rate of fire.  But they're a must-have on maps that require long distance sniping.
Cons:
low player base.  for a multiplayer game, it relies entirely on there being other people online to play against.  i've had a few instances where i simply had to close the game because there were no open games.

This game recreates the battlefields of the western front from the forts in Verdun to the trench lines of the Somme and everything in between.
There are several different types of units and squads to choose from allowing you to play as all of the warring nations that fought in France. There are 12 squad types to be played: 5 for Germany and 7 for the Entent Powers. Every squad has 4 types of soldier to pick from and each soldier has three unique loadouts to choose. This gives you a lot of veriety and choice in how you play the game but keeps a realistic composition of guns on the battlefield; most people will be using bolt action rifles but there is the occasional machine gun or even flame thrower to have to contend with!
You will die a lot to begin with but if you have the patience for it and enjoy a slower paced yet unforgiving FPS then Verdun is a great buy!
