Receiver is an interesting rouge-like FPS (In that death is permanent and the game generates randomly). Most notable is the gun mechanics, where you must go through all the motions of reloading your gun manually, from inserting bullets individually into magazines to pulling back the slide. If this sounds complicated, it is. However, the game is nice enough to provide a help overlay that shows you the next button you need to press. Eventually, like handling a real gun, doing every action will become muscle memory, and you'll no longer need the help screen.
The game has three different guns that you will get randomly when you spawn: a Colt 1911, a Smith & Western Victory Revolver, and a Glock. All three weapons handle differently. Probably the simplest to master is the Victory Revolver, as it is the least complicated to reload. The Cold and Glock are fairly similar in reloading and maintaining but are different enough to be noticeable. It would have been nice if there were more guns included, but it isn't a huge deal.
The 'story' of the game is pretty simple and only exists to give you a reason because it needs to. You must find 11 cassette tapes randomly strewn around the generated environment, avoiding a couple different types of automated enemies. The game is really challenging, and how far you get in the game seems to be based on luck (There have been many times where I've failed to find any tapes despite surviving for quite a while and other times I've found most of the tapes without running into too much resistance). The many times you die won't frustrate you too much, but will only drive you to try "one more time". Unfortunately, the level generation isn't really that interesting, and you will quickly become bored of the same rooms over and over again.
Ammo is fairly limited, only spawning in random places, so you will need to make every shot count. Enemies have certain weak spots that are more suitable to damage. You can also disable certain parts of enemy robots by shooting them, such as motors or cameras, that disable those functions. For instance, destroying a flying "Killdrone"'s taser leaves it unable to damage you. The poor thing will continue to follow you around trying to zap you, like a lost puppy.
The dynamic lighting won't work on some computers with some medium or low end graphics cards, like mine. This causes many rooms to be too dark to explore properly. There is a flashlight item in the game that also does not work if the lighting is broken, making the purposefully-dark rooms very hard to navigate, but not impossible. It really frustrated me when I realized it, but eventually I got used to it.
Overall, Receiver is a fun, challenging, and addictive game that I like to enjoy in short bursts, but lacks a lot of content. It's very realistic gun simulation compared to pretty much any other FPS out there.
Don't worry, this ain't no No Man's Sky.

I'm mixed on this game. While it is quite enjoyable, in my opinion, there's a fundamental design flaw. At its core, Banished is a fun, yet simple builder, survival game only made difficult by the "flaw". Toward the bottom of Maslow's heirarchy of needs are the physiological and safey needs of self. Yet, Banished violates this premise with its breeding model; the citizens will breed until all open houses are filled. This one, simple fact, makes it nearly impossible to recover from late game mistakes or natural disasters, making the game too finicky.
Anectdotally (populatation graph in profile), in my fourth Banished game, this flaw occurred again. A tornado destroyed part of my town, nearly 500 strong. Even though the damage was small, it caused a chain reaction--a tool shortage, led to resource shortage (food and raw materials for tools and clothing), which led to 320 people dying before it recovered.
Important note: the town had housing for 500+ people.
Food stores slowly began to recover, all the while the adults were still breeding, never slowing. With a 500-citizen occupancy on housing, they kept procreating, but the resources didn't exist and after reaching 400 citizens (270 adults), the population crashes again down to one, lone hunter.
TL;DR. The breeding model is flawed, which is an exercise in frustration instead of an enjoyable challenge.  I can't recommend it at this time; I'll revist my review if a patch is released.

This is not Simcity.
Rather, this is Simcity retold with the struggle underpinning Dwarf Fortress. You will build a city, but the primary aspect of the game is the struggle to avoid resource crashes. Populations age and die off, land is often in short supply, forcing you to decide how to build in suboptimal areas and manage traffic. Tools wear out and break, traders bringing vital resources like seeds or livestock charge a pretty penny for the priviledge.
Initially, you may even struggle to keep the most basic aspects of your city in line. Starvation, hypothermia, disease, fires - I've seen references to a tornado, though I've never experienced one.
The game is still in development, and often feels brutally short on information, but it is playable, and the challenge is definitely there. It needs some UI and logistics improvements (stockpile item control, for instance, is notably absent).
If you like a challenging city builder, this may be for you. If you want a cakewalk, look elsewhere - this game is determined to make success difficult to achieve, in the vein of games of yesteryear. This gets a thumbs up from me after ~30(!) hours of trying to manae cities, but I may be a masochist.
You were warned.

This is a very odd title. Imagine Crysis got a actually good sequel, before it escalated waaaay too fast and got the aliens and all that. They are on the island with North Korea in Crysis 1, and lets just imagine it ends with North Korea finding out about the attack and them invading America and winning. Boom, Homefront The Revolution right there but with less super suit. This really does feel like Crysis and how 2 should have played in terms of free roam in a city. Urban Guerrilla warfare for days. Keep in mind each part if a section but each sector is usually 400m-1000m with lots to find.
You are in an occupied Philly, part of the resistance tasked with miltant attacks to take your country back. The game itself is beautiful, since it is in CryEngine. There's moments I find myself staring at the ground while the rain falls watching the drops lets completely coat the road drop by drop until they turn into puddles and I get shot.
This game has a slight feel of what STALKER/Metro 2033 has, but really feels more like Crysis meets the Saboteur/Far Cry. I have really been enjoying the game, and would easily pay 20+. The game suffered from terrible publisher disorder and was released with a ton of bugs, I haven't had any real issues with the game, I did have a load error issue but that was due to a validation.
Tips for getting started. Turn off the music. Just do it. Set your FOV to something more tolerable and then finally remove the MipMap/Onscreenmap since that thing makes the game feel completely different with it enabled and by removing it forces you to take things slow since you don't have telekenetic abilites to see every enemy in real time.
AI is pretty good all things considered and is on point with flanking and covering. Gunplay is fun, finding out what bullets penetrate what is one of most fun things in the game. Lots of enviromental hazards and multiple types of ways to play. Supposedly there is a way to stealth, but I end up just running around shooting people through walls.
Shame the game had a rocky release, but excited to see new DLC's and support the developers on this. According to the developers, there are 2 more DLCs and the final one adding a massive new zone to operate in.
Tl;dr Like Crysis, Far Cry, Red Faction Guerrilla, & The Saboteur? Buy it.

After playing Dark Souls, I knew what I was getting myself into.
Immediately, the graphics are improved tenfold, but that's to be expected given the time the game was released compared to Dark Souls.
The NPC's are engaging and interesting to listen to, the lore discovery is much more strong in Dark Souls 2 than it ever was in Dark Souls, and the different environments the player travels through are stunning and gorgeous. (Praise the sun!)
As for actual game mechanics:
Combat feels more fluid compared to Dark Souls. (However I have had a few embarassing moments where lock-on has killed me, quite violently I might add.)
For the reviews complaining about co-op play and connecting with friends... I have never had an issue in Dark Souls 2 summoning my friend. When he got out of my Soul Memory range we simply bought the Name-Engraved Rings, chose the same God, and boom! instantly able to see each others soapstone signs. This ring also limits those who do not have the ring on and the same God chosen from summoning you so your friends have a chance to actually pull you into their game. (Don't be cheap! Buy the ring... The Cat in Majula sells it for around 5000 souls which is pretty damn cheap if you ask me!)
As for "always" being online, that just isn't true :) you can set your game to offline mode if you want to play solo. Or! if you are online and want to farm souls in peace, burn an effigy at the bonfire in the area you are farming and voila! no invades possible. From Software has made it insanely easy in Dark Souls 2 to not, for the most part, be invaded by jerks who just want to f*** with you. Effigy effect, however, will not negate NPC invades, like Forlorn. (He always invades at the worst possible moments!...Jerk!)
Overall, those that thoroughly enjoyed Dark Souls, the old style RPG, discover lore, learn from deaths game, you will love Dark Souls 2.

The gun handling is awesome and near perfect, being able to disable a standing sentry 10 feet away is less than acceptable though and that's my main complaint which is preventing me from wanting to play the game anymore. I can waste 2 clips on a single sentry and not disable it at all (with bullet marks all over it)... the only way I seem to be able to disable them is to hit that tiny little red dot on the front where the gun sights are, so not only is it already difficult to hit a bullseye with a gun (because at high resolution, lining up the sights on the gun is difficult because it's so dark and small... which I'm ok with), but you have to hit that red dot a split second before it unloads it's bullets on you... not acceptable. Realistically, a sentry would be easy to take down because of all the moving parts and circuitry and wires, etc... If they were going for realism with this game, they failed. Also, there isn't enough random swaying back and forth when aiming a gun...
I've shot a nice 9mm beretta handgun a bunch of times and I know how difficult it is to hit a bullseye at just 10 feet away and hitting close to bullseye at 20 feet away. Worst Souls games ever. Ruined every mechanic possible. Before I begin to list my greivances, let the record show that I platinumed Demon Souls on ps3 and 100%ed Dark Souls 1 on steam. So I am not a scrub that needs to "git gud".
Soul memory is a dumb metric that made far less sense than using soul level. The idea behind it is that every soul a character ever earned is used to determine matchmaking. This discriminates against archers because they must waste souls on arrows, which a caster/melee build would not need to do. This also screws over people who fail to get their retreivals and people who like to upgrade a diverse set of weapons to try them out.
Shades have inconsistant functionality when it comes to invaiders. Sometimes the shade will be locked in for the duration of the invasion and sometimes the shade will expire mid-invasion. I play an intentionally super fragile glass cannon sorceress because the person I play with all the time is a 100% tank build. Invasions tend to work real nice for us unless he is the shade and he mysteriously disappears half way through the fight (as a super tank, he can just sit there and block for days if I am the shade and that happens until he can summon me again, I do not get that luxury). Most of the time the shade will stay in for the entire invasion even if they are completely blacked out, but 10% of the time we get burned by a weird exception that is either shoddy design or bad programming.
All trash mobs now have finite spawns per game. After killing something as many as 15 times, you will never see it spawn until NG+. This makes bosses too easy because you can clear the path to them and have a full spellbook going into each boss. It also makes it so that you can be screwed over by not getting your rare drop and needing to wait until the next playthrough to get the item you need now. It can also screw over the noobs because if there are no more trash mobs left in the universe and they let all their bloodstains rot before making use of the souls, they will have no means to improve their characters.
In Dark 1 and Demon it always felt on some level clear what I needed to do next. While we were presented with choices on what order to do certain things, it was always clear how to move forward. In Dark 2, it is just a set of dead ends after dead ends with a bunch of guessing as to what minascule detail we happened to overlook that will give us access to more content. I doubt I have ever played another game where I combed the entire world multiple times and failed to find the way to progress.
I could probably write a 10 page report on why this game is inferior to the predecessors, but I decided to cut it down to just this for the purposes of this review.

Going into this game, I told myself to "imagine" I was the character in the house. That's what these types of games are about. sure, games are meant to immerse you into the game on it's own (which I feel the game does decently enough) but adding the air of imagination to increase your own personal feelings about the given situation at hand in said game can go a long way.
now one thing I'll say right now, for $20 bucks... if you REALLY want to play this game and can't wait for a sale, then go ahead, but I recommend getting it on sale. only reason being, it's just not that long.
now back to me imagining things:
so, I'm a daughter, come home from college. I come home.... and... well... no one is home. if this were me in real life, I would be relatively scared for my loved ones. and given the state of th house... it's not in great shape.... so either my parent's stopped caring about cleaning as much anymore, or.... some♥♥♥♥♥♥went down.
this builds an air of "oh my god, were is my family? I have to find out what the hell happened!" to the game. I mean, if you don't wish to put yourself into this characters shoes, then I understand that some people wouldn't like this. but trust me, shut off your BS meter when playing this game and just remember "this is happening to YOU". Sure ths story may not be the "six sense" of the gaming industry, but playing this game I had a lot of questions as to certain things around the house that usually gave me a chill down my spine as if I were a 7 year old who has to go into the creepy basement to get the laundry, but you don't want to cause "there be monster down there". putting yourself into the right shoes when playing this game can make you relive those feelings, as ludacris as it may make you feel.
is it a great game? well, with how I experianced it, it was worth my time and I had fun. so it was a good game, but not great.
The story? It knows how to hint a certain things that make you start coming up with your own theories as to what happened. and you just feel like you just HAVE to find the truth. so the story in my opinon is a pretty darn good story. and on top of that, at the end, though I may have wanted more resolution, I found myself with a hopeful smile. I might be a sentimentalist, but that made the game worth my time and money.
should you play it? well, I say yes. But as I mentioned, price is a bit of an issue.
will I fault you for not liking the game? Absolutely not. every game appeals to a different person in MANY ways. I just gave you my general experiance and how it made me feel. you can read this review and hope it leads you down the right path, but it's ultimately up to you to decide if this game is a journey you want to take.

Likes:
* When the game wasn't crashing or chugging along under 30fps, there were a few things like reflections that impressed me. I otherwise found the environments forgettable and drab.
* (potential early game spoiler) The first time you "sneak" back into the main residential area, you are tasked with inciting a riot by committing acts of vandalism and assaulting kpa personnel. For a brief moment, the city actually feels alive; the more acts of domestic terrorism you commit, the more civilians will start to gather in protest near the kpa structures in the area. It would have been interesting to feel more involved with the people but instead you're just running around breaking things and♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥people off until the little counter in the top corner fills up and says you've caused enough unrest for the next cutscene to play.
* While i like the idea of on-the-fly gun customization, i feel like it fell a bit short.
Dislikes:
* Controls are as clunky as can be expected for a fps deep silver game
* Gun customization is difficult to pull off with a controller and nigh impossible to do with m+kb
* Awkward, shoe-horned racism and racial slurs. I actually felt more uncomfortable around the "rebellion" than anything i heard from the big baddies that were supposed to be opressing me.
* Incredibly long, unskippable, awkwardly written cutscenes
* Clearing outposts and completing objectives somehow feel even more hollow than the standard sandbox ubisoft games that clearly inspired this. After clearing a section of the map, no soldiers spawn, making traversal boring and tedious.
* Incredibly buggy. In the short span that i played this game, i had three secondary objectives break, which prevented me from taking on more bounties and even making it impossible to clear one of the sections of the map because the enemies would not spawn.

A great sequel, even though I didn't find it nearly as scary as the original. The animatronics, new and old, are still just as creepy if not more so. The atmosphere is, once again, excellent. I just found the jump scare deaths to have a lot less of an impact, due to the fact that I played the original so much. At this point, the jump scares frustrate me more than they scare me. This game is also much more challenging than the original. The original had four (Golden Freddy doesn't count) animatronics to keep track of. The sequel, by the final night, has a total of eleven. In the later nights, its more or less luck that determines whether or not you make it through the night, as opposed to skill. However, the game is still an enjoyable challenge, even though the deaths feel cheap at times. If you have not played the original, this game is more than likely to scare the absolute hell out of you. I absolutely recommend this game, but I also recommend you play the original first. The graphics are pleasant if you don't expect too much, and there's some pretty serious calculations going on behind the scenes. And this is a game that screams out for mods...which is why it's so exciting that the developer has confirmed that he'll release a mod kit. All in all, if you are into the "building" genre, you have to check out Banished. Highly recommended.

Everything this game does Red Orchestra 2 or even 1 does better.
It does not take advantage of its setting to do anything interesting. It's like a generic shooter but you die in 1 or 2 hits. It even has the white cross in the crosshair everytime you hit, and the exp-bonus per kill and headshot like CoD.
It is clunky, movement does not feel good. You get often blocked by teammates in the trenches and there's no way to circumvent that.
Trench warfare is not fleshed out. Melee is auto-aim and the most simple system you can have. Just press the melee key and kill, whoever presses the key sooner wins...
There is not a single unique or interesting thing going for this game, except the game-mode "Frontlines" which in the end is just a capture point game-mode mixed with some attack-defense mechanics.
Graphically is not very well polished and runs badly for what it is, it looks like a 2004-ish shooter.
Again, it's not well optimized.
Finally you need a group of 4 friends to enjoy the multiplayer to its full potential, since there is a squad system where you level up as a squad. So you're forced to play with the same people over and over to get special benefits like better armor and weponry.
Finally the community is not very good, there almost no communication or strategy. There is also not much room for strategizing, since the map give you very limited options in terms of cover and approaching enemy trenches, which are not much more than a straight horizontal line, the corridors are so tight that you will not have any cover, so it often comes down to who shoots first, a well landed granade or an RNG mortar shoot.
WW1 was famous for the battles in the trenches, which were melee battles. The thing that would have made this game unique is to recreate those aspects of the war. Instead, melee is less efective than a gun almost all the time in the trenches, since guns are so easy and fast to reload or bolt, and so easy to aim and fire. So the game even lacks any kind of historical recreation appeal that could of had. As I said, there is no intricacies to the melee fighting, just as complex as any other shooter in which you press V to stab.
The ragdoll physics are pretty awful, most of the times the trenches will be covered in gliched out bodies standing in weird and impossible positions.
This game is not worth 20 bucks.
Buy Red Orchestra 2.

I can't recommend it because of the price. Right from the start, this should be at the most a $5 game. It's too short and too feature-light to ne taken seriously as a $20 game, and that's where I believe a lot of the negative reviews to be coming from. I personally got it as part of a humble bundle.
It is not a horror game, but it's pleasantly eerie. It honestly does a fairly good job at what it sets out to do. You're a young woman returning home after a year of absence, in which time your family has moved into a new home, so it helps to put you into Kaitlin's shoes, the fact that you're both seeing this new house for the first time. There's a lot to discover if you've got the patience, but it's been said before (and is true) that once you know where a certain item is, the game can be 'completed' in less than a minute. Otherwise, if you're playing it for the first time and you don't get stuck looking for a key or a note, you'll probably get through it in a little over an hour.
It's good. The story is good, not great, the atmosphere is very nice, the sense of discovery and learning about what has gone on with your family in the time you were gone, it all works very well together. But there's just no feasible way this should cost what it does. Find a quiet LPer that isn't irritating (tall order, I know) and experience the story that way, because that's all the game really has going for it in the end.

It's not the most interesting game, but I have to admit that I actually had fun with it during the free weekend they did. And once we got used to the coop, the boyfriend and I had quite a lot of fun in that actually.
The weapon customization is actually pretty damn nice and the standout element of the gameplay. Swapping out different receivers for each weapon to make them do something different is actually really good. While technically only carrying three weapons, the pistol and two primary weapons, the alternate receivers are always available meaning you effectively have nine weapons at all times if you have all the receivers for each weapon. It's something I'd really love to see in a lot of other games.
The open world is what you'd expect from the recent Far Cry titles, or any open world game from Ubisoft really. Clear out rather meaningless outpost/checkpoint style zones until you've filled up a meter. At least there is an actual change in the world, albeit minor, when you fill up that meter. People start appearing on the streets of the "yellow zones" protesting and fighting with the KPA, things are lit on fire, it at least feels like there is some response to your actions.
Gunplay is fairly solid, some guns feel a little weightless and meager, but some really feel good to fire.
Coop is the highlight of the whole game though. While set up just as preset missions set in the singleplayer maps, usually with restrictions on where you can go without completing certain objectives, it feels fun playing alongside others. As opposed to the singleplayer, you also have character customization in the form of picking various skills and wearable equipment to give you different passive perks and different cosmetics. I feel like the only downside is that I really wanted even more to do in the coop because it was genuinely that fun.
For $15 it's definitely worth it, even for $20 though I'd say it's certainly worth it if you aren't opposed to the more typical Ubisoft style open world in the singleplayer.

This is a really interesting game, which makes the gun mechanics of "hard" military sims such as the Arma series look absolutely primitive. Here you have to manually reload a limited supply of rounds into clips and chamber rounds before they can be fired. As someone who's actually fired real world weapons, it's nice to see the real world mechanics of actually handing rounds and guns replicated faithfully in a videogame. There's no one button, instant reload here; and the game's all the better for it. The premise of the game is also interesting, too, and the procedurally generated levels allied to one-hit vulnerabilty and permadeath add lots of replayability - but  if there's one major flaw, the AI is *way* too twitchy.
As an experiment in replicating real world gun mechanics in a virtual world, Receiver is an unqualified success - by playing it you'll gain a much greater understanding and respect for how handguns actually work - but as a game, slightly less agressive AI would greatly enhance the experience for those of us who don't have the reflexes of house flies on amphetamines.

Receiver is an outstandingly realistic FPS game when it comes to firearms. Pretty much the only thing lacking in it is jamming, but you're talking about the M1911A1, Glock, and a revolver. S&M Model 10 or something like that. .38 Spl.  Not a whole lot of jamming to be found there, however it does happen on the rare occasion. There are the scatter complaint I have about this game, but a lot of positive aspects to point out as well, let's start with them.
First off; individual magazine, not an ammo pool. LOVE it! Ability to manually remove ammo from a magazine, or load ammo into a mag. That's a first for me in a videogame, and it's outstanding. Ability to activate safety on an M1911A1, love the realism, however it should NOT be able to be activated when the hammer is decocked. I own a Springfield Armory 2008 M1911A1 Mil Spec, and it cannot be put on safe unless it is cocked.
Select fire on Glock 18. Now I don't like that they chose the Glock 18 because it's very rare for gun owners to ever handle one, however at the same time I'm glad they implimented it; it's almost useless in full auto, wastes ammo faster than you can say 'yeehaw', and will do more missing than hitting on anything beyond 10m. That's good, it shows people realism. Many people love the G18 because "Full auto pistol! 1337!" No, full auto is pretty much useless on a pistol unless it's got a stock on it. Even then, it will still eat up ammo insanely fast. Keep it on semi auto, or you won't last very long. Ultimately, I think it would have been better if they chose Glock 17 or Glock 22 (.40 S&W), but I love that they at least made it realistic!
You can also go magazine +1 (M1911A1 has 7 round mags (Even though 8 round mags are more common nowadays but I digress) so you can have a full 7 round mag, +1 in the chamber making a total of 8. Or with Glock 18 with 17 round mag, have than +1 in the chamber and you have 18 rounds before having to reload!) It's also cool being able to spin the cylinder of that .38 revolver. Load just one round, spin it, and play Russian Roulette. Will you have a live round, or an empty chamber? :o
I think now I'll touch on the bad aspects; as said, M1911A1 shouldn't be able to be on safe while hammer is cocked. Also, for some reason, when you have a full mag loaded, with the slide locked back, if you press the 'pull slide' button or whatever it's called, then a round will eject. If you choose the 'slide release' button or whatever it's called in the game, then you will simply chamber a round. Realistically, either should be able to be used without a live round leaping out of the chamber.
I think that's about all I have to say about the game other than the obvious; obvious to just about anyone who played it anyways... GODDAMN FLIERS! You'll see what I mean, they have to do something about them. SO annoying! Anyways, I hope they continue to develop this game, and come to include the ability to find more mags, use more firearms (More than one if you're lucky enough to find another firearm), ability to choose difficulty (I WANT TO PLAY WITHOUT THOSE DAMN FLIERS!), and if at all possible, please develop some rifles, as well as potential long distance shooting with adjustable sights!
Don't stop now that you have a (Albeit kind of simple beyond the controls) revolutionary game made; keep going! Try making a more in depth story line! Character creater! Inventory! Weight management! Perhaps leveling up because I know from experience that it takes time and practice to become an accurate shot! How about long-term gaming? Hunger, thirst, oh and don't forget about different types of ammo! 9mm isn't much use when all you have is an M1911A1 and an SKS (Just throwing an idea out there for potential rifles/carbines that could be found!) :) To a bright future for this futuristically realistic game! Cheers!

Whether your looking  for a realistic Indie FPS, a fun and exciting new twist on first-person shooters, or a realistic gun simulator with a classic arcade feel, there is something for everybody in a game that can be fun but rather burdensome oftentimes.
The game features realistic gun errors, (i.e jamming, safe reloads, and bullets getting stuck in the cylinder) excellent gun mechanics, and awesome bullet physics. The game while fun, has some major performance issues. I will often be on an important part of the game when suddenly I start to get major lag. This should not be happening on a game like this, as the graphics are not even that good. This takes away from much of the game's fun. When the game is not lagging (something which is a rare commodity) it is extremely fun to play. When you encounter a flying mind tech you feel this true sense of fear for your life as you either fight or run. Shooting and reloading the gun is rather interesting because every single part of the gun is controllable. While this adds uniqueness to the game it slows the pace down considerably and has nothing to help speed it up.
The verdict: An exciting and adrenaline pumping experiment that is hindered majorly by its massive performance issues. While the game is fun to play it badly needs to be optimized. If you have beast gaming computer or something "good enough" to run most games, then I would definitely recommend picking this up!

This game is an interesting concept piece, but falls utterly flat on it's face. Everything about the game is in need of polish, from an awful UI (for such an extremely sparse UI as it is), to intentionally poor control layout, to the combination of these factors exacerbating its brutal difficulty. It's impressive how such a simple game can fail on so many levels.
The game is brutal in it's difficulty. Not because the enemies can kill you with a single hit, or that they greatly outnumber you, or that you have very limited ammo, or that it's intentionally difficult to aim your weapon properly, or that some enemies appear to be able to absorb prodigious amounts of ammo for little to no good reason. No, the biggest difficulty creator is the fact that there is no rhyme or reason to the control layout beyond the normal movement and aiming and firing controls. Yes, the game is supposed to have a difficult mechanic of maintaining your weapon. But the button placements make no sense - they neither emulate the firearm that you are using, nor are they set up in a way that encourages a logical pattern. They're just generally clustered around the WASD keys like the developer just slapped them down whenever he thought of a new feature that guns have that he had yet to implement.
The only hook into the plot (what little plot there appears be) is from audio tapes that have a poor voice over that you may or may not find near the beginning of your adventure. There is nothing that will make you feel like you have a need to complete the plot, other than any intrinsic desire you may still harbor for completing the game for the sake of completion alone.
Also, a very special frustration that I managed to encounter is the fact that the game offers no way to reset one's controls to the defaults, but the UI that gives you control hints entirely works on having the default controls. So if you change your controls you'll either need to give up on using the tutorial UI, or find them online (at the time I write this I was incapable of finding them listed), or delete your registry keys from Windows so the game is forced into returning your defaults to you.
The only people who should buy this game are the heedlessly masochistic and the curious game developers who want to explore the concept and how not to approach it. Even then, wait until it's on sale.

This game, put simply is just so bloody good, so bloody hard and yet INCREDIBLY simple. There are essentially three layers to this game: gun mechanics, exploration and a thin veil of storyline that is actually really interesting.
Gun mechanics is actually a bit more detailed than you might be expecting. Basically you need to not only load your gun manually, but understand each part of the gun (and there are different models with different functions). If you have a revolver, you have to be able to pop out the cylinder, empty rounds, load them manually. For pistols, you need to be able to eject magazines, clear chambers, unlock safeties, etc etc. The exploration part is finding tapes which contain the storyline. You have to go through somewhat plain enviironments in order to find 12 cassettes which explain what is going on. But then, there's the robots. Differing types are all out to kill you, and your defence comes in understanding and operating the guns, as well as learning the weak spots on each opponent. It is MADDENINGLY tough at times, and you can get a mad fright when a robot comes out of nowhere, especially when you can't just shoot, you need to understand how to shoot.
Honestly, this is an addictive, clever game. Get on it.

Woo, what can I say? Aside from being a remaster, this is truly a great collection for folks who didn't get to experience the International Edition's bonus content, as well as the bonus Last Mission to Final Fantasy X-2 that was previously exclusive to Japan.
The bold colors of the updated textures of this remaster make the characters and environments far more vibrant and "pop" compared to the older PS2 textures, where in comparison look entirely washed out, which really helps put the "fantasy" in these games.
The audio in the game is also great, giving players the choice to choose between the new or old tracks when starting a new game. I'm personally giving the new a go, and so far I haven't been disappointed.
As for controls, it recognised my Xbox 360 controller just fine, and with how smoothly it works, I haven't given, nor will I probably give keyboard and mouse a go, lest my controller bites the dust.
Now for the bad. The really, really bad.
The only complaint I have isn't one of either games themselves, but of the bonus stories that follow the events of Final Fantasy X-2, of which only one is actually included (the latter of the two). Now I won't spoil any actual content, but in my opinion they completely dropped the ball, undermining the plot of both X and X-2, and entirely disregarding character development like some rubbish fanfiction you'd find by accident. Worse yet, fans are not only to be left with a bad taste in their mouths, but an ugly stain after the company confirmed for the worst, that there will not be any follow up to the horrendous ending they have left us with. This is truly one case where they should have spent far more time on the story, or better yet, left it alone.
All in all, I still recommend this collection. The gameplay is great, as well as the graphics, which are far more than decent for a game of its caliber, let alone a remaster. Just be sure to avoid the above mentioned bonus stories like the plague if you want a wonderfully deep plot.

My experience with the first Homefront game was not especially pleasant.  Although the setting was well done and interesting (even allowing for the ludicrous plot) the game itself felt like every linear FPS single-player campaign criticism rolled into one.  So when Homefront: Revolution was announced, I scoffed and then ignored it until recently when a free weekend had some friends reporting good things and I tried it.  Glad I did.
I think most people compare HF:R to an urban Far Cry 3/4 but that's because it's largely true.  Enter a region, note your plot objective, then ignore it as you fight your way through buildings, conquering then and flipping the map from red to blue.  Actions can increase your standing with the city residents until they are finally inspired to rise up and riot, attacking their Korean occupiers.  It's repetitive and, like Far Cry (or games like Mad Max or Shadow of Mordor), by the second strike point you'll probably know if you feel like playing 30 more hours because the game won't change significantly.  The story is serviceable even if nothing amazing or thought-provoking.  It's an excuse to run around a ruined city and shoot dudes and take over territory.  The simple bottom line is that if you enjoy games in the Ubisoft "point control" model, you'll likely enjoy Homefront: Revolution.
Guns were interesting though the system took me a little while to appreciate. You have your Primary/Secondary weapon but each of them can convert into two additional weapons.  So your semi-auto pistol can convert into a small SMG and/or a silenced pneumatic pistol depending on your needs.  Add in attachments (scopes, silencers, etc) and you get an impressive amount of flexibility and essentially seven weapons at a time (3x Primary, 3x Secondary plus an RPG) though you'll need to plan tactically and find cover to convert your assault rifle into a light machine gun on the fly.  Still, it nicely bridges the gap between console-based limited gun slots and becoming a walking arsenal.
Finally, the game includes a co-op system where you and up to three friends can band together for missions and gain experience and money for skill/weapon/gear unlocks.  Although there's an air of randomness about it (you buy a crate and hope for a good weapon), it's all self-contained and there's no item store or cash shops.  The system is in addition to the single player game rather than the focus and it adds some additional play once you're done.
To be fair, trying Homefront: Revolution well after its initial release meant that I avoided its rocky, buggy launch and got in after the worst of it was ironed out.  When I played, it was relatively bug free.  No game-breaking issues for me, although once I dropped through the map and once had a physics glitch fatally launch me into the air.  Out of 50 hours of play, I can't complain though. It played well on my aging system (i7-860 @ 3.6GHz, R9 290X, 12GB) with a consistent 60fps at 1080p on High settings.

The CoD of fantasy games; re-release the same game every year with a few minor tweaks and new maps.  This series is not hard.  It is poorly designed and intentionally unbalanced.  There is a difference.  QWOP
Difficult to coop with friends, though random coop is functional.  If the game was purely this, or more built around this, it could be great.  Currently, however, its mostly for boss fights and removes all difficulty, as enemies aren't designed to fight multiple players.
As if the game wasn't poorly balanced enough to begin with, enjoy being spawn camp 'invaded' by a player who is multiple times stronger than you.  They're also immune to monsters in your world for some reason, so you can't even combat them creatively.
+ Fast travel
+ Talking cat
+ Refillable potions
+ Equipment variety
+ Random friendly NPCs
+ Infinite inventory space
+ Not the worst PC port of all time, like Dark Souls 1 was
+ Helping someone in coop restores humanity and farms souls
+- Slow sense of progression
+- Weak character customization
+- Single currency system, no bank
+- Coop makes the game pathetically easy, and is basically just extra DPS for boss fights, they might as well add NPC companions.
+- Low quality graphics, most textures look like they belong on the PS2, but things run at a solid 60 FPS, and there are interesting sights
- Ultra simplistic combat.  Hit enemy, dodge roll away, repeat.  'Difficulty' comes from unbalanced numbers.  You have to hit an enemy more than they do you, they usually outrange and/or outnumber you, and they can stunlock you.  Sound fair?  OK, have fun.
- Dodge roll doesn't animation cancel, making the game a test of patience instead of skill.
- Parrying, which is arguably the only skill based thing in this entire series, is so frame/millisecond specific, and must be learned by trial&error, that it falls to luck
- Awful weird controls that have been bad since Demon's Souls.  Triggers to attack, buttons don't match to the HUD layout; the left button uses the bottom item.  Hold B to sprint, click left stick while sprinting to jump?  So bad.
- Cheap enemy placement/traps.  Such trial and error pitfalls are the other source of 'difficulty' in this series.
- Lockon doesn't instantly lockoff/change target when enemies die
- The first real boss is pathetically easy and disapointing, beat him on my first attempt, easier than half the trash leading up to him
- Attacks can miss targets, even if locked on and at point blank range
- Hit trading with enemies and/or walls blocking hits
- NPC chat interferes with gameplay
- Weird weapon durability system
- Doesn't work with DS4 controller unless hidden
- Messages and Death Replays are distracting, though don't fully interfere with gameplay
- Monotonous oldschool MMO style 'pull 1 enemy at a time or die' styled pacing
- Aside from a few shield upgrades, the gear I started the game with has been better than anything found in ~8 hours
- I assume this game would only be ~2 hours long if you didn't have to retrace your steps 10 times over
- Clunky menu system that interferes with gameplay
- No quests, story, direction, or motivation
- Game can't be paused
- Pointless torches?
- Can't sell items?
- No Map
- Short lockon range
- Respawning enemies
- No borderless window option
- So many breakable objects, so few loots
- Disgusting stamina system.  Stamina should only be effected by blocking.
- Countless locked doors with no context
- Shops don't show comparisons to your current gear
- Alt equipment slots increase weight, even though theyre basicaly in your bag either way?
- Armor makes almost no difference in damage taken, but has a huge impact on speed, best to just run around naked
- Can't freely save, do you lose hours of play if the game crashes?
- Starting the game as a mage class is nearly required, as they have access to a feature not easily obtained by others
- Can't jump over the tiniest wall, and sprinting/jumping controls seem backwards if not entirely broken
- 'Metroidvania' style world.  This has worked well in one game ever; Castlevania SOTN.  That was like 20 years ago on the PS1, stop trying to use it.
- Unbalanced dual weilding.  Takes 3 hits to kill an enemy with sword & shield, still takes 3 hits if wielding that sword with both hands, but you're slower and less protected, so whats the point?  Seems to be a 10% damage increase, but a 100% stamina cost and 50% speed cost.  Not worth. Also completely pointless to have a weapon in each hand, since you can't attack with both at once or attack any faster or any benefit whatsoever.
- Troll messages, bad message ranking system (can't downvote)
- Punishing corpse runs, worse than WoW, lower HP each death, because if you couldn't beat that enemy with 100% HP, you can definetly do it with 50
- Limited arrows
- Fall damage
- Can't swim

This is my first review I've ever wrote. It's feels strange that it should be about this game, a game that has been so positively scored and yet left me completely disappointed.
For a game that has prided itself on being a 'Story Exploration Video Game' to have committed a basic narrative mistake such as mixing up genres is something that baffles me.
For the first ten minutes of gameplay it will feel like an Agatha Christie novel, which is a great compliment, and raised my hopes about this game to an incredible level. The tone of the game itself promises a deep old mystery, it even flirts with the paranormal... but that's it. That's the best you'll have, from then on you'll find yourself in a teen-punk-lesbian love story filled with almost every cliché and stereotype from the 90's.
And even if you can go over that and you start investigating and exploring everything, as I did, as a reward you'll have the most obvious and foreseeable conclusion: nothing remarkable happened.
I spent 2.4 hours in an unremarkable place trying to figure out what was wrong about it, just to find out nothing was out of place. No mystery to be solved, no hidden past, just inconvinient schedules and lack of communication between family members.
In hindsight, this game promised great potential but instead left me with a sense of being cheated by a cups-and-balls performer. I bought it during the summer sales, I highly recommend you save yourself the 19.99 USD and go spend it on an honest game.

Make no mistake - this is a positive review for the game, as it is indeed a well-crafted thing of beauty for its time, and still is. But this is a negative review for the currently perceived state of Square Enix and/or whatever development team was responsible for the PC port. As much as I love the Final Fantasy franchise, their PC ports have always been unfinished jobs upon release (and even years after). They have somehow managed to do this with every -single- release thus far.
I can't stress this point enough: Every...single...title. And there are quite a lot of them by now.
Japanese audio is available, but with no English subtitles. The reason posted on the news feed is "technical difficulties," yet someone from the Steam community already fixed it with a simple hex edit within 30 minutes of release, and is currently distributing the corrected .exe via Dropbox. Others on Steam are reporting numerous stability issues, but I can't vouche for that yet myself.
I still purchased the game, knowing this full in advance. I simply love it too much not to. It is unfortunate that they are likely aware a great number of peoople - with the exact same reservations - will make the purchase for the very same reason as me: Simply for the love of the piece of art that it is. (Immediately available modding definitely contributed to my decision to buy, as well.)
I honestly don't know if it's an intentional oversight or not, but this constant trend of relying on modders to finish the job gives the appearence of being unprofessional, if not dishonerable. That being said, I wish to remain civil, and I sincerely would like a response from a developer for clarity on this issue, so I can give this product the positive review it deserves - not that it needs my lone voice added, as it has rightfully already won the hearts of millions. Speaking personally however, it would go a long way toward restoring my faith in - not to mention my enjoyment of - future releases by Square Enix.

Final Fantasy X was an amazing experience when I was young. Now, replaying it in HD glory is a huge nostalgia hit. The score (both revised, and original) is outstanding. The story is deep, rich, and an emotional journey for both the characters and the player. The gameplay may seem tedious to those that don't find RPGs appealing, but many will be love it. If not the animations and art style, simply fly through a battle and take in the music. Even now I have the menu in the background for the music alone. Added 'cheat' features give replayability, and something to mess with if you get bored. The graphics have (obviously) been redone to look good, but it doesn't lose the feel of the original.
Final Fantasy X alone is worth the full price. If you've played the original, you'll love going back. If not, you're in for an incredible journey. However, you also get Final Fantasy X-2...
While not as good as Final Fantasy X, FFX2 is still a very enjoyable game. The score is once again brilliant, the cutscenes breathtaking, and it gives closure to the story. The gameplay and RPG elements are different, but fun to play with and experiment. It's a nice balance of difficulty too.
Keep an eye out for cutscenes in both FFX & FFX2 then glue your finger to the screenshot button, trust me.

Having played the original PS2 version of this game, the PS3 remaster and its Vita port, this is easily the best adaption although not tremendously different from the PS3 version and if you own that one I wouldn't necessarily recommend it.
The game's minimum requirements suggest that this is a well optimised port capable of running on the now-antiquated (and midrange for the time) 9600GT, among others. There are a number of graphical settings which I assume run the gamut between the Vita and recent PS4 release, and any surplus of graphical horsepower can be put towards higher resolutions/downsampling and anti-aliasing; I'm running at 4k (1080p display) with 8xMSAA and SMAA, which cleans up any aliasing without distorting the details (although I don't recommend running SMAA or FXAA on less than a 4k resolution unless you have no other option). This game has some mixed reviews, and from what I've seen, a lot of the negative ones are based on frustration bred from laziness and an inability to properly apply one's common sense in a city building simulator.
All negativity aside, Banished is an excellent city building game, but could do with some fine tuning where information is concerned. When I first started playing, it took one or two towns (what I like to call my trial and error period) to figure out how to set things up, and what the natural ebb and flow was. This was - maybe - two or three hours of experimentation, and certainly post-tutorial. When I figured out the very basics, it was relaxing and fulfilling to watch my tiny population grow into something a bit more impressive.
My only critiques would have to be regarding the placement of buildings, as that seems to be the hangup for a lot of players. Tooltips would be grand, even an in-game FAQ of sorts for people to refer to when they had questions about what buildings work best, and where. Otherwise, Banished lives up to everything it promises to offer in a city building sim.
+ The benefit of a

Establish a comfortable population, wait for the initial ebb in numbers, where the founding members of your new town die out (and they will, usually one after another) and once you've compensated for that loss and have a few new kids on the way, build a schoolhouse and let the grooming begin.
+

+ In the beginning, I like to take stock of my seed (map) and will immediately pause, zoom out and start mentally zoning areas, everything from places suitable for livestock and crops, to dense forest areas fit for cultivation.
+ Foresters, Herbalists, Hunting Lodges and Gatherers should never, ever, be placed in a residential area. The further they are from your main buildings, the better.
+

+

+

+

Possibly the most underappreciated, and infrequently mentioned tool in this game is the

in hard mode.) They can live without houses for a season or two, but food is a must have if you want them to survive until they can build those houses. I also cannot live without my
and

In conclusion! Don't be afraid to let your game plateau a little bit and build an excess of resources. Manage this with your birth rates, and workers coming of age, of course, but building stores is always good when you're trying to grow and for the longterm.

At one time this was a decent game, but unfortunately there are several things that make it a headache to play on most days.  One happens to be the updates.  Though I realize updates are a necessary part of any game, Warface has exceptionally large ones often that cause a crimp in my plans to play when I'm finished with work.  They need to be broken into smaller increments so that there are fewer disruptions AND they need to be tested BEFORE released so that many players don't have to reinstall the game to get it to work again.
Another issue is game lag and glitching/cheating.  Yep...just like other FPS games, there are plenty, but there are some known players and clans that purposely glitch and cheat and get away with it.  I suspect that it's because they are paying VIP players and it's a revenue stream that the developers are unwilling to part with.  It doesn't help that VIP weapons (gold weapons) are so much more powerful that snipers can slide and use their rifles like shotguns from distance while doing so.
Finally, quit letting South American players join the North American server.  GIVE THEM THEIR OWN SERVER!  Though they claim there is now a lag limit, I constantly see players from Colombia or Venezuela connecting to the Virginia server (the ONLY server in NA).  These are often the players that take advantage of problems in the game (glitching) and use aimbots and ridiculously resistant armor in the game (yes, boys and girls...there ARE ways around EasyAntiCheat).
So, the game was once okay, but now it sucks.  I'm sitting here right now waiting on an almost 7 Gb update to complete.  Why the hell so large?  Because Crytek likes to reinstall large portions of the game with the updates.  Do yourself a favor and find another publisher's game to play.

It's not a good game, but that's not what you should buy it for. It's about the gun handling. Once you have gotten the hang of it and played a while, you'll want mechanics like these in other games, too, and I'm not aware if there are any so far. I do not feel like these mechanics must be the focus of a game (And they indeed aren't in this game, they'll only seem like that to a beginner for whom they'll be the main obstacle.), they could just be a nice element of realism, but the game would of course have to be balanced accordingly.
At first, I had real trouble getting the hang of the gun mechanics, even though there's on-screen help in the game (that you can toggle). But then I did this, and it helped a lot:
In the game's launcher, I edited the keyboard configuration to a set of keys that I could easily remember and that made logical sense to me. This plus the key function texts in the configuration window made it easy for me to start handling the guns in a routine way. Downside: The in-game help does not adapt to the changed keyboard config. :(
So, the gun handling and mechanics are fun. What about the game itself? Well, it has very limited gameplay. You sneak through a (procedurally assembled, so somewhat different play-through each time) facility, trying to obtain bullets, magazines, guns, a flashlight, and a few audio tapes. You'll encounter flying turrets that you have to fend off, and there are floor-mounted turrets. It's interesting that both consist of various parts, and shooting those has varying effect depending on what you hit.
Is it fun? Yes, for a few hours, and it's mostly interesting because of the gun mechanics. It's not a full game, rather a prototype. Worth the purchase? Definitely when discounted, but €5 isn't all that much, either.

リロードに手順が必要だけどボタンさえ覚えればやることは

Banished is a willage building sandbox simulation set in medieval era. Feels like a mix of Cultures, Stronghold and ANNO series, except there is no combat involved.
But soon, you will realize that there are more dangerous things than armed enemy approaching your carefully designed willage. Things like aging of your citizens, whom after death have to be replaced, otherwise there will be no production and most of your people will die. Vicious and unreliable weather which WILL now and then freeze the soil and prevent your farmers from planting new crops in early spring. Yes, and the same weather which will insidiously freeze your crops in autumm, thus preventing the farmers from harvesting those few left shrunken potatoes. The potatoes that you were praying for all summer to be last chance of feeding your starving population. Logically there is no escape from starving so most of your people will die. What's next ?. Yes..Does your food production relie on those lazy hunters ? Bad luck ! deers have moved on the other side of the map so there is a slight possibility that your people will die. Nice ! a merchant has arrived to the city ! He sells sheep and chicken ! Quiclky bulid some space for them to multiply ! Now there is a nice herd and is succesfully reproducing itself and providing your population with some meat resource... But look ! what's that green cloud over there ?! Is it a death cloud from Baldur's Gate ? Yes it IS !!! Now in Baldur's Gate it could kill a Boss Dragon.. so.. yeah,, you get the picture...
Banished is good and addicive game. It has quite simple logic : you just have to let your people multiply and keep them alive, that means happy and healthy. The circumstances that cause your people to die are well balanced. In a while you will be able to guess the chance of your stonemasons to be killed by a falling rock, or your other citizens to freeze to death because of lack of a firewood. Yes you did't cut enough trees to survive the winter ! But don't worry you can always train some foresters so there is someone taking care of planting new trees.
If you like detailed and production systems you will be in heaven when seeing your chicken farms producing not only eggs but also fresh meat from chicken above limit. Yes, you can easily set a number of chicken allowed in the pasture by draging your mouse on the scrollbar. All other chicken gets slaughtered generating a meat income. Also sheep are fun, and aditionally they produce wool for making warm clothes. Really nice is the possibility to combine resources to make more valuable and more durable versions of a standard products like clothes and tools, and if your barns are overflowing with equippment you can always sell it to a merchant and buy for example new seeds or animals. Just bear in mind that there is lots of events that will randomly change your resource flow, one year making you rich of food because of a good harvest and the other year losing third of your population just because yo have sold your food to a merchant expecting the weather and harvest to be as good as the last year.
I would recommend this game to players with adiction to simcity, anno, cultures and stronghold games. Just don't expect it to be a walk in the park.

Short:
Definitely recommended, since it's a very promising concept. I recommend it specially to those who love SimCity, SimFarm, Anno 1404 and many other city-building related games.
This game, however, is much more difficult and meaner to the player. It's a survival town-building game where you can screw up pretty easily and have your citizens die from hunger, frozen to death, or in many other painful ways, specially if you're negligent at managing and building your town.
Long:
This is a town-building survival game. You have to make sure your civilians get food, clothes and shelter. At times everything looks stable and easy, wonderful isn't it? Not so fast. Once you start facing problems like running out of food, tools or clothes (mostly after a baby boom), that's when the whole town can start crumbling like a deck of cards, faster than you might expect. Prudence is your friend here, dear reader, and this game will be pretty mean and unforgiving if you're negligent.
You might be thinking: "All I have to do is avoid the baby booms, easy peasy". So what do you do? You logically stop building more houses because that means less room for families to expand (and have babies), and then it's all good, right? Wrong. If you wait too long you'll have to face the problem of regress, with a population that's too old to make babies. With very few births your population will die off faster than it reproduces and that's obviously a problem. While babies and students mature you gotta have enough workers left to produce food and clothes for everybody. That being said: It's hard to maintain a stable population. It's challenging, and that's great if you love challenges. If you don't -- if you want a walk in the park until a screen pops up saying "VICTORY!" -- this game is not for you. Also: There is no victory (that I know of), there's no apotheotic triumph. Only despair and misery awaits you. The question is: how long will you last? How far can you expand your town before everybody is wiped out by your incompetence or lack of resources (usually both)? The game is still delicious even though the future of your town won't look pretty in the long run.
Trade:
There is no money, it's all about trading resources of a kind (raw materials and produced goods) in exchange for resources of another kind... For instance: trading a bunch of firewood for some chickens.
Producing food:
You can buy seeds and plant your crops and orchards too, it's actually nice when it comes to agriculture, there's a lot of variety to choose from (once you're powerful enough to afford all the seeds).
If you don't want to produce food through artificial means (agriculture and pastures) you can always treat your town as a hunter-gatherer society, but that's likely to be troublesome once the population growth hits a variable threshold (it depends on how much food you can collect at any given time). Remember that, historically speaking, human societies have thrived thanks to agriculture and other technological advancements (read "Guns, Germs and Steel" by Jared Diamond for more info, if you enjoy anthropology), so you might wanna invest in agriculture if you wanna survive later on.

Amazing game that is highly specialized, and masters it's niche beautifully. Many multi-million dollar projects have been unable to accomplish what this single man has done.
My gaming rig is pretty powerful, and I was pleasantly surprised to see high resolutions and advanced graphics features. The game looks stunning when maxed out.
My wife and kids have been mesmerized by the detail while watching me play for hours. We've tried all kinds of things and my wife has had a lot of input on decisions made for our towns despite not being much of a gamer herself. The kids almost cried when bad decisions on my part cost us our first town.
This game is so well thought out and realistic that it brings a natural focus to increased realism. You find yourself wanting to tweak certain things because of how close they are to real life. Citizen behaviors are impressively detailed and easy to believe in.  Decisions have to be made carefully, because the impact is very noticeable. At the start of the game you are dealing with such small numbers of people that everyone in the town counts.
The trickiest part of the game is managing the generation cycles. It requires a lot of careful attention to produce a wide spectrum of citizen ages rather than getting locked into spaced generations that result in large death cycles. I'm not sure this is a problem so much as an aspect of realism. What happens if your town has only a few children because of limited resources and then all of the adults pass out of child-bearing age? Eventually the townsfolk might all die of old age, leaving the town without enough of a labor force to service it's own basic needs.
These are the more advanced management decisions required once you get beyond basic town building. The game requires a lot of future planning to be successful, and will be very hard for anyone trying to just live in the moment. It simply isn't enough to only solve today's problems. This is especially true when it comes to the cycle of seasons, which has been handled extremely well. This is the first game I've played where the crop cycle really is as important as it was in real life centuries ago.
One of my takeaways from playing has been an increased understanding and respect for how hard it must have been to establish the early American colonies.
In closing, while the developer has expressed a desire to eventually explore other projects, it is my hope that he will invest as much time as he can into expanding the core functionality and content of the game before moving on. This is truly one of the great town games  of the modern era, and an incredible achievement for one man working alone.

At the time of writing this, I have invested 10 hours on Scholar of the First Sin on Steam and 200+ hours on my long-gone PS3 version.
Although Dark Souls 2 is definitely the weakest entry in the Souls series, that hardly makes it a bad game. If you have already played Dark Souls 2, then I recommend spending some time on the other Soulsborne games and then updating to Scholar of the First Sin when you're ready to revisit Drangleic. That's what I did, and everything feels both familiar and slightly different.
The new enemy placement isn't bothering me because the game isn't freshly etched into my mind. Scholar of the First Sin certainly isn't enough to make the original Dark Souls 2 feel fresh again-- it's just polish and tweaks. I will admit, however, that the addition of Fragrant Branch Statues is irritating because I already know where to go, and it feels like I can't carve my own path into the world. We've also got a special surprise added just before the Blue Sentinels covenant, which makes an already dead covenant more difficult to get to. (Hell, for all I know the guy might not even be there. I haven't figured out how to circumvent the special surprise yet.)
The game runs beautifully; has never dropped below 60FPS once. And although I normally use a controller, I think M+KB are perfectly viable options. The mouse camera control has been fixed since Dark Souls 1 (although it felt a bit sensitive to me, I would only be able to play from between 0-3 sensitivity out of about 10, not a lot of room to dial it in).
Summons are also very quick. They pop in within 10 seconds.
Yeah Soul Memory is an unfortunate addition, but it isn't game breaking. The levels aren't interconnected, but then again they aren't interconnected in Dark Souls 3, Demon's Souls, or Bloodborne either. Dark Souls 1 definitely outshines the rest in level design and art direction (I said direction, not graphics).
Where Dark Souls 2 really shines is that it fixes gameplay annoyances from its predecessor. The GUI is beautiful and easy to navigate, this is the first time we were able to use multiple soul items with the click of a button, the menu doesn't disappear once they're gone, you can re-allocate your character with Soul Vessels, and you can replay bosses ad infinitum with Bonfire Ascetics without starting the whole journey over, and defeating the last boss doesn't rudely force you into New Game Plus.
My take on Souls 2 is this: Novice players will get similar enjoyment from this version compared to Dark Souls 1. Intermediate players will get annoyed at the differences and missteps and whine. True Souls vets will appreciate the things Dark Souls 2 really does right, and will adapt to and overcome what has been changed.
When you buy Scholar of the First Sin, as you probably already know, you are also getting all three of the Dark Souls 2 DLC's. This game is absolutely monolithic. But if the price tag of $40 isn't worth it to you, that's fine. I never buy games at full price either. On a good sale (at the time of writing), it's 14 bucks, and you get a hell of a lot of game for it.
Highly recommended. Don't let the others overshadow it. Git good.

Verdun is a pretty unique shooter and very well made, but the trailers and screenshots are horribly misleading. You won't be running and gunning, players aren't going to charge forward...it's mostly just lying down or crouching in a hole, slowly moving up and then slowly retreating. It's extremely slow paced and yet there's no tension unlike similar "realistic" shooters like Insurgency. There are no "clutch" moments, or brief surges of action.
The maps are pretty dull to look at as they're mostly just holes in the dirt surrounded by barbed wire and wooden fences...realistic, but pretty boring to play. Sound design is good. Gunplay is okay but hit detection seems a bit off at times. The game seems to be optimised well for lower-end systems, as even my aging laptop could run it smoothly with no issues.
I can see the appeal and if you're interested World War 1 or slow-paced shooters, I can recommend Verdun. It's unlike anything else on the market and I'm sure there are people out there who love it. I'm just not one of them!

Pros:
Beautiful graphics
Varied game styles (Yellow zone stealth, Red zone aggressive)
Tried and tested Far Cry formula
Weapon customisation
RC Car bombs!
Cons:
Unlikeable allies
No reason for your character to be a mute
Ridiculously fast respawns for the yellow zone Hearts and Minds activities
Loot system could be more varied (e.g weapon mods, more craftable items)
I'd give this a solid 75% in its curent state and would highly recommend it if you can pick it up on sale. I purchased it, after trying it for free, at 40% off so it was £17.99. At that price it's well worth it

When you look at this game at first, you might think that it is another old city building game. No, it is not just another city building game. This game is detailed and beautiful in every way. At first I had a hard time keeping my people from starving, but I learned that my strategy was all wrong. A tip for when you play this AMAZING game and want to keep your food storage high: start with two nice sized crop feilds and then build up each spring. Then on the second or third year, place a fishing post. Keep building up thos farm feilds until you have five feilds. Then get a hunting lodge and a gatherer. Just prepare to be building oober amounts of storage barns. Try to keep a good focus on the wood because if you let it go down, you will find it hard to build the storage barns fast enough to get your produce into shelter.

A very interesting experience with a compelling story that makes the player explore all the small pieces and memories inside the house while unravelling the story.
Gone Home makes sure the game doesn't feel like just walking and listening to a story - it includes enough interaction to keep the player entertained with both the story as it unravels and exploring the house, finding the different objects and documents found throughout the house. There is very little repetition among objects found and even a few humorous moments.
You work your way through the memories found in the game, but in the end of it all, the game itself is a memory to be kept.

A must have.
An FPS that lets you take full control of your weapon. No more R to reload, no more resupplying by walking over ammo, etc. One button to pull the slide, one to eject the magazine, one to put a round into the magazine, one to chamber a round, one to engage safety, one to eject a round, one to pick stuff up, one to fire... it does have a bit of a learning curve, but I can tell you it's really worth it. Once you've mastered your weapon, using it will be thrilling. You have to shoot drones that'll try to kill you. Once you die, you start over on a new, randomly generated map (well, more like existing rooms put together in a random order). It also has an eerie backstory and "quest", of which I'm not going to reveal anything other than you collect cassette tapes and listen to them.
If you have ever played FPS games, corridor shooters, shoot-em-ups, whatever, you need to play this game.
If you like guns, you absolutely need to play this game. I'm not especially into firearms, but this game made me more interested in them :)
Cons: The game was made in about ten days (for a game jam), so it's far from polished. The graphics won't astonish you (think minimalistic Unity3D), and there are some optimization problems, but overall it's still a very enjoyable and definitely unique experience.
Oh, and it's made by the Wolfire guys who are like the best indie devs ever. So buy it nao.

So, this is the last Dark Souls game I played through to completion; I started my first playthrough quite a while ago, but never got very far because both the clunkier controls and muddier visuals put me off, plus I heard a lot of people calling this the worst game in the series. However, after exhausting everything Dark Souls 3 had to offer, I still craved for more Dark Souls gameplay, so the black sheep in the series was my only option. So what did I think of it? I thought it was a lot better than people make it out to be.
Okay, it definitely has some legitimate flaws, like the controls being somewhat stiff, the hitboxes being massive trolls from time to time, and the enemy placement being a bit of a pain in certain areas, but I still got a lot of enjoyment out of it. The fire mechanic is right up my alley, I just adore being able to manipulate the levels in a meaningful way, and lighting up all the little torches just tickled my brain in a very delightful manner. I also am a big fan of being able to change the boss arenas a la Dragonrider, Lost Sinner and Fume Knight; it makes the stages feel like more of a puzzle you have to put together, and it carries a great sense of discovery with it, at least for me.
The story and world are definitely a downgrade compared to the other two Souls games, I have to admit, but I still found a lot of the characters likable. Okay, there were no real Solaires or Andres among them, but to be fair, those are some high bars to reach. Considering the mastermind Miyazaki wasn't working on this one, I think his lackeys did a fairly good job at putting together a competent game in its own right.
So, is it the worst in the series? Sure, it's really hard to argue against that. Is it still a good game? Absolutely. It does some things I like that the other games don't do, and even if its core mechanics are inferior to its siblings, they are still far superior to the mechanics of a lot of other high budget games in my experiences. So, take it for what it's worth. I enjoyed it and got a lot of playtime out of it, so I'm satisfied.

I avoided this game in the beginning after hearing so many terrible reviews due to optimization. However, after playing it over the free weekend, I immediately bought it. The game runs smooth as glass, the graphics and gameplay are both great, it's not a massive system hog, and the story is actually very good and quite long. It took about 30 hours to beat. The co-op play is a lot of fun as well and finally you can play a game with friends without having to be amped up on cocaine and Red Bull to have enough reflexes just to kill something.
The story is quite a bit of a stretch, what with the US being beholden to North Korea for its technology and finances. Yes, you will need to suspend reality a bit to enjoy it, but it IS enjoyable. I have a sneaking suspicion that originally it was about China, but possibly due to real-world political and PR fallout they decided to substitute China for North Korea. This is just my opinion and speculation. Think of it more of an alternate reality than an actual cold war Red Dawn scenario, where there really was a credible fear of a Soviet attack.
All in all, I give it an 8.5 out of 10. I would give it a 9, but I would have liked more weapons in the game. Yes, I do like the system of customization and cannabilizing weapons for parts to create new upgrades, but I would have liked to do that with different types of rifles and submachine guns, not just an AR-15 that turns into a SAW and a pistol that turns into some half♥♥♥♥♥SMG. Also, being unable to pick up enemies' weapons is pretty lame, although I guess it could be argued that they would all have electronic trigger locks for each individual. Finally, I would have liked to have more accessories, such as silencers for the sniper rifle. It's not a big deal, but it would've added more to the stealth aspect, which is lacking. But, then again, you're a resistance fighter, not a ninja.
The obvious parallels to Far Cry are there, with the only real difference being there is no vehicle usage in the game. I actually kinda liked that, because it's not very realistic that the average resistance fighter would know how to drive a futuristic North Korean tank.
Finally, I'm very excited that they're planning DLCs in the form of both Co-Op multiplayer maps and big single player maps as well. I will be keeping this game on my hard drive for a while, and I might just replay the single player again. It's a lot of fun and you would be missing out on a great experience if you don't buy this massively (at least now) underrated game. If you like FPS games but despise the spastic 11-year-old♥♥♥♥♥♥talking CoD scene, get this game.
Is it worth the full price? Yes, in my opinion. Others may disagree but I think 50 bucks is fair for this game, especially since it runs so well now.
Is it worth the sale price? Absolutely. It would be criminal to overlook it on sale.

Your opponents and you typically die after one rifle shot, making running around like a child with a toy gun impossible. You HAVE to take cover, you HAVE to treat your opponents as threats, and you HAVE to shoot straight. This all makes for some very immersive gameplay, and some very angry BF and CoD fanatics. Another thing is that this game revolves around teamwork; your team's success or failure often relying on communication between teammates. On some maps, it can seem impossible to take the enemies' first trench, which makes it all the more satisfying when you do.
So basically, if you like realistic, immersive FPS -and don't mind a bit of trial and error- I'd definitely recommend this game.
