Think you'd survive an action movie if you had a gun?
Spoiler: No, no you wouldn't.
This is the FPS equivalent of Super Meat Boy, and it has what are indisputably the most immersive gun mechanics of any game ever.
The gameplay itself, outside of the gun mechanics is as simple as its minimalist aesthetic, but severely punishing for any misstep or corner left unchecked. It only takes one bullet to bring you down, and there's no going back. The game has a permadeath system, and any failure brings you back to square one with randomized equipment at a randomized spot of the randomized world.
Tasks which would be simple motions for action heroes are challenging feats here. It may take you several playthroughs to swiftly reload a colt 1911a, but to finally accomplish a swift reload is incredibly satisfying.
Receiver is Wolfire Games' submission for 7DFPS, and though it lacks polish, it's an extremely successful experiment in game design.

The game was recently up for a free weekend, and despite the mixed reviews, I enjoyed the game enough to purchase it on sale. All in all I think there's a lot to enjoy here. First the bad - the noted frame rate drops, and the occasional minor bug typical of open world games - NPCs mispathing, or blocking doors or staircases; a few minor  missteps when jumping or looting, etc., and some audio bugs with speeches playing over each other, but over all there were no game breaking bugs and no crashes or freezes at all.
The good - in terms of gameplay, the story and world gameplay both unfold nicely. The open world setting works very well for the style of game - some areas start out clean and pristine, and there's a good mix of stealth gameplay and action as you move throughout the zones, sabatoging and taking on random events and exploration. As you progress the citizens around you start to rise up, attacking guards, spraypainting walls, etc. You see the effects of your progress on the world and it helps create a lot of immersion.
In terms of mechanics, the gunplay is average - there are some fairly bullet spongey enemies, but you're able to upgrade your weapons in order to reduce that. AI is decent - enemies will take cover and throw grenades, but they're fairly same-ish for the most part. There's not a massive variety of weapons, but it makes sense in the context of the game world. Ambushing patrols with remote explosives is a lot of fun and definitely makes you feel like you're playing the part of a revolutionary.
The story and voice acting are acceptable and move the action forward but they're not winning any awards. Graphics are good and it runs well on older hardware, aside from the aformentioned frame rate drops, which seem to occur regardless of your specs.
Overall if you get this game on sale, it's a good time and I found myself wanting to play more. Unfortunatly any online play seems to be dead, but I bought this mainly for single player and it lived up to my expectations.

You are given a rough post ice age landscape, covered in glacial eratics, including (unusually for a planet with free oxygen) lumps of pure iron. The terrain has a patchy covering of trees and far too many mountains hills and rivers. The task is to direct your hapless exiles to create the things they need to firstly survive and secondly thrive. You would expect this little band of brothers to work for the common good? Far from it they hoard resources in their little huts and do not help their comrades  in their hour of need. I watched one person starve to death while another had plenty. The setting of priorities is very clunky I would expect to be able to direct individuals, This is not possible the citizens go about their tasks with a order that I have yet to fathom. Rather like the workers at a factory would if all the managers were on holiday at the same time and the computers went down. So despite this group being what can only be described as an awkward rabble, if you take the care to not give them too much to do at once, and create the task in the right sequence, you will not only get them to survive but also thrive. What then you might ask? Well more of the same there are no more challanges apart from dealing with a not very enterprising trader (I would get into the boat with him and introduce him to an AK47 to motivate him, if I could),who instead of bringing a low quantitity of many things, often comes with large quantity of things you don't need. Missing are gold and currency, a better way of directing 'the rabble', reasonable trading, and progression. They come by cart but they never use the cart to move goods around and can't build new carts. The rabble walk through virgin forest at nearly the same speed as when you build them a path. I expected to see them building boats but are totally incapable. The game for all of this is reasonably good, but it could have been great, what a pity.

The first-person shooter has become nearly as anicent as the platformer.  Once you figure out the basic formula behind it, it's all downhill from there because everything else is just so much salad dressing.  Or is it?
Receiver brings to the table some crazy ideas to go with a bright, unique one: realistic gun mechanics.  You will soon understand just how complicated actual firearms really are and that aiming is no walk in the park either.  It takes patience and persistence despite only being the tip of the iceberg.  When you get down to it though, the realism of how reloading and aiming actually works is a fascinating spin on this tired genre of gaming.  I mean, what other game has made you feel so close to a measely pistol of all things?
Seven days worth of game design and we are introduced to Receiver.  You're a man (or woman) with brittle bones that can't survive a ten-foot drop and such nerves that a taser will implode your frightened little heart.  Death is one mistake away and the world and its resources are never the same should you die.  You're on a quest to find eleven cassette tapes of valuable information pretaining to the setting of the game and your own circumstances.  All you have to defend yourself is one of two handguns or a revolver and you can bet you need to be frugal with your insurance policy.
Despite the game's simplicity and lack of polish, Receiver is a game that most definitely deserves to be played.  There are few games that capture and embrace the qualities of curiousity and tension.
One could say that it's absolutely impossible to be faithful of your own ability to survive when there is no room for error.  The consequences of missing a single shot can hurt you in ways you never thought possible.  You might even take a  wrong step in the middle of a wild dash from hot pursuers and go careening right off a third story overlook.  We're only human, after all.
Yet, regardless of the peril, you can't avoid feeling compelled to explore.  Every bullet you find ups your chances of survival and every tape brings you one step closer to victory.  The gun mechanics themselves are an obstacle to be understood and overcome.  Emptying cartridges into a magazine to be loaded into a Colt M1911A1 pistol, then pulling the slide back to chamber the first round, is a deceptively simple and absorbing activity.  Then you pull off an amazing shot at one of a hostile killer bot's weakpoints and see it crash to the ground with a satisfying clash of short-circuitry and metallic clanking.
All these elements come together for an incredibly immersive game.  It really does feel like you're left to your own wits to survive a situation that would otherwise be placed in the hands of a superpowered space marine or badass super spy.  It's far from perfect (obviously) but it shines as an example of what the gaming industry needs more of.  For five bucks, you owe it to yourself to play it.  Once you get past the learning curve, you'll see for yourself that glimpse of hope that novelty still lives on in the heart of gaming.  Even in first-person shooters.

Gone Home is an exploration of family, love, discontent, life's disappointments and life's joys.  It is, ultimately, a video game for people who enjoy the art of well-told stories.  Enhanced by the creators' choices in music and art style, each character is delicately drawn, using only the detritus of their lives (and deaths?).  Playing through the game, I could have wept that, finally, finally, a story that reflects me (in some small measure) was both central and yet, not fetishised, not a punch-line, not an inevitable tragedy. The beginning passage of the game definitely evokes unease and the penultimate part real fear, for those attrached to the game for its creepy aesthetics. Ultimately, this is more than a game, more than ineractive fiction with added graphics - it transcends genre. I hope as many people as possible get to experience it.

In short, should you buy Receiver?  Yes.
Keep in mind this one thing when evaluating Receiver: it was made in SEVEN DAYS by THREE GUYS.
Considering that, it's amazing Receiver exists at all.  But to top it off, the game offers a new and very unique element within the FPS genre: massive attention focused on the process of reloading.  It's a surprisingly fun and rewarding test of dexterity FPS players aren't used to.  And if you enjoy the real-life sport of shooting, the experience is all the more enjoyable.
No, you won't simply hit "R" when your clip is empty in THIS game, Spanky!  First, you'll press "E" to remove the magazine from your M1911A1 or Glock, "`" to holster the gun, then cartridges (bullets) are inserted individually by pressing "Z" for each.  Pressing "`" again draws your gun, "Z" loads the magazine, and "R" racks the slide to chamber a round.  So don't expect a long life if you empty a magazine in combat.  Even if you have a spare, loaded mag, it's still "E" > "E" > "1" > "1" > "R" to reload, and by that time you've probably died.
Did I mention you die from a single hit?
Yes, while Receiver is 100% beatable, doing so is hard as heck.  Managing to collect all 11 audio tapes to complete the game leaves you feeling like you've accomplished something significant, earned a higher status, and achieved a new milestone in your career as a gamer.
Each game world is generated dynamically, and starting equipment is assigned randomly, so Receiver is never the same twice.  Do you start with the 1911, Glock, or S&W revolver?  Is it loaded?  If so, with how many rounds?
Better be sure.

Sometimes, a game comes along that makes you redefine what a game really is.  A lot of individuals like to limit things with their definition.  To claim a video game isn't a game because it doesn't have the particular mechanics you are accustomed to seeing in a game, is absurd.  What I'm trying to say, is, that the definition of a word is flexible.  As independent developers continue to emerge, we begin to see more and more creative ways to define a video game, and I find that exciting!
Gone Home is one of those games; a game that really makes you reconsider your definition.  Gone Home lacks any sort of combat system, leveling system, or even a scoring system.  Gone Home is simply a first-person interactive experience, devoid of any type of traditional gameplay mechanic besides story and the interaction of objects within the game's environment.
This may seem like an alien concept to those unaccustomed to such a concept.  However, Gone Home shows an evolution in gaming: the ability to tell a compelling story without the conventional gameplay hooks required to engage an audience.  Gone Home is not the first game to do this, but it's one of the first games of its kind to attract so much attention.
Gone Home begins with the return of your character from a year-long trip abroad.  You arrive home in the dead of night to an abandoned house.  The home is large and expansive with many things to interact with and investigate.  The game doesn't even give you an objective; you only explore the home and make your way through it, piecing together the last year of events that you've missed.  Throughout the journey, the large house creaks and the storm outside rages, creating some odd noises.  The setting is unnerving as you make your way through the house, switching on lights as if you're ten years old all over again, reaching around the door frame, groping for the light switch.  (Admit it! You did it!)
Gone Home isn't only an interactive story, but also a period piece.  The game takes place in the 1990s, complete with X-File references and anything else you can imagine.  Growing up during that time really made Gone Home hit even harder for me, referencing fond memories from my early childhood.  The pace of the story and the accuracy of the period culminate into a very enjoyable experience that stands on its own, despite lacking customary game mechanics.

Gone Home tells the story of a young girl home after a long trip overseas.  Before you even open the door to begin your story, a note is left on the door to pull you along.  Your sister is gone, and she doesn't want you looking for her.  As the game progresses, you learn more about your family, and the house.
This 'game' is labeled on Wikipedia as a first person interactive story adventure.  Specifically in Gone Home, you walk around the house, pick up items, read notes, and figure out ways to explore more of the house.  Your carrot on the stick is the story, and it's a good one.
There are puzzles in the house, but they are only there to pace the story they are trying to tell.  They really didn't give me my puzzle game fix like games like Myst would.  The interactive part of this story adventure amounts to picking up items to examine them and putting them back down.  It fleshes out the story.
On the negative side, while the story was good, it wasn't great.  The finale was lacking, but maybe that was my fault.  The atmosphere made me feel like I was in a spooky house.  Some of the history that you learn also puts you in this creepy vibe.  The game really isn't creepy or really all that mysterious.  I thought it was going to be a mysterious adventure, but it wasn't.  They told me a story, and as interesting as it was, it was still underwhelming.
I still recommend a play through though.  I've never played a game like this before and I couldn't stop once I started.  It only took a couple hours to finish, so go for it.

Is £15 worth it for only four hours of game? Yes, in the same way that £15 is worth it for a great movie on DVD or Blu Ray. Highly recommended.

Unlike most FPS shooters where even the most gun-inept moron can be a hero, this game's mechanics puts a very tense spin on things by mimicing reality moreso than conventional shooters - such as no HUD, lack of "automatic" reloading, and the ability to take a bullet or two without collapsing. This game also includes a system for reloading your magazines, which means unlike most FPS's where you just run around and magically pick up ammo in fully loaded, ready to use magazines, you will have to stop and load rounds into magazines by hand. Or remove them, depending on your preference - unless you're using the revolver.
It's simple. It's tense. And I recommend it.

Alright so, let me give full disclosure to start, I played this game in the free weekend that Steam offered on the 9th-11th September.
First of all, there were things to enjoy about this game. The gameplay wasn’t too bad - Far-Cry esque in an occupied city where the underground revolution (you) has to take down the occupants he can, destroy their equipment and earn his freedom. It was almost Terminator 2 like, popping out of a ruined building to lob a pipe-bomb at a passing mech and quickly get back down to snipe a few soldiers advancing towards you.
The exploration, taking over districts by doing a variety of different tasks (Strike Points through hacking, killing soldiers stationed there, finding HAM radios, etc.), helping civilians there, and a number of collectables (radios, propaganda speakers, fuel storage tanks) - all of this was fairly enjoyable. I like open world gameplay where you start off outnumbered and hopeless and become the main force by the end of the game - standard linear progression yes, but it makes for a fun experience of being the hero.
The story is an interesting concept. North Koreans started up the tech giants, Americans flooded to buy their gear (computers, tablets, phones, and even military equipment) only for it all to have a backdoor allowing NK to easily invade. The large zeppelin airships that watch over cities, looking out for trouble with their spotlights which you have to avoid (or be faced with endless soldiers until you get to safety/hide somewhere), patrolling armoured vehicles and mechs, it was all pretty cool and eerie.
Graphically, this game looks pretty good. Textures are nice, effects are pretty good, once you get into an area that’s been gassed you get to see all the particle effects of toxins in the air and all the dust from the dilapidated factories and structures that are in the area.
Though of course, this is a negative rating I’m giving. And it’s probably expected. The performance.
The performance can be pretty abysmal at times - even on a pretty good machine (i7-6700k, GTX 980ti, 16GB RAM). It started off alright, but frame drops can be frequent (be warned, CLOSE ALL BACKGROUND PROGRAMS. I had YouTube open on my other monitor to watch some stuff whilst I took over districts and my framerate tanked hard - dropping to unplayable rates and stuttering every 10-20 seconds sometimes). It gets worse the longer you play - I recommend restarting the game now and then whilst you play so it doesn’t tank as hard.
The game also gets glitches. One strikepoint was unavailable to me (chop shop) and it appears to be a common occurrence according to the Internet. I had to download a trainer to allow me to float upwards (cheat my way basically) up and through the side of the building as the garage door refused to open once the generator was running. I also spawned once in a mission with no resistance soldiers with me - facing a few dozen NK soldiers, the game then gave me a game over screen as my “resistance soldiers had died” when they never even spawned in game. Achievements are also pretty glitched. They stop tracking when you play, so there are quite a few I am missing which I clearly achieved (I liberated all Strike Points, free’d every district yet apparently I barely got over half of them according to the Steam achievement tracker. Several other ones didn’t unlock either).
If this game got fixed - polished up a bit with the performance optimised and the glitches buffed out I’d buy this game no problem. It seems alright - it’s not too long but it’s long enough and doesn’t outstay it’s welcome at all and is what you’d want out of this style of game. Too long and it drags on. The devs seem pretty honest people, with the credits opening with some story about the development problems that plagued this game, and even after all the disasters post-launch they are doing things to progress it a bit at least. Time will tell, if the problems do get fixed then this will change into a positive review for sure.

Banished is full of ripple effects:  Everything's running smoothly and you feel confident in building another house?  20 years later, because of that extra house, everyone is dying of starvation, freezing to death or dying of diptheria.
My laborious little laborers have been trampled, stabbed, plagued, frozen, crushed, drowned, burnt, swept away, and one lucky teacher went batshit crazy.  And yet, humanity persevered and thrived.
It's a game filled with subtleties and harsh lessons, but definitely worth playing!

This game, while simplistic in graphics, is well worth the five bucks  - and then some. Unlike most FPS shooters where even the most gun-inept moron can be a hero, this game's mechanics puts a very tense spin on things by mimicing reality moreso than conventional shooters - such as no HUD, lack of "automatic" reloading, and the ability to take a bullet or two without collapsing. If caught unawares, the game is unforgiving. Get hit even once, and you are dead.
This game also includes a system for reloading your magazines, which means unlike most FPS's where you just run around and magically pick up ammo in fully loaded, ready to use magazines, you will have to stop and load rounds into magazines by hand. Or remove them, depending on your preference - unless you're using the revolver.
It's simple. It's tense. And I recommend it.

Thank you Deep Silver and Dambuster for the free weekend. Unfortunately, this game is not very good.
Ostensibly a mix of Far Cry, Stalker and Freedom Fighters, it soon reveals itself to be a mere Crysis-alike with a gimmick. The weapon customization menu probably gave that away to some of you.
The story is very predictable and at times comically vile. And it's absolutely terrible! There's no reason to play Homefront: The Revolution for the story, its perfunctory rah-rah patriot ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t doesn't even compare favorably to the Call of Duty garbage of a few years back.
But does it at least play well? Eh... not really.
The gunplay and movement is typical for CryEngine - that is to say not very good. Even smooth 60+ fps can't hide the weird player movement and unsatisfying gun action. The novel weapons aren't really fun to use, which is an absolute bummer.
Painting the map blue by liberating outposts and strongholds also loses its draw after the first map. The concept of Yellow Zones is interesting on the surface, but completely wasted in practice. Sprinting past guards takes care of every problem. The world just doesn't feel believable or internally consistent.
Homefront certainly isn't a terrible game, but with the amount of quality games available today, why play a thoroughly mediocre one?

A lot of reviews here seem to miss the point of the game- yes, there is a main story told through journal entires that get spoken to you as you explore the house and yeah, that main story is a little hamfisted in a "teenage coming-of-age love story" kind of way that's pretty predicatble. But if you take your time and really pay attention to all the little details, there are a lot of subplots that get told in a really interesting way through scattered papers and pictures and documents. A lot if it hit a little close to home for me, so maybe I enjoyed it more than others would- it's a pretty personal game, and if you've never dealt with some of the family issues the game deals with, you may not have as much of a connection to the main character.
That being said, yes, it is short. And yes, the puzzles are pretty simple. But this is not a puzzle game, and if it was any longer it would have detracted from the story (maybe some games are *meant* to be short?). It's not really that replayable either, second time around it would have nowhere near as much impact as the first.

My thoughts:
This is not actually a review but rather a few comments on the game since it has been 15 years since I have played this game and it's just brought back so much memories. After ~10 hrs of game there are a few things that I like and not fond/grey area of about this version:
What I liked:
Turbo mode:
Kudos to whoever came up with this. I have been grinding the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of the game when I was a kid and I have seen the animation over and over again. Probably close to 1k+ times now so I love this feature to cut back the time spent on those animations.
Enemy Encounter:
Increase the chance of spawning enemies. VERY GOOD for leveling and maxing out stats for late game. You gonna need this to farm for some materials too for your Sphere Grid skill.
Arranged OST:
THIS!!!! THIS IS GOOOOOOOOOOOD!!!!!!!!!!!! Just listen to the OST darn it!!!!
Lulu's figure:
Yea I can't lie about this...she has been...somewhat a teaser with her outfit. It's been 15 years and I still can't look at her straight in the eyes sometimes....
Not fond of:
Load Save:
Where the hell is the load Save feature? I don't wanna quit the game then reload it again. Give me a load save built-in feature within the menu so I can reload the game to the previous point without exiting it. There are multiple occasion that I needed to reload to the previous inaccessible area to pick up some stuff and I had to exit the game then reload back. More time consuming, just do it SE. Build a load function in the game.
Grey area:
Graphic:
It is to be expected that this game is ~16 years old and therefore it can't match up with the graphic that we have seen today so I put this in a grey area cos it's subjective to personal taste.
Other features such as max skills, max gils...etc:
I personally don't like the game when it's too easy but some people may find these features useful to assist them finishing the game while maintaining their busy work schedule. So it's good that SE has made this an optional that can activate when needed.
30 FPS:
I know that the game is capped at 30 FPS. However, this should be noted that this is an old game and thus 60 FPS back in PS2 day wasn't a thing. Me personally I'm comfortable with this but I know some may have problem with 30 FPS. There may be a mod or something to unlock the game to 60 FPS so you may want to hold off on purchasing the game if 60 FPS is a must for you.

Amazing World is an interesting idea, and one that I can honestly say I enjoy almost completely. Despite being a child's MMO game, it has enough in it to interest most MMO fans, at least to a certain degree.
Originally, I downloaded this game on my sister's laptop to see if she would enjoy it (she didn't really have anything except The Sims 2 & 3). We were both instantly drawn in to the cutesy style and well-designed world that the game presented, and played it for a day straight, max-leveling one of the accouts we made to the highest non-pay level. Once we got back home, I downloaded it on THIS steam account to see if the multiplayer worked. Amazing World is similar to Skyrim in that you cannot play it for just a few minutes, at least if you enjoy the game. Whilst I initally only went on to try the multiplayer, I ended up completing a full character story and earning about 6000 coins!
Speaking of characters, all are well-voiced and each have their own personalities. While I won't list them all, the best by far were Annoying (a navi-like little probe robot with a very teenage-girl-like attitude and style of speech) and Brick (a carpenter who sees himself as fearless but gets scared very easily). Whilst some are locked until levels higher than 10, the ones that we have had a chance to meet are charming and well-made.
Overall, whilst I do enjoy the game, I always feel a bit awkward playing it seperately to my sister (since we spent a while playing it on the same device at the same time). It's worth at least an hour or two of play even if you don't like anything about it. As my sister said, "it's Moshi Monsters, but better".

1) The netcode is simply the worst. The server trusts the client, this means: Client A says "I hit Client B" and the server informs Client B that he has been hit and is dead. That Client B allready had his head down in the trench is of no interest. See the problem there ? People with high pings will♥♥♥♥♥♥you good, especially if you are on a very good connection. Because your information where you move reaches them faster, than their movement info reaches you.
Also this kind of client-trust makes the game very vunerable for "hacking-tools" - something that had The Divison loose a lot of players. But in all my play time, i never really experienced obvious skript kiddies and i dont consider it a problem.
2) The game randomly disconnects you upon map change, or when you try to join with a squad. If youre lucky and on of your squad-mates made it through the map-change progress you have to join him quick via steam overlay. Otherwise some other player might take your spot ...
3) The maps are filled with stupid bugs that make you fly up in the air or randomly for example.
4) All the above problems are not new. They exist for long. And yet what do the devs do ? They work on a silly console version which will fail hard because of Battlefield 1.

While some of the sections above may sound either fanboy-ish or cynical-old-man-ish, that’s simply because there are so many either really good or really bad things that come with Mists of Pandaria.
Pros:
Once again the collector’s edition is gorgeous. Blizzard does CE versions very well, and this is no exception. Sure it is a few extra bucks, but for that you get a great looking box, a nice art book, a mouse pad, a DVD, a soundtrack CD, and an in game mount and pet.
The new Pandaren race and Monk class are both really nice additions to the game. I love the whole panda thing, and have since they were introduced way back in Warcraft as an April fools joke.
The Monk class is cool as well since it offers another hybrid class that can tank (my favorite spec). Better yet the tank spec is completely different than any other tank spec, making it a whole lot of fun to play.
The overall look and feel of the game, as well as the music, voice, and storytelling aspects. There are so many more cut scenes included that the game feels like I am participating in a movie rather than just playing a game. It also helps that once again Blizzard has nailed the story lines in each zone, and that really pulls me into the game.
The new dungeons and raids look stunning and are a whole lot of fun to play. While the dungeons are not as hard as the Cataclysm ones were initially, they do have a lot more going on in them. Blizzard has really started to add more abilities to dungeon bosses since Cataclysm, and that makes them much more interesting to fight against.
For once the launch went amazingly well! The game just flowed right into the launch and while there was some congestion at key points in quest chains, there was never a serious holdup. This was probably the best launch yet for a WoW expansion.
Cons
The leveling in the game is once again way to fast. It is just insane to me that after all this waiting for a game players can power through it in less than a day. Sure there is a lot of end game content, and that is what most players want to get to, but it was still too fast by far.
The whole idea of adding Pokemon to the game is more than a little strange to me. While I know the idea is popular with the younger crowd, it seems downright disrespectful to the more serious gamers.
While scenarios looked to be an awesome idea, they fall seriously short. They are way to easy and require way to little cooperation to offer any serious lasting enjoyment.
The simplified talent system is just way to simplified. While I do agree that it offers more meaningful choice when compared to the old talent system, it does so at the expense of a feel of accomplishment or customization. Getting 1 talent every 15 levels doesn’t feel like you are accomplishing anything or able to customize your character at all. Worst of all, all specializations for each class all have access to the same talents. I can think of only one word to describe that: lame.

Find an FOV calculator, enter in your desired horizontal FOV and then use the calculated vertical FOV number to set your FOV higher in the files.
Go to: (user name)\Saved Games\homefront2\game.cfg and open the file in Notepad.
Find the below text, which should be right at the top.
cl_defaultnearfov = 50
cl_fov = 50
The default vertical is set at 50. But I like to play it at 68, which is 100 horizontal FOV.
Save the file after the changes, boot up the game and enjoy your new perspective on the world.

The game itself though, I honestly find really enjoyable. I have not played another game that has really nailed the feeling of urban warfare and guerrilla tactics like Homefront: The Revolution has. You will frequently feel outmanned and outgunned, which I find incredibly refreshing compared to the mass of games that treat you like a super soldier.
The difficulty is no walk in the park either, even on Easy a shotgun to the face will kill you instantly if you aren't at full health. Again, I very much enjoy this kind of feeling where engagements have to be planned out and taken seriously.
The co-op is a real high point, adding a very positive team dynamic to the guerrilla warfare, but unfortunately it is pretty dead. This is a huge shame, as some of the best fun in the game can be found in these missions playing with other people and sharing the experience.
Bring friends for the great co-op or buy it just for the singleplayer.

Since a recent update you also may spawn with either an M1911, a revolver of some kind (a bit fiddly to reload, but quite simple otherwise), and a Glock 17 (with a full-auto mod, kind of pointless as ammo is so scarce).
There's a couple playthroughs on YouTube, check 'em out!

My thoughts:
This is not actually a review but rather a few comments on the game since it has been 15 years since I have played this game and it's just brought back so much memories. After ~10 hrs of game there are a few things that I like and not fond/grey area of about this version:
What I liked:
Turbo mode:
Kudos to whoever came up with this. I have been grinding the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of the game when I was a kid and I have seen the animation over and over again. Probably close to 1k+ times now so I love this feature to cut back the time spent on those animations.
Enemy Encounter:
Increase the chance of spawning enemies. VERY GOOD for leveling and maxing out stats for late game. You gonna need this to farm for some materials too for your Sphere Grid skill.
Arranged OST:
THIS!!!! THIS IS GOOOOOOOOOOOD!!!!!!!!!!!! Just listen to the OST darn it!!!!
Lulu's figure:
Yea I can't lie about this...she has been...somewhat a teaser with her outfit. It's been 15 years and I still can't look at her straight in the eyes sometimes....
Not fond of:
Load Save:
Where the hell is the load Save feature? I don't wanna quit the game then reload it again. Give me a load save built-in feature within the menu so I can reload the game to the previous point without exiting it. There are multiple occasion that I needed to reload to the previous inaccessible area to pick up some stuff and I had to exit the game then reload back. More time consuming, just do it SE. Build a load function in the game.
Grey area:
Graphic:
It is to be expected that this game is ~16 years old and therefore it can't match up with the graphic that we have seen today so I put this in a grey area cos it's subjective to personal taste.
Other features such as max skills, max gils...etc:
I personally don't like the game when it's too easy but some people may find these features useful to assist them finishing the game while maintaining their busy work schedule. So it's good that SE has made this an optional that can activate when needed.
30 FPS:
I know that the game is capped at 30 FPS. However, this should be noted that this is an old game and thus 60 FPS back in PS2 day wasn't a thing. Me personally I'm comfortable with this but I know some may have problem with 30 FPS. There may be a mod or something to unlock the game to 60 FPS so you may want to hold off on purchasing the game if 60 FPS is a must for you.

Receiver is an amazing proof-of-concept. The guns are more realistic, and take more knowledge to handle than just "press R to reload". Having to manually insert each bullet into the magazine (and remember to manually chamber the first round) makes each gun feel like a tool, like something more solid and tangible. That builds a strong connection between you and your gun, making the shooting more exciting. I would love to see the ideas of Receiver used in a mainstream game. Would love to.
That said, Receiver itself is a fun distraction, but not much of a "game". After a half hour you'll likely feel you've seen everything worth seeing, and not be wrong. It's worth buying to experience what FPS games could do, as that proof-of-concept, and support the developers.

Dark Souls II, although it's not connected to Dark Souls I in any big way, but has some hints to their connection in small easy to miss dialogue in the Lost Bastille. Although they aren't connected, some level design has hints of similarity to the first game. If you enjoyed Dark Souls I, you most likely will enjoy any game in the Souls series, Dark Souls II may be the least enjoyable, but it still gives you many hours of enjoyment, and frusteration. Getting further into the game, it become clear that the directors, Tomohiro Shibuya and Yui Tanimura (not the one who directed ds1), seemed to drop off on the abundance of unique clutter for areas, and just used boxes and a few other smashables throughout the game past FoFG where everything seemed place to either distract or make you curious on what was under. Level design feels alot more linear than Dark Souls I, at some points there is only 1 path to take with a few side halls that end after a couple yards with either nothing or a chest/item of some sort, and that one main path you have to take, leads straight through all the bosses of the area and into the next. It feels like they didn't try as hard with designing the levels to have many different paths with lots of backtracking (which was by far the most annoying yet relieving feeling I felt in DS1) and went for the kind where it gets you to your destination faster, but at the cost of letting the player explore and experience relief when they cleared out a path of loot. The enemies, oh god. A few generic movesets and lots of old knights throughout the game. The feeling I had when encountering an enemy with a completely new attack or way of trying to dispatch me was greatly appreciated, because it kept me wondering if more was to come. I'm glad the scrapped the Humanity system that reduces max health on death, although if you have lots of Human Effigies early in the game, it may not be such a problem for you, but when you're trying to take out the dragon before the Cathedral of Blue, you may get a little frusterated having less heath than before to take out the beast.

The original Just Cause came back in 2006, a year when the transition from the last gen consoles to the current ones was in full scale, a thing that made new titles easy to slide away from the hands of the gamers and it pretty much did. Even with those problems Avalanche Studios didn't give up and so the ideas of a sequel came along; with a new storyline, current gen graphics and a larger map to explore. Just Cause was from the beginning a game of exploration, completion and basically a constant satisfaction of achieving new things, something that Just Cause 2 does in an amazing way. The new island of Panau is enormous, with over 350 settlements to explore; a larger vehicle collection, a deeper story and much more. The story follows the same Rico Rodriguez working for a secret organization known as the Agency, whose job is to eliminate unmerciful dictators from the face of the Earth and bring democracy, because for some unknown reason people enjoy killing dictators. The main story is divided into different missions, which will unlock as you cause more and more chaos around the island, but even so, it is short and easily forgettable. While the story may not leave you with a memory that will last for years to come, the universe created around this game surely will, as each area of the island has a particular look and there are plenty of activities to satisfy your needs; in the end Just Cause 2 is more about the experiences you create yourself jumping from a corner to the next one of the island rather than the ones the story will provide you with. It's easy to jump into the game at any time and the loading screens are decent, however the black market could use some refreshing ideas as browsing into three menus to call for transport isn't exactly the definition of accessible.
The gameplay is what shines in this game, simply because it is so much fun to travel around the island, collect things and most of all destroy things. There is a lot, and I really mean a lot to destroy in here, each village or military base has things that were built by the old regime and must be destroyed in order to free the people of Panau, everything from transformers to gas tanks, communication dishes and so on is destructible and even more, the game will reward you for doing so. All locations have a certain amount of collectibles and destructible items that you must deal with in order to get 100% completion, depending on the size of the village or governmental base. The island is huge, so the game provides you plenty of options to travel around, you can use your grappling hook in combination with the parachute for a fast travel over small distances, call for transport, or just use a vehicle, and trust me there is a lots to chose from; everything from cars to motorcycles, bikes, choppers, boats, and fast jets are present in game, all making the adrenaline pump, which is good since this is the main objective of the game. When you are not dealing with the environment, you are dealing with the government, and as big the vehicle collection is, the weapons don't disappoint either, everything from machine guns to grenades and missiles are here for you to use. The combat works well, however during missions checkpoints will be rare and dying during one may send you a few minutes back, which can be annoying since you will die a lot, at least until you get some cash to upgrade your gear.
When Just Cause came out it was clearly outdated graphically speaking, but with Just Cause 2 that ain't the case; the island of Panau looks amazing, having a huge variety of locations, from snowy secret army bases, to sunny beach villages, it is all in here. The background and location design is undoubtedly one of the best of 2010 and why not one of the best on the current gen consoles. On the other side character designs are done okay, but they lack personality and can be easily erased after completing the game, sometimes even while I was playing I forgot Rico's face and who that guy I'm currently working for is. For a game this size it's impressive how there are almost no visual glitches, however there is a lot of repetition in design which is understandable considering the size of the map, but I did get tired of seeing the same house from a village to another.
One thing that could use some work in this game is voice acting, I mean sure it makes Baby Panay sound like an idiotic dictator, but it does lack a lot of personality per character, and spending a lot of time travelling around will make you realize how repetitive the secondary characters are; cops usually have few quotes in their minds, but those governmental patrols take stupidity to a whole new level. With that said, the soundtrack does a better job to improve the sound quality in the game, keeping you enraged to slaughter your enemies with everything you can imagine; and combining the great explosion effects with that does make up a little for the horrible voice acting.
There is no doubt about the size of this game, and the main storyline is only an introduction to what the game has to offer; after that you have the whole map to explore and explode, which is awesome, completing side missions, races, destroying army bases and completing villages will take you up to 70 hours, all of them spent into an enormous shot of adrenaline and pure action. Completing all those will unlock most of the achievements, however there are a few more special that are fun to do and make you try new things in the game. There is a lot to do in this game by yourself, but now with the additional of a free multiplayer mode there is even more to explore, and while this may not be the most beautifully crafted experience since it was created by the fans and not by the actual developers, it does it's job: putting you and your friends together in the enormous world of Just Cause 2, giving you freedom to kill each other, drive cars, jets, boats, helicopters, crash into stuff and a lot more.
There are hours and hours of countless fun to enjoy in Just Cause 2, and if you enjoy exploding things and travelling around this is a must have; sure the story is weak, but that doesn't even matter when the game is so much fun to play, after completing it once you'll probably just stick with exploring and killing people around the island, too bad you must do that on your own with no friend to watch your back online or in co-op. With such a huge amount of content you can just ignore the story and stick to what this game does best, kicking♥♥♥♥♥in every corner and all over the contested Panau.

Dark Souls 2 is a good game. It is good, not great, not fantastic, just good. It is deeply flawed, and I do mean deeply.
The Souls series follows the same logic that Castlevania (for the NES) followed: High difficulty and a steep learning curve, but fairness in that difficulty. You know what you did wrong and get better each time. Once you know what you're doing, the game is a cakewalk. Each attack can be avoided and countered, and smart play, combined with patience, are rewarded.
Dark Souls 2 stumbles on this formula, particularly in the DLC. This is a shame, since there were many parts of the game that were highly enjoyable and challenging. Invariably, the comparison to Dark Souls 1 will be made:
Dark Souls 2 is mechanically superior but suffers from an inferior sense of design. The weapons are better, the port is better (The DS1 port has serious framerate issues), there's more magic, more build options, everything is better.
However, most of your enemies are dudes with weapons. While DS 1 had a lot of this, it really shows in DS2. After battling my way through the Lost Bastille, fighting dudes with weapons (and some dogs), I catalogued the bosses:
There is a miniboss (The Pursuer) who is a dude with a two-handed weapon.
The mid-boss is three dudes with two-handed weapons.
The final boss is a dude with a two-handed weapon.
Lazy. Just straight lazy. The bosses who are really enjoyable are fairly easy while the bosses who are dudes with weapons  are, while not particularly difficult, tedious. They have a lot of health and do a lot of damage, so you dance around while chipping their health off for 5-6 minutes at a time. Yawn.
In DS1, we all loved the clever level design. The levels were vertically stacked corkscrews with clever dropoffs and shortcuts. DS2 has barely any of that, with poor or no shortcut placement and tedious straight pathways. The DLC is easily the worst, with Crown of the Ivory King forcing the player to fight through 20+ of the same enemy to reach a bonfire. You cannot go around them (they will chase you quite a distance and have ranged attacks) and there are no shortcuts or dropoffs or anything at all. They take 2-3 full stamina bars to kill and deal a lot of damage. It's just boring.
Finally, DS2 is fascinated with group combat. You will fight large groups of enemies (mostly dudes with weapons) who cannot be pulled individually, they are chained together. Attack one and they all come. The entirety of the battle consists of dodging until they all attack at once and give you an opening to poke them. Screw up and you die. Yawn.
This is not to say DS2 is a bad game, it's just a good game. It's not great, and that's its biggest issue. If you're a hardcore fan and want to play all of them, play DS2 once and then forget it. If you're looking for a game to start in the series, try Dark Souls 1, Dark Souls 3, or Bloodborne (a PS4 exclusive) first. Leave this one for last if you do decide to play it, because it's a letdown.

Surprising indie gem. One of the tightest FPS experiences I've everplayed.
Premise of the game is simple--you're dumped into a kind of 'dream world', and you need to recover a series of tapes to 'wake up' (think The Matrix meets Videodrome meets Vanilla Sky. Or something.)
You're moving through a series of what are, apparently, interconnected apartment buildings, each with multiple floors that connect across. There are enemies scattered throughout, but only two types: flying kill drones, and turrets. Kill drones will fly straight for you and electrocute you at close range, turrets will shoot a spray of bullets at you from afar.
So far, so generic, and a lot less content than most FPS. So why play?
Well, what makes the game work so well are the detailed mechanics.
First off, if you're struck even once, or fall, that's it--you're dead. Going gun blazing into a room is pretty much game over.
Second, you control every mechanic of your gun with a separate keyboard key. Just arming and firing your weapon will take you a few playthroughs to learn, but when you do--it's amazing how rewarding your actions feel.
Third, running requires that you 'tap' the forward key, lending a neat kinetic element to the game.
Fourth, ammo is scarce, and you'll have to selectively choose which fights you want to engage in... and which to bypass or run for it.
Despite the sparse world and somewhat rudimentary graphics, sound design and aesthetics are brilliant, and I haven't been so kinetically into a game since the days of Atari 2600. Bravo!
It's hard to explain the culmination of all of the above elements; you'll simply have to try it out for yourself. It's unlike any oher FPS and revolutionary at what it does. I guess I would call Receiver the 'thinking man's shooter'.
It's terrific; buy it, then go yell at the devs to show it a little love and update it rather than spending all their time making rabbit-fighting games.

This game is pretty damn awesome. It's a basic, relatively simple game that doesn't look amazing, but what's actually there is great. Each level is procedurally generated so the map is never the same, you always have randomized ammo/equipment, and one bullet from a turret or shock from a flying drone will kill you. It makes piecing together the 2spooky story that's told across 11 tapes randomly placed on the map very difficult, but wonderfully tense.
And of course, there's the game's real star - three guns that operate the same way actual firearms do. There's no crosshair, no ammo counter, and your mags don't magically refill themselves - assuming you have more than one, anyway. Doing a brass check and topping off magazines with loose rounds are actually things you'll find yourself doing in this game, as are other gun-specific actions like releasing the slide, dropping empty brass from a revolver, and spinning a cylinder to a loaded chamber, all of which require multiple button presses to accomplish. Sometimes, you'll even find it necessary to holster your weapon to complete an action such as filling a magazine, or pull the weapon down from the "aimed" position into a low ready to sprint away from danger. It's not the prettiest or most action-packed game out there, but Receiver is the closest a game has ever come to recreating the sensation of using an actual firearm. Very, very much worth the $5 purchase price.

I really like the concept of this game. I bought the game after simply viewing the promo video.
The game is fun to play. The mechanics are easy to handle. The graphics are smooth and did not have any noticeable glitches. Similar to DayZ, I really love that Banished has taken the next step on developing a different kind of game in a genre filled with look-a-likes. However, the fun of a city builder, for me, is being able to watch a city flourish and reap the satisfaction of knowing I made great decisions to inspire a great city.
Banished feels incomplete, and is, for all I know, admittedly so; houses can be upgraded once to stone, but the other buildings you place in your city (to this point) are forever log cabins. After exhausting the limited number of unique buildings, the only thing left is to increase your population to add jobs to add more houses to increase your population, and so on and so forth. What's the end game?
After three or four enjoyable evenings of exploring the offerings of Banished, I've found that in it's current state I'm torn between whether I'd recommend it at it's current price point, though I will say yes* because it has so much room for expansive and positive growth.

Let me start by saying that I loved FFX when it came out. I still have the PS2 game from 2002, and the sequel FFX-2 (not my cup of tea). The game has a beautiful story, which is why I bought this version, so I could experience that story again fourteen years later on my PC. However, the quality of the product is what prompted a Steam refund after an hour.
I can't believe this is classed as HD. The picture quality is, for lack of a better term, jagged. It looks like an old PS1 game. Hair is angular, cloth is angular, pixelated rough edges abound. Some character faces seem airbrushed or changed for no reason.
You can't truly rebind the keys on keyboard, as A is required to do some odd boss fight move within the first hour. Using WASD isn't feasible because of this, and there are other keys that we're informed can't be changed. This isn't great.
If this is HD then I'm a carrot. It's so atrociously poor quality that I have dusted off my PS2 and am replaying the game on that.
However, a lot of people won't have that option. I understand that. But know what you're getting into. This game looks like it belongs on the PS1, it actually feels like a downgrade from the PS2 version. If you haven't played this before, £16 for both games is a bargain. If you can get around terrible controls, go for it and revel in the story. But for Square to proclaim this as HD and a 'remastered' version feels like an insult. They could have made this shine like a gem instead of the amateurish offering they give here.
Too long, didn't read? The game of Final Fantasy X is fantastic. Square's sloppy effort to port it to PC isn't. What I saw in my hour of playing was, in gaming terms, disheartening. Buy if you've never experienced it, but don't expect great graphics or controls.

Imagine four hundred square kilometers of open-world terrain, with scenic vistas all around and wonderful sunsets.
And now, add a healthy dose of madness, with explosions and car crashes all around, deafening you with every step you take through this island paradise laced with government corruption. But, more often than not, you won't be walking. Cars abound, and the convenient military base filled with helicopters, jets, or other destructive methods of transportation is never terribly far, and that's just counting the conventional means of transport.  You are equipped with a very strong and speedy grappling hook with a good 200ft of range and the ability to take you almost anywhere, when combined with your parachute. It can also tether objects (including people) to each other, for towing or lifting (or, much more commonly, for comedic purposes)
And that's just in singleplayer! With the addition of a multiplayer mod, the chaos is multiplied by however many (the record is somewhere around 1600, but the only limit is the strength of the server) other players are there with you. Of course, the NPCs don't exist in multiplayer, but that doesn't matter. There's plenty of chaos and laughs to be had without them.

Dark souls 2 is better than the first by the widest margin possible in gaming. And after years of supporting this game I have finally decided to speak up.
Does it run?
Dark souls 2 works, in my entire 230+ hours of playing, the game has NEVER crashed for me not once, on my ps4 I have well over double that play time, it didn’t crash there either, if you go to my 360 I have near 200 hours, it didn’t crash there either.
Dark souls 1 does not, I have over 100 hours on PC and the game crashed dozens of times occasionally forcing me to restart the entire game in order to recover, but that’s not just on PC that was on my 360 and my ps3 as well
Conclusion: from a "does it run" standpoint alone dark souls 2 is infinitely better
How does it play?
Dark souls 2 has omni-directional rolling allowing for what I find to be undeniably better and more fluid combat system
Dark souls 1 does not often causing you to roll backward off a cliff when you do not intend to and you never intend to.
Conclusion: Dark souls 2 is better from a mechanical standpoint.
Yea but what about the pvp?
Even most dark souls 1 verterans will tell you the pvp is better by a wide margin and I am no exception, sure you have some occasional laggy back stabs, but its better than being invaded by someone who you literally can’t beat no matter how many times you hit them, or if your unlucky like me and you parry an invader every single hit and get him to a sliver of health, and then he one shots you from full hp, almost as if he let you get him that far down, just to♥♥♥♥♥♥on your head.
Conclusion: Dark souls 2 all the way
But I heard the atmosphere isn’t as good as the first one...
I never understood this argument, it isn’t, the complaints I have heard about "area transitions" are obnoxious at best and flat out wrong at worst. "oh but I have to go up this elevator to this place with a castle and lava, that doesn’t make sense" of course it does! it’s at the top of the mountain! And dark souls 1 had a far worse atmosphere then demon souls, demon souls felt lonely and oppressive, dark souls 1 i just wanted to get the ♥♥♥♥ out of at every turn! Dark souls 2 however, it’s a harsh world, but saying its unforgiving wouldn’t be near accurate, it’s a world i would want to live, and die, and repeat in, over and over.
Conclusion: Dark souls 2!
What about the bosses?
Dark souls 2 has 32 bosses! Sure some would say only 5 or 6 are any good, but for dark souls 1 it has 26 and in my opinion only 3 are any good. Dark souls 1 also features what is without a doubt the worst and most RNG filled boss fight in the series, the bed of chaos! It’s a boring boss fight and the only thing interesting about it is its lore!
Conclusion: Dark souls 2 for sure!
What about that lore you just mentioned?
Now that is the one and only redeeming quality of dark souls 1, I wouldn’t quite say its better than dark souls 2, but its very good! And in the end the lore is the one reason I forced myself to finish the game.
Conclusion: Lore does not a good game make, and its not enough to redeem dark souls 1.
In conclusion, get this game, you know what no one tells you? on metacritic dark souls 2 on PC has a score 91, dark souls 1 is an 89! sure its only 2 points, but the game is simply better. And as for dark souls 3, until it gets some DLC dark souls 2 is better by a long shot.

Homefront: The Revolution is a game I've been interested in since it was originally announced. After playing the first game in the series in 2011, I was impressed by what I initially saw in the sequel. Although the game is a huge improvemant over the original game in terms of ideas, it's still not a good game. The main character's are sort of cookie cutter and not very well developed. The story is shallow, not well thought out, and in the end feels unimportant. The world design is boring and doesnt feel alive or real. The A.I. in this game is terrible. Strange scripting, like npc's hitting walls with melee weapons for no reason. The gameplay is "ok" but feels outdated, the gunplay could have been a lot better. I really believe if this game came out 10 years ago (minus the modern graphics obviously) people really would have liked it. Sadly this game doesn't meet todays standards.
The optimization leaves a lot to be desired and I experienced frame drops/hitching/stuttering throughout my 10 hour playthrough of the game. This was on a 980 Ti mind you. I understand performance used to be worse before the latest update, but in my opionion it's nowhere near where it should be. I have seen worse though. Your experience may vary.
This game does have things I really liked. The graphics in some environmonts were great. The game also features a great gun customization resembling the one featured in the 'Crysis' series. There was some great character design throughout the game. I was very impressed by the way faces looked in this game as well. Besides the terrible animations, the characters looked real. The game does have a lot going for it, just not enough...
Overall I really think this game should have had A LOT more work. I know people don't like to hear this, but this game really should have been pushed back farther for optimization and gameplay improvements. I really feel this series and game have/had a lot of potential. This series and gamers deserve better.

Watch out, it's an actual review instead of yet another joke review for this game!
The first Five Nights at Freddy's, while overhyped, is still a pretty solid game. Barely over two months later, this sequel was released. That right there should ring some alarm bells. It certainly is rushed and shows some signs of the creator jumping on to the hype train while the series is still popular, rather than taking his time with a worthy sequel.
Two of the strongest aspects of the original game's horror were how good the atmosphere was and the spooky sound design. The latter is mostly gone in the sequel, with the former pretty much missing. The first game did a good job of making the pizzeria look frightening, while still matching with the description of a place that is joyous in the day. It doesn't seem like a whole lot of time was put into recreating that feel for the sequel, as the pizzeria is simply bright and colourful this time around, with no spookiness to the appearance of the diner. The only exception is the parts and services room, but of course kids aren't supposed to be there, so no attempt to blur the line of friendly and frightening was needed.
The sound design isn't even close to matching the quality of the first game's, however some of it shows promise. With some more time testing what does and doesn't work (read: not rushing the game out in barely over two months) the sound design could have been absolutely fantastic. For example, the animatronics Balloon Boy and Mangle have their own unique sounds, which excellently use common horror techniques. Balloon Boy has creepy childish sounds and Mangle pretty much is a ghost box, constant white noise and distorted voices, showing the fear behind chaos. Unfortunately there isn't really a whole lot more special going on in the sound department. The atmospheric sounds are sadly far inferior. They do their job of indicating something dangerous is nearby and that's it. Especially lazy is the sound indicating an animatronic passing through the main hall. It took me a while to realise the sound was indicating an animatronic was so close, since, well... I'm having a hard time figuring out how "extremely repetitive alarm-type noise" ties into someone being in front of you? Somehow the loud footsteps from the first game conveyed that expression better. Additionally, you may know an animatronic is close to you by the sounds of someone moving through the vents. Even this isn't without its flaws however, as the sound has to keep looping if multiple animatronics are active at once, and thus the sound very noticably gets cut off and resets commonly on future nights.
Oh yes, the vents... there are many more animatronics in this game than the previous one and most of them travel through the vents. This means there can be more than one in the exact same spot at one time and the only way to really be aware of this oftentimes is to simply guess. Fake difficulty, which doesn't make a whole lot of sense. This was present to a small extent in the first game, although it made more sense as those areas weren't cramped vents.
The gameplay is much less satisfying than the first game's. This installment requires manic activity from the player. While later nights in the first game certainly required the player to be on their toes, there were still brief pauses while the player had to conserve power, and observation of multiple cameras was necessary to keep an eye on the more active Freddy.
This game seems to be confused in what it's trying to do, in its attempts to be different, it actually amplifies what it may have been trying to fix. There is no longer a limit to the building's power usage, so cameras can be viewed freely. At first I assumed this meant the player could spend more time checking all the cameras instead of constantly switching back to the office to conserve power, which is a neat idea. However, it's necessary for there to be a vital reason to view the cameras. But oh dear, is that vital reason a drag in this game. There's a music box in the prize corner video feed that needs to be wound up remotely, which for some reason is only possible while looking at that camera. This means the only camera that actually ever needs to be looked at is the prize corner. This becomes MORE repetitive than looking at the office. A mechanic where at least one animatronic needs to be followed camera-to-camera would not only fill the criteria of making camera viewing a necessity, but add some variety. This was achieved with Freddy in the first game, unfortunately not the case in the sequel.
Speaking of the nonsensical remote music box winding that somehow requires looking at a video feed, there is also a flashlight in this game. You're not just restricted to using it in the office, however. The flashlight can also be used in other rooms to light up dark corners. However, you're still only viewing these rooms on a camera. How can a flashlight light up something you're only viewing on a video feed? Huh? What?
As for difficulty, this game is even harder than the first, which was not a step in the right direction. The horror also fades much more quickly this time around due to having to go through the same things over and over. There isn't a whole lot of horror in the sequel, so cue falling back on jumpscares harder than ever. Some of the jumpscares are actually pretty good, aside from being overused but then there's laughable ones like Toy Freddy and Toy Bonnie just kinda jumping around being colourful, which is supposed to be scary because a loud noise is playing at the same time.
One thing I was really looking forward to, even as my opinion on this game got more negative, was unlocking the "custom night." With even more animatronics to choose from than last time, I thought that'd mean even more customisation. Nope. Foxy is locked to being active even on 0. The music box winds down extremely quickly, maybe even faster than it did on night 5, and there's no setting to change this. It might seem silly bringing up an unlockable mode in a serious review but the fact is that the mode got ♥♥♥♥ed up so badly that I feel it deserves a mention. There is the nice addition of presets in the custom mode to try, which reward the player with some cute bonuses, but I'd rather have a custom night that actually feels fully customisable.
I still sort of enjoy the game, to an extent, maybe as a guilty pleasure. It's however very disappointing, and I can't say I got much substantial enjoyment out of it. The next installment in the series is apparently very close to release, so that one's getting rushed out too. I'm kind of wary about buying it. Should that one be a rushed jumpscare fest as well, it may be safe to say that Five Nights at Freddy's was a pretty good horror game that got way out of hand and spawned nothing but bad sequels that don't use any scare tactic other than jumpscares.

I played this game for about 2hrs. when I first bought it. Now, before I bought the game, I spent at least 3hrs. watching "Let's Play" footage on YouTube, much like I do when I plan on buying a game. But while watching the "Let's Plays," I fell in love with this game. It is a great simulation game. Playing the tourtorial from the get go will help players get a true feeling for the game, which may seem simple at first, but it will soon turn south if you try to expand too quickly or do not worry about the three basic needs; food, supplies, and meds. The supplies are used to build the buildings which supplie the food and meds, along with shealter.
The graphics for this game were very surprising to me. Since this game was not created by a big time corporation (instead from what I've heard it was created by just one man), I was expecting pretty crapy graphics. Hold and behold, the graphics were almost top of the line, even for my crappy laptop. The soundtrack was also very good. I enjoyed listening to the music while I played.
The game does have a few issues with AI being stupid and a bit slow, but this game just came out; so that is natural. On the flip side of that, this game is much like SimCity or CivRome where you try to build up a settlement and keep your peeps happy and safe. I highly recommend this game to everyone, and for $19.99, that is not a bad deal for a game that I forsee becoming very popular for the gaming community.

Dark Souls 2 is a good game. It is good, not great, not fantastic, just good. It is deeply flawed, and I do mean deeply.
The Souls series follows the same logic that Castlevania (for the NES) followed: High difficulty and a steep learning curve, but fairness in that difficulty. You know what you did wrong and get better each time. Once you know what you're doing, the game is a cakewalk. Each attack can be avoided and countered, and smart play, combined with patience, are rewarded.
Dark Souls 2 stumbles on this formula, particularly in the DLC. This is a shame, since there were many parts of the game that were highly enjoyable and challenging. Invariably, the comparison to Dark Souls 1 will be made:
Dark Souls 2 is mechanically superior but suffers from an inferior sense of design. The weapons are better, the port is better (The DS1 port has serious framerate issues), there's more magic, more build options, everything is better.
However, most of your enemies are dudes with weapons. While DS 1 had a lot of this, it really shows in DS2. After battling my way through the Lost Bastille, fighting dudes with weapons (and some dogs), I catalogued the bosses:
There is a miniboss (The Pursuer) who is a dude with a two-handed weapon.
The mid-boss is three dudes with two-handed weapons.
The final boss is a dude with a two-handed weapon.
Lazy. Just straight lazy. The bosses who are really enjoyable are fairly easy while the bosses who are dudes with weapons  are, while not particularly difficult, tedious. They have a lot of health and do a lot of damage, so you dance around while chipping their health off for 5-6 minutes at a time. Yawn.
In DS1, we all loved the clever level design. The levels were vertically stacked corkscrews with clever dropoffs and shortcuts. DS2 has barely any of that, with poor or no shortcut placement and tedious straight pathways. The DLC is easily the worst, with Crown of the Ivory King forcing the player to fight through 20+ of the same enemy to reach a bonfire. You cannot go around them (they will chase you quite a distance and have ranged attacks) and there are no shortcuts or dropoffs or anything at all. They take 2-3 full stamina bars to kill and deal a lot of damage. It's just boring.
Finally, DS2 is fascinated with group combat. You will fight large groups of enemies (mostly dudes with weapons) who cannot be pulled individually, they are chained together. Attack one and they all come. The entirety of the battle consists of dodging until they all attack at once and give you an opening to poke them. Screw up and you die. Yawn.
This is not to say DS2 is a bad game, it's just a good game. It's not great, and that's its biggest issue. If you're a hardcore fan and want to play all of them, play DS2 once and then forget it. If you're looking for a game to start in the series, try Dark Souls 1, Dark Souls 3, or Bloodborne (a PS4 exclusive) first. Leave this one for last if you do decide to play it, because it's a letdown.
It just could have been so much better. What a shame.

The War of 1812 was a military conflict that lasted from June 18, 1812 to February 18, 1815, fought by the United States of America against Great Britain, its North American colonies, and its North American Indian allies. Historians in the United States and Canada see it as a war in its own right, but Europeans sometimes see it as a minor theatre of the Napoleonic Wars, as it was caused by issues related to that war (especially the Continental System). By the war's end in early 1815 the key issues had been resolved and peace came with no boundary changes.
The United States declared war for several reasons, including trade restrictions brought about by the British war with France, the impressment of as many as 10,000 American merchant sailors into the Royal Navy,[5] British support for Native American tribes fighting American settlers on the frontier, outrage over insults to national honor during the Chesapeake–Leopard Affair, and possible American interest in annexing British territory.[6] The primary British war goal was to defend their North American colonies, although they also hoped to set up a neutral Indian buffer state in the Midwest.
The war was fought in three theatres. First, at sea, warships and privateers of each side attacked the other's merchant ships, while the British blockaded the Atlantic coast of the United States and mounted large raids in the later stages of the war. Second, land and naval battles were fought on the U.S.–Canadian frontier. Third, large-scale battles were fought in the Southern United States and Gulf Coast. At the end of the war, both sides signed and ratified the Treaty of Ghent and, in accordance with the treaty, returned occupied land, prisoners of war and captured ships (though neither side returned the other's warships due to frequent re-commissioning upon capture) to its pre-war owner and resumed friendly trade relations without restriction.
With the majority of its land and naval forces tied down in Europe fighting the Napoleonic Wars, the British used a predominantly defensive strategy in the Provinces of Upper and Lower Canada. Early victories over poorly-led U.S. armies, such as in the Battle of Queenston Heights, demonstrated that the conquest of the Canadas would prove more difficult than anticipated. Despite this, the U.S. was able to inflict serious defeats on Britain's Native American allies, ending the prospect of an Indian confederacy and an independent Native American state in the Midwest under British sponsorship. U.S. forces were also able to make several gains and score victories on the Canadian frontier; taking control of Lake Erie in 1813, seizing western parts of Upper Canada. However, a large-scale U.S. attempt to capture Montreal was repulsed in November 1813. Despite the major U.S. victory at Chippawa on July 5, 1814, serious U.S. attempts to fully conquer Upper Canada were ultimately abandoned following the bloody Battle of Lundy's Lane on July 25, 1814. The U.S. then fell back roughly 30 km (19 mi) from Lundy's Lane to Fort Erie, where they withstood a siege for several months. The British eventually withdrew, but as winter set in, the Americans demolished the fort and fell back across the Niagara.
In April 1814, with the defeat of Napoleon, the British adopted a more aggressive strategy, sending larger invasion armies and tightening their naval blockade. However, with the end of the Napoleonic Wars in Europe, both governments were eager for a return to normality and peace negotiations began in Ghent in August 1814. In the Deep South, General Andrew Jackson destroyed the military strength of the Muscogee (Creek) Nation at the Battle of Horseshoe Bend. In September 1814, the British won the Battle of Hampden, allowing them to occupy eastern Maine, and the British victory at the Battle of Bladensburg in August 1814 allowed them to capture and burn Washington, D.C. They were repulsed, however, in an attempt to take Baltimore and Fort Bowyer, and during their assault at Fayal. An American victory in September 1814 at the Battle of Plattsburgh repulsed the British invasions of New York, which, along with pressure from merchants on the British government, prompted British diplomats to drop their demands at Ghent for an independent native buffer state and territorial claims that London previously sought. Given that it took six weeks for ships to cross the Atlantic, news of the peace treaty did not arrive before the British suffered a major defeat at New Orleans in January 1815.[7]
In the United States, late victories over invading British armies at the battles of Plattsburg, Baltimore (inspiring the United States national anthem, "The Star-Spangled Banner") and New Orleans produced a sense of euphoria over a "second war of independence" against Britain.[8][9] The war ended on a high note for Americans, winning the final engagements of the war and bringing an "Era of Good Feelings" in which partisan animosity nearly vanished in the face of strengthened American nationalism. The war was also a major turning point in the development of the U.S. military. The poor performance of several U.S. militia units, particularly during the 1812–13 invasions of Canada and the 1814 defence of Washington, convinced the U.S. government of the need to move away from its Revolutionary-era reliance on militia and focus on creating a more professional regular force. Spain was involved in fighting in Florida but was not an official belligerent; some Spanish forces fought alongside the British during the Occupation of Pensacola. The U.S. took permanent ownership of Spain's Mobile District.
In Upper and Lower Canada, British and local Canadian militia victories over invading U.S. armies became iconic and promoted the development of a distinct Canadian identity, which included strong loyalty to Britain. Today, particularly in Ontario, memory of the war retains its significance, because the defeat of the invasions ensured that the Canadas would remain part of the British Empire, rather than be annexed by the United States. In Canada, numerous ceremonies took place in 2012 to commemorate the war, offer historical lessons and celebrate 200 years of peace across the border.[10] The conflict has not been commemorated on nearly the same level in the modern-day United States, though it is still taught as an important part of early American history,[11] and Dolley Madison's and Andrew Jackson's respective roles in the war are especially emphasized.[12][13] The war is scarcely remembered in Britain, being heavily overshadowed by the much larger Napoleonic Wars occurring in Europe.
