I have read through many of the negative reviews. Most of them were simply just expecting a different game and were then disappointed with what the game was. I, too, would be disappointed if I were to play Skyrim expecting it to be Call of Duty. They are not the same games and thus many of the negative reviews have no basis.
Many other negative reviews address the price. While I agree that the full price is high for the length of the game, I personally would pay it. More importantly, though, is that this game drops below $5 during sales and is often on sale and, at that price, is well, well worth it. With that said, many games on Steam and many things in general are like jewelry: Never pay full price for it.
As for the actual game, I found it to be an excellent experience. The story is deep and develops well throughout the game at a good pace. If you take the time to play it, you will discover many tangents and paraboles to the story, as well. The story itself is very well written. The voice acting is good, as well. The music is fantastic, it does a great job of setting the atmosphere. The best part for me, however, was the environment. The era in which it is set is essentially when I was growing up and so it created this ridiculously deep sense of nostalgia throughout. That alone warrants a 10/10 for me. This game was stuck in my head for weeks after I finished it.
There is the possibility that the time setting also affects how people experience and rate this game. The ones who grew up around this time and can relate to the story and environment are more likely to enjoy it, whereas a younger audience may not appreciate the full experience because they cannot relate to the setting. It would also explain why many of the negative reviews feel like a bunch of children whining.
In conclusion: 10/10, a great, nostalgic experience. I would play it again just to look around.

It's funny that I'm recommending Receiver when I can't recommend Evoland.
Receiver is a rogue-like adventure-esque FPS game in a spy setting. Your goal is to collected 11 cassette tapes from around the randomly generated complex you find yourself in. One bullet or taser shock from your robot adversaries (two kinds) will kill you instantly. There are no save points either. Given that death is a little too easy to achieve and dying means you start again from the very beginning and there are 11 tapes to achieve to finish the game, how is this fun? Well, that lies in what makes it an FPS.
The game's main mechanic revolves around its manipulation of your gun in a realistic way. One button opens the chamber of a revolver, another loads it, another dumps the casings/bullets onto the floor, another button closes it. You also have other weapons, such as a glock, or a semi-automatic pistol. Which one you have differs by playthrough. You could also start with additional bullets, magazines, or a flashlight. Surprisingly, what sounds tedious actually adds a layer of atmosphere and depth to the game. Every bullet counts as well as how you reload and wield your weapon. Things can go wrong that you have to fix. Just by how you use your gun and the uncertainty of how things could go gives great immersion.
Aiming your weapon to properly neutralize your foes takes a good amount of trial and error (and the ♥♥♥♥ing flying taser bots MOVE CONSTANTLY), so you will die a lot. But eventually you'll get it. That said, I never found more than two tapes per run and even then I feel like I've seen what the game itself has to offer me. But, it's also $5 which is why I can recommend it, despite some frustrating experiences I had. Overall it's a unique experience that is worth trying once.

Remember when you were a little kid and you had army men, often engaging in crazy battles between transformers, Batman, and even dinosaurs? Those timeless days spent by yourself, picking up tiny pieces of plastic and following along with insane campaigns of your own demented design?
That's sort of what it's like playing Dino D-Day. You might be spraying tiny carnivores with your tommy gun one second, and the next, you'll be ragdolled against a wall, instantly slain by a flying goat. Or you might be courageously defending an ally with your trusty M1 Garand, clips flinging out of your weapon hither and thither, when suddenly you hear a mighty roar behind you, and you are mowed down by the twin chain guns of the Tyrannosaurus Rex. These things have happened to me and will assuredly happen to you.
The game is just great, goofy fun. You'll never feel TOO mad losing in this game, because there's always something dopey to laugh at. Even the loading screens, which are for my taste, a bit long, are still dominated by silly wartime documents detailing the Nazi war machine with their new reptillian additions. I am particularly fond of the newspaper article concerning a dino rendition of a grand Wagnerian opera that goes horribly wrong.
In terms of gameplay, the multiplayer is indeed frantic, and requires you to do some thinking. If you choose the wrong class for your situation/map, then that could spell doom for your team. Alternatively, a well-placed tank dino might be just what you need to hold the point long enough. And although not many people necessarily play games with that much thought, I am confident that the construction of the class system is actually well-balanced and caters to any play style.
Going back to that previous point, some may argue that certain classes are too powerful. To that I say, "phooey!" Each class has a counter-class, and the sooner you realize this, the better you'll play. As the most specific example, I've heard many people complain about the Allied character with the Garand. Yeah, he's pretty strong, especially in the hands of an expert marksman. But you put him in front of a tank dino and he's toast. Really. My point: if you're sucking, it's your own freakin' fault.
If you don't have the DLC (and I don't, although I'm going to pick it up soon), there are three basic match types: deathmatch, king of the hill, and demolition. The T-Rex spawns on a couple maps, and adds a whole new dynamic to the gameplay. The maps are also well-made and don't allow players to hide anywhere indefinitely, save for the flying raptor, who often needs that upper hand/deception to stalk and make great kills.
Anyway, if you're on the fence, I am all about this game. It's really excellent, and incredibly rewarding to people who play it either casually or otherwise. The only downside is that there is not a huge amount of people playing at the moment, which is really a shame, because this game rocks. I am looking forward to what other games the developers make.

This game was an unexpected gem.
I picked it up on sale and became immediately intrigued by the premise of someone coming home from an extended absence, only to find their entire family missing.
The terrific narration and the well-written and poignant monologues paint the picture that the only adequate graphics can't. There are a great many clues laying about the house that led me down one path, but then some new audio recording, written note or what-not would put what I'd seen in a different context and lead me in a new direction.
This is a difficult game to write much about because giving too much information about the state of affairs at the protagonist's home would spoil the story. The other aspect that makes this game difficult to describe in any way that appeals is that it is a walking simulator. There are some inventory management puzzles to open new areas, but most of the rewards and insights come from small clues and learning just a touch more about the sister that your character thought she knew so well.
As a side note, the game is set int he middle nineties, so there are all sorts of cultural touchstones and things such as VCRs and audio cassettes that make the set of Gone Home into a sort of creepy, virtual time capsule. I found the video game references particularly entertaining.
Not a lot happens in Gone Home and the running time is short; that said, I'd certainly recommend it if you can get it on sale.  Anyone who relishes stories that come apart like onion skins, revealing new information and casting previously discovered evidence in a new light, would likely enjoy Gone Home.

You will ACCIDENTALLY JACK A LIVE ROUND OUT OF THE CHAMBER FOREVER, and you'll only have yourself to judge for it, since all the enemies are unmanned weaponry.
In all seriousness, though, this is an interesting little game. You have no real character, as such, but you have a fully-realistically-featured handgun at your disposal.
Learning this weapon and keeping it fed is all the character development you really need, given the addition of maybe a dozen extra control-buttons devoted purely to manipulating the firearm.
The game is sort of a roguelike, meaning a randomized map, incredibly easy deaths, and you spawn in with one of three guns in varying condition with a small but randomized inventory.
Your first goal in each new life is to check your weapon and ensure it is loaded and ready to fire. Otherwise, you may be faced with a turret or stun-drone and find your gun is jacked. Or, even more simply, that you never took the safety off.
(Protip: with magazine-fed pistols, holster your weapon and press Z to load loose ammo into the mag, or R to pull it back out. Also totally use the help thing, it's great for getting used to the controls.)

I'm happy I bought this game on sale because I was completely disappointed when I finished it.  It took me about 3-4 hours (and a few walkthrough tips) and the ending just felt so anticlimatic.  I will explain as best as I can without including any spoilers.
Over the years I've played a lot of games with a storyline that requires you to explore, complete puzzles, etc. to solve the mystery and finish the game.  I'm including all the Nancy Drew mystery games I played when I was younger too.  Well...this game kinda sucked compared to those other ones.  At first though, it seems like it's going to be really cool.  The whole atmosphere of the game is this amazingly creepy mansion, in the middle of the night, with a wicked thunderstorm going on outside.  If you wear headphones while you play it really helps immerse you in the game, with all the weird noises and sounds that surround you as you investigate the house.  However, I think it's misleading because the actual storyline itself, wasn't scary or intense, and you realize this pretty early on as you begin to understand more.  It was an interesting storyline but it was predictable in the end. I felt like there was all this buildup and then...well, you know how you watch a movie and it really keeps your attention and you're enjoying it and then it ends and you think, "Really? That's it??".  Yeah, that's how I felt when I finished this game.  Who knows though, maybe I missed stuff in the story that would have amped up the creepy part (beyond the actually house itself).  Frankly though, I have no desire to play again and bother trying to find out.

A cheap, and somewhat simple game( atleast the objective is simple.) Receiver follows the formula of games such as Slender, were as you walk around a map hunting for objects, in this case cassette tapes. But thats were the similarities end. You are not a lonely wanderer being preyed upon by a menacing monster. You are armed and on the hunt. This game pays close attention to detail with the 3 handguns currently available(1911, Glock 18, and S&W Model 10.) The player controls every lever on the gun and must manually eject the magazine, load it, replace it, and then place a round in the chamber. Or in the case of the revolver, eject the cylinder, eject the spent rounds, replace them, and close the cylinder. At first this is complicated because there is a plethra of buttons to use but after a while it turns into the simple combination of E,~,Z,~,and then T/R and in a short time you won't even have to use the guide. This along with a one hit death makes for difficult experience. My main issue with the game is the lack of options. As stated before there are only 3 handguns in 3 different calibres, One map, and 2 enemies(a flying drone with a taser and a sentry turret.) Mainly this is because it was the product of the 7-Day FPS challenge and was created in only 7 days. But i hope that with the source code open that eventually this game will gain a little bit of popularity and with that, mods. All in all, the game retails at $5.00 so you're not risking much.

Dark souls 2 is better than the first by the widest margin possible in gaming. And after years of supporting this game I have finally decided to speak up.
Does it run?
Dark souls 2 works, in my entire 230+ hours of playing, the game has NEVER crashed for me not once, on my ps4 I have well over double that play time, it didn’t crash there either, if you go to my 360 I have near 200 hours, it didn’t crash there either.
Dark souls 1 does not, I have over 100 hours on PC and the game crashed dozens of times occasionally forcing me to restart the entire game in order to recover, but that’s not just on PC that was on my 360 and my ps3 as well
Conclusion: from a "does it run" standpoint alone dark souls 2 is infinitely better
How does it play?
Dark souls 2 has omni-directional rolling allowing for what I find to be undeniably better and more fluid combat system
Dark souls 1 does not often causing you to roll backward off a cliff when you do not intend to and you never intend to.
Conclusion: Dark souls 2 is better from a mechanical standpoint.
Yea but what about the pvp?
Even most dark souls 1 verterans will tell you the pvp is better by a wide margin and I am no exception, sure you have some occasional laggy back stabs, but its better than being invaded by someone who you literally can’t beat no matter how many times you hit them, or if your unlucky like me and you parry an invader every single hit and get him to a sliver of health, and then he one shots you from full hp, almost as if he let you get him that far down, just to♥♥♥♥♥♥on your head.
Conclusion: Dark souls 2 all the way
But I heard the atmosphere isn’t as good as the first one...
I never understood this argument, it isn’t, the complaints I have heard about "area transitions" are obnoxious at best and flat out wrong at worst. "oh but I have to go up this elevator to this place with a castle and lava, that doesn’t make sense" of course it does! it’s at the top of the mountain! And dark souls 1 had a far worse atmosphere then demon souls, demon souls felt lonely and oppressive, dark souls 1 i just wanted to get the ♥♥♥♥ out of at every turn! Dark souls 2 however, it’s a harsh world, but saying its unforgiving wouldn’t be near accurate, it’s a world i would want to live, and die, and repeat in, over and over.
Conclusion: Dark souls 2!
What about the bosses?
Dark souls 2 has 32 bosses! Sure some would say only 5 or 6 are any good, but for dark souls 1 it has 26 and in my opinion only 3 are any good. Dark souls 1 also features what is without a doubt the worst and most RNG filled boss fight in the series, the bed of chaos! It’s a boring boss fight and the only thing interesting about it is its lore!
Conclusion: Dark souls 2 for sure!
What about that lore you just mentioned?
Now that is the one and only redeeming quality of dark souls 1, I wouldn’t quite say its better than dark souls 2, but its very good! And in the end the lore is the one reason I forced myself to finish the game.
Conclusion: Lore does not a good game make, and its not enough to redeem dark souls 1.
In conclusion, get this game, you know what no one tells you? on metacritic dark souls 2 on PC has a score 91, dark souls 1 is an 89! sure its only 2 points, but the game is simply better. And as for dark souls 3, until it gets some DLC dark souls 2 is better by a long shot.

Most games assign you a single button to reload your gun. Most games provide you enough ammo to get the job done. Most games start you with the same equipment, in the same location on the map. Receiver is not most games.
You start with one of three weapons at a random location on the single, large map. The amount of ammo you have appears to be random, as does whether or not you have a flashlight or spare magazines. In a normal FPS, you'd start with a full clip and pressing "fire" would do just that. With Receiver, that would make you extremely lucky. The first thing to do is examine your weapon. Is it a revolver, a semi-automatic, or a machine pistol? Is it loaded? How full is the magazine? Is the safety on? Is it set to full auto? All of this matters.
While this can sound tedious, the surprising thing about Receiver is that it works. The graphics are terrible, the sound and story are nothing to write home about, but the gameplay more than makes up for everything else. As frustrating as the first few rounds can be, it's extremely rewarding when you finally start to pick things up. You'll quickly learn to count your shots because you don't have an ammo counter. You'll quickly learn to take cover and look around corners because the enemies are lethal. Pretty soon checking your gun, loading your magazines when you get ammo and checking every corner for turrets will be second nature.

Going to Dark Souls 2 after Dark Souls 1,
Its not good. Nothing feels right. I beat it, however I did not feel rewarded. Instead I felt like I wasted my time and money on a game that feels like a spin-off rather than a sequel. I can't say for much about the weapons, cause I could not remember them from the base game that's not SotFS, and the fact that I only had a Batman-based build during the whole game (Caestus on both arms and an endless arsenal of throwable items). But, because I did this, shouldn't I go replay the game using actual weapons?
The answer is no.
I felt no need to, sure there's the interesting aspect of power stances on many different items, but the whole time the combat in the game lacked impact. I mean, sure I beat bosses with my fists and a ton of knives, but getting to these places was a pain, and even moreso in SotFS, as enemy placements were annoying and for the record only made things worse. Its like playing one of those gimmick rage games like I Wanna Be The Guy or Bloody Trapland.
also on a personal note I really don't like how I still take damage during the animation of a backstab or a riposte. It makes sense, but it really makes me not want to attempt to try to riposte or backstab anything because of that.
Another problem why I haven't felt the need to play through it again is because it fails to bring up any interest for me to explore the areas. Don't get me wrong, at times the game can be beautiful and that's when I want to explore. But most of the areas look like a rehashed version of Blighttown. I'm not dealing with that, I barely explored Blighttown in the first game as well. Still not gonna deal with that.
For the final nail in the coffin for this game, its the way you summon people, soul memory.
You want to play with friends? Make sure you have the near same amount of souls as them, and if they went ahead and killed a couple of bosses, and want to help you with a very difficult boss? Nah. They're too good for that. Instead hope to god that some kind soul out there decided to help pair up with a random that has the near same amount of souls you have,
By the way, soul memory is how many souls you get during the ENTIRETY of your playthrough, not how many souls you have on hand.
Do I like this game? Not at all.
Will newcomers to the Souls series like this game? Probably.

Absolutely brilliant
It looks so simple all of it, the style the controls.
It plays so simple, it has a tutorial thats a great help, and you should look it over, but when you see the interface you'll be playing right away its very easy to learn.
But! the guy that made this has his coding down because it's not as easy as it looks.
yes I do really mean one guy, the developer did everything artwork sound, coding. And he came up with 200 MB of awesomeness, that you may not see until it's kicking your backside and your poor villagers start dying because you thought it was just another sim game.
You'll find out real quick that you're not just building a town to live in but a town you need to survive in. Possible starvation, and cold winter's, even accidents can happen like a tree falling on your logger, or a rock crushing someone in the quarry.
There are even natural disasters such as a tornado or fire can happen in your village and you will wish you had built that water well. You can't just build your way out of problems, by throwing down a half dozen of the same building. This game will make you think about how you want to expand, and you always have to take into account available Manpower Food Supply and resource management.
You will get to know your villagers, they have names, live work and have children, you send to school, and when they die they go to the graveyard.
Things people may not like about the game there's always a few.
It's not a fast paced game, you can speed up the game world, but the game play is very mellow and it will take hours of playing before your map reaches capacity.
Also the game does not have hundreds of different building to choose from it's not going to end up looking like New York. I personally don't care it's quite difficult to get to use all the buildings it does have.
I can't think of anything else, it's a brilliant game the developer did an outstanding job of creating what looks to be a simple city builder on the outside, but it's coding will keep you coming back for a long long time.

If Dark Souls 1 was a 10/10 (which in my books it is)...
Dark Souls 2 is a 7/10. There are so many changes that are good for the game such as more fluid combat, it looks WAY prettier then its predecessor and feels much smoother in general. The game has almost 40 bosses and far more content then Dark Souls 1. Sounds amazing, right?
This game would've been a solid 9/10 or maybe even eclipsed its predessor if not for TWO things.
#1: Losing max HP upon death, only to be restored via Human Effegies.
#2: The addition of lifegems/less estus flasks in general.
Both of these issues can be solved by grinding out extra souls to buy said items. However this is the problem in iteslf. One of the things in Dark Souls that kept me going was the continous sense of progression. With the addition of these soul dumps (the expendable items) I personally felt as if I was wasting my time/resources by purchasing them. Every death became more frustrating because I wasted the lifegems I used that life to try and clear the area/kill the boss. it also became more frustrating because I would then have to seek out human effegies.
Dark Souls is known for its difficulty, and these games are advertised for them. Difficulty in Dark Souls 1 is perfect (level design, enemy placement, pacing, etc). One could make the argument that these added mechanics in Dark Souls 2 make the game harder. However they don't in a way. This is because these mechanics can be completely forgone by grinding to get more of the items you need to negate the mechanic's downsides.
If health and death was managed exactly how it was in Dark Souls 1, I truly feel this game would be on par with its predecessor. It wouldn't have recaptured the magic of Dark Souls 1, but it would've at least felt more fun. I'm curious if someone made a mod to change the game by the two aspects I listed.
Overall... 7/10.

Always heard so many people talking badly about this game like it was horrible or something. Mostly I think it's mostly just those typical 'hardcore' Souls fans that are usually toxic about everything. Reading through the reviews it seems the biggest compliant is that this game is not as good as the first one. While that is true, it doesn't make it a bad game in any respect, it just wasn't as good as it's predecessor. Though it really is not as hard as the original and doesn't offer that completely open experience as the first one, it is still one of the best games on the market and follows the base Souls formula.
Some reviews talk about how the controls are crap. Crap compared to what? Dark Souls 1? A huge amount of my deaths on the first one was just due to my character not responding in the way I wanted him to. This installment I think was actually a lot better controlled than the first one and it made dual-wielding actually viable. Some things I actually didn't like was the lock-on system; I found myself switching targets a lot by accident and missing my attacks. This was because as I'm moving around enemies naturally I lean the camera a little and instead of leaning the camera it switches targets. I may have had the same problem on the first one but I just don't remember it being as big of a problem.
Game mechanics just seemed a lot smoother than the original as well. One of my biggest memories in the first one was spending over an hour trying to regain my souls. I would keep getting back to them but where my bloodstain was was at a place where I would slip as soon as I picked my souls back up. So just over and over I came back trying to get them and kept dying due to no fault of my own but the game design. Eventually I died right before picking them up and just threw my hands in the air and said I'm done. It was a really frustrating memory that had nothing to do with difficulty and more to do with design. I never had that problem in this version.
Bosses are easier, a lot easier. On the first game I died to almost every boss at least once. And you had to just to learn how to fight the boss! In this version I rarely ever died to any boss. And if a certain boss was hard there was usually 1-2 NPC shades you can summon to help and even summon up to three different shades. I enjoyed it a bit more on the first one where it was just you and one other guy struggling to defeat the boss together and you had to rely on each other a lot more.
I didn't like the hollowing system on this version as opposed to the first one. I get they were trying to make dying more punishing and all that but losing more and more health each time kinda sucked. Not that I had much room to complain, I just stayed human almost all game long and the playerbase isn't really large enough now for that to be hazardous. It was rare an enemy ever really killed me so, unlike the first one where I stayed hollow unless I needed to summon, I just stayed human to keep full health.
One of my biggest complaints though is the sucky soul memory system. It seemed like they tried to fix the problem where people didn't level and just leveled their gear to destroy in pvp. But the problem with this system is it punishes you even more for dying which is essential for learning in the Souls series. If you don't grab your souls again after death you're just getting left further and further behind in the dust by your soul memory peers that aren't dying as much. So if you suck as new players are bound to suck then you're just gonna hate dying even more and more.
Overall I still really enjoyed it despite all the trash talk it seems to get. I didn't really have any real complaints and it was still the same Souls vibe I was looking for in the last game. As I stated earlier, it's not the best game in the Souls series but it's still one of the best games on the market. 5/5

I am not usually a huge fan of "Worker Placement" games. This goes for both Board games (L'Harvre, Agricola, Stone age, etc.) and Video games (Towns being one of the biggest turn offs for me). So it was with a bit of hesitation that I opened the Store page to Banished, a higher resolution game of building a settlement from nearly scratch and making it survive. I purchased it yesterday, and for those people who want a short, quick review: TL;DR GET THIS GAME.
My play time right now is very limited. I have only clocked a few hours of this game, but I PLAN ON CLOCKING MORE. Please take this into consideration while reading this.
Starting from when I viewed the original trailer upon its release, I had hope that I may finally turn around my stroke of bad luck conscerning games like these. The game looks beautiful, runs smoothly even on somewhat dated systems, and the feel of it as you watch it run for the first time is very good. It may sound weird reading that last sentence, but it is really the only way I can explain it after seeing many games have a small lag time from when you see the title screen and when you can actually select anything from it.
The game comes with a tutorial that has a decent amount of depth to it, explaining and teaching you the basics of how to start up a small community of workers and labourers, and then does exactly what SHOULD happen after this stage: Leaves you alone. This game is set to be a strategic development game, so I would have been slightly put off if the tutorial held your hand the whole time while explaining when, why, and how you use each and every building. After learning the basic controls and solutions to problems players would experience in the first 15 minutes of game time, I found it pleasantly surprising how much of overall setting creation players get. Different seeds can be loaded, Resource availability, starting conditions, weather, even Disasters that may or may not be toggled (Cant wait till I get hit by my first tornado! :D) are all at the players fingertips right before s/he dives in to playing god.
During actual gameplay, the thing I like most is the freedom to do what you want, whether or not you will actually SURVIVE. My first town considsted of houses, a foresting agency, a fishing dock, and a mine. And by the 2nd or third year i had run out of food, had too many workers working the mine and dying of starvation, and realistically got my butt whooped by the in game Mother Nature after a half hour of game time. Starting again, I made a new town with more food production and less of other resources. Another failure, most of my food supplies died off during winter. Oh Well!
Time and Time again I have lost to this game, be it by starvation, population lock, disease, cold... And every time I lose I find myself renewed and refreshed, ready to start again and push my town further. The difficulty of the game is high, and a player will definetly need a good sense of planning and forethought to expand greatly, yet I think anyone who enjoyed games like Prison Architect, Roller Coaster Tycoon, Towns (Yikes!), and even the old Sim City games would easily fall in love with this piece.
So to end my Wall of Text review, I leave you with a Pro/Con list:
PRO
- Looks great
- Easy to navigate HUD and menus
- Freedom
- Plenty of replayability
- Lots of fun.
CON
- Difficulty is fairly high.
- (From what Ive read) Some events such as diseaased crops only give visual cues, like changed colors. Considering my play style, these might be hard to notice.

Gameplay: The gameplay wasn't the worse but it did lack storyline other than "fight the government". Basically you're the resistance fighting against the government thru most of the game. Bugs: The AI was ocassionally glitchy. I was able to hide in a dumpster while KPA agents were shooting me. The AI that follow you would also block you in a corner and wouldn't move no matter what you do.... unless you reload from last checkpoint was really annoying. Certain areas of the map you could glitch it where you can sometimes get up to the next floor without going around or basically fall thru the map. Banished is challenging, addicting, strategy/management game and it is a must for anyone who is a fan of games such as SimCity, Dwarf Fortress and Tycoon series.
Contradicting the theory present in most of AAA games of nowadays, that "modern games" should be casual, simple and easy to pick up to appeal to a large audience. Banished is a challenging, highly complex, successful game, top seller on steam for a few days, selling at full price. Showing us that core games still appeal to a large audience.
The game is complex and can look scary at first. But after you go through the basics tutorials, you are pretty much ready to get going. The interface is very intuitive and easy to pick up, there are keyboard shortcuts for almost every action, which is great. The game mechanics are deep, it takes a bit to get your head around it, it resembles in some aspects Dwarf Fortress. The game is challenging and addicting, each failure will make you learn more, and make you want to try again with new village compositions. The achievements are rock hard (as they should be).
The game provides dozens of hours of entertainment, it is definitely a must for strategy/management games fans and if you are not in the genre, it is a very good game to get started.

Always heard so many people talking badly about this game like it was horrible or something. Mostly I think it's mostly just those typical 'hardcore' Souls fans that are usually toxic about everything. Reading through the reviews it seems the biggest compliant is that this game is not as good as the first one. While that is true, it doesn't make it a bad game in any respect, it just wasn't as good as it's predecessor. Though it really is not as hard as the original and doesn't offer that completely open experience as the first one, it is still one of the best games on the market and follows the base Souls formula.
Some reviews talk about how the controls are crap. Crap compared to what? Dark Souls 1? A huge amount of my deaths on the first one was just due to my character not responding in the way I wanted him to. This installment I think was actually a lot better controlled than the first one and it made dual-wielding actually viable. Some things I actually didn't like was the lock-on system; I found myself switching targets a lot by accident and missing my attacks. This was because as I'm moving around enemies naturally I lean the camera a little and instead of leaning the camera it switches targets. I may have had the same problem on the first one but I just don't remember it being as big of a problem.
Game mechanics just seemed a lot smoother than the original as well. One of my biggest memories in the first one was spending over an hour trying to regain my souls. I would keep getting back to them but where my bloodstain was was at a place where I would slip as soon as I picked my souls back up. So just over and over I came back trying to get them and kept dying due to no fault of my own but the game design. Eventually I died right before picking them up and just threw my hands in the air and said I'm done. It was a really frustrating memory that had nothing to do with difficulty and more to do with design. I never had that problem in this version.
Bosses are easier, a lot easier. On the first game I died to almost every boss at least once. And you had to just to learn how to fight the boss! In this version I rarely ever died to any boss. And if a certain boss was hard there was usually 1-2 NPC shades you can summon to help and even summon up to three different shades. I enjoyed it a bit more on the first one where it was just you and one other guy struggling to defeat the boss together and you had to rely on each other a lot more.
I didn't like the hollowing system on this version as opposed to the first one. I get they were trying to make dying more punishing and all that but losing more and more health each time kinda sucked. Not that I had much room to complain, I just stayed human almost all game long and the playerbase isn't really large enough now for that to be hazardous. It was rare an enemy ever really killed me so, unlike the first one where I stayed hollow unless I needed to summon, I just stayed human to keep full health.
One of my biggest complaints though is the sucky soul memory system. It seemed like they tried to fix the problem where people didn't level and just leveled their gear to destroy in pvp. But the problem with this system is it punishes you even more for dying which is essential for learning in the Souls series. If you don't grab your souls again after death you're just getting left further and further behind in the dust by your soul memory peers that aren't dying as much. So if you suck as new players are bound to suck then you're just gonna hate dying even more and more.
Overall I still really enjoyed it despite all the trash talk it seems to get. I didn't really have any real complaints and it was still the same Souls vibe I was looking for in the last game. As I stated earlier, it's not the best game in the Souls series but it's still one of the best games on the market. 5/5

Not without it flaws, but very fun game nonetheless. It's basically a Far Cry in urban setting and that worked spectacularly for me. Fights are fun, gunplay is solid, bots are fairly stupid to abuse but still competent enough to fight.
World is divided in several regions that you will "liberate" by hacking/blowing different objects of interest inside it, these regions can "red" or "yellow" zones, which I've found very interesting.
Red Zones are pretty large open areas with a lot of ruins and rubble, where enemies shoot on sight and your gameplay is mainly kill everybody and capture everything. Also ride on bike on every stairwell.
Yellow Zones are more like City 17 in Half-Life 2. Building are mostly intact, there are lots of alleys, civilians and patrols. Fighting there is a little tricky, thanks to constant enemy reinforcements - you should run away and fight smart.
Both zone types feel a little different while keeping focus and gameplay loop intact. That results in pretty varied but consistent experience, which is pretty hard for a sandbox. Maybe there will be a green zone, I haven't reached it yet.
Being pretty much happy with the game it the current state, I must mention that it is very clunky. It does suffer from the lack of polish you expect from AAA open-world games, but mainly because in a game of this scale there is a LOT you need to polish. Some voice actors are really dull, radio chatter is extensive, human models are pretty bad and it is a little buggy. From minor physics glitches to disappearing enemies on long distances.
And oh my god the intro sequence was horrendous. Cutscene, cutscene, walk, instant failure if you walk wrong, cutscene, walk, cutscene, loading, walking cutscene. You'll see all the flaws in this intro: bugs, clunkiness, bad acting, bad character models and it's pretty lengthy too.
I do hope that intro won't scare you, because after that you'll be dropped inside a Red Zone and it's a great fun. With ruins you can run and bike inside, stronghold to capture, koreans to ambush and random flashpoints the game generates for you - it's really fun. Clunky, but fun... Funky?..
Also, there is a coop Resistance mode. It's... weaker, but still fun. Missions are heavily scripted and linear, while progression and loot systems are not very interesting. So I can't say there is a lot of replayability after you beat all missions on Hard. Which by the way IS hard, so you know, it's fine as a side activity.
In the end I can see why people was unhappy on the release of this game, but right now, without anything gamebreaking, with fixed performance and lowered price - this game is very, very solid.

Receiver is an experiment with realistic gun handling in a game setting that hasn't really been done before (to my knowledge). It gives you full control over weapon operations - you can release the magazine, insert/remove bullets, release the slide lock, toggle the safety, and even use full auto - and it lets you see real gun mechanics at work. It may seem mundane to some but you'll soon find that reloading and operating a virtual firearm becomes mechanical as you play through and is quite satisfying - and it's a lot more interesting than simply pressing R to reload.
The game itself is surprisingly tense and suspenseful. Because your opposition (turrets and flying stun-drones) can kill you in one hit, you are forced to be practical and careful in your movements and actions. And, as you DO have a task in the game - of collecting 11 cassette tapes that are lying around in various places in the randomly generated world - it's a lot more challenging than you might think!
All in all - it's an interesting experiment in realism and definitely worth checking out.

A much more accurate portrayal of The Great War than Battlefield 1 will ever be. Everybody starts with either a bolt-action rifle or a pistol (and most classes continue using it even in their higher unlocks), and there's trenches everywhere. You'll be blown up by artillery, you'll die cut by barbed wire, you'll be executed for deserting, you'll die from inhaling toxic gas, you'll be mowed down by machinegun fire and blown up by a stray grenade.
The game consists of 32 player maps, 4 squads of 4 players on each side of the conflict, so it's recommended that you get 3 friends and create a pre-made squad for this: cooperation and communication is key in this game, you can not, I repeat, CAN NOT be a one man army: you'll usually die in one hit.
Bullet balistics are an existing game mechanic: for targets that are far away you need to adjust your aim to compensate for gravity and the speed+direction of your target.
Although more accurate, this is not as unforgiving as other FPS games such as Red Orchestra 2: you can see how much ammo you have left, you have a working radar where you can see all your allies, and friendly fire doesn't exist, so if you're not sure who you're aiming at... shoot anyway.
Be sure to check out some starting guides for this game, and good luck!

The graphics are better, the framerate isn't capped to 30 and there are just some combat improvements that are nice.
Sadly, though, the game is much worse than the first Dark Souls game, or just about any other game because of the artificial difficulty: The game isn't hard. It's annoying.
Most bosses are really easy and keep doing the same, easy-to-dodge moveset and only some bosses has different phases. Some bosses are made 'difficult' by adding a stupid gimmick to it, like this one boss (I forgot her name, that's how unmemorable and boring she was) that is only somewhat difficult because the floor is poisonous water. The only point of damage I took was from that water and I was forced to heal during the fight because I was poisoned. She herself took less than 10 hits to kill (with a strength/dex mix build).
Some locations are just not fun to traverse, like the Black Gulch. You are continuously poisoned by these ♥♥♥♥♥♥ statues. They can be destroyed, but on the way to the boss there are legit 100+. I know that not every single statue shoots poison, but plenty do for it to still be annoying as ♥♥♥♥. Ther are also just difficult to dodge. This honestly isn't even difficult to go through, but just annoying.
Throughout the game you'll notice that enemies are not greatly placed and often to make the game seem difficult, you'll be gangbanged by 5+ dudes. That also happened in DS, but less frequently and less enemies at a time.
TL;DR: The devs were very lazy and in stead of making a difficult game they made it seem difficult with ♥♥♥♥♥♥ gimmicks and gangbangin you.

This game did a lot of things write but I feel like it took many steps back when compared to the original. Let me just give some quick examples.
Pro: I love being able to quick travel so early in the game.
Con: Must spend sould at only a single location.
Con: World becomes way more disconnected and frankly doesn't make sense sometimes. For example, you climb a tall tower in a grassland and eventually fight the boss. From that room, you take a starcase that leads you into the iron keep which is surrounded by lava as far as the eye can see... Why was I not able to see that earlier? Surely, I could not have missed it.
*The world of Dark Souls 1 may have not given the player quick travel so soon, but it made for a much more interconnected world*
DS1: Many enemy's would react fairly when compared to how your character reacts. Example, I hit an enemy while he has his shield fully up? I get staggered. The enemy hits me while I have my shield up, he gets staggered. Example, I swing a huge mace over and over, I get extremely low on stamina and have to let it regenerate. If an enemy does the same, the same thing occurs.
These types of 1 to 1 mechanics are alot less common in dark souls 2 which can be frustrating at times.
Additionally, I feel like dark souls 2 was created with the sole purpose of being "difficult". Dark souls 1 became a classic due to its difficulty but it seemed to be always fair. Always learning what certain enemys do. Always adjusting the way you play. In dark souls 2, too often I found myself faced at a boss/ room, that was simply a large mob of enemys running towards me instead of it being designed it a much more sophisticated manner. It seemed like lazy design when compared to the first.
Overall, I have to say that I think I enjoyed Dark Souls 1 more, however, at the end of the day, Dark souls 2 was still a great game.

A monotonous romp through a series of amateur Tomb Raider climbing quests, repetitive tasks and shoot-outs with poorly programmed AI enemies using your own tedious weapons (on an annoying weapon wheel) come to characterize the disappointing sequel to the surprisingly fun original, Homefront.
A widely expected but eventually omitted player-versus-player multiplayer mode hammered the last nail in the coffin on a title that saw its potential squandered by developers who chose to ignore the wishes of the two million strong userbase of the original.

Receiver, a game made in under seventy-two hours by Overgrowth developers, Wolfire Games, is a procedurally generated first person shooter with hyper detailed gun mechanics; even actions as seemingly simple as reloading require a great deal of familiarity with how the weapon works. Your opposition consists of stationary turrets and flying taser-bots, all of which can and will kill you very quickly.
Being made under such time contraints, the game can appear a little undercooked, but once the admittedly steep learning curve is overcome, the result is an intense, immersive, challenging experience that is difficult to walk away from. I highly recommend this game if you're looking for a nice change of pace from your typical FPS fare.

Warning: This is an addicting game. The gameplay is not unlike the '-Shock' series, where you're looking for audio tapes whilst trying to avoid and/or get-the-drop-on drones and turrets. The real difference in Reciever is in the shooting/gun mechanics.
The gun you have in 'shooter' games is usually little more than a fancy finger that goes 'pew pew' wherever you're pointing it. In Reciever, your weapon is a very realistic *system* with which you must learn to interact, both successfully and quickly, in order to survive combat scenarios. This means knowing how many bullets you have in your clip, replacing a clip when you need to, not dropping bullets by accident as you're trying to refill a clip on the fly. All of this is in your direct control. No random dice-rolls... if you get caught with your pants down, it's on you.
It's that direct relation of personal skill and performance that really draws you in. You will die quickly, and often. But each time you load up the game, or 'respawn', the environment is shuffled randomly. Even the equipment you start with is randomized. No two games are the same. And with almost zero load time. Just get killed by a drone that you didn't know was there until it was too late? It's okay, you immediately find yourself in a totally different place with a new weapon(1 of 3 , that I've seen) to familiarize yourself with and the lessons you learned from your previous life still fresh in your memory... now go see how long you live this time!
This is a great game and I honestly think every person who's ever played a FPS before should play it. If for no other reason than to gain a little more respect for the weaponry that so many of us have grown to take for granted.

The fact that a game made in seven days is more unique, interesting, and entertaining than  modern AAA FPS is really telling about the genre and the gaming industry as a whole... Completely risk-averse, just like Hollywood.
Receiver is quite an experimental game, and the trailer pretty much shows the entire scope of it, so I'll spare talking too much about gameplay. The handling and bullet physics of the guns are the game's main selling points, and they perform quite well. You need to load every magazine yourself, eject spent casings, bullets will ricochet if fired at bad angles, etc. etc.
The two enemies shown in the trailer are the only two enemies in the game, the flying drones which rush you really fast and try and stun you and the turrets. Both kill you in one hit. Not much of a variety at all, but it doesn't really need one. The drones clearly test your reflexes and the turrets your marksmanship. It could use one more to test handling in some way but that seems impossible to implement unless it somehow magically jammed your gun.
All in all it works together quite nicely. The levels and your starting equipment are randomly generated and there's always some unique challenge to overcome. That said the level generation could use a few tweaks... as it tends to make impossibly hard levels with 0 ammo and about 8 turrets down a single one way path. The way you see the developers shooting multiple rounds at things in the trailer? Not a good idea. You generally want to take everything out in one shot if you can because ammo is very, very scarce, though you may get lucky! Aside from the obvious crappy graphics (the game seems to have problems with V-sync, by the way) that is my only negative.
7/10 seems about right.

An urban warfare variation of the Far Cry formula with a better level design, but overall more clunky.
Pros:
- Good level design, especially some environmental puzzles in some of the strike points (think towers in Far Cry). They get better as you progress in the game. My favourite one: Hospital where you have to find medical supplies before unlocking the point.
- The city is a much better environment for the Far Cry formula than a jungle or mountains, in my opinion. In Far Cry I found the travelling between bases and towers boring, here it's fun and you have to be wary of your surroundings all the time.
- Vaulting over obstacles and mantling on higher platforms is used naturally everywhere
- The writing in the later parts of the game
- Voice acting
- Diverse environments. From rich villas to gassed and desolate industrial zones
Cons:
- The shooting is not very satisfying and some weapons behave strangely. A fully upgraded silenced SMG has more recoil than a LMG, for example
- Rudimentary stealth with few options. Stealth is required as in some maps if you raise an alarm, the game spawns soldiers infinitely, unless you hide. But the tools you have at your disposal are lacking.
- The movement system (vaulting, mantling) is quite slow, the PC feels like an elephant. Fast movement feels more fluid, see Dishonored or Titanfall
- Writing in the earlier parts of the game is cliched and quite bad. I feel it gets better in later parts, where the situation is more desperate.
- Some bugs (wrongly placed objects, levitating NPCs, even a show-stopping bug in the main quest, that was luckily solved by reloading)
Overall I recommend the game if the idea of a Far Cry formula in a city appeals to you. Just be ready for some clunkiness and a few bugs.

This game did a lot of things write but I feel like it took many steps back when compared to the original. Let me just give some quick examples.
Pro: I love being able to quick travel so early in the game.
Con: Must spend sould at only a single location.
Con: World becomes way more disconnected and frankly doesn't make sense sometimes. For example, you climb a tall tower in a grassland and eventually fight the boss. From that room, you take a starcase that leads you into the iron keep which is surrounded by lava as far as the eye can see... Why was I not able to see that earlier? Surely, I could not have missed it.
*The world of Dark Souls 1 may have not given the player quick travel so soon, but it made for a much more interconnected world*
DS1: Many enemy's would react fairly when compared to how your character reacts. Example, I hit an enemy while he has his shield fully up? I get staggered. The enemy hits me while I have my shield up, he gets staggered. Example, I swing a huge mace over and over, I get extremely low on stamina and have to let it regenerate. If an enemy does the same, the same thing occurs.
These types of 1 to 1 mechanics are alot less common in dark souls 2 which can be frustrating at times.
Additionally, I feel like dark souls 2 was created with the sole purpose of being "difficult". Dark souls 1 became a classic due to its difficulty but it seemed to be always fair. Always learning what certain enemys do. Always adjusting the way you play. In dark souls 2, too often I found myself faced at a boss/ room, that was simply a large mob of enemys running towards me instead of it being designed it a much more sophisticated manner. It seemed like lazy design when compared to the first.
Overall, I have to say that I think I enjoyed Dark Souls 1 more, however, at the end of the day, Dark souls 2 was still a great game.

Okay, but seriously... here is my review.
Listen to my story… this… may be our last chance.
What can I say? To many, this game is an absolute classic, and to me one of my favourite games of all time. Never before have I been so moved by a video game’s story.
Final Fantasy X was made to make the huge leap to PS2, and also to pay homage to the classic Final Fantasy’s combat system. It is an undeniable masterpiece, showing off that Square Enix were more than ready to make the next step in RPG gaming. In 2015, more than 13 years after its initial release, we were blessed with a HD Remaster to take us all back to how we felt all those many years ago. But now, in 2016, we are now blessed with the nostalgia bomb; our beloved Final Fantasy X on glorious PC. When this game popped up on my steam homepage I had to restrain myself from going bat♥♥♥♥♥♥crazy.
Enough about my story with this game, let’s get on to the easy-to-digest pros and cons:
Port Analysis: It’s a very good port (especially for Square Enix standards), probably even better than the PS3’s port, no graphics bugs or glitches so to speak of so far. My main gripe is that there is a 30FPS lock, but with a game like this it’s tolerable. There are also a few sound bugs with footsteps and lag on attacks but these are minor. Emulator-esque game boosters come with this port which can speed up the game (except for cut scenes, annoyingly…), increase or completely remove random encounters, supercharge your characters to ridiculous levels, and remove the HUD. There are also ‘cheats’ which can give you 99 of all items or maximum AP. EDIT: I have discovered advanced graphics settings. They are accessed in game in the Esc menu. Many resolution options, borderless windowed and some basic low, medium, high graphic settings are available.
Pros (Brace yourself, there are many):
+ One of the best soundtracks in a video game you’ll ever hear.
+ One of the most emotional roller coasters of a story in gaming. You will laugh, you will cry, you will fume, you will smile, this game is perfect for the sensitive soul.
+ An assortment of likable characters, no stale personalities here (‘cept for maybe Yuna, but you gotta have one straight man).
+ Very flexible levelling system with the sphere grid.
+ Beautiful CGI-cutscenes, even by today’s standards.
+ Combat System is classic turn based in X; solid, easy to pick up, and engaging. Some people may like the faster paced, ATB based system and those that do can play X-2 which uses that system instead.
+ Very good English dub. No Japanese voice option (modding can probably solve this), but if you’re like me you mostly remember the English dub.
+ Upgraded visuals improve the game’s look and feel without detracting from its charm.
+ No need to grind too much. I played through the game fighting every encounter without fleeing and I was about high enough level to beat bosses.
+ Choice between original and remastered soundtracks.
+ Blitzball is exciting and luck based fun!
+ Addition of autosaves.
+ Controller intergration in great for the 360 Controller. Buttons are mapped fine with onscreen instructions. Vibration support as well.
+ Plenty of side quests and other hidden treasures to discover.
+ Extras previously only available in Japanese versions.
+ Over 40 hours of gameplay, and that’s just the main storyline!
Procons
~ Port is iffy. Works fine, plenty of graphics of options, but the dreaded 30FPS lock. Also there are sound glitches with footsteps and occasional lag.
~ CGI Cutscenes are unchanged. They still look good, I was just hoping SE would remake these cut scenes with their updated graphics engine. Then again, it’s great for the nostalgia seekers like me.
~ For people unfamiliar with this game the Sphere grid may be confusing
~ Final Fantasy X-2
Cons
- People new to this game may think it is still dated, which it kind of is, let’s be honest…
- Game is slow to progress in the first 8 or so hours.
- No Japanese voice (mods will fix this I’m sure).
- Un-skippable cutscenes (can’t even be sped up through using the in-game boosters).
- Blitzball can be very infuriating when the RNG hates you. Also if you want to 100% the game and get all ultimate weapons you HAVE to play Blitzball.
- Combat is slower than ATB systems but can be mitigated with the hyperspeed boosters.
- One of the most cringiest cutscenes in the history of gaming, you all know the one I mean.
Overall:  Solid port, game lives up to its legacy as a widely regarded gaming masterpiece. To those who have never played this game and considering it, do it. Ignore the slightly dated animations and graphics, this game is one you’ll never forget.

A belated review for Dark Souls II. I actually played this originally on the PS3 (got the platinum for it too) and loved it, before picking it up for a second time on PC. Dark Souls II unfairly received a lot of flak for not being produced by Miyazaki, but the 'Team B' crew still did a fantastic job.
I loved the locations. You had your fire and ice settings, along with very green, very dark settings, and then some almost blind areas (Shaded Woods) which were quite enjoyable to travel through. The overall world layout could have been done better as some of it didn't quite make sense. For example travelling up from Harvest Valley to the lava filled area of Iron Keep doesn't make any sense geographically.
The new Adaptability stat was an odd inclusion. It seemed quite unnecessary, with most players getting it to 20 and then forgetting about it.
Magic was really well done, with sorcery, faith, pyro and dark magic all being totally viable playstyle options. Faith did take some heavy nerfs later on which was a shame, but to be fair it was probably a little OP at launch, with Lightning Spears able to take out most mobs and bosses quite easily.
The network side of things was really solid. I have almost zero issues with summoning other players or being summoned myself. I was definitely not a fan of the new Souls Memory mechanic. I think it did more harm than good with it really limiting how much co-op you could do before being out of range of other players.
The three DLC's were all absolutely excellent, definitely worth the asking price. All of them had brilliantly crafted levels with lots of shortcuts and secrets to unlock, and all had some really well designed and very challenging bosses.
Anyway Dark Souls II is a solid addition to the series and highly recommended. Not as good as the first Dark Souls IMO but still very much worth a play.

The gun mechanics are pretty neat - it is indeed a satisfying feeling to be able to figure out the nuances of the weapon. I don't know anything about guns, but I'd assume they resemble reality decently.
Unfortunately, the rest of the game is plagued with problems. The design of the game itself is so poor that the furthest I have ever gone in any of my games is finding 2 of the 11 objective items. Frequently, sentries and drones would be placed in locations where they cannot be disabled without being killed. The random initial gun/ammo state meant that I frequently ran out of ammo at inopportune times, with no reliable hope of finding more. The random chance of finding or starting with a flashlight meant that often, I'd find myself in a pitch-black area with no means of exploring. And in one worst-case scenario, a drone killed me right after I spawned, before I had any opportunity to react at all.
Then there's the lag. This game has a horribly severe lag problem. On my laptop, which is capable of running Just Cause 2 on medium-high, this game struggles to run at 800x600 on lowest graphical settings. On my desktop, running it at full 1080p resolution with the lowest graphical settings causes my GPU fan to spin up and create a considerable din. For a game this graphically simple, optimization this bad is simply disappointing.
Receiver is good as a novelty and exploration of game mechanics, but as a game itself, is a poorly produced product and not worth your time.

I played DS1 before this obviously...
This is a substantially different game from either 1 or 3 (I havnt played 3 but have read its very similar to 1). The main Dark Souls mechanics are there, but a lot of other things are pretty different.
It's a pretty common opinion that DS2 is the weakest of the series, and with its shortcomings I can see why people say that. In fact, the very fact that Iron Keep exists makes this game the weakest for me, as that place imo is a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, pardon my French
DS1 never ever made me say "omg ♥♥♥ this game" but DS2 made me say more than once with the ammount of bs it throws at you compared to DS1. DS1 and levels could be learned and mastered that you could traverse most of them without taking a single hit. DS2 levels... not so much. In Iron Keep, there's no way to get to the boss without fighting at least 5 enemies, notably the Smelter Demon. Some of the enemies in Iron Keep are even shoved in narrow hallways that you can't even swing your sword while you die, or crowded onto narrow bridges such that they push you off with a single hit and kill you, and not to ention with all the narrow hallways with enemies in them you find youself hitting walls alot and thus canceling your attack. This kind of enemy placement never occurs in 1 so it akes it very frustrating when combined with the fact that many actions in DS1 made you invincible to damage (opening doors, passing through fog gates, etc.). It feels like instead of intelligently placing enemies they've just been increased in quantity so that they can't be avoided at all.
That being said, it does some things way better than 1, namely replay value. Dark Souls 3 'apparently' had a bad NG+ system, where enemies simply gain more health and damage. (I just read this as i don't own DS3) but In DS2, going NG+ will change enemy locations, and even give some bosses new moves, so a NG+ will always leave you feeling surprised. On top of this, there is the bonfire ascetic item that changes an area to NG+ which you can do at any point during the game, aslong as you have the item of course.
So I would say that this game did a lot of things better than the previous Souls titles, but overall it will cause more needless frustration than the others in the series. When you die in DS1, you nod your head and know exactly what you did wrong. When you die in DS2, sometimes it's not even your fault, and I believe that's what gives this game its rep.
Overall worthwhile game, but expect more ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t then anything else
EDIT: The Smelter Demon triggered this review, hardest boss in the game for me personally

Five Nights at Freddy's is back and while still a fun experience, this game is a step back from its glorious predecessor. Of course, I'm writing this review OVER A YEAR (dear god) from when it came out, but I still feel like I should express my opinion. Lorewise, this game knocks it out of the park. The introduction of the 8-bit minigames we all know and love are a nice and disturbing addition to the franchise. As for the end-of-night cutscenes, they're great too, and its a shame the later games don't include them. Also, the calls provided by the ever lovely Phone Guy really get the mind racing and speculating on the hidden secrets behind this troubled restaurant chain.
Gameplay and/or horror isn't as strong though. The flashlight and mask mechanics are fine...its just that damn music box. And no, I'm not criticising it because of how many times it cost me the night (ugh), I just think its too much to handle along with eveyrthing else. Every second you're worrying about it, which is a bit too far in my opinion. This prequel-sequel's horror aspect is lacking as well, since your surroundings seem a lot brighter and more comfortable than the previous game, which isn't a good thing. Not to mention how many animatronics act the same way, causing it to be pretty predictable. But nevertheless, this game's good qualities outweigh the bad, which is why I think its definitely worth playing.
I recommend you to play the Deathrun mod in GFL Clan server. It's really enjoyable...

Although I've only played 9 or so hours at the time of me writing this review, I can confidently say that this is one of the best FPS games that I've ever played.
In my eyes, it is only matched by games like Insurgency.  Other than that not many other games come close to the immersiveness and inventiveness that this game brings to the table.
As an amateur historian and lover of all things war history, it is really refreshing to see a very well done video game about WW1.  To take that point even further, it is great to see a WW1 game be done with incredible historical accuracy, unlike a certain AAA title that is coming out in a few months...
From a technical standpoint, I'm playing this game on a ♥♥♥♥♥♥, ♥♥♥♥♥♥ laptop, and I can still get decent framerates and nice textures.  So I would have to say that it is well optimized.  I have yet to come across any technical difficulties as well.  No glitches or bugs.
I would also like to add that the community is very nice and welcoming.  Everyone is a team player.  No trolls or asshats.  Everyone is immersed in the game and makes it a nice experience.
Dim the lights, put on a good pair of headphones, and prepair yourself mentally to get PTSD from this realistic depiction of war that seemingly lives up to, and pays rememberence by simply existing to a collossal point in history.

Iron keep is a shameful attempt at videogame design.
From a studio with many titles under it's belt and awards for said titles, The final state Iron Keep was left in at release is apalling. A kingdom so enamored with its splendor and strength, sinking under the weight of its very greed and narcrissim is a perfect allergory to this Dark Souls: Prepare to Die. sequel.
The very first assault to any kind of logic is met upon reaching the area. Before getting to the Iron keep you must fight up a tall building/windmill. Clearing the area and reaching the top, you take a elevator going even higher only to find the Iron Keep. A land that is sinking in lava. How this is even possible even for a cryptic lore series as this uncertain. This should not be here.
Soon after you are met with the general denizen of the keep, The Alonne Knights.
Most of the faults with Dark Souls 2 enemy difficulty can be found bundled in this one enemy. With their mach 10 movement speed, 500 mile eagle eye vision, instant attack animations, and their tendancy to gank in groups of 3 or more, They attempt to uphold the Dark Souls legacy of being "a hard game".
This enemy was haphazardly dotted around the map with no sense of logic or reason. Along with  a few Greatbow wielding Alonne Captains to make sure the notion of this being "The hardest game ever" was being properly displayed. Attempting to avoid these knights and rush the optional boss is nearly impossible thanks to the added animation time to entering fog-gates - which was a simple task in the previous game.
The game is a tedious dance of trial and error, With no sense of a well fought fight. Bosses are either extremely easy, or slapped with a gimmick to make them seem like a challenge.
This game is trash and you should not buy it.

Amazing game, probably the most realistic/best war game for me.
This game features:
-About 30 weapons which can all be used (mainly Bolt-action rifles, but there are also MGs, very little SMGs, knives, grenades and even a flamethrower)
-Very realistic gameplay (1 shot kill, Gas attacks, Very good graphics which can be altered, slow-paced as most players stay in prone, wise decision)
-The most accurate gameplay to the era I have seen, very detailed maps, bullet ballistics, mortar barrages, limbs being blown off, dying corpses in the mud writhing and crying and screaming for help before choking on their own blood and getting blown up by another mortar, cheerful stuff like that. -TIP: don't poke your head up from the trench for more than 3 seconds, else you'll have about 50 enemy snipers with you in their crosshairs. Unless you like looking like swiss cheese, of course.

-It may be WW1, but charging at the enemy sewing machines (or machineguns, if army slang hasn't found it's way to you yet) ISN'T as glorious as the old BBC propaganda makes it out to be. (swiss cheese... remember?!)
-Also, the gas right now is really not as dangerous as it was then. You can just casually walk through the DEADLIEST gas for about 5 seconds, put your gas mask on, and you'd be fine. No need to worry. Unless there are enemy soldiers in your trench... then you should worry...

I must say that I'm quite impressed by the quality of this game, and at the same time I'm ashamed by the gaming community as a whole for bashing this game so much (maybe because it wasn't made by some "developers" who inexplicably get a free pass everytime they milk a franchise without making anything new).
Homefront The Revolution starts up with a heist in your haven by the North Korean Force, which slays your partners while you watch everything. This after a complete overview of the story so far in a beautifully made cutscene. So, let's get to the point here:
This time the game has an open world system split into zones, which we have the yellow and the red ones. In the red ones, you've got a more Stalker/Metro-ish kind of environment, in a post war Philadelphia. Everything is in rubles, and in this zones is where you get more of the action while you progress in the plot and make side missions. You've got even a bike to traverse the environments more quickly.
In the red zones, we've got a more "civilized" view of the America after the invasion, with military propagandas and Soldiers patrolling the streets; it's a very nice change of pace and mechanics as whole, because in these zones you have to blend in with the population, trying not to attract any attention to yourself while you accomplish missions. It's hard... Well, Homefront The Revolution is a hard game, but not the frustrating kind; you simply have to plan your approach, because it's not a simply run and gun FPS, but more of a stealth one.
The side missions isn't what you might expect, it isn't a mindless to do list with various icons pesting the world map with bland and repetitive activities and useless collectibles, as in... Well, I won't mention other games here, you've got the picture already!
Those missions involves you having to take pictures of patrols and drones with your phone, taking outposts, reclaiming apartments and other points of interest to the resistance, destroying certain kinds of enemies with certain kinds of weapons, etc; in other words, it keeps a nice pace as a whole, mixing perfectly with the main missions. And I noticed that you don't have much of those side missions around the map, they are well distributed and far between, and doesn't make your map look like a christmas tree.
Now, about the weapon customization: oh man, I wish every game has this kind of weapon customization, but well, if every single one of them had it, it wouldn't be so special here; it looks like the known Crysis series system, where you hold your weapon near the screen and change some attachments, but in here you actually see the protagonist changing pieces and sometimes dismantling big portions of the weapons to, for instance, turn a pistol into a SMG. It's awesome, it never gets old and it's always nice to see what kind of arsenal you can customize for yourself based on the missions you are about to do.
It runs on CryEngine, has a day and night cicle (which is beautiful, to be honest) and one of the best face sync I've ever seen in a game. Just in the beginning you have this woman who talks to you while you're tied to a chair, and her facial expressions, together with the voice acting, accomplish a level of quality here that we don't see very often, not even with AAA famous titles. and it isn't just with facial expressions, the body sync also made a lot of NPCs in other games looks like clay dolls.
Most of people who bashed Homefront The Revolution was saying it runs badly, wasn't them?! Well, I played it with everything on high (not
high, high) with a stable experience, no CTD, and with 42-50 fps most of the time. I have a GTX 760, 8Gb RAM and an i5 2400, so you can take your conclusions with that.
Overall, Homefront The Revolution is a must have for any shooter fan out there; I suggest you simply ignore all the press and the critics, and most of the players who said it's bugged and/or unplayable, I'm almost sure most of them didn't even played the game.

I know this game is getting a lot of crap, and I can understand why, but I'm going to just put this out there: This is in NO WAY a BAD GAME. The mechanics work and, while there could be some improvements to the story, it works. The fact is I think it is poorly priced; because while it is a good game, it is a very SHORT game.

Anyway, I took a little longer than average because I re-read most things and listened to all the journal entries twice after gathering the whole lot. I also had a ton of fun throwing random sh*t around because I could.
ANYWAY, back to the actual review stuff.
Pros:
90s nostalgia. Nintendo, cassets, tapes, and crappy tv's galore.
Good music (also 90s and some original score)
Enjoyable story delivery (journal entries read to you when picking up/finding certain objects and letters)
Good Story
Cons:
You can't run (least I didn't find a button that let me)
While the music is good and it's fun to find a casset player and look for the casset to match so you can listen to some Bratmobile or Heavens to Betsy while you read papers, there isn't too much of it when you go through the house. Lot of quiet moments broken by you throwing glasses at the floor in the hope they'll combust.
Random elements that don't really connect to the main story (like the fact that the mom works as some type of forest park ranger supervisor, or that her dad is a reviewer and somewhat-failed fiction writer. There are some hints to a poor marriage that could tie in with the rest of it, but there is a lot of random papers that you don't really have to read for the purpose of the story).
In general I'd say wait for this game to go on sale for at least 5 bucks. I got it for about 3 and I don't regret the buy; I'm ather happy I did purchase the game, actually. If you wanna listen to Sam's journal entries again - because they are very nice to listen too - you can just go to the journal tab in your finished game and go ahead and do that.
Overall a 7.5/10 because I really did enjoy the story and the Sam character.

Your goal is to collect all 11 tapes and listen to them, which are, not surprisingly, placed in random locations. Also randomly placed is extra ammo, which you'll need to destroy the turrets and Manhack-type things that are, GASP, randomly placed. The reloading mechanics, while nonsensical at first, begin to make sense the more you play and are actually really quite logical. I played a little over 8 hours of the singleplayer game throughout the free weekend and was pleasantly surprised. Highly recommend this game for the price and heres why.
Gameplay: 8/10 - Everything about the game from the characters movement to the shooting mechanics is solid. You really feel the weight of the character and the first person animations are on point. Enemy A.I. is generic but not ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ in any way. The side missions are also generic but fast paced, challenging, and did not become too tedious to do. The weapons are the highlight of the game. They are satisfying to use, look and feel realistic (comparable to Arma), and are customizable in many ways (similar to Crysis).
Sound: 6/10 - This is where the game is unfortunately lacking. Although the gun sounds and voice acting are pretty good, the rest of the world feels dead. Civs and other npcs repeat themselves too often atleast for me and it just seemed like if there were more sounds placed throughout the city it would've felt more life like and immersive. I did encounter a sound bug at one point and sometimes I noticed sounds didnt register at all like explosions.
Graphics: 10/10 - If you have the hardware for it, these graphics are beautiful and amongst one of the best. Everything from the lighting to the special effects are awesome and really does a good job of keeping you hooked.
Replayability: 5/10 -The singleplayer is the typical open world you should all be accustomed to by now. You're placed on a big map with missions and objectives to complete. You unlock more of the map as you progress and can get around pretty easily with dirt bikes. The incentives to do the side missions are worth it atleast at first but after about 5 hours you unlock the majority of the weapons you want and I dont see myself wanting to do more. Its a game you will probably play once and not really play again
Final thoughts: 7.5/10 -The game is definitely worth a playthrough for 20 bucks. Its not anything you havent seen before but its damn good entertainment. All the previous bugs and problems the game had before were fixed by the devs so it is definitely playable now and the campaign will last you over 12 hours to complete. I did not try out the multiplayer but I dont think this game was really mp focused but it may provide more play time if you like it.
