This is a very pretty village builder which can be quite relaxing, but very often challenging. The most important aspect of the game is micro-managing all the different types of workers to ensure abundance of all resources. Things in the village can always quickly turn for the worse with a couple of different disasters that could occur. The game is very entertaining and even though at a certain point a village can reach a level where it has all the different possible buildings built, the primary purpose of the game: to build an ever bigger sustainable settlement is always enough to keep me interested in the game.
My first village was quickly overcome by famine, but on my second try, I have managed to always have a stable settlement which even survived a few crop infestations and a fire, all achieved with slow paced careful expansion.
It might not be that the newest graphics technology is used in this game, but it still looks good, the aesthetics are great and I have found myself following different little people around numerous times. The game certainly has a charm. All in all, it's a job well done and considering the price, this is a builder which I can recommend.
NOTE: The game is almost completely clean of bugs in my experience, but some people have reported minor AI bugs. I haven't really suffered any.

I played DS1 and DS3 before this.
This is a substantially different game from either 1 or 3. The main Dark Souls mechanics are there, but a lot of other things are pretty different.
It\'s a pretty common opinion that DS2 is the weakest of the series, and with its shortcomings I can see why people say that. In fact, the very fact that Iron Keep exists makes this game the weakest for me.
Neither DS1 nor DS3 ever made me say \"omg♥♥♥♥♥this game\" but DS2 made me say it twice. DS1 and 3 levels could be learned and mastered such that you could traverse most of them without taking as much as a single hit. DS2 levels... not so much. In Iron Keep, there\'s no way to get to the boss without fighting at least 5 enemies. Some of the enemies in Iron Keep are even shoved in narrow hallways such that you can\'t even swing your sword while you die, or crowded onto narrow bridges such that they push you off with a single hit and kill you. This kind of enemy placement never occurs in 1/3 so it\'s very frustrating when combined with the fact that many actions that were invincible in 1/3 (opening doors, passing through fog gates) are no longer so. It feels like instead of intelligently placing enemies such that they could be avoided with a proper strategy, they\'ve just been increased in quantity so that they can\'t be avoided at all.
That being said, it does some things way better than 1/3, namely replay value. Dark Souls 3 has a notably bad NG+ system, where enemies simply gain more health and damage. In DS2, going NG+ will change enemy locations, give bosses new gimmicks, and is generally full of surprises. On top of this, there is the bonfire ascetic mechanic to NG+ an area at any point during the game.
So I would say that this game did a lot of things better than the Miyazaki Souls titles, but overall it will cause more needless frustration than the others in the series. Unlike many games these days, this title differs greatly in the fact that is is more like a user controlled film or short story. A tale that (in my humble opinion) is on the scale of the film 'American Beauty'. Something strange is occuring in the suburbs in this rural town, Something strange, yet intimat, and beautiful. Harnessing the creativity of the writers, this game has the power to envoke emotions which may be entirely familiar and nostalgic to you, or perhaps those which you may have never known. This is a tale of exploration and wonder. With my hair standing on end, I entered the next room to learn of its curiosity. Most of all this is a tale of love. The story is not long, and may leave you wondering about a few details, however you will come away filled with a new feeling, which is very rich and satifying. This is an amazing first person shooter for many reasons. One of the main eye-catching reasons is its advanced reloading system that makes you feel like you are controlling a real firearm. You can take out your magazine, put bullets in it, then put it back into your gun. It's so immersive in terms of mechanics. You gotta worry about ammo consevation, though, because ammo isn't cheap. It gets tough to find and when you run out of ammo.
The game is also randomly generated. Each time you star the game, a new level, new starting place, new item position, and a new inventory is picked. You could start with 1 of 3 pistols. A glock, which has an automatic firing mode, a Colt pistol, and a "Victory" revolver. You can start with 1 clip, or 5. You sometimes start with a maglight!
Your goal is to find tapes throughout the level. There is 11 to collect, and each of them unlock a piece of a puzzle. But the game is tough, with two types of enemies that always kill you in one hit. There's a flying 'tazer' bot, and a stationary sentry bot. They can both be disabled in a number of ways. You can shoot out the camera, the guns, and the motor.
For a game that started as a seven-day project, it's pretty amazing. It runs smoothly and plays smoothly. If you're a fan of indie FPS games, I highly recomend getting this game.

Created by a team of 4 in a week for a FPS game design challenge, Receiver revolves around realistic gun mechanics in a (very) randomly generated world. Despite being an FPS game, the gameplay focuses more on actually controlling and preparing your firearm and stealth rather than on modern "realistic" cover shooting concepts. Reloading magazines manually,  emptying revolver chambers, and juggling your inventory are actually all very enjoyable, even more so when you manage to learn the controls. The randomization is very strong, starting you off with one of three random handguns, a random amount of ammo, and occasionally a mag light. Room objects, enemies, pickups, and lighting all are randomized, making you want to explore. However, the randomization also causes issues; one game I spawned right next to a taser drone with 3 bullets. Overall, I think this is worth picking up just to experience it, especially with the low asking price.

Homefront: The Revolution is a mixed bag, but I think it ultimately prevails as an above average open world FPS. I played this game a good bit through its free weekend, and I enjoyed it. There's many reasons why its a mixed bag, so lets get to those reasons, shall we?
The best thing this game pulls off with flying colors is its visuals. The open world of this abused rundown urban city you explore looks great. There's lots of detail everywhere. There's also a great urban apocalypase art style, especially in the Resistance. Paired with the game's fantastic Cryengine graphics, it's a glorious looking game. Its heavy hopelessness feeling atmosphere is also great. It's fun to climb to a high point and look at the view. The art and graphics team kicked♥♥♥♥♥ There's great weapon customization. Different guns can be taken apart and swapped to transform into different guns. You can transform your assault rifle to a LMG with the hit of just two buttons, so you basically carry 6 guns when you're only carrying 2. You can carry up to two primary weapons and a pistol. That's 9 weapons you carry around, which is crazy, and it's unique how they pull it off. This is complimented by the ability to add attachments like sights, underbarrel stuff like grips and lasers, and muzzle brakes. Sadly, there's no weapon camos (as far as I know). Running around in the world is fun. You can climb up buildings if you can reach the ledges, and there's these big airships that beam down scanners that scan for Resistance soliders like you, so if one gets close, you have to dive for the nearest building and hide for them, which is pretty cool. You can also sneak past the numerous KPA patrols in Red Zones, or get immersed by blending into the civilian population in Yellow Zones. Yellow Zones is one of the best parts of the game. You have to sneakily sabatoge stuff like speakers, and save prisoners from the KPA. Eventually, the civilian population will join you in fighting back, and soon the whole Yellow Zone will be a big riot. This system is really awesome, and one of the most cool things you can do in this game.
The game is demanding. This might not be a legit negative thing, as it happens with these new titles, but it alienates people with low end machines. I know it isn't unoptimized, as my GPU is always at 95%-99% in GPU-Z, which means it's being pushed as hard as it can. My 960 4GB runs this game as a mix of Med-High with 2x SMAA at 40-60 FPS, which isn't too bad. The AI is pretty bad. They'll take cover behind a piece of cover two feet in front of you instead of fighting back, so you can take 3 steps and shoot their head. They also sprint towards you out in the open like a bunch of morons, and will also react to you slowly if you walk around the corner and surprise them. The game can also get repetitive. You go to an area, maybe kill some KPA, liberate it, and then do it all over again. This doesn't bother me, as I enjoy this kind of formula, but for people that don't like repeating the same process over and over in a video game, you might get annoyed and you'll lose any enjoyment. Although they have such a great weapon customization engine, they make one huge glaring mistake. You can't silence assault rifles and snipers. You can only silence pistols and SMGs. WHY? I was hoping to be this badass Sam Fisher kind of character with silenced weapons, but I can't do that. Why can't I silence my primary weapons? That's so stupid. There's also not much variety in weapons. There's one assault rifle, one marksman rifle, one pistol (well, two if you count the dart shooting pistol), etc. So everyone's gun looks exactly the same, which is pretty bland. It's also pretty buggy. I notice a lot of clipping, audio glitches like pausing the game and unpausing can sometimes just kill the voices of the guy that's talking to you, and just weird stuff like a low textured iron sight floating in mid air after I changed my sight one time.
Homefront: The Revolution is a mixed bag, but an enjoyable mixed bag in my opinion. It's a beautiful looking game that's fun to roam around, sniping KPA for torn down buildings. I enjoyed the time I had to play it during the free weekend it had. If I can find it for around $15-$20, I might end up getting it eventually. Also, most of the negative reviews are trash, simply saying "Game is♥♥♥♥♥♥ Don't buy it." I
reviews like that because they don't tell you why it's bad. There's also some saying it's the worst game of 2016 or even the worst game ever. Those reviews are blatant lies. Ignore them. There's way worse game in 2016 and WAY worse games in the past.

Receiver is similar to the original indie game Slender, but with killbots and functionally detailed firearms instead of a horror theme.  You are dropped into an environment randomly generated from a variety of interconnected prefab rooms and must locate eleven randomly placed tape cassettes.  You are given a random handgun (at this time there are three available) and a random amount of ammo (I have started with as little as 4 bullets).  The weapons feature action similar to real handguns, with clips or cylinders that must be reloaded one bullet at a time.  As you navigate away from the "safezone" you randomly encounter two types of killbots and must use your weapon to disable them before they kill you.  Ammo and flashlights are also placed at random drop points throughtout the environment.  I have played and replayed this game numerous times and expect to do so for some time.  For the price of $5 it is worth your money.

I admire the effort put into this game to model and skin nearly every grab-able object. It's an attention to detail that makes it worthwhile to explore the house. The gameplay is very good. It controls like a polished game. And I think the developers accomplished their goal. However, I didn't like the audio creepiness, like the sudden crack of thunder, or creaking floors. It seems like this was used to bait players who thought the game was a horror/suspense game. This is an unscrupulous way to sell your game! I'm also disappointed in the regular price. I've played plenty of short-form or indie games and Gone Home is an especially brief, "cheap" experience that doesn't merit the high price.
This is a hard game to recommend. Technically it is a good game, nothing to dismiss in that regard. On the other hand, I never liked "sign posted" games, where the storytelling is delivered through billboards. The Bioshock games were bad for that. It's because it presumes a world where no-one thinks it strange that someone is projecting their private thoughts and feelings on public surfaces; It's just unrealistic. If this is how you want to tell a story then turn it into an interactive novel where the storytelling method actually makes sense. Automatically turning every possible artistic experience into a 3D gaming experience is disingenuous.

: The Fullbright Company
: The Fullbright Company
==========
Gone Home is an excellent example of how amazing an exploratory story game can be. The story is told as you explore each room, and bits and pieces of the story are shown to you for you to put them together. When everything is said and done, you have a great overall picture of what's happened/happening in the game. Gone HOme does a very good job laying everything out before you.
==========
Played entirely in first person, Gone Home drops you off at the front door of your home after a trip abroad. A note on the door clues you in that your sister is gone and asks you not to try and find out where she went. As you go along, you find out what happened through little notes and pictures that you find hidden around the house. At certain points you need to find a key to open up a new section of the house, opening up new bits of story, clues, and notes to find to help you piece together the overall story. Not going to spoil anything, but the story is well written and you can totally see it as an event that could really happen.
There are sections where you might expect something to happen, or some baddie to jump out and get you (due to the ambience), but nothing of the sort is present in this game. So if you are expecting that, you will be disappointed. Gone Home is purely a story game.
==========
The house you explore is very realistic. The layout is a bit weird and unconventional at places, but overall it works. Furniture and other props such as cups and cabinets all look great. Doors, windows, etc all have the same detail.
Lightning is questionable, where everything is almost completely dark until you turn on a light. Even then, some areas aren't very realistic when lit. It works though, I suppose. You will make a habit of looking fo rlight switches or lamps when you enter a new room.
If you look close enough,  you will find a myriad of obscure references to the 80's and 90's, especially in a few of the bedrooms, on the cassette tapes you find near tape players, and on postes in various rooms. There are tons to find, try to find all you can!
==========
The music is very calming, but as said above, there are points where it might make you think something will jump out at you. Gone Home is a very ambient game, with lots of backgrounds noise and weather effects to set the mood and atmosphere. It's all very fitting for the theme of the game, and well placed.
==========
I had absolutely no issues running this game. It ran at a constant 60FPS and had no stuttering or frame loss. It didn't crash at any point either. Most users should have no issues running this game, as it didn't seem to be very 'heavy' on my rig. No complaints here!
==========
A great story driven exploratory adventure, Gone Home is a nice, relaxing game that you can enjoy at your pace for a few hours. The only downside is that it is extremely short. It took me approximately 2-3 hours to complete the story. This included actually reading everything I found, taking screenshots, and picking up/looking at most of the objects scattered about. Regardless, it's worth the price of admission (on sale) because it tells a great, moving story.

TL;DR: There is currently an issue with FFXHD not flagging itself for use on a dedicated GPU in a system with switchable graphics. In addition to this, during my testing (unknowing running on the iGPU), the game has a tendency to crash when transitioning between areas. It's hard to say why, but regardless until these issues are resolved I'd suggest holding off. Users running into issues where FFXHD does not use their dedicated graphics are advised to manually run the executable and forcing the game to use the dedicated graphics in their system.
## OVERVIEW AND MAJOR COMPLAINTS
At this point in time, Final Fantasy X/X-2 HD is a known quantity. You can read any review of the previous incarnations of FFXHD to know what the gameplay is like. FFX is a legendary PS2 title, pushing the barrier for graphical fidelity at the time.
My biggest gripe so far is the tendency to crash. I've encountered issues where the renderer stops updating the display, causing the game to appear frozen but still be 'playable'. I believe this was an issue with my Intel graphics driver crashing, but haven't done enough testing to see if the issue is still present after a driver update. This could be linked to an issue I talk about in the performance section of this review.
The far more common issue is a straight crash-to-desktop when transitioning between areas. It has happened twice during the first underwater segment, and again on Besaid after Wakka asks Tidus to join the blitzball tournament. This is a frustrating problem.
## GRAPHICS AND PERFORMANCE
This PC release offers a variety of graphical options and improvements over the various console releases. While gameplay is locked to 30fps, menus appear to render at the refresh rate of your display (which for me is 60Hz). This might be a cause of concern for some, but personally while I'd prefer there be no framerate cap, a game like FFX is perfectly playable at 30fps.
In terms of performance, I've been playing FFXHD on my laptop, hardware wise it's a ZenBook UX303LN with a dual-core Core i5-4210U @ 1.7 GHz, a 2GB GeForce 840M and 12GB of RAM.
Currently, there appears to be an issue where FFXHD is flagged to run on the iGPU instead of the dGPU, meaning instead of using the GeForce 840M, FFXHD has been running on Intel HD Graphics 4400. This is my primary reason for not recommending this just yet, in addition to the crashes.
Performance on the HD 4400 has been above expectations. The game runs at 1080p on the Low preset with textures on High at 30fps in most environments. Typical for integrated graphics, the framerate dips into the mid-20s in scenes with lots of lighting effects. Combat for the most part runs at 30fps (again depending on the environment), but attacks with lots of effects or explosions cause the framerate to tank fairly sharply. The GPU is given full license to clock up to 1,000 MHz with memory at 800 MHz and a temperature of around 73C-75C. I'm fairly impressed with these results given how limited the shader performance and memory bandwidth is on the HD 4400.
As for performance on the GeForce 840M, the game runs at 1080p on the Medium preset with textures on High and anti-aliasing turned off. Exploring around the early areas of Besaid the game sticks to 30fps with GPU usage around 95%-98%. In a battle scene on Besaid, GPU usage drops to around 85%. The 840M is allowed to turbo to its full 1,124 MHz core speed and 900 MHz memory speed and temperatures sit at around 73C in my ZenBook UX303LN. Once again, I'm pleased with these results, given the 840M isn't exactly a gaming powerhouse.
However, In reality I shouldn't even have to have two sections for performance. The game should be running on dedicated graphics in systems that have it. Whether this is an issue for Square Enix to resolve, or if Nvidia can resolve this with a driver update, it's still dissapppointing to see. Performance numbers across the board are better than I expected, so I see no isses with optimisation here, just the issue with GPU switching and crashes.
## CONCLUSIONS
The issues outlined here form the basis of my decision to not recommend this game at this time. Crashing to the desktop is a frustrating experience, and users should not have to manually set a game to run on their dedicated graphics.
However, when these issues are resolved, I will ammend this review and give FFXHD a solid recommendation. If you believe you're happy to work around these issues as they currently stand, by all means the game has my recommendation. But until they're resolved, this review ends without a recommendation from me.

A story-telling exploration game with a somewhat eerie atmosphere - as eerie as coming back to an empty home in the middle of a thunderstorm can be. The level design plays with that and does so quite well, making reveals slow and deliberate. But you do not have to expect any pop-up in-your-face horror elements.
The story itself is told in little audio snippets and text notes all over the house, while the level design ensures that you get them in the best possible order.
Some might consider the story obvious, but it is the "how", not the "what" that makes it engaging. There is a reason this game is brought up regularly when talking about fresh indy approaches to gaming. But also be warned that this is a rather short game. Still, in my opinion, worth it.

War is terrible thing. Verdun will show you that. The screams, the bullets whizzing over my head, the mortars exploding nearby, the choking gas, the blood, the gore,the bodies so many bodies...They all give me nightmares. But nothing, absolutely nothing is worse than the damn barbed wire...
Seriously though, this is a fun game. Graphics are good, sound is great, and the gameplay is wonderful. It's definitely a different experience from a game like Call of Duty or Battlefield.
It's more brutal. You see people exploding from mortars, people laying on the ground bleeding to death and crying. You see limbs torn from bodies and blood everywhere. And that damn barbed wire...
It's slower paced. You pop your head out of trenches, scan for enemies, and quickly get back down. You can either get your head blown off right away or live long enough to off a couple enemies and get back into cover. Don't expect to be able to run out into the open for longer than 5 seconds without getting shot. It's a one shot, one kill deal. There is also a respawn timer to simulate reinforcements.
You have squads with specific roles that you have to play as. You can't custom select your weapons much at all, you choose a role and use what they give you.
It's also a nice change from the Americans vs Russians/Chinese/terrorists thing that's been going on. Here we have a few different factions that you can be a part of.
I recommend this game to people who like historical shooters. It's really fun, possibly due to it being more slower paced and adding to the realism. As of the writing of this review I have 25 hours in but I'm looking forward to playing much longer. If you're interested,

PLAYED ON FREE WEEKEND.
This review has been made using my feedback from playing during the free weekend.
I am one of the few who actually enjoyed the first Homefront game made by THQ. However I'm not a fan of this one. Performance wise, I had a rather poor experience, I had numerous game crashes and freezes. The longest I went without one was about 15mins. The framerate was ok on ultra settings using a 1070 founders, but not as high as I anticipated. Otherwise the game visually does look pretty good.
However, my main issue is with the free mode style gameplay, after the first 10 minutes of interductory cutscenes/gameplay, the story completely fell apart for me. Instead of a group of resistance fighters, the game turns into a one man resistance, you single handedly taking on the whole occupation forces of the KPA. This ruined the story for me as at least the previous game had a sense of a group of people not just a single man, even with it's fixed mission based playthrough.
Another thing I wasn't keen on was the repetitive nature of getting to missions, the motorbike controls are far too poor to use and also wasn't very immersive just driving past an entire platoon of KPA, and running 200+ meters made me feel like I was playing ARMA at some points of the game.
However on a side note I do like the weapon customisation to a degree, the way in which a pistol can be made into an SMG, or a Marksman Rifle into a Sniper Rifle is an awesome idea expecially when done in the game, not in a menu. However, on the counterside, I would have wanted more customisation as It's rather lacking.
In comparison this review may be biased as I haven't played the whole game, and for a more in depth review for longer playtimes should be considered alongside this review. However I recommend this game, ONLY if you are really interested in the purchase and the franchise, and when the game is discounted as even I wouldn't buy this game for less than 50% or more of retail price.

On the other hand, sometimes people don't like surprises.  On one hand, I played it alone in the dark and it was creepy.  On the other hand, it has some thematic elements certain people won't like.  On one hand, there isn't as much narration as say, The Stanley Parable.  On the other hand, The Stanley Parable is digital garbage.
TL;DR - I have 8 hands, I only recommend Gone Home during a sale, and I hate the Stanley Parable.

The story is classic but well told with well defined characters and interesting dynamics.
The game sufferrs from minor performance issue but  it's running fine on 1080p medium on my old toaster.
In all honestly, I don't understand the torrent of negative reviews as it's one of the best and most refreshing  open world shooters I have played in years.

Just Cause 2 is one of the most thrilling shooters that I have ever played in my life.  No other third-person shooter has quite held my attention as much as this, with its incredible action-movie plot and its huge open world.  A thumbs-up is simply not enough.
This game is incredible.  What it lacks in variety is made up by the huge number of challenges, islands and vehicles that populate this huge open world.  And it is huge.  Very huge.  All of the weapons have their good and bad points, and the ability to duel weild one-handed weapons is incredibly cool when you can juggle enemies in the air with a barrage of smg rounds.  The explosions feel chunky and pack a real punch, and you will be seeing a lot of them on your journey round Panau.  The island itself is beautiful, with lush green forests mixed up with deserts and alpine regions, all populated with various villages, challenges, missions and military bases.
However, some of these places lack variety.  While the huge number of settlements is incredible, they lack variety.   One village looks like the one next door, and a military base is a military base, no matter what way you look at it.  Also, don't purchase this expecting some realistic driving mechanics either.  The cars will react to the environment in a very action-movie way, which means that they cannot provide a realistic driving experience.  However, Rico's grappling hook combined with his stunt parachute make a much better way of getting around.
Overall, Just Cause 2 provides a wide range of incredible action-movie moments, from jumping on cars and shooting the police's tyres out to make them flip over and explode, to making incredible vehicle jumps in order to escape the torrent of military soldiers on your tail.  For its current price, as of writing, of £10, or £5 if you are in the Christmas sale, it is a must-buy.  I myself have played over 100 hours (over a long period of time, of course), as I couldn't simply let the game go once I had completed the story.  Causing chaos is just too good, I guess.

I would probably recommend not enabling chat if you are a parent letting their kid play this.
The good:
Amazing World is an MMO designed for children, but has just enough personality to be entertaining to the parents of those children, too (not in a 'main MMO' way, but that shouldn't be expected).  I could also see this being a wonderful thing for anyone with a mental disability (being serious, not making joke), as it really is very easy to grasp what's going on (and even if you don't, I could see just running around looking at the scenery being enjoyable). There are a variety of activities, like quests, "run around and find all the bunnies", minigames, races, fishing, etc.
It is vibrant, well designed, colorful, has great music, sound, and voice acting. The controls are responsive and simple (though you can't change the control setup- see 'the bad' below). It seems like a fairly safe environment for kids (naming restrictions, "pick 3 words from these lists to make your name"), though I of course would still want to supervise kids playing any MMO.
______________
The bad:
* The lack of a menu option to re-assign hotkeys is a shame- I know this leaves lefties (and anyone picky about controls) out    of luck.
* For some reason, the game is extremely picky about resolution- it will only work at 1280x720 or above. Not a huge deal, but still, could be a slight hassle.
* The "free to play" aspect. You cannot progress past level 10 with one "Zing" (character/avatar) as a free account. There are still public activities, games, and a few other things you can do once you hit that wall, but progression is impossible without subscribing. The good news here is, subscribing is extremely cheap- only $4 (USA) per month, when you pay one month at a time (there are 6 and 12 month options available, as well). Also, if this is just a child spending a bit of time playing an MMO, the level 10 restriction may not matter, anyway- the repeatable activities are a lot more content than I had on a Tiger handheld game when I was a kid- and I sure kept playing the heck out of those.

In short, I love Dark Souls, but this doesn't feel like Dark Souls.
And now I present to you the longer version: The game tries to be like the original, but it relies on cheap and unfair gimmicks to make up for the fact that it is not a difficult game.

In the beginning I had no idea where to go. I wandered around in Majula for what seemed like ages until I found my way.
I had no idea why I was doing anything. The exposition from the hag in the opening cinematic even says, "But one day, you will stand before its decrepit gate. Without really knowing why..."
The basic mechanic of dodge-rolling is dependant on the agility stat. Until that stat reaches 105, your rolling is pathetic. Unless you intend on hiding behind a shield through the entire game, you must reach that soft cap before you can truly level up your other stats.
Statues block your every path forcing you to release the petrified victim with a rare/expensive item in order to proceed. Many of these statues lead nowhere, where as some are necessary to progress.
DS2 recycles bosses from DS1.
You are frequently invaded by NPCs with provocation.
Most enemies are too easy on their own, so you are forced into fighting multiple of the same enemy at the same time.
There are many death traps that serve no other purpose than to slow your progression.
Nearly all bosses are just some guy with armor and a weapon and are defeated the same way.
Bosses become become common enemies after defeating them because the game HAS to try to be hard.
Ornstein, no Smough!
Poison is EVERYWHERE!
Several enemies only exist to specifically destroy your armor while dealing little to no damage, not acting as a threat but rather a nuisance.
You can easily get caught on the terrain and be killed because of it.
The unbreakable Dragon Tooth weapon weilded by Havel, I mean Woodland Child Gully, is literally as durable as a wooden club.
Most NPCs are miserable ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s.
You start with a single estus flask. Drinking from it takes an unfairly long amount of time.
You will frequantly die after drinking from your flask due to the slow healing rate.
Fog gates litter the land with no other purpose than to obscure your view of the next room whether it's safe or not.
You can be killed while walking through a fog gate.
After defeating a boss, all previously aggroed enemies will storm into the boss room and murder you.
You can not farm for souls since enemies stop respawning after being killed so many times. This can really punish people who are not too great at the game and need to grind some souls to increase their stats.
Attacking a mimic in the back will result in it still grabbing you even though it only reaches out in front of itself.
Poison is like toxic, and toxic is like curse.
Every time you die you lose up to 10% of your maximum health.
You will be stun locked time and time again if you do not stack poise.
A swarm of rats is a boss, lolwut?
The land is not connected. You will go through multiple cutscenes of traveling methods showing how disconnected the land is.
You need to equip a specific ring every time you want to go through a certain door.

You will fight the same NPC invaders time and time again.

Just Cause 2 is an action-adventure video game developed by Avalanche Studios, published by Eidos Interactive, and distributed by Square Enix. It is the sequel to the 2006 video game Just Cause.
Just Cause 2 employs the Avalanche Engine 2.0, an updated version of the engine used in Just Cause. Rico Rodriguez returns as the protagonist, aiming to overthrow the evil dictator Pandak "Baby" Panay and confront his former mentor, Tom Sheldon.
Notable features of Just Cause 2 include the grappling hook, which gives players the ability to tether objects to each other. For example, in a high speed vehicle chase, the player can use the grappling hook to attach a pursuing vehicle to the ground, forcing it to stop and often flipping or turning the vehicle causing damage to it. The grappling hook also allows the player to pull himself, and hold onto objects such as walls or helicopters.
In addition, the player has a parachute which is always ready to be deployed, even if it has been deployed and discarded only moments before. This can be combined with the grappling hook and used as a fast method of transport.
The PlayStation 3 version of the game allows the user to capture video of their gameplay and either export it to the XMB or upload it to YouTube from within the game.
Plot
Just Cause 2 is set four years after the first Just Cause, with Agency operative Rico Rodriguez being dropped into Panau, a fictional dystopian island nation in Maritime Southeast Asia. Formerly a U.S. ally, Panau is ruled by Pandak "Baby" Panay  who institutes a harsh, oppressive dictatorship and cuts off all ties to the United States due to his Anti-American views. Rico's mission is to oust Panay from office, as well as track down and assassinate his old mentor, Tom Sheldon, who the Agency fears has gone rogue after disappearing during the regime change. In order to find Sheldon, Rico allies himself with the three dominant criminal gangs on the island: the Roaches, an organized crime syndicate, the Reapers, an insurgent Socialist militia and the Ular Boys, an ultranationalist rebel group that espouses traditionalism and opposes foreign influence. He gathers enough information to track down Sheldon, who not only reveals that he's been investigating a larger conspiracy behind Panau, but that he is in fact the "Sloth Demon", the Black Market dealer that often calls Rico to give information on the gangs and that Rico calls to be provided with weapons and vehicles . Rico establishes that Sheldon has not gone rogue, and Sheldon tells him to continue causing chaos on Panau while he goes to explain the situation to the Agency.
After clearing everything up, Sheldon demands that Rico quickly make his way over to his hideout. They tell him that Jade Tan, a mysterious Agency asset whom Rico had met earlier, has been caught in Panay's military base, and is to be tortured and possibly killed without question. Rico heads to rescue her, and destroys the base where she is held. However, Jade is bundled into a truck and a fleet of gunmen attempt to make a getaway along a frozen lake. En route, a nuclear submarine emerges from the ice, but Rico hijacks the truck carrying Jade, and they are both airlifted to safety by Sheldon and Kane  Later, Jade reveals that the Roaches, Reapers, and Ular Boys are secretly being supported by benefactors of Russia, China, and Japan respectively in an effort to bring down Panay, and Rico and Sheldon wonder what the small nation that is Panau has that is able to attract such dominant superpowers. Nonetheless, Rico and Sheldon track down the foreign intelligence officers liaising with the factions and assassinate them. Soon after, the island is amidst so much chaos that Panay is forced to leave the capital and take refuge in his fortified military base. Enlisting the aid of the factions, whether it be from the Ular Boys, Reapers, or the Roaches, Rico assaults Panay's hideout, but all of Rico's followers are killed during the raid. Panay is apparently killed during the assault by Karl Blaine in a murder-suicide, and Rico discovers that Russia, China, Japan, and the US have been secretly fighting over Panau for its oil supply, which is supposedly the richest in the world.
With Panay dead, the situation in Panau turns into a free-for-all as foreign nations scramble to claim the oil. Russia, China, and Japan send a fleet of supertankers to Panau, while the U.S. begins scrambling military forces to defend the island. Rico is tasked with holding off the supertankers until reinforcements arrive. However, a nuclear submarine surfaces from the sea. Rico investigates the submarine and discovers Panay, who is still alive but injured from Karl Blaine's suicide attack. Panay proceeds to fire four nuclear missiles at Russia, China, Japan, and the U.S., but his clothing is accidentally snagged on one of the missiles and he is hauled off with it. In pursuit, Rico grapples onto one of them and both men battle in mid air as Rico disarms each missile one by one. Finally, on the U.S. missile, Rico pins Panay into the exposed missile core and reprograms the targeting computer before leaping to safety. The final missile changes course and explodes over Panau's oil fields, killing Panay and destroying Panau's oil reserves. Rico reunites with Sheldon, Kane and Jade, who express their dismay at this decision as the oil was worth billions, but Rico explains that the oil is not worth dying over, and now that it's destroyed, all interest in Panau will be lost, preventing a war between the major superpowers and sparing the innocents of the island. Sheldon agrees, and assures Rico that a US-friendly president will be installed on Panau, and that the nation will be closely monitored. The group raise their glasses, to good friends, and a job well done.
Development
Eidos originally announced a Christmas 2008 release date for Just Cause 2. However, on October 10, 2008, Eurogamer reported that Just Cause 2 was pushed back to 2009, and later, 2010. On November 24, Square-Enix announced that the game was set to be released in North America on March 23, 2010, three days later on March 26, 2010 in Europe, Middle East, and Asia, six days later on April 1, 2010 in Australia and New Zealand, and June 10, 2010 in Japan.
The PC version only runs on DirectX 10 hardware and is thus incompatible with Windows XP. It supports several features and graphical effects that are missing from the console versions such as screen space ambient occlusion, soft shadows and increased detail. Compatible Nvidia graphics cards additionally support Bokeh lens effects, enhanced water simulation and stereoscopic 3-D.

Final Fantasy X and X-2 are some of the most iconic games there are in existence, let alone the Final Fantasy series. This review will talk more about the differences between the Steam release and the original PS2 games, but in short, Final Fantasy X is a completely standalone game from the other games in the Final Fantasy series, and X-2 leads on from where X left off. Final Fantasy X sees you play as Tidus, a Blitzball payer from Zanarkand who gets flung into the world of Spira where he must assist Yuna on her pilgrimage to defeat Sin. X-2 switches control to Yuna, who has formed a group of Sphere Hunters with old friend Rikku and new friend Paine.
All in all, this is a pretty decent port. There's only 'partial' controller support, but the only important things that can't be controlled using a controller are the new boosters. Both keyboard and controller controls are bindable, which is very nice. There's multiple language selections, with both English and Japanese audio. The Japanese is a little buggy, though modders are already hard at work fixing that. For some reason, when I fired the game up for the first time, the game defaulted to Japanese text. This includes menu navigation, which can make it a little confusing to change back to English. Hopefully this is just a glitch, and not intended behaviour. Additionally, my game defaulted to a 1280x760 windowed resolution with 'low' graphic settings. This can easily be changed, but nonetheless is a slight gripe that others may encounter. Another nice feature of the port is achievements. The PS3 and PS4 versions had trophies, but the Steam version adds achievements for the truly hardcore players to try and complete. Can you get them all?
This Steam version is the equivalent of the PS3 & PS4's HD remaster, with a few differences. The HD remaster attempts to modernise the original PS2 game by improving the musical score and the graphics. Whether or not these are an improvement over the original music and graphics in the PS2 version is open to debate. Some of the new music sounds really great, but it naturally won't have the nostalgia of the original music -- there really is quite a difference. However, in this version all of the audio channels are on sliders. Want to increase the SFX while decreasing the background music? Now you can! The graphics are undoubtedly a vast improvement over the background objects from the original, with some smoother edges to the characters. Unfortunately, the character's eyes have been completely re-done, and in the process appear to have lost all emotion. Despite the facial 'improvements', they still haven't fixed the problem with the lip-syncing from the original Japanese audio to the English audio. The Steam version builds on the HD Remaster by allowing you to further customise the graphics, with adjustments to things such as screen resolution, brightness, shadow quality and anti-aliasing.
There were a number of exclusives to the original PS2 game based on geographic region. The Steam version is based on the International Version, meaning you have access to them all! In Final Fantasy X, there's access to the new Expert Sphere Grid, for advanced players already familiar with the original game. There's also 10 new powerful optional bosses, plus one new powerful super-boss to track down and defeat. Included in the game selection menu is a video that fills in a bit of the story between the two games, along with some developer interviews as well. Finally, there are a few new skills for you to try out on the Sphere Grid. Final Fantasy X-2 boasts new Dresspheres, along with a new 'Creature Creator' and Field Arena tournaments. Now you can train monsters to fight alongside you! While it does make the game quite a bit easier, it is a nice new feature to play around with. There's also a brand new mission in Final Fantasy X-2 to try out, available from the game selection menu.
In addition to the features from the International Version, the Steam version adds a number of features that none of the previous versions have. These come in the form of 'boosters', that previous Steam Final Fantasy players may be familiar with. Essentially, they're little add-ons that make the game easier for you. In Final Fantasy X, you have a turbo mode that will increase the game by 2x or 4x speed, an option to always perform overdrives, an option to eliminate or change the rate of encounters, an option to have the characters battle automatically for you, and an option to disable the HUD. While the turbo feature can really come in handy on your 20th playthrough of the game, it sadly doesn't fast-forward through cut-scenes or FMVs, only actual gameplay. Some FMVs can be skipped, which is nice. The other features do feel a little like cheating, but some may find benefit in their use. If you really want to cheat, there's the option to max out your items, max out your Gil, and teach your characters all abilities.
These two games are absolutely amazing, and this port does a decent job at bringing these classics to Steam. The price is cheap, and the games are well worth the money. For the games themselves, I'd give Final Fantasy X a 10/10, and Final Fantasy X-2 an 8/10. With regards to the Steam port, I'd give it a 7/10. If you haven't played either of the games before, I say that you simply must try them out. If you have played them before, you already know how amazing they are, so what are you waiting for? Go ahead and pick up this release right now! :)

Also optionally, [Z], [~], [Z], [~] (now you have an extra bullet, 7 in the magazine, one in the chamber.
I was joking about how awkward it might seem at first, but after playing this for a while, it becomes surprisingly easy and fun. And if you ever get stuck, just hold [?] (or actually just [/]), to see what you need to do to get the weapon ready to fire.

In short, I love Dark Souls, but this doesn't feel like Dark Souls.
And now I present to you the longer version: The game tries to be like the original, but it relies on cheap and unfair gimmicks to make up for the fact that it is not a difficult game.
Where to start with this attrocity?
In the beginning I had no idea where to go. I wandered around in Majula for what seemed like ages until I found my way.
I had no idea why I was doing anything. The exposition from the hag in the opening cinematic even says, "But one day, you will stand before its decrepit gate. Without really knowing why..."
The basic mechanic of dodge-rolling is dependant on the agility stat. Until that stat reaches 105, your rolling is pathetic. Unless you intend on hiding behind a shield through the entire game, you must reach that soft cap before you can truly level up your other stats.
Statues block your every path forcing you to release the petrified victim with a rare/expensive item in order to proceed. Many of these statues lead nowhere, where as some are necessary to progress.
DS2 recycles bosses from DS1.
You are frequently invaded by NPCs with provocation.
Most enemies are too easy on their own, so you are forced into fighting multiple of the same enemy at the same time.
There are many death traps that serve no other purpose than to slow your progression.
Nearly all bosses are just some guy with armor and a weapon and are defeated the same way.
Bosses become become common enemies after defeating them because the game HAS to try to be hard.
Ornstein, no Smough!
Poison is EVERYWHERE!
Several enemies only exist to specifically destroy your armor while dealing little to no damage, not acting as a threat but rather a nuisance.
You can easily get caught on the terrain and be killed because of it.
The unbreakable Dragon Tooth weapon weilded by Havel, I mean Woodland Child Gully, is literally as durable as a wooden club.
Most NPCs are miserable ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s.
You start with a single estus flask. Drinking from it takes an unfairly long amount of time.
You will frequantly die after drinking from your flask due to the slow healing rate.
Fog gates litter the land with no other purpose than to obscure your view of the next room whether it's safe or not.
You can be killed while walking through a fog gate.
After defeating a boss, all previously aggroed enemies will storm into the boss room and murder you.
You can not farm for souls since enemies stop respawning after being killed so many times. This can really punish people who are not too great at the game and need to grind some souls to increase their stats.
Attacking a mimic in the back will result in it still grabbing you even though it only reaches out in front of itself.
Poison is like toxic, and toxic is like curse.
Every time you die you lose up to 10% of your maximum health.
You will be stun locked time and time again if you do not stack poise.
A swarm of rats is a boss, lolwut?
The land is not connected. You will go through multiple cutscenes of traveling methods showing how disconnected the land is.
You need to equip a specific ring every time you want to go through a certain door.
Controls can be unresponsive or cause you to do things you never intended, such as using "X" to use an item when you actually hit "B" to roll.
You will fight the same NPC invaders time and time again.
The ending credits kept flashing on the screen giving me a headache.
I could go on forever about this game's flaws, but I'll save you the trouble by ending it here and warning you to skip this sequal. Your sanity is not worth it!

Just Cause 2 is an action-adventure video game developed by Avalanche Studios, published by Eidos Interactive, and distributed by Square Enix. It is the sequel to the 2006 video game Just Cause.
Just Cause 2 employs the Avalanche Engine 2.0, an updated version of the engine used in Just Cause. Rico Rodriguez returns as the protagonist, aiming to overthrow the evil dictator Pandak "Baby" Panay and confront his former mentor, Tom Sheldon.
Notable features of Just Cause 2 include the grappling hook, which gives players the ability to tether objects to each other. For example, in a high speed vehicle chase, the player can use the grappling hook to attach a pursuing vehicle to the ground, forcing it to stop and often flipping or turning the vehicle causing damage to it. The grappling hook also allows the player to pull himself, and hold onto objects such as walls or helicopters.
In addition, the player has a parachute which is always ready to be deployed, even if it has been deployed and discarded only moments before. This can be combined with the grappling hook and used as a fast method of transport.
The PlayStation 3 version of the game allows the user to capture video of their gameplay and either export it to the XMB or upload it to YouTube from within the game.
Plot
Just Cause 2 is set four years after the first Just Cause, with Agency operative Rico Rodriguez being dropped into Panau, a fictional dystopian island nation in Maritime Southeast Asia. Formerly a U.S. ally, Panau is ruled by Pandak "Baby" Panay  who institutes a harsh, oppressive dictatorship and cuts off all ties to the United States due to his Anti-American views. Rico's mission is to oust Panay from office, as well as track down and assassinate his old mentor, Tom Sheldon, who the Agency fears has gone rogue after disappearing during the regime change. In order to find Sheldon, Rico allies himself with the three dominant criminal gangs on the island: the Roaches, an organized crime syndicate, the Reapers, an insurgent Socialist militia and the Ular Boys, an ultranationalist rebel group that espouses traditionalism and opposes foreign influence. He gathers enough information to track down Sheldon, who not only reveals that he's been investigating a larger conspiracy behind Panau, but that he is in fact the "Sloth Demon", the Black Market dealer that often calls Rico to give information on the gangs and that Rico calls to be provided with weapons and vehicles . Rico establishes that Sheldon has not gone rogue, and Sheldon tells him to continue causing chaos on Panau while he goes to explain the situation to the Agency.
After clearing everything up, Sheldon demands that Rico quickly make his way over to his hideout. They tell him that Jade Tan, a mysterious Agency asset whom Rico had met earlier, has been caught in Panay's military base, and is to be tortured and possibly killed without question. Rico heads to rescue her, and destroys the base where she is held. However, Jade is bundled into a truck and a fleet of gunmen attempt to make a getaway along a frozen lake. En route, a nuclear submarine emerges from the ice, but Rico hijacks the truck carrying Jade, and they are both airlifted to safety by Sheldon and Kane  Later, Jade reveals that the Roaches, Reapers, and Ular Boys are secretly being supported by benefactors of Russia, China, and Japan respectively in an effort to bring down Panay, and Rico and Sheldon wonder what the small nation that is Panau has that is able to attract such dominant superpowers. Nonetheless, Rico and Sheldon track down the foreign intelligence officers liaising with the factions and assassinate them. Soon after, the island is amidst so much chaos that Panay is forced to leave the capital and take refuge in his fortified military base. Enlisting the aid of the factions, whether it be from the Ular Boys, Reapers, or the Roaches, Rico assaults Panay's hideout, but all of Rico's followers are killed during the raid. Panay is apparently killed during the assault by Karl Blaine in a murder-suicide, and Rico discovers that Russia, China, Japan, and the US have been secretly fighting over Panau for its oil supply, which is supposedly the richest in the world.
With Panay dead, the situation in Panau turns into a free-for-all as foreign nations scramble to claim the oil. Russia, China, and Japan send a fleet of supertankers to Panau, while the U.S. begins scrambling military forces to defend the island. Rico is tasked with holding off the supertankers until reinforcements arrive. However, a nuclear submarine surfaces from the sea. Rico investigates the submarine and discovers Panay, who is still alive but injured from Karl Blaine's suicide attack. Panay proceeds to fire four nuclear missiles at Russia, China, Japan, and the U.S., but his clothing is accidentally snagged on one of the missiles and he is hauled off with it. In pursuit, Rico grapples onto one of them and both men battle in mid air as Rico disarms each missile one by one. Finally, on the U.S. missile, Rico pins Panay into the exposed missile core and reprograms the targeting computer before leaping to safety. The final missile changes course and explodes over Panau's oil fields, killing Panay and destroying Panau's oil reserves. Rico reunites with Sheldon, Kane and Jade, who express their dismay at this decision as the oil was worth billions, but Rico explains that the oil is not worth dying over, and now that it's destroyed, all interest in Panau will be lost, preventing a war between the major superpowers and sparing the innocents of the island. Sheldon agrees, and assures Rico that a US-friendly president will be installed on Panau, and that the nation will be closely monitored. The group raise their glasses, to good friends, and a job well done.
Development
Eidos originally announced a Christmas 2008 release date for Just Cause 2. However, on October 10, 2008, Eurogamer reported that Just Cause 2 was pushed back to 2009, and later, 2010. On November 24, Square-Enix announced that the game was set to be released in North America on March 23, 2010, three days later on March 26, 2010 in Europe, Middle East, and Asia, six days later on April 1, 2010 in Australia and New Zealand, and June 10, 2010 in Japan.
The PC version only runs on DirectX 10 hardware and is thus incompatible with Windows XP. It supports several features and graphical effects that are missing from the console versions such as screen space ambient occlusion, soft shadows and increased detail. Compatible Nvidia graphics cards additionally support Bokeh lens effects, enhanced water simulation and stereoscopic 3-D.

This is a great way to learn the mechanics of a modern firearm. Reloading is much more fun than the standard 'reload button'.
Take the magine out, place bullets in the magazine, or get a full magazine, put the magazine in the weapon, chamber a round by releasing the slide. So, in stead of pressing R to reload, you perform the incredibly intuitive  [E], [~], [Z],[Z],[Z],[Z],[Z],[Z],[Z],[~], [Z], [R]. Optionally, Hold [T] and press [R] to check if the round is chambered. Also optionally, [Z], [~], [Z], [~] (now you have an extra bullet, 7 in the magazine, one in the chamber.
I was joking about how awkward it might seem at first, but after playing this for a while, it becomes surprisingly easy and fun. And if you ever get stuck, just hold [?] (or actually just [/]), to see what you need to do to get the weapon ready to fire.

The game markets itself as a great big mystery. You come home, and your parents and sister are not there. Surely there will be some deep reasoning behind this... WRONG. Your parents are
and your sister
which you can EASILY guess within 30 minutes of playing the game. Other than that the game tries to make you think there is some significance to the former owner of the house,
however there really isn't any. Also, this game has horrible optimization. You can look at screenshots to see this game is by no means winning any awards in the graphics department, yet my PC which can run pretty much any modern AAA game at High to Max Settings at 1080p and 60fps, gets framerate drops to 40 fps!

I'm the type of gamer who isn't into the usual 'shooters' (barring Half Life series, Mass Effect series, and their ilk that have engaging stories and role playing adventures). So games like "Vanishing of Ethan Carter" and "Gone Home" really speak to me. I really appreciate the story delving into experiences that aren't often included in North American overculture, particularly ones that feature female leading characters. If you are seeking a different kind of gaming experience, one that focuses more on story, mystery, and discovery, this game is for you. This is a game for indie fans.
Only draw backs are the puzzle elements aren't too much of a challenege, and the game is short. I completed it in about 2 hours, and I thought I was "taking my time" really exploring everything.
There were some creepy moments, especially when you enter dark rooms and can't find the light switches, the TV's are playing looping messages, and other subtle but effective "jumpy" experiences. The voice acting, art, and stories were very well crafted and believable. This is truly a story that could have happened, and most likely has, representing a well produced piece of historical fiction.
As I was also a teenager in the mid-1990's, it was very nostalgic to see references to homemade "casette tapes" and references to Kurt Cobain, 'zines, and punk/grunge bands of that area. The game creators captured the ambience of that area well.
Give this game 30 minutes, and it will blow your mind.

I really wanted to like Homefront: The Revolution too. And I do... to a point. Unfortunately, there's also a lot not to like. It's a shame too, since it feels like given a few more months of work, The Revolution could have been a real winner.
What I liked:
- The idea for the story is something I can get behind. However it wasn't well explained, and there were gaps missing which were left to the imagination.
- It's an open world FPS, like modern Far Cry games, Dying Light, Middle-earth: Shadow of Mordor, etc. I don't mind that they took the series in a new direction, although I was surprised.
- The artwork, voice acting, etc. were (for the most part) top notch.
- No in-game nagging for DLC content. There was actually no mention of DLC at all in-game. Good.
- Hidden Time Splitters 2 game, available from Extras under the main menu once unlocked.
What I disliked:
- Bugs. Bugs everywhere! Let's see...
I fell through the floor a few times. I once got stuck in the level causing me to need to restart from a checkpoint. Enemies sometimes fell through the floor after they died. There is a part where you need to stand in line, but the people in front of you get stuck and you can't pass - you have to reload a save (twice, in my case) to continue, with no ability to skip a lengthy cut scene. There was plenty of AI pathing issues. Enemies in the distance would spawn and de-spawning whenever they felt like it (even when looking right at them) making sniping from any significant distance useless. Some jobs could not be achieved if they were not attempted early in the game. Some achievements only activated upon closing the game, leading me to retry things I unknowingly already achieved.
At one point the game loaded a checkpoint without me telling it to (and without me dying). The game also crashed to the desktop multiple times. One time the game would not show anything on screen at launch (but the process was running in the background and had to be killed off through Task Manager). Explosives could be selected when you had none, which caused strange hand animations suggesting the player was carrying something invisible.
One issue I found one time was that I was unable to get back on a motorcycle because I accidentally drove it a few centimetres outside of the mission area, even though I was standing right next to it and there was no other motorcycle nearby. At another point I had to load a previous checkpoint because an audio loop (beeping indicating the close proximity to a Resistance stash) wouldn't stop playing once the stash was found and I had walked away.
Consider the game beta quality at best. It's really no wonder the game received such bad reviews in the face of so many problems. I didn't even try multiplayer!
- Still no sign of the promised GNU/Linux support. If the game had this at launch, I would have purchased it despite the bugs.
- Inability to fast travel to any point to the map which has been captured. Travelling to try to finish off uncompleted jobs is frustrating. Selecting a destination on the map is not remembered when you die and re-spawn. Further, the map is not accessible on the motorcycle.
- The store menu is a pain. If you want to purchase 10 consumable items (such as explosives), you need to select the explosive, confirm the purchase, and repeat this 10 times. I didn't even notice how to get to the job menu until late in the game due to the bad layout. If you don't specifically look for the active jobs menu, you won't notice it. You can also die looking at the menu, even though the game audio has stopped and you are in a single-player campaign.
- Gun-play needs work. It's more frustrating than it should be. If you're using the shotgun, there's one guy left nearby and you need to reload, the game won't let you insert just one or two shells and fire away - you need to fill it up completely with shells before the reload animation will stop and you can fire. This caused me to die on many occasions.
If an airship spots you, enemies will spawn from all around you almost instantly - even from areas you know you just cleared out. This forces you to play in a trigger-happy style, but the gun-play is not well geared for it.
Grenade and cover systems are horrible for keyboard+mouse. There is also no “Hold to duck” key binding option, so duck can only be toggled.
- Dying is frustrating. You won't generally lose much progress, but repawning takes too long. When you die, the game is unresponsive for a few seconds, eventually some text slowly fades in telling you to press enter. If you press enter too early (ie. before the text has fully faded in) the key press won't register. And you can't press or click any other button to continue - only enter will work. This causes me to constantly bash the key in frustration! Next, the game will start loading the level again. On my overclocked i7-6700k, that takes another 10 or so seconds I guess.
For me, this is perhaps the single most frustrating part of the entire game. If you die in a single player campaign, you should always be able to get back in the action immediately.
- No Crossfire support. It's 2016, and this isn't a Bethesda title (which typically run amazingly well even on a single GPU anyway). If you want to call yourself a AAA developer, Crossfire is the expectation. I played the game at 2560x1440 on a Fury X with basically everything maxed out, and I was getting anything from just under 40 FPS to just under 60 FPS. That's significantly worse than running Far Cry Primal on a single Fury X. Of course, Far Cry Primal can use Crossfire anyway.
- Lack of originality. The story was fine (although the last few minutes were somewhat painful), but the general game mechanics (capturing structures, unlocking parts of the map, finding hidden loot, etc. all feels a bit too familiar. This isn't in itself a problem provided there is also something new brought to the table, or the overall approach is polished and improved in some way. Unfortunately that just hasn't happened here, and actually a lot of the similarities to comparable titles seem like a step backwards. Obviously Ubisoft is a massive company with a lot of experience in making these types of games, so I'm not at all surprised that Homefront hasn't turned out better than a Far Cry experience. However Homefront developers should have anticipated this and provided something new to compensate.
- The original Homefront advertised the game with a metal compilation CD including tracks such as a Metalica cover by Periphery. Sadly, that never received much promotion, is no longer available and doesn't even appear to have been attempted for The Revolution.
- The textures all seem to be high resolution and generally look great, but occasionally I came across something strange. eg. a truck that was completely green, including the tires. The shading was drawn correctly, but possibly the textures were missing. It's unclear if that was another bug or the artwork was unfinished.
- Parkour really isn't a strong point here. The Revolution has it, but feels very limited compared to what the Far Cry and Dying Light universes offer. Climbing a building is generally a matter of walking around the outside of it (and nearby buildings) looking for a wooden ramp, as opposed to trying to perform risky manoeuvres from a great height. It all feels very dumbed down. The game also imposes significant impact damage if you fall.
- No benchmark mode.
In summary, the game feels like a poor-man's Far Cry. It's frustrating, both because the game causes you frustration, and also because the game feels like it was very close to becoming something much greater than it turned out to be.

So many thoughts on Gone Home but I'm going with a vague review to not spoil the experience.
Your character arrives "Home" to a house she has never been in before this late stormy night.  The house is completely empty.  Unpacked moving boxes linger throughout the house.  Someone has left a message on the answering machine pleading in panic/fear for your sister to answer the phone.  You explore the house.  You discover things about the house and your family.  You experience an existential dread of what may have happened to your family, and, if their fate will be your own.  You hear sounds of something in the house.  You explore and learn more.  You start to fear the worst with your mind manufacturing the worst possible scenarios and outcomes.  You continue on.
This was my experience with the first 2-3 hours of Gone Home.
Continuing on, you begin to realize that things are not quite what you had feared, but you still expect the worst as many of those horrible scenarios you conceived are still completely possible and you need to see, read, and hear the truth.  The only way to do that is to go forward unflinchingly.  All is revealed in the end.
(So, I really enjoyed Gone Home, and I hate to label or price out the hard work of others, but in a fair review for people who have not yet purchased Gone Home, I do have to say that the $19.99 price point feels too high.  Gone Home is a great experience, and while I understand and appreciate the hard work that Fullbright put into Gone Home, I think that, at minimum, $14.99 would be a more appropriate price to value ratio.  I don't personally remember the price point at which I purchased it, but I believe it was around $9.99 or even $7.99.  I feel I got my time and money's worth.)

Receiver is excellent. The gameplay is one of the most unique and tense things I've played all year. The gun mechanics are obviously the big selling point for this game, and they work quite well. Figuring out how to work the weapons is quite satisfying and within an hour or so I was able to operate each of the weapons without relying on the on-screen help. There are 11 tapes to collect to 'win' but these are scattered around the randomized world and surviving the robots long enough to collect them is not easy. Each death starts you over in a new world with different starting conditions and each of the pistols play differently and require you to adjust your strategy from try to try. It all comes together as you push forward with little or no ammo, dodging behind whatever cover you can find to avoid robots while scrounging for supplies and making sure every shot counts.

I know this is an unpopular opinion (like the fact I think season 7 of The Walking Dead was one of the best seasons of the show) but I simply can't like this game.
So let me start by saying this: I LOVE Dark Souls series. The first game was challenging, fun, and extremely interesting. I feel like FromSoftware made this game and decided that it was going to be their last, but after realizing they screwed it up, made a (very awesome) third game. This game feels very alien to the DS series. The bosses are a joke, having the toughest bosses (Flexile Sentry and The Rotten) up front as your first few boss battles, then EVERY boss after that is easy as heck (Except the Chariot boss, haven't fought him yet. I'm doing another run-through to find the Chariot boss). The game's poor balance makes for a very awkward play while the lack of a proper lore really makes the game a "beat it as fast as you can" type because it is very easy to lose interest in games without an interesting story behind it. The one apsect of this game that drives the nail in the coffin is its play on the humanity system. You die, you lose maximum health (the more hollowed you are). So after about 3-4 deaths, your max health is 75% (and it doesn't stop there, more deaths and it will keep lowering). I say skip this game entirely unless you are VERY bored. Play Dark Souls -> Dark Souls 3 THEN maybe play this game. But I just can't get myself to recommend it. Sorry, guys.
After playing another 20+ hours of the game, I have started noticing things I have not before, mainly with the difficulty. Dark Souls is known to be tough, but also very strategic. Dark Souls II simply lacks that. For example, go into Black Gulch (the reskin of blighttown), notice anything? The enemeies (including statue) are spammed everywhere. There's no strategy to how they place them. They are literally just spammed across the map. If this had been in Dark Souls 1 or 3, there would be some fake statues placed to make the player memorize which are fake and which are real. This game doesn't do that. Instead, Dark Souls II relies on the player hitting everything in sight. That's not very fun. This game is difficult just to be difficult, there's no logic or reason other than to enrage the player.
Another major issue I have with the game is the lack of mimic chests. Those were always something that I got paranoid about, you know? Like, you run up to a chest and you accidentally open it without thinking and get munched on by a horrendous creature. In this game, it has removed mimic chests (or at least I can't find any) so there isn't any punishment for trust.
The Scholar of the First Sin also makes this game more annoying with the amount of NPC invasions. I kill one, he somehow respawns in the world. Doesn't make sense other than to give the player a harder time.

It's okay. It's a decently executed exploration mechanic, in a well executed, yet mundane, atmosphere, where piece by piece you uncover what turns out to be an unremarkable an uninteresting story.
What it does well:
+Atmosphere. It captures the irrational eeriness of walking around a dark and unfamiliar home perhaps too well. Don't be misled into thinking it's an actual scary game, though. It's exactly as creepy as walking around the basement alone at night. The house feels old, mysterious, and creepy, and the premise of the game (you coming home from school to a different house) perfectly sets you up for the feeling of exploring a place you're a stranger in, but are allowed to be in.
+Exploration. Your "progress" (a loose term, in this game) in the game unfolds smoothly as you discover information and explore the house.
+Voice acting. There's roughly one voice actor in the game, and she knocks it out of the park.
What it does okay:
+ Details. There's a lot of detail in the house that make it feel real and lived in, and lots of small things to discover which help to piece together a picture of the family. Some objects relate to each other really elegantly and naturally, which help make the house feel like more than just box of independent 3D models. However, you quickly learn that the ability to pick up and examine a roll of toiler paper is just a novelty for filler, and sorting the wheat from the chaff becomes your main objective.
What it does poorly:
-Logic. The family clearly recently moved into the house, but there are also indications they've been living there for several months at least. Also, there are years old letters and notes just lying in random places that would barely make sense normally, but make none at all if they'd recently moved. And the girl hiding a secret from her parents is amazingly comfortable leaving personal notes literally all over the place.
-Story. It's just not very interesting, but it's presented like it's momentous. The central plot is about your younger sister falling in love with another girl at school. (That's not a spoiler. I'd assumed as much from watching the trailer, and it becomes obvious quickly.) I'm certain that some people will find it personally meaningful, but if you're not particularly interested in a teenage girl's crush or the ensuing stereotypical conflict with her parents, you'll be starved for something to care about. There are some side bits about the house and the rest of the family, but the game shows no interest in developing those into interesting stories. They're ultimately just background detail in the same vein as the toilet paper in the cupboard.
-Storytelling. The backstory for the rest of the family is discovered organically, but the central story about your sister is largely handed down through audio diaries that materialize in your head at certain points. It feels a little heavy handed for a game so clearly designed to be about exploratory narrative. It isn't clear what these audio sections are supposed to represent, or whether your character is supposed to be aware of them (as opposed to just you, the player). Finding that out was actually the most interesting part of the ending for me.
Bottom line: I can't recommend, because it's just not interesting enough. It's great to see a game try to be more about exploration, but it doesn't do that well enough to be amazing. And the story being told is mediocre. The only thing it excels at is atmosphere, but the atmosphere in question isn't remarkable. It's just a house with the lights turned off, which isn't exactly like being transported to another world.
Get it on sale if you're *really* curious, but don't expect much.

Is it Dark Souls? Yes

Is there still an active community? You won't always struggle to find sunbros, or to get invaded, but it is certainly harder after DS3 came out.
Is it worth the buy?

Fans of the Souls series will have to take some time to get used to the changes here, but in the end, that's part of the fun. If you're like me and you don't want to get soft banned after spending $60 on DS3, spend $40 on this instead, it's well worth your time.

Played the game from start to finish on Deathwish difficulty during the free weekend. I'm glad I waited, because it's fantastic.
I know the game was off to a troubled start, and so I waited until the invetible free wekend after the latest (as of Sep 11, 2016) patch to try the game out.
Finally, after all these patches, the game is now complete. And it's pretty good.
The combat is rock solid - I love the feel of the weapons. Some of them aren't really viable, but they're fun to play around with anyways. The story seems to jump around a lot towards the end, but it was overall coherent and emotional. Not Oscar-level, but good enough to keep me interested.
You really do get the feeling of a desperate, scrappy urban combat. The difficulty ramps up nicely and I always felt challenged. Being able to recruit up to 4 resistance members to chum around with takes the game from good to great - the game is nearly impossible on the hardest difficulty without support and knowing when to just run.
Overall, I would say this game is as good as Far Cry 3 - maybe even better, since I prefer the urban combat.

A quick disclaimer; it's been a long time since I've played this thing. However, in viewing this store page, I had some thoughts to share.
The developers put an INSANE amount of detail into this game. You can interact with just about anything. Papers in desks? Yes, you can pick them up, and you can read them, and each paper will have a different story to tell. Coffee cup? Go ahead, pick it up. You don't even have to put it back. This game clones the experience of looking around someone's house for clues into their lives. Gone Home uses this element to tell a story in a way no other game does.
That said, Gone Home does leave something to be desired, as many people have pointed out in their reviews. The story will likely disappoint you. It tries to go somewhere most games stay away from, but doesn't make much of a meaningful statement. Don't let that ruin the experience for you. Gone Home is the Avatar of gaming. The story is plain, but the visual experience is unprecedented and unforgettable.

Welcome to Freddy Fazbear's Pizza, where animatronics, no matter how much of a state of disrepair they are in, run around at night, completely ignoring the wet floor signs, simply to murder a single guy who's just trying to earn his paycheck.
Five Nights at Freddy's 2, whilst not as good as it's predecessor, really brings a lot to the table. It's amazing at building stress, particularly on the earlier nights. This is mainly because of the fact that you have no real way to protect yourself. There are different routines you have to carry out to fend off the animatronics, such as quickly placing Freddy's dismembered head upon yours, which will soon be dismembered if you didn't catch that millisecond time window, which can be quite frustrating. The story is amazing, but it's got as many holes as a minefield, but they may be answered in the third installment, which I hope to god is the last one. A fourth one just isn't necessary. The game is quite scary, so I wouldn't recommend it if you're easily scared, but if you think you're ready for Freddy, then go ahead.
In my opinion I'd give overall a 7/10.
