SOME MINOR SPOILERS HERE: But then again, the whole plot is very small in and of itself, so it's likely most of the plot I'll be spoiling anyways.
This game is interesting in a number of ways and there's a few things I like about the atmosphere, although I think some things might be unintentional. One of the problems though is that the gameplay is literally just walking around pointing and clicking on things and interacting with objects, which could be interesting at times, but often ends up being pointless and there's really not as much hidden stuff in it as a game like this should have.
The story is okay, I suppose. It could have - and should have been written better though. First of all, the game's atmosphere freaked me out and made me feel like I was in a horror game - empty house with all the lights turned off, tonnes of supernatural objects throughout the house, including conspiracy theory stuff, a Ouija board, and an alien poster. At one part you turn a light out in a small dark corridor, and the light shuts off promptly. There's loud thunder sounds at times and the music is subtly unsettling. There is a lot of mention of your pscho uncle, but this is never really explained in the game. Instead, the game is based around clues you find which although sidetrack to give you information on the family and your own character, they are almost always entirely focused on your sister's relationship with a punky military girl named Lorrie. Although I did enjoy elements of the diary at this point, some of it being cutesy, there were points in which it was absolutely too cheesy or too forced, especially the ridiculous ending in which Lorrie ditches her bus, and subsequently the military, which she had been passionate about, because she suddenly felt an overwhelming feeling that Sam (your sister) is more important despite not feeling this way leading right up to this point. I couldn't suspend my disbelief for this, even for the fact at how risky it is to dodge the military. Not only this, but leading up to this point, the game really hints there's going to be much more, and there isn't. I was almost wanting a Five Nights at Freddy's jumpscare where I'd least expect it just to keep me interested enough to enjoy the game. This game is basically Sucker Punch - The Game.
There was also a bit of SJW feminist propoganda sprinkled throughout the game - such as girly magazines claiming to allow you to "subvert a man's gaze" and short stories and a comic featuring women who are strong and don't need no man. I'm totally cool with LGBT stuff, but I've always been anti-feminism. Feminism isn't about equality - it's about putting men down and raising women above men, focusing on men's faults and ignoring those of women. The fact of the matter is that women aren't perfect, and neither are the characters in this game, and that's fine. But I can't help but feel that if it were male characters the game was dealing with, then the entire plot would have been handled differently.
The game was also much too short. There's a lot of little things in it that aren't even worth looking at that fill up the game, like any food items or most notes in the game or basically anything that doesn't have a code written on it or a map of secret passageways. Even if you do explore every single aspect of the game possible, this would only constitute maybe four or five hours of gameplay if you REALLY take your time inspecting every last detail. I got this game for about $3, and I think that's as much as I think is worth spending on this game to consider it a decent value. $20 is basically robbery, and I think I'll have to not reccomend this game mostly for that reason.
Other than that, the time period felt right. The game did feel very 90's and had a lot of little things accurate and relevant to the time periods it was referencing. References to things like The X Files and NES games are sure to hit people right in the nostaligia bone, but reminiscing aside, there isn't much more to it. It keeps you in it to the point where you're interested enough to keep playing and searching for things, but also at the point where you feel you might become board enough to stop. It's an overwhelmingly mediocre experience and a bittersweet nostalgia trip.
Pros:
-Creepy atmosphere.
-Decent voice acting, for the most part.
-The aesthetics of the notes and drawings felt believable, and often cute or funny.
-The characters are almost likeable at times.
-Decent story.
Cons:
-Simple point and click puzzles throughout.
-Completely linear, with no replay value whatsoever.
-Incredibly short.
-Game has many misleading elements and lots of red herrings.
-I pretty much didn't like any of the music whatsoever.
-The ending could easily have been done much better.
-SJW propoganda.
-Not enough easter eggs considering how much potential there is for a game like this.
-$20 price tag is way too high.

-First note, this is not Pay 2 Win- This game is pretty garbarge, unless you like co-op. What do I like about this game? The co-op. Thats it. And its pretty similar to survival from CoD. And in my opinion this game is basically CoD: Ghosts, only with worse graphics and debatably worse maps.
Now lets talk about the maps. They are smaller versions of cod ghosts maps. So basically its like combining the chaos of Nuketown and adding the camping of CoD Ghosts. Everyone camps. Thats how people get high scores basically. Also there is another mechanic that is in this game. Sliding. Now sliding is incredibly op, and you can take down any player with sliding and maybe proning.
Now lets talk about the guns. For one, the hit detection is AWFUL. Sometimes it will take 2 seconds for bullets to register. The guns also do very low damage (except for snipers and a couple rifles rifle). This can be very very annoying if you are running engineer with the starter SMG, (by the way, there are 4 classes. Sniper, Medic, Engineer, and Rifleman, which I will get to later) then its really annoying because it has lots of recoil, (more than in almost any game i've played) and takes around 10 bullets to kill with a 30 bullet magazine. Not to mention the guns aren't very accurate. So basically with the starter SMG you can only get about 1 maybe 2 kills with it.
The Sniping. Its pretty bad, considering that it wavers really weirdly and its uncontrollable. It just takes to long to hit someone.
Explosives: the grenades have range even more than CoD4, and they're pretty dang OP. The claymores are more overpowered than in cod, so take it or leave it as you wish
Now lets talk about classes. Like I mentioned before there are 4 classes. The sniper is pretty straightforward. A 1-2 shot knife (there is a right and left click attack for the knife), a grenade, and of course, a sniper.  Every class has a grenade, and the Rifleman is I believe to be the only class without  knife. The Engineer has an SMG, a claymore, and grenade. The starting smg is pretty horrible (like I mentioned before) with the bad hitreg, high recoil, and low damage, and he also can restore armor. Later SMG's are really OP and do high dmg with better mags. The Rifleman is a pretty straightforward class. He comes with an LMG, a grenade, and a pistol (every class comes with a pistol). The medic can heal people (including yourself) and revive people. The medic comes with a shotgun, and is incredibly OP with sliding.
The Health system. Its the same as Counter-Strike, with armor and non-regening health. Nothing more to be said.
Ranking system- pretty crap, considering that after Lvl 13 you get  matched with Lvl 80s, who slide and camp their asses off. I simply cannot recommend this game.
Cons:
-Awful Hitreg
-Unbalanced damage
-Multiplayer is a campfest
-Sliding is overpowered
-Maps are unstrategic
-Bad ranking system
Pros:
-Non P2W
-Co-Op can be fun

You can kill this person, kill that person, have choice and weight to story progression, effect other NPCs lives, choice of what you want to be, and tons. and Tons. of items. +Excellent music. The music in this game always amazes me with how perfect it fits with the setting, which is a doomed, twisted, apocolyptic medieval world.
+Amazing aesthetics/lore. I pretty much said it already, it's a doomed, twisted apocyptic medieval world. They splice everything together perfectly, perfect design with the theme, dark, sinister, sickening, twisted, with sites of what could of been, or what was still barely being there. First and formost, this is a Souls Game. If you expect this game to hold your hand for you, and guide you ever so gently from place to place, or to help you in any realy way, you probably shouldn't play it. If you grew up in the worlds of the old, where games were hard, unforgiving and funner than anything, then you will love this game.
This game has many improvements on the original, one big one being a noticebly more relaxed difficulty at the begining than the first one. Don't let this fool you, like I did. The difficulty RAPIDLY ramps up VERY early, with no warning at all, arguably beginning with The Pursuer (a recurring boss fight, that is more or less optional).
Leveling is NOT done at a bonfire as before, but at a central hub. I personally missed the bonfire levelling mechanic, as this does make the game feel slower (even though combat is literally twice as fast as the previous games) it does encourage you to return more often to the hub, where useful NPC's who are found will congregate after you've met their requirements (usually exhausting their dialogue). Many (like me) will find the change jarring, as I did, but I warmed up to it eventually.
Combat is SO much faster. The new power stance mode is great, letting you dual wield your weapons and opening new moves for you to utilise. Spellcasting is far better, if still way too OP for my liking (♥♥♥♥ you PvP mages), and bows work better now, with move-aim actually an option now.
Graphically, it makes the original look like a pancake. Yep. this game is beautiful. you may find a couple of odd textures here and there (mostly if you're looking for them) but overall, it's highly polished, and isn't too hardware intensive. You can lower the seetings now, if it isn't running too well.
Still laggy in a lot of PvP if you have a bad connection, but there's no cheating that I've come across now. The community is good.
all in all, a worthy addition to the Souls Franchise, and it should be in your library. The Scholar of The First SIn version, with the added DLC.

Five Nights at Freddy's 2 took what made the game great and amplified it 10 fold. Though a lot of the scare factor was left behind, Five Nights at Freddy's 2 trumps its predecessor in almost every way. For those new to the fnaf series, Five Nights at Freddy's is a indie horror game made by a single man named Scott Cawthon. It puts you in the role of a night guard at a Chuck-E Cheese esc resterant named Freddy Fazbear's Pizza. In order to beat this game you have to survive for 5 nights whale 5 new and shiny anamatronic creatures attempt to get into your office, along with the old withered anamatronics from the old location. As i said before, a lot of the scare factor from the 1st game was lost one this one. though it is still hororfing, it dosent have the atmousfear and sound design of the original. Then again, the camera is much smoother, the graphics are refined, the game mechanics are a lot more fleshed out and, of course, with 9 anamatronics insted of the inisial 4, this game is a lot harder then the original. all and all, though i personaly prefer the original, Five Nights at Freddy's 2 still clocks in at around 80 hours for me so kin my eye it is well worth the tiny price tag that it currently holds. 8/10

As you play more of a squad you get more bonuses for that squad. It's a nice system.
- Varied maps. Not all the same muddy field, there are maps that consist of nothing but CQB trench areas and bunkers and more open field and hill maps.
- Career Points. Career points are a clever system for unlocking equipment and weapons. As you level up you receive career points, these let you unlock two more equipment presets for each unit type of each squad. It means that you can get slightly varied equipment (e.g. Rifleman style units can spend a career point or two to get a scoped variant of their rifle) but also balances it so you don't just unlock everything as every single separate unit of every squad costs its own points.
- Great to play with friends. The squad system means you can create a squad with up to three friends. Given the diversified roles and the NCO commands it makes it a good social game too.
- Active development. The developers are still constantly working on Verdun to fix problems and add new features. Not often you see that in developers these days.
Cons:
- Too many career points. While I am not complaining about being able to unlock a decent amount of stuff, I feel like the balance is sightly withdrawn with how many points you get. I am only level 19 and I have 39 spare points, with decent unlocks already maxed with a couple of units.
- Minor Bugs. Every now and again I do experience a few minor bugs such as being teleported/glitched into the air sometimes when against a trench wall.
- Often not any/many players in any other gamemode than the default attack/defend frontline one.

First of all, for those who are arguing this is supposed to be a horror game, it's not. The basic storyline is 'you come home and nobody is there, find out why' and not 'zombies have taken over the house and lurk in the basement'.
Yes, "Gone Home" is short, once you know where to find the information and the keys, you can play it in a little over 10 minutes ... but that means only going through the house and triggering the ending sequence, that kind of playing will not give you the complete story. The story, however, is not just about Sam (the sister). You can also find out about your father's troubles with writing, about his weird uncle, who owned the house before the family moved in, and other stuff. Basically, the game lets you catch up with the family history during the time you were in Europe.
It's an everyday story, not something great or heroic or scary. It's just the unease everyone would feel alone in a house they've never been in before, at after 1 a.m. on a night with a thunderstorm, not atmospheric horror like in "Amnesia."
$20 might indeed be a little much for the game... and 'game' a little too much of a word for "Gone Home" but it does not deserve all the bad reviews it has gotten. If you want an action game, this is not for you... but that should be obvious from the description. If you like uncovering a story for yourself, you might want to give it a chance.

A good PC port. Square did well with this PC port and it's much better than some of their previous PC Final Fantasy ports.
Final Fantasy X is a turn based RPG. You get into battles with random encounters. In combat the combat is a departure from previous entries of the series. The Active Time Battle system(ATB) from previous FF games is gone and now a more traditional turn based system is in place. With this system you can see when each character is going to get their turn and plan ahead accordingly. Furthermore, a cool aspect is you can switch between characters in combat on the fly and each character has different pros/cons in combat. This helps add more strategy to the fights. The leveling of FFX is a bit strange though.
Leveling in FFX is done with a Sphere Grid system. You gain EXP from winning fights and move across the Sphere Grid and each time you fill out a node on it you either get a stat boosted or learn a skill. The annoying aspect about the leveling in FFX is for each party member to get EXP from combat you must have everyone hit a enemy. This makes battles take a little longer then they should since you need to level everyone and constantly have to switch characters in/out to ensure they all get EXP. The combat difficulty of the game is increased from it's predecessor FFIX. The random battles are fairly easy, but some of the bosses can be quite challenging for beginner RPG players. Final Fantasy X really emphasizes moreso then other games of the series using status effects in combat like Haste and whatnot to give you an edge in combat. It's very important to use buffs/debuffs on allies/enemies to allow yourself to win some of the harder boss fights. Last, regarding gameplay the exploration is very linear. If you don't like linearity you may not like FFX. Now for the story.
The story of FFX is quite good. You're put into the shoes of Tidus a Blitzball player from the city of Zanarkand. One day Zanarkand is under attack by a mysterious entity known as Sin. Sin begins a siege on the city and Tidus escapes with a friend of his father named Auron who seems to know about the mysterious creature Sin. Tidus manages to escape, to an entirely different place and time to the world of Spira. Here he learns about the culture of Spira. In Spira a summoner goes on a pilgrimage to obtain summon monsters to combat Sin and ultimately sacrifice themselves to keep Sin away for a temporary amount of time. Tidus joins a summoner named Yuna on her pilgrimage as one her guardians and goes on a journey wth her to learn the truth about Sin and to put an end to Sin. So characters...
Tidus is a great protagonist in my opinion because we get to see inside his mind often. Often, he introspects and reflects on what is going on and it's great to see that in a FF protagonist. He feels like a down to earth character with whom the player can relate to despite his at times silliness. The rest of the cast like Auron, Yuna, Rikku and Wakka etc. are all great characters as well and get developed over the course of the game. We see them change as the game goes on and we learn about them more and more as the story progresses. Unfortunately, one character Kimhari felt kind of shoehorned in. He's a cool character, but he gets almost no character development til near the very end of the game. So it just kind of feels like they didn't have time to develop his character out. One of the best parts of the story is some of the plot twists. There's a lot of major plot twists about Tidus, Yuna, Sin and several of the main characters of the story. Finally, the music.
Final Fantasy X's soundtrack was composed by not just Nobuo Uematsu, but also Masashi Hamauzu. Hamauzu Square fans may be familiar with because he worked on SaGa Frontier 1/2's soundtrack. The soundtrack is incredible in the game and many of the songs are some of the best of the Final Fantasy series. Many of the battle, boss and area themes of the game are either catchy or incredibly memorable. One of the first songs the player is introduced to as soon as they begin a New Game is called To Zanarkand and it's one of the finest pieces of video game music that has ever been composed and is truly ingrained into my memory. I would highly suggest buying this for Final Fantasy X. In my opinion, one of the best Final Fantasy games ever made and one of the best RPG's ever made. Overall, FFX is a must play RPG in my opinion. I played through it on PS2, PS3 and now plan to play it again on PC.

I was going to write a short "yeah, this game is good, buy it," type of review, but after seeing all of the negative reviews, I feel the need to defend it. I won't go into any specifics, because this game would be RUINED by even minute spoilers.
I feel like all of the negative reviews here are for people who didn't understand what they were getting into when they bought the game, and were let down by that.
What I will say is this: What this game does, it does well. Atmosphere, pacing (which, for the record, is slow, but that's okay,) and manipulating the player's emotions - these are all executed flawlessly. It is an incredibly emotional experience, with more twists than I expected.
As far as cons go, the game is short, and it's kind of expensive. I got it on sale, and feel like I got my money's worth, but at the normal price of 20 dollars, it's kind of a toss-up. It really comes down to what you want in a game. If you're willing to spend 20 dollars for a 2 hour long emotional experience, (like if you've gone to the movies in the past 10 years, since that's almost 20 ♥♥♥♥ing bucks now,) I'd buy this game immediately. I probably wouldn't have bought this game were it not on sale, but having played it, I think it's worth the 20 dollars to a certain group of people.
Additionally, if you're looking for a "video gamey" video game, this is not it. The gameplay literally consists of walking around and examining♥♥♥♥♥♥ There aren't quick time events or active reloads, but that's alright. This game sets out to tell a story in the most immersive medium that exists today. Again, you have to know exactly what it is you're signing up for, or you run the risk of being disappointed.
That said, this was one of the most engaging and emotionally impactful games I've played in a while. I highly recommend it.

I cannot recommend this game in comparison to the much cleaner CS:GO.
CSS is a classic Counter-Strike game that features a lively community that continues to survive and thrive. But boy is it flawed.
Two words: Lag. Compensation.
This is the biggest issue I have with this game. Its lag compensation system really drags the game into the dirt, making all those BS shots around a corner a common occurance. I cannot tell you how many times I died while behind a sturdy wall. It's happened almost every time I've peaked around a corner, making peaking something near impossible if there's a good player shooting at you.
"Get better internet!" I hear as I type this paragraph. I have/had pretty good internet, with an average ping way below 60. It's the fault of the server and the other players, which is a nice segway into the next topic of this review.
The ratio of modded servers to vanilla servers is about 10:1, and I'm being nice. When I say "vanilla" I mean that the server retains the fundamentals of a CSmatch: pistol round, (so you don't start at $16000) not deathrun, jailbreak, no shop of any kind, or any other gamemodes that belong in GMOD, and
When you find a vanilla (or close, because most servers have a stat tracking mod) server, good luck having fun. Between the aforementioned lag compensation, the CS elitists, the stacked teams, and huge player count, (ranging in the 30s-40s) you will be getting stomped if you are even remotely fresh.
The game is a testament to how long a game lasts, with its large predecessor, Counter-Strike, still racking in plenty of players with double the modded servers and $16000 to start. People (namely self-proclaimed pros)  prefer the classics because they have found all the exploits and have established themselves in the CS community some how: through maps, sound packs, textures, or server mods.
The game is old and dated when compared to CSGO. CSS and it's predcessors are full of people grasping tightly to a game on its last legs, and would rather call players of CSGO "scrubs" than move on.

In comparison to the vanilla versions (x360 ps3 dx9), things have changed a lot. Areas have better and often more sensical/lore friendly enemy placements and the game feels a lot less empty. General progression is much more fluid in contrast to the game's general difficulty increase; vanilla may have been easier, but having to reach Iron Keep just to get the dull ember, or having to go through the Belfry Luna just to get the bastille key were a pain. In Scholar of the First Sin, these items exist in their appropriate areas.
I haven't finished Scholar just yet, but it already feels like the definitive version. General difficulty improvements and bug fixes are implemented from the get-go and the difficulty increase of the PvE experience never feels too over the top. There are more NPC summons in place to prevent people getting too stuck in certain areas after the game dies, NPCs appear in stranger places, sometimes more appropriate ones. A few hiccups remain from the conversion to 60fps, however, including some erratic movement from enemies that may attack far too quickly for you to parry, although capping your framerate somehow will fix these issues.
It still has the same problem Dark Souls 2 and 3 have - coming from the original Dark Souls, where poise was a gamekiller and parrying was almost a necessity, DS2 and 3 feel much easier and harder, allowing for viable dex builds and with less enemies having crazy amounts of poise, but parrying has been made a much more difficult and often pointless endeavour that is hard to drill out from your mind. The games went from a slow and clunky mess where parrying and poise breaking caused you to min/max and optimize, to a much more fluid game where dual wielding isn't awful and all weapons feel impactful, although some have their niche appeal.
It's a hack and slash, now.
But after all that, it's still Dark Souls, just with a roll that isn't locked to four directions upon locking on, and with more friendliness towards fashion or whatever you specifically want to use, without the instant backstabs or the horrendous lag. People's main complaint come from the fact that it isn't a direct sequel. That's part of what makes DS2's story so great. To quote Arin Hanson of GameGrumps regarding these games: "You just go." That's precisely what DS2's story and level design is about. You aren't supposed to be clear on anything, not until the last second. Spend some time looking through the lore descriptions, listening to dialogue, or even just watching VaatiVidya's youtube videos and DS2 suddenly becomes an amazing evolution of the established Dark Souls plot, all hidden away under a shroud of player confusion and unclear goals.
"I believe they called it Drangleic. Perhaps you're familiar. No, how could you be. But one day, you will stand before its decrepit gate. Without really knowing why."
I don't wish to spoil much for DS2 newbies, but the plot being masked with a lack of information is both the game's strong point and its weakness. In DS1, you are given three distinct goals from a potential three different NPCs. In DS2 everything is vague; level design makes no sense and worlds seem to be connected together by dull, empty rooms with barely designed lifts that seem to shatter real-world physics, something often criticized by fans. But remember the epidemic of memory loss sweeping Drangleic? How would you remember how you really found yourself at your destination? All those dull, dark, empty, impossible and badly designed rooms are symbolic of the curse eating away at your memory, which is a strong focus of much of the game's story and characters. Nobody reliably remembers why they came or how they came. The symbolism simply compliments those barren rooms being necessary transitional/loading areas. It's amazing to me that all the prerequisites to truly understanding the story and the journey are given to you in the FIRST CUTSCENE OF THE GAME.
Dark Souls 2 is a shining example of an underappreciated and fine sequel. Not bogging around in what was, no matter how great, but reimagining what was. A fresh new take on something you're already very familiar with, yet it suffered for the art. It doesn't have as many memorable moments in the base game as Dark Souls 1 did until the very end, whereas Dark Souls 1 had you venturing through painting worlds, falling through collapsed prisons and fighting remarkable bosses to great music, DS2's base game has a few decent bosses and gets much better as you access the DLC areas. Dark Souls 2 may not have as huge an impact on you as the first game did, but it certainly outclasses the first mechanically. You no longer have to be a tryhard to drive away invaders or stay hollowed for fear of constant OHKO invasions. It plays better, runs better, but being developed for the x360 and ps3 at the time, DS2 isn't going to leave your mouth agape too often.

Gone Home is one of the best-constructed narratives I have ever played in a video game. Its gameplay is rudimentary but evokes a prime feeling of progression as you unlock secret areas and find keys to other parts of the game. The game is very linear so it's not really possible to miss anything important, but the feeling it evokes is still the same as an environment such as the mansion in the original Resident Evil - that is to say, that you yourself are discovering these areas, and you yourself are responsible for discovering the plot - and speaking of that plot...
Gone Home is the best example that I have experienced of environmental storytelling in gaming. The audio logs tell the story, but the environment tells the plot. If you were to just listen to the audio logs, you would have a well-presented audio drama coming-of-age story. If you were to play the game without the audio logs, you would still have that, and you would have so much more. They work together to compliment each other and together they present a spellbinding and thoroughly enjoyable story.
That said, the story is not for everyone. Gone Home's plot hit me harder than few other games ever have. I would put it up there with some of my favorite movies. The problem is that it felt very personal to me, and I will avoid saying more for the sake of spoilers, though a lot of people already know the biggest one. Most people are nothing like me, and they won't identify so strongly with this game's plot. I don't think that's necessarily a problem, but I think it is the reason that a lot of people seem to not be as taken with this game as I am. If you don't relate to Gone Home's characters and identify with their struggles, you won't experience this game as intently as I did. Someone who hates this game because of its plot needs to understand that people are fundamentally different, and some identify with different things than others. By the end of my time with the game, my eyes were sore from crying. This experience will obviously not be shared by everyone, and I can't blame someone for having a lesser opinion than me based on the fact that they did not have this experience.
The other problem with this game is one of length. The game took me exactly 100 minutes to play through, and I wasn't even particularly fast. Most people seem to report an average of two hours. I will probably play this game again in the future, like returning to a favorite book or movie, but I don't think that will be the case for most people, and at $20, the price is a bit steep. As much as I loved this game, I can't say it's worth $20. I think that price is a grave mistake on the part of the developers, and I can't understand why it hasn't been lowered since release. I believe that a lower price point would have made the game much more accessible for a lot of people.

I cannot recommend this game in comparison to the much cleaner CS:GO.
CSS is a classic Counter-Strike game that features a lively community that continues to survive and thrive. But boy is it flawed.
Two words: Lag. Compensation.
This is the biggest issue I have with this game. Its lag compensation system really drags the game into the dirt, making all those BS shots around a corner a common occurance. I cannot tell you how many times I died while behind a sturdy wall. It's happened almost every time I've peaked around a corner, making peaking something near impossible if there's a good player shooting at you.
"Get better internet!" I hear as I type this paragraph. I have/had pretty good internet, with an average ping way below 60. It's the fault of the server and the other players, which is a nice segway into the next topic of this review.
The ratio of modded servers to vanilla servers is about 10:1, and I'm being nice. When I say "vanilla" I mean that the server retains the fundamentals of a CSmatch: pistol round, (so you don't start at $16000) not deathrun, jailbreak, no shop of any kind, or any other gamemodes that belong in GMOD, and
When you find a vanilla (or close, because most servers have a stat tracking mod) server, good luck having fun. Between the aforementioned lag compensation, the CS elitists, the stacked teams, and huge player count, (ranging in the 30s-40s) you will be getting stomped if you are even remotely fresh.
The game is a testament to how long a game lasts, with its large predecessor, Counter-Strike, still racking in plenty of players with double the modded servers and $16000 to start. People (namely self-proclaimed pros)  prefer the classics because they have found all the exploits and have established themselves in the CS community some how: through maps, sound packs, textures, or server mods.
The game is old and dated when compared to CSGO. CSS and it's predcessors are full of people grasping tightly to a game on its last legs, and would rather call players of CSGO "scrubs" than move on.

TL;DR: it's not a game for everyone, but if you're looking for something different, something a little slower paced, this is a great game with an interesting story. It's only about two and a half hours long if you play like I do (and I'm fairly average at figuring things out and I like to poke around, exploring things, but I'm not a 100% completionist), and there's not a lot to revisit, so replay value is kind of low--on that front, it's more like a good book than a video game. You'll pick it up again in a few months, already knowing everything, but just wanting to experience it again. The dev's added a commentary mode, so I guess that adds some replay value, but I haven't checked it out yet.
A lot of the complaints I read about this game mentioned that it was repetitive; you're just wandering a house. Find this clue, go to the next room, find another clue. And it is exactly this. Exploring a house, finding clues as to what's going on, trying to piece together the mystery of an empty house after you come back from a trip.
It's no less repetitive than more mainstream games "go here, kill this guy, grab this item, use it to go there and kill that guy". It's just different. If different bothers you this is not the game for you.
If you're looking for a change of pace, a short breather and palate cleanser between one "go here, kill him" game and the next, this is the game for you.
The primary story is intriguing; it definitely leads you towards certain assumptions, building tension as you find more and more clues and hear more and more of Katie's little sister's story. The subplots are also very interesting--trying to piece together the life that's going on around Katie's little sister as she tells her story is just as interesting as hearing hers. Figuring out Katie's parents' marriage, her father's relationship to the house, the house's relationship to the community and how that all flows in and out and around the little sister's story is so great.

I'll try to make this short and avoid using any childish puns.
Final Fantasy X is a jRPG which tells the story of Tidus, a boy who enjoys Blitzball (basically Underwater Hand-ball) and has severe family issues. He's playing a blitzball game until he gets thrown several thousand years into the future by a giant whale thing. It's up to the player to help him figure out what's going on and how to go back home. The story isn't particularly original, but it can keep the player's interest until the end, and most characters are pretty cool
Combat is turn-based and lets you use all of your characters in battle, with only 3 appearing on screen at the same time that can be switched during each of your turns, leading to many tactical possibilities
The character growth system is very unique and involves a huge grid where your characters earn abilities and stat boosts by moving in it through the use of AP which can be acquired by killing enemies. Each character also has unique abilities called Overdrives, which can be obtained in many different ways, incentivating the player to explore the game in order to find new Overdrives and become stronger.
You can also take on several sidequests and minigames which can be fun timesinks (like Blitzball) or dreadful minigames designed by Satan himself (the lightning dodging and the butterfly catching)
FFX's graphics are nice, clean and smooth. The cutscenes still look enjoyable today (and some of them can be skipped now!) and watching Aeons wreck stuff is always amazing to look at.
Final Fantasy X-2 is the ignorant sequel to FFX which tells the tale of Yuna, who has somehow lost all dignity after the end of FFX, and her two friends, Rikku and Shadow the Hedgehog---I mean Paine.
Together they do all sorts of weird jobs, dressed like K-Pop idols and striking poses at every possible occasion, The main quest-line barely gets mentioned during the entire game but it involves Yuna finding a sphere that looks like "Him", which leads her to join a "Sphere-Hunters" gang in order to gather clues that might help her finding "Him" so that they can 'laugh it up' together again ...that's right, he's called "Him" for the entirety of FFX-2.
As cringy and stupid the story may be, the game itself is actually pretty fun. It is more open-ended than FFX, as you get access to the airship immediately after starting the game and you can go wherever you want. There's tons of side-quests and a lot more mini-games to do this time around, and Blitzball also makes a return (though it is dumbed down from FFX's blitzball)
The combat is revamped into an 'active turns' based system, with emphasis on timing and cooldown management. Said combat is spiced up even further by the 'Dress-Sphere' system, which is like the Job System from some of the older games in the series, except you can also switch jobs on the fly during battle.
The HD Remaster has all extra content from the previously Japan-only 'International' release, like the Colosseum which lets you fight old and new faces in arena fights of increasing difficulty, or Creature Capturing which lets you capture every monster in the game and make them fight by your side.
When you're done playing FFX-2, you can still find a good challenge in 'The Last Mission', which completes the game's story and takes place in a randomly generated, 80-floor dungeon that you must beat with limited items and party setups.
Graphics took a step up from FFX, with tons of new flashy effects and updated characted models which look gorgeous in HD.
The HD remaster is really good, and it runs smoothly even on toasters.
It also comes with a lot of new goodies, including an extra novel which is supposedly the Sequel to FFX-2.
If you haven't bought the FFX/X-2 HD before, then the PC version is easily the best version to get, as it comes already patched from all the issues which plagued the console releases, and the ability to choose text language and new/old soundtrack (which is lacking from the console versions).
The PC version even comes with a few optional cheats if you want to use them for whatever reason, and it even has a button to skip encounters and another button to make the entire game run 2 times or even 4 times faster than normal, which makes much of the walking/battles a lot less TEDIOUS.

When I first bought "Gone Home" on sale, I had no idea what to expect from it, and neighter did I know what kind of game this was. But it looked like a interesting mystery type of game, set back in the 90s, which is a interesting time period for a game, especially if you have a childhood from the 90s (not me though). There is no combat or puzzels in the game, all though the game is a puzzel it self......
To enjoy "Gone Home", you have to like slow-paced games, and you need to have patience, because you are going to read A LOT in the game to find out more about your missing family. This is a story-driven game, so if you don't engage in the story, there it's no point in playing it. You must search every corner, read every piece of paper, and  listen to every tape you find, because that's how you get ahead in the game, and experience the amazing story.
After 5 minuttes of playing, I quickly got a creepy feeling, because you learn fast that this is a real SCARY game, more scary then many horror games out there. You are all alone in this big old house, and the game doesn't even try to help you out. You have to turn on all the lamps in the house, because you have no flashlight or anything. What's great about the game, is that while you are playing, you will probably come up with many conclusions about your family's disappearance. Is it something supernatural, or maybe not? Inside every room there is somehow a clue to find out the deeper truth.
I would strongly recommend to use a headset while playing at night. The game should be 3-4 hours, and has no replay value, but this is the kind of game that you only need to experience once, despite of how short the game is. I would also recommend not to play the game in more then on period, because of how short the game is. It would be like watching half a movie one day, and the rest another day, it kind of looses that "vibe".
This is an outstanding game that differs from the rest. I don't normally play games like this, but I think it's good for everyone to play something else then "Dota" and COD".  All in all, this is a must own game on steam, trust me on this one.

There are attachments that can be gained and maintained for free, and that's it.  You also have to choose to unlock them over weapons and armor.  What?  If you aren't paying with real dollars: The repair bills for using weapons and armor, with in-game currency, are excessively high and will often leave you losing money per mission unless you're being very conservative with it.  That means an upgraded pistol for Insane missions and keep everything else default or use time-limited guns that can sometimes be gained from level ups. “Gone Home is the greatest video game love story ever told.”
No it's not. And it's not worth 20 dollars unless you have excess spending money to blow or really want to support indie developers. There's about 2 hours of game here, plus or minus a few minutes depending on how literate you are. Or if you're an idiot like me and can't read maps.
Aside from the 90's kitsch and the fact that the main storyline is based off of teenagers and the adolescent rage that goes with it, the three stories (daughter, father, mother) found here are told well. There are no cutscenes or other video game mechanics to pull you out of the gameplay. Instead, you are free to explore and uncover clues and evidence at your own pace. The game designers did a great job of following the writing goal of "show, don't tell." There is no hand holding here and the player is forced to construct their own narrative about their screwed up family. The stories diverge and converge throughout, and the game teases you with classic horror tropes as you creep through this desolate house. The game is deeply personal, and shows the complexities of families and relationships.

I've played FInal Fantasy X through at least 4-5 times in my life, but this is my first time with the remaster. Still haven't played X-2, so this review strictly covers X.
PROS
- Gameplay encourages creativity in how you use each character, and difficulty of boss fights and monsters scales well.
- Story is engaging and well-paced.
- Blitzball is a fun diversion every once in a while.
- Voice acting is largely quite good.
- Lots of additional content to keep you playing after the main story ends.
- New graphics look gorgeous, and I love that you can choose the original or remastered soundtrack (protip: original).
CONS
- Cutscenes can be long and are not skippable. I like them, but that's probably a nostalgia thing.
- If you're going for full completion (i.e. all Celestial weapons, etc.) it can get VERY grind-y (a problem that isn't present for the most part in the main storyline unless you flee a ton of battles).
- 30 FPS lock - which apparently is something people get very mad about. I personally don't care.
Overall score: 10/10. Game has aged well, is tons of fun to play, and is very engaging from the first few minutes.

I don’t even know where to start with Dark Souls II.  This game was an absolutely horrible experience.  It was like a Dark Souls abortion.  After my first 10 minutes of playing I realized that I had made a big mistake with this purchase.  To start out, I went through the character creation and perfectly designed and sculpted a character that looked really close to me. This isn’t a Skyrim experience, that’s for sure.  With this game being the remastered version, I would have hated to see the original.
I should probably note that I started the game with a Mage.  That said, most of my combat was done with a knife since the spell system is kinda screwed.  You have to charge your spells by resting at a campfire, somewhat Dungeons and Dragons style, but you seem to always run out of spells right when you need them the most. At any rate, I really can’t recommend this version of Dark Souls II.  Having never played the original, I can’t really recommend it either.  From what I hear the first DS is better, and the latest Dark Souls III absolutely blows them all away… Save your money, skip this one.

This is a conditional recommendation. If you're looking for the latest iteration of Kill Simulator 9000, you're definitely in the wrong place. If you're looking for intricate, heavy puzzles, you're also in the wrong place. If you're looking for a horror experience, you are approximately 98% in the wrong place (I dunno, a big, empty mansion is kinda creepy, plus some of the things revealed about the previous owner's life are a bit unsettling, but there's no jump scares or horror here- just some mild discomfort).
First off, don't think of this as a game. It's almost like a self-guided graphic novel, if that makes any sense. Secondly, as someone who was about the same age as the protagonist at the time this game takes place, this was a huge nostalgia trip- some good, some bad, some sad. I remember people being into the bands that are name-checked (and on cassettes) throughout the game. Hell, the "hanging out with someone because they have an NES" mention struck a chord with me because I did that to someone (poor lass).
Without spoiling anything- you've just returned from a big trip to Europe. Your folks moved to a big new mansion while you were gone. You pick up the spare key, let yourself in, and find the place empty. Your own voice is on the answering machine. You thought your sister would be here to greet you but she's nowhere to be found. You find a scrap of paper, and then the game plays a small piece of narration from your younger sister Sam. Explore the house. Find out what's been going on with Sam, your parents, the eccentric great uncle who owned the house originally, and why the house is empty.
This is a story/time capsule, told through the mechanics of a first-person video game. It's quite good at that. It's not a video game in the usual sense, and that will throw a lot of people off. If you were a 90s teen, or like the idea of a game engine being used to tell a story, get this when it goes on sale. As of this writing it's $2.39 US and worth that- I can't think of a comic book that's cheaper than that these days.
TL;DR Gone Home is a novella told through the medium of a first person exploration game. The story is the core, not the gameplay, and it's a fantastic snapshot of mid-90s pop culture (they really did their homework in terms of accuracy). If that sounds interesting, pick it up when it's $5 or less (I feel that it's a bit too short to justify the full $19.99 price tag).

Been playing CSS since High School and still get a kick out of it everytime I join a server. The original CS was great, but Source improves everything you loved in the first CS and adds in so many customizable levels, skins, textures, items, mods, etc. that it makes it hard to stop playing even though the game is now fairly old in age. PROS:
- Great shelf-life
- Hours of playability
- Definition of an FPS
- Strong fan-base/community
- Runs on older PCs
CONS:
- Camping is rampant in certain levels
- Hacking is still apparent
- Mic spamming / trolling
- Difficult for those new to the FPS genre
Overall, if you're looking for a great game with plently of hours of playtime and customization, this game's for you. If you're not familiar with FPShooters and want a game to practice and hone your skills, look no further than Counter-Strike: Source.
If you're not a fan of intense mutiplayer games, or you don't like getting shot at/dominated by experienced players, I'd pass on this game. If you easily get angered at losing, or prone to rage-quitting, this game's probably not for you.
On a scale from 1 to 10, with 1 being the lowest score and 10 being the highest, my personal rating for Counter-Strike: Source would be an 8/10.

If your looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an outstanding cheese cake recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1 cup digestive plain sweet biscuit crumbs
3 tablespoons sugar
3 tablespoons melted butter
40 ounces softened cream cheese
1 cup sugar
3 tablespoons flour
1 tablespoon vanilla
1 cup sour cream
4 eggs
Directions:
For The base:.
If you're using a dark pan, preheat the oven to 350. If you are using a shiny pan, 375.
Combine the crumbs, melted butter and 3 tbsp sugar well and pat onto the bottom of a 9 inch springform pan. I also like to very very lightly butter the sides of the pan so that the cheesecake will not stick later on.
Bake for 10 mins in your preheated oven and remove. Let it cool while you prepare your batter.
For the batter:.
Make sure everything is at room temperature.
Combine sugar, cheese, flour and vanilla in a big bowl and mix on medium speed till well combined. Don't forget to scrape the bowl as you're doing this.
Mix in the sour cream till its incorporated well. Then, add the eggs one by one, mixing well after each addition.
Pour the batter into the springform and let it bake for 1 hour and 10 minutes After the baking time, turn off the oven and leave the door ajar. Let the cake cool in there for about 1 1/2 hours.
Remove the cake and let it cool thoroughly. Refrigerate overnight.
Release the sides of the springform.
Eat.

After having this on my wishlist for a very long time I finally bought it on sale for about 3 bucks.. and I think that's the right price.
When I first saw this game, I thought it was some kind of horror title.  Spooky house, walking simulator, no sign of weapons.. it sounded like and looked like a kind of a 'Amnesia: the Dark Descent' ripoff.  I was intrigued and put it on my wishlist.
I spent the better part of a year avoiding spoilers, but it was impossible.  Going in, I knew these things:
"It's an exploration simulator."
"You won't die."
"Great story."
"Pretty short. Not a lot of replyability."
"There's some LGBT themes in there."
"This game is so great, if you don't buy it I'll buy it for you." - some podcaster from the Laser Time network
Finally, after the price went to three bucks, I bought it.
As a kid from the 90s, it just didn't evoke the 90s feeling that I was hoping... I imagine that wandering through and empty house doesn't help.   Yes, there were items to look at and interact with that were from the 90s, but I never felt like I was playing in the 90s.  It actually felt more like I was walking through an old-timey home filled with items that were not from its time period.
Without spoiling more than I have, I do applaud this experience.  It's not a game, folks.. if anything, it's a role playing game - where you, Mr. Steam Player, play the role of a teenage girl coming home to an empty house after a whirlwind vacation around Europe. Except noone's home, not even your sister.
Look, if you want to experience something new and you don't mind supporting a developer who's trying something new, give Gone Home a chance. Just be warned, this is a very cerbral experience that requires a certain level of empty toward others and an appreciation of developers taking a risk on breaking new ground.

This is a tough review because the game does some things really good and some things really bad.Homefront : The Revolution is a FPS open world game that tries to be Far Cry but fails due to repetitive gameplay and bad gunplay.
The game plays like Far Cry a lot.It borrows a lot of mechanics such as the ability to capture bases and the battle between two factions(Rebels and North Koreans).Sadly,capturing bases is not nearly as fun as in the Far Cry series.
The gameplay is not linear as some might say.You have plenty of choices besides following the campaign.You can raise the ''Hearts and Minds'' meter by doing certain activities like capturing bases,disabling North Korean machinery,destroying armored cars and shuting down radios.
When you create enough chaos in a region of the city,the citizens will start to riot and join you.The game does a very good job at this.The level design changes as the citizens get more and more fed up with the occupation.
Random events are among the good things that this game has to offer.You can save citizens from police brutality,kill Korean officials and aid the rebels against attacking North Koreans.
Populated areas are very frustrating.Stealth in the game is very bad and when you are in a urban area,it is very hard for you to move around without getting spotted and have to fight endless waves of attackers.Why can't you just have a disguise?They recognise you instantly.
Platforming in the game is also very bad and not intuitive.The game sometimes fails to register jumps and sometimes you can't jump/climb somewhere even if you should have.
Gunplay...this is one of the most disappointng things in the game.You'd think a shooter game would have decent gunplay,but Homefront : The Revolution does not.The guns feel clunky and unresponsive.The conversions kinda save the gunplay and make it bearable.
Another clunky mechanic of the game is driving.The motorcycles in the game don't feel right.
The A.I in the game are pretty dumb and probably glitch out a lot and that's why they are so dumb.
Overall,the gameplay is repetitive and because of the bad gunplay,at times it is painful.Some levels are chaotic and badly scripted also.It's a good thing the actual gameplay gets better as the game progresses because I would have stopped two or three hours in.
The game suffered an awful launch and even after several months and several patches,the game still has bugs,glitches and performance issues.One bug kept happening to me over and over again.When I would get down from a motorcycle,I would get thrown into the air a few meters and then fall and take damage from the fall.NPCs kept getting stuck in objects or just went through them and so on.Those bugs don't happen enough for me to say that the game is unplayable...but I noticed them.
I saw people complaining about ugly graphics.The game actually looks really nice.The level design is pure eye-candy.If Homefront did one thing right,it's world building with those pretty graphics.
The soundtrack is serviceable and the voice acting is top notch.
SPOILERS DON'T READ
After reading through reviews I expected a bad plot but it's actually not that bad.It has great moments,decent dialogue and a few memorable characters.Maybe having North Korea invade and conquer the US is a bit too imaginative.But it's a game after all.I think they messed up a bit towards the end with a very weird self-sacrifice.Also,they scrapped the first Homefront game and recreated the backstory.I don't know what to say about that.
Homefront : The Revolution is a mediocre game at best.The Open World is beautiful in design but offers next to nothing in content.Gunplay is bad but gets better throughout the game while the storyline can be great at times but they mess up towards the end.That coupled with the performance issues make it very hard game to recommend.Why I am recommending it?Because I enjoyed the storyline and the dialogue and also enjoyed the level designs and some mechanics of the game.
I give the game a 6/10.
It may not be a good game,but I enjoyed going through it with all it's faults.Hopefully the Devs won't abandon patching the game since I heard they are going to release more singleplayer/multiplayer DLCs.

I was ready to refund this game after the 2 hour trial period. I am very glad I didn’t, it took some time getting used to it and liking it. This shooter is not like many others out there, it is very original, which is of course a good thing. The first good thing about this game is it’s setting of WWI, a period that not a lot of games explore. The gameplay is dark, brutal and unforgiving. With extra gore enabled you can see body parts missing and screams of agony in the background. Trench warfare is what makes this game unique - where troops advance or retreat trench by trench and where camping and careful advancement is a must. One shot kills (or a few with a pistol) also adds to the intensity and different approach from your regular shooter. The squad progression system is also very unique where you need to stick with the same people if you want to level up your squad (lvl 100 max). The higher the squad level the better abilities the whole squad enjoys. The roles within the squad can be unlocked with skill points you get as you level up.
Verdun is far from perfect though. The main problem is the player base. On a daily the game has 600 - 1000 players. Voice chat users are pretty rare - even though it is an extremely squad based game people don’t communicate. The game is very unpolished - there are many glitches that made me die numerous times and hit registry is not the greatest. The squad leveling system even though original has its flaws - because of the small player base and not knowing anybody that plays, it is hard to level up the squad.
The game is very solid but the standard price of $28 CAD is ridiculous. That is the main reason why it has such a small community. I think this game should compete with Insurgency at $10 CAD and go on frequent sales of $5. For that price I would pick it up.

Decent game, a good story, but not a lot of replay value: And this from someone who can play through practically any game at least 5 times, before getting bored with it. In short: if it hadn't been 88% off, it would have been a massive waste of money, bordering on criminal.
The story itself is (I believe) interesting, compelling, and worth playing the game for; but only if you're the type of person that enjoys emotional drama. I'd like to point out, that the game's description clearly states that there are no puzzles, and no fighting - so if you're looking for action and thrills, keep looking, this isn't the game for you - Gone Home is a nice, short story about love, and can barely be classified as a "game".
The atmosphere, soundtrack, and graphics is masterfully done, equal to great games developed by the greatest companies, which is perhaps, why the gameplay and storyline feels like a let down - its like the developers spent all their time on the setting, the gloomy atmosphere, the creepy environs, and just plain forgot that it needed a plotline?
As I said, the story itself is sweet and emotionally stimulating, but hardly original. Its a basic, cliché lovestory, the only "twists" being the fact that one expects something more sinister or paranormal happening, and that the lovestory refers to a same-sex type relationship. Wow, groundbreaking stuff, right there (sarcasm!).
In short: at full price this is basically a bait-and-switch scam; but if you can get it on sale, its worth playing. Perhaps a price adjustment is required?

Alright...Where should i start.
Let's start with the fact, that i have more than 5 hours, i played this game when it was in the beta back when it wasn't even on steam. It was an "ok" game, with a quite decent community, but too few coop levels and bad pvp map design, so it turned me away from the game on the long rung.
But here came the end of the years of beta testing, and the "release " of the game, with extra content, but the question is, did it improved in any way? Long story short...no.
Let me explain:
We got a few new maps which are finally a lot better than what we had before, but that's way too little effort, and sadly they are barely played, the community just votes for the basic maps that mostly end up in a team getting spawned camped, literally you can walk into their spawn, and trust me it happens often.
And yes the community, remember what i said above? The game had a decent community back in it's "golden days", but now it's all gone. In every game, you encounter at least once cheater if you are lucky, they are even proud of it.
English is almost non existant, so communicating can be more than tricky.
Players never talk, but when they do, they are toxic.
The weapon balance is also way worse than it was before, the game is filled with even more one shot body kill weapons now, so i wouldn't even mention warface and balance on the same page.
And you want to know what's the worst part of all this? The simple fact that this game had...hell it still has potential.
The pvp is a disaster yes, but coop wise this could be such a great game, the 3 "raid" or longer coop levels alone prove that. If you somehow manage to find players who speak your language and are willing to work with you (  having class balance for example) than it can be a really great experience.
In my opinion it would have been much better if the game wasn't free to play , because that's what gave the cheaters and toxic players a warm welcome, and the balance a goodbye filled with tears.  If this game was a 15 euros budget game, or even 20, but with more content and balanced aspects i would recommend it right away...maybe i would still do, if things were better, but there are not too many players left, and what's left of the community is certainly not good.
It's sad to say, but...stay away from this game, it had potential to be a hidden gem in the free to play market, but it made a wrong turn and it resulted in a disaster. It's a shame, really.

Just Cause 2 gives you a massive island nation to freely explore, wreaking havok as you slowly discover hundreds of locations and find over a thousand items. JC2 is so insanely fun because it completely indulges the player while minimizing the tedious elements of open world games.
Other open world games require slow walking, but JC2 gives you over 50 vehicles (cars, tanks, fighter jets, and more) plus your essential grappling hook and parachute. If you’re hoofing it, you’re doing it wrong. Rather, open up the anywhere-accessible black market and buy a helicopter with dual-machine guns.
JC2’s biggest achievement is how it makes you feel totally in control, able to go anywhere and do anything. There are no invisible walls or disconnected “levels”. And visually, JC2 is really, really attractive. The weather and water are standouts still looking good years after release. The artwork is all very well-crafted, with amazing attention to detail.
The story is fun, too, with a very B-movie feel, intentionally hokey, but it works very well because of very solid voice work. The game also has a great self-awareness, featuring a hilarious dictator who will make you chuckle as he spouts his pontifications from loud speakers.
Are there downsides? A few. You run out of ammo often, but after 5 hours or so you learn to simply order new guns. There’s no stealth elements but that’s ok. Very few buildings have accessible interiors but no biggie.
Overall, the large scope, consistent quality, and accessible controls of JC2 make it one of the purest video games ever created. When you’re tired of “serious” games let JC2 cleanse your gaming palette.

So, there has been a lot of controversy about this game which I think is somewhat warranted. I got this game at 88% off, but many of the critiques have pointed out that you are paying $20 for about 90 minutes of content. And in that sense, I would agree - it is a very short game, and probably deserves an overall price cut to better match the amount of content currently available.
I have also seen criticisms that state that it feels like "Oscar bait", in the sense that it deals with issues (LGBT rights, white family dynamics) that would resonate with viewers. These criticisms feel less justified to me - I think the story itself would work fine with any combination of demographic and/or lifestyle combinations.
That being said, it manages to deal with LGBT issues in a serious and heartfelt way that should be commended. LGBT relationships are criminally under-represented in games, and I personally felt that the incorporation of those issues into the story did not feel forced at all. It seemed like a natural part of the storyline.
Above all, the game sets out to do several things: tell a very personal story, provide environmental interactivity, and develop a sense of mystery. It does all three incredibly well. As you walk through the house, there is a feeling of foreboding, a sense that something terrible happened. But as the game progresses and you interact with what starts to feel like a more and more familiar environment, you unravel what happened. You quickly realize that nothing supernatural is at play; instead, the issues coming to bear in this game are much closer to home and much more poignant.
Anyway, if you want a good story told in a very interactive manner, pick up this game while it is on sale. It was easily worth the ~$3, and I would certainly have paid more. But if you are looking for a traditional gaming experience (zombies, guns, fantasy tropes, etc.) then this game may not resonate as well as it could.

This will be a in depth review on Gone Home, instead of the usual one line joke because I believe the negative reviews for this game are unwarranted. This being said I want to give my personal context, and what games I personally enjoy. I do not usually like Indy titles, though have given MANY a chance. Fez, Meat Boy, ect. I understand why they are liked. But I lean towards story based gameplay.
That being said I will start this review.
Gone Home starts off with a odd feeling to it. You arrive after a small call home and a general backstory to literally just a empty house. After searching around for a few minutes, you begin to realize that this game is a investigation psychological thriller piece that allows you to go through the home and story at your own pace. The dialogue is well voice-acted, and the physics of the game though can be a bit clunky end up feeling completely natural. The story itself keeps you driven to read, and find more clues to the investigation.
If you go hearing spoilers about the game, it will ruin the original experience this title could have delievered for you. If you are coming in to this with no spoilers, and a general idea of the investigative piece. Then you will have a AMAZING time with this game.
This game is only for people that want a good story, and something that allows you to tie clues together to form a hypothesis on the plot before its final reveal. This is not Borderlands 2, Fall Out, or something that has story equal to gameplay. The gameplay is a aid towards the atmosphere of the story. Not the other way around.
All this being said, it is a amazing game that I am beyond happy with. I WOULD NOT pay full price for this game. It simply is not worth 20$. However if this is on sale for even 50% off, it is a must buy. Extremely happy with the purchase.

CONS: From what I've played, the game is basically a hack'n'slash inspired by the original DS. Swarms of enemies seem to pop up out of nowhere, and seem to exist for the sake of the game saying "Hah! Bet'cha Can't Do This! GIT GUD SCRUB!" ignoring the sort of smooth difficulty ramp from dark souls one that made you feel like a powerful badass. I don't know how widespread this issue is, but it's had a noticable impact on my enjoyment of the game. The other main bugbear I have with the game is the lack of map design that made Lordran feel like a world. PROS: Has none of the revolting issues that the original DS PC port had (that I've noticed). The game runs smoothly at a decent FPS, and still keeps the aesthetic from the original game with improved quality. The game, including the DLC of DS2 has a wide veriety of locations and bosses that still keep enough of what made the original Dark Souls fantastic that  makes it a good source of just more Dark Souls for those who have (and this is completely hypothetical) gotten a bit tired of DS NG+7.
Overall, it's a great game that just isn't quite the followup of Dark Souls 1 that one could hope for.

I got this one one of the occasional fire sales they have on it, so I just paid a couple of bucks.
This isn't really a game in the usual sense, because your existence at all is irrelevant to the plot, and to the extent there are any challenges they are rapidly self-evident.
You can pick up and handle a whole lot of objects in the game, but for 99% of them there really is no point.
The game keeps you interested through the process by playing a lot of bait-and-switch, telling you that there are stories going on that never actually mean anything.  If you start getting interested in anything occult going on, it's just a distraction.
The actual story (spoilers here) is another fake-out, looking like it's building towards a suicide pact and instead building to the "happy ending" of two teenaged girls running off to live with each other.  Without any means of support.  Or money.  If you project this one forward a few months the ending could be pretty dark.  But this isn't the sort of game that's going to think through the implications of this sort of thing.  We're supposed to just celebrate their decision to pursue their teenage romance in favour of social oppression.  Given the lifespan of the average teenage relationship it'd probably have been a far happier ending if they were all just sad for awhile and then moved on and pursued other relationships later.
All in all, expect this game to dangle you around with false plot threads for no more than a couple of hours before it gets to the point, which really could have been done in a single expository sequence.  This feels like a tiny fragment of a much bigger (and theoretically better) game.

A good immersive game. I was originally looking for exploration and a efficient fighting system, inspired as I was by an old Codemasters' game named Severance. Well... Dark Souls II SoFS stands somewhere between Shadow of the Colossus and Severance: Blade of Darkness.
So... you are doomed and explore a good number of different and unique environments in order to find peace, facing numerous enemies and collecting souls to empower yourself, exchange them for weapons and other stuff.
This game first rebuked me, then I got very enthusiast about it and then, approaching the end, I got a bit bored by some of its mechanisms and situations. It is a game to be tamed to be enjoyed, but it may be a bit too long for what it "packs".
The pros:
- Most of the levels, enjoyable or unnerving, sometime both, have a unique ambiance that you won't forget that soon.
- Bots or players invasions add drama. It can be either a good or bad thing, depending on how you appreciate the level where and when it happens.
- Different ways to polish your character, either with experience or equipment.
- Many boss' fights.
- You can use and abuse your opponents' weaknesses without many limits. But using tricks often calls for going through boring processes.
- Many ambushes which means a lot of looking around and careful steps, which means that you don't run through levels but actually look at them too. A good thing for fully observing and enjoying the developpers' job.
- A bit of platforming.
- A bit of backtracking, but not at an annoying level. More felt to me as a welcome way to discover a bit more of a previously done level.
- A recurrent nemesis.
- The possibility to farm experience to make things smoother, or to engage bots or other online players to help you fight if needed.
- You can play half an hour and stop, or play three hours in a row. You will still feel like having had an experience. Playing a short time here doesn't necessarily mean you will feel like having done nothing as it is in many other long videogames.
- It ranges from about hard to really tough depending on how you want to play it. A bit of difficulty isn't bad in the videogames' industry nowadays.
The cons:
- The fighting system isn't near half as good as Severance's unfortunately. And well, the hope it would cope with this old game's fighting system was what led me there at first. But it's still way better than Witcher's 3 for that specific matter.
- Too much rolling left or right in order to dodge.
- Mostly lore unfriendly stuff. I hate that... and spit on it. Fortunately, there are a few pieces of equipment which are ok and playable.
- The plot and mood of most of the game. I don't care a bit about their thing. It would have clearly been an experience breaker if the exploration and difficulty didn't make me enjoy the game and carry on regardless of that.
- No tutorial whatsoever. You'll constantly need to check things on the web. It helped to build some sort of passive community among players, sure. But still...
- Facing magic users suck when you are not one yourself.
- No pause, except while activating the soothing effect of bonfires. It's logical considering some of the situations you will face, but that still disturbs me. Things do happen in life while you are playing.
- You must play with a control pad. I've tried with keyboard and mouse at first, out of laziness to plug my stuff and sheer curiosity. I don't tell it's not possible, but it's even more unforgiving.
- The Crown of the Sunken King DLC stuff didn't get my attention. I felt like going through some generic, interchangeable rooms and abandoned it after half an hour. Sure it felt more challenging, but less because of the enemies' behaviour than exaggeration and their sheer number in somewhat cramped, contrastless and repetitive environments. Though there may be more about it considering the short time I invested in it...

Knowledge is knowing that Gone Home isn't a horror game. Wisdom is knowing that Gone Home really is a horror game. While there aren't any scary monsters or cursed artifacts, and in all likelihood the house isn't even haunted as is originally suspected, growing up as an LGBT youth even now, let alone 20 years ago, is one of the scariest things a teenager can go through. At one point, there's even a clipping indicating that Sam's parents were looking into conversion therapy, which has recently been debunked as tortuous and abusive, but is still highly favored by homophobic parents who wish to control who their children are. This game is a very emotional ride that left me in bitterweet tears as the ending credits rolled.

Rating: 8.8/10
Good: This game definitely gets the feel in terms of World War 1. The weapons, uniforms, grenades, maps, and even has the stories of the battles in each one, making it historically accurate. The atmosphere is absolutely stunning, you truly feel as though you are fighting in the trenches, and the gigantic holes from mortars is gorgeous. If gore is your thing, it has some great options in that department too, such as limbs coming off, lots of blood, and of course, screaming/gargling as you die from a gun shot. The trench warfare mode is REALLY fun, even if it is basically a skinned version of attack/defense. Also, the community is amazing, no real flamers/hackers that I've run into, definitely being a good sign.
Bad: And now for the bad points of said game. One shot almost ALWAYS determines a kill, which to me, sucks. I feel like if you shoot them in the chest, you should be able to be revived, and maybe with half health (thus introducing a health bar with no regeneration, except from health packs, etc.) I also feel like some of the maps are well...too flat. Yes, they look awesome (as they all do) BUT, strategically, the attacking team has to crawl their way to the enemy's bunker, and HOPE they dont get picked off/run out of time, which stink bollucks. I also feel that in some parts of certain maps, chokeholds can easily be one sided, but that could be entirely subjective.
Overall, a SOLID game with lots to offer. Definitely worth it if you enjoy history.
