Summary: It is a strange, sad, happy game and you have to be open to new things in order to enjoy the experience.
First off:
I bought the game cheap and under the impression that it was horror, which it is not, at least in the traditional sense. After I learned that it was not a survival horror game (10 seconds internet research), I started it again, this time not defaulting to the "Scared Victim" style of playing, instead playing the role I was intended to play, that of a teenager coming home.
Story:
Without spoiling the game, it is a very nice story. in the end I was emotionally exhausted and thought to myself "totally worth it." while rather short it made that up in intensity. Soaps are usually extremely dense in story development, the same goes for movies. In the game you experience one year worth of family drama in about 4 hours. The events are not Soap dense as in "more stuff happens" but more "let's ignore the unimportant stuff", even though the story itself is only about 2 hours i would guess (in game) long, you experience all the things that happened to your family in the last year.
It feels not like a soap because the events in the game did play out over a long time, you just get the abrdged version.
Gameplay (Played on Linux laptop):
It is your regular first person experience, walking picking stuff up, interacting nothing new to which I can point and say "that". The graphics I can't really judge, because i had to turn the quality all the way down and it still wasn't smooth. Audio was great quality, i liked that it was only ambient noise, no music, unless it made sense (you turned something on). Playing it immersive is and advice as close to a "must do" as I can give without being part of the creation team and immersive doesn't mean "headphones and emulate lighting levels of game". I mean willingness to play the part of someone who was gone a year and finds an empty home. Not with friends not let's playing it or watching a let's play. Immersive does not mean ambient lighting and super hedphones, immersive is becoming the character in mind. I still recommend headphones and a dark room, though.
Rant:
So many people say this game is "deep" and I would tell them in their face "No, other games are just shallow"
A game is usually described as deep the second characters become humans. When a game charakter says "let's poke things with sticks because yay!" noone bats an eye, when in a game strangers approach you and ask you to join their adventure the answer "Yes" because that is expected from the player.
But when someone approaches you in real live holds out their hand and says "The world is great and interesting, take my hand and we will see it together." many think 'what is wrong with that guy?' (Some said that to my face)
Why is that? Because making adventures for humans is hard, for characters it is not. I am a gamemaster and I know the problems one has when trying to create a world that breathes, so I blame noone for taking the "easy route", because sometimes you have to do that to create a fun experience.
A "deep" game is one where you have to think for yourself. Where the way is not that straightforward, where the answer is not what is expected. Being "deep" is being human. And being human is hard, many play games to stop being humans, in a sense.
But sometimes we want to be someone else, not just a hero, and that is when deep is what you want.

I got this game on the free weekend (sept 2016) and it was a BLAST! I just bought it from bundlestars for $8, with DLC!
Steam's review system should document if the reviewer's system meets specs and has up to date drivers (or at least if the reviewer claims they do), because I think a lot of people grabbed a free game hoping it'd run on a sub-spec system and they lashed out at the game when it didn't. Why else would someone make a complaint that isn't even legit... "too few guns?" It has at least pistol, pneumatic pistol, smg, crossbow, blunderbuss, AR, battle rifle, LMG, shotgun, limpet gun, and RPG. Add to that 4 types of thrown weapons (incendiary, explosive, hack tool, distractor) each with 4 subtypes, total 16. Plus knife, bolt cutters, flashlight...
With the difficulty on recruit mode it was non-stop action. I'm sure more stealth is needed at higher diffuculties. Free-running though controlled zones looking for targets of opportunity like equipment sabotage targets and lone soldiers to silent-takedown... jumping from scaffolding to rooftops and through upper floor windows, looting valuables... frantically looking for a dumpster or portapotty to hide in... what's not to love? It's like Mirror's Edge meets Far Cry. Plenty of side missions can be done in any order or ignored as you like. It took 16 hours for the main mission and about half the side missions, none of the job missions, and very few of the flash missions (optional missions that appear without warning).
I love the game's moral choices... imagine you are an operative in an occupied zone on an important mission and you get an opportunity to save some civilians getting a beatdown from bully occupiers, but only by blowing your cover. Take the chance or sacrifice them... clock's ticking! Will you use remote explosives blindly with the possibility an innocent will walk by them?
The characters are well fleshed out. Dana's a complete psychopath, the doc has his own priorities, reasonable characters all have different outlooks on the occupation, the NPC chatter is diverse and on topic, and I didn't see the game re-use any faces for different people, very well done. The graphics are amazing - at one point while hiding behind a dirty old dumpster next to a chain fence with ivy growing on it I felt like I was looking at a real photo.
I had 2 crashes to desktop during the my entire 16 hour campaign. Core i7, 16gb, GTX970.

The review I had posted before was a bit of a rant, but basically I don't like 2 as much as 1 as far as the Dark Souls series goes. That's not to say this is a bad game, far from it, it just loses some of the points that 1 had and instead gains some aspects. PvP is far more enjoyable, at least for me, and I actually wanted to fight people in this game. Instead of being able to simply hide behind shields, players now have a standoff waiting for the first move and having a battle of reactions, as guard breaking and the amount of stunlocking (while infuriating) allows for more need of protecting yourself through dodging and prediction rather than tanking behind a shield. The weapon and armor designs are far superior, in my opinion, particularly the Greatsword, as it feels like the title, a great sword that's massive and does boatloads of damage. However there are aspects that leave much to be desired. Boss designs feel far less varied as they are either rehashes of previous boss fights of the first game, variations of melee soldiers, "ganks" of multiple enemies varying from large sums of ordinary mobs to multiple boss level monsters, or on rare occasions new and unique bosses. Bosses also feel weaker, at least to me, as I have been able to beat most with little to no help from other players and with less knowledge on each of them. I've never died to a good chunk, unlike in 1 (although it was my first souls game so I have more experience in the design with this one but it's still not good that you can go into a boss fight with literally no knowledge of it and still win, barely healing sometimes even). And there's the Shrine of Amana, a location that I and many others have many misgivings with, especially as a melee character. I still say 1 is a better game, but 2 isn't exactly inferior just far different. Whether that's a good or bad thing is up to you, to me it's both. It's still Souls though and still feels amazing when you beat a boss you've been having trouble with, or get through a hard area.

This game became something of a lightning rod- politics outside this game's actual content have made it a favorite of some to hate, and some to promote. Assuming that you're looking for a review of the game itself, I'll say this.
This is a somewhat artistic, story-driven game based on exploration.
The major critisism that you'll see of it calls it a "Walking simulator". There are many other games that don't involve hit points and other such stats. This game primarily boasts the overall feel of what is going on, and while there are puzzle elements, it's not like a point and click adventure like your Monkey Island-type games. If you're looking for a horror game where you shoot zombies, you'll have to settle for one of the 10,000 other games that feature that.
Replayability isn't high, in the same way that once you've ready a mystery novel, you might read it another time to see the things you didn't notice, or read it again after a good amount of time has passed to enjoy it again, even though you know the ending. This isn't the sort of game that you'll be playing every weekend, nor was it ever intended to be.
I enjoyed this game, I found it's story interesting, and although it isn't especially long, the time spent was very engaging. This game has been out for a while, and is on sale rather often, so if you've gotten past the negative reviews long enough to see this one, I'd say it's definitely worth a play through.

I had the change to try the game during a free weekend event.
All in all I think not every negative review is justified and the game can be fun. Think of it as the following game mix:
Far Cry 3 missions and movement set in a dystopian scenario using the typical Crysis engine and weapon modification features.
Story / Missions:
The missions are not very innovative and can be copied 1:1 from Far Cry 3. Kill/destroy, defend, collect, use/hack. It can get boring to hack another console for the 100 time, but if you liked to simply stray in FC3, you might also like it here.
I can't say much about the story, but from what I've seen it's more like a no brainer. More like a medium to get you through the scenario. Dont't expect crazy drug dreams like in FC3. So don't play it if you expect much story.
Maps / Levels:
The game has no big open world map like FC3, more like about 7 bigger levels with tasks. Each area has a distinctive look, although the alltogether look similar due to the destruction of the city (ruins, kinda grey). What i like about those semi-open-world levels is that most actions change the level. Buildings look different, when you liberate them. You can even notice more and more rebels moving around or civilians revolting, which is nice for the atmosphere. In the end, if you begin the real rebellion in a sector it starts to look more like a warzone.
Graphics:
The game is by far not ugly. It sometimes looks very "Call of Duty" / grey-in-grey mid day. But I guess thats only realistic in cities. Sunrise and sundown look very nice and give a nice touch of colors to the greyness of mid day. The night is usually really dark, so you need your flashlight (think pitch black darnkess like in S.T.A.L.K.E.R. with mods). So in the end the graphics are atmospheric considering the scenario.
AI:
Quite dumb. More like Call of Duty AI / quantity instead of quality.
TL;DR:
Mix Far Cry 3 with Crysis set in a dystopian scenario without much story. If you liked doing mischief in FC3, give it a try. But don't play it for story.

Vast open world. There is some semblance of a story involving a cruel dictator etc. but honestly it isn't that engrossing nor is it really in your face as a selling point to the game. This game speaks for itself through sheer size and gameplay as well as the amount of things you can do to occupy yourself.
You can go on missions from story to collections if you have to grab them all as well as take part in races. There is a reason my friends and I have spent 100s of hours on this game and that is that over every hill, around every corner there is something to see, do or collect.
There is a huge amount of vehicles in the game, locations (bases) to destroy to basically snub your nose at the Dictator who is keeping the populace down. Even when I had completely nearly 100% of the game I wanted to start over so I had a whole world to skillfully and artistically (movie-style-like) destroy all over again.
I did encounter one glitch with the game and that was that on occasion the world will go devoid of NPCs and only be populated by the few soldiers roaming the world. A quick save and restart of the game would usually resolve that.
If you love open world and have the creativity to "set your own goals outside story" then this is your game. Back when the other guys were doing more linear "open-ish-world" this game came out and really redefined what an open world could be.

So, I had hesitated to get into this series for the last several years and a friend of mine talked me into purchasing this game about a month prior to Dark Souls 3's release.  I have to say, that this was the best purchase for a video game that I have made since the late 2000's.
I have not had this much immersion into a game for a very long time, due to the fact that the majority of the games nowadays are on easy mode.  Even at the highest difficulty settings, some games can be a little challenging at times, but still a breeze at most.  This game challenges me, even after becoming an intermediate at the combat system, and I LOVE it!  There's never a moment where I feel like I can just blow through any content at all in this game, not even after leveling past 220 and going to the early game content.  There is a sense of dread that I feel when going into certain locations that I remember being very tough, and that makes the adrenaline flow very easily.
Dark Souls 2 has changed my perspective of what a Triple A game needs to be.  It doesn't need a cast of real actors, it doesn't need flashy graphics, and it doesn't need a super strong story shoved down your throat.  No, all it needs is the best gameplay I've played in an RPG, ever.
I recommend this game to anyone that wants a challenge and is tired of the "no child left behind" library of games we have been given over the past 10 years or so.

This game is extremely good, but the amount of bugs and broken mechanics overshadows a good amount of fun that could otherwise be visible.
Combat is very wonky. Range for every weapon is quite awkward. It's not uncommon to be sniped from across the map with a luger or a c96, or be taken out 2 trenches over from an Mp18. The flamethrower's range can annihilate an entire team in seconds and its awfully overpowered. Many guns aren't leveled for fun, but rather for realism - yet when realistic features are suggested to the community and devs, they're excused for "not being realistic".
The game doesn't know if it wants to be a gritty WW1 Simulator or a fun shooter. So it tries to do both, leaving it lukewarm on both elements.
One of the largest issues with how the gameplay works is matching. It's done very awkwardly and it's off balanced. You'll have one team full of level 1s who bought the game yesterday and are still trying to understand the controls, put up against a team of seasoned veterans who have been with the project since its alpha launch. The team is a squad full of 100s who bunnyhop around the map and trickshot the newbies to nothing.
The community around the game is alright in most areas but can be very toxic. Many times during gameplay two or three people will start a match-long argument and you can barely talk to your fellow teammates while they drone on about nothing. The playerbase has adopted a very "git gud" attitude and most folks are not very welcoming of new players.
The game essentially shuts itself off from new demographics and unfortunately the playerbase seems to be getting smaller. I notice it takes hours for any teams to come up until like noon, and even then all I find are simular situations to my previous point - One team absolutely curbstomps another with no real challenge involved.
The graphics, sound design, and environmental elements are second-to-none, however. They're excellently crafted and I really feel like I'm there. The in-game music is quite good, and the combat can be very fun at times.
Weaponry is absolutely amazing - And the map design is fantastic.
Mechanic-wise, The game works, but only selectively. The game is sound, but awkward.
I simply cannot endorse this game, but at the same time want to show people it.
It's fun, but makes me want to tear my hair out in rage at the same time.
I often find I'll redownload it once every 7 months, have fun, and then learn to re-hate the game so much I uninstall it again. Rince and repeat forever. It's so much more trouble than what its worth - with gamebreaking features that haven't been patched since day 1 and combat bugs galore, you start fresh and hyped to start a round but you'll be just generally frusterated with the game's mechanics before long.
But the absolute worst issue out of all of them is balance.
Nothing in the game is ♥♥♥♥ing balanced. At all. The word "Balance" is a lie in Verdun Context.
Some weapons require skill, others - you press Mouse 1 and Move Forward and the entire trench falls over.
The biggest culprits are the Webley, M1911, Lewis Gun, Wex, and the Mp18. Each of these listed have ridiculous range (AKA, Submachine-gun and Flamethrower Sniping), and are balanced so poorly you can have 1 player on one team absolutely curb-stomp over 6 players with the same two guns over and over. Skill isn't relevant - the guns are broken.
Weapons should not be beefed up for no reason - It becomes immensely un-fun.
"yeah, but historically-"

World War One was hardly a balanced fight, but games should be. Or else you come out with Verdun.
It's a combination of both a Realism Simulator and a videogame, so you come out with a half-baked videogame with half-baked realism.
Bullets should still be bullets. A belly-shot with a rifle should tip you on your♥♥♥♥♥the same way you can get insta-killed from the leg by an Mp18.
Rifle shots got nerfed - so essentially, any riflemen are carrying sticks, while anyone using automatic or otherwise weaker guns (Luger, M1911, Webley) will absolutely kick everyones'♥♥♥♥♥
Everything about the game is so good, but the infuriating mechanics and absolute lack of direction takes this game down from a solid 9/10 to a god-damned 4.5. I'm honestly dissapointed, because my reviews over the years have gone on-and-off from positive to negative each time I've played the game, but recently all I get is more bugs, more bad features, and more anger-enducing moments. Balance has gotten worse, combat is getting worse every patch.

Vast open world. There is some semblance of a story involving a cruel dictator etc. but honestly it isn't that engrossing nor is it really in your face as a selling point to the game. This game speaks for itself through sheer size and gameplay as well as the amount of things you can do to occupy yourself.
You can go on missions from story to collections if you have to grab them all as well as take part in races. There is a reason my friends and I have spent 100s of hours on this game and that is that over every hill, around every corner there is something to see, do or collect.
There is a huge amount of vehicles in the game, locations (bases) to destroy to basically snub your nose at the Dictator who is keeping the populace down. Even when I had completely nearly 100% of the game I wanted to start over so I had a whole world to skillfully and artistically (movie-style-like) destroy all over again.
I did encounter one glitch with the game and that was that on occasion the world will go devoid of NPCs and only be populated by the few soldiers roaming the world. A quick save and restart of the game would usually resolve that.
If you love open world and have the creativity to "set your own goals outside story" then this is your game. Back when the other guys were doing more linear "open-ish-world" this game came out and really redefined what an open world could be.

This game is extremely good, but the amount of bugs and broken mechanics overshadows a good amount of fun that could otherwise be visible.
Combat is very wonky. Range for every weapon is quite awkward. It's not uncommon to be sniped from across the map with a luger or a c96, or be taken out 2 trenches over from an Mp18. The flamethrower's range can annihilate an entire team in seconds and its awfully overpowered. Many guns aren't leveled for fun, but rather for realism - yet when realistic features are suggested to the community and devs, they're excused for "not being realistic".
The game doesn't know if it wants to be a gritty WW1 Simulator or a fun shooter. So it tries to do both, leaving it lukewarm on both elements.
One of the largest issues with how the gameplay works is matching. It's done very awkwardly and it's off balanced. You'll have one team full of level 1s who bought the game yesterday and are still trying to understand the controls, put up against a team of seasoned veterans who have been with the project since its alpha launch. The team is a squad full of 100s who bunnyhop around the map and trickshot the newbies to nothing.
The community around the game is alright in most areas but can be very toxic. Many times during gameplay two or three people will start a match-long argument and you can barely talk to your fellow teammates while they drone on about nothing. The playerbase has adopted a very "git gud" attitude and most folks are not very welcoming of new players.
The game essentially shuts itself off from new demographics and unfortunately the playerbase seems to be getting smaller. I notice it takes hours for any teams to come up until like noon, and even then all I find are simular situations to my previous point - One team absolutely curbstomps another with no real challenge involved.
The graphics, sound design, and environmental elements are second-to-none, however. They're excellently crafted and I really feel like I'm there. The in-game music is quite good, and the combat can be very fun at times.
Weaponry is absolutely amazing - And the map design is fantastic.
Mechanic-wise, The game works, but only selectively. The game is sound, but awkward.
I simply cannot endorse this game, but at the same time want to show people it.
It's fun, but makes me want to tear my hair out in rage at the same time.
I often find I'll redownload it once every 7 months, have fun, and then learn to re-hate the game so much I uninstall it again. Rince and repeat forever. It's so much more trouble than what its worth - with gamebreaking features that haven't been patched since day 1 and combat bugs galore, you start fresh and hyped to start a round but you'll be just generally frusterated with the game's mechanics before long.
But the absolute worst issue out of all of them is balance.
Nothing in the game is ♥♥♥♥ing balanced. At all. The word "Balance" is a lie in Verdun Context.
Some weapons require skill, others - you press Mouse 1 and Move Forward and the entire trench falls over.
The biggest culprits are the Webley, M1911, Lewis Gun, Wex, and the Mp18. Each of these listed have ridiculous range (AKA, Submachine-gun and Flamethrower Sniping), and are balanced so poorly you can have 1 player on one team absolutely curb-stomp over 6 players with the same two guns over and over. Skill isn't relevant - the guns are broken.
Weapons should not be beefed up for no reason - It becomes immensely un-fun.
"yeah, but historically-"

World War One was hardly a balanced fight, but games should be. Or else you come out with Verdun.
It's a combination of both a Realism Simulator and a videogame, so you come out with a half-baked videogame with half-baked realism.
Bullets should still be bullets. A belly-shot with a rifle should tip you on your♥♥♥♥♥the same way you can get insta-killed from the leg by an Mp18.
Rifle shots got nerfed - so essentially, any riflemen are carrying sticks, while anyone using automatic or otherwise weaker guns (Luger, M1911, Webley) will absolutely kick everyones'♥♥♥♥♥
Everything about the game is so good, but the infuriating mechanics and absolute lack of direction takes this game down from a solid 9/10 to a god-damned 4.5. I'm honestly dissapointed, because my reviews over the years have gone on-and-off from positive to negative each time I've played the game, but recently all I get is more bugs, more bad features, and more anger-enducing moments. I remember a warm summerday in august 1914, people were gathering around a poster, a poster that will set a force of unimaginable powers loose. But back then we were naive, there was so much hate towards the Germans after the Franco-Prussian War. We were ready to annihilate them, or at least humiliate them like they did to us. Without a second thought me and my friends enlisted the next day. It will be a great adventure some say. We will drink a cold beer on the Alexanderplatz in Berlin within a few months others say. Too much imagination. Now 2 years have passed, i'm sitting in the mud of our trench. Fighting on our own turf. Berlin isn't even close. I saw all my friend die, but i still had the lucky number, for now. My compagnie is mostly fresh recruits, they will die within a few days. They jump from every piece of arty that hits the ground. Our orders came in, we have to attack. Another suicide mission, going straight to the enemy lines. The previous compagnie that attacked a few days ago was completely annihilated, their corpses still rotting on the barbed wires, food for the rats. There is still one thing i hope for, that this slaughter called a war will probably be the war to end all wars. I go now, may god have mercy on my soul .Take good care of our 4 children, love you and miss you with all my heart. Pfc René. Died 20 march 1916 at Verdun

“Trench fighting is the bloodiest, wildest, most brutal of all ... Of all the war's exciting moments none is so powerful as the meeting of two storm troop leaders between narrow trench walls. There's no mercy there, no going back, the blood speaks from a shrill cry of recognition that tears itself from one's breast like a nightmare.”
― Ernst Jünger, Storm of Steel
This is a damn well made indie game. While not as polished or smooth as other AAA FPS titles, this is definitely the best WW1 FPS out there, and will continue to be even after Battlefield 1's release. The squad system is well fleshed out, and doesn't leave out many major combatants(from the western front anyway), with great variety of different classes and tactics to choose from. The classes range from machine gunners, to officers that can call in artillery/gas attacks and add "buffs" to nearby team mates, to melee/ close range focused assault classes, to sniper units. The different equipment and class types make it feel like you need to "roleplay" your role, as that's what your equipment is for. Leveling up these classes through play adds a neat progression system that gives your character more weapons, more abilities, etc. In addition to class leveling, there is a very unique squad leveling system that makes it feel like you are part of an epic war, as they are persistent across matches. Teamwork is essential, and you really get the sense that your squad is its own self sufficient unit in a much larger conflict.
The variety of squad types is awesome too, ranging from U.S. Doughboys to elite Alpenjägers, to the scrappy Belgians, to the rough and tough French Poilus. As your squad levels up, your player models become better armed and tougher looking, just like a squad would in real life. The ability to name squads whatever you want, from "Donald Trump's Royal Guard" to "The Really Bad Marksmen" or something adds a lot of personality and a feeling of pride as you fight with other players on your team. The original FFX used to be one of my favorite games as a kid. Growing up, I always held it in the highest regard, and I've always had a huge amount of nostalgia for it... Up until I played it again as a 22 year old adult. What an eye-opening experience.
This game was clearly made for a much younger audience. The writing is an atrocity for almost the entire game, and by the writing I particularly mean the dialogue. It is incredibly cumbersome to force myself to sit through almost every cutscene (minus the CGI cutscenes, which are the only ones that hold my interest). The fact that the developers didn't include an option to skip the cutscenes, or at the very least fast-forward through the cutscenes, is a huge ♥♥♥♥ you to the players that have already played the game before, and to the players who play this game specifically for the gameplay. Before the Yunalesca fight, there is literally a 10-minute cutscene. The problem with that is since there's no option to skip it, if you die during the boss fight, you have to sit through that entire cutscene again. Not to mention the cutscene isn't by any means an intriguing cutscene in the first place. So you have to sit through this incredibly boring cutscene, only to have one chance to beat the boss. If you don't beat her, you have to sit through that entire cutscene again while gouging your eyes out due to the boredom... Or you could just alt-tab out and browse the interwebs to your heart's content. Either one works.
What bothers me most about 99% of the cutscenes in this game is the fact that the characters speak in a snail-like pace to each other, and in between each line there would be a few seconds of silence. The conversations didn't have a natural flow to them, and they didn't feel authentic in the slightest. Not only that, but the dialogue had little to no substance. The writing is just extremely poor, and there are no original ideas. There is a♥♥♥♥♥♥ton of exposition through the dialogue between the characters, and particularly from Tidus himself during his narrations throughout the game. The exposition isn't even subtle or intelligently told, it's in your face and from time to time it felt like through their conversations the characters would indirectly remind the player what's going on in the story so far and where it's headed, and there's not even a single moment in the plot where I felt like I needed it. It's not a difficult story to understand in the slightest, unless you get manipulated due to your young age (like me).
Let's talk about the characters. Tidus is an annoying ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. He's extremely optimistic and cheerful, which both contribute to his obnoxious cluelessness. Wakka is similar to Tidus in terms of his optimism, but he's more irritable and, ultimately, more human. His weapon is also a blitzball. He actually has superhuman strength. Lulu is the realist goth of the party. Her black magic-al♥♥♥♥♥♥in HD are reason enough to buy this game. Yuna is the innocent one in the group, and she's also about as clueless as Tidus is. Kimahri is the silent guardian of the group, and his silence alone is ultimately the reason why he's the second most interesting character in the party.  The two best and most interesting characters in the game are Auron and Seymour. Seymour had some originality to him, and he glosses over some intriguing ideas through his poorly written dialogue. His vibes alone stole every scene he was in. He had a subtle wickedness to him, especially through the voice acting. Auron's role was akin to Lulu's in that he acted as the realist of the group. He's the most badass character, and his backstory is one of the most intriguing aspects of the plot. But like every other aspect of this game, it was horribly executed. The reminscent scenes of Auron, Jecht, and Braska felt more like expositional robots speaking indirectly to the player, rather than three best friends speaking casually directly to each other. Like I mentioned before, almost every conversation in this game almost completely lacks authenticity, and they don't have a natural flow to them.
Overall, I just wanted to talk about the story and the writing rather than the gameplay in this review because that is ultimately what I look most forward to in any single-player video game. I can confidently say that I was blinded by the nostalgia I had for this game, but not anymore. If you want a game that has an original story, that contains unique ideas that are fleshed out intelligently, and has compelling characters, then this isn't the game for you.

I loved Dark Souls, so I came into this expecting more of the same. Well, I got what I expected, but on steroids.
From the beginning, it was practically unplayable. I could barely kill anything and I was dying from even the most basic of trash. Most things even one-shotted me, so it took all I had to keep playing. After I finally defeated the Lost Giant, the Dragonrider (though I cheesed that, and he fell off the edge), the Skeleton lords and got to a point of fighting a Medusa-looking boss, I just couldn't do it any more. I decided to look up and see if I could get a summon NPC for it.
Well, it turns out that I couldn't summon anything, even in human form. It took me ages to work out why. What I'd done from the start was join a covenant in Majula, thinking nothing of it. But what that did was set all the enemies to a much, much higher difficulty than it should have been (as if I was on a 3rd play through). It also meant I couldn't summon anything.
Now that I've left the covenant, the game is back to a more bearable level and I can carry on knowing I was so amazing at the game that I unknowingly went hard and didn't go home. Stupidity is punished in Dark Souls II.

My only complaint really is that the game tends to be buggy and the thought "Pls don't crash pls don't crash" often pops up in my head while playing.

Hopefully the game keeps growing!

Who knew a game from 15 years ago could still be so damn good today!
+ LOADS of content, expect to get 40-60+ hours worth of enjoyable content from FFX, and another 30+ hours from FFX-2
+ Visually the game looks fantastic, especially for a PS2 game that came out in 2001. It's almost unbelievable. The higher resolution mixed with some updated textures does nothing but improve upon the original, although some areas do look a bit nicer than others.
+ The story is amazing, filled with mystery, adventure, and loads of surprises. To put it in very simple terms, you are trying to defeat a huge Godzilla-like magical creature born from sin that has been causing massive destruction, death, and suffering throughout the world. (there's also a ton of interesting lore to discover throughout the game)
+ Many voice acted characters with fantastic dialogue and great personalities.
+ In FFX you have 7 characters to choose from, each with their own unique traits and abilities, although normally you choose your 3 favorites and can switch between characters at anytime even during battle.
+ The turn based combat system is surprisingly a lot of fun and much deeper than you would expect. There's tons of skills, abilities, special moves, "overdrives" (very powerful attacks), spells, an overload of weapons / armor custimizations, and so much more. In combination with the amount of characters you get to use, every player will likely have a different strategy to defeat many of the bosses.
+ Challenging Bosses! Trust me this game is no walk in the park, and revolves around the many, many bosses you will encounter throughout the game. Each one is unique and actually pretty thrilling to fight as you learn their weaknesses and strategeize your plan of attack.
+ Aeons which are summoned powerful magical creatures to fight for you are an amazing addition although optional. They each look great, come with some fantastic animations and skills, can be customized, and really just add another layer of greatness on top of everything else.
+ Hidden / Extra content, there's at least 10-15hours worth of "Extra" content in FFX that most people skip over. This content is mainly for people who finished the game and are looking for "more", although it's absolutely incredible to me that the developers decided to add so much! There's "Celestrial Weapons" which are the best weapons in the game that you must find parts often in hidden areas or obtained through completing difficult minigames / sidequests. There's a TON of extra end-game bosses like Dark Aeons or the bosses in the Monster Hunter area. Monster Hunting in itself is quite a large chunk of extra content that essentially has you go around capturing monsters to create new very challenging bosses with very unique rewards. There's 3 "hidden" and yet very powerful optional aeons that are absolutely worth getting. There's also new dungeons with powerful creatures and loot.
+ Blitzball...sort of like underwater soccer using your hands is basically a game within a game. You can hire new players, level them up and learn unique blitzball abilities, and there's leagues and championships which give their own rare and unique items. This game in itself adds an extra like 1-5+ hours of content although again completely optional
+ The game runs perfectly on my PC. Fast load times and I didn't experience any problems or any crashes whatsoever with max settings. Some may complain that it's 30fps, but this game was designed for 30fps so you will not notice any slowdown or stutter whatsoever.
+
, I played through the entire game with an Xbox One Wireless controller. I did NOT have to keybind anything, it auto-detects it, and even changes the in-game button prompts to display Xbox buttons which was very nice of them to do.
- The new arranged soundtrack isn't nearly as good as the original, but it IS OPTIONAL and you can switch between the two throughout the game if you wish. (Again Original is best)
- The Remastered character faces look a bit odd and expressionlist at times, I mean at times Tidus looks like he's wearing some heavy eyeliner lol.
- You still can't skip cutscenes...this is especially bad if you fail a boss and have to rewatch a 5minute scene
- I know for a fact, many people think the bosses in the game are "too challenging" most people will get stuck at some point and many will end up giving up. (if this is you, please look up some strategy guides!)
- There are some cringe-worthy moments during a few scenes, and the facial animations are a bit dated. Personally I enjoy them, but new players may be turned off a bit at first.
- This is a personal note, but there's one character named Kimahri who is practically useless throughout the entire game, and has very little character development throughout the story.
- The Story while being very interesting can also be extremely confusing. Especially once you reach the end of the game, and want to know more details about how the game began, how sin was born, how Jecht and Tidus got to Spira, about the Machina War, and about the timeline. The game is quite vague on many of these questions.
Turbo: Speed up the game x2 or x4 (this is amazing for grinding late game)
Supercharge: Characters will be supercharged
Enemy Encounter Override: Increase or Decrease encounter rate
Auto battle: Characters fight using AI
Hide HUD: For Screenshots
Using anything above will NOT prohibit earning achievements
New Arranged Soundtrack that is completely optional and can be changed at any point in the game to the Original Soundtrack (ORIGINAL IS BEST)
There's also an "expert spheregrid" which lets you greatly customize the characters beyond what the normal sphere grid allows, although entirely optional and unneeded.
+ Very lighthearted game with a lot of amusing characters and cutscenes
+ Cute and Sexy outfits / Dresspheres which effectively act as class changes. Every character basically has the same stats and can use and switch between any class although you must train each character to learn skills as each class.
+ Lots of sidequests and addional lore
+ Extremely challening, I found some parts to X-2 to be considerably more difficult than X, especially if you choose not to do the sidequests to level up your characters. (There's a reason why only 2% or less of players have beaten FFX-2 on Steam...the bosses are insane!)
- The combat system has completely changed. It is now a Active Time Battle system similar to FFVII or XIII. It can be hard to get familiar with as battles are very fast paced, and I often found myself making a lot of mistakes feeling rushed to make decisions during difficult encounters.
- The story is not very good, and is extremely confusing to understand. Yuna becomes a sphere hunter looking for Tidus (who should not exist), and finds a man who looks exactly like Tidus named "Shuyin"but is not him....   I won't go further then that.... But I felt like FFX had a very nice concise ending....and  X-2 kinda ruins it for me.
- Sidequests are extremely easy to miss, and you can not go back to do them if you've already advanced the story. (Forcing you to use a guide so you don't miss large portions of the game)
- Some enemies are ridiculously overpowered

First off, let's address the criticism: Yes, the game is a walking simulator.  Yes, the only gameplay elements are meandering through a house, reading notes, turning lights on and/or off, and picking up miscellaneous items to spin them around and examine their features - often for no substantial reason.  No, there are not any jump scares or really any horror elements.  It's pure exploration and piecing together a family's story.  And it takes about 2 hours to finish.
That aside, I genuinely enjoyed this game.  It's one of those few examples where learning more about the story is a reward in itself.  The subject matter is quite mundane, but that's why it's so effective; it's a story that is grounded, believable, engrossing, and - at the risk of sounding like a pretentious snob - utterly human.  It did not thrill or challenge me, but it did affect me emotionally; not quite on the level that, say The Cat Lady or Silent Hill 2 did, but more than a lot of games.  And for that, I enjoyed it quite a bit.
I can see why people hate this game; it hardly even qualifies as a game.  But for what it is - an experience of exploration and gradually uncovering an emotional story - it is excellent.  I will probably never play it again, but for the two hours that I did play it, it made a substantial impact on me.  It is also pertinent to note that I only paid $2.39, and I would say that is a fair price; $20 is too high for such a short experience - even though it is very well done.

I've finished the story on PS4 so I can comment to the game's story and everything in global.
The Revolution as a first person shooter game is set in, as the name suggests "THE REVOLUTION" type of open world (sorta) location with lot of details and stuff laying around. I won't spoil anything for the story, as it's not great, but decent. Characters are decent and relatable, graphics are awesome (not something next level obviously but awesome for the eye in every way, details on characters are greatly done), and system requirements aren't that scary at all. I have a weird Metro Last Light feeling while walking around, I don't know why.
They patched the game in the beginning of September so the game is very stable now. Considering the requirements it was playable even on a Core 2 Duo processor (30+ FPS with drops as expected from an older architecture), also Core 2 Quad (40+ almost stable with few minor dips, nothing too serious).
I tested the game myself on a GTX970, i5 6600 and 8GB of RAM (because it's free for two days, so why not?) and it's pretty stable (compared to before patch - it was a mess), 60+ FPS all the time on all settings maxed out, not optimized? What are you talking about? With a decent specs you can max the game easily without anti-aliasing and super-sampling.
BIG LIKE FOR THE CUTSCENES - MOVIE LIKE FEELING! GREAT ANIMATIONS COMPARED TO SOME OTHER GAMES
As for the bad part, there are...not just a few issues with the game. I was unable to get the game working on anything but 1080p resolution, it doesn't support 4K display for some reason, it always keeps me in the 1080p resolution, 1440p resolution obviously DOESN'T WORK TOO.
This game have had so much potentioal once it was released - but not anymore, considering it's ruined by bad reviews. I guess that's what you get for releasing an unfinished product nowadays (and thereee are alot of them, but compared to other disasters they actually fixed it - so The Revolution wins a point for that).
As for the AI - it's a mess, I can't think of any game that has worse AI than this game, it's...ahh...terrible, horrible, there's no word to describe how stupid the AI is actually.
Homefront The Revolutions is obviously NOT WORTH THE FULL PRICE TAG, catch it on a sale or some third party websites for half the price.

Trench warfare like you wouldnt find it in a game like Call of Duty and Battlefield. Yes, even Battlefield 1 will probably not feature this kind of trench warfare. The game is alot slower than traditional FPS games, since its pretty much a sniper fest with bolt action rifles and big old school machine guns. In your trench you're pretty well protected from small arms fire, but then there's always the enemies artillery bombardments you're gonna want to watch out for. If you actually want to score some kills though, you're going to have to put your head above the trenches and take out the advancing enemy. My best tip for this game is to never stay in a single area for too long, or you'll risk being shot. Use cover where you can. If you're looking out over a spot with something like a machine gun, cover the frontline diagonally with some cover at the sides. It gives you the best chance at picking off attackers without them being able to snipe you head on. Watch out for grenades, and get the hell around a corner when the enemy throws a grenade into your trench.
The most prominent gamemode is named Frontlines and is VERY different from the default deathmatch kind of games you see in other shooters. The match switches between defending and attacking. During defence you are more or less forced to stay in your trench and defend it as the other team tries to cross no mans land and capture your trench. After this, its your team's turn to attack or counter attack. This goes back and forth along multiple trench lines and gives a VERY authentic WW1 feeling, as there's an actual frontline. Games like Call of Duty never have a frontline, because you never really know where the enemy is coming from. Both teams are pretty much looking in eachothers directions in this game.
I can really recommend this game. Its a very refreshing shooter after getting SO bored of games like Call of Duty and Battlefield. It does get frustrating to get shot from out of nowhere sometimes, but its only a reminder that you didnt keep your head down or recon well enough. Surviving what you need to learn, though dying is also part of the game, as sometimes survival is just not possible. Trench warfare is known to be brutal and unforgiving, its a challenge to get good at, but its also great fun at the same time. Seeing how far you can get before inevitable death is pretty addicting.

An excellent 90's themed game with a story told through slow, controlled exploration. It may be criticized for it's lack of "gameplay" (whatever that means), but it's another one of those games that sacrifices traditional puzzle gameplay for something much more organic and straight-forward, similiar to The Vanishing of Ethan Carter, and to a lesser extent, Dear Esther (Dear Esther however does not have much interactivity at all). It simply uses a bit of interactivity to tell a story without unnecessary filler content.
I think what's important to consider before playing this game is that: You have to play it in one sitting, and you have to pay attention to everything you encounter and read in order to reconstruct the narrative space, to understand the characters, their background and interests, to nourish empathy with these characters.
It's not exactly a game for gamers. It's something that you have to make an effort to play (granted, not much effort at all), it's not a game that will entertain you after work. It's a game that contains a heartwarming message with many underlying themes. A tad of social criticism here, a tad of 90s nostalgia there. It's something that you should play when you have nothing else to do, and are feeling particularly adventurous,
There really isn't much to say about the game, objectively. I can tell you that the graphics are just completely utilitarian, it has everything it needs to have and has a great 90's atmosphere that is likely to resonate well with anyone who grew up in the US in the 90s or even early 00's. And the game is just about 2 hours long. Which is ok, considering the price.
Definitely recommend it for anyone who is patient and remotely open minded.

After finishing Dark Souls III I wanted a little more so when I saw Dark Souls II: SotFS up for sale I jumped on it and for the most part I'm glad I did.
First I want to talk about the port, which is great this time, the complete opposite of Dark Souls I: Prepare To Die on PC which we all know has a laundry list of issues and is only made somewhat playable by DSFix but I'm happy to say that's not the case here, I was getting a locked 60fps throughout on max settings and I didn't have a single technical issue in over 40 hours. The game looks, sounds and runs really nicely.
Content wise it's a big game with the included DLC, I actually still have two optional bosses left to kill and I've sunk 43 hours into it already so you're getting plenty of bang for your buck (I'd highly recommend shopping around, I picked it up for £9.59). On the whole the game is enjoyable in a Dark Souls sort of way, but there were a few areas that went past "Dark Souls" and just ended up being extremely tedious, not hard or challenging just plain boring and those areas did tarnish the overall game for me a bit, but thankfully there's only a few truly poorly designed areas in the game so in the grand scheme of things it's not too bad.
I found the bosses to be on the whole too easy, the base game bosses especially. I killed every boss in under 5 tries apart from a select few. The DLC bosses are much harder in general though, and the final boss of part II is currently kicking my butt after many tries, he's by far the hardest boss in the game and one of the hardest I've faced in the "Soulsborne" universe [EDIT: He's down!]. I haven't been using phantoms or summons either, so I imagine if you do get truly stuck using these options will help you out a lot.
For me it's worth playing if you enjoy these types of games, I actually put it above Dark Souls I purely because of the quality of the port, it was just more enjoyable to play without all the issues, but it's a few pegs behind both Bloodborne and Dark Souls III which is the top of the pile IMO.

The story(Spoiler free) sees you play as Tidus fighting monsters that appear all over Spira, in true epic Final Fantasy fashion there are twists and turns along the way. Even though the voice acting is a little weak(HA-HA-HA-HA scene...) you fall in love with the characters and share some truely heart-wrenching moments. The main antagonist is a massive monster named Sin that appears in Spira to punish the world for using "machina". To beat Sin a "Summoner" must fight him with his/her followers every time he re-appears. Along the way you will deal with marriages, undead monster birds, Final Fantasy classics like Biggs, Wedge and Cid, Movie spheres, a complete new language to learn and much much more!
If story doesn't draw you in, gameplay should, there is a huuuuge and complex levelling system called "the sphere grid" using it you can tailor your gameplay how you like by upgrading skills such as the FF classics like Fire, Fira, Firaga. Using the advanced grid you can "mix and match" and make the ultimate all powerful character.

I've only played about an hour, but I can't take any more. This game gets all the small things wrong, and they pile up to make for an absolutely infuriating experience.
Controlling the game is a nightmare. The mouse smoothing is crazy strong - I know it can be turned off in .ini files, but that's not acceptable in 2016. The guns feel like Nerf guns (although at least they're Nerf guns that actually kill people, at least in the intro levels I played) - no recoil, poor sound effects. Driving a motorcycle is quite possibly the worst driving experience I've ever had in a video game: it controls exactly like walking, just faster. Why does an over-the-top action shooter have a handbrake control if it doesn't let you drift around corners and you stop within a second of letting off the gas anyway? Oh, and the first time I tried to get *off* a motorcycle, I was magically catapulted 50 feet into the air and died on impact, so that was fun.
The sound is hilariously bad. I knew Yahtzee had complained about it, but I was still amazed by the terribleness. In one of the opening scenes, an important character (I know he's important because literally every NPC I've talked to can't shut up about how important he is) gets arrested on the street. According to the subtitles, he's yelling at the cops. All you can actually hear is the civilians, who are *all shouting the same line, one after another*. In a pre-rendered cutscene. Yeah.
The graphics... well, they're not exactly bad, but again, they're annoying in a lot of little ways. The motion blur is sickening (motion blur on moving the mouse? Who thought that was a good idea?). The lip-syncing isn't synced. The NPC animation quality is poor. Ground and wall textures leave something to be desired.
The setting is kind of cool, but that's not enough to redeem a game whose actual gameplay feels like a trip to the dentist.

I doubt this review will see the light of day, as Steam seems intent on burying this game for whatever reason.
Is it short? Yes, it is. The house is big, but in the end it's just a house, and there are only so many places to explore.
Is there any replay value? That depends. Personally I think that, like a good movie, the value of experiencing it a second time drastically improves if there's someone else with you for whom it's the first time. So yeah, replay value if you've got a friend to play it or watch alongside.
Is it worth $20? That's really up to you. I picked it up for $15 in a Steam Sale and I don't regret it. If you like that's what you can do as well.
Is it a good story?
It's a story that made me see the world through the eyes of a frustrated and lovestruck teenage girl, a beleaguered writer, a mother whose Christian values don't quite hold up under the strain of life. It's a story that, despite all evidence to the contrary, made me fear the worst for a sister that I never even had. It's a story that partially tells itself, through audio journal entries, but partially it forces you to look through and assemble its pieces yourself.
It's a compelling story and an utterly unique game. I would pay full price for it knowing now that there has never been a game exactly like it. Go for it - for $20, or for whatever its rate is on the next Steam sale. It's worth playing for yourself.

I can't believe this port is finally here! I've had my steam user image set as Tidus and Yuna sixty-nineing each other since I installed steam way back when. This just shows my love for the game.
This game has changed my life. If you have never played it, I highly suggest setting some time aside to enjoy a true masterpiece (This game originally came out on the PS2 where I spent a thorough amount of time completing the game so don't hate for the limited time with this port. Like I said, this is a review on the port only.)
This review is only going to consist of the quality of the port (only tested FFX because FFX-2 is like a toy in a happy meal. It provides some low grade entertainment for about 30 seconds and gets dull real quick. Then you look back at your time with the toy and think, "why the hell did they even think this was a good idea" and "I want my 30 seconds of life back so I can play more FFX").
Pro's:
1. The first thing I like about a port is when it ACTUALLY WORK ON LAUNCH. So far so good! (Very limited testing so far, however... just keep that in mind.)
2. I don't know what people are talking about in these reviews, but yes, you CAN choose which version of music you prefer. Whether that be the OST or the arranged HD remake version. So if you want hardcore nostalgia, go original.
3. The game supports resolutions up to 3840x2160 with multiple options for graphical settings, a nice touch. Running this port at ultra looks great, at least for a game that was designed more than a decade ago.
4. Xbox 360 controller support. Always a plus.
5. Achievements! Huzzah!
6. After spending some time with the game, I realize that the function keys are actually a great addition. The port has some function keybindings that allow manipulation of the game. For example, the F1 key allows a turbo mode which puts the game in a x2 setting, pressing F1 again allows x4, and then back to the original. This is super helpful if you want to skip through something you've already seen a dozen times like an aeon summon cinematic (they also give you an option for allowing "quick summons" which cuts the cinematic time down)
The F2 key allows your team of FFX heroes to allows be supercharged for use of their special abilities. Already an easy cheat with a touch of a button. Probably going to avoid this one for now.
F3 alters random enemy encounters. I think this is great, I already have used this with no regrets. Sometimes you just want to run around and explore without getting a spontaneous heart attack from the random battle sequences screen crash.
F4 automates battles so you can watch. Tedious fights are of the past.
Also, in the game options, you can open up a menu which allows you to change the game's parameters. If you want infinite money, BOOM, it's yours. I feel these added functions will stay as a con. I personally like to earn achievements genuinely, makes me feel like I worked to get that mark. That's just me.
I will expand on the pro's when I have more time put into the game. For now, I think this will suffice. Here's the bad.
Con's:
1. Yeah, I'm sure you have seen it so far. 30 fps lock.
I get it, there has to be a reason. Bringing a game from the early 2000's into 2016 with new resolutions, rendering, operating systems, etc., is not a small feat. However, I am very biased because my monitor has G-SYNC support. I use an Acer XB280HK, and the game looks like it runs at ~50 fps. Read up on G-SYNC. It's a great tool for this kind of fps cap.
2. The price. 24 dollars is not bad, but come on. Lets be honest, we are all only buying this port to play FFX. FFX-2 doesn't exist. I am convinced it doesn't. I am not going to even start with that. I'm assuming that's why they packaged them together so they could be like "Hey, instead of charging 15 bucks for FFX standalone, let's throw FFX-2 and make it a dual purchase so the kiddies think they are getting a good deal for double the price!" I see through your marketing strategy Square Enix... and I approve, it was smart ;)
3. That's it for cons so far. Once I have a play-through completed, I will be sure to update any bugs or crashes.

I typed out like... a lot of words and... uhhh.... may have failed and lost it.
I'll retype this tomorrow maybe... Sad times.
In short - 7.5/10
Ds3>Ds1>Ds2 - Solid game. Great game yet only a good Souls game.
I'M BACK! I shall review the game. I know I said I would do it tomorrow like half a year ago but, well, I forgot.
Anyway.
Graphics/Sound - 7/10:  Nothing to write home about but they do look nice. Dark and grim it still looks pretty. The scenery and atmosphere is fitting and adds to the world as does the background music.
Gameplay - 8/10: Compared to the poor port of Dark Souls 1 this game plays very nicely. Combat is smooth, upgrade system is intuitive, different bosses and enemies help keep it fresh throughout.
Replayability - 8/10: Out of the 3 games I found this one the most replayable. I found this was the best game for messing around with different builds, etc. and NG+ has some nice additions.
Difficulty - 5/10: You could argue this both ways but as it's a Dark Souls game I would favor difficulty and this game is relatively easy. I'm not saying it's an easy game, it isn't, but comparing it to the other two games this one provided the least of a challenge and I found it was probably the easiest to become overpowered in (Miracle builds I found OP for example).
Story 6/10: It's Dark Souls. The story isn't all that obvious. How much of the story you learn depends on how much you want to learn, none of it is really told to you. I tried to get into the story but there didn't seem to be that much to it. There's a lot of lore to Dark Souls but your character's story is kinda basic (Basically 'Go do dis' 'OK')
Writing 7/10: While there isn't much dialogue in the game the parts that do have dialogue do give some nice information about characters. Most of the information you get is gotten from reading descriptions of stuff you find, it's nice background but a lot of it is uninteresting (IMO). Reading this stuff is entirely optional which is nice.
Characters 7/10: There's a few characters with stories throughout the game. The backstories of these characters is interesting but I kind of wish there was more too them. In someway the mystery around them is good but at the same time it would be nice to find out more about them. The small quest lines they do have to give some nice story to the characters and deepens the story of the world in general.
Great game in general, good game by Dark Souls standards. I'd recommend you pick it up and the DLC (Inc in SotFS) are pretty nice too. This review is kinda♥♥♥♥♥♥♥but I felt like letting down exactly no one for half a year I should finish it!

Gone Home is not a game for everyone.
Its an atmospheric and rather slow paced immersion game.
You are basically walking around the house, and learning about its story and the people that live here through the environment, letters and audio diarys.
There is no fighting, no enemy, no horror and just a touch of mystery, but you get a highly detailed and immersive interactive environment, a great story of love, growing up and self discovery and believable well crafted and characters you can identify yourself with.
Many exploration games are often boring or too high concept, however Gone Home grips you instantly and makes you care deeply for the characters as you uncover their lives in a very intimate way.
A great addition if you like exploration and stories that unfold in a nonlinear fashion.

One of the worst feelings I know is when the cause of your death in a game is not your own incompetence, but the game designers'. This game makes me relive that feeling again and again and again. The fact that I not only lose my mind but often also my time doesn't make it better, with at times scarsely placed checkpoints. I don't mind games being hard, as long as they're fair. The problem is, 90 % of my deaths aren't fair. And yet I recommend this game. Why?
Too begin with, I would like to explain more precisely what is so unfair with this game. The absolutely worst thing is the hitboxes. They are just ridiculously and does often not seem to be in any way connected with the animations. Not range or the area covered by the attack nor the timing seems to make any sense. For example, I've got hit by a spear when I stand next to the enemy, who thrust the spear forward. Another quite terrible thing is the general game design (at times, most of the time it's great). Sometimes scenarios are created where the game design, attacks of the enemies and placement of everything makes an situation almost impossible or actually impossible to survive. Or it is completely unreasonable to expect the player to do the extremely specific thing which is required to get of the situation. One of the more simple scenarios are on a dragon boss. One of its attacks consists of jumping up in the air and hovering there, while breathing out flames which cover a very large area which you have to get out of. This can be easily done by running  towards the tail of the dragon, which seems to be safe. But if you're unlucky, the seemingly random movement of the dragon has placed it on the very edge of the platform you both stand on. This could create a situation were the tail of the dragon is outside the platform, and you will have a very hard time running away from the flames which will kill you. I guess it is possible to get out of this situation, but I find it unreasonably hard, complicated and time-consuming to do what is needed for that.
Now that I've got the negative out of the way, let's start with the more fun stuff. Pretty much every part of the game - except the one I mentionened in my little essay up there - is greatly designed and very engaging. The combat system is responsive and very satisfying. There are a lot of different weapons with completely different attack patterns, and other gear like rings, armors, and shields. The level up-system is also great, were you spend the souls which you have acquired from the defeated enemies to gain levels. There are many different stats to invest in to make the character just as you want it. The level design is also quite good, with many hidden areas, different paths and cool locations. It's not as amazing as the interconnected world of Dark Souls (1), but still good. Then we have the enemies, and there are lots of them. Every new location you arrive too means a lot of new enemies, and of course almost always at least one boss. While the bosses sometimes feel a bit too generic with not that imaginative design nor attacks, they're still very well designed, and many of them are still really cool. The art direction of the game is truly amazing, and everything has this dark, decayed look to it. Especially the locations are extremely fantastic and varying, and entering a new one is often followed by a feeling of aw and wonder.
I would say that while Dark Souls was a masterpiece and in my opinion felt a lot like a piece of art, Dark Souls 2 succeeds in just being a great game.

Homefront: The Revolution is like, an urban Far Cry, but with North Korea having taken over the world so you've kinda got some themes from Wolfenstein: The New Order in there with the bad guys having taken over the world and all.
However, the gameplay is nothing like Wolfenstein: TNO and it doesn't have the animal hunting seen in Far Cry 3. As for the graphics, I find them pretty nice and the faces also are visually appealing as well although I do hate it when designers give facial piercings to a character (as I hate facial piercings).
Pros:
-Great gunplay
-Fun weapon modding system
-It's like an urban Far Cry 3
-Runs great on my PC (thanks, performance patch)
-Interesting concept
-Neat soundtrack
Cons:
-Multiplayer resources should've been spent on the game itself, as no one would play Homefront for the multiplayer (and no one plays FPS multiplayer if it isn't CS:GO or CoD). While the multiplayer is fun (I only played solo as I couldn't find any lobby), I'd have avoided creating it altogether as people only play CS:GO or Call of Duty or hell, why not make the multiplayer a standalone experience instead?
-Some collision with some meshes like tarps are stupid and immersion-breaking, I should be able to go over those IRL.

Ds3>Ds1>Ds2 - Solid game. Great game yet only a good Souls game.
I'M BACK! I shall review the game. I know I said I would do it tomorrow like half a year ago but, well, I forgot.
Anyway.
Graphics/Sound - 7/10:  Nothing to write home about but they do look nice. Dark and grim it still looks pretty. The scenery and atmosphere is fitting and adds to the world as does the background music.
Gameplay - 8/10: Compared to the poor port of Dark Souls 1 this game plays very nicely. Combat is smooth, upgrade system is intuitive, different bosses and enemies help keep it fresh throughout.
Replayability - 8/10: Out of the 3 games I found this one the most replayable. I found this was the best game for messing around with different builds, etc. and NG+ has some nice additions.
Difficulty - 5/10: You could argue this both ways but as it's a Dark Souls game I would favor difficulty and this game is relatively easy. I'm not saying it's an easy game, it isn't, but comparing it to the other two games this one provided the least of a challenge and I found it was probably the easiest to become overpowered in (Miracle builds I found OP for example).
Story 6/10: It's Dark Souls. The story isn't all that obvious. How much of the story you learn depends on how much you want to learn, none of it is really told to you. I tried to get into the story but there didn't seem to be that much to it. There's a lot of lore to Dark Souls but your character's story is kinda basic (Basically 'Go do dis' 'OK')
Writing 7/10: While there isn't much dialogue in the game the parts that do have dialogue do give some nice information about characters. Most of the information you get is gotten from reading descriptions of stuff you find, it's nice background but a lot of it is uninteresting (IMO). Reading this stuff is entirely optional which is nice.
Characters 7/10: There's a few characters with stories throughout the game. The backstories of these characters is interesting but I kind of wish there was more too them. In someway the mystery around them is good but at the same time it would be nice to find out more about them. The small quest lines they do have to give some nice story to the characters and deepens the story of the world in general.
Great game in general, good game by Dark Souls standards. I'd recommend you pick it up and the DLC (Inc in SotFS) are pretty nice too. This review is kinda♥♥♥♥♥♥♥but I felt like letting down exactly no one for half a year I should finish it!

Well to start, multiplayer is broken on most maps (See edit). Terrain doesn't spawn in, audio glitches, etc. Customization is quite fun, but to advance in it you have to play the same glitched maps. The only map that isn't broken for me is the Vehicle escort. (Can't recall the name)
The campaign is a different story, for the most part, the main story missions are quite good and mostly enjoyable. Though it is plagued by some rather terrible design choices.
*****SPOILER WARNING*****
You play as Brady, a new recruit to the Revolution. Your Revolution buddies get murdered by the KPA etc ect. Anywho, you get rescued by Walker, the leader of the Revolution, A couple boring capture the zone quests later and boom you take Phillidelphia. Obviously this is not all the game has to offer, one particularly good part is when you steal a Goliath, a armored tank. The ending is quite rewarding, with some of your friends being killed off in a Game of Thrones style.
*****Spoiler over*****
Now, the one main downside is aweful, unresponsive, unreliable, parkour. You will often find yourself frustrated by trying to jump from place to place. Mix that with horrible capture the district quests, and you have a one-way ticket to Rage quit.
Overall its a pretty decent game, maybe, MAYBE pick it up if its on sale for 10$ or less.
But for 40$? Pass on it and pick up a game like Far Cry 3, which it clearly has borrowed heavily from.
I have to not recommend it due to the pricepoint, and horrible design choices, but on sale, it is quite fun to play.

One of the worst feelings I know is when the cause of your death in a game is not your own incompetence, but the game designers'. This game makes me relive that feeling again and again and again. The fact that I not only lose my mind but often also my time doesn't make it better, with at times scarsely placed checkpoints. I don't mind games being hard, as long as they're fair. The problem is, 90 % of my deaths aren't fair. And yet I recommend this game. Why?
Too begin with, I would like to explain more precisely what is so unfair with this game. The absolutely worst thing is the hitboxes. They are just ridiculously and does often not seem to be in any way connected with the animations. Not range or the area covered by the attack nor the timing seems to make any sense. For example, I've got hit by a spear when I stand next to the enemy, who thrust the spear forward. Another quite terrible thing is the general game design (at times, most of the time it's great). Sometimes scenarios are created where the game design, attacks of the enemies and placement of everything makes an situation almost impossible or actually impossible to survive. Or it is completely unreasonable to expect the player to do the extremely specific thing which is required to get of the situation. One of the more simple scenarios are on a dragon boss. One of its attacks consists of jumping up in the air and hovering there, while breathing out flames which cover a very large area which you have to get out of. This can be easily done by running  towards the tail of the dragon, which seems to be safe. But if you're unlucky, the seemingly random movement of the dragon has placed it on the very edge of the platform you both stand on. This could create a situation were the tail of the dragon is outside the platform, and you will have a very hard time running away from the flames which will kill you. I guess it is possible to get out of this situation, but I find it unreasonably hard, complicated and time-consuming to do what is needed for that.
Now that I've got the negative out of the way, let's start with the more fun stuff. Pretty much every part of the game - except the one I mentionened in my little essay up there - is greatly designed and very engaging. The combat system is responsive and very satisfying. There are a lot of different weapons with completely different attack patterns, and other gear like rings, armors, and shields. The level up-system is also great, were you spend the souls which you have acquired from the defeated enemies to gain levels. There are many different stats to invest in to make the character just as you want it. The level design is also quite good, with many hidden areas, different paths and cool locations. It's not as amazing as the interconnected world of Dark Souls (1), but still good. Then we have the enemies, and there are lots of them. Every new location you arrive too means a lot of new enemies, and of course almost always at least one boss. While the bosses sometimes feel a bit too generic with not that imaginative design nor attacks, they're still very well designed, and many of them are still really cool. The art direction of the game is truly amazing, and everything has this dark, decayed look to it. Especially the locations are extremely fantastic and varying, and entering a new one is often followed by a feeling of aw and wonder.
I would say that while Dark Souls was a masterpiece and in my opinion felt a lot like a piece of art, Dark Souls 2 succeeds in just being a great game.

I feel conflicted about this game, but overall, I would recommend it. It was very well executed in terms of the detail of the world and the story, but for as short as it was, I found myself wanting it to be over toward the end. There are virtually no puzzles to solve; the main thing you do is go from room to room picking up personal items, notes, forms, letters, etc. and as you do, you unravel the story. However, after a while, it got tedious, and when I felt like I was making progress toward the story's resolution, I kept finding more--it started to feel like a grind.
I can say though, that the voice acting was top notch, and the use of sounds and music did a good job of instilling fear and dread, even though this is NOT a horror game. The game was constantly throwing red herrings at you trying to convince you that it was a horror game and it sort of colored the story for me. I wonder how I would have responded to the story if the game took place on a bright sunshiny day instead of a dark and stormy night.
Anyway, at some point in the game I got over the "blue balls" of anticipating some jump scare that never came and I found the calculated lightning strikes and thunder peals at opportune moments to be a little annoying. It was definitely an interesting experience, playing this walking simulator, but, as I said, it was short and has no replay value whatsoever, at least for me. In the end I am glad I played it, but it's hard to recommend it whole-heartedly as I can see that it's not for everyone. I commend the developers for trying something different and succeeding on some level.

I'M BACK! I shall review the game. I know I said I would do it tomorrow like half a year ago but, well, I forgot.

Graphics/Sound - 7/10:  Nothing to write home about but they do look nice. Dark and grim it still looks pretty. The scenery and atmosphere is fitting and adds to the world as does the background music.
Gameplay - 8/10: Compared to the poor port of Dark Souls 1 this game plays very nicely. Combat is smooth, upgrade system is intuitive, different bosses and enemies help keep it fresh throughout.
