I don't know what to say about this game. I thought it was going to be a horror game. Instead I found myself caught up in unravelling the tale of a the main character's sister Sam, a seventeen year old girl struggling, not with her sexual identity (as she puts it, "I've known since She-Rah"), but how her world reacts to it.
All the while, I was waiting for the ghost of the girls' father's uncle to pop out and scare me. This didn't happen, and the way this game is structred, I can tell you right now that it can't happen. Some people are annoyed at this deception. I'm a little confused, but it did provide some tension to to the gameplay, and I honestly have no idea what playing without it would be like.
I mention it in this review for the world to see in the interests of fairness. I think the game tried to treat the ghost plot as a red herring. They would have succeeded at this if not for the fact that the leadup clues to it weren't so much hints as they were blatant lies.
Really, the subtlety-fu was strong with this game most places but the opening. Gone Home really did use the game medium as a way to tell a story in such a naturalistic way that you can't help but admire how well they pulled it off--but still, there were issues (not to mention, you sometimes find crucially lesbian notes in the most public of places).
As another reviewer put it, Sam becomes less an individual and more a placeholder over the course of the game, and I'm inclined to agree. While her relationship with her girlfriend Lonnie remains beautifully fleshed out, there are 'fight the patriarchy!' signs here and there, and copies of a feminist zine which don't gell with the rest of her character--a creative young tomboy who accepts herself even if others don't, is not about flouting a little authority, and who tries to live in the moment. Sam isn't fighting against the patriarchy--she's fighting against those who don't want her to be in love with another girl. This includes her mother, who is also a woman.
So these rallying cries for girl power don't fit in to her character. I'm not saying she's not a feminist, but from all other indications of her character, she's not *that* kind of feminist. It's a major misstep by the designers of the game, and it rings hollow. In a game that's all about the natural discovery of story, something like this sticks out like a sore thumb.
By the way, if you want to talk representation, those who laud the game as a departure from catering to young white straight male gamers should probably remember that this is a game about a young white queer female gamer. While most young white teenagers were probably not thinking about race or able-bodiedness or what have you in the 90s, the people who play this game are, and the people who designed this game could (and arguably should) have been if representation was intended to be a theme in Gone Home. There are ways to acknowledge these things without going overboard.
(In all fairness if I'm going to go on about this I should state that Lonnie, Sam's girlfriend, has a Hispanic last name, Desoto. There is never any discussion of race in-game.)
So, should you buy Gone Home? My gut feeling is that you shouldn't pay full price. It's worth paying *some* money for, out of respect for what the developers were trying to do, and half succeeded at. And I want to see them try again, and succeed better this time. Hence the money. But for what the game actually was, it's honestly not worth the full amount.
To be honest, while I mostly enjoyed playing it, I was a little disappointed with the ending, too. Without being spoileriffic, it's exactly what you would expect a seventeen year old to do--but not one as intelligent as Sam. Not exactly good life decisions, let's put it that way. And the game did not acknowledge this.
Should you play Gone Home? It only took me about an hour and a half, and I now know more about how to craft narrative in games than I did before--what to do and what not to do. I loved the character of Sam as a whole, and the story, while not what I was expecting at all, sucked me in. The voice acting and the scoring was top notch, and the world detail was very impressive. So absolutely. Play this game. Just don't expect it to live up to the hype, cause it won't, and don't go in hating it, because it doesn't deserve it.
It's just a game, but one that I think makes a couple of points for rather than against the notion that games can be art.

One of the worst feelings I know is when the cause of your death in a game is not your own incompetence, but the game designers'. This game makes me relive that feeling again and again and again. The fact that I not only lose my mind but often also my time doesn't make it better, with at times scarsely placed checkpoints. I don't mind games being hard, as long as they're fair. The problem is, 90 % of my deaths aren't fair. And yet I recommend this game. Why?
Too begin with, I would like to explain more precisely what is so unfair with this game. The absolutely worst thing is the hitboxes. They are just ridiculously and does often not seem to be in any way connected with the animations. Not range or the area covered by the attack nor the timing seems to make any sense. For example, I've got hit by a spear when I stand next to the enemy, who thrust the spear forward. Another quite terrible thing is the general game design (at times, most of the time it's great). Sometimes scenarios are created where the game design, attacks of the enemies and placement of everything makes an situation almost impossible or actually impossible to survive. Or it is completely unreasonable to expect the player to do the extremely specific thing which is required to get of the situation. One of the more simple scenarios are on a dragon boss. One of its attacks consists of jumping up in the air and hovering there, while breathing out flames which cover a very large area which you have to get out of. This can be easily done by running  towards the tail of the dragon, which seems to be safe. But if you're unlucky, the seemingly random movement of the dragon has placed it on the very edge of the platform you both stand on. This could create a situation were the tail of the dragon is outside the platform, and you will have a very hard time running away from the flames which will kill you. I guess it is possible to get out of this situation, but I find it unreasonably hard, complicated and time-consuming to do what is needed for that.
Now that I've got the negative out of the way, let's start with the more fun stuff. Pretty much every part of the game - except the one I mentionened in my little essay up there - is greatly designed and very engaging. The combat system is responsive and very satisfying. There are a lot of different weapons with completely different attack patterns, and other gear like rings, armors, and shields. The level up-system is also great, were you spend the souls which you have acquired from the defeated enemies to gain levels. There are many different stats to invest in to make the character just as you want it. The level design is also quite good, with many hidden areas, different paths and cool locations. It's not as amazing as the interconnected world of Dark Souls (1), but still good. Then we have the enemies, and there are lots of them. Every new location you arrive too means a lot of new enemies, and of course almost always at least one boss. While the bosses sometimes feel a bit too generic with not that imaginative design nor attacks, they're still very well designed, and many of them are still really cool. NOTE: I am a singleplayer gamer, so I'll only be reviewing the singleplayer portion(s) of this game.
TL;DR - Great game, and I do recommend it for others. But since you can't play past the ending, it's not a game I'm going to play more than once. Thanks for the free weekend so that I didn't end up regretting a purchase.
Now that that's out of the way...
Played through story mode from beginning to end. Story itself had potential to be really great through-and-through, but certain climactic moments were full of cliche and uniformity (especially the end bit). While I was quite disappointed that it didn't follow the original concepts of the original Homefront (esp. because John Milius was a consultant for the original Homefront story) it ended up being capable of standing on its own feet, as it were. I did rather appreciate the constant fear of betrayal, and even being on the receiving end of suspected betrayal, but I didn't like how the KPA took over the US via waging economic war. I much preferred the original story, and this one would have been great as a game of its own, without sharing the spirit of another.
With all that said however, it broke my biggest rule in "open world" gaming; in Homefront: The Revolution, you can't play past the ending. That, in itself, is normally a dealbreaker for me. There have been a few exceptions to this (especially Fallout: New Vegas since you can just 'fix' that with a mod). But unfortunately, this game is not the exception, but the rule. Sure, it has other "modes" you can play in singleplayer, but if I can't get the story out of the way so that I can freely muck about in the worldspace(s) without that main mission marker making me avoid certain areas and/or safehouses, then I simply won't play it again. This is functionally a quasi-clone of the latest Far Cry games, and both FC3 and FC4 let you play past the story. And before anyone suggests it; NO, reloading the checkpoint from before accepting the "Point of No Return" mission is NOT acceptable.
Now, if they ever release a "free roam" DLC where the story bit is removed from the entire worldspace whereby all the yellow and red zones are unlocked, and you can continually do random jobs, I might consider purchasing the Freedom Fighter Bundle when it's on sale again. But until that happens, no sale. By the way, yes, I am indeed suggesting I'd buy it as a DLC.
Aside from that... Even though they released the "performance patch," I still got quite a bit of lag playing through the story. My rig only just barely exceeds the recommended requirements, but even still, I don't think they're quite done with their optimisations. Either that, or they may want to up their recommended requirements to match what is actually required to not have the game completely freeze for a few seconds upon entering a new zone.
At the end of the day, I do like the game. I just don't like it enough to support devs who make open-world games yet keep the ending closed. So while I greatly appreciate the free weekend that allowed me to make a well-informed purchase decision, I won't be buying it until that huge mistake is corrected.
I already know a lot of people don't care about the whole "open world; closed ending" thing, and [sarcasm]good for you[/sarcasm] if that's the case. But shut up, this ain't your review, nor your wallet.

okay, negl the environment is gorgeous and immersive. despite the fact that many items are cloned and reused, there are still much more that are detailed and it really captures that era--mind u i don't know it too well. detailed letters and scraps lying around, brand designs of books/cereal/misc with labels on the front and back. so yes, they reused some things (toiler paper) but many others have a lot of writing that could be extraneous but adds to the reality. the rain & lightning creeped me out. the first time i booted up the game, i didn't want to play the game after like 10 minutes of having to turn on the lights by myself and listen to the storm. i did return eventually.
so it's not a  traditional game. and it's better than you walk into this knowing that. you pick up stuff and observe them if you want. you can skip through everything and only pick up story-moving items. but i tried to get to as much as i could while leaving a mess behind. so is it a ~fun~ replayable game? i'd say no. but it is a lovely coming of age story with gal pal feels (c what i did thar) and even sister feels, with one coming home and the other explaining what led up to her leaving. so sister & home feels = slay me. gone home runs in the line of an interactive visual novel with more control than one might have in a traditional japanese VN. learning about the family background, their respective problems and their dynamic via found objects was a great way to utilize the medium (in this case GAME); so i'd actually count this as a success. it's not something for everyone; i can see how one might get bored. but i'm thinking more like how epistolary novels can have scraps of letters &c as an anthology. this does the same thing except you find the pieces by yourself, controlling via first person pov the older sister. choosing and maximizing the use of a medium is very important to me--from using pen or pencil, to whether to tell a story via commentbombs or logs--there isn't always a right answer but if you're going to go with one, do the best you can. and in gone home, i think they did a great job merging interactive play with a found object-story.

This is probably the only F2P shooter I'd recommend downloading. It was a P2W in the past, but this company did what most F2P game developers should do, which is taking away obnoxious microtransactions. Sure, there are boosters and some guns that are paywalled, but these honestly don't affect gameplay much, if at all. You will have more difficulty facing a  skilled player with typical gear than a player who sucks with a bunch of premium gear. But to keep this review short, I will go over the pros and cons.
PROS:
-Good looking game with low system requirements.
-The way you customize your guns is very innovative and useful.
-Not a P2W.
-Vast selection of guns and gear you can unlock with in game currency.
-Ranking up is pretty easy if you're a decent player.
-Sound design is well done.
-The gamemodes are very fun and the game moves at a comfortable pace.
-The guns feel good and a bunch of the guns you don't typically see in a shooter.
-The classes are balanced.
-The slide mechanic feels nice and adds an interesting twist to gameplay.
-The maps are nicely sized and are well designed.
CONS:
-A few bugs and glitches.
-The community is generally friendly, but it can be annoying at times.
-Even though the game modes are fun, they aren't that creative or new, with the possible exception of Bag and Tag.
-The progression can feel a little slow, but generally isn't that big of a problem.
Verdict: Go ahead and download it. It's one of the few F2P shooters that isn't a pay to win, and the gameplay itself is very fun and entertaining.

Dark Souls II swaps out a lot of the core mechanics and design elements from Dark Souls for new mechanics/designs in order to provide a streamlined single player experience, totally devoid of nuance, intended to faciltiate arena-style multiplayer PVP and boss raids.
In a nutshell, here are the game's major issues:
- total abandonment of the game's signature difficulty and emphasis on precise gameplay: rather than challenging/interesting combat based on risk assessment and reflexes, Dark Souls II ties accuracy and evasion to a single statistic (cf. Bethsoft games where you can visibly miss a target, but still hit because of a stat buff).
- removal of challenge-based progression: rather than requiring players to proceed from one area to the next by carefully managing resources/heals/etc., Dark Souls II implements unlimited healing and incredibly frequent save points. Progress becomes a matter of running forward in a straight line, not carefully weighing your resources and ability versus what you know about the path in front of you.
- incoherent and abritary level and envionment design: long tunnels connect to other long tunnels and big box rooms connect sequences of long tunnels to one another; Dark Souls signature level design and environmental connectivity (i.e. where all areas connect to all other areas seamlessly) is totally removed from Dark Souls II.
- repetitive and obvious modular design: in terms of the overall single player experience, Dark Souls II is a collage of modular exploration and combat areas. While the other games in the series are also broken into similar loops, they make an effort to conceal the mechanic. In Dark Souls II, however, you can set your watch by the fact that each area will have four or five "hub" areas and each boss will have a hidden save point right outside his door, etc.
- equally repetitive boss battles: rather than giant, bizarre boss monsters with unique designs and battle mechanics, Dark Souls II is an endbless parade of giant knights in armor and dragons.
- ill-concieved new multiplayer modes that ruin the game's pacing and facilitate the game's novel/new focus on extended PVP and boss-raids.
- the representation of the series' lore and mythology is paltry at best: not only does this game, which is dramatically longer/larger than Dark Souls, feel like a footnote to the first game, the new characters it enters into the mythology are childishly simple and reflect a very poor understanding of the first game.
I could go on, but hopefully the point is clear: there are so many important departures from the design and mechanics of Dark Souls, it hardly even makes sense to call this game an entry in the series/franchise, let alone a numbered sequel to Dark Souls.
But, at the end of the day, I do not hold that against the game's developer, From Software.
At some point during the development process, From Software lost control of this game and ended up going to market with a half-baked spin-off that incorporates some formal/design elements and creative assets from the original game, but which ultimately delivers a tedious, simplistic and not very challenging game focused on competitive multiplayer.
The main reason that this game is such a hot mess is that during most of its development cycle, Hidetaka Miyazaki, the series' heart and soul, was moving from being a lead game director to being the president of From Software. Miyazaki was also lead director on Bloodbourne while Dark Souls II was being developed.
Rumormill reporting at the time held that Miyazaki was barely involved in the project at all. Anyone who played the first or third games in the series knows beyond any shadow of a doubt that his involvement in Dark Souls II was purely nominal.
(i.e. his name ended up on the tin for marketing purposes, not because he had anything to do with the game's development.)
This essentially resulted in a situation that is familiar from other popular franchises: the main creative force leaves the project (for whatever reason), the studio puts a less qualified team in charge and they botch the delivery.
The second reason why not to hold the total failure of Dark Souls II to deliver a proper Dark Souls game against From Software is that the studio just released Dark Souls III, which not only reverts/fixes many of the ill-concieved design and mechanical changes and mistakes outlined above, but which also restores Miyazaki to the helm and, with him, the game's focus on a robust single player experience and an immersive world/lore/exploration experience.
All of which is to say that Dark Souls II is a numbered entry in the Dark Souls series for commercial/marketing purposes only: ideally, to prevent confusion, it would have been called "Dark Souls Arena" or "Dark Souls Battle Network" or something like that.
Anyone new to the franchise should probably skip this game. If you're a beginner, you should play Dark Souls, then play Dark Souls III and then, if you're interested in a different take on the series, you could try out From Software's multiplayer/raid/arena spin-off, Dark Souls II.

I really like this game. This game brings out some of the harsh truth about war especially WWI which occurs more than 100 years ago. It is an age where you do not have robots to help you find the enemy nor fully automatic weapons that can empty a 30 round magazine in 4 seconds. This is an age where melee weapons such as bayonet, clubs, and knives had a major role. In most FPS games that came out lately, this game stands out for choosing this age whereas the other choose the futuristic era like Call of Duty: Modern Warfare for example. Another thing that stands out from this game is it's very realistic features (except for the desertion system that is quite unrealistic and the ballistics that is not as good as the one in Sniper Elite) like the iron sight and scoped sight that wobbles after running around and it doesn't always score you a hit. Overall this game highlighted an era that is not very popular among game developers and the weapons are old (like VERY old) but it is very realistic which other games lack. It is the first WWI game that I found and personally speaking I like to read about WWI a lot and this game gave me a chance to experience a glimpse of the Great War. The map are sometimes quite small in width but not in length. Some factions which is still missing are the Austrians, Turkish, ANZAC, Russians, Japanese, and Bulgarian. The game seems to focus on the Western Front and still missing the Eastern Front, the African Front, the Arab Front, and the Far East front which is fine if the developers only wants to highlight the Western Front but I'd love to see some of these fronts that I mention.
It is a good game and anyone who hasn't played this game yet, you should try it.

Dark Souls II swaps out a lot of the core mechanics and design elements from Dark Souls for new mechanics/designs in order to provide a streamlined single player experience, totally devoid of nuance, intended to faciltiate arena-style multiplayer PVP and boss raids.
In a nutshell, here are the game's major issues:
- total abandonment of the game's signature difficulty and emphasis on precise gameplay: rather than challenging/interesting combat based on risk assessment and reflexes, Dark Souls II ties accuracy and evasion to a single statistic (cf. Bethsoft games where you can visibly miss a target, but still hit because of a stat buff).
- removal of challenge-based progression: rather than requiring players to proceed from one area to the next by carefully managing resources/heals/etc., Dark Souls II implements unlimited healing and incredibly frequent save points. Progress becomes a matter of running forward in a straight line, not carefully weighing your resources and ability versus what you know about the path in front of you.
- incoherent and abritary level and envionment design: long tunnels connect to other long tunnels and big box rooms connect sequences of long tunnels to one another; Dark Souls signature level design and environmental connectivity (i.e. where all areas connect to all other areas seamlessly) is totally removed from Dark Souls II.
- repetitive and obvious modular design: in terms of the overall single player experience, Dark Souls II is a collage of modular exploration and combat areas. While the other games in the series are also broken into similar loops, they make an effort to conceal the mechanic. In Dark Souls II, however, you can set your watch by the fact that each area will have four or five "hub" areas and each boss will have a hidden save point right outside his door, etc.
- equally repetitive boss battles: rather than giant, bizarre boss monsters with unique designs and battle mechanics, Dark Souls II is an endbless parade of giant knights in armor and dragons.
- ill-concieved new multiplayer modes that ruin the game's pacing and facilitate the game's novel/new focus on extended PVP and boss-raids.
- the representation of the series' lore and mythology is paltry at best: not only does this game, which is dramatically longer/larger than Dark Souls, feel like a footnote to the first game, the new characters it enters into the mythology are childishly simple and reflect a very poor understanding of the first game.
I could go on, but hopefully the point is clear: there are so many important departures from the design and mechanics of Dark Souls, it hardly even makes sense to call this game an entry in the series/franchise, let alone a numbered sequel to Dark Souls.
But, at the end of the day, I do not hold that against the game's developer, From Software.
At some point during the development process, From Software lost control of this game and ended up going to market with a half-baked spin-off that incorporates some formal/design elements and creative assets from the original game, but which ultimately delivers a tedious, simplistic and not very challenging game focused on competitive multiplayer.
The main reason that this game is such a hot mess is that during most of its development cycle, Hidetaka Miyazaki, the series' heart and soul, was moving from being a lead game director to being the president of From Software. Miyazaki was also lead director on Bloodbourne while Dark Souls II was being developed.
Rumormill reporting at the time held that Miyazaki was barely involved in the project at all. Anyone who played the first or third games in the series knows beyond any shadow of a doubt that his involvement in Dark Souls II was purely nominal.
(i.e. his name ended up on the tin for marketing purposes, not because he had anything to do with the game's development.)
This essentially resulted in a situation that is familiar from other popular franchises: the main creative force leaves the project (for whatever reason), the studio puts a less qualified team in charge and they botch the delivery.
The second reason why not to hold the total failure of Dark Souls II to deliver a proper Dark Souls game against From Software is that the studio just released Dark Souls III, which not only reverts/fixes many of the ill-concieved design and mechanical changes and mistakes outlined above, but which also restores Miyazaki to the helm and, with him, the game's focus on a robust single player experience and an immersive world/lore/exploration experience.
All of which is to say that Dark Souls II is a numbered entry in the Dark Souls series for commercial/marketing purposes only: ideally, to prevent confusion, it would have been called "Dark Souls Arena" or "Dark Souls Battle Network" or something like that.
Anyone new to the franchise should probably skip this game. If you're a beginner, you should play Dark Souls, then play Dark Souls III and then, if you're interested in a different take on the series, you could try out From Software's multiplayer/raid/arena spin-off, Dark Souls II.

I did like the first Homefront, making me part of a very small group of people.
For better or for worse, this game is entirely different in all regards except for the setting; instead of story based linear missions, it is an open world liberation fest that allows for almost unlimited freedom to do what you want (past the scripted intro segments), which in theory should be great.
However, the game just doesn't feel fun to play. The gunplay is unsatisfying on keyboard and mouse because of some funky mouse handling (and I tried the acceleration fix, so I'm not sure what exactly the problem is, but it just feels wrong to me, like the sensitivity is both too low to aim rapidly, ala SMG, but too high to aim precisely, ala sniper rifles. Now, some people might say "But you can fix it", but honestly, who wants mouse acceleration? If you use a mouse for anything other than gaming, you're used to how a mouse works. It's a stupid idea and always implemented in such a way as to make it worse for players who are proficient with their mice) and gameplay (getting shot at is tedious because you never know exactly how much damage you'll take, so you die unexpectedly while other times you can survive incredible amounts of damage, seemingly based on a coin toss). The aesthetic is also a bit tedious; it feels like someone took Homefront and was like "But what if it looked like Terminator?" which is not a terrible idea except for implementation; on low settings, it looks like sludge (and my rig can't hit high) with performance hits and unholy amounts of bloom when you transition from a lit area to a dark area, to the point where operating during the day is tedious because your screen will wash out if you step into shadows. While the performance was stable, it was unimpressive for the graphical fidelity delivered.

FIrst things first: 20 bucks is way too much. Also, this is not a game. Yup, do not expect a game, do not ♥♥♥♥♥ and whine if you run through the whole house in 30 mins (in which case you have missed the point). Those issues seem to be the root of why such a beautiful narrative was slammed widely by consumers. Gone Home is a story, and it is magnificent.
In this kind of narrative, atmosphere and immersion are everything. I'm happy to report the atmosphere is incredible, with great sound and visual design. While textures are not super-detailed, where it mattered they were stellar (rain flowing down windows, pale moonlight shining through curtains). Voice acting was spot on, and provided you with just enough story each time.
The story itself? It's simple, and that's what I believe makes this a masterpiece. It is a simple concept,  perfectly executed. I felt some feels guys, even when I just found a story-related object lying around the house. FInding out little snippets of what are (really the quite ordinary) lives of the parents was somehow made satisfying. The story was presented to you with perfect pacing, and perfect sequencing throughout the house.
Many thought this game set out to break boundaries and address controversial social issues; I disagree. I view this as a triumphant demonstration of how powerful video games can be. The story is simple, but the magical atmosphere, the perfect pacing, the teasing exposition.... that is what makes this experience (that would be ordinary in any other medium) so brilliant. That is something only video games can do.

Verdun, the game that will give you PTSD. I've seen my fellow players torn to pieces by grenades, decapitated by gun fire, maimed by sniper shots, and even die charging out of trenches. If you aim to exit the trench, more than likely you will be killed by a sniper, machine gun, or just random gun fire. Gas will kill you quick if you don't get your gas mask on. Bullets are usually one hit kills, making reloading without cover a deadly mistake. You will watch your fellow man be dismantled, maimed, and killed before your eyes. You will see bodies stacked on top of bodies, and those still alive, moaning in pain before they finally die. This game is truely brutal and intense, but this is just a game. People live this in real life, and unlike us gamers, they don't respawn when they take a bullet to the brain. Hat's off to soldiers past, present, and future who have to live the Hell that is war. If all war games were like Verdun, I think we'd all find new respect for soldiers.

I started playing the demo on PS3 some days after it initially released. Hours of gameplay on that demo alone, restarting from scratch and doing something different each time.
Then, after a while, I got the game on X360, when a friend said that it was "just not his cup of tea" and gifted it to me. MAybe I was a little not in the mood for it, so I played it for some more then traded it to GS for something else.
Fast forward to january 2013, I bought it as a PS3 Platinum and it just clicked. More than 80 hours of gameplay later I've yet to complete that version...but Steam has ruined my plans, offering me the best version of the game for a mere 3 €.
Restarted from scratch, and the game is still as fun as ever.
Just Cause 2 is that type of game: you can get lost into it, hopping around from village to military installation in any way you see fit: by fast travel (but let's be honest: it's just more fun to slow travel and have "random encounters" on the way), by heli, by plane, by car, by bike...heck, even by parachute and hook.
There are a lot of missions, sidequests, distractions, collectibles, scenarios, vehicles, ways to do things. And each and every one of then can be lots of fun.
Just Cause 2 is just that: an almost endless joyride in an enormous and varied environment.
Because, let's admit it: a game where you can plant an explosive on a double decker bus, drive it to a nearby Colonel, jump out of it at the last second and hookchute away while blowing it up, with Colonel and guards along it, is just priceless fun. And then, to top it off, Rico's evil laughs.

I quit playing FPS games a long time ago because they just didn't keep my interest anymore. Too many times I spent the money and then got bored before I got my money's worth. Most new FPS games feel like re-skins of the same games we've all been playing for years... and I just couldn't get into it anymore.
I'd never played a WWI FPS before and it was something I always thought would be pretty cool. So when I saw this pop up on Steam I followed it for a while. After a few months I was bored and looking for a new game so I decided to take a chance on Verdun. Personally I feel like it's the best game purchase I've made in a while. This has been the most fun I've had with a FPS game since I can remember.
The trench warfare is just a totally different feel than anything I've ever played before. The pace of combat changes constantly depending on whether you are attacking or defending - and there are multiple ways to attack and defend depending on your load out. The squad system is actually pretty unique too.
The learning curve isn't too steep - and so far the community has been pretty cool.
I highly recommend this game!

It surprises me that this game is a mere 15 dollars.  It has an incredibly large and beautiful open world, a satisfying grapple hook that creates scenes that look right out of a spy movie.  It has a large array of vehicles you can steal, a day/night cycle, and it's open-endedness is perfect for this type of game.  However, the one and only thing that bugs me is the lack of emotion and life in the citizens.  Most of them have the same skin except MAYBE different colors, and how they look depends somewhat on the location they are on the island.  So, often times you can find a rice farmer driving a ridiculously fast sports car at 20 mph or a lady wearing lower-end clothing driving a limo.  The citizens all have the same animation if you bump into them, they hardly talk, and you can't interact with many things inside the game aside from shooting them.  Of course, that hardly makes this game a bad game, and it's an action game anyways, most people don't buy action games do talk to citizens on the street.  All in all, worth 15 dollars, ridiculously fun, and with the multiplayer mod, it's also now a multiplayer game, all a 40$-50$ value for 15 bucks.

Ok, sooo...
After experiencing Verdun for quite a few months by now (heck, what am I talking about, I got it since May 2015, that's two damn years ago!!!), I can see myself fit to write an, at least half-legible, poorly-translated-from-my-native-language, review about this fine work of entertainment.
200 hours? In two years? Maybe a bit too little time - some may say - to give a full, in depth, description of the game's subtelties about why it is indeed a superior form of art. But, due to the nature of my work, I just couldn't invest more in it... bear with me please!
On a positive note; well, this game has offered me something that I have not experienced in quite some years now – heck too many years to be honest - playing a FPS in which I am not bothered by extreme discrepancies between veteran players and fresh recruits; dare I call them like this; and a game that truthly encompasses what a shooter should feel like.
There is no pay to win mentality, unlike most triple A shooters today (looking at you Crap of Duty). The community is almost overwhelmingly and annoyingly friendly; to be honest with you, I haven't met anyone hostile really, well at least not too hostile to be a hinderence (expect the average troll from time to time, "for teh lulz", you know...). But with all the humor aside, the players are cool people! You get this sense of - how to put it - community. It is a relaxed atmosphere (quite ironic considering what this game simulates), players are playing mostly for fun; yet that doesn't mean it lacks the sense of competition.
It’s realistic – yes! ArmA like realistic – not quite. But truth be said if we were to make a 100% realistic WWI shooter, that would just mean creating a getting-mowed-down-by-machine-guns simulator 2017, and I guess nobody would really play that, would it now? It has balance in it, yet the balance is quite subtle. Don’t get me wrong machine guns will mow you down, but maybe not as often as you would expect.
For most players that are out there and are tired of all these damn pieces of publicly appealing crap (ahem! again COD), Verdun might sound for a good alternative and believe me, it is. Honestly enough I am really glad that I decided to spend - what I vaguely remember as being - 10 Euros on that late May day, wanting to buy this game; it really feels it was worth it.
Another strong point to this game is the setting; I mean, to this date, WWI hasn't got its proper FPS (yeah, yeah BF1, I know; but honestly do you want a somewhat legit representation of The War to End All Wars, or do you want Hollywood-style special effects?). I know that game developers see this historical period as something rather dull; truth is that this war was indeed a meat grinder. And, as the war was, expect to die in this game, and die a lot. Yet despite all this death and misery, you realise the true value of this game and the awesome work the devs have done. I mean they turned one of the saddest and most brutal chapters from the history of mankind into a quite exciting and – well, I say it now - authentic experience.
Thus, if you feel it's worth a shot, try this game out; one may be pleasantly surprised by it.

This game is made to be an accurate historical respresentation of WW1 trench warfare. It does a hell of a job doing just that. As someone who likes WW1 and WW2 history, I love it.
Fighting in the Great War through Verdun is an experience I will never forget. In the deadliest battlefields of WW1, there is no greenery. your only landmarks are sandbags, downed planes, muddy hills and even bodies. The bodies fill the trenches and shell holes. More and more bodies hit the mud as the machine guns keep firing. The wounded lay writhing and screaming in pain. The waterlogged trenches run red with blood. Artillery shells blow the legs off of men, leaving them to scream in pain as they bleed out. The shells leave craters to take cover in... if you don't mind the putrid odor of the corpses that lie in them. GAS GAS GAS! You are quick and throw on your gas mask as the yellow green cloud creeps into your trench. Your fellow soldier is not quick enough. He staggers around, choking, clutching his throat before he collapses, blood flowing from his mouth. Soon after, the opposing army drops into the trenches, bayonets and clubs and shovels and other brutal weapons at the ready. It's a massacre. Men are impaled and bludgeoned as chaotic hand to hand combat insues. Death and blood and rot are everywhere. Your fellow countrymen are dead. Your best friend just took a bullet to the neck and lays gurgling, choking, sputtering next to you, bleeding all over himself and you and the ground. Now he is dead. You're next. You could retreat, but that would be deserting. You know what happens to those poor, shell shocked ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s. There is no escaping your own gruesome, agonizing death. War is Hell. Do not play this game unless you are ready to experience all of this.
No other game I have played conveys the brutality, destruction, endless trench warfare and sheer loss of life in the Great War like this game does. And war in general at that. It accurately shows you exactly what WW1 was like, with attention to every detail. It shows you exactly what the cost of war is. It may be a game, and it may be fun, but it has a much deeper meaning to it than just that. If you learn anything from playing this game and experiencing the horrors of the most brutal war ever, it is that War is Hell.

This game is still suffering quite a lot from the stigma of its launch fiasco, so you see a lot of reviews even today downvoting the game, while either not giving an explenation, or talking about trivial things that you find in many succesful titles. I wouldn't rely too much on reviews that say "0.2 hours played".
I would carefully recommend this game. I haven't encountered any bugs other than the odd popping in/out of objects. The game runs very smoothly and loading screens are swift. So let's get into the gameplay.
The way weapons work in this game is satisfying, and requires a little skill with the feedback. It's just right. However, travelling through the city is a bit of a pain, because enemies are everywhere. Too many if you ask me. So it's good to be aware of hiding spots like containers and toilet cabins that you can hide in. Otherwise you'd be fighting forever.
The story is nothing extraordinary, it's basically a story about trying to liberate Philadelphia from the control of the North Korean occupiers. The way it's executed is actually pretty good. The missions are varied, the character progression feels pretty organic, as it's entwined with the story. I love doing the main missions in this game.
So all in all, I will recommend this game, but not at full price. Get it on sale.

So I'll start with the obvious, do not buy this game at full price. I enjoyed my time with this game, depsite how short it is but the fact that it has been up on the store for twenty dollars is just ridiculous. I picked it up on sale for about three and to be honest, three to five dollars feels like a better price point for what you actually get here.
You can probably guess from the other reviews and my comments about the price, that there isn't much to the game. Your character is coming home from a trip and finds the house empty, where your family was supposed to be there to greet you. The gameplay consists of walking around the house and attempting to discover what happened. There's some very easy puzzles and a bit of thinking to do, but for the most part, you just walk around this house.
Personally, I quite enjoyed my time with it. I appreciated the atmosphere and the story was surprisingly engaging, despite being almost completely narration and reading notes. It was dark and gloomy, two elements which I love to see when used correctly.Then I got to the ending and left with a bad taste in my mouth. Without spoiling anything, the game builds to something, and then goes in a completely different direction. There is also a pretty big couple of hints in the environment that go nowhere and I really would like to know the story behind those.
All in all, I can't recommend it for the base price. Even though I did have fun with what I played, if I had reached the ending after putting out twenty dollars for it, I would have been livid.
